He states whether there has been any resignation of the statutory auditors during the year and, if so, whether he has taken into consideration the issues, objections or concerns raised by the outgoing auditors. Two things follow. The clause is answered by the auditor now in office, about a predecessor, and it is engaged by any resignation during the year, whether or not the resignation was connected with a dispute. And "taken into consideration" reports what the incoming auditor did with what he was told: it does not require him to adopt the outgoing auditor's conclusions, and it does not discharge Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, which makes it misconduct to accept a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing. The outgoing auditor's own obligation is different again: section 140(2) makes him file a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within thirty days of resigning, giving the reasons and other facts relevant to his resignation.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xviii)

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xx)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xx) reports on where unspent corporate social responsibility money went, and it splits by whether the project was an ongoing one. Under clause 3(xx)(a) the auditor states whether, in respect of other than ongoing projects, the company has transferred the unspent amount to a Fund specified in Schedule VII to the Companies Act within a period of six months of the expiry of the financial year, in compliance with the second proviso to section 135(5). Under clause 3(xx)(b) he states whether any amount remaining unspent under section 135(5) pursuant to any ongoing project has been transferred to a special account in compliance with section 135(6) — the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account, into which the unspent amount goes within thirty days from the end of the financial year, to be spent by the company towards that ongoing project within three financial years, failing which it is transferred to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days of the end of the third financial year. The two limbs have different destinations and different clocks, and the clause reports a transfer, not the quality of the spending.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xx)(a) and 3(xx)(b), reporting compliance with the second proviso to section 135(5) and with section 135(6) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: CARO 2020 — Clause 3(xiii)
concepts.statement: Clause 3(xiii) has the auditor state whether all transactions with related parties are in compliance with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 where applicable, and whether the details have been disclosed in the financial statements as required by the applicable accounting standards. Three things are reported at once and each can fail on its own: the audit committee's approval under section 177 where the company has an audit committee; the approval regime of section 188, which reaches the transactions that section specifies where they are not in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis; and disclosure under the applicable accounting standard. The words "where applicable" work in both directions — a transaction outside section 188 because it is in the ordinary course of business and at arm's length still has to be disclosed under the accounting standard, and a company with no audit committee still answers the section 188 and the disclosure limbs. The population the clause reports on is all transactions with related parties, which is wider than the list of transactions section 188 regulates.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiii), reporting compliance with sections 177 and 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 and disclosure as required by the applicable accounting standards

concepts.subsection: Section 132 — National Financial Reporting Authority
concepts.statement: The National Financial Reporting Authority is a statutory body constituted by the Central Government under section 132 to make recommendations on accounting and auditing policies and standards, to monitor and enforce compliance with them, to oversee the quality of service of the professions associated with ensuring that compliance, and to suggest measures for improvement. Its jurisdiction runs over the classes of companies and bodies corporate prescribed by the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018 — the listed and large end of the population, not every company. Within it, the Authority may investigate, either suo motu or on a reference made to it by the Central Government, matters of professional or other misconduct committed by any member or firm of chartered accountants registered under the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, and the proviso is the part that decides most questions: where the Authority has initiated an investigation, no other institute or body shall initiate or continue any proceedings in such matters of misconduct. Where misconduct is proved the Authority may impose a monetary penalty, and may debar the member or the firm from being appointed as an auditor or internal auditor, or from undertaking any audit or internal audit of any company or body corporate, or from performing any valuation under section 247, for a minimum period of six months and up to a maximum of ten years. An appeal against such an order lies to the Appellate Tribunal.

citation.ref: Section 132(2) and section 132(4) with its proviso barring proceedings by any other institute or body, read with the National Financial Reporting Authority Rules, 2018

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — the conceptual framework and threats to independence
concepts.statement: The Code of Ethics does not work by a list of banned acts alone. It sets out a conceptual framework requiring a professional accountant to identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, to evaluate whether the threats identified are at an acceptable level, and to address those that are not — by eliminating the circumstances that create the threat, by applying safeguards to reduce it to an acceptable level, or, where neither is possible, by declining or ending the professional activity. An acceptable level is the level at which a reasonable and informed third party would be likely to conclude that the accountant complies with the fundamental principles. Threats fall into five categories. A self-interest threat arises where a financial or other interest will inappropriately influence judgement. A self-review threat arises where the accountant will not appropriately evaluate the results of a previous judgement made, or activity performed, by himself or by someone in his firm, on which he will rely in forming a current judgement. An advocacy threat arises where he promotes a client's position to the point that objectivity is compromised. A familiarity threat arises from a long or close relationship making him too sympathetic to the client's interests or too accepting of its work. An intimidation threat arises where he is deterred from acting objectively by pressures, actual or perceived, including attempts to exercise undue influence. For an audit engagement the accountant must be independent both in mind and in appearance, and a threat that cannot be brought to an acceptable level ends the engagement rather than being disclosed away.

citation.ref: the conceptual framework — identify, evaluate and address threats to compliance with the fundamental principles — with the five categories of threats and the requirement of independence in mind and in appearance for audit and review engagements

concepts.subsection: SA 200 — Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor
concepts.statement: Two things SA 200 says about what an audit cannot do are constantly turned into an excuse for what the auditor did not do. The auditor shall comply with relevant ethical requirements, including those pertaining to independence, relating to financial statement audit engagements. Reasonable assurance is a high level of assurance but not absolute, because an audit has inherent limitations, with the result that most of the audit evidence on which the auditor draws conclusions is persuasive rather than conclusive. Those limitations arise from the nature of financial reporting, which involves judgement and estimates; from the nature of audit procedures, since management may not provide complete information, fraud may involve sophisticated and carefully organised schemes designed to conceal it, and the auditor is neither trained as nor expected to be an expert in the authentication of documents; and from the need for the audit to be conducted within a reasonable period of time and at a reasonable cost. What the standard then refuses is the inference. The inherent limitations are not a basis for the auditor to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, and the difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for omitting an audit procedure for which there is no alternative. The auditor shall not represent compliance with the Standards on Auditing unless he has complied with all the SAs relevant to the audit.

citation.ref: para 14 on compliance with relevant ethical requirements, including those pertaining to independence, read with para 5 on reasonable assurance and para 15 on professional skepticism, and with the inherent limitations of an audit and the rule that they are not a basis for being satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive

concepts.subsection: SA 240 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud
concepts.statement: Fraud is distinguished from error by intent, and SA 240 describes three conditions generally present when it occurs. There is an incentive or pressure to commit fraud — a target, a covenant, a bonus that turns on a number. There is a perceived opportunity, which is what a weak control or a position allowing management override supplies. And there is an ability to rationalise the act, an attitude or set of values that lets a person justify committing it. These are fraud risk factors: events or conditions that indicate an incentive or pressure, or provide an opportunity, and their presence is not evidence that fraud has occurred. The auditor's inquiries are a set of topics, not one question. He inquires of management regarding its assessment of the risk that the financial statements may be materially misstated due to fraud, including the nature, extent and frequency of such assessments; management's process for identifying and responding to the risks of fraud in the entity, including any specific risks of fraud that management has identified or that have been brought to its attention; management's communication, if any, to those charged with governance regarding its processes for identifying and responding to those risks; and management's communication, if any, to employees regarding its views on business practices and ethical behaviour. He inquires of management, and of others within the entity as appropriate, to determine whether they have knowledge of any actual, suspected or alleged fraud affecting the entity, and unless all of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity he makes the same inquiry of them and obtains an understanding of how they exercise oversight of management's processes. Primary responsibility for the prevention and detection of fraud rests with those charged with governance and management; the responsibility for identifying and assessing the risks of material misstatement due to fraud is the auditor's, and no inquiry answer discharges it.

citation.ref: the three conditions generally present when fraud occurs — an incentive or pressure, a perceived opportunity and an ability to rationalise the act — and the required inquiries of management, of others within the entity and of those charged with governance, read with the presumed risk of fraud in revenue recognition at para 26 and management override at para 31

concepts.subsection: SA 250 — Consideration of Laws and Regulations
concepts.statement: SA 250 begins by giving the duty away. It is the responsibility of management, with the oversight of those charged with governance, to ensure that the entity's operations are conducted in accordance with the provisions of laws and regulations, including compliance with those that determine the reported amounts and disclosures in the financial statements. The auditor is not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations. His responsibility is to obtain reasonable assurance that the financial statements as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error, and in doing so he takes into account the applicable legal and regulatory framework. The risk of not detecting a material misstatement arising from non-compliance is higher than the risk of not detecting one arising from error, for three reasons the standard names: many laws relate principally to the operating aspects of the entity, do not affect the financial statements and are not captured by the information systems relevant to financial reporting; non-compliance may involve conduct designed to conceal it, such as collusion, forgery, deliberate failure to record transactions, management override of controls or intentional misrepresentations made to the auditor; and whether an act constitutes non-compliance is ultimately a matter for legal determination by a court or other appropriate adjudicative body. That last reason has a consequence in the report — the auditor never certifies that the entity has complied with the law, and a written representation about compliance is evidence he obtains, not a conclusion he may express.

citation.ref: the responsibility of management, with the oversight of those charged with governance, to ensure the entity's operations are conducted in accordance with laws and regulations; the position that the auditor is not responsible for preventing non-compliance and cannot be expected to detect non-compliance with all laws and regulations; and the point that whether an act constitutes non-compliance is ultimately a matter for legal determination by a court — read with the two categories of law at para 6

concepts.subsection: SA 260 (Revised) — Communication with Those Charged with Governance
concepts.statement: Before SA 260 says what is communicated it settles who. Those charged with governance are the person or persons or the organisation with responsibility for overseeing the strategic direction of the entity and the obligations related to its accountability, including overseeing the financial reporting process. The auditor determines the appropriate person or persons within the entity's governance structure with whom to communicate. Where he communicates with a subgroup, such as an audit committee or an individual, he determines whether he also needs to communicate with the governing body. And where all of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity — the small company whose only directors are its managers — matters required by the standard that have already been communicated with those persons in their management capacity need not be communicated again with the same persons in their governance capacity; the auditor must nevertheless satisfy himself that communicating with them adequately informs all of those with whom he would otherwise communicate in their governance capacity. Outside that express case, communicating with management does not relieve the auditor of communicating with those charged with governance. The auditor communicates the form, the timing and the expected general content of the communications, and at the end evaluates whether the two-way communication between him and those charged with governance has been adequate for the purpose of the audit; where it has not, he evaluates the effect on his assessment of the risks of material misstatement and on his ability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence, and takes appropriate action.

citation.ref: the determination of the appropriate person or persons within the entity's governance structure, the requirement where the auditor communicates with a subgroup to determine whether he also needs to communicate with the governing body, the relief where all of those charged with governance are involved in managing the entity, and the evaluation of the adequacy of the two-way communication — read with the planning communication at para 15 and the significant findings at para 16

concepts.subsection: SA 300 — Planning an Audit of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: Planning does not start with the strategy. SA 300 requires the auditor to undertake three preliminary engagement activities at the beginning of the current audit engagement: performing the procedures required by SA 220 regarding the continuance of the client relationship and the specific audit engagement; evaluating compliance with relevant ethical requirements, including independence, in accordance with SA 220; and establishing an understanding of the terms of the engagement as required by SA 210. The words "the current audit engagement" are the whole point. These are not acceptance activities done once in year one and rolled forward — they are done afresh every year, because what they exist to catch changes every year: a matter arising during the year that would have caused the firm to decline the engagement had it been known earlier, a new financial interest or a new non-audit service that has cost the firm its independence, a change in the entity that means the existing terms no longer describe what is being done. For an initial audit engagement the auditor additionally performs the SA 220 procedures on acceptance of the client relationship and, where there has been a change of auditors, communicates with the predecessor auditor in compliance with relevant ethical requirements — that step, and only that step, belongs to the first year alone. The engagement partner and other key members of the engagement team are involved in planning, including in the discussion among engagement team members.

citation.ref: the preliminary engagement activities at the beginning of the current audit engagement — client and engagement continuance under SA 220, evaluation of compliance with relevant ethical requirements including independence, and establishing an understanding of the terms of the engagement under SA 210 — and the additional activities required prior to starting an initial audit engagement

concepts.subsection: SA 315 (Revised) — Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement
concepts.statement: The auditor obtains an understanding of the entity and its environment, the applicable financial reporting framework and the entity's system of internal control, and that understanding is the basis on which risks of material misstatement are identified and assessed. The system of internal control is understood through its components — the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, the entity's process to monitor the system of internal control, the information system and communication, and control activities. What the standard asks of the auditor for the controls he identifies is precise and is routinely overstated: he evaluates the design of those controls and determines whether they have been implemented, by performing procedures in addition to inquiry of the entity's personnel. Inquiry alone establishes neither. Evaluating design asks whether the control, individually or with others, is capable of effectively preventing, or detecting and correcting, material misstatements; determining implementation asks whether the control exists and the entity is using it. Neither is a conclusion about operating effectiveness — whether the control operated as designed throughout the relevant period — which is tested under SA 330 and only where the auditor intends to rely on controls, or where substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence at the assertion level. Risk assessment procedures by themselves do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base the audit opinion.

citation.ref: the requirement to obtain an understanding of the entity's system of internal control through its components — the control environment, the entity's risk assessment process, the entity's process to monitor the system of internal control, the information system and communication, and control activities — and the requirement to evaluate the design of identified controls and determine whether they have been implemented by performing procedures in addition to inquiry of the entity's personnel, read with the significant risk definition at para 12(l)

concepts.subsection: SA 320 — Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit
concepts.statement: The materiality set when the audit was planned was set on an expectation, and SA 320 does not let it stand once the expectation is known to be wrong. The auditor revises materiality for the financial statements as a whole, and where applicable the materiality level or levels for particular classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures, in the event of becoming aware of information during the audit that would have caused him to have determined a different amount or amounts initially. A division sold, a business lost, a loss where a profit was budgeted, a benchmark that turns out to be unrepresentative — each is such information. And the revision does not stop at one number. If the auditor concludes that a lower materiality than that initially determined is appropriate, he determines whether it is necessary to revise performance materiality, and whether the nature, timing and extent of the further audit procedures remain appropriate — sample sizes computed against the old figure, scoping decisions about which components or balances to test, analytical thresholds. The trigger is the arrival of information, not a point in the calendar, and this revision is a different requirement from the reassessment SA 450 makes the auditor perform at the end, before evaluating the effect of uncorrected misstatements. The auditor documents the amounts determined, the factors considered in determining them, and any revision as the audit progressed.

citation.ref: para 12 and para 13, read with para 9 and para 11

concepts.subsection: SA 501 — Audit Evidence: Specific Considerations
concepts.statement: Segment information is the third specific item SA 501 singles out, after inventory and litigation and claims. The auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding the presentation and disclosure of segment information in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework by obtaining an understanding of the methods used by management in determining segment information — evaluating whether those methods are likely to result in disclosure in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework and, where appropriate, testing the application of those methods — and by performing analytical procedures or other audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances. The methods worth understanding are the ones where the number is made rather than found: sales, transfers and charges between segments and the elimination of inter-segment amounts; comparisons with budgets and other expected results, such as operating profits as a percentage of sales; and the allocation of assets and of costs among segments, including the treatment of costs that serve more than one segment. The limit on the work is stated as plainly as the work: the auditor is not required to perform audit procedures that would be necessary to express an opinion on the segment information presented on a standalone basis. Segment information is a disclosure within the financial statements he is reporting on, not a separate set of accounts and not other information.

citation.ref: para 13, read with the litigation and claims requirements at para 9 to para 11

concepts.subsection: SA 530 — Audit Sampling
concepts.statement: Three decisions are made before a single item is examined, and a sample that fails any of them cannot be rescued afterwards. When designing an audit sample the auditor considers the purpose of the audit procedure and the characteristics of the population from which the sample will be drawn — the population has to be appropriate for the objective of the procedure and it has to be complete, and stratifying it or selecting a value-weighted approach is part of the design. He determines a sample size sufficient to reduce sampling risk to an acceptably low level; the size responds to the level of sampling risk he is willing to accept, to the tolerable misstatement or tolerable rate of deviation, and to the misstatement or deviation he expects to find. And he selects items in such a way that each sampling unit in the population has a chance of selection. Sampling risk is the risk that the auditor's conclusion based on a sample may differ from the conclusion if the entire population were subjected to the same audit procedure; non-sampling risk is the risk of an erroneous conclusion for any reason not related to sampling risk. Of the selection methods, random and systematic selection and monetary unit sampling give every unit its chance; haphazard selection is acceptable because the auditor selects without following a structured technique while still avoiding conscious bias or predictability, though it is not available where a statistical evaluation is intended; and block selection of contiguous items is ordinarily not appropriate, because most populations are structured so that items in a sequence share characteristics with each other and differ from the rest.

citation.ref: para 6, para 7 and para 8, read with para 13 and para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 550 — Related Parties
concepts.statement: Where management has made an assertion in the financial statements to the effect that a related party transaction was conducted on terms equivalent to those prevailing in an arm's length transaction, the auditor obtains sufficient appropriate audit evidence about the assertion. It is an assertion like any other and it is audited like any other; what makes it hard is that the support may not exist. There may be no identical or similar transaction with an unrelated party to compare with, the item may have no open market, and management's process for supporting the assertion may amount to an internal opinion recorded in a minute. The procedures available are to compare the terms of the transaction with those of an identical or similar transaction with one or more unrelated parties, or with known market terms for broadly similar transactions on an open market; to evaluate the appropriateness of management's process for supporting the assertion; and to verify the source of the internal or external data supporting the assertion and test the data for accuracy, completeness and relevance. Where the audit evidence contradicts the assertion, the disclosure is misstated. Where the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence about an assertion the applicable financial reporting framework requires to be disclosed, that is an inability to obtain evidence, with the consequences SA 705 (Revised) attaches. Management asserting it is not the auditor evidencing it, and this requirement is separate from the significant risk that a related party transaction outside the entity's normal course of business creates.

citation.ref: para 24, read with para 23

concepts.subsection: SA 610 (Revised) — Using the Work of Internal Auditors
concepts.statement: Before any of the internal audit function's work may be used, the external auditor determines whether it can be used, and the determination is made by evaluating three things: the extent to which the function's organisational status and relevant policies and procedures support the objectivity of the internal auditors; the level of competence of the function; and whether the function applies a systematic and disciplined approach, including quality control. Each is a gate. The external auditor shall not use the work of the function if the organisational status and relevant policies and procedures do not adequately support the objectivity of internal auditors, if the function lacks sufficient competence, or if it does not apply a systematic and disciplined approach. Where the work may be used, he determines the areas and the extent of the work that can be used by considering the nature and scope of the work and its relevance to his own strategy and plan, and by considering the amount of judgement involved in planning, performing and evaluating that work and the assessed risk of material misstatement at the assertion level — the more judgement, the higher the risk, the weaker the objectivity or competence, the less can be used and the more the external auditor performs himself. He plans to use the work in a way that leaves all significant judgements in the audit made by him, and the more of them there are, the less the aggregate use. Before using the work he reads the reports, evaluates whether it was properly planned, performed, supervised, reviewed and documented, whether sufficient appropriate audit evidence was obtained to enable reasonable conclusions, and whether the conclusions reached are appropriate and the reports consistent with the results of the work; and he performs sufficient audit procedures on the body of work as a whole, including reperformance. Using the work never reduces his sole responsibility for the opinion. This is a different question from direct assistance, which the standard permits on its own separate and stricter conditions.

citation.ref: the requirement to determine whether the work of the internal audit function can be used by evaluating the extent to which its organisational status and relevant policies and procedures support the objectivity of the internal auditors, the level of competence of the function, and whether the function applies a systematic and disciplined approach including quality control; the prohibition on using the work where any of the three fails; and the evaluation of the work performed, including reperformance — read with the direct assistance conditions at para 28, para 30 and para 33

concepts.subsection: SA 620 — Using the Work of an Auditor's Expert
concepts.statement: SA 620 puts a written agreement between the decision to use an expert and the expert starting work. The auditor agrees, in writing when appropriate, on four matters with the auditor's expert: the nature, scope and objectives of that expert's work; the respective roles and responsibilities of the auditor and that expert; the nature, timing and extent of communication between the auditor and that expert, including the form of any report to be provided by that expert; and the need for the auditor's expert to observe confidentiality requirements. Whether writing is appropriate turns on matters such as whether the expert will have access to sensitive or confidential entity information, the respective roles of the auditor and the expert, any legal and regulatory requirements, the extent and complexity of the work, and whether the expert is an auditor's internal expert or an auditor's external expert. The fourth matter is the one most often assumed away: an auditor's external expert is not bound by the auditor's own professional duty of confidentiality merely by being engaged, which is precisely why the standard makes it a matter to be agreed. The agreement sits alongside two other duties that come before the work — evaluating whether the expert has the necessary competence, capabilities and objectivity for the auditor's purposes, and obtaining a sufficient understanding of the expert's field of expertise to enable the auditor to determine the nature, scope and objectives of that expert's work and to evaluate its adequacy afterwards. Agreeing the scope is not directing the expert's judgement; it is what makes the later evaluation of the adequacy of the work possible at all.

citation.ref: para 11, read with para 12 and para 13

concepts.subsection: SA 700 (Revised) — Forming an Opinion and Reporting
concepts.statement: Past the Opinion and Basis for Opinion sections, SA 700 (Revised) prescribes elements that are routinely treated as formalities and are routinely got wrong. The name of the engagement partner is included in the auditor's report for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities, unless, in rare circumstances, such disclosure is reasonably expected to lead to a significant personal security threat — and where the auditor intends not to include it, he discusses that intention with those charged with governance. The report is signed, and it names the place of signature, being the location where the auditor signs it. And the date is not administrative: the auditor's report is dated no earlier than the date on which he has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence on which to base the opinion, including evidence that all the statements that comprise the financial statements, including the related notes, have been prepared and that those with the recognised authority have asserted that they have taken responsibility for them. So the date can never precede the day the board approved the accounts, and it is not the day fieldwork ended. The report also carries a title indicating it is the report of an independent auditor, an addressee, a section describing the responsibilities of management and, where appropriate, of those charged with governance for the financial statements, and a section describing the auditor's responsibilities for the audit; where the auditor has other reporting responsibilities under law or regulation, they go in a separate section headed Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements, so that the opinion on the financial statements is not diluted by them.

citation.ref: the requirement that the name of the engagement partner be included for audits of complete sets of general purpose financial statements of listed entities unless disclosure is reasonably expected to lead to a significant personal security threat; the requirements that the report be signed and name the place of signature; and the requirement that it be dated no earlier than the date on which the auditor has obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence, including evidence that those with the recognised authority have asserted that they have taken responsibility for the financial statements — read with the Opinion section at para 23 and the Basis for Opinion at para 28

concepts.subsection: SA 701 — Communicating Key Audit Matters
concepts.statement: Key audit matters come out of a funnel with three stages, and each stage narrows the last. The auditor starts from the matters communicated with those charged with governance. From those he determines the matters that required significant auditor attention in performing the audit, taking into account areas of higher assessed risk of material misstatement or significant risks identified in accordance with SA 315; significant auditor judgements relating to areas in the financial statements that involved significant management judgement, including accounting estimates identified as having high estimation uncertainty; and the effect on the audit of significant events or transactions that occurred during the period. From those he determines which were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period, and those, and only those, are the key audit matters. The description is prescribed. Each key audit matter is described using an appropriate subheading in a separate section headed Key Audit Matters, the description includes a reference to the related disclosure or disclosures, if any, in the financial statements, and it addresses why the matter was considered to be one of most significance in the audit and therefore determined to be a key audit matter, and how the matter was addressed in the audit. The introduction to the section states that these are the matters that, in the auditor's professional judgement, were of most significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period, that they were addressed in the context of the audit of the financial statements as a whole and in forming the auditor's opinion thereon, and that the auditor does not provide a separate opinion on these matters. Materiality alone is not a reason a matter required significant auditor attention, and where the auditor determines that there are no key audit matters to communicate, he says so in the section.

citation.ref: para 13 on the description of each key audit matter, read with the three-stage determination — matters communicated with those charged with governance, those that required significant auditor attention, and those of most significance in the audit of the current period — and with para 14

concepts.subsection: SA 705 (Revised) — Modifications to the Opinion
concepts.statement: Choosing the modification is half the answer; SA 705 (Revised) then changes the report in several places at once, and a report that carries the right label over the wrong words is worse than one that carries neither. The heading of the Opinion section becomes Qualified Opinion, Adverse Opinion or Disclaimer of Opinion as appropriate. A qualified opinion arising from a material misstatement says that, except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the financial statements give a true and fair view; a qualified opinion arising from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence says except for the possible effects of the matter. An adverse opinion says that, because of the significance of the matter described, the financial statements do not give a true and fair view. A disclaimer says that the auditor does not express an opinion, and that because of the significance of the matter described he has not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide a basis for an audit opinion. The Basis for Opinion heading is amended to match the opinion, and that section describes the matter giving rise to the modification and, where the misstatement relates to specific amounts, includes a description and quantification of the financial effects unless impracticable, in which case the report says so. Two further changes belong to a disclaimer alone: the statement that the audit was conducted in accordance with the Standards on Auditing is replaced by a statement that the auditor was engaged to audit the financial statements, the description of the auditor's responsibilities is amended accordingly, and the report does not include a Key Audit Matters section unless the auditor is required by law or regulation to communicate key audit matters.

citation.ref: para 16 on the heading of the Opinion section, para 20 on amending the Basis for Opinion heading and para 21 on describing and quantifying the matter, read with para 11 to para 14 and with the requirements that apply where the auditor disclaims an opinion

concepts.subsection: SRE 2400 (Revised) — Engagements to Review Historical Financial Statements
concepts.statement: A review is designed to obtain limited assurance, and its procedures are primarily inquiry and analytical procedures — but that is where a review starts, not a ceiling on it. If a matter comes to the practitioner's attention that causes him to believe the financial statements may be materially misstated, he designs and performs additional procedures sufficient to enable him to conclude on the matter or to determine that a modified conclusion is needed. The conclusion is expressed in the negative form: nothing has come to the practitioner's attention that causes him to believe that the financial statements do not give a true and fair view, or are not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. Modification then follows the same two-by-two grid as a report. Where the financial statements are materially misstated, the conclusion is qualified where the effects are material but not pervasive and adverse where they are material and pervasive. Where the practitioner is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence, he qualifies where the possible effects are material but not pervasive and disclaims a conclusion where they could be material and pervasive; and where management imposes a limitation such that he believes he may need to disclaim, and the engagement is not required by law or regulation, he withdraws where practicable and possible. What a review does not require is what separates it from an audit: it does not ordinarily require tests of accounting records through inspection, observation or confirmation, an understanding of internal control sufficient to identify and assess risks of material misstatement, or tests of controls, and the practitioner expresses no audit opinion. He must still comply with relevant ethical requirements including independence, and exercise professional skepticism and professional judgement throughout.

citation.ref: the requirement to design and perform additional procedures where a matter comes to the practitioner's attention causing him to believe the financial statements may be materially misstated, the negative form of the conclusion, the four modified conclusions and the withdrawal on a management-imposed limitation, and the statement that a review does not ordinarily require tests of accounting records, an understanding of internal control sufficient to identify and assess risks of material misstatement, or tests of controls

concepts.subsection: SAE 3420 — Reporting on the Compilation of Pro Forma Financial Information
concepts.statement: Pro forma financial information shows what the effect of a significant event or a transaction would have been on unadjusted financial information, had the event occurred or the transaction been undertaken at an earlier date selected for purposes of the illustration. It appears in a prospectus, and its purpose is illustration. SAE 3420 gives the practitioner a reasonable assurance engagement, but on a narrow question, and the narrowness is the examinable part: his opinion is on whether the pro forma financial information has been compiled, in all material respects, by the responsible party on the basis of the applicable criteria. He expresses no opinion on whether the actual outcome of the event or transaction will be as illustrated, and he does not re-audit or update the unadjusted financial information from which the pro forma information is derived. Three tests decide the opinion. The source from which the unadjusted financial information has been extracted must be appropriately identified. The pro forma adjustments must be directly attributable to the event or transaction, factually supportable, and consistent with the entity's applicable financial reporting framework and its accounting policies under that framework. And the applicable criteria must be suitable and adequately disclosed. Because an illustration only works if the reader knows it is one, the practitioner also considers whether the pro forma financial information is appropriately presented and adequately explained, and reads the other information in the prospectus to identify any material inconsistency with it. An adjustment resting on savings management hopes to achieve is not factually supportable, whatever the quality of the hope.

citation.ref: the opinion on whether the pro forma financial information has been compiled, in all material respects, on the basis of the applicable criteria; the position that the practitioner expresses no opinion on whether the actual outcome will be as illustrated; and the requirements that the source of the unadjusted financial information be appropriately identified and that the pro forma adjustments be directly attributable to the event or transaction, factually supportable, and consistent with the entity's applicable financial reporting framework and accounting policies

concepts.subsection: Digital auditing — audit data analytics
concepts.statement: Audit data analytics let the auditor examine an entire population rather than a sample — every journal entry, every sales invoice, every vendor payment — and they change what the auditor gets, not what he owes. Three limits hold, and each is where a file goes wrong. First, the output of an analytic is a set of items carrying the characteristic the auditor asked it to find; it is not a list of misstatements. Every exception is investigated, and most of them usually have an ordinary explanation. Second, an analytic is only as good as the data it ran on. Data extracted from the entity's systems is information produced by the entity, so the auditor obtains audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness — reconciling the extraction to the general ledger or to another control total, and checking the parameters the extraction was run with — and where the analysis depends on system-generated data he must first be satisfied about the general IT controls over that system, because a weak change-management or access control undermines everything the system produced. Third, testing one hundred per cent of a population removes sampling risk, which is the risk that a conclusion based on a sample differs from the conclusion on the whole population. It removes nothing else. A rule written to the wrong threshold, an analytic that tests the wrong attribute, and an auditor who accepts what the tool produced without a critical assessment are all non-sampling risk, and that is exactly where professional skepticism is still required. Analytics are used across the audit — in risk assessment, as substantive procedures, and in the overall review at the end — but they never make the significant judgements, which remain the auditor's.

citation.ref: Ch. Digital Auditing and Assurance, read with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

concepts.subsection: Section 138 — Internal audit
concepts.statement: Section 138 requires such class or classes of companies as may be prescribed to appoint an internal auditor to conduct internal audit of the functions and activities of the company. Who may hold the office is set by the section itself, and it is wider than the profession's own boundary: the internal auditor shall either be a chartered accountant or a cost accountant, or such other professional as may be decided by the Board. The Explanation to the section settles the point most often got wrong — the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company. The Central Government may, by rules, prescribe the manner and the intervals in which the internal audit shall be conducted and reported to the Board. Two boundaries run off it. The company's statutory auditor cannot be its internal auditor, because section 144 lists internal audit among the services an auditor appointed under the Act shall not render, directly or indirectly, to the company, to its holding company or to its subsidiary company. And appointing an internal auditor is a different question from whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business, which is what CARO 2020 asks the statutory auditor to report on; the existence of the function does not decide whether the statutory auditor may use its work, which SA 610 (Revised) alone governs.

citation.ref: Section 138(1) with its Explanation that the internal auditor may or may not be an employee of the company, and section 138(2), read with section 144

concepts.subsection: SA 720 — The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Other Information
concepts.statement: SA 720's work begins before there is anything to read. Other information is financial or non-financial information, other than the financial statements and the auditor's report thereon, included in an entity's annual report — the annual report being a document, or a combination of documents, prepared typically on an annual basis by management or those charged with governance in accordance with law, regulation or custom, the purpose of which is to provide owners with information on the entity's operations and its financial results and financial position as set out in the financial statements. The auditor determines, through discussion with management, which documents comprise the annual report and the entity's planned manner and timing of the issuance of those documents. He makes appropriate arrangements with management to obtain, in a timely manner and if possible prior to the date of the auditor's report, the final version of those documents. And where some or all of them will not be available until after the date of the auditor's report, he requests management to provide a written representation that the final version will be provided to him when available and prior to its issuance by the entity, so that he can complete the procedures the standard requires. A press release, an investor presentation or a separate analyst pack is not by itself the annual report — a document is other information because it forms part of the annual report, not because it was published near it — and the auditor expresses no opinion or conclusion on the other information whenever it arrives.

citation.ref: para 13, read with the reading requirement at para 14

concepts.subsection: Bank audit — verification of advances
concepts.statement: Advances are where a bank audit is won or lost, and the work on an advance runs on four questions that come before any question of classification. Is it within sanction — the drawing power recomputed by the auditor from the latest stock and book-debt statement, after deducting the margin stipulated in the sanction and after deducting creditors for goods, because a drawing power worked out on the gross value of stock is a limit the borrower never had. Is it properly secured — the charge created and, where the law requires it, registered; the security in existence, inspected and valued on a basis the auditor can see; the valuation not simply carried forward from the year before. Is the documentation complete and enforceable — the loan and security documents executed by persons authorised to execute them, stamped, and not time-barred, which is why acknowledgements of debt and revival letters are examined and why a document that has run out of time is a defect however good the borrower looks. And are the terms of the sanction being observed — the end use of the funds, the conditions precedent, the financial covenants, the periodicity of the statements the borrower is required to submit. Only then comes classification, and there the discipline is that the auditor tests the branch's identification of non-performing assets rather than accepting the list the system produced. That list is generated on parameters configured by the entity, so it is information produced by the entity: the auditor establishes its accuracy and completeness, and he independently examines accounts showing the symptoms the norms care about — no credits, credits insufficient to cover the interest debited, an outstanding persistently above the limit or the drawing power, a limit renewed on paper without a fresh appraisal, and a facility whose overdue position was cured by a fresh advance from the same bank.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — verification of advances: drawing power and the margin stipulated in the sanction, creation and registration of the charge, enforceability and limitation of the documents, and the auditor's own testing of the branch's identification of non-performing assets, read with the RBI Prudential norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning and with SA 500 on information produced by the entity

concepts.subsection: Bank audit — treasury operations
concepts.statement: Treasury is a small number of people moving very large sums very quickly, so the first control the auditor looks for is not a limit but a separation. The front office deals. The mid office measures exposure, monitors the limits and reports independently. The back office confirms with the counterparty, settles and accounts. No person straddles two of the three, and a dealer who confirms his own deals has removed the only independent check on what he says he did. From that structure the procedures follow. The auditor confirms deals against the counterparty's confirmation and the exchange or clearing corporation record rather than against the dealer's own slip. He tests that deals were struck inside the counterparty, currency, instrument and open-position limits sanctioned by the board, and that a breach was reported and approved rather than absorbed. He examines rates against the market rate ruling at the time of the deal, because a deal put through away from the market is how value is moved out of the bank or a loss is moved into another book. And he looks specifically for deals cancelled and rebooked with the same counterparty, for deals done outside dealing hours or outside the dealing room, and for a pattern of late confirmations, all of which are the recognised means of postponing a loss to a later period. Existence is verified from the bank's own account with the depository or from a confirmation obtained directly from the custodian, never from the front office's own record, and a security shown as sold is traced to delivery. Because the volumes are large and the period between statutory audits is long, treasury is one of the areas ordinarily covered by concurrent audit, and the statutory auditor reads the concurrent auditor's reports and the action taken on them rather than treating their existence as assurance.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — treasury operations: segregation of the front office, the mid office and the back office, independent confirmation of deals with the counterparty and the exchange, dealing within the limits sanctioned by the board, scrutiny of off-market rates and of deals cancelled and rebooked, and verification of the existence of securities from the depository or the custodian, read with SA 265 on communicating deficiencies in internal control

concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the Ghosh and Jilani Committee recommendations
concepts.statement: Two committee reports sit permanently in the bank auditor's checklist and students routinely swap them, so learn them by subject. The Ghosh Committee was on frauds and malpractices in banks, and what it recommended is anti-fraud housekeeping: rotation of staff holding sensitive positions and compulsory leave, so that no one seat is held by one person indefinitely; joint custody of cash, of security documents and of the keys; control over the issue, custody and record of security stationery such as demand drafts, cheque books and pay orders; verification of specimen signatures and of the powers under which an instrument is signed; prompt reconciliation of inter-branch accounts, of nostro accounts and of suspense and sundry accounts, since an unreconciled account is where a fraud lives undisturbed; and prompt reporting of frauds through the prescribed channel. The Jilani Committee was on the internal control and inspection or audit system in banks, and what it recommended is the machinery that checks: an independent inspection and audit department reporting to the top of the organisation rather than to the executives it inspects; coverage of every branch on a defined cycle, with the interval between inspections set by the risk and the size of the branch; a proper system of concurrent audit for large and sensitive branches and for treasury; a system for the rectification of the irregularities reported rather than the mere listing of them again in the next report; and a report to the audit committee of the board. The statutory auditor reports on the implementation of both sets of recommendations in the long form audit report, and what he reports is compliance and not recital: a recommendation not implemented is reported as not implemented, and a recommendation implemented on paper with no evidence that it operated is not implemented.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the Ghosh Committee on frauds and malpractices in banks and the Jilani Committee on the internal control and inspection or audit system in banks, and the reporting on the implementation of their recommendations in the long form audit report

concepts.subsection: Bank audit — the memorandum of changes
concepts.statement: A branch auditor cannot alter the branch's books, so what he does with a figure he disagrees with is a memorandum of changes: a statement annexed to and forming part of his branch audit report setting out every change he considers necessary in the returns the branch has submitted, each change described, quantified, and grouped by its effect — on the profit and loss account, on the classification of advances, on provisioning, on the balance sheet heads, and on the asset classification returns the head office consolidates. It exists because the branch's figures are consolidated at the head office, and the central statutory auditors and the head office need each proposed change in a form they can apply without re-doing the branch audit. Two rules decide its contents and neither is about size alone. A change goes in whether or not the branch has accepted it, because the memorandum is the auditor's statement and not a negotiated one. And a change the branch has already carried out in its books before the report is not a change at all and does not go in, because it is already in the figures being reported on. The memorandum is a supplement to the report and never a place to park an opinion: where changes the branch has refused to make are material to the branch's own financial statements, the branch auditor qualifies his branch audit report and the memorandum quantifies what he has qualified. Where he proposes no change he states the memorandum is nil rather than omitting it, since a missing memorandum reads at the head office as one not yet received. Changes touching the classification of an advance are always set out with their consequence for the provision, because classification and provisioning move together and a reclassification carried without its provision is only half the change.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Banks — the memorandum of changes annexed to the branch audit report: changes proposed whether or not accepted by the branch, changes already carried out in the books excluded, a nil memorandum stated as nil, and the rule that the memorandum supplements the branch audit report and does not substitute for a qualification of it

concepts.subsection: NBFC audit — the auditor's report to the Reserve Bank
concepts.statement: The statutory auditor of a non-banking financial company carries a reporting duty the Companies Act alone does not give him. Under the directions the Reserve Bank issues to auditors of non-banking financial companies he makes an additional report to the Board of Directors of the company, separate from and in addition to his report under section 143 on the financial statements, on the matters those directions specify: whether the company is engaged in the business of a non-banking financial institution and holds a certificate of registration granted under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934; whether, on the basis of its asset pattern and its income pattern as at the year end, it is entitled to continue to hold that certificate; where the company does not accept public deposits, whether the board has passed the resolution the directions require to that effect and whether the company has in fact accepted any; whether the company has complied with the prudential norms on income recognition, accounting standards, asset classification and provisioning applicable to it; and, where applicable to the company, whether the capital adequacy ratio has been correctly determined and reported to the Reserve Bank. The examinable part is the exception route. Where any of those statements is in the negative or is unfavourable, the auditor does not stop at the Board. He reports the matter directly to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank in whose jurisdiction the company's registered office is situated, within the period the directions allow. That duty is the auditor's own; it does not depend on the Board agreeing with him, on the Board forwarding anything, or on the matter being material to the financial statements. And it stands alongside, not instead of, his duty under section 143(12) of the Companies Act where he has reason to believe that an offence involving fraud is being or has been committed — a regulatory non-compliance is not by itself such an offence, and a fraud is not discharged by a report to the Regional Office.

citation.source: Reserve Bank of India directions to auditors of non-banking financial companies
citation.ref: the additional report to the Board of Directors on the matters specified, including registration under section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and continued entitlement on the asset and income pattern, and the obligation to report a negative or unfavourable statement directly to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank in whose jurisdiction the registered office is situated, read with section 143(12) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Sections 139(5) and 139(7) — appointment of the auditor of a government company
concepts.statement: In a government company, and in any other company owned or controlled directly or indirectly by the Central Government, by any State Government or Governments, or partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments, the appointment of the auditor does not run through the Board and the members in the ordinary way. Section 139(5) provides that the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India shall appoint an auditor duly qualified to be appointed as an auditor of companies under the Act within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year, and the auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the annual general meeting. Section 139(7) deals with the first auditor of such a company and sets out a cascade: the Comptroller and Auditor-General appoints the first auditor within sixty days from the date of registration of the company; if he does not appoint within that period, the Board of Directors appoints within the next thirty days; and if the Board also fails to appoint within those thirty days, it informs the members, who appoint the first auditor within sixty days at an extraordinary general meeting. The first auditor so appointed holds office till the conclusion of the first annual general meeting. The cascade is the examinable part — it moves outward from the Comptroller and Auditor-General to the Board and only then to the members, and each step opens only on the failure of the step before, never by choice. This is the government-company track, and it is not the section 139(6) track under which the Board of any other company appoints the first auditor within thirty days of registration and, failing that, the members appoint within ninety days at an extraordinary general meeting. Reading one cascade into the other is the commonest way this question is lost.

citation.ref: Section 139(5) — appointment by the Comptroller and Auditor-General within one hundred and eighty days from the commencement of the financial year — and Section 139(7) with its cascade of sixty days for the Comptroller and Auditor-General, the next thirty days for the Board and sixty days for the members at an extraordinary general meeting, read against Section 139(6) for a company that is not a government company

concepts.subsection: Government audit — comprehensive audit of a public enterprise
concepts.statement: A public enterprise is set up with public money for a stated purpose, and comprehensive audit is the Comptroller and Auditor-General's examination of whether the way it is being run is serving that purpose. It goes past the accounts and past the vouchers into management's decisions and their results: whether the capacity created is being used and, where it is not, why; whether projects were completed to time and to cost and what the overrun cost; whether the price at which the product or service is sold recovers what it should; whether inventory, receivables and idle assets are being carried far beyond what the operation needs; whether the return on the capital employed justifies the investment made; and whether the objectives for which the enterprise was created are being achieved at all. The areas are not fixed by any rule. They are selected after a study of the enterprise, its stated objectives, its published policy, the decisions of its board and the reports it makes to Government, and the criteria against which performance is judged are drawn from those sources rather than from the auditor's own preference — which is precisely what keeps the exercise from collapsing into an opinion about management. Two boundaries are examined. Comprehensive audit expresses no opinion on the financial statements and certifies nothing; it reports findings, the reasons behind them and recommendations, and its reader is Parliament through the Comptroller and Auditor-General's report. And it is not the transaction-level prudence test that propriety audit applies to a particular item of expenditure: comprehensive audit asks how the enterprise as a whole has performed against the objectives for which it was set up, not whether one payment was wisely made.

citation.ref: Ch. Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — comprehensive audit of a public enterprise: the areas examined, including capacity utilisation, project execution and cost overrun, inventory and receivables, pricing and return on capital employed; the selection of those areas after a study of the enterprise and its objectives; and the reporting of findings and recommendations rather than an opinion

concepts.subsection: Internal audit — scope, independence and reporting line
concepts.statement: Internal audit is an independent appraisal activity established within an entity to examine and evaluate its activities as a service to the entity, and the two words carrying the weight are "independent" and "within". Because the function sits inside the organisation, its independence cannot come from being an outsider; it comes from where it reports and from what it is kept out of. The function reports to the audit committee, or where there is none to the board or to the highest level of management able to act on what it finds, and it never reports to the head of the activity it audits. Its scope is settled by the audit committee or the board and not by the managers whose work it examines, and it has unrestricted access to records, to personnel and to premises. And the internal auditor does not design, install or operate the controls he later evaluates and owns no part of the process he reviews, because a person reviewing his own work is not appraising it. The scope reaches wherever the entity's risks are — the adequacy and the operating effectiveness of the internal control system, compliance with law and with the entity's own policies, the reliability and integrity of financial and operating information, the safeguarding of assets, and the economy, efficiency and effectiveness with which resources are used — which is wider than the financial statements the statutory auditor reports on. That difference in scope is why the two are not substitutes in either direction. The statutory auditor may use the internal audit function's work only on the conditions SA 610 (Revised) lays down, and using it never reduces his sole responsibility for the opinion; equally, having a statutory auditor does not relieve a company of appointing an internal auditor where the Act requires one, and a well-run internal audit function does not narrow the statutory audit.

citation.ref: Ch. Internal Audit — internal audit as an independent appraisal activity established within the entity; its reporting to the audit committee or the board rather than to the management it audits; the scope settled by the audit committee or the board and unrestricted access; the bar on evaluating controls the internal auditor himself designed or operates; and the relationship with the statutory audit, read with SA 610 (Revised) and section 138 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Due diligence — normalised earnings and hidden liabilities
concepts.statement: A financial due diligence does not verify last year's profit; it works out what the buyer is actually buying, and two numbers come out of it. The first is normalised or sustainable earnings: reported profit adjusted to strip out what will not recur and to put in what the seller's own arrangements have been suppressing. Out come one-off gains and losses — profit on the sale of an asset, the write-back of a provision no longer required, an insurance recovery, income from a business the seller is retaining. Out also come the effects of arrangements that end at completion: a proprietor's remuneration far below or above the market rate, rent paid to a related party at a concessional rate, a group service charge, a sale to a group company at a price nobody outside the group would pay. In come the costs the business will bear after completion and has not been bearing — a market rent, a full management team, the audit and compliance costs of a standalone company. The second number is net debt together with the working capital the business normally needs, because a price agreed on a multiple of earnings is settled in cash against a debt-free, cash-free position, and everything debt-like is pulled into net debt: unfunded gratuity and leave obligations, deferred consideration on an earlier acquisition, receivables factored with recourse, statutory dues in arrears. Then come the hidden liabilities, which is where the assignment earns its fee — disputed tax and duty demands and their likely outcome, guarantees given for group companies, undisclosed contingent liabilities, litigation, pending regulatory action, an onerous long-term contract, environmental obligations, disputed employee dues, and a lease or a borrowing carrying a change-of-control clause that the transaction itself will trigger. The reporting is not an audit's. A due diligence report states findings of fact, is addressed to the party who engaged it and for the purpose for which it was engaged, expresses no opinion on the financial statements, and feeds the price, the warranties and the indemnities rather than a report to members.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — financial due diligence: the normalisation of reported earnings for non-recurring items and for arrangements that end at completion, the computation of net debt and normal working capital against a debt-free cash-free price, and the identification of hidden liabilities including disputed demands, guarantees, onerous contracts and change-of-control clauses

concepts.subsection: Sections 210 and 213 — investigation into a company's affairs
concepts.statement: Two sections open an investigation into a company's affairs and they differ in who moves. Section 210 is the Central Government's. It may order an investigation where it is of the opinion that it is necessary to do so, on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or of an inspector under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest; and where a court or the Tribunal, in any proceeding before it, orders that the affairs of a company ought to be investigated, the Central Government shall order an investigation. In every case the Central Government appoints one or more persons as inspectors to investigate and to report in the manner and within the period it directs. Section 213 is the Tribunal's, and it starts with an applicant rather than with the Government. The Tribunal may order an investigation on an application by members of the requisite number the section prescribes, or by any other person, on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest what the section lists: that the business of the company is being conducted with intent to defraud its creditors, members or any other person, or for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or in a manner oppressive to any of its members, or that the company was formed for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose; that persons concerned in the formation of the company or the management of its affairs have been guilty of fraud, misfeasance or other misconduct towards the company or towards any of its members; or that the members have not been given all the information with respect to its affairs which they might reasonably expect. The applicant is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard and the Tribunal may require security for costs. Where the Tribunal so orders, the Central Government appoints the inspectors, and where the report makes out a case the section provides for action against those responsible. Neither section is a route a member takes by writing to the auditor, and neither is section 212, under which the Central Government assigns an investigation to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office.

citation.ref: Section 210 — investigation ordered by the Central Government on a report under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution, in the public interest, or on the order of a court or the Tribunal — and Section 213, under which the Tribunal may order an investigation on an application by the requisite number of members or by any other person on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest the matters the section lists, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard

concepts.subsection: Audit of consolidated financial statements — reporting on components audited by other auditors
concepts.statement: The parent's auditor signs one report on the consolidated financial statements and he alone is responsible for the opinion in it, however many other auditors audited the components inside it. What the report does is disclose the extent of what he did not audit himself. Where components have been audited by other auditors, the parent's auditor includes an Other Matter paragraph stating that he did not audit the financial statements of those components, giving the number of components concerned and the quantum they represent — total assets, total revenues and net cash flows, and the group's share of profit or loss for associates and joint ventures accounted for on the equity method — that those financial statements have been audited by other auditors whose reports have been furnished to him, and that his opinion, in so far as it relates to the amounts and disclosures included in respect of those components, is based solely on the reports of the other auditors. The paragraph is a disclosure of division and not a disclaimer. It does not qualify the opinion, it does not reduce the parent auditor's responsibility for the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and it does not excuse him from the work the framework requires of him on the consolidation itself — the uniformity of accounting policies across components, the consolidation adjustments and eliminations, the computation of non-controlling interests, and the treatment of a component whose figures are unaudited. Where a component auditor has modified his opinion, the parent's auditor evaluates whether the matter is material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole and modifies his own opinion only if it is; a matter material to the component but not to the group does not travel up. And an Other Matter paragraph is never the way to deal with a matter that requires a modification, exactly as an Emphasis of Matter paragraph is not — a paragraph that describes a matter is not an opinion about it.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: the Other Matter paragraph in the parent auditor's report stating the number of components not audited by him, the total assets, total revenues and net cash flows they represent, and that his opinion on the amounts and disclosures in respect of those components is based solely on the reports of the other auditors, read with SA 706 (Revised) paras 8 and 10 on Emphasis of Matter and Other Matter paragraphs and with SA 705 (Revised) on when a modification is required

concepts.subsection: Sections 177(4) and 177(5) — terms of reference of the audit committee
concepts.statement: Section 177(4) requires the Board to specify the audit committee's terms of reference in writing, and it lists what those terms include. The recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors of the company. Review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance, and of the effectiveness of the audit process. Examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report on it. Approval of, or any subsequent modification of, transactions of the company with related parties. Scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments. Valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary. Evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems. And monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers and related matters. Section 177(5) then gives the committee the means to do it: it may call for the comments of the auditors about internal control systems, the scope of audit including the observations of the auditors, and review of the financial statement before their submission to the Board, and it may discuss any related issues with the internal and statutory auditors and the management of the company. Two consequences run off that list and both are examined. Because the committee recommends the auditor's appointment and reviews his independence and performance, the auditor's relationship with the company on those matters runs through the committee and not through the management whose figures he is auditing — which is what makes the committee, and not the finance function, the right addressee for a difficulty encountered during the audit. And because the committee approves related party transactions, a transaction entered into without its approval is an identified non-compliance with law, which the auditor treats as one under SA 250, communicates to those charged with governance, and considers for its effect on the financial statements and on his risk assessment.

citation.ref: Section 177(4) — the terms of reference of the audit committee specified by the Board, including the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors, review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance, examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report, approval of related party transactions, scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, valuation of undertakings or assets, evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers — and Section 177(5), read with Section 177(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 148 — cost records and cost audit
