concepts.subsection: Section 72A — Carry forward of losses in amalgamation
concepts.statement: Section 72A lets the accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation of an amalgamating company be treated as the amalgamated company's own loss and depreciation for the year of amalgamation, opening a fresh period of carry forward — but only where the amalgamating company is an industrial undertaking, a ship, a hotel, a banking company, or another class the section names, and specified continuity conditions on the business and its fixed assets are met before and after the amalgamation. Failing those conditions after the set-off has been claimed reverses it: the set-off amount becomes the amalgamated company's taxable income in the year the conditions fail.

citation.ref: Section 72A

concepts.subsection: Section 92E — Transfer pricing accountant's report
concepts.statement: Every person who has entered into an international transaction or a specified domestic transaction during the previous year must obtain a report from an accountant in the prescribed form, and furnish it on or before the specified date — the same extended due date section 139(1) gives a person required to furnish a transfer pricing report. The obligation attaches to the existence of the transaction itself, not to whether it actually shifted profit, and for an international transaction it carries no minimum value threshold.

citation.ref: Section 92E

concepts.subsection: Section 195 — TDS on payments to non-residents
concepts.statement: Section 195 requires tax deduction at source on any sum chargeable to tax under the Act paid or credited to a non-resident — chargeability itself is the trigger, not a named list of payments — at the time of credit or payment, whichever is earlier, at the rates in force under the Finance Act or the applicable DTAA, whichever is more beneficial to the payee. A payer unsure how much of a composite sum is chargeable may apply under section 195(2) for the Assessing Officer to determine the taxable proportion, while the recipient may separately seek a nil or lower deduction certificate under section 197.

citation.ref: Section 195 (with Sections 195(2) and 197)

concepts.subsection: Section 253 — Appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal
concepts.statement: An assessee aggrieved by an order of the Commissioner (Appeals), among other specified orders, may appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal; the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may likewise direct an appeal against such an order. Once an appeal is filed, the other side may file a memorandum of cross-objections without needing to file a separate appeal of its own. The Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority in the appeal hierarchy — a further appeal to the High Court under section 260A lies only on a substantial question of law, not a fresh look at facts the Tribunal has settled.

citation.ref: Sections 253 and 260A

concepts.subsection: Section 92BA — Specified domestic transaction
concepts.statement: A specified domestic transaction is a transaction between related domestic parties that the transfer pricing machinery reaches even though no foreign party is involved — but only where the aggregate of all such transactions in the previous year exceeds twenty crore rupees. What remains inside the definition are transactions of an undertaking claiming a profit-linked deduction, such as inter-unit transfers to which section 80-IA(8) or 80-IA(10) applies, and similar transactions under section 10AA. Payments to related persons covered by section 40A(2)(b) were dropped from the definition when clause (i) of section 92BA was omitted with effect from 1 April 2017, so those payments are tested for reasonableness under section 40A(2) alone and never counted towards the twenty crore aggregate.

citation.ref: Section 92BA (clause (i) omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2017) read with Section 80-IA(8) and (10)

concepts.subsection: Sections 92CA and 92C(4) — Reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer
concepts.statement: The Assessing Officer may, with the approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, refer the computation of the arm's length price to a Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA; the TPO's order determining the arm's length price binds the Assessing Officer, who then computes total income in conformity with it. Where the arm's length price so determined increases the assessee's income, the proviso to section 92C(4) denies any deduction under section 10AA or under Chapter VI-A on the amount of that enhancement — a tax-holiday unit therefore gains nothing by understating its transfer price, because the adjustment lands as fully taxable income.

citation.ref: Section 92CA read with the proviso to Section 92C(4)

concepts.subsection: Sections 92CC and 92CD — Advance pricing agreement
concepts.statement: An advance pricing agreement fixes the arm's length price, or the manner of determining it, in advance for an international transaction, and binds both the assessee and the tax authorities for the previous years the agreement covers — not exceeding five consecutive previous years. A rollback may be sought so that the same agreed position applies to as many as four previous years preceding the first year of the agreement, and the applicant must seek the rollback for every one of those years in which the transaction was undertaken; picking only the favourable years is not open to it. Section 92CD then requires a modified return within three months of the month in which the agreement is entered into, for each earlier year the agreement covers.

citation.ref: Sections 92CC and 92CD read with Rules 10MA and 10RA

concepts.subsection: Sections 115JC and 115JD — Alternate minimum tax
concepts.statement: Alternate minimum tax applies to a person other than a company that has claimed a deduction under Chapter VI-A heading "C" (deductions in respect of certain incomes, such as section 80-IA), or under section 10AA, or under section 35AD. It is charged on adjusted total income, which is total income with those deductions added back. The twenty lakh rupee floor in section 115JC(4) is not a general exemption: it protects only an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons, a body of individuals or an artificial juridical person. A firm or a limited liability partnership gets no such floor and is inside the AMT net whatever its adjusted total income. Tax paid in excess of the regular liability becomes AMT credit under section 115JD, carried forward for fifteen assessment years and set off only in a year when regular tax exceeds AMT; no interest is payable on the credit.

citation.ref: Sections 115JC(1), 115JC(2), 115JC(4) and 115JD

concepts.subsection: Section 2(19AA) — Demerger
concepts.statement: A transfer of an undertaking is a demerger for tax purposes only if it satisfies every condition in section 2(19AA) together. Two do most of the work in an examination. First, all the property and all the liabilities of the undertaking must be transferred at values appearing in the books of account immediately before the demerger — any increase on revaluation is ignored, so recording the assets in the resulting company at fair value breaks the definition. Second, shareholders holding not less than three-fourths in value of the shares of the demerged company must become shareholders of the resulting company. Fail any condition and the transaction is not a demerger at all, which means the exemptions in section 47 and the loss carry-forward in section 72A(4) are simply unavailable.

citation.ref: Section 2(19AA) read with Sections 47(vib), 47(vid) and 72A(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 12AB — Registration of a charitable trust and its validity
concepts.statement: Registration under section 12AB is never permanent, unlike the old section 12AA registration it replaced. Provisional registration runs for three years. On renewal, the period depends on the size of the trust: ten years where the trust's total income, computed without giving effect to sections 11 and 12, did not exceed five crore rupees in each of the two previous years immediately preceding the previous year in which the application is made, and five years otherwise. The ten-year period comes from the proviso to section 12AB(1), inserted with effect from 1 April 2025. In every case the trust must apply for renewal at least six months before the registration expires, and the registration lapses if it does not.

citation.ref: Section 12AB(1) with its proviso (inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2025), read with Section 12A(1)(ac)

concepts.subsection: Section 115TD — Tax on accreted income of a trust
concepts.statement: Section 115TD is an exit charge on a registered trust or institution that leaves the charitable régime — where its registration is cancelled, where it converts into a form not eligible for registration, where it merges with an entity not having similar objects and registration, or where on dissolution it fails to transfer its assets to another registered trust within twelve months. Accreted income is the fair market value of the total assets on the specified date reduced by the liabilities on that date, and it bears additional income-tax at the maximum marginal rate. The charge is on accreted net worth, not on income, so it is payable whether or not the trust earned anything that year, and it is in addition to any income-tax otherwise payable.

citation.ref: Sections 115TD(1), 115TD(2) and 115TD(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 206C(1H) omitted — TCS on sale of goods and its overlap with Section 194Q
concepts.statement: Section 206C(1H), which made a seller with turnover above ten crore rupees collect tax at source on sale consideration beyond fifty lakh rupees from a buyer, stands omitted with effect from 1 April 2025. For previous year 2025-26 it does not operate at all, and the old tie-break rule — where both provisions applied to one transaction, section 194Q prevailed and the seller was relieved — has nothing left to resolve. What survives is section 194Q: a buyer whose total sales, turnover or gross receipts exceeded ten crore rupees in the immediately preceding financial year deducts tax at 0.1 per cent on the value of goods purchased from a resident seller in excess of fifty lakh rupees in the year. The obligation now sits on the buyer alone.

citation.ref: Section 206C(1H) (omitted w.e.f. 1-4-2025) read with Section 194Q

concepts.subsection: Sections 201(1) and 201(1A) — Assessee in default for a TDS failure
concepts.statement: A payer who fails to deduct tax at source is deemed an assessee in default under section 201(1) and can be recovered from as though the tax were his own. The first proviso rescues him where the resident payee has furnished a return under section 139, has taken the sum into account in computing income in that return, has paid the tax due on the income declared, and the payer furnishes an accountant's certificate in the prescribed form. That relief is from the tax alone. Interest under section 201(1A) still runs at one per cent for every month or part of a month from the date on which the tax was deductible to the date on which the payee furnished his return of income — the compensation for the delay survives the payee's compliance.

citation.ref: Section 201(1) with its first proviso, and Section 201(1A)

concepts.subsection: Section 149 — Time limit for a notice of reassessment
concepts.statement: For a notice under section 148 issued on or after 1 September 2024, section 149 allows three years and three months from the end of the relevant assessment year in the ordinary case. That stretches to five years and three months, but only where the Assessing Officer has books, documents or evidence revealing that income chargeable to tax which has escaped assessment amounts to, or is likely to amount to, fifty lakh rupees or more for that year. The extended limb is not confined to search cases, and the ten-year outer limit that existed before this amendment is gone. The period runs from the end of the assessment year, never from the end of the financial year in which the income was earned.

citation.ref: Section 149(1) as substituted with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Section 148A

concepts.subsection: Section 144C — Draft order and the Dispute Resolution Panel
concepts.statement: Where the Assessing Officer proposes a variation prejudicial to an eligible assessee — a person in whose case a transfer pricing adjustment has been made under section 92CA(3), or a non-resident, or a foreign company — he must first forward a draft of the proposed assessment order. The assessee then has thirty days from receipt of the draft order to either accept the variation or file objections with the Dispute Resolution Panel and the Assessing Officer. Miss those thirty days and the Assessing Officer may complete the assessment on the basis of the draft. Where objections are filed, the Panel's directions bind the Assessing Officer and must issue within nine months from the end of the month in which the draft order was forwarded.

concepts.subsection: Equalisation levy — both levies withdrawn
concepts.statement: Neither equalisation levy operates in previous year 2025-26. The two per cent levy on the consideration of an e-commerce operator for e-commerce supply or services ceased to apply to consideration received or receivable on or after 1 August 2024, and the six per cent levy on consideration for online advertisement and related services ceased on or after 1 April 2025. The exemption in section 10(50), which kept income already bearing the levy outside the Income-tax Act, falls away with the levy it was tied to. The consequence is that these payments are now tested for chargeability in the ordinary way — under section 9 for a business connection or significant economic presence, under section 195 for withholding, and against the applicable double taxation avoidance agreement.

citation.ref: Chapter VIII, Sections 165 and 165A of the Finance Act, 2016 (levies withdrawn w.e.f. 1-8-2024 and 1-4-2025), read with Section 10(50) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Section 9(1)(vii) — Fees for technical services deemed to accrue in India
concepts.statement: Fees for technical services payable by a resident are deemed to accrue or arise in India under section 9(1)(vii), except where the services are utilised for a business carried on outside India or for earning income from a source outside India. The Explanation to section 9(2) settles the argument that once succeeded before the courts: such income is deemed to accrue in India whether or not the non-resident has a residence, a place of business or a business connection in India, and whether or not the services were rendered in India. Physical presence is therefore irrelevant to the source rule. What is not irrelevant is the treaty — section 90(2) lets the non-resident take the double taxation avoidance agreement where it is more beneficial, and many treaties tax fees for technical services only if the services make available technical knowledge or skill to the recipient.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(vii) with the Explanation to Section 9(2), read with Section 90(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 44B — Presumptive profits of a non-resident shipping business
concepts.statement: For a non-resident carrying on the business of operating ships, other than cruise shipping, section 44B deems seven and a half per cent of a specified aggregate to be the profits chargeable under the head profits and gains of business or profession. The aggregate has two limbs. The first takes the amount paid or payable, whether in India or outside India, for the carriage of passengers, livestock, mail or goods shipped at any port in India — so a freight collected abroad still counts if the cargo loaded in India. The second takes the amount received or deemed to be received in India for carriage from a port outside India. Compare the neighbouring presumptive rates before answering: section 44BB, for services connected with the extraction of mineral oils, deems ten per cent, and section 44BBA, for the operation of aircraft, deems five per cent.

citation.ref: Section 44B(1) and (2), read with Sections 44BB and 44BBA

concepts.subsection: Section 194A — TDS on interest and the thresholds from 1 April 2025
concepts.statement: Section 194A requires tax at ten per cent to be deducted from interest other than interest on securities paid to a resident, and the threshold below which nothing is deducted was raised on 1 April 2025. Where the payer is a banking company, a co-operative society engaged in the business of banking or a post office, the threshold is one lakh rupees for a resident senior citizen and fifty thousand rupees for anyone else. In any other case — a company, a firm or a non-banking finance company paying interest on a loan or a deposit — the threshold is ten thousand rupees. Two traps sit in the section. The threshold is tested on the aggregate for the financial year, not on each payment, and once it is crossed the deduction is on the whole sum and not merely on the excess over the threshold.

citation.ref: Section 194A(1) and Section 194A(3)(i) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194-I — TDS on rent and the threshold from 1 April 2025
concepts.statement: Section 194-I makes a payer other than an individual or Hindu undivided family not liable to tax audit deduct tax from rent paid to a resident, at two per cent where the rent is for the use of plant, machinery or equipment and at ten per cent where it is for the use of land, a building, furniture or fittings. From 1 April 2025 the threshold is fifty thousand rupees for a month or part of a month, replacing the old figure of two lakh forty thousand rupees for the financial year; on an even rent that works out at six lakh rupees for the year. The two rates are the examinable half of the section, because the equipment limb is often given the ten per cent rate by reflex. As everywhere in Chapter XVII-B, once the threshold is crossed the deduction is on the whole rent and not on the excess.

citation.ref: Section 194-I(a) and (b) with its second proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194J — TDS on professional and technical fees and the category-wise threshold
concepts.statement: Section 194J covers four different payments to a resident — fees for professional services, fees for technical services, royalty, and a sum for not carrying out any activity or not sharing any know-how. The rate is ten per cent, except that it is two per cent for fees for technical services other than professional services, for royalty in the nature of consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films, and for a payee engaged only in the business of operating a call centre. From 1 April 2025 the threshold is fifty thousand rupees, raised from thirty thousand rupees, and the proviso applies that figure separately to each of the four categories rather than to their aggregate. A payee can therefore take forty-nine thousand rupees of professional fees and forty-nine thousand rupees of technical fees from the same payer in a year with nothing deducted from either.

citation.ref: Section 194J(1) with its first proviso, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 194H — TDS on commission or brokerage after the rate and threshold changes
concepts.statement: Section 194H requires deduction from commission or brokerage paid to a resident, and both its numbers moved recently. The rate fell from five per cent to two per cent for sums credited or paid on or after 1 October 2024, and the threshold rose from fifteen thousand rupees to twenty thousand rupees on 1 April 2025. The threshold is on the aggregate credited or paid during the financial year, so a series of small payments that individually fall below it still triggers deduction once they add up past twenty thousand rupees, and the deduction is then on the whole aggregate including the earlier payments from which nothing was taken. Insurance commission is outside this section and falls under section 194D.

citation.ref: Section 194H with its first proviso, rate amended with effect from 1 October 2024 and threshold with effect from 1 April 2025

concepts.subsection: Section 206C(1G) — TCS on remittance under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme
concepts.statement: An authorised dealer remitting money abroad under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme collects tax at source under section 206C(1G). From 1 April 2025 the threshold is ten lakh rupees, raised from seven lakh rupees, and the collection is on the amount in excess of that figure and not on the whole remittance — which makes this section behave differently from the deduction provisions in Chapter XVII-B. The rate is five per cent on the excess where the remittance is for education or for medical treatment and twenty per cent on the excess for any other purpose. Also from 1 April 2025, where the remittance for education is made out of a loan obtained from a financial institution as defined in section 80E(3)(b), no tax is collected at all, whatever the amount.

citation.ref: Section 206C(1G) with its provisos, as amended with effect from 1 April 2025, read with Section 80E(3)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 286 and Rule 10DA — Country-by-Country report and the master file
concepts.statement: Two separate documentation duties sit on an Indian member of a multinational group and they have different triggers. The master file under Rule 10DA is required where the consolidated group revenue of the international group for the preceding accounting year exceeds five hundred crore rupees and, in addition, either the aggregate value of the entity's international transactions exceeds fifty crore rupees or its international transactions in intangible property exceed ten crore rupees; it is furnished in Form 3CEAA, and Form 3CEAB designates which of several Indian entities will file. The Country-by-Country report under section 286 is required only where the consolidated group revenue exceeds six thousand four hundred crore rupees, the figure aligned with the OECD's 750 million euro standard; it is filed in Form 3CEAD by the parent entity or the alternate reporting entity, with the intimation in Form 3CEAC. A group can therefore owe a master file and owe no Country-by-Country report at all.

citation.ref: Rule 10DA and Rule 10DB read with Section 286 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, and Notification No. 31/2021

concepts.subsection: Rule 128 — Foreign tax credit and Form 67
concepts.statement: A resident who has paid tax in a foreign country on income also taxed in India takes credit under Rule 128. Two limits define the credit. It is available against tax, surcharge and cess payable under the Income-tax Act, 1961 and never against interest, fee or penalty; and it cannot exceed the amount of tax arrived at by applying the Indian rate of tax to that same doubly taxed income, so where the foreign rate is the higher one the excess is simply lost, being neither refunded nor carried forward. The procedure changed in 2022: the statement in Form 67 may now be furnished at any time on or before the end of the relevant assessment year, where it previously had to accompany a return filed by the due date under section 139(1).

citation.ref: Rule 128(1), 128(2) and 128(9) as amended by Notification No. 100/2022, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Sections 115A and 44DA — Royalty and fees for technical services of a non-resident
concepts.statement: Whether a non-resident's royalty or fees for technical services is taxed gross or net turns on one fact: whether the right, property or contract is effectively connected with a permanent establishment or fixed place of profession in India. Where it is not, section 115A charges the gross amount at twenty per cent — raised from ten per cent with effect from assessment year 2024-25 — with no deduction for any expenditure and no allowance under sections 28 to 44C. Where it is, section 115A steps aside and section 44DA taxes the income as business profits on a net basis at the ordinary rate, which for a foreign company is thirty-five per cent from assessment year 2025-26; the non-resident must then keep books under section 44AA and furnish an audit report in Form 3CE, and section 44DA disallows head-office reimbursements and any expenditure not wholly and exclusively for the permanent establishment. Section 90(2) still lets the non-resident take a lower treaty rate.

citation.ref: Section 115A(1)(b) and Section 44DA(1) with its provisos, read with Section 90(2) and Rule 6GA (Form 3CE)

concepts.subsection: Article 4(2) of a treaty — Tie-breaker for a dual resident individual
concepts.statement: An individual can be a resident of India under section 6 and a resident of the other country under its own law at the same time. Section 90(2) then lets him take the treaty, and Article 4(2) breaks the tie by a strict order that must be worked in sequence and abandoned the moment one test decides. He is treated as a resident of the state in which he has a permanent home available to him; if a permanent home is available in both, of the state with which his personal and economic relations are closer, that is his centre of vital interests; if that cannot be determined, of the state in which he has an habitual abode; if he has an habitual abode in both or in neither, of the state of which he is a national; and if he is a national of both or of neither, the two competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement. Winning the tie-breaker does not change his residential status under section 6 for the Act's own purposes; it decides which state may tax what under the treaty.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital
citation.ref: Article 4(2), as adopted in India's double taxation avoidance agreements, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Sections 158B and 113 — Block assessment in search cases
concepts.statement: Block assessment came back with the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 and applies where a search under section 132 is initiated, or a requisition under section 132A is made, on or after 1 September 2024. Section 158B(b) defines the block period in these words — the period comprising previous years relevant to six assessment years preceding the previous year in which the search was initiated or the requisition was made, and also including the period starting from the first day of April of the previous year in which the search was initiated or the requisition was made and ending on the date of execution of the last of the authorisations. All of it is assessed as one under section 158BC rather than year by year, and any assessment for a year inside the block period that is pending on the date of the search abates under section 158BA. Section 113 then charges the total undisclosed income of the block period at a flat sixty per cent, whatever the status of the assessee, increased by the surcharge levied by the Central Act applicable in the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the search was initiated, and by cess.

citation.ref: Sections 158B(b), 158BA and 158BC read with Section 113, as inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024

concepts.subsection: Sections 143(2) and 153(1) — Time limits for the scrutiny notice and the assessment order
concepts.statement: Two different clocks govern a scrutiny assessment and they start from different events. The notice under section 143(2) must be served within three months from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished — a period cut from six months to three by the Finance Act, 2021 — so it runs from the end of that financial year and never from the date of filing. The order under section 143(3) or section 144 must then be passed within twelve months from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable, which is the limit for assessment year 2022-23 and every year after it. Where a reference is made to the Transfer Pricing Officer under section 92CA the twelve months is extended by a further twelve months.

citation.ref: Section 143(2) proviso as amended by the Finance Act, 2021, and Section 153(1) with Section 153(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 245MA — Dispute Resolution Committee and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022
concepts.statement: Section 245MA gives a small taxpayer a route that is neither an appeal nor a revision. The committee may be approached only against a specified order, defined in the Explanation to the section as one where the aggregate of the variations proposed or made does not exceed ten lakh rupees and the returned income for the relevant assessment year does not exceed fifty lakh rupees. Both tests must hold. An order founded on a search or survey, or on information received under an agreement referred to in section 90 or section 90A, is excluded whatever the figures. What the committee can do that an appellate authority cannot is grant a reduction or waiver of penalty and immunity from prosecution, under Rule 44DAC, and it must pass its order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is admitted.

citation.ref: Section 245MA with the Explanation defining a specified order, read with Rule 44DAC and the e-Dispute Resolution Scheme, 2022

concepts.subsection: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted — share premium of a closely held company
concepts.statement: Section 56(2)(viib), the provision known as angel tax, charged a company in which the public are not substantially interested on the amount by which consideration received for shares exceeded their fair market value. It was omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from assessment year 2025-26, so for previous year 2025-26 no charge arises on share premium at all, and the extension of the charge to non-resident subscribers made only a year earlier goes with it. Two things survive the omission and are the examinable half of the topic. Section 68 still lets the Assessing Officer treat the share application money as an unexplained cash credit where the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of the subscriber are not established, and section 56(2)(x) still taxes a person who receives shares for less than their fair market value — a charge on the recipient, which section 56(2)(viib) never was.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(viib) omitted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 April 2025 (A.Y. 2025-26), read with Sections 68 and 56(2)(x)

concepts.subsection: Section 115BBI — Tax on the specified income of a trust
concepts.statement: Section 115BBI charges specified income of a registered trust or institution at a flat thirty per cent, plus surcharge and cess. Specified income is defined by the section and includes income accumulated or set apart in excess of fifteen per cent where it is not applied as required, income deemed under section 11(1B) or 11(3), income applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of a person referred to in section 13(3), income not invested in a mode specified in section 11(5), and income applied outside India without approval. Sub-section (2) is where the marks sit: no deduction is allowed for any expenditure, allowance or set-off of loss against specified income, so the charge falls on the gross figure. Only the specified income is taken out; the rest of the trust's income continues to be governed by sections 11 to 13 in the ordinary way.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBI(1) and 115BBI(2) with the Explanation, read with Sections 11(5) and 13(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 32(2) — Unabsorbed depreciation and the order of set-off
concepts.statement: Unabsorbed depreciation is not a loss and is not governed by the rules that govern one. Section 32(2) deems it to be part of the depreciation allowance of the following year, which gives it three privileges a business loss does not have: it may be set off against income under any head except salaries, it is carried forward indefinitely with no eight-year limit, and it survives even where the return was not filed within the time allowed by section 139(1), because section 80 does not reach it. Nor does it need the same business to continue. The price of those privileges is that it goes last. The settled order of set-off is current year depreciation first, then brought forward business loss under section 72, and only then brought forward unabsorbed depreciation — which matters, because a business loss can only meet business income and would otherwise be stranded.

citation.ref: Section 32(2) read with Sections 72(2), 72(3) and 80

concepts.subsection: Section 14A and Rule 8D — Disallowance of expenditure relating to exempt income
concepts.statement: Section 14A disallows expenditure incurred in relation to income that does not form part of total income. The Finance Act, 2022 settled the long-running argument by inserting a non-obstante clause and an Explanation saying that the section applies, and the disallowance is made, whether or not such exempt income has accrued or arisen or been received during the previous year — so a year with no dividend is no defence. Where the Assessing Officer is not satisfied with the assessee's own working, Rule 8D fixes the amount as the sum of the expenditure directly relating to the exempt income and one per cent of the annual average of the monthly averages of the opening and closing balances of the investments the income from which does not or shall not form part of total income. The rule carries its own ceiling: the total disallowed can never exceed the total expenditure claimed by the assessee.

citation.ref: Section 14A(1) with its Explanation inserted by the Finance Act, 2022, read with Rule 8D(2) and 8D(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.subsection: Section 45(2) — Conversion of a capital asset into stock-in-trade
concepts.statement: Turning a capital asset into stock-in-trade of one's own business is a transfer, but section 45(2) postpones the tax. The capital gain is chargeable in the previous year in which the stock is actually sold, not in the year of conversion, and the fair market value of the asset on the date of conversion is deemed to be the full value of the consideration for computing it. Indexation, where it is available at all, runs only to the year of conversion, because that is when the asset stopped being a capital asset. The surplus above that fair market value is business income of the year of sale. One transaction therefore produces two heads of income in the same year, split at the conversion-date value, and the holding period for deciding long or short-term is measured to the date of conversion and not to the date of sale.

citation.ref: Section 45(2) read with Section 2(47)(iv) and Section 48

concepts.subsection: Section 51 and Section 56(2)(ix) — Advance money received and forfeited
concepts.statement: An advance taken on a negotiation for the transfer of a capital asset and then forfeited is dealt with by two provisions divided by one date. Where the sum was received on or after 1 April 2014, section 56(2)(ix) charges it as income from other sources in the previous year of forfeiture, and the proviso to section 51 then stops it being deducted from the cost of acquisition, so it is taxed once and only once. Where the sum was received before that date, section 51 alone applies and the amount is not taxed at the time; it is deducted from the cost of acquisition when the asset is eventually sold. Two conditions run through both limbs. The negotiation must have failed, so an advance that becomes part of the price is not touched, and the charge falls on the owner who kept the asset, there being no transfer at the moment of forfeiture.

citation.ref: Section 56(2)(ix) inserted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 with effect from assessment year 2015-16, read with Section 51 and its proviso

concepts.subsection: Section 55A — Reference to a Valuation Officer
concepts.statement: Section 55A lets the Assessing Officer send a valuation to a Valuation Officer for the purposes of the capital gains Chapter, and the section has two clauses that are easy to mix up. Clause (a) applies where the value the assessee claims is in accordance with the estimate of a registered valuer, and the Assessing Officer is of opinion that it is at variance with its fair market value. Those last words replaced the words "is less than the fair market value" with effect from 1 July 2012, and that change is the whole point of the section now — before it, an inflated valuation could not be referred at all, and after it the variance may run in either direction. Clause (b) covers a case not supported by a registered valuer's report, and it is still one-directional: it needs the Assessing Officer to be of opinion that fair market value exceeds the value claimed by more than the prescribed margin, or that the nature of the asset makes a reference necessary. The section reaches a cost of acquisition as much as a sale consideration, which is why it is most often seen on a fair market value adopted as on 1 April 2001.

citation.ref: Section 55A(a) as amended by the Finance Act, 2012 with effect from 1 July 2012, and Section 55A(b) read with Rule 111AA of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

concepts.subsection: Section 115BAC(1A) — The default personal regime for assessment year 2026-27
concepts.statement: Section 115BAC(1A) is the default for an individual, a Hindu undivided family, an association of persons other than a co-operative society, a body of individuals and an artificial juridical person, and a taxpayer now has to act to leave it rather than to enter it. For assessment year 2026-27 the slabs run nil up to four lakh rupees, five per cent to eight lakh, ten per cent to twelve lakh, fifteen per cent to sixteen lakh, twenty per cent to twenty lakh, twenty-five per cent to twenty-four lakh and thirty per cent above that. A resident individual gets a rebate under section 87A of sixty thousand rupees where total income does not exceed twelve lakh rupees, with marginal relief just above that figure, and a salaried person gets the standard deduction of seventy-five thousand rupees under section 16(ia). The rebate is tested on total income after that deduction, not on gross salary. Almost every Chapter VI-A deduction is off, the survivors being section 80CCD(2), section 80CCH(2) and section 80JJAA. A person with no business income may opt out and back every year in the return; a person with business income opts out once in Form 10-IEA and may return to the default only once, and never leave again.

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(1A) and Section 87A as amended by the Finance Act, 2025 for assessment year 2026-27, read with Sections 16(ia) and 115BAC(6)

concepts.subsection: Sections 23 and 24 — Annual value, municipal taxes and the two deductions
concepts.statement: House property income is built in a fixed order and each step has a trap. Gross annual value under section 23(1) is the higher of the expected rent and the actual rent received or receivable, the expected rent itself being the higher of municipal value and fair rent but capped at standard rent where rent control applies. Municipal taxes come off next, and the first proviso to section 23 allows only the taxes borne by the owner and actually paid during the previous year — taxes charged but unpaid at the year end are not deductible, and taxes for an earlier year paid this year are. What is left is net annual value. Section 24 then gives exactly two deductions and no others. Clause (a) is thirty per cent of net annual value, a flat allowance that has nothing to do with what was actually spent on repairs, insurance or collection; clause (b) is interest on borrowed capital, allowed on an accrual basis, with interest for the period before the year of completion allowed in five equal annual instalments beginning with the year the construction was completed.

citation.ref: Section 23(1) with its first proviso, and Section 24(a) and 24(b) with its Explanation

concepts.subsection: Section 41(1) — Remission or cessation of a trading liability
concepts.statement: Section 41(1) is the mirror of a deduction already taken. Where an allowance or deduction has been made in any assessment year in respect of loss, expenditure or a trading liability, and the assessee later obtains any amount in respect of it or any benefit by way of remission or cessation of it, the value of that benefit is deemed to be profits and gains of business of the previous year in which it is obtained. Two words carry the section. It charges the year of remission, not the year in which the deduction was allowed, so nothing is reopened; and it applies whether or not the business to which the liability related is still in existence in that year. Explanation 1 catches a unilateral write-back in the assessee's own books. What the section cannot reach is a liability for which no deduction was ever allowed, which is why the waiver of a loan taken to buy a capital asset falls outside both section 41(1) and section 28(iv) — the borrowing was never claimed as an expense.

citation.ref: Section 41(1) with Explanation 1, read with Commissioner of Income Tax v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd (2018) 404 ITR 1 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Section 36(1)(iii) — Interest on borrowed capital and the put-to-use proviso
concepts.statement: Interest on capital borrowed for the purposes of the business is deductible under section 36(1)(iii), and the proviso carves one slice out of it. Interest for any period beginning from the date on which the capital was borrowed for acquisition of an asset and ending on the date on which such asset was first put to use is not allowed as a deduction; Explanation 8 to section 43(1) adds it to the actual cost instead, where it is recovered through depreciation. Two dates decide the split and neither of them is the obvious one. The clock stops on the date the asset is first put to use, not the date it was delivered or capitalised in the books, and it does not run to the end of the previous year. The words "for extension of existing business or profession" were omitted with effect from assessment year 2016-17, so the proviso now bites on any asset acquired out of borrowed money, whether the business is being extended or merely re-equipped.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(iii) with its proviso as amended by the Finance Act, 2015 with effect from assessment year 2016-17, read with Explanation 8 to Section 43(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 80JJAA — Deduction for the cost of additional employees
concepts.statement: Section 80JJAA gives an assessee whose accounts are audited under section 44AB a deduction of thirty per cent of additional employee cost, for three assessment years beginning with the year in which the employment is provided, on a report in Form 10DA furnished by the due date under section 139(1). The definition of an additional employee is where the marks are, because it excludes four kinds of person. One whose total emoluments exceed twenty-five thousand rupees a month is out. One employed for fewer than two hundred and forty days in the previous year is out, and the relaxed figure of a hundred and fifty days applies only to a business manufacturing apparel, footwear or leather products. One who does not participate in a recognised provident fund is out. So is one whose entire contribution is paid by the Government under the Employees' Pension Scheme. Emoluments paid otherwise than by account payee cheque, draft or electronic transfer do not count at all, and there must be a net increase in the total number of employees. The deduction survives inside sections 115BAA, 115BAB and 115BAC, which is unusual for Chapter VI-A.

citation.ref: Section 80JJAA(1) and (2) with Explanation, read with Rule 19AB (Form 10DA) and Sections 115BAA(2), 115BAB(2) and 115BAC(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 80M — Deduction for dividend passed on by a domestic company
concepts.statement: Once dividend became taxable in the shareholder's hands, the same money could be taxed at every layer of a group. Section 80M answers that, and it answers it only so far as the money is passed on. A domestic company that receives dividend from another domestic company, a foreign company or a business trust may deduct an amount equal to that dividend, but the deduction cannot exceed the dividend it itself distributes on or before one month prior to the due date for furnishing its return under section 139(1). Three limits follow. The deduction is capped by the dividend received, so distributing more than was received buys nothing extra; the cut-off is one month before the due date and not the due date itself; and the same received dividend cannot be used twice, the section allowing the deduction only in one assessment year.

citation.ref: Section 80M with its proviso, inserted by the Finance Act, 2020 with effect from assessment year 2021-22

concepts.subsection: Sections 115BBE and 271AAC — Tax and penalty on unexplained income
concepts.statement: Income assessed under section 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C or 69D is priced separately from everything else. Section 115BBE(1) charges it at sixty per cent, the Finance Act adds a flat surcharge of twenty-five per cent of that tax whatever the assessee's income, and cess rides on the total, so the effective burden is seventy-eight per cent. Section 115BBE(2) is the harder half — no deduction for any expenditure or allowance, and no set-off of any loss, is allowed against such income, and since assessment year 2017-18 that bar applies to a set-off as well as to a deduction. Section 271AAC then adds a penalty of ten per cent of the tax payable under section 115BBE(1)(i), which is ten per cent of the sixty per cent and not of the income. The penalty is not levied where the income was included in the return and the tax was paid on or before the end of the relevant previous year, and no penalty under section 270A may be imposed on the same income.

citation.ref: Sections 115BBE(1) and 115BBE(2), and Section 271AAC(1) with its proviso and 271AAC(2)

concepts.subsection: Sections 184 and 185 — What a firm loses when the deed is defective
concepts.statement: Section 184 sets three conditions for a firm to be assessed as a firm. The partnership must be evidenced by an instrument, the individual shares of the partners must be specified in that instrument, and a certified copy of it must accompany the return for the previous year in which the partnership was formed or the instrument was changed. Section 185 says what happens when a condition is not met, and it is not what most people expect. The firm continues to be assessed as a firm — its status does not change to an association of persons — but no deduction by way of interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration paid to any partner is allowed in computing its income. Section 40(b) never comes into the picture, because section 185 has already removed the whole claim before any limit could be applied to it. The proviso to section 28(v) then keeps the amount out of the partners' hands as well, so what the firm cannot deduct the partner is not taxed on.

citation.ref: Sections 184(1), 184(2) and 185, read with the proviso to Section 28(v) and Section 40(b)

concepts.subsection: Sections 60 and 61 — Transferring income without transferring the asset
concepts.statement: Two sections stop a taxpayer giving away the fruit while keeping the tree. Section 60 includes in the transferor's total income any income he has transferred without transferring the asset from which it arises, and it does this whether the transfer is revocable or not revocable and whether it was made before or after the Act came into force — an irrevocable deed is no answer to section 60 at all. Section 61 reaches the other case, where the asset itself is transferred but the transfer is revocable; the income is then the transferor's. Section 63 defines revocable widely enough to catch any arrangement giving the transferor a right to reassume power over the income or the asset, directly or indirectly. Section 62 is the only real relief, and it is narrow: a transfer by way of trust not revocable during the lifetime of the beneficiary, or any transfer not revocable during the lifetime of the transferee, escapes section 61 until the power to revoke actually arises. A right to take the asset back after a fixed number of years is not that, so section 61 applies from the first year.

citation.ref: Sections 60, 61, 62(1) and 63

concepts.subsection: Sections 234A and 234B — Interest for a late return and for short advance tax
concepts.statement: Both sections charge one per cent for every month or part of a month, and each answers a different failure on a different base. Section 234A runs from the day after the due date under section 139(1) to the date the return is actually furnished, on the tax on total income as reduced by advance tax, tax deducted or collected at source, relief and credits — so a return filed fifteen days late costs a full month. Section 234B is not about the return at all. It applies where the assessee has paid no advance tax, or has paid less than ninety per cent of the assessed tax, and it runs from 1 April of the assessment year to the date of the assessment, on the shortfall between assessed tax and advance tax paid — never on the whole assessed tax. Assessed tax means the tax on total income reduced by tax deducted or collected at source and by the reliefs and credits, which is why a taxpayer whose income is largely covered by deduction at source rarely faces section 234B at all.

citation.ref: Section 234A(1) and Section 234B(1) with Explanation 1

concepts.subsection: Section 244A — Interest on a refund
concepts.statement: Where a refund becomes due, section 244A pays interest at half a per cent for every month or part of a month — half the rate the taxpayer pays the department under sections 234A and 234B. The period is where the section is examined. For a refund out of tax deducted or collected at source or advance tax, interest runs from 1 April of the assessment year only if the return was furnished on or before the due date under section 139(1); where the return is late, it runs from the date the return was furnished, and the months before that are simply lost. For a refund out of self-assessment tax, clause (aa) starts the clock on the date of furnishing the return or of payment of the tax, whichever is later. Section 244A(2) then excludes any period of delay attributable to the assessee, decided by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner whose decision is final. No interest is payable at all where the refund is less than ten per cent of the tax determined.

citation.ref: Section 244A(1)(a) with its proviso, Section 244A(1)(aa) and Section 244A(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 270AA — Immunity from penalty and prosecution
concepts.statement: Section 270AA lets an assessee buy peace after an assessment, and the price is that he gives up the appeal. He must pay the tax and interest in the notice of demand within the time specified there, and he must not file an appeal against the assessment order; he then applies in Form 68 within one month from the end of the month in which the order was received — the clock runs from the end of the month, not from the date of the order. The Assessing Officer shall grant immunity from the penalty under section 270A and from prosecution under section 276C or section 276CC where those two conditions are satisfied, but only where the penalty proceedings are for under-reporting; sub-section (3) expressly withholds immunity where the case is one of misreporting under section 270A(9). The order accepting or rejecting is to be passed within one month from the end of the month in which the application is received, no rejection may be made without hearing the assessee, and that order is final — neither an appeal under section 246A nor a revision under section 264 lies against it.

citation.ref: Sections 270AA(1) to 270AA(6), read with Section 270A(9) and Rule 129 (Form 68)

concepts.subsection: Sections 269SS, 269T and 269ST — Three cash limits and three penalties
concepts.statement: Three sections restrict cash and each carries its own limit and its own penalty. Section 269SS forbids taking or accepting a loan, deposit or specified sum of twenty thousand rupees or more otherwise than by account payee cheque, account payee draft or an electronic mode, and section 271D prices a breach at a penalty equal to the amount taken. Section 269T mirrors it on repayment, with section 271E charging a penalty equal to the amount repaid, so one loan taken and repaid in cash is penalised twice over. Section 269ST is wider and newer: no person shall receive two lakh rupees or more in cash from a person in a day, or in respect of a single transaction, or in respect of transactions relating to one event or occasion, and section 271DA charges a penalty equal to the amount received. The three limbs of section 269ST are alternatives, so breaking a single bill into daily instalments below two lakh rupees defeats nothing. Every one of these penalties is imposed by the Joint Commissioner, and section 273B saves an assessee who proves reasonable cause.

citation.ref: Sections 269SS, 269T and 269ST with their provisos, read with Sections 271D, 271E, 271DA and 273B

concepts.subsection: Section 276CC — Prosecution for wilful failure to furnish a return
concepts.statement: Section 276CC punishes a wilful failure to furnish a return in due time under section 139(1), or in response to a notice under section 142(1)(i), section 148 or section 153A. Where the amount of tax sought to be evaded exceeds twenty-five lakh rupees the sentence is rigorous imprisonment for six months to seven years with fine, and in any other case three months to two years with fine. The proviso is what actually decides most questions, and it bars prosecution altogether for a section 139(1) failure in two situations — where the return is furnished before the end of the relevant assessment year, whatever the tax involved, or where the tax payable on the total income determined on regular assessment, as reduced by advance tax and tax deducted or collected at source, does not exceed ten thousand rupees. Where the proviso does not save him, section 278E leaves the accused very little room: the court shall presume the existence of a culpable mental state, and he must prove its absence beyond reasonable doubt, not merely on a preponderance of probability.

citation.ref: Section 276CC with its proviso, read with Section 278E

concepts.subsection: Section 197 and Section 197A — Lower deduction certificate and the self-declaration
concepts.statement: There are two ways out of deduction at source and they are not interchangeable. Section 197 is the general route: the payee applies in Form 13, and where the Assessing Officer is satisfied that the recipient's total income justifies it he issues a certificate for deduction at a lower rate or for no deduction, for the sections section 197 names — which include sections 192, 193, 194A, 194C, 194H, 194-I, 194J, 194Q and 195. Rule 28AA fixes the rate on the existing and estimated liability, taking the average rate of tax of the last three previous years and the tax payable on the estimated income of the current year. The certificate is issued to the named deductor, is valid for the assessment year stated in it, and operates from the date it is issued — it never reaches back over deductions already made, which the payee recovers as a refund on his own return. Section 197A is the narrow route: a self-declaration in Form 15G, or Form 15H for a resident senior citizen, works only for the handful of sections that provision lists and only where the estimated total income is nil after rebate. Section 194C is not one of them.

citation.ref: Section 197(1) read with Rule 28AA and Rule 28 (Form 13), and Sections 197A(1A) and 197A(1C)

concepts.subsection: Section 5 — Scope of total income and the not-ordinarily-resident window
concepts.statement: Residential status decides nothing by itself; section 5 is what turns it into a tax bill. For a resident and ordinarily resident, total income takes in everything — income received or deemed to be received in India, income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India, and income accruing or arising outside India. For a non-resident, only the first two limbs apply. The resident but not ordinarily resident sits between them under the proviso to section 5(1), and the proviso adds exactly one thing to the non-resident's charge — income which accrues or arises outside India from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Two words in the section do most of the damage in an exam. Received means first received, so money that accrued abroad and was later remitted to India is not received in India; and Explanation 1 to section 5 says income once included on the basis of accrual is not included again when it is received.

citation.ref: Section 5(1) with its proviso and Section 5(2), read with Explanation 1 to Section 5

concepts.subsection: Section 9(1)(ii), (iii) and (v) — Where salary and interest are sourced
concepts.statement: Section 9 deems certain income to accrue in India, and each clause has its own connecting factor. Clause (ii) catches salary earned in India, the Explanation making the place where the services are rendered decisive, so the employer's residence and the place of payment are both beside the point. Clause (iii) is the narrow special case — salary payable by the Government to a citizen of India for service outside India is deemed to accrue here, though section 10(7) then exempts the allowances and perquisites paid outside India for rendering that service. Clause (v) sources interest by looking at who pays and what the money was used for. Interest payable by the Government is Indian-source. Interest payable by a resident is Indian-source unless the money was borrowed and used for a business or profession carried on outside India or for earning any income from a source outside India, and interest payable by a non-resident is Indian-source only where the money was borrowed and used for a business or profession carried on in India. The payer's residence therefore decides which limb applies, and the use of the money decides the answer inside it.

citation.ref: Section 9(1)(ii) with its Explanation, Section 9(1)(iii) and Section 9(1)(v)(a) to (c), read with Section 10(7)

concepts.subsection: Section 2(47) — What counts as a transfer
concepts.statement: Capital gains are charged on a transfer, and section 2(47) defines transfer inclusively so that it reaches a good deal more than a sale. It takes in sale, exchange and relinquishment of the asset, the extinguishment of any rights in it, its compulsory acquisition under any law, and its conversion into stock-in-trade. Clause (v) is the one that decides most questions — any transaction involving the allowing of the possession of immovable property to be taken or retained in part performance of a contract of the nature referred to in section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Once the contract is in writing and registered, the price is paid or the buyer is willing to perform, and possession has passed, the transfer has happened for tax, whatever the conveyance deed says or when it is executed. Clause (vi) adds the other route people use to avoid a deed — a transaction which has the effect of transferring or enabling the enjoyment of immovable property, including becoming a member of a co-operative society or entering into an arrangement of any other manner whatsoever. Legal ownership is simply not the test.

citation.ref: Section 2(47)(i) to (vi) read with Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882

concepts.subsection: Section 49(1) — Cost where the asset came without a purchase
concepts.statement: Where a capital asset came to the assessee on a total or partial partition of a Hindu undivided family, under a gift or will, by succession, inheritance or devolution, or on a distribution on the liquidation or dissolution of a company, firm or other body, section 49(1) deems the cost of acquisition to be the cost to the previous owner who last acquired it by a mode other than those listed, increased by the cost of any improvement. The section does not stop there. Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) makes the period for which the previous owner held the asset part of the assessee's holding period, and section 55(2)(b)(ii) lets the assessee substitute the fair market value as on 1 April 2001 where the previous owner acquired the asset before that date, capped by the stamp duty value on that date for land or a building. The value at which the asset came to the assessee — a probate valuation, a gift deed figure, an accounting entry — has no place in the computation at all.

citation.ref: Section 49(1) with Explanation, read with Section 55(2)(b)(ii) and Explanation 1(i)(b) to Section 2(42A)

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Capital gain on a block of depreciable assets
concepts.statement: Section 50 opens with the words "notwithstanding anything contained in clause (42A) of section 2", and that opening decides the whole section. Where a capital asset forms part of a block on which depreciation has been allowed, the gain is deemed to arise from the transfer of a short-term capital asset however long the asset was held, so no long-term rate and no section 54 style exemption keyed to a long-term gain is available. The computation under section 50(1) is a subtraction, not a matching of individual assets. Take the whole of the consideration for every asset of the block transferred during the year, and deduct three things — expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer, the written down value of the block at the beginning of the previous year, and the actual cost of any asset falling within the block acquired during the previous year. Any excess is the deemed short-term capital gain. Section 50(2) reaches the other case, where the block ceases to exist because every asset in it has gone. In either year no depreciation is allowed on that block, because there is nothing left on which to compute it.

citation.ref: Sections 50(1) and 50(2), read with Section 2(11) and Section 32(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 45(5) — Compensation on compulsory acquisition and the enhancement
concepts.statement: Compulsory acquisition breaks the ordinary rule that a capital gain is charged in the year of transfer, because the money often arrives years after the land goes. Section 45(5)(a) charges the gain on the compensation awarded in the first instance in the previous year in which that compensation, or any part of it, is first received — the year of the award and the year of the transfer are both irrelevant. Section 45(5)(b) then charges any amount by which a court, Tribunal or other authority enhances the compensation as a capital gain of the previous year in which that enhanced amount is received, so an enhancement decreed but unpaid is charged to nothing until it arrives. The Explanation to section 45(5) makes the cost of acquisition and the cost of improvement nil for the enhancement, since both were already used against the original award; expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with getting the enhancement remains deductible under section 48(i). Interest on compensation is a different animal altogether — section 56(2)(viii) puts it under income from other sources in the year of receipt, with a flat fifty per cent deduction under section 57(iv), and it never joins the capital gain.

citation.ref: Sections 45(5)(a) and 45(5)(b) with the Explanation, read with Section 48(i), Section 56(2)(viii) and Section 57(iv)

concepts.subsection: Section 28 — What the charge of business income actually covers
concepts.statement: Section 28 is the charging section, and most of its work is done by the clauses that follow the obvious first one. Clause (i) charges the profits of any business or profession carried on during the previous year. Clause (ii) charges compensation on the termination or modification of a managing agency or of any contract relating to the business. Clauses (iiia) to (iiie) charge export incentives — cash assistance against exports, duty drawback, the sale of an import licence and profit on the transfer of a duty entitlement — none of which are trading receipts in any commercial sense and all of which Parliament had to name. Clause (va) charges any sum received under an agreement for not carrying on any business or profession or for not sharing know-how, patent, copyright, trade mark or a similar commercial right, which reversed the older law that a non-compete receipt was a capital receipt. Its own proviso keeps out a sum received for the transfer of a right to manufacture or a sum chargeable under the head capital gains. Clause (vi) charges a sum received under a keyman insurance policy including the bonus, which is exactly what section 10(10D) carves out of its exemption.

citation.ref: Section 28(i), (ii), (iiia) to (iiie), (va) with its proviso and (vi), read with Section 10(10D) and Section 55(2)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 37(1) — The residuary deduction and the four gates
concepts.statement: Section 37(1) allows an expenditure only after it has passed four gates. It must not be described in sections 30 to 36, so a claim that belongs to one of those sections is judged there and cannot be rescued here. It must not be capital expenditure. It must not be personal expenditure of the assessee. And it must be laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business or profession. Three Explanations then close the obvious escapes. Explanation 1 denies any expenditure incurred for a purpose which is an offence or which is prohibited by law, which is why a penalty for breaking a statute is not deductible while a contractual damages payment for a commercial default is. Explanation 2 denies expenditure on corporate social responsibility referred to in section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013. Explanation 3 spells Explanation 1 out to include a benefit or perquisite given to any person where that person's acceptance of it violates a law, rule, regulation or guideline governing him. Section 37(2B) sits beside them and bars advertisement in a souvenir, brochure, tract or pamphlet published by a political party outright.

citation.ref: Section 37(1) with Explanations 1, 2 and 3, and Section 37(2B)

concepts.subsection: Sections 57 and 58 — What other sources allows and what it refuses
concepts.statement: Income from other sources is a real head with a real deduction section, not a bucket taxed gross. Section 57 names some deductions specifically — a collection commission on interest on securities or dividend under clause (i), the repairs, insurance and depreciation on plant or a building let out under clauses (ii) and (iii) where the letting is taxed here, and fifty per cent of interest on compensation under clause (iv) — and then clause (iii) adds the general one, any other expenditure, not being capital expenditure, laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purpose of making or earning such income. That general clause is what allows interest on money borrowed to buy an investment whose income is taxed under this head. Section 58 is the matching list of refusals. Clause (1)(a)(i) bars personal expenses, clause (1)(a)(ii) bars interest paid outside India without deduction of tax, clause (1)(a)(iii) picks up section 40(a) style disallowances, and clause (2) applies section 40A here as well. Sub-section (4) is the hardest of them — no deduction of any expenditure or allowance at all against winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, races, card games and other games of any sort or from gambling or betting, so the cost of winning is simply not recognised.

citation.ref: Sections 57(i) to (iv), Section 58(1)(a), Section 58(2) and Section 58(4), read with the Explanation to Section 2(24)(ix)

concepts.subsection: Sections 70, 71 and 74 — Setting off and carrying a capital loss
concepts.statement: A capital loss travels along one road and it is a narrow one. Section 70(2) lets a short-term capital loss be set off against income under the head capital gains in respect of any capital asset, so it may go against a long-term gain as freely as against a short-term one. Section 70(3) is the restriction, and it runs the other way — a long-term capital loss may be set off only against a long-term capital gain. Section 71(3) then closes the head off entirely: a loss under capital gains cannot be set against income under any other head, whatever is left of it, which is why a capital loss can never reduce salary, house property or business income. Whatever survives is carried forward under section 74 for eight assessment years immediately succeeding, and the same asymmetry follows it — a carried short-term loss may be set against any capital gain, a carried long-term loss only against a long-term gain. Section 80 puts one condition on the carry forward, that the loss be determined in a return furnished within the time allowed under section 139(1), and section 74 requires the same business or asset in no sense at all, which is where it differs from section 72.

citation.ref: Sections 70(2), 70(3), 71(3) and 74(1) and 74(2), read with Section 80 and Section 139(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143(1) — Intimation and the adjustments it may make
concepts.statement: Processing under section 143(1) is not a scrutiny and it is not a rubber stamp either. The return is taken, the total income or loss is computed after a closed list of adjustments in section 143(1)(a), tax, interest and fee are worked out, and an intimation follows which is deemed to be a notice of demand under section 156 where any sum is payable. The list is what must be known. Clause (i) an arithmetical error in the return; clause (ii) an incorrect claim apparent from any information in the return itself; clause (iii) disallowance of a loss claimed where the return of the year in which the loss arose was furnished beyond the due date under section 139(1); clause (iv) disallowance of expenditure or increase in income indicated in the audit report but not taken into account in the return; and clause (v) disallowance of a deduction claimed under section 10AA or under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A where the return is furnished beyond the due date. Nothing outside that list may be done, so no question of fact and no view about whether an expense was excessive belongs here. The first proviso bars any adjustment unless an intimation of it is given to the assessee in writing or electronically, and the second requires the response to be considered, the adjustment being made if none comes within thirty days. The intimation itself must go within nine months from the end of the financial year in which the return is furnished.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(a) clauses (i) to (v) with its first and second provisos, read with Section 156

concepts.subsection: Section 142 — Inquiry before assessment and the special audit
concepts.statement: Section 142(1) gives the Assessing Officer three powers before he assesses. Clause (i) is a notice requiring a person who has not made a return within the time allowed under section 139(1) to furnish one — no escapement need be alleged and section 148 is not involved. Clause (ii) is a notice to produce such accounts or documents as he may require. Clause (iii) is a notice to furnish information in writing, including a statement of assets and liabilities. Two provisos fence them. A statement of assets and liabilities not included in the accounts may be required only with the previous approval of the Joint Commissioner, and no accounts may be required relating to a period more than three years prior to the previous year. Section 142(2A) is the heavier power. Having regard to the nature and complexity of the accounts, the volume of the accounts, doubts about their correctness, the multiplicity of transactions or the specialised nature of the business, and the interests of the revenue, the Assessing Officer may direct the assessee to get the accounts audited by an accountant nominated by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner or Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. It needs that authority's previous approval, and the proviso requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard for the assessee — his consent is nowhere in the section. Since 1 June 2007 the expenses of the audit are determined by that authority and paid by the Central Government under section 142(2D).

citation.ref: Section 142(1) clauses (i) to (iii) with provisos (a) and (b), and Sections 142(2A), 142(2C) and 142(2D)

concepts.subsection: Section 144 — Best judgement assessment
concepts.statement: Section 144(1) is triggered by any one of four failures — failure to make the return required under section 139(1) and no return under section 139(4) or 139(5) either, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 142(1), failure to comply with a direction for a special audit under section 142(2A), or, having made a return, failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 143(2). On any of them the Assessing Officer shall, after taking into account all relevant material he has gathered, make the assessment to the best of his judgement. Best judgement means an honest estimate resting on some material, not a guess and not a punishment, and the assessment is appealable like any other. Two provisos govern the hearing. The first says no such assessment shall be made without giving the assessee an opportunity of being heard by serving a notice calling on him to show cause why the assessment should not be completed to the best of the officer's judgement. The second removes that requirement altogether where a notice under section 142(1) has already been issued before the assessment is made, on the footing that the assessee has already been asked and has already not answered. No approval of any superior officer is required — that belongs to section 153D, which governs a search assessment.

citation.ref: Section 144(1) with its first and second provisos, read with Sections 142(1), 143(2) and 153D

concepts.subsection: Sections 148 and 148A — The stage that comes before a reassessment notice
concepts.statement: Reassessment stopped being a matter of the officer's private reasons in 2021. Section 148 now permits a notice only where there is information which suggests that income chargeable to tax has escaped assessment, only after the procedure in section 148A has been followed, and only with the prior approval of the specified authority under section 151. Section 148A is the pre-notice stage. The Assessing Officer serves a show cause notice on the assessee setting out the information relied on and giving a period specified in the notice, of not less than seven days and not more than thirty days, to explain why a notice under section 148 should not be issued; the assessee replies; and the Assessing Officer then passes an order under section 148A(3), on the material on record and that reply, deciding whether it is a fit case. This replaced the practice built on GKN Driveshafts, under which the assessee filed a return, asked for the reasons recorded and objected afterwards — the objection is now heard before the notice rather than after it. Cases where a search is initiated or books are requisitioned are outside section 148A and go down the block assessment route in section 158BA instead.

citation.ref: Section 148 with its provisos and Section 148A as substituted by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024 with effect from 1 September 2024, read with Sections 151 and 158BA

concepts.subsection: Section 154 — Rectification of a mistake apparent from the record
concepts.statement: Section 154 lets an income-tax authority amend any order it has passed, any intimation under section 143(1) and any intimation under section 200A(1) or 206CB(1), to rectify a mistake apparent from the record. Four things fix its shape. The mistake must be apparent — an error of fact or of law that stares from the record and needs no long argument; a point on which two views are reasonably possible is outside the section, which is what T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers decided. The power runs both ways, and section 154(2)(b) expressly allows an amendment on an application made by the assessee, so it is not confined to the authority's own motion. Section 154(3) requires notice and a hearing before any amendment that has the effect of enhancing an assessment or reducing a refund. And section 154(7) sets the outer limit — no amendment after the expiry of four years from the end of the financial year in which the order sought to be amended was passed, a period measured from the order and not from the assessment year. Where the assessee applies, section 154(8) requires the authority to pass an order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is received.

citation.ref: Sections 154(1), 154(2)(b), 154(3), 154(7) and 154(8), read with T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers (1971) 82 ITR 50 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Section 264 — Revision at the assessee's instance
concepts.statement: Section 264 is the assessee's revision and section 263 is the revenue's, and almost every difference between them follows from that. The Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may act either on his own motion or on an application by the assessee, may call for the record of any proceeding under the Act, and may pass such order thereon, not being an order prejudicial to the assessee, as he thinks fit — so the worst outcome of a section 264 application is that it is refused. There is no requirement that the order be erroneous or that it be prejudicial to the revenue; those words belong to section 263. The power is wide enough to grant relief on a claim that was never made in the return, the restriction in Goetze (India) being a restriction on the Assessing Officer and not on the revisional authority. Section 264(3) gives the assessee one year from the date on which the order was communicated to him or he otherwise came to know of it, with power to condone delay, and section 264(5) requires a fee of five hundred rupees. Section 264(4) is the bar — no revision while the time for an appeal has not expired and the right of appeal has not been waived, and none where the order has been made the subject of an appeal; once the appeal time has run out unused, the bar lifts. Section 264(6) requires the order within one year from the end of the financial year in which the application is made.

citation.ref: Sections 264(1) to 264(6), read with Section 263(1) and Goetze (India) Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC)

concepts.subsection: Sections 260A and 261 — Appeal to the High Court and to the Supreme Court
concepts.statement: The Appellate Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority, and everything above it is about law only. Section 260A(1) gives an appeal to the High Court from every order passed in appeal by the Tribunal, but only if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law.
