The practice clause sits in Part I of the Second Schedule and turns on the client's consent; this one sits in Part II, binds every member whether in practice or not, and turns on the employer's permission. The person who can release him is the employer, not the client, not the new employer and not his own conscience. Two doors lead out and no third — a law for the time being in force that requires the disclosure, and the employer's permission. The duty does not end when the employment does: information acquired at a previous employer stays confidential after he has moved on, which is exactly the situation a new employer will press him about.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 2

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part II — Clauses 3 and 4
concepts.statement: Two clauses of Part II of the Second Schedule punish dishonesty by any member, in practice or not. Clause 3 — includes in any information, statement, return or form to be submitted to the Institute, the Council or any of its Committees, the Director (Discipline), the Board of Discipline, the Disciplinary Committee, the Quality Review Board or the Appellate Authority any particulars knowing them to be false. Clause 4 — defalcates or embezzles moneys received in his professional capacity. Each has a lighter neighbour that a candidate must not confuse it with. Against Clause 3 stands Clause 2 of Part III of the First Schedule, which punishes not supplying the information at all: staying silent is a First Schedule matter, telling the Institute something the member knows to be false is a Second Schedule matter, and knowledge is what moves it across. Against Clause 4 stands Clause 10 of Part I of the Second Schedule, which punishes failing to keep a client's moneys in a separate banking account: that is a custody failure and it survives repayment, whereas defalcation is taking the money for himself. Both clauses here route the case to the Disciplinary Committee.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clauses 3 and 4

concepts.subsection: Section 27 — Maintenance of branch offices
concepts.statement: Where a chartered accountant in practice or a firm of such chartered accountants has more than one office in India, section 27 requires that each one of such offices shall be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute, and failure to do so renders the member liable to disciplinary action. The member in separate charge must be a member of the Institute and, where the office belongs to a firm, must ordinarily be either a partner of the firm or a member in whole-time employment with it; he is expected to be actually in charge, attending the office, not merely named on a letter. The Council's general exemptions relieve the requirement of a second member where the second office is located in the same premises in which the first office is situated, or in the same city as the first office, or within the distance from the municipal limits of a city that the Council's guidelines prescribe — this bank does not recite that distance. In those cases both offices may be under the same charge. What counts as an office is decided by how the place is held out, not by how often it is used: a room at a member's residence carrying the firm's name board, or a place described to clients as an office where the member attends on appointed days, is a second office and section 27 applies to it.

citation.ref: Section 27, read with the Council's general exemptions from separate charge of a second office

concepts.subsection: Sections 22A and 22G — the Appellate Authority
concepts.statement: Section 22A requires the Central Government to constitute an Appellate Authority consisting of a person who is or has been a judge of a High Court as Chairperson, two members nominated by the Council from among its own members, and two members nominated by the Central Government from among persons of ability, integrity and standing having special knowledge of law, economics, business, commerce or accountancy. Under section 22G a member aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or of the Disciplinary Committee imposing a penalty may prefer an appeal to the Authority within the period the section allows from the date on which the order is communicated to him — this bank does not recite that period — and the Director (Discipline) may also appeal where the Council so authorises him. The Authority's powers on the appeal are wide: it may confirm, modify or set aside the order; it may impose any penalty, or set aside, reduce or enhance the penalty imposed; it may remit the case to the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee for such further enquiry as it considers proper; or it may pass such other order as it thinks fit. A proviso requires that the parties concerned be given an opportunity of being heard before any such order is passed. So an appeal is not a one-way door — the penalty can come back heavier — and the Authority sits above both disciplinary forums rather than beside them.

citation.ref: Sections 22A and 22G, with the proviso to section 22G

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — management responsibilities and non-assurance services
concepts.statement: A firm shall not assume a management responsibility for an audit client. This is one of the few places where the Code stops applying its usual machinery and simply says no: the threats created by taking the client's decisions cannot be reduced to an acceptable level, so there is no safeguard, and the only answer is not to do it. A management responsibility involves controlling, leading and directing an entity, including making decisions about the acquisition, deployment and control of human, financial, technological, physical and intangible resources. Setting policies and strategic direction, hiring or dismissing employees, directing and taking responsibility for the actions of employees, authorising transactions, controlling or managing bank accounts or investments, deciding which recommendations of the firm to implement, reporting to those charged with governance on behalf of management, and taking responsibility for the design, implementation, monitoring or maintenance of internal control are all management responsibilities. Providing advice and recommendations to assist management is not, provided management makes the decision. To stay on the right side the firm must be satisfied that client management makes all judgements and decisions that are the proper responsibility of management, and the client should assign an individual who possesses suitable skill, knowledge and experience to be responsible for the client's decisions and to oversee the services. Section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013 lays a statutory list of forbidden services on top of this for a company auditor, and the two have to be answered separately.

citation.ref: the prohibition on a firm assuming a management responsibility for an audit client, with the requirement that client management make all judgements and decisions and assign an individual with suitable skill, knowledge and experience to oversee the services, read with section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — long association and cooling-off
concepts.statement: Long association of an individual with an audit client creates a familiarity threat and a self-interest threat, because the individual becomes too sympathetic to the client's interests or too accepting of its work. The firm must evaluate the threat, weighing the nature and length of the individual's relationship with the client, his role on the engagement, how far the client's management has changed, and the nature and complexity of the client's accounting and reporting issues. It then addresses what it finds — by rotating the individual off the engagement team, by changing his role, by having an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the team review his work, or by an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement. For an audit client that is a public interest entity the Code stops evaluating and starts prescribing: an individual shall not act as the engagement partner, as the engagement quality control reviewer, or in any other key audit partner role for more than the number of consecutive years the Code specifies, and must then serve a cooling-off period of the length the Code specifies for that role — this bank does not recite either number. During the cooling-off period he shall not be a member of the engagement team, provide quality control for the engagement, consult with the team on technical or industry-specific issues, or otherwise directly influence the outcome of the engagement. This rotation of the individual sits beside, and does not replace, the statutory rotation of the audit firm and of the individual auditor under section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013.

citation.ref: the long association provisions — evaluation of the familiarity and self-interest threats created by long association, and the mandatory rotation and cooling-off of key audit partners on a public interest entity — read with section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — fee dependency and overdue fees
concepts.statement: Fees create threats in three directions and the Code deals with each separately. Where the total fees from an audit client represent a large proportion of the total fees of the firm, the firm's dependence on that client and its concern about losing it create a self-interest threat and an intimidation threat; the firm evaluates the threat and addresses it, for example by reducing the dependency, by increasing the client base, by having an appropriate reviewer who is not a member of the engagement team review the work, or by an independent internal or external quality review of the engagement. Where the client is a public interest entity and the total fees from it and its related entities exceed the proportion of the firm's total fees that the Code specifies for two consecutive years, the firm must disclose that fact to those charged with governance and discuss which action it will take — this bank does not recite that proportion. Fees remaining unpaid from an audit client for a long time, and especially where a significant part is still unpaid before the current year's audit report is issued, create a self-interest threat: the firm must determine whether the overdue fees are equivalent to a loan to the client, and whether it is appropriate to be re-appointed or to continue. Nothing here is cured by telling the reader of the audit report about it — disclosure to those charged with governance is a step in managing the threat, not a substitute for managing it.

citation.ref: the fees provisions — the self-interest and intimidation threats created by fee dependency, the disclosure to those charged with governance for a public interest entity, and the treatment of overdue fees as possibly equivalent to a loan

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — gifts, hospitality and inducements
concepts.statement: An inducement is an object, situation or action used as a means to influence another individual's behaviour — gifts, hospitality, entertainment, political or charitable donations, appeals to friendship or loyalty, employment or other commercial opportunities, and preferential treatment or rights. The Code splits the question in two. Where the inducement is offered or accepted with the intent to improperly influence the behaviour of the recipient or of another individual, it is prohibited outright, whatever its value; the accountant shall neither offer nor accept it, and shall not allow another to offer or accept it for him. Where there is no such intent, the accountant applies the conceptual framework, considering the nature, frequency, value and cumulative effect of the inducement, the timing of it relative to any decision or work being performed, whether it is customary in the circumstances, and the roles of the persons involved. On top of that sits a bright line for audit work: a firm, a network firm, or a member of the audit team shall not accept gifts and hospitality from an audit client unless the value is trivial and inconsequential. Intent is judged by what a reasonable and informed third party would conclude from the circumstances, not by what the giver or the receiver says he meant, and a gift timed to arrive while a disputed accounting question is open will not read innocently however small it is.

citation.ref: the inducements provisions — the outright prohibition where there is intent to improperly influence behaviour, and the rule that gifts and hospitality from an audit client may be accepted only where the value is trivial and inconsequential

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — network firms and what makes a network
concepts.statement: A network is a larger structure that is aimed at co-operation between firms and that is clearly aimed at profit or cost sharing, or shares common ownership, control or management, or shares common quality control policies and procedures, or shares a common business strategy, or uses a common brand name, or shares a significant part of professional resources. A firm belonging to such a structure is a network firm. Each of those tests stands on its own — a common brand name alone makes a network, and separate partnership deeds, separate profits and separate client lists do not undo it. What does not make a network is co-operation with nothing more behind it: an arrangement to refer work to one another, sharing an immaterial cost, or an association formed for a single joint engagement. The consequence is the whole point of the definition. Where a firm is a network firm, the independence requirements that apply to an audit client of the firm apply to the network firm too, so a financial interest, a business relationship, an employment relationship or a prohibited non-assurance service on the part of a sister firm is treated as though the auditor had it himself. The question in the examination is therefore never whether the sister firm is independent; it is whether the two firms are a network.

citation.ref: the definition of a network and a network firm, and the application of the independence requirements for an audit client to a network firm

concepts.subsection: Section 141(3)(g) — the ceiling on company audits
concepts.statement: Section 141(3)(g) disqualifies from appointment as auditor of a company a person who is in full-time employment elsewhere, and a person or a partner of a firm holding appointment as its auditor who, at the date of such appointment or re-appointment, is holding appointment as auditor of more than the specified number of companies. This bank does not recite the specified number, and no question here turns on it — what is examinable is the shape of the count. Companies excluded from the count are one person companies, dormant companies, small companies, and private companies having paid-up share capital below the amount the section prescribes. The ceiling belongs to the individual, not to the firm: where a firm is appointed, the count is applied to each partner separately, so a firm cannot multiply its own headroom by putting a different partner's name on each report, and a person who is a partner in more than one firm adds together every appointment he holds anywhere. A partner in full-time employment elsewhere, and a partner who has already reached the ceiling, are simply not available to be counted. Before appointing, the company obtains from the auditor written consent and a certificate that the appointment, if made, will be in accordance with the conditions prescribed, which is where section 139(1) makes the auditor put his own compliance with section 141 in writing.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(g) with its proviso, read with section 139(1)

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — service with and employment by an audit client
concepts.statement: People move between an audit firm and its client in both directions, and the Code answers each direction differently. A partner or employee of the firm shall not serve as a director or officer of an audit client, and shall not act as company secretary for one unless the role is purely administrative and law permits it; this is an outright bar, not a threat to be weighed. Coming in: where an individual who was a director or officer of the audit client, or an employee in a position to exert significant influence over the preparation of the accounting records or the financial statements, joins the firm, he shall not be assigned to the audit team if that service or employment occurred during the period covered by the audit report; where it was before that period, the firm evaluates the self-interest, self-review and familiarity threats and addresses them, for example by having an appropriate reviewer review the work he does. Going out: where a former member of the audit team or a former partner joins the audit client as a director or officer, or as an employee in a position to exert significant influence, the familiarity or intimidation threat is at an unacceptable level unless he has no significant connection remaining with the firm — no payments due to him except fixed pre-determined amounts, and nothing owing that is material to the firm — and he does not participate, or appear to participate, in the firm's business or professional activities. For a public interest entity a cooling-off period applies before a key audit partner may take such a position with the client.

citation.ref: the provisions on serving as a director or officer of an audit client, on recent service with an audit client, and on employment with an audit client, including the requirement that no significant connection remain between a departing partner and the firm

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 8
concepts.statement: Accepting an audit previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing is professional misconduct. The duty is to communicate — the outgoing auditor's permission or no-objection is not required, and the purpose is to learn whether the change hides something the incoming auditor should weigh.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 8

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 1
concepts.statement: Disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement to anyone other than the client, without the client's consent, is professional misconduct — unless law requires the disclosure. Legal compulsion and client consent are the only two doors out of the duty.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 1

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 4
concepts.statement: Expressing an opinion on the financial statements of any business in which the member, his firm, or a partner in his firm has a substantial interest is professional misconduct. The clause reaches the firm and the partners, not only the signing member, and no disclosure cures it — the opinion itself is barred.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 4

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 7
concepts.statement: Failing to exercise due diligence, or being grossly negligent in the conduct of professional duties, is professional misconduct. The clause needs no dishonesty and no client loss — signing what was never examined is the classic case.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 7

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 11
concepts.statement: A chartered accountant in practice may not engage in any business or occupation other than the profession unless the Council permits it. The clause's own proviso allows a directorship simpliciter — an ordinary board seat without managing or whole-time office — unless the member or a partner is interested in the company as its auditor. General and specific permissions of the Council carve the remaining space.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 11

concepts.subsection: Second Schedule Part I — Clause 10
concepts.statement: Failing to keep a client's moneys — other than fees or money meant to be spent — in a separate banking account, or failing to use such moneys for their intended purpose within a reasonable time, is professional misconduct. The office account is for the firm's money; the client account is for the client's, and mixing them is the offence regardless of eventual repayment.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 10

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 7
concepts.statement: Advertising professional attainments or services, or using any designation other than chartered accountant on professional documents, cards or sign boards, is misconduct — a recognised university degree or a title indicating membership of an institute may be used. The Council's guidelines carve narrow permissions — write-ups within prescribed norms, websites on a pull basis — but self-praise pushed at the public stays barred.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 7

concepts.subsection: First Schedule Part I — Clause 2
concepts.statement: Paying or allowing any share, commission or brokerage out of professional fees to anyone other than a member of the Institute, a partner, a retired partner, a deceased partner's legal representative, or a member of a permitted other professional body is misconduct. The clause polices the outflow of fees; referral commissions to clients, agents or relatives all fall on the wrong side.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 2

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Costs to obtain and fulfil a contract
concepts.statement: The incremental costs of obtaining a contract are recognised as an asset if the entity expects to recover them, with a practical expedient to expense them if the amortisation period is one year or less. Costs to fulfil a contract that are not within another Standard's scope are capitalised only if they relate directly to an identified contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy performance obligations, and are expected to be recovered.

citation.ref: para 91 to 98

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Hedge accounting
concepts.statement: Hedge accounting is available only where the hedging relationship consists solely of eligible hedging instruments and eligible hedged items, there is formal designation and documentation at inception of the risk management objective and strategy, and the relationship meets the effectiveness requirements — an economic relationship between the hedged item and the hedging instrument, credit risk not dominating the value changes, and a hedge ratio consistent with actual risk management.

citation.ref: para 6.4.1

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Derecognition of financial assets
concepts.statement: A financial asset is derecognised when the contractual rights to its cash flows expire, or when it is transferred and that transfer qualifies for derecognition — which turns on evaluating the extent to which the risks and rewards of ownership are retained. Substantially transferring risks and rewards derecognises the asset; substantially retaining them keeps it recognised in full, with a financial liability for the consideration received; only when neither is clear does the entity move on to a control test.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Deferred tax in a business combination
concepts.statement: Fair value adjustments to identifiable assets and liabilities recognised on a business combination create temporary differences whenever the tax base does not move to match, and the resulting deferred tax asset or liability is recognised as part of the acquisition accounting — increasing or decreasing goodwill or the bargain purchase gain. The one carve-out is goodwill itself — no deferred tax liability is recognised on its initial recognition, because that would only inflate goodwill further.

citation.ref: para 15 and 19

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Net investment in a foreign operation
concepts.statement: Exchange differences on a monetary item that in substance forms part of an entity's net investment in a foreign operation are recognised in profit or loss in the separate or individual financial statements of the entity concerned, but in the financial statements that include the foreign operation — such as the group's consolidated statements — those exchange differences go to other comprehensive income and are reclassified to profit or loss only on disposal of the net investment.

citation.ref: para 32 and 48

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Sale and leaseback
concepts.statement: In a sale and leaseback, the seller-lessee applies the Ind AS 115 requirements for identifying when a performance obligation is satisfied to judge whether the transfer is a sale. If it is, the seller-lessee measures the right-of-use asset retained at the proportion of the previous carrying amount relating to the rights retained, and recognises only the gain or loss relating to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor — not the full gain on the asset. If the transfer fails the sale test, both parties account for it as a financing.

citation.ref: para 99 and 100

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Timing of the goodwill impairment test
concepts.statement: A cash-generating unit to which goodwill has been allocated is tested for impairment at least annually, and the test may be performed at any time during the annual period provided it is performed at the same time every year; different units may be tested at different times. If some or all of the goodwill allocated to a unit was acquired in a business combination during the current period, that unit is tested before the end of the current annual period — the entity cannot wait for next year's cycle.

citation.ref: para 96

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 33 — Diluted EPS and antidilution
concepts.statement: Diluted EPS adjusts profit and the weighted average number of shares for the effect of all dilutive potential equity shares, but a potential equity share that would increase EPS (or reduce a loss per share) is antidilutive and is excluded from the diluted EPS computation. Each issue or series of potential equity shares is tested for dilutive or antidilutive effect separately, not in aggregate.

citation.ref: para 41

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Contingent assets
concepts.statement: A contingent asset is never recognised, because that could bring in income that may never be realised — but it is disclosed when an inflow of economic benefits is probable. Once realisation becomes virtually certain, the asset is no longer contingent and is recognised, together with the related income, in the period the change occurs.

citation.ref: para 33 to 35

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 — Cash-settled share-based payment
concepts.statement: For a cash-settled share-based payment, the entity measures the goods or services received and the liability incurred at the fair value of the liability, and remeasures that fair value at the end of every reporting period and at settlement, with all changes recognised in profit or loss. Unlike an equity-settled award, the amount charged is never frozen at grant date — it moves with the liability's fair value until the award is paid.

citation.ref: para 30 to 33

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — Going concern disclosure
concepts.statement: Management assesses the entity's ability to continue as a going concern, looking at least twelve months from the reporting date, and prepares the financial statements on that basis unless it intends to liquidate or cease trading or has no realistic alternative. Where management identifies material uncertainties that cast significant doubt on that ability, those uncertainties are disclosed — disclosure, not abandonment of the going concern basis, is the standard's response short of an actual intention to liquidate.

citation.ref: para 25 and 26

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Correction of prior period errors
concepts.statement: A material prior period error is corrected retrospectively in the first financial statements approved after its discovery, by restating the comparative amounts for the period the error occurred, or restating opening balances if the error predates the earliest period presented. The correction bypasses profit or loss for the period of discovery — it adjusts the periods actually affected, not the current period's result.

citation.ref: para 42 and 46

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 103 — Contingent consideration after the acquisition
concepts.statement: How contingent consideration moves after the acquisition date is decided by how it was classified on that date. Classified as equity, it is never remeasured and its settlement is accounted for within equity. Classified as an asset or a liability within the scope of Ind AS 109, it is remeasured to fair value at every reporting date with the change in profit or loss. Only a change that reflects new information about facts existing at the acquisition date is a measurement period adjustment that touches goodwill; a change caused by the acquiree's later performance never does.

citation.ref: para 58, read with para 45

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Ownership change without loss of control
concepts.statement: Once control exists, buying more of a subsidiary or selling part of it without losing control is a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners, not an acquisition or a disposal. The carrying amounts of the controlling and non-controlling interests are adjusted to their new relative shares, and any difference between that adjustment and the fair value of the consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity and attributed to the owners of the parent. No goodwill is created or released, and nothing reaches profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 23 and B96

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Reclassifying financial assets
concepts.statement: Financial assets are reclassified when, and only when, the entity changes the business model for managing them. Financial liabilities are never reclassified. The change bites on the reclassification date, which the Standard defines as the first day of the first reporting period following the change of business model, so measurement carries on unchanged until the period ends. From that date the new classification applies prospectively, and previously recognised interest, gains and losses are not restated.

citation.ref: para 4.4.1 and 5.6.1, with the Appendix A definition of reclassification date

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Modifying a financial liability
concepts.statement: Renegotiating a borrowing is tested before it is accounted for. Terms are substantially different if the present value of the cash flows under the new terms, including fees paid net of fees received and discounted at the original effective interest rate, differs by at least 10 per cent from the present value of the remaining cash flows of the old liability. Substantially different means the old liability is extinguished and a new one recognised, with the difference between the old carrying amount and the consideration paid taken to profit or loss. Below the threshold, the liability survives and only its carrying amount is recomputed.

citation.ref: para 3.3.2 and 3.3.3, with the 10 per cent test in para B3.3.6

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Significant financing component
concepts.statement: Where the timing of payments gives either the customer or the entity a significant benefit of financing the transfer of goods or services, the promised consideration is adjusted for the time value of money, so that revenue is recognised at the amount the customer would have paid in cash on the date of transfer. It works in both directions, a long advance as much as long credit. A practical expedient excuses the adjustment where the gap between transfer and payment is expected at inception to be one year or less. The discount rate is the one implicit in a separate financing transaction between the two parties at inception, and it is never updated afterwards.

citation.ref: para 60, 63 and 64

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Lessee accounting for a lease modification
concepts.statement: A lessee treats a modification as a separate lease only when both gates open, the scope increases by adding the right to use one or more underlying assets and the consideration goes up by an amount commensurate with the stand-alone price for that increase. Otherwise the lessee reallocates the consideration, redetermines the lease term, and remeasures the lease liability at a revised discount rate. Where the modification decreases the scope, the right-of-use asset is first cut back to reflect the partial or full termination and the resulting gain or loss goes to profit or loss; for every other modification the whole remeasurement is absorbed by the right-of-use asset.

citation.ref: para 44, 45 and 46

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Deferred tax on investments in subsidiaries and associates
concepts.statement: Undistributed profits of a subsidiary, branch, associate or joint arrangement create a taxable temporary difference between the carrying amount of the investment in the consolidated financial statements and its tax base. A deferred tax liability is recognised on all of them except where both conditions hold together, the investor can control the timing of the reversal and it is probable the difference will not reverse in the foreseeable future. A parent controls its subsidiary's dividend policy and can meet both; an investor in an associate cannot control that policy, so the exception is rarely available there.

citation.ref: para 39, read with para 38 and 40

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Allocating an impairment loss within a unit
concepts.statement: An impairment loss on a cash-generating unit is allocated in a fixed order, first against any goodwill allocated to the unit until that goodwill is nil, and only then across the unit's other assets pro rata on their carrying amounts. No individual asset may be written below the highest of its own fair value less costs of disposal where measurable, its value in use where determinable, and zero; whatever the floor blocks is reallocated pro rata to the remaining assets. Goodwill written off this way can never be reversed in a later period, even if the unit recovers.

citation.ref: para 104 and 105, with the reversal bar in para 124

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 113 — Principal market and the price used
concepts.statement: Fair value is measured in the principal market, the market with the greatest volume and level of activity that the entity can access, and only where no principal market exists does the most advantageous market answer. Where a principal market exists, its price is used even if a different market would net the entity more. That price is not adjusted for transaction costs, which are specific to a transaction rather than a characteristic of the asset, but it is adjusted for transport costs where location is a characteristic of the asset.

citation.ref: para 16, 18, 25 and 26

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — Presenting a discontinued operation
concepts.statement: A discontinued operation is a component disposed of or classified as held for sale that is a separate major line of business or geographical area, part of a single coordinated plan to dispose of one, or a subsidiary acquired exclusively for resale. Its post-tax result and the post-tax gain or loss on measurement or disposal are collapsed into a single amount in the statement of profit and loss, with the analysis given in the notes. The profit or loss figures for prior periods are re-presented on the same basis; the balance sheets of prior periods are expressly left alone.

citation.ref: para 32, 33, 34 and 40

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 19 — Past service cost
concepts.statement: Past service cost is the change in the present value of the defined benefit obligation caused by a plan amendment or a curtailment. It is recognised as an expense in full at the earlier of the date the amendment or curtailment occurs and the date the entity recognises related restructuring costs or termination benefits. There is no spreading over a vesting period and no distinction between vested and unvested benefits, and past service cost is part of service cost in profit or loss, not a remeasurement in other comprehensive income.

citation.ref: para 102 and 103, with the components in para 120

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Attributing results to non-controlling interests
concepts.statement: Profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income are attributed to the owners of the parent and to the non-controlling interests, and total comprehensive income is attributed to both even where this leaves the non-controlling interests with a deficit balance — there is no floor at nil, unlike the equity method for an associate. Where a subsidiary has cumulative preference shares classified as equity and held by non-controlling interests, the group computes its share only after adjusting for the dividends on those shares, whether or not they have been declared.

citation.ref: para B94, read with B95

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — The investment entity exception
concepts.statement: An investment entity is one that takes funds from investors to provide them with investment management services, commits to invest solely for capital appreciation or investment income, and measures performance on a fair value basis. It does not consolidate its subsidiaries and does not apply Ind AS 103 on obtaining control; it measures each investment in a subsidiary at fair value through profit or loss. The one carve-out is a subsidiary providing services relating to the investment entity's own investment activities, which is consolidated. A parent that is not itself an investment entity consolidates everything it controls, including what it controls through an investment entity subsidiary.

citation.ref: para 27, 31, 32 and 33

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — Upstream and downstream transactions with an associate
concepts.statement: Gains and losses on sales between an investor and its associate or joint venture are recognised only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests, so the investor's own percentage of the unrealised profit is eliminated and no more. A downstream sale reduces the investor's own profit by its share; an upstream sale reduces its share of the associate's profit. Elimination is never in full, which is where an associate parts company with a consolidated subsidiary. Where the transaction evidences a fall in net realisable value or an impairment, that loss is recognised in full on a downstream sale.

citation.ref: para 28, read with para 29

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 111 — Acquiring an interest in a joint operation that is a business
concepts.statement: Where the activity of a joint operation constitutes a business, an entity acquiring an interest in it applies, to the extent of its share, all the Ind AS 103 business combination principles that do not conflict with Ind AS 111 — identifiable assets and liabilities at fair value, acquisition-related costs expensed, goodwill recognised and tested annually. This holds for an additional interest as much as the first. The departure from a step acquisition is that previously held interests are not remeasured where the joint operator retains joint control.

citation.ref: para 21A, with B33A and B33C

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — Translating a foreign operation into the presentation currency
concepts.statement: To carry a foreign operation into a different presentation currency, assets and liabilities for every balance sheet presented go at the closing rate at that balance sheet date, income and expenses go at the exchange rates at the dates of the transactions with an average rate accepted as an approximation, and all resulting exchange differences go to other comprehensive income. Those differences come from two sources, retranslating the opening net assets at a new closing rate and translating the result at a rate that is not the closing rate, and they accumulate in a separate component of equity until disposal.

citation.ref: para 39, read with 40 and 41

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Measuring a cash flow hedge
concepts.statement: The cash flow hedge reserve is adjusted to the lower, in absolute amounts, of the cumulative gain or loss on the hedging instrument and the cumulative change in the present value of the hedged expected future cash flows, both from inception. That effective portion goes to other comprehensive income and everything left over is hedge ineffectiveness in profit or loss. If the hedged forecast transaction later produces a non-financial asset or liability, the accumulated reserve is removed and included directly in that item's initial cost, which is not a reclassification adjustment; in every other case it is reclassified to profit or loss in the periods the hedged cash flows affect profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 6.5.11(a) to (d)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — The general expected credit loss model
concepts.statement: Outside the simplified approach, a loss allowance is measured at 12-month expected credit losses unless credit risk has increased significantly since initial recognition, when it moves to lifetime expected credit losses. The test compares the risk of a default occurring at the reporting date with that risk at initial recognition, not the change in the amount of the losses. Two shortcuts sit either side of it — an entity may assume no significant increase where the instrument has low credit risk at the reporting date, and there is a rebuttable presumption of a significant increase once contractual payments are more than 30 days past due.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Measuring a provision
concepts.statement: A provision is the best estimate of the expenditure required to settle the present obligation at the end of the reporting period. Where a large population of items is involved the estimate is the expected value, weighting all possible outcomes by their probabilities; where a single obligation is involved the most likely outcome may be the best estimate. Discounting is required only where the effect of the time value of money is material, at a pre-tax rate reflecting current market assessments and the risks specific to the liability. A reimbursement is recognised only when it is virtually certain, as a separate asset capped at the provision, and may be netted only in the statement of profit and loss.

citation.ref: para 36, 39, 45, 47 and 53, with the presentation in para 54

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 20 — Repaying a government grant
concepts.statement: A government grant that becomes repayable is a change in accounting estimate, never a prior period error. Repayment of a grant related to income is applied first against any unamortised deferred credit, with the excess straight to profit or loss. Repayment of a grant related to an asset is recognised by increasing the carrying amount of the asset or reducing the deferred income balance, and the cumulative additional depreciation that would have been charged in the absence of the grant goes immediately to profit or loss. The pre-2018 Indian text allowed only the deferred income route and carried no depreciation catch-up.

citation.ref: para 32 as substituted in 2018, with para 33

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 41 — Government grants for biological assets
concepts.statement: Ind AS 41 deliberately departs from Ind AS 20 for a biological asset measured at fair value less costs to sell. An unconditional grant on such an asset goes to profit or loss when, and only when, it becomes receivable — not when it is received and not spread over anything. A conditional grant goes to profit or loss when, and only when, the conditions are met, with time-apportionment allowed only where the terms let part of the grant be retained as time passes. Ind AS 20 returns only where the biological asset is measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment.

citation.ref: para 34, 35 and 36, with the scope split in para 37 and 38

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix C — Service concession arrangements
concepts.statement: Infrastructure inside a public-to-private service concession is never the operator's property, plant and equipment, because the arrangement does not convey the right to control its use. The operator is a service provider, and what it books for construction depends on what the grantor gives back. An unconditional contractual right to receive cash from the grantor produces a financial asset; a right, or licence, to charge users of the public service produces an intangible asset, because those amounts turn on how much the public uses the service. That split also decides borrowing costs — expensed under the financial asset model, capitalised during construction under the intangible asset model.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 11, 16, 17 and 22

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 23 — Capitalisation rate on general borrowings
concepts.statement: Funds borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset yield the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing less any investment income on the temporary investment of those borrowings. Funds borrowed generally yield a capitalisation rate applied to the expenditure on the asset, the rate being the weighted average of the borrowing costs on the entity's borrowings outstanding during the period other than those made specifically for a qualifying asset. Whatever the two limbs produce, the amount capitalised in a period can never exceed the borrowing costs actually incurred in that period.

citation.ref: para 12 and 14

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 33 — Rights issue and the bonus element
concepts.statement: A rights issue priced below fair value is part fresh money and part gift, and only the gift is retrospective. The shares outstanding before the issue are multiplied by the fair value per share immediately before the exercise of rights over the theoretical ex-rights fair value per share, that theoretical price being the aggregate fair value of the existing shares plus the proceeds of the rights, divided by the shares outstanding after the exercise. The adjusted number is used for all periods before the rights issue, so the comparative earnings per share is restated, while the new shares themselves enter the weighted average from their own date.

citation.ref: para 27(b), with Appendix A, para A2

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 34 — Income tax in an interim period
concepts.statement: Interim income tax expense is recognised on the best estimate of the weighted average annual income tax rate expected for the full financial year, applied to the year-to-date profit. When the estimate of that annual rate changes, the amount accrued in an earlier interim period of the same financial year is adjusted through the later interim period, so the catch-up lands in the current quarter. Amounts reported in earlier interim periods are not retrospectively adjusted, and no interim period is measured as though it stood alone.

citation.ref: para 30(c), read with para 28 and para 36

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 108 — Entity-wide disclosures
concepts.statement: Three disclosures bind every entity within Ind AS 108, including one with a single reportable segment, and are given only where the segment note has not already given them. Revenues from external customers by product or service; revenues and non-current assets other than financial instruments, deferred tax assets, post-employment benefit assets and insurance rights, split between the country of domicile and all foreign countries in total with any material individual country shown separately; and the fact of any single external customer at 10 per cent or more of revenues, with the amount and the reporting segment but not the customer's name.

citation.ref: para 31, 33 and 34

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 — Modifying and cancelling an equity-settled award
concepts.statement: Whatever is done to an equity-settled award afterwards, the entity recognises as a minimum the services received at the grant date fair value of the instruments granted, unless they fail a vesting condition other than a market condition. On top of that it recognises the effects of modifications that increase the total fair value or are otherwise beneficial to the employee. The incremental fair value is the difference between the modified and the original instrument, both measured at the modification date, spread from that date to vesting. A modification that reduces fair value is ignored, and a cancellation or settlement during the vesting period is an acceleration of vesting.

citation.ref: para 27 and 28, with Appendix B, para B43 and B44

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Changes in liabilities arising from financing activities
concepts.statement: An entity must let a reader move from the opening to the closing balance of every liability whose cash flows sit in financing activities, and the movement is split five ways — changes from financing cash flows, changes from obtaining or losing control of subsidiaries or other businesses, the effect of changes in foreign exchange rates, changes in fair values, and other changes. The disclosure covers the non-cash movements as well as the cash ones, which is what makes it more than a repeat of the financing section, and a reconciliation between opening and closing balance sheet amounts is the way the Standard itself suggests fulfilling it.

citation.ref: para 44A, 44B, 44C and 44D

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Supplier finance arrangements
concepts.statement: A supplier finance arrangement is one where a finance provider offers to pay what the entity owes its suppliers and the entity agrees to pay the provider on the same date or later, so the entity gets extended payment terms or its suppliers get early payment. Reverse factoring, payables finance and supply chain finance are the usual names. Two things are expressly not such arrangements — instruments that are solely credit enhancements for the entity, such as letters of credit used as guarantees, and instruments used to settle directly with a supplier, such as credit cards. Where the arrangement exists the entity discloses the terms and conditions, the carrying amounts and the balance sheet line items, how much of that the finance providers have already paid the suppliers, the range of payment due dates against comparable ordinary trade payables, and the non-cash changes. In India this bites for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 April 2025.

citation.ref: para 44F, 44G and 44H, with the Indian application date in the effective date section

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Choosing a policy where no Ind AS applies
concepts.statement: Where no Ind AS covers a transaction, management develops a policy giving information that is relevant to users and reliable, and it must first work down a two-step order it cannot skip — the requirements in Ind ASs dealing with similar and related issues, then the definitions, recognition criteria and measurement concepts in the Framework. Only after that may it look further, and the Indian text orders even that optional layer: it may first consider the most recent pronouncements of the International Accounting Standards Board, and in the absence of those, the pronouncements of other standard-setting bodies using a similar conceptual framework, other accounting literature and accepted industry practice — none of which may conflict with the mandatory two steps.

citation.ref: para 10, 11 and 12

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 — Depreciating significant parts separately
concepts.statement: Each part of an item of property, plant and equipment with a cost significant in relation to the total cost of the item is depreciated separately, the airframe and the engines of an aircraft being the Standard's own example. Parts with the same useful life and the same depreciation method may be grouped. Once any part is depreciated separately the remainder of the item — the parts that are individually not significant — is depreciated separately too, with approximation techniques allowed where expectations for those parts vary. An entity may also choose to depreciate a part separately even where its cost is not significant.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 Appendix A — Changes in an existing decommissioning liability
concepts.statement: A change in the estimated timing or amount of a decommissioning outflow, or in the discount rate, is not a gain or a loss on the day it happens. Under the cost model the change is added to or deducted from the cost of the related asset in the current period, the deduction is capped at the asset's carrying amount, and any excess of a decrease over that carrying amount goes immediately to profit or loss; an addition is an indication to test the asset for impairment. Under the revaluation model the change moves the revaluation surplus instead. Once the asset has reached the end of its useful life every later change goes straight to profit or loss. The periodic unwinding of the discount is a finance cost in profit or loss, and capitalisation of it under Ind AS 23 is not permitted.

citation.ref: Appendix A, para 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 38 — Recognising expenditure in the development phase
concepts.statement: An intangible asset arising from development is recognised if, and only if, the entity can demonstrate all six of technical feasibility of completing the asset so that it will be available for use or sale, its intention to complete and use or sell it, its ability to use or sell it, how it will generate probable future economic benefits, the availability of adequate technical, financial and other resources to complete it, and its ability to measure reliably the expenditure attributable to it during development. The cost is the sum of expenditure incurred from the date the criteria are first met and no earlier, and expenditure once recognised as an expense may never be reinstated as part of the cost of the asset.

citation.ref: para 57, read with 65, 67 and 71

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 40 — Transfers into and out of investment property
concepts.statement: A transfer to or from investment property is made when, and only when, there is a change in use, evidenced by commencement of owner-occupation, commencement of development with a view to sale, end of owner-occupation, or commencement of an operating lease to another party. A decision to dispose of an investment property without developing it is not a change in use, so the property stays investment property until it is derecognised; redevelopment of an investment property for continued use as investment property is not one either. Because India permits only the cost model for investment property, no transfer between investment property, owner-occupied property and inventories changes the carrying amount of the property or its cost for measurement or disclosure.

citation.ref: para 57, 58 and 59, read with para 56

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 2 — Costs that stay out of the cost of inventories
concepts.statement: Cost of inventories is costs of purchase, costs of conversion and other costs of bringing the inventories to their present location and condition. Costs of purchase take in the purchase price, import duties and other taxes not subsequently recoverable, and transport and handling, less trade discounts and rebates. Four things are named as excluded and expensed as incurred — abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour or other production costs; storage costs, unless those costs are necessary in the production process before a further production stage; administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing inventories to their present location and condition; and selling costs. Where inventories are bought on deferred settlement terms containing a financing element, that element is interest expense over the period of the financing, not part of cost.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix B — A licence as a right to access or a right to use
concepts.statement: Where a licence of intellectual property is a separate performance obligation, its nature is a right to access only if three criteria are all met — the contract requires, or the customer reasonably expects, activities by the entity that significantly affect the intellectual property; the licence directly exposes the customer to the positive or negative effects of those activities; and those activities do not themselves transfer a good or service. Activities significantly affect the property where they are expected to change its form or functionality, or where the customer's benefit substantially depends on them, which is why a brand usually differs from a completed film or a piece of software with significant stand-alone functionality. A right to access is satisfied over time; a right to use is satisfied at a point in time, and never before the customer can use and benefit from the licence. A sales-based or usage-based royalty is recognised only at the later of the sale or usage occurring and the performance obligation being satisfied.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, B59A, B60, B61, B62 and B63

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 Appendix B — Assurance-type and service-type warranties
concepts.statement: A warranty the customer can buy separately is a distinct service and therefore a performance obligation, and part of the transaction price is allocated to it. A warranty the customer cannot buy separately goes to Ind AS 37 as a provision, unless it, or part of it, gives the customer a service beyond the assurance that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications, in which case that part is a performance obligation. Where both kinds are promised and cannot reasonably be accounted for separately, they are accounted for together as a single performance obligation. A law making the entity liable for damage its products cause, and an indemnity against infringement claims, create no performance obligation at all.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B28 to B33, with para 74, 76 and 81

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Classifying a sublease
concepts.statement: An intermediate lessor classifies a sublease by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, not by reference to the underlying asset, so the comparison is with what is left of the head lease term rather than with the economic life of the building or the machine. The one exception runs the other way — where the head lease is a short-term lease the entity has taken the recognition exemption on, the sublease is an operating lease. Where the sublease comes out as a finance lease the intermediate lessor uses the interest rate implicit in the sublease, and if that cannot be readily determined it may use the discount rate used for the head lease, adjusted for initial direct costs on the sublease.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, with para 68 and the Appendix A definition of a sublease

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 Appendix C — Uncertainty over income tax treatments
concepts.statement: An uncertain tax treatment is one where it is uncertain whether the taxation authority will accept it under tax law. The entity first decides whether to look at each uncertainty on its own or grouped with others, on whichever better predicts the resolution. It must then assume the authority will examine every amount it has a right to examine and will have full knowledge of all related information — there is no allowance for the chance of not being caught. If acceptance is probable, the filed treatment is used. If it is not probable, the effect of the uncertainty is reflected using either the most likely amount, where the outcomes are binary or concentrated on one value, or the expected value, being the probability-weighted sum, where they are neither. A later change in facts or new information is a change in accounting estimate.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 24 — The government-related entity exemption
concepts.statement: A reporting entity is exempt from the paragraph 18 disclosures for transactions and balances with a government that controls, jointly controls or significantly influences it, and with any other entity the same government controls, jointly controls or significantly influences. The exemption is bought, not free: the entity must instead give the name of the government and the nature of the relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction, and a qualitative or quantitative indication of the extent of the transactions that are collectively but not individually significant. Judgement on how much detail turns on the closeness of the relationship, the size of the transaction and whether it was on non-market terms. Nothing in the exemption reaches key management personnel compensation or the disclosure of the parent's name.

citation.ref: para 25, 26 and 27

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Splitting a compound financial instrument
concepts.statement: A bond convertible by the holder into a fixed number of the issuer's own ordinary shares is a single non-derivative instrument holding both a liability and an equity component, and the two are presented separately in the balance sheet. The split is a residual one and only in that direction: the liability component is measured first, as the fair value of a similar liability without the conversion feature, and the equity component is whatever is left of the fair value of the instrument as a whole. Any embedded derivative other than the equity conversion option stays inside the liability component. No gain or loss arises on splitting, and the classification is never revised because conversion has become more or less likely.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 107 — Liquidity and market risk disclosures
concepts.statement: For each type of risk arising from financial instruments the entity gives the qualitative picture — the exposures and how they arise, its objectives, policies and processes for managing the risk, the methods used to measure it, and any change from last year — and summary quantitative data on the basis of what goes internally to key management personnel. For liquidity risk it gives a maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities and a separate one for derivative financial liabilities showing remaining contractual maturities, at contractual undiscounted cash flows rather than balance sheet carrying amounts, with an issued financial guarantee contract entering at its maximum amount in the earliest period the guarantee could be called. For market risk it gives a sensitivity analysis for each type, showing the effect on profit or loss and on equity of changes that were reasonably possible at the reporting date, unless it uses a value-at-risk analysis instead.

citation.ref: para 33, 34, 39 and 40, with Appendix B, para B11C and B11D

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 27 — Measuring investments in separate financial statements
concepts.statement: In separate financial statements an entity accounts for investments in subsidiaries, joint ventures and associates either at cost or in accordance with Ind AS 109, and it must apply the same accounting for each category of investments. There is no third option: the equity method that IAS 27 permits was deliberately left out of Ind AS 27, on the reasoning that the equity method is a manner of consolidation rather than a measurement basis like cost or fair value. An investment carried at cost moves to Ind AS 105 when it is classified as held for sale, while one carried under Ind AS 109 does not change. A dividend from a subsidiary, joint venture or associate is recognised in profit or loss when the right to receive it is established.

citation.ref: para 10, 11A and 12, with the Comparison with IAS 27, item 2

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 29 — Restating in a hyperinflationary economy
concepts.statement: Ind AS 29 sets no absolute rate at which hyperinflation arises; it lists indicators, of which cumulative inflation over three years approaching or exceeding 100 per cent is only one, and leaves the call to judgement. Once made, the Standard applies from the beginning of the reporting period in which the entity identifies the hyperinflation, not from the day the index crossed anything. Financial statements are then stated in the measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period, comparatives included. Balance sheet amounts not already in that unit are restated by a general price index; monetary items are not restated because they are already in it; all items in the statement of profit and loss are restated; and the gain or loss on the net monetary position goes to profit or loss and is separately disclosed.

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 106 — Exploration and evaluation assets
concepts.statement: Exploration and evaluation assets are measured at cost on recognition, and after recognition the entity may keep the cost model or apply a revaluation model consistent with whether it has classified the assets as tangible or intangible. Expenditure on the development of mineral resources is outside the definition and cannot be recognised as an exploration and evaluation asset. The moment the technical feasibility and commercial viability of extracting a mineral resource are demonstrable the assets stop being exploration and evaluation assets, and they must be tested for impairment and any loss recognised before they are reclassified. For impairment the entity sets its own policy for allocating the assets to cash-generating units, but no such unit or group of units may be larger than an operating segment.

concepts.subsection: Corporate social responsibility — accounting for the amount left unspent
concepts.statement: Since 22 January 2021 an unspent corporate social responsibility amount is a statutory obligation rather than a matter for explanation in the Board's report alone, so at the reporting date it is a liability and not merely a disclosure. Where the unspent amount relates to an ongoing project it is transferred within thirty days of the end of the financial year to a special account with a scheduled bank called the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account for that financial year, and must be spent within three financial years of the transfer, failing which it goes to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days of the end of the third financial year. Where it does not relate to an ongoing project it goes straight to a Fund specified in Schedule VII, within six months of the expiry of the financial year. The Board still gives its reasons for not spending.

citation.ref: section 135(5), third proviso, and section 135(6), both as substituted with effect from 22 January 2021

concepts.subsection: Integrated reporting — capitals, guiding principles and content elements
concepts.statement: The International <IR> Framework categorises the resources an organisation uses and affects into six capitals — financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, and natural. Seven guiding principles underpin how a report is prepared and presented, and eight content elements are put as questions to be answered rather than as a checklist of specific disclosures. The categories are a guideline, not a template: the Framework does not require an integrated report to adopt them or to be structured along the lines of the capitals, and an organisation may categorise differently, the point of the list being that it does not overlook a capital it uses or affects.

citation.ref: January 2021 revision, para 2.15, 2.17, 2.19, 3.1, 4.1 and 4.3

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 117 — The general measurement model
concepts.statement: A group of insurance contracts is measured, on initial recognition, as the total of two things and no others — the fulfilment cash flows and the contractual service margin. The fulfilment cash flows are themselves three components: an explicit, unbiased and probability-weighted estimate of the future cash flows within the contract boundary, an adjustment discounting those cash flows for the time value of money and for financial risk, and a risk adjustment for non-financial risk, which is the compensation the entity requires for bearing the uncertainty about the amount and timing of those cash flows. Where the fulfilment cash flows are a net inflow, the contractual service margin is set at exactly the amount that leaves no income and no expense arising on initial recognition, so the group is carried at nil and there is no day-one profit.

citation.ref: the general measurement model — measurement on initial recognition as the fulfilment cash flows plus the contractual service margin, and the three components of the fulfilment cash flows (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 117 — The contractual service margin
concepts.statement: The contractual service margin is the unearned profit in a group of insurance contracts, and it is carried forward rather than earned. Over the life of the group it is rolled forward in a fixed order — the effect of contracts added to the group, interest accreted on the margin at the discount rate fixed when the group was first recognised, the effect of changes in fulfilment cash flows that relate to FUTURE service, the effect of currency exchange differences, and last of all the amount released to profit or loss for the insurance contract services actually transferred in the period, measured by coverage units. The dividing line that matters is service: a change in estimate touching future service adjusts the margin, while a change touching current or past service — an adverse development on claims already incurred, for instance — goes straight to profit or loss and never near the margin.

citation.ref: subsequent measurement of the contractual service margin — the roll-forward for contracts without direct participation features, and the future service versus past service divide (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 117 — A group of contracts that is onerous
concepts.statement: A group of insurance contracts is onerous on initial recognition when its fulfilment cash flows are a net outflow. There is no negative contractual service margin to absorb it: the margin is nil, the whole net outflow is recognised as a loss in profit or loss immediately, and the entity establishes a loss component of the liability for remaining coverage equal to that loss. The loss component is then tracked separately, and subsequent favourable changes in fulfilment cash flows relating to future service reverse the loss component down to nil before any contractual service margin can be re-established.

citation.ref: onerous contracts — a group whose fulfilment cash flows are a net outflow on initial recognition, the immediate loss, and the loss component of the liability for remaining coverage (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 117 — The premium allocation approach
concepts.statement: The premium allocation approach is a permitted simplification of the liability for remaining coverage, not the default and not a requirement. An entity may choose it for a group only if one of two gates opens at the inception of that group — either the entity reasonably expects the simplification would produce a measurement of the liability for remaining coverage not materially different from the general measurement model, or the coverage period of every contract in the group is a year or less. The first gate is closed where the entity expects significant variability in the fulfilment cash flows before a claim is paid. Choosing the simplification changes how the remaining coverage is measured; it does not switch off the onerous test, and it does not touch the liability for incurred claims, which is still measured on fulfilment cash flows.

citation.ref: the premium allocation approach — its optional character, the two eligibility gates tested at inception of the group, the significant-variability bar on the first gate, and the onerous test surviving (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Cash flows on acquiring and disposing of a subsidiary
concepts.statement: The aggregate cash flows from obtaining or losing control of a subsidiary are presented as a single separate line and classified as investing, and the amount shown is the cash consideration actually paid or received NET of the cash and cash equivalents that came in or went out with the subsidiary. Consideration settled in the acquirer's own shares is a non-cash transaction and never enters the statement. A change in ownership interest that does NOT cost the parent control is a transaction with owners, so its cash flows are financing, not investing. Alongside all this the entity discloses in aggregate the total consideration, how much of it was cash and cash equivalents, the cash and cash equivalents in the subsidiary, and the other assets and liabilities involved.

citation.ref: para 39 to 42B, with the exclusion of non-cash transactions in para 43

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Treasury shares
concepts.statement: An entity's own equity instruments reacquired by the entity, or by any other member of the consolidated group, are treasury shares and are deducted from equity. No gain and no loss goes to profit or loss on their purchase, sale, issue or cancellation, whatever happens to the market price, and the consideration paid or received is recognised directly in equity. The shares are not a financial asset of the group, so they are never fair-valued through profit or loss and never impaired. The amount of treasury shares held is disclosed separately, in the balance sheet or in the notes.

citation.ref: para 33 and 34

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Offsetting a financial asset against a financial liability
concepts.statement: A financial asset and a financial liability are offset and the net amount presented when, and only when, both conditions hold together — the entity currently has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts, and it intends either to settle net or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. Currently is the word that does the work: a right exercisable only on a future event such as the counterparty's default is not a current right, which is why an ordinary master netting arrangement does not on its own permit offsetting. Both conditions must also survive the ordinary course of business, not merely the event of default or insolvency.

citation.ref: para 42, read with the conditions elaborated in paras 43 to 50

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Reversing an impairment loss
concepts.statement: At the end of every reporting period the entity looks for any indication that an impairment loss recognised in an earlier period on an asset other than goodwill no longer exists or has decreased, and reverses it if, and only if, the estimates used to determine recoverable amount have changed since that loss was recognised. The reversal is capped: the increased carrying amount must not exceed the carrying amount, net of depreciation, that would have stood had no impairment loss ever been recognised. The reversal goes to profit or loss unless the asset is carried at a revalued amount, and the depreciation charge is then reset over the remaining life. An impairment loss recognised for goodwill is never reversed.

citation.ref: para 110, 114, 117 and 119, with the goodwill bar in para 124

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — What goes into a restructuring provision
concepts.statement: Once a restructuring provision is due to be recognised, its amount is confined to the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring — those both necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. Retraining or relocating continuing staff, marketing, and investment in new systems and distribution networks are named as excluded, because they relate to the future conduct of the business. Identifiable future operating losses up to the date of the restructuring are excluded too, unless they arise on a contract that is itself onerous.

citation.ref: para 80, 81 and 82, read with the obligating event in para 72

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Offsetting and presenting tax balances
concepts.statement: Current tax assets and current tax liabilities are offset only where there is a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net or to realise and settle simultaneously. Deferred tax assets and liabilities carry a harder test: the same legally enforceable right to set off CURRENT tax balances must exist, and the deferred balances must relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation authority on either the same taxable entity or different taxable entities that intend to settle net in every future period in which material amounts reverse. Two members of one group are two taxable entities, so their deferred tax balances do not offset in the consolidated balance sheet merely because they are consolidated. No deferred tax balance is ever classified as current.

citation.ref: para 71 and 74, with the classification bar in Ind AS 1 para 56

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 19 — The asset ceiling on a plan surplus
concepts.statement: A surplus in a defined benefit plan is not automatically an asset of the employer. Where plan assets exceed the present value of the obligation, the net defined benefit asset is measured at the LOWER of that surplus and the asset ceiling, the asset ceiling being the present value of the economic benefits actually available to the entity in the form of refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions to it. Any change in the effect of the asset ceiling, other than the part already inside net interest, is a remeasurement: it goes to other comprehensive income and is never reclassified to profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 64, with the remeasurement components in para 127 and the OCI treatment in para 120 and 122

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — A change in functional currency
concepts.statement: A functional currency, once determined, changes only when the underlying transactions, events and conditions relevant to it change — it is not a policy choice and it is not revisited for convenience. When it does change, the translation procedures for the new functional currency are applied PROSPECTIVELY from the date of the change: every item is translated into the new functional currency at the exchange rate ruling on that date, and the translated amounts of non-monetary items are treated from then on as their historical cost. Nothing is restated, and exchange differences already accumulated in other comprehensive income on translating a foreign operation stay in equity until that operation is disposed of.

citation.ref: para 35 to 37 on a change in functional currency, read with the reclassification on disposal in para 48

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — When the plan of sale changes
