concepts.statement: When an asset no longer meets the held-for-sale criteria, classification ceases, and the asset comes back onto the balance sheet at the LOWER of two figures: its carrying amount before it was ever classified as held for sale, adjusted for the depreciation, amortisation or revaluation that would have been recognised had it never been classified; and its recoverable amount at the date of the decision not to sell. The suspended depreciation is caught up, not forgiven. Any adjustment falls in profit or loss from CONTINUING operations in the period the criteria stop being met, in the same caption used for a gain or loss on remeasurement.

citation.ref: para 26, 27 and 28

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 108 — Aggregating operating segments
concepts.statement: Two or more operating segments may be combined into one only where the aggregation is consistent with the core principle of the Standard, the segments have similar economic characteristics, AND they are similar in each of five respects — the nature of the products and services, the nature of the production processes, the type or class of customer, the methods used to distribute the products or provide the services, and, where applicable, the nature of the regulatory environment. Similar economic characteristics alone is not enough, and geography is not on the list. Segments that fail the quantitative thresholds may be combined with each other only where they share similar economic characteristics and a majority of those five respects; anything left over goes into an all other segments category.

citation.ref: para 12, read with para 14 and 16

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 112 — Disclosing interests in other entities
concepts.statement: Ind AS 112 is the disclosure standard that sits behind Ind AS 110, 111 and 28, and it asks two distinct things. First, the significant judgements and assumptions made in deciding that the entity has control, joint control or significant influence, and in deciding the type of joint arrangement — so a conclusion of control on less than half the voting rights has to be explained, not merely reached. Second, entity-by-entity information about each subsidiary whose NON-CONTROLLING INTERESTS are material to the reporting entity, including the proportion of ownership interests and voting rights held by those interests, the profit or loss allocated to them, their accumulated balance, and summarised financial information about the subsidiary. The trigger is the materiality of the non-controlling interests, not the size of the subsidiary. Ind AS 112 does not apply to separate financial statements prepared under Ind AS 27.

citation.ref: para 7 and 12, with the separate financial statements carve-out in para 6

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 113 — Highest and best use of a non-financial asset
concepts.statement: The fair value of a non-financial asset assumes the use that maximises its value in the hands of MARKET PARTICIPANTS, whether by using the asset themselves or by selling it to another market participant who would. The use must be physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible, and all three are tested. The entity's own current use is presumed to be the highest and best use, but the presumption falls the moment market or other factors show a different use would maximise value, and the entity's intention is irrelevant — an asset bought and deliberately left idle to protect a competitive position is still measured on the use a market participant would make of it. Costs a market participant would have to incur to reach that use, such as clearing a site, come off the price.

citation.ref: para 27, 28, 29 and 30

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — The discount rate and variable lease payments
concepts.statement: A lessee discounts the lease payments at the interest rate implicit in the lease where that rate can be readily determined, and otherwise at its own incremental borrowing rate — the rate it would have to pay to borrow, over a similar term and with similar security, the funds needed to obtain an asset of similar value in a similar economic environment. A cost of capital is not that rate. The payments discounted are fixed payments less lease incentives receivable, variable payments that depend on an INDEX OR A RATE measured using the index or rate at the commencement date, amounts expected to be payable under residual value guarantees, the exercise price of a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, and termination penalties. A payment that varies with sales or usage is none of those, so it stays out of the liability and is charged to profit or loss in the period the triggering event occurs.

citation.ref: para 26 and 27, with the treatment of excluded variable payments in para 38(b)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — The statement of changes in equity
concepts.statement: The statement of changes in equity is a primary statement, not a note. It shows total comprehensive income for the period split between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests, the effects of retrospective application or retrospective restatement recognised under Ind AS 8 shown for each component of equity, and, for each component, a reconciliation from opening to closing balance separately disclosing the changes from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income, and from transactions with owners in their capacity as owners. Dividends are a distribution to owners: they are presented here or in the notes, with the amount per share, and never as an expense in profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 106, 106A and 107, read with the restatement requirement in Ind AS 8 para 42

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 Appendix B — A cash-settled award modified to equity-settled
concepts.statement: Where the terms of a cash-settled share-based payment are modified so that it becomes equity-settled, three things happen on the modification date and all three happen at once. The equity-settled award is measured by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments granted AT THE MODIFICATION DATE, and the amount taken to equity is the portion of that fair value relating to the goods or services already received up to that date. The liability for the cash-settled award is derecognised on that date. Any difference between the carrying amount of the liability derecognised and the amount recognised in equity goes immediately to profit or loss. Nothing is carried forward and nothing is remeasured afterwards.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B44A, B44B and B44C

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 34 — Segment disclosure in an interim report
concepts.statement: Segment information appears in an interim report only where Ind AS 108 requires that same entity to disclose segment information in its ANNUAL financial statements — an entity outside Ind AS 108 does not acquire segment reporting by publishing a half-year report. Where it does apply, what is given is a short list, not the annual note: revenues from external customers and intersegment revenues where they sit in or are provided to the chief operating decision maker's measure, a measure of segment profit or loss, total assets and liabilities of a segment only where those are regularly provided to the chief operating decision maker AND have changed materially since the last annual balance sheet, a description of any change in the basis of segmentation or of measurement, and a reconciliation of the reportable segments' profit or loss to the entity's own.

citation.ref: para 16A(g), read with para 15

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — What Schedule III prescribes and what it does not
concepts.statement: Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 fixes the format and content of a company's financial statements and stops there. It does not prescribe the accounting treatment to be adopted, so the fact that a particular item appears in the format of the balance sheet does not imply that the item may be recognised — recognition is a matter for the notified standards, which Schedule III itself acknowledges and to which it grants overriding status. Three further consequences follow. Schedule III prescribes only the vertical format of the balance sheet and offers no horizontal alternative, though it allows line items, sub-line items and sub-totals to be added or substituted where that is relevant to understanding the company's position or performance. Its disclosure requirements are in addition to, and not in substitution of, those in the notified standards, and the terms it uses take their meaning from those standards. And the proviso to section 129(1) keeps insurance companies and banking companies outside it altogether, their formats being prescribed by their own regulators.

citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — Schedule III, read with the proviso to section 129(1)

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — Materiality as the filter for disclosure
concepts.statement: Materiality is the filter that decides what goes into the financial statements and what stays out, and the lack of clarity in how to apply it is one of the main drivers of overloaded financial statements. Information is disclosed only if it is material, meaning only if it could influence the decisions users take on the basis of those statements. The filter runs in both directions. Downwards it strips clutter. Upwards it catches what is individually immaterial and material in aggregate — several separately small commitments to buy items of property, plant and equipment together amount to a material capital commitment and are disclosed as one. Size is not the whole of the judgement either: a revenue stream under five per cent of total revenue may still warrant separate segment disclosure where the company has told its stakeholders that it is the strategic direction of the business and the revenue is growing rapidly, even though other streams of similar size are combined into other revenue. Once the line items needing disclosure are settled, the same judgement decides how much detail to give about each and how best to organise it.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, materiality

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — Integrating notes, policies and judgements
concepts.statement: The notes cover the largest portion of a set of financial statements and have the greatest effect on how well those statements communicate, so best practice is to group them into categories, place the most critical information prominently, and integrate the main note on a line item with the accounting policy for that item and with the key estimates and judgements behind it. An inventory note carries the cost formula, the lower of cost and net realisable value policy, the estimation uncertainty in net realisable value and the figures together, in one place. The matching discipline is that accounting policies are disclosed in one place and not scattered across various notes — a policy of writing off in full assets costing less than five thousand rupees belongs in the accounting policy for fixed assets, not buried in the fixed asset note. Only material accounting policies are disclosed, and non-material policy text that adds no value is removed. Disclosures about estimates focus on the most difficult, subjective and complex of them, with how the estimate was derived, the key assumptions, the review process and a sensitivity analysis.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, integration of notes and disclosure of material accounting policies

concepts.subsection: Analysis of financial statements — A staff housing loan below the market rate
concepts.statement: A housing loan advanced to an employee below the market rate is a financial asset and an employee benefit at the same time, and recording it at the amount disbursed gets both of them wrong. Ind AS 109 measures the loan on initial recognition at fair value, which here is the contracted receipts discounted at the market rate for a similar housing loan, so a loan carrying a below-market rate comes on to the balance sheet below the sum lent. The shortfall is not a loss of the year. It is the value the employee receives, and because the employee has to remain in service to keep the concession it is carried as prepaid employee cost and amortised over the loan period on a straight line basis as an employee benefit under Ind AS 19 — irrespective of the employee not being required to give any specific performance against the benefit. Interest is then recognised as finance income at the effective interest rate, which is the market rate used to discount, not at the rate contracted. Deferred tax is recognised on the temporary differences the restatement creates.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — case study on a concessional staff housing loan, read with Ind AS 109 and Ind AS 19

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — The five fundamental principles
concepts.statement: ICAI's Code of Ethics of 2019, applicable from 1 July 2020 and derived from the IESBA Code of 2018, sets five fundamental principles and a Chartered Accountant shall comply with each of them. Integrity is to be straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships. Objectivity is not to compromise professional or business judgement because of bias, conflict of interest or the undue influence of others. Professional competence and due care is to attain and maintain the knowledge and skill a client or employing organisation needs for competent service, and to act diligently in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards. Confidentiality is to respect information acquired through professional and business relationships. Professional behaviour is to comply with relevant laws and regulations and to avoid any conduct the accountant knows or should know might discredit the profession. Where local regulation differs from the Code the more stringent provision applies unless the law forbids it. Where two principles conflict the accountant might consult others in the firm or employing organisation, those charged with governance, the Institute or legal counsel — but no consultation relieves him of the responsibility to exercise professional judgement and, if necessary, to disassociate from the matter creating the conflict.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the fundamental principles

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — The conceptual framework and the informed third party test
concepts.statement: The Code does not attempt to list every situation. It gives a conceptual framework the accountant applies in three steps — identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, evaluate the threats identified, and address them by eliminating them or reducing them to an acceptable level. In applying it the accountant shall exercise professional judgement, remain alert for new information and for changes in facts and circumstances, and use the reasonable and informed third party test. That test asks whether the same conclusions would likely be reached by another party weighing all the relevant facts and circumstances the accountant knows, or could reasonably be expected to know, at the time the conclusions are made. The third party need not be an accountant; what is required is the knowledge and experience to understand and evaluate the appropriateness of the conclusions impartially. Professional judgement here means asking whether relevant information might be missing, whether the known facts sit oddly against expectations, whether the accountant's own expertise is sufficient, whether someone else should be consulted, and whether the accountant's own preconception or bias might be affecting the judgement.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the conceptual framework

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Confidentiality and the circumstances that override it
concepts.statement: Confidentiality binds the accountant to information acquired through professional and employment relationships, and it survives the relationship: on changing employer or taking a new client the accountant is entitled to use prior experience but shall not use or disclose confidential information acquired or received earlier. It is not absolute. Disclosure may be required by law — producing documents or other evidence in legal proceedings, or disclosing infringements of law that come to light to the appropriate public authorities. It may be permitted by law and authorised by the client or employing organisation. And there may be a professional duty or right to disclose where the law does not prohibit it: to comply with a peer review or quality review of the Institute, to respond to an inquiry or investigation by a professional or regulatory body, to protect the accountant's professional interests in legal proceedings, and to comply with technical and professional standards including ethics requirements. Confidentiality is never a cover for the accountant's own advantage or a third party's, which is why insider trading breaches it, and it is not a reason to hide material facts that require disclosure — reporting fraud, illegal activity or non-compliance with laws and regulations does not constitute a breach at all.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — confidentiality

concepts.subsection: Code of Ethics — Information that is or might be misleading
concepts.statement: When preparing or presenting information the accountant shall use a relevant reporting framework, shall not intend to mislead or to influence a contractual or regulatory outcome inappropriately, shall represent the facts accurately and completely in all material respects, describe clearly the true nature of the transactions, classify and record in a timely and proper manner, and omit nothing with the intention of misleading. Discretion is where this bites, and the Code names the misuses: determining a fair value estimate in order to misrepresent profit or loss, selecting between policies permitted by the framework in order to misrepresent profit or loss, timing the sale of an asset near the year end in order to mislead, structuring a financing transaction in order to misrepresent assets and liabilities or the classification of cash flows, and selecting disclosures so as to omit or obscure information about financial or operating risk. Where the accountant knows or has reason to believe that information he is associated with is misleading, the response is a ladder — raise it with the superior, management or those charged with governance and ask for correction and, where it has already gone out, for the users to be told; consult the organisation's own ethics or whistle-blowing policy; then consult the Institute, the internal or external auditor or legal counsel, and determine whether anything must be communicated to third parties or to regulatory and oversight authorities. If after exhausting all feasible options the information is still misleading, the accountant shall refuse to be or to remain associated with the information, and resignation might be appropriate.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — preparation and presentation of information

concepts.subsection: Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 — The clause a member in service is charged under
concepts.statement: A member in employment who lets a wrong accounting treatment through is not charged under the clauses written for a member in practice, and knowing which Schedule and Part applies is the whole of the answer. Section 22 makes professional or other misconduct include any act or omission in any of the Schedules, and section 21 is the disciplinary route. Professional misconduct sits in Parts I, II and III of the First Schedule and Parts I and II of the Second Schedule; other misconduct sits in Part IV of the First Schedule and Part III of the Second Schedule. Part I of the Second Schedule holds ten clauses and applies to a Chartered Accountant in practice — among them failing to disclose a material fact necessary to a financial statement he is concerned with professionally (clause 5), failing to report a known material misstatement (clause 6), not exercising due diligence or being grossly negligent in professional duties (clause 7), and failing to obtain information sufficient for the expression of an opinion (clause 8). Part II of the Second Schedule holds four clauses and applies to members generally, and its clause 1 is contravening any provision of the Act, the regulations, or any guidelines issued by the Council — read with the Council Guidelines, which state that a member who is an employee shall exercise due diligence and shall not be grossly negligent in the conduct of his duties. That is the route by which a CFO or an accountant in service is held guilty. Part III of the Second Schedule holds one clause: a member, whether in practice or not, is guilty of other misconduct if held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the Schedules, read with sections 21 and 22 and the Council Guidelines

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Robotic process automation in the reporting cycle
concepts.statement: Robotic process automation puts software robots, called bots, on the manual, repetitive and rule-bound parts of financial data processing, analysis and reporting. The bots mimic a person's interactions with the digital systems rather than replacing those systems. On a group consolidation they extract financial data from each subsidiary's own system and consolidate it into the parent's, perform the necessary currency conversions, identify and reconcile intercompany transactions and generate the elimination entries Ind AS 110 requires so that nothing is counted twice, compute the amounts attributable to non-controlling interests and the comprehensive income attributable to the parent, and produce the consolidated balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, statement of changes in equity and cash flow statement. What that buys is accuracy, timely reporting, cost saving and data integrity, and it frees finance people for work that needs judgement. What it does not buy is judgement itself — a bot applies the rules it was given and nothing more.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — robotic process automation, read with Ind AS 110

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Cloud service models and what they change
concepts.statement: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet, and the shapes it takes differ by how much of the stack the provider runs. Cloud storage keeps files reachable and synchronised from any connected device. Software as a service delivers finished cloud-based applications over the internet, with nothing installed — accounting and financial management, customer relationship management, team collaboration. Infrastructure as a service rents virtualised computing resources, being servers, storage and networking, on a pay-as-you-go basis, so a business scales its IT infrastructure on demand without buying physical hardware. Platform as a service gives developers a cloud-based platform on which to build, deploy and manage applications without the complexity of managing the infrastructure underneath. What the accounting function gains is accessibility from any location, security features such as encryption, firewalls and multi-factor authentication, scalability without new hardware, lower upfront and maintenance cost, real-time collaboration with version control that leaves an audit trail of revisions, and stronger reporting and analytics. What it risks is that an entirely online system is exposed to attackers who could steal data or passwords or compromise the integrity of processed data, and that it depends on connectivity, which is not evenly developed outside the metros.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — cloud computing, its applications, benefits and challenges

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Building internal control over financial reporting into an ERP
concepts.statement: An ERP is designed around a single defined data structure with a common database, so information entered by one department is immediately available to authorised users across the business and there is one source of authentication instead of several reconciled versions. Integrating internal control over financial reporting into it turns controls into system behaviour rather than a checklist run afterwards. The illustrative steps include keeping the financial closing process aligned with the reporting requirements and deadlines the regulators set; tracking and validating every change to the closing and reporting process through the system's change management functionality, and confirming from the system logs and audit trail that the change was authorised by a designated individual with the appropriate authority; defining roles through the user access matrix configuration together with a responsibility assignment matrix, which records who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed; assessing the qualifications and training records of the people in financial reporting roles; documenting and approving the choice between alternative accounting treatments and communicating it to the audit committee; running KYC validation controls on account masters and separate ledger coding for related parties so that Schedule III disclosure can be tabulated automatically; and using the audit trail with the accounting period configuration controls, and the posting date against the transaction date, to confirm every posting fell in the correct period and to prevent backdating or unauthorised adjustments.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — illustrative steps for integrating internal control over financial reporting within an ERP

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Cybersecurity threats and the measures against them
concepts.statement: The threats an accounting function faces are named and distinct, and each aims at stealing sensitive financial data, disrupting operations or extracting a ransom. Phishing tricks a user into clicking a malicious link or providing sensitive information. Malware infects computers or networks with software that steals data or disrupts operations. Ransomware encrypts files or locks users out of systems and demands a payment in exchange for restoring access. An insider threat is a malicious act by an employee or other insider who already has access to sensitive data. A denial of service attack overwhelms a system or network with traffic to disrupt it. A supply chain attack compromises third-party software or hardware in order to get in. The proactive measures are equally specific: complex passwords changed regularly, encryption of sensitive data in transmission and in storage, access control limited to authorised personnel and reviewed whenever the management or employee structure changes, network security with firewalls, employee training, regular data backups stored securely, and an incident response plan with procedures for detecting, containing and mitigating an attack. A breach is not only an IT matter — the Information Technology Act, 2000 governs the collection, storage and transmission of financial data, organisations have legal and ethical obligations to disclose incidents with financial implications, and the reporting guidelines of regulators such as SEBI and RBI address disclosure of cybersecurity incidents in financial statements.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — cybersecurity in accounting

concepts.subsection: Accounting and technology — Blockchain and financial reporting
concepts.statement: A blockchain is a decentralised ledger shared across a network, in which each transaction is verified by multiple participants and encrypted so that it cannot afterwards be altered, which removes the need for intermediaries and central authorities. For financial reporting that changes several things at once. Transparency, because the record is visible and tamper-proof and can be audited easily. Data integrity, because unauthorised modification is prevented rather than merely detected afterwards. Audit, because the auditor can access the ledger directly to verify transactions instead of reconciling data pulled from different systems. Reconciliation, because a single shared source of truth removes the need to reconcile multiple versions of the same data across systems. Cost, because third-party verification and reconciliation fall away. The audit trail, which is comprehensive and immutable, so an irregularity or discrepancy is easier to identify and investigate. And timeliness, because real-time data availability lets financial reporting be done more frequently and still accurately.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — key impacts of blockchain on financial reporting

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — Convergence with IFRS is not adoption of IFRS
concepts.statement: Adoption means the country applies IFRS in the same manner as issued by the IASB and is one hundred per cent compliant with it. Convergence means the national standard setter works with the IASB to develop the standards over time, having adopted IFRS with some exceptions and working towards a point where no differences are left. India converged. Ind AS carry carve-outs and carve-ins made for the local regulatory landscape, business practice, tax and other provisions, so they are not IFRS as issued. The consequence is a hard one and it comes from the IASB's own rule: full application of its standards and interpretations, including IFRS 1 on first-time adoption, is what allows an entity to assert that its financial statements comply with IFRS, and an entity that applies IFRS as amended by a local authority cannot assert compliance with IFRS. Canada, Bahrain and Cambodia are among the jurisdictions that adopted; India, China and Hong Kong are among those that converged.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — convergence versus adoption of IFRS

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — Net worth for the Ind AS roadmap
concepts.statement: Whether Ind AS applies to a company under the MCA roadmap turns on net worth, and net worth carries the meaning in clause 57 of section 2 of the Companies Act, 2013 — the aggregate value of the paid-up share capital and all reserves created out of the profits and the securities premium account, after deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not written off, as per the audited balance sheet, but not including reserves created out of revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation or amalgamation. It is computed on the standalone financial statements as at 31 March 2014, or on the first audited financial statements for a period ending after that date for a company not then in existence or crossing a threshold for the first time later. A company that does not meet the criteria on the cut-off date reassesses at each balance sheet date, and a company that meets them once stays in, whatever its net worth does afterwards. Ind AS once required applies to the standalone and the consolidated financial statements alike. Phase I covers listed companies with net worth of five hundred crore or more and unlisted companies of that size, plus their holding, subsidiary, joint venture and associate companies, from periods beginning on or after 1 April 2016; Phase II covers listed companies below five hundred crore and unlisted companies of two hundred and fifty crore or more, and their group companies, from 1 April 2017. Companies listed only on an SME exchange are outside the roadmap.

citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — roadmap for applicability, read with section 2(57) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Introduction to Ind AS — How an Ind AS is made and who notifies it
concepts.statement: Accounting standards in India are formulated by the Accounting Standards Board of the ICAI, but the ICAI does not put them into force. The sequence is fixed. The ASB prepares a preliminary draft carrying the carve-ins and carve-outs it considers necessary, giving weight to the local regulatory landscape, business practice and tax provisions. The draft goes to the Council members of the ICAI and to specified outside bodies — the MCA, SEBI, the C&AG and the CBDT among them — and the ASB meets their representatives to hear their views. An exposure draft is then finalised and issued for public comment. The comments are considered, the ASB finalises and submits to the Council of the ICAI for approval, and the Council may modify the draft in consultation with the ASB. The final draft goes to the NFRA with the ICAI's recommendation, the NFRA reviews and provides its inputs, and only then does the MCA notify the standard under the Companies Act by publishing it in the Gazette of India, with an announcement of the applicability date. The central government prescribes the standards as recommended by the ICAI, in consultation with and after examination of the recommendations made by the NFRA, and only a notified standard is authoritative under Indian law.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — process of development and finalisation of Indian Accounting Standards

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — Previous GAAP carrying amount as deemed cost, all or nothing
concepts.statement: A first-time adopter has four ways of measuring property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and right-of-use assets in the opening Ind AS balance sheet, and they do not all behave the same way. Applying the relevant standards retrospectively, using fair value at the date of transition, and using a previous GAAP revaluation that was at its date broadly comparable to fair value or to cost or depreciated cost adjusted for a general or specific price index may each be chosen item by item, one plant retrospectively and another at fair value. The fourth is different: continuing with the previous GAAP carrying amount is available only where there is no change in functional currency, and only if it is applied to all of the asset classes and every item within them. It also extends to investment property, which is the only route to deemed cost there, since Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model and fair value as deemed cost is therefore not available for investment property. Carrying amount means the net book value on the date of transition and not the original cost, so future depreciation runs on that net book value over the remaining useful life, reviewed at least annually as Ind AS 16 requires. Different entities within a group may choose different bases in their own standalone financial statements; for the consolidated financial statements the entire group is treated as one reporting entity and different bases across its entities are not permissible.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — deemed cost for property, plant and equipment, intangible assets and right-of-use assets, paragraphs D5 to D7AA

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — The mandatory exception for derecognition
concepts.statement: Ind AS 101 has two kinds of relief and they run in opposite directions. An optional exemption is an election the first-time adopter may take. A mandatory exception is a prohibition on going back, and it binds whether the entity wants it or not. For derecognition the exception is that a first-time adopter shall apply the derecognition requirements in Ind AS 109 prospectively for transactions occurring on or after the date of transition. A non-derivative financial asset or liability derecognised under previous GAAP as the result of a transaction occurring before that date is therefore not recognised again under Ind AS, even where the Ind AS 109 criteria would not have been met — an NBFC that securitised a loan portfolio to a trust before transition, and derecognised it under Indian GAAP, does not bring it back on to the balance sheet. The items return only if a later transaction or event qualifies them for recognition. One door is left open: the entity may apply the derecognition requirements retrospectively from a date of the entity's choosing, but only where the information needed to apply Ind AS 109 to those past transactions was obtained at the time of initially accounting for them, not reconstructed afterwards.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — mandatory exceptions, derecognition of financial assets and financial liabilities

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — Resetting cumulative translation differences at transition
concepts.statement: Ind AS 21 accumulates the exchange differences on translating a foreign operation in a separate component of equity and reclassifies them to profit or loss when the operation is disposed of, so a first-time adopter would in principle have to rebuild that accumulated balance for every foreign operation from the day each was acquired. Ind AS 101 offers an election out of it. If the exemption is used, the first-time adopter need not recognise those translation differences in other comprehensive income from the beginning and need not reclassify the pre-transition cumulative amounts on a later disposal, and the cumulative translation differences are deemed to be zero for all foreign operations at the date of transition. It is not available for one foreign operation and refused for another. The consequence carries to the far end: the gain or loss on a subsequent disposal of a foreign operation shall exclude the translation differences that arose before the date of transition and shall include only those arising after it.

citation.ref: Ch. Ind AS 101 First Time Adoption of Ind AS — optional exemptions, cumulative translation differences

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.statement: Revenue is recognised when (or as) a performance obligation is satisfied by transferring control of the promised good or service to the customer. Transfer of control, not transfer of risks and rewards, is the recognition trigger.

citation.ref: para 31

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 2 — Inventories
concepts.statement: Inventories of items that are not ordinarily interchangeable are costed by specific identification. For the rest, FIFO or weighted average is used. LIFO is not permitted.

citation.ref: para 23 to 25

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Consolidated Financial Statements
concepts.statement: An investor controls an investee only when it has all three elements together — power over the investee, exposure or rights to variable returns, and the ability to use its power to affect those returns. Control does not require a majority shareholding.

citation.ref: para 7

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Financial Instruments
concepts.statement: Loss allowances are measured on an expected credit loss basis, recognised from initial recognition without waiting for a default. For trade receivables the simplified approach applies, and the allowance is always lifetime expected credit losses.

citation.ref: para 5.5.15

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 103 — Business Combinations
concepts.statement: Under the Indian carve-out, a gain on a bargain purchase is recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in capital reserve, not in profit or loss — unlike IFRS 3, which takes it to profit or loss.

citation.ref: para 34 and 36

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers
concepts.statement: A performance obligation is satisfied over time only when one of three criteria is met — the customer consumes the benefit as the entity performs, the customer controls the asset as it is created, or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date. Otherwise control passes at a point in time.

citation.ref: para 35

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
concepts.statement: A provision is recognised only when all three conditions hold — a present obligation, legal or constructive, from a past event; a probable outflow of resources; and a reliable estimate. For a restructuring, the obligating event is announcing the plan to those affected or beginning to implement it, never the board decision alone.

citation.ref: para 14 and 72

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 — Property, Plant and Equipment
concepts.statement: The cost of a major inspection or overhaul that is a condition of continuing to operate an asset is capitalised into the asset's carrying amount when incurred, and any remaining carrying amount of the previous inspection is derecognised — even if the previous inspection's cost was never separately identified.

citation.ref: para 13 and 14

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 21 — The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
concepts.statement: At each reporting date, foreign currency monetary items are translated at the closing rate, with exchange differences to profit or loss. Non-monetary items carried at historical cost stay at the transaction-date rate. Whether an item is money fixes which rate it gets.

citation.ref: para 23

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 38 — Intangible Assets
concepts.statement: Internally generated goodwill is never recognised as an asset, and internally generated brands, mastheads, customer lists and similar items are barred with it. Development costs are the exception, capitalised only from the day all six conditions are demonstrated; research is always expensed.

citation.ref: para 48, 54 and 63

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 108 — Operating Segments
concepts.statement: An operating segment is separately reportable if it crosses ten per cent of combined revenue (internal plus external), of the greater of combined profits or combined losses, or of combined assets — and reportable segments must together cover seventy-five per cent of external revenue, adding segments until they do.

citation.ref: para 13 and 15

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 1 — Presentation of Financial Statements
concepts.statement: A liability is current when the entity lacks, at the reporting date, the right to defer settlement for at least twelve months. A covenant breached by the year end makes the loan payable on demand and therefore current — unless the lender agreed, on or before the reporting date, not to demand payment; a waiver arriving after the year end comes too late to change the classification.

citation.ref: para 74 and 75

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Statement of Cash Flows
concepts.statement: Under the Indian carve-out, an entity other than a financial institution classifies interest paid as a financing cash flow and interest and dividends received as investing — the options IFRS offers are removed. A bank classifies all of them as operating, because lending is its business.

citation.ref: para 33

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Leases
concepts.statement: A lessee recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for every lease, with two elections out — leases of twelve months or less with no purchase option, and leases of low-value assets. The exemptions are elections about recognition, not about whether the contract is a lease.

citation.ref: para 5 and 6

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 36 — Impairment of Assets
concepts.statement: An asset is impaired when its carrying amount exceeds its recoverable amount, and recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use. Higher — the entity keeps the better of selling and using, so either measure alone can clear the asset of impairment.

citation.ref: para 6

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 10 — Events after the Reporting Period
concepts.statement: An event after the reporting period adjusts the financial statements only when it evidences a condition that existed at the reporting date; a condition that arose afterwards is disclosed, not adjusted. Dividends declared after the reporting period are the standard's own worked example — no liability at the reporting date, however certain the declaration.

citation.ref: para 3 and 12

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 105 — Non-current Assets Held for Sale
concepts.statement: Held-for-sale classification needs the asset available for immediate sale in its present condition and the sale highly probable — management committed to a plan, an active programme to find a buyer, active marketing at a reasonable price, and completion expected within a year. Once classified, the asset is measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, and depreciation stops.

citation.ref: para 6-8

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 8 — Policies, Estimates and Errors
concepts.statement: A change in accounting policy is applied retrospectively, restating comparatives as if the new policy had always applied; a change in accounting estimate is recognised prospectively, in the period of change and the future. Where the two are hard to tell apart, the standard itself says treat the change as an estimate. Depreciation method and useful life are estimates; measurement basis is policy.

citation.ref: para 19 and 36

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 23 — Borrowing Costs
concepts.statement: Borrowing costs directly attributable to acquiring, constructing or producing a qualifying asset — one that necessarily takes a substantial period to get ready for its intended use or sale — are capitalised as part of the asset's cost; all other borrowing costs are expensed. Capitalisation is suspended during extended periods when active development pauses, and ends when the asset is substantially ready.

citation.ref: para 8

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 40 — Investment Property
concepts.statement: Ind AS 40 permits only the cost model for investment property — the Indian carve-out removed IAS 40's fair value model. Fair value is still measured and disclosed in the notes, but the balance sheet carries cost less depreciation and impairment. Property held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, not for use in production or administration, is what the standard covers.

citation.ref: measurement after recognition (cost model; fair value model not permitted)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 113 — Fair Value Measurement
concepts.statement: The fair value hierarchy ranks inputs, not techniques: Level 1 is unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical items; Level 2 is other observable inputs — quoted prices for similar items, or corroborated market data; Level 3 is unobservable inputs. A measurement sits at the lowest level of any input significant to it, and Level 1 prices are used unadjusted where available.

citation.ref: para 76, 81 and 86

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 102 — Share-based Payment
concepts.statement: For equity-settled awards to employees, the expense is measured at the fair value of the equity instruments at grant date — and that value is never remeasured, however the share price moves. What does move is the number of awards expected to vest under service and non-market conditions, trued up each period until vesting. Market conditions are priced into grant-date value once and never trued up.

citation.ref: para 10-11

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 19 — Employee Benefits
concepts.statement: Defined benefit cost splits three ways: service cost and net interest go to profit or loss; remeasurements — actuarial gains and losses, and the return on plan assets beyond the amount already in net interest — go to other comprehensive income, and once there they are never reclassified to profit or loss. The split keeps the operating result clear of actuarial volatility without hiding it.

citation.ref: para 120 and 122

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — Investments in Associates
concepts.statement: Twenty per cent or more of voting power presumes significant influence — the power to participate in financial and operating policy decisions — and less than twenty presumes its absence; both presumptions yield to clear demonstration otherwise. Board representation, policy participation, material transactions, interchange of personnel or essential technical dependence can evidence influence below the line. An associate is equity accounted, not consolidated.

citation.ref: para 5-6

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 12 — Income Taxes
concepts.statement: A deferred tax asset on unused tax losses is recognised only to the extent future taxable profit is probable — and a history of recent losses is itself evidence against that. A loss-making entity records the asset only to the extent of taxable temporary differences or convincing other evidence of future profit, such as a firm order book from a cause that has demonstrably ended.

citation.ref: para 34-35

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 109 — Classification of financial assets
concepts.statement: A financial asset is carried at amortised cost only when both tests pass: the business model is to hold and collect contractual cash flows, and those cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest. Held-to-collect with equity-linked returns fails the second; plain-interest bonds bought for trading fail the first. Failures land in fair value categories.

citation.ref: para 4.1.2

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 103 — Non-controlling interest at acquisition
concepts.statement: For each business combination, the acquirer measures qualifying non-controlling interest at either full fair value or the proportionate share of the acquiree's identifiable net assets — a choice made combination by combination, not as a standing policy. The choice sets goodwill: fair value NCI produces full goodwill including the minority's share; the proportionate route recognises only the acquirer's goodwill.

citation.ref: para 19

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 116 — Lessor accounting
concepts.statement: Lessors still classify: a lease that transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership is a finance lease — derecognise the asset, recognise a receivable; otherwise it is an operating lease — keep the asset, book income over the term. Indicators include ownership transfer, a bargain purchase option, the term covering the major part of economic life, and present value of payments amounting to substantially all the fair value. Lessee accounting became single-model; lessor accounting did not.

citation.ref: lessor classification (finance vs operating)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 32 — Liability or equity
concepts.statement: An instrument is classified by substance against the definitions, not by its legal name: a contractual obligation to deliver cash — mandatory redemption, compulsory dividends — makes a financial liability, however the instrument is titled. Preference shares redeemable at the holder's option or on a fixed date are debt; pure discretion over both dividends and redemption keeps an instrument in equity. Classification happens once, at issue.

citation.ref: para 11 and 15

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 33 — EPS and bonus issues
concepts.statement: A bonus issue, split or similar event changes the share count without changing resources, so EPS treats the new count as if it had existed from the beginning of the earliest period presented — restating the comparative EPS too. A fresh issue for cash, by contrast, enters the weighted average only from its date, because new resources arrived then.

citation.ref: para 27-28

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 24 — Related Party Disclosures
concepts.statement: Key management personnel compensation is disclosed in total and by category — short-term, post-employment, other long-term, termination, share-based. Related party disclosure is about relationships and transactions, not approval: arm's length terms may be claimed only if they can be substantiated, and a government-related entity gets a partial exemption for dealings with its government and its sister entities, disclosing the nature and extent instead of every transaction.

citation.ref: para 17

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 34 — Interim Financial Reporting
concepts.statement: Interim statements apply the same accounting policies as the annual ones — a quarter is not a licence for different measurement — and reporting frequency must not change the annual result: measurements run year-to-date, so a third-quarter estimate correction adjusts the year-to-date figures rather than fabricating a standalone quarter. Costs that fail asset definitions at year-end fail them equally at a quarter's end.

citation.ref: para 28

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 37 — Onerous contracts
concepts.statement: A contract whose unavoidable costs of fulfilment exceed the benefits expected under it is onerous, and the present obligation is provided for at once — the unavoidable cost being the lower of the cost of fulfilling and the penalty of exiting. Routine cancellable purchase orders create no obligation, and expected future operating losses of the business generally are never provided for; the onerous contract is the exception because the loss is contracted, not merely forecast.

citation.ref: para 66-68

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 111 — Joint operations and joint ventures
concepts.statement: Joint control is contractually agreed sharing of control where the relevant decisions need unanimous consent. The arrangement's type decides the accounting: joint operators have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities and record their share of each, line by line; joint venturers have rights only to the net assets and equity-account the investment. Structure through a separate vehicle starts, not ends, the classification.

citation.ref: para 7 and 15-16

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 20 — Government grants
concepts.statement: A government grant is recognised only when there is reasonable assurance the entity will comply with its conditions and the grant will be received. Since the 2018 amendment, a grant related to an asset may be presented either as deferred income released over the asset's life, or by deducting it from the asset's carrying amount — the pre-2018 Indian text had removed the deduction option, and stale materials still teach that removal.

citation.ref: para 7 and 24 (as amended 2018)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 101 — First-time adoption
concepts.statement: A first-time adopter may elect deemed cost for property, plant and equipment at the transition date: fair value at that date, or the previous GAAP carrying amount where eligible — instead of rebuilding depreciated cost as if Ind AS had always applied. The elections are optional exemptions from full retrospective application; the general rule remains retrospective, and mandatory exceptions forbid hindsight in estimates.

citation.ref: deemed cost exemption for PPE at transition

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Principal versus agent
concepts.statement: An entity is a principal when it controls the promised good or service before transfer to the customer, reporting gross revenue; an agent arranges for another to provide it, reporting only its fee or commission. Momentary legal title on the way through does not make a principal; inventory risk, primary responsibility for fulfilment and discretion in setting prices indicate control. The revenue difference is presentation, not profit.

citation.ref: para B34-B35

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Loss of control
concepts.statement: When a parent loses control of a subsidiary it derecognises the subsidiary's assets, liabilities and NCI, recognises the consideration received, and measures any retained interest at fair value at that date — that fair value becomes the cost of the new associate or investment. The gain or loss in profit or loss thus includes a remeasurement of the stake kept, not only the stake sold; control is an all-or-nothing line.

citation.ref: para 25

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 16 — Revaluation model
concepts.statement: Under the revaluation model an upward revaluation goes to other comprehensive income and accumulates in equity as revaluation surplus — except to the extent it reverses a decrease earlier charged to profit or loss. A downward revaluation charges profit or loss — except to the extent a surplus for that same asset exists to absorb it. The surplus never passes through profit or loss: on disposal it transfers directly to retained earnings.

citation.ref: para 39-40

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 2 — NRV and the raw materials exception
concepts.statement: Inventories are carried at the lower of cost and net realisable value, item by item — but raw materials are not written down below cost while the finished products they will enter are expected to sell at or above cost. Only when the materials' price decline signals that the finished product's cost exceeds its NRV do the materials write down, with replacement cost as their best available measure.

citation.ref: para 32

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 41 — Agriculture
concepts.statement: Biological assets are measured at each reporting date at fair value less costs to sell, with changes through profit or loss — cost models yield to the market's verdict on living, growing assets. Bearer plants — the tea bush, not the tea leaf — are carved out to Ind AS 16 as plant-like assets, while the produce growing on them stays in Ind AS 41 until harvest, when it moves to Ind AS 2 at its harvest-date fair value as deemed cost.

citation.ref: para 12-13 and scope

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Mandated ratios and disclosures
concepts.statement: Division II of Schedule III requires eleven named ratios in the notes — current ratio, debt-equity, debt service coverage, return on equity, inventory and receivables and payables turnover, net capital turnover, net profit, return on capital employed, return on investment — with the elements of each computation and an explanation wherever a ratio moved more than twenty-five per cent from the prior year. The amendments also demand disclosure of benami proceedings, undisclosed income surrendered, and crypto holdings.

citation.ref: Schedule III Division II (2021 amendments)

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 28 — Sharing an associate's losses
concepts.statement: Equity accounting absorbs an associate's losses only down to zero: once the investor's share of losses equals its interest — the equity-method carrying amount plus long-term interests that are in substance part of the net investment — recognition of further losses stops, resuming only after future profits rebuild the base. Losses beyond zero are provided only where the investor has legal or constructive obligations or made payments for the associate.

citation.ref: para 38-39

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 115 — Constraining variable consideration
concepts.statement: Variable consideration — bonuses, penalties, volume rebates, royalties — enters the transaction price only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur when the uncertainty resolves. Estimation uses the expected value or the most likely amount, whichever predicts better; the constraint then trims the estimate. Booking the hopeful number and reversing later is the pattern the rule exists to stop.

citation.ref: para 56

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 7 — Cash and cash equivalents
concepts.statement: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of value change — normally maturing within about three months of acquisition. Equity investments are excluded save in-substance equivalents. Bank overdrafts repayable on demand that form an integral part of cash management join cash and cash equivalents, turning the statement's bottom line negative-capable.

citation.ref: para 7-8

concepts.subsection: Ind AS 110 — Consolidation procedures
concepts.statement: Consolidation combines like items line by line, eliminates the parent's investment against its share of each subsidiary's equity, and eliminates intragroup balances, transactions and unrealised profits in full — not merely the parent's share. The group reports as one economic entity under uniform accounting policies for like transactions, restating a subsidiary's numbers where its policies differ.

citation.ref: para 19 and B86

concepts.subsection: Board meeting quorum — section 174
concepts.statement: Quorum for a board meeting is the higher of one-third of the total strength of directors (any fraction rounded up) or two directors. A director interested in an item under section 184(2) is left out of the count for that item, and telephonic assent from a director not participating by the prescribed video-conferencing means does not count as presence. Absent quorum, the meeting stands automatically adjourned to the same day the following week, same time and place, unless the articles say otherwise.

citation.ref: Section 174

concepts.subsection: Frequency of board meetings — section 173
concepts.statement: Every company holds at least four board meetings a year, with the gap between two consecutive meetings never exceeding one hundred and twenty days, and the first meeting within thirty days of incorporation. A one person company, small company, dormant company or private start-up needs only one meeting in each half of the calendar year, with a minimum gap of ninety days between the two — a relaxation, not the general rule.

citation.ref: Section 173

concepts.subsection: Board powers needing shareholder approval — section 180
concepts.statement: The board cannot, by its own resolution, sell, lease or otherwise dispose of the whole or substantially the whole of an undertaking, or borrow beyond the aggregate of paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium (ordinary-course temporary bank loans excepted) — both need a special resolution of the shareholders first, obtained before the act, not disclosed to them after it.

citation.ref: Section 180

concepts.subsection: Retirement by rotation — section 152
concepts.statement: Independent directors are never liable to retire by rotation. Of the remaining directors of a public company, at least two-thirds must be liable to rotation, of which one-third (or the number nearest to one-third) retires at every annual general meeting, the director longest in office retiring first and being eligible for reappointment. Articles cannot exempt directors from rotation below this statutory floor.

citation.ref: Section 152(6)

concepts.subsection: Disclosure of directors' interest — section 184
concepts.statement: Every director discloses his concern or interest in any company, body corporate, firm or association of individuals at the first board meeting he attends in a financial year, and again on any change — a duty owed regardless of the size of the interest. Separately, an interested director discloses that interest in a specific contract or arrangement and does not participate in the board's discussion or vote on it; a contract entered in breach is voidable at the company's option.

citation.ref: Section 184

concepts.subsection: Contract of employment with managing or whole-time director — section 190
concepts.statement: A company keeps at its registered office a copy of its managing or whole-time director's contract of service, or a written memorandum of its terms where the contract is not in writing, open for inspection by members without charge during business hours — a members' right the board or the company secretary cannot narrow to itself or to the auditor.

citation.ref: Section 190

concepts.subsection: Consolidated financial statements — section 129(3)
concepts.statement: A company with one or more subsidiaries, including associate companies and joint ventures, prepares a consolidated financial statement in addition to its standalone statements, in the same form and manner, following the applicable accounting standards, and lays it before the annual general meeting alongside the standalone statements. Consolidation covers every subsidiary; it is not a management choice of which ones to fold in.

citation.ref: Section 129(3)

concepts.subsection: Board's report contents — section 134
concepts.statement: The board's report states, among other prescribed particulars, a director's responsibility statement under section 134(5), particulars of loans, guarantees and investments under section 186, particulars of related-party contracts in the prescribed form, the CSR policy and initiatives, and — for listed and other prescribed companies — a statement on the formal annual evaluation of the board, its committees and individual directors. These are matters the report must itself state, not particulars merely available on request.

citation.ref: Section 134(3)

concepts.subsection: Annual return and its certification — section 92
concepts.statement: Every company files its annual return with the Registrar within sixty days of the annual general meeting, or of the date by which the AGM should have been held where none took place, in which case a statement of the reasons for the default goes with it. Section 92(2) leaves the size line to the rules, and Rule 11(2) draws it at a listed company, or a company with paid-up share capital of ₹10 crore or more, or turnover of ₹50 crore or more: such a return must additionally be certified by a company secretary in practice in Form MGT-8. The two size tests are alternatives — crossing either is enough — and listing is a third, independent route in.

citation.ref: Sections 92(2) and 92(4), read with Rule 11(2) of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014 (Form MGT-8)

concepts.subsection: Rights issue procedure — section 62
concepts.statement: A rights issue offer goes to existing equity shareholders in proportion to their holding, stays open for not less than fifteen days and not more than thirty days, and carries a right of renunciation in favour of another person unless the articles exclude it. The board cannot allot before the offer period lapses or ahead of renunciation choices being exercised or declined.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Debentures — trustee and redemption reserve, section 71
concepts.statement: Section 71(5) stops a company from issuing a prospectus, or making an offer or invitation to the public or to more than five hundred of its members, for subscription of its debentures unless it has appointed one or more debenture trustees before that issue or offer. What pulls the trustee in is the kind of offer, not the size of the borrowing — the section names no rupee figure at all. Rule 18(1)(c) adds that the trustee comes before the prospectus or letter of offer goes out, and the debenture trust deed is executed within sixty days of allotment, so an independent party holds the security and enforces the debenture-holders' rights; the issuer's own guarantee is not a substitute for that office. Section 71(4) separately requires a debenture redemption reserve out of profits available for dividend, but Rule 18(7) as it now stands excuses listed companies, NBFCs registered under section 45-IA of the RBI Act and housing finance companies registered with the National Housing Bank; other unlisted companies keep a reserve of ten per cent of the outstanding value of the debentures.

citation.ref: Sections 71(4) and 71(5), read with Rules 18(1)(c) and 18(7) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014

concepts.subsection: Moratorium under the IBC — section 14
concepts.statement: On admission of a corporate insolvency resolution application, the adjudicating authority declares a moratorium barring institution or continuation of suits against the corporate debtor, transfer or disposal of its assets, enforcement of any security interest, and recovery of property by an owner or lessor in the debtor's possession; supply of essential goods and services to the debtor cannot be terminated during this period. The moratorium does not extend to a surety in a contract of guarantee for the corporate debtor.

citation.ref: Section 14

concepts.subsection: CIRP time limit — section 12 of the IBC
concepts.statement: A corporate insolvency resolution process must be completed within one hundred and eighty days of the insolvency commencement date. The committee of creditors may resolve, by a vote of sixty-six per cent of voting share under section 12(2), to instruct the resolution professional to seek one extension of up to ninety days — one only, never a second. The proviso to section 12(3) then caps the whole process at three hundred and thirty days from the insolvency commencement date, and that outer figure expressly swallows the time taken in legal proceedings relating to the process. The Supreme Court in Essar Steel read down the word "mandatorily" so a tribunal may go past three hundred and thirty days in an exceptional case where the delay is the tribunal's own, but that is a rescue, not the rule.

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and the proviso to section 12(3), as inserted by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2019

concepts.subsection: Committee of creditors — related parties and voting thresholds
concepts.statement: The committee of creditors comprises all financial creditors of the corporate debtor, but the first proviso to section 21(2) strips a financial creditor that is a related party of the corporate debtor of any right of representation, participation or voting in the committee. Losing the vote is not losing the claim — the related party remains a financial creditor whose debt is admitted and paid in its class. The committee's ordinary decisions need fifty-one per cent of voting share under section 21(8); the actions listed in section 28(1) need sixty-six per cent under section 28(3), and so does approval of a resolution plan under section 30(4). "Related party" here is the IBC's own definition in section 5(24), which is wider than section 2(76) of the Companies Act — and the corporate debtor's related-party disclosure under Ind AS 24 continues through the process regardless of who may vote.

citation.ref: Sections 5(24), 21(2) first proviso, 21(8), 28(3) and 30(4)

concepts.subsection: Liquidation waterfall — section 53 of the IBC
concepts.statement: Section 53(1) distributes liquidation proceeds in a fixed order that overrides anything to the contrary in any other law - (a) insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs in full; (b) workmen's dues for the twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished its security, ranking equally between themselves; (c) wages and unpaid dues of employees other than workmen for the twelve months preceding that date; (d) financial debts owed to unsecured creditors; (e) government dues for the two years preceding that date and any amount left unpaid to a secured creditor that enforced its own security, ranking equally; (f) any remaining debts and dues; (g) preference shareholders; (h) equity shareholders or partners. Section 327(7) of the Companies Act, 2013 shuts sections 326 and 327 — the Companies Act's own preferential payments — out of a liquidation under the Code, and the Supreme Court upheld that exclusion in Moser Baer Karamchari Union.

citation.ref: Section 53(1), read with section 327(7) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Ineligible resolution applicant — section 29A and the MSME relaxation
concepts.statement: Section 29A lists the persons who may not submit a resolution plan, and section 30(4) obliges the committee of creditors to check eligibility before approving one. Clause (c) catches a person whose account, or an account of a corporate debtor under his management, has been classified as a non-performing asset with at least one year gone from that classification to the insolvency commencement date. Clause (h) catches a person who has executed a guarantee in favour of a creditor of the corporate debtor where that guarantee has been invoked and remains unpaid. Section 240A switches off clauses (c) and (h) alone where the corporate debtor is a micro, small or medium enterprise, so a promoter of an MSME may bid for his own company — but every other clause of section 29A, including clause (b) on an undischarged insolvent and clause (d) on a conviction, applies to him unchanged.

citation.ref: Sections 29A(b), 29A(c), 29A(h), 30(4) and 240A

concepts.subsection: Pre-packaged insolvency resolution process — Chapter III-A of the IBC
concepts.statement: Chapter III-A, sections 54A to 54P, opens the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process to one class of debtor only — a corporate debtor classified as a micro, small or medium enterprise under section 7(1) of the MSMED Act, 2006. The minimum default is ten lakh rupees, notified under the second proviso to section 4 by S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021, against the one crore rupees that gates an ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process. Before filing, the corporate debtor must obtain the approval of unrelated financial creditors representing not less than sixty-six per cent in value of the financial debt owed to them, and must place a base resolution plan on the table. The whole process is built to close within one hundred and twenty days, against the outer three hundred and thirty of a full process, and management stays with the existing board — a debtor-in-possession process supervised by a resolution professional, not an ouster of the board.

citation.ref: Sections 54A and 54C of Chapter III-A, read with the second proviso to section 4 and notification S.O. 1543(E) dated 9 April 2021

concepts.subsection: FDI receipt — the Companies Act clock and the FEMA clock
concepts.statement: A single foreign investment starts two clocks with two regulators. Under company law, section 42(6) requires allotment within sixty days of receipt of the application money, refund within fifteen days of that period if allotment does not happen, and interest at twelve per cent beyond that; section 42(8) then requires the return of allotment with the Registrar within fifteen days of the allotment, and section 42(4) blocks the company from using the money until it is filed. Under FEMA, Regulation 4(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019 requires the issue to be reported to the Reserve Bank in Form FC-GPR not later than thirty days from the date of issue of the equity instruments, and Regulation 5 makes a late filing payable through a late submission fee. The two filings run from the same allotment, to different authorities, on different lengths of leash — filing one never satisfies the other.

citation.ref: Regulations 4(1) and 5 of the FEM (Mode of Payment and Reporting of Non-Debt Instruments) Regulations, 2019, read with sections 42(4), 42(6) and 42(8) of the Companies Act, 2013

concepts.subsection: Overseas direct investment against overseas portfolio investment
concepts.statement: Rule 2(1)(q) of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 makes an investment overseas direct investment where it is an acquisition of unlisted equity capital of a foreign entity, or a subscription to its memorandum, or an acquisition of ten per cent or more of the paid-up equity capital of a listed foreign entity, or any investment below ten per cent that carries control. Rule 2(1)(s) leaves everything else in foreign securities as overseas portfolio investment. The Explanation to Rule 2(1)(q) is the sting — once an investment is classified as ODI it stays ODI even if the holding later falls below ten per cent or control is lost, so the reporting and exit discipline follows the original classification, not today's percentage. Paragraph 3(1) of Schedule I caps an Indian entity's total financial commitment in all foreign entities at four hundred per cent of its net worth as per the last audited balance sheet, Rule 19(1) bars ODI into real estate activity, gambling and rupee-linked financial products without approval, and reporting, including the Annual Performance Report, runs through Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022.

citation.ref: Rules 2(1)(q) with its Explanation, 2(1)(s) and 19(1), and paragraph 3(1) of Schedule I, of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, read with Regulation 10 of the FEM (Overseas Investment) Regulations, 2022

concepts.subsection: Compounding a FEMA contravention — section 15 and the 2024 Rules
concepts.statement: A contravention of FEMA carries a penalty under section 13, and section 15 lets the contravener compound it — admit it, pay a sum, and close the matter — on an application made after the contravention. The Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024, notified on 12 September 2024, superseded the 2000 Rules and moved every figure: the application fee is now ten thousand rupees plus tax, and the Reserve Bank officer who may compound is fixed by the amount involved — an Assistant General Manager below sixty lakh rupees, a Deputy General Manager below two crore fifty lakh rupees, a General Manager below five crore rupees, and a Chief General Manager above five crore rupees. The compounding order is to be passed within one hundred and eighty days of receipt of a complete application, and the amount is payable within fifteen days of the order, failing which the application is void and FEMA applies to the contravention as though nothing had happened. A contravention of clause (a) of section 3 — dealing in foreign exchange with an unauthorised person — is not compounded by the Reserve Bank at all; it goes to the Directorate of Enforcement.

citation.ref: Sections 13 and 15, read with the Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024 (notified 12 September 2024)

concepts.subsection: Insider trading — continual disclosure and the contra trade bar
concepts.statement: Regulation 7(2)(a) of the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 makes every promoter, member of the promoter group, designated person and director disclose to the company the securities acquired or disposed of, within two trading days, once the value traded — in one transaction or a series over any calendar quarter — exceeds ten lakh rupees. Regulation 7(2)(b) then makes the company notify the stock exchange within two trading days of receiving that disclosure. Separately, clause 10 of Schedule B to Regulation 9 makes the company's code of conduct forbid a designated person who has traded from executing a contra trade for a period that can never be shorter than six months; a contra trade done in breach has its profits disgorged to SEBI for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund. The compliance officer may relax the restriction for reasons recorded in writing, but a relaxation can never permit what the Regulations themselves prohibit.
