The company pays, and because reverse charge liability is not output tax within section 2(82) it pays in cash, not out of the credit ledger. Three payments to the same person can therefore be treated three different ways. Remuneration to a whole-time or executive director that the company books as salary and on which it deducts tax at source under section 192 of the Income-tax Act is not a supply at all — entry 1 of Schedule III puts services by an employee to the employer in the course of or in relation to his employment outside the scope of supply. Sitting fees, commission and similar payments to a non-executive or independent director, on which tax is deducted under section 194J, are not employment income and do fall under entry 6, so the company pays under reverse charge. That split is what Circular No. 140/10/2020-GST settled. And where a director supplies something to the company in his private or personal capacity rather than as a director — renting out immovable property he owns personally being the standing example — Circular No. 201/13/2023-GST says entry 6 does not reach it, so there is no reverse charge on the company and the director accounts for the tax himself if he is otherwise liable. The test is the capacity in which the service is supplied, not the identity of the person supplying it.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with entry 6 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), read with entry 1 of Schedule III, section 2(82), Circular No. 140/10/2020-GST and Circular No. 201/13/2023-GST

concepts.subsection: Schedule II paragraph 5(b) — Construction sold before completion, and the entire-consideration test
concepts.statement: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II treats as a supply of services the construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority, or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier. Read the exception backwards and it is the whole rule. The carve-out needs the entire consideration to have arrived after the relevant event; a single rupee taken before it — a booking amount, a token, an instalment — pulls the transaction back inside the levy and the whole value becomes a supply of services, not merely the part received early. The relevant event is the earlier of two, and the second of them has nothing to do with any certificate. First occupation can precede a completion certificate, and where it does, it is first occupation that starts the clock. Paragraph 5 of Schedule III sits beside this and is expressly made subject to it — sale of land, and, subject to paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II, sale of a building, are neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services. A completed building sold outright is therefore outside GST altogether, while the same building sold under a booking taken during construction is a service throughout. The Explanation to paragraph 5 defines the competent authority and treats construction as including additions, alterations, replacements or remodelling of any existing civil structure.

citation.ref: Paragraph 5(b) of Schedule II with its Explanation, read with paragraph 5 of Schedule III and section 7(1A)

concepts.subsection: Rule 46 and Notification 14/2020 — The dynamic QR code on a business-to-consumer invoice
concepts.statement: Two separate obligations put a machine-readable code on an invoice and they point in opposite directions. Rule 48(4) is electronic invoicing — a registered person above the notified turnover must prepare an invoice for a supply to a registered person, for an export, or for a supply to a special economic zone unit or developer, by uploading the particulars to the Invoice Registration Portal, which returns an Invoice Reference Number together with a signed QR code. That code is static. It carries the identity of the invoice so anyone can verify it, and an invoice within rule 48(4) that has not been issued this way is not a valid invoice at all. Business-to-consumer invoices are outside rule 48(4) entirely and are never uploaded to the Portal. Rule 46 carries the other obligation, notified by Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax — an invoice issued by a registered person above the notified turnover to an unregistered person must have a Dynamic Quick Response code. A dynamic code is not an identity token but a payment instruction; it carries the payee details and the amount so that the customer can scan it and pay. The notification treats the requirement as met where the supplier makes the dynamic code available to the recipient through a digital display and the invoice carries a cross-reference of the payment made using that code, and where payment is made by any other mode the invoice must carry a cross-reference of that payment instead. So the same supplier may owe both duties at once, on different invoices, and the code printed by the Portal on a business-to-business invoice does nothing for the counter invoice handed to a walk-in customer.

citation.ref: Rule 46 (the Dynamic Quick Response code requirement) read with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax and rule 48(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1) — Getting money back out of the cash ledger
concepts.statement: Money deposited by challan sits in the electronic cash ledger and is not yet tax. It becomes tax only when it is debited against a liability, and until then it belongs to the person who deposited it. Section 49(6) says so — the balance in the electronic cash ledger or electronic credit ledger after payment of tax, interest, penalty, fee or any other amount payable may be refunded in accordance with section 54. The proviso to section 54(1) gives the cash balance its own simple route, letting a registered person claiming refund of any balance in the electronic cash ledger claim it in the return furnished under section 39, in the prescribed manner. Nothing lapses and nothing is forfeited, however long the balance sits. The credit ledger is not the same animal. Input tax credit is refundable only in the two situations section 54(3) allows — zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and an inverted duty structure where the rate on inputs is higher than the rate on output supplies, subject to the exclusions in the provisos to that sub-section. A registered person making ordinary domestic taxable supplies who has accumulated credit simply carries it forward and uses it; he cannot ask for it back. There is also a middle route for cash that avoids a refund altogether — section 49(10) with FORM GST PMT-09 lets an amount in the cash ledger be transferred from one head or major head to another, and between registrations of the same person holding the same Permanent Account Number. Nothing similar exists for the credit ledger.

citation.ref: Section 49(6) and the proviso to section 54(1), read with section 54(3) and section 49(10)

concepts.subsection: Section 56 — Interest when a refund is late, and the date the clock starts
concepts.statement: Section 56 makes the Government pay for its own delay, and it fixes the starting point at an event the applicant controls rather than one the department controls. Where any tax ordered to be refunded under section 54(5) is not refunded within sixty days from the date of receipt of application under section 54(1), interest is payable from the date immediately after the expiry of those sixty days till the date of refund, at a rate the section caps at six per cent and a notification fixes. The date the officer got round to sanctioning is irrelevant, and so is the date of any order. The proviso raises the stakes where the claim comes out of litigation — where a refund arises from an order passed by an adjudicating authority, an Appellate Authority, the Appellate Tribunal or a court which has attained finality, and is not refunded within sixty days from the date of receipt of the application filed consequent to such order, interest runs from the date immediately after the expiry of those sixty days till the date of refund, at a rate the section caps at nine per cent. Note what the proviso does and does not do. It lifts the rate, but it keeps the same trigger — sixty days from the receipt of an application, and specifically the application filed consequent to the order, not the original claim that was rejected years earlier. The Explanation closes the circle by deeming an order of refund made by an appellate authority, the Tribunal or a court against an order of the proper officer to be an order passed under section 54(5), so a refund the department never sanctioned is still a refund ordered under that sub-section for the purposes of the section.

citation.ref: Section 56 with its proviso and Explanation, read with sections 54(1) and 54(5)

concepts.subsection: Sections 107(2) and 107(11) — What the Appellate Authority may do, and the one thing it may not
concepts.statement: The first appeal is not only the taxpayer's. Section 107(1) lets any person aggrieved by a decision or order appeal to the Appellate Authority within three months of its communication, extendable by a further month on sufficient cause under section 107(4). Section 107(2) gives the department a mirror route that is not called an appeal in the section but works as one — the Commissioner may, on his own motion or on a request from his State counterpart, call for and examine the record of any proceeding in which an adjudicating authority has passed a decision or order, to satisfy himself as to its legality or propriety, and may by order direct a subordinate officer to apply to the Appellate Authority for determination of the points he specifies. That application is treated as an appeal. Section 107(11) is where the marks are. The Appellate Authority shall, after making such further inquiry as may be necessary, pass such order, confirming, modifying or annulling the decision or order appealed against, but shall not refer the case back to the adjudicating authority that passed it. There is no power of remand in the first appeal under GST, so an incomplete record has to be completed by the Appellate Authority itself through its own further inquiry. Two provisos then fence the power. An order enhancing any fee or penalty or fine in lieu of confiscation, or confiscating goods of greater value, or reducing the amount of refund or input tax credit, shall not be passed unless the appellant has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the proposed order. And where the Appellate Authority forms the opinion that tax has not been paid, has been short paid or erroneously refunded, or that credit has been wrongly availed or utilised, it cannot order payment without a show cause notice and without observing the time limits of the demand sections. Section 107(12) requires the order to state the points for determination, the decision and the reasons; section 107(13) sets one year from filing as the target where it is possible to do so.

citation.ref: Sections 107(2), 107(11) with its two provisos, 107(12) and 107(13), read with sections 107(1) and 107(4)

concepts.subsection: Section 108 — Revision, and the four bars on the Revisional Authority
concepts.statement: Revision is the department's own second look at an order nobody has appealed. Subject to section 121, the Revisional Authority may, on his own motion, on information received, or on a request from the Commissioner of State tax or Union territory tax, call for and examine the record of any proceeding, and if he considers that a decision or order passed by an officer subordinate to him is erroneous in so far as it is prejudicial to the interest of revenue and is illegal or improper or has not taken into account certain material facts, whether available at the time of the order or not, or in consequence of an observation by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India, he may stay the operation of that order and, after giving the person concerned an opportunity of being heard and making such further inquiry as may be necessary, pass such order as he thinks just and proper, including enhancing, modifying or annulling the decision or order. Note the direction of travel — the power exists for orders prejudicial to the revenue, not for orders prejudicial to the taxpayer. Sub-section (2) then shuts four doors. He shall not exercise the power where the order has been the subject of an appeal under section 107, 112, 117 or 118; where the period specified under section 107(2) has not yet expired or more than three years have expired after the order sought to be revised was passed; where the order has already been taken for revision at an earlier stage; or where the order was itself passed in revision. The first of those is qualified by a proviso that is worth as much as the bar — the Revisional Authority may pass an order on any point which has not been raised and decided in the appeal, before the expiry of one year from the date of the order in such appeal or the three years in clause (b), whichever is later. A second proviso excludes any period during which the making of the order is stayed by a court or the Appellate Tribunal. The Explanation makes clear that record covers everything available at the time of examination, and that a decision includes an intimation given by an officer lower in rank than the Revisional Authority.

citation.ref: Section 108(1), section 108(2) clauses (a) to (d) with its two provisos, and the Explanation to section 108, read with section 121

concepts.subsection: Section 161 — Rectifying an error apparent on the face of the record
concepts.statement: Section 161 is the small repair kit, and it is deliberately narrow. Any authority who has passed or issued a decision, order, notice, certificate or any other document may rectify any error which is apparent on the face of record in it, either on its own motion, or where the error is brought to its notice by an officer under the CGST Act or the State or Union territory Act, or by the affected person within three months from the date of issue of the document. Two limits and a safeguard follow. The first proviso says no rectification shall be done after six months from the date of issue of the document — the authority's own outer limit, longer than the affected person's three months to point the error out. The second proviso lifts that six-month limit entirely where the rectification is purely in the nature of correction of a clerical or arithmetical error arising from any accidental slip or omission; a wrong addition or a transposed digit can be put right whenever it is found. The third proviso is the safeguard — where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice shall be followed by the authority carrying it out. What section 161 will not do is reopen a matter. An error apparent on the face of record is one visible without argument; a debatable question of law, a fresh appreciation of evidence, or a change of mind is not one, and the route for those is appeal or revision. The section opens without prejudice to section 160, which protects a notice or order from being held invalid merely for a mistake, defect or omission where it is in substance in conformity with the Act.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its three provisos, read with section 160

concepts.subsection: Section 171 — Passing the benefit on, and what an order against a profiteer contains
concepts.statement: Section 171(1) states an obligation in one sentence — any reduction in rate of tax on any supply of goods or services, or the benefit of input tax credit, shall be passed on to the recipient by way of commensurate reduction in prices. Two triggers, and only two. A fall in the supplier's own costs, a cheaper raw material, a better freight contract, none of these engage the section, and a supplier who has cut his price for one of those reasons has not thereby discharged an obligation created by a rate cut. Commensurate is measured against the benefit, not against last year's price list. Section 171(2) lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, constitute an Authority or empower an existing authority to examine whether input tax credits availed or a reduction in the tax rate have actually resulted in a commensurate reduction in price, and a proviso added in 2024 lets the Government notify a date from which that Authority shall not accept any request for examination. The machinery has moved twice — the National Anti-profiteering Authority first, then the Competition Commission of India, and then the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 109, with a notified cut-off after which no fresh request is entertained. Read the current notification for the dates before quoting them. What an order does is fixed by section 171(3) with the rules — it may direct a reduction in prices, and the return of the amount not passed on to the recipient with interest, and where the recipient does not claim it or cannot be identified, deposit of that amount in the Consumer Welfare Fund. Section 171(3A) adds a penalty equivalent to ten per cent of the profiteered amount, with no penalty if that amount is deposited within thirty days of the order. The profiteered amount is the recipient's money being routed back to him; it is not a demand of tax, and it does not travel through sections 73, 74 or 74A.

citation.ref: Section 171(1), 171(2) with its proviso, 171(3) and 171(3A) with the Explanation to section 171, read with rules 127 and 133 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and section 109

concepts.subsection: Sections 151 and 152 — Calling for information, and the bar on using it unheard
concepts.statement: Section 151, as substituted by the Finance Act, 2021, is short and wide — the Commissioner or an officer authorised by him may, by an order, direct any person to furnish information relating to any matter dealt with in connection with the Act, within such time, in such form and in such manner as may be specified in the order. It stands beside section 150, which obliges specified persons — registering authorities, banks, stock exchanges, income-tax authorities and others — to furnish an information return. Between them the department can build a picture of a taxpayer out of material the taxpayer never supplied and may never have seen. Section 152 is the fence around that power and it has two limbs. Sub-section (1) says no information of any individual return or part of it, given for the purposes of section 150 or section 151, shall without the previous consent in writing of the person concerned or his authorised representative be published in a manner enabling the particulars to be identified as referring to a particular person; and no such information shall be used for the purposes of any proceedings under this Act without giving an opportunity of being heard to the person concerned. Publication and use are two separate prohibitions, and the second is the one that bites in an assessment. A proviso lets the Commissioner publish information about a class of taxable persons or a class of transactions where he considers it desirable in the public interest, because nothing there identifies an individual. Sub-section (2) keeps the files shut — no person not engaged in the collection of statistics under the Act, or in compiling or computer processing it for the purposes of the Act, shall be permitted to see or have access to any information or any individual return referred to in section 151.

citation.ref: Sections 151 and 152(1) with its proviso and 152(2), as substituted and amended by the Finance Act, 2021, read with section 150

concepts.subsection: Section 23 — Persons not liable to register, and the overriding words added in 2023
concepts.statement: Section 23(1) names two classes who shall not be liable to registration — any person engaged exclusively in the business of supplying goods or services or both that are not liable to tax or wholly exempt from tax under the CGST Act or the IGST Act, and an agriculturist, to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of land. Sub-section (2) lets the Government, on the recommendations of the Council, notify further categories exempted from obtaining registration. Two words in sub-section (1) carry the work. Not liable to tax points at a non-taxable supply under section 2(78) — alcoholic liquor for human consumption, and the petroleum products on which GST is not yet levied — while wholly exempt points at section 2(47). And exclusively means exclusively; one taxable supply, however small, takes a person out of the clause and back to sections 22 and 24. The important change is at the front of the sub-section. As originally enacted, section 23 sat awkwardly against section 24, which opens with its own overriding words and makes registration compulsory for named categories irrespective of turnover, among them a person required to pay tax under reverse charge and a person making an inter-State taxable supply. Which provision won was argued for years. The Finance Act, 2023 substituted the opening of section 23(1) so that it now reads notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in sub-section (1) of section 22 or section 24, and the substitution was given retrospective effect from 1 July 2017. Section 23 therefore prevails. A person who supplies nothing but exempt or non-taxable goods is outside the register even where a compulsory category in section 24 would otherwise have caught him — and he was outside it from the first day of the levy, not from the date of the amendment.

citation.ref: Section 23(1) as substituted by the Finance Act, 2023 with retrospective effect from 1 July 2017, and section 23(2), read with sections 22(1), 24, 2(47) and 2(78)

concepts.subsection: Section 121 — The four orders no appeal lies against
concepts.statement: Not every decision of a tax officer can be appealed, and section 121 says which cannot. Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any provision of the Act, no appeal shall lie against any decision taken or order passed by an officer of central tax if it relates to any one or more of four matters. First, an order of the Commissioner or other authority empowered to direct transfer of proceedings from one officer to another. Second, an order pertaining to the seizure or retention of books of account, register and other documents. Third, an order sanctioning prosecution under the Act. Fourth, an order passed under section 80, which is the provision allowing the Commissioner to extend time for payment or to permit payment of any amount other than self-assessed tax in monthly instalments. What the four have in common is that each is a step in the administration of a case rather than a determination of liability — who will hear it, what papers the department may keep, whether a criminal complaint will be filed, and how long the taxpayer has to pay. The liability itself remains fully appealable. Two consequences follow. The bar is on an appeal, not on every remedy, so a writ to the High Court against an arbitrary order in one of these matters is untouched by the section. And section 108(1) opens with the words subject to the provisions of section 121, so the same four matters are outside the revisional power as well; the department cannot revise what the taxpayer cannot appeal.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (a) to (d), read with sections 80, 107(1) and 108(1)

concepts.subsection: Sections 59 and 73 — The warehousing bond, and when it comes back
concepts.statement: Warehousing defers duty, and the security for the deferred duty is a bond. Section 59(1) requires the importer of goods for which a bill of entry for warehousing has been presented under section 46 and assessed under section 17 or section 18 to execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed, binding himself to comply with all the provisions of the Act, the rules and the regulations in respect of those goods, to pay on or before the date specified in a notice of demand all duties and interest payable under section 61(2), and to pay all penalties and fines incurred for any contravention in respect of those goods. Section 59(2) lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner permit a general bond covering goods to be imported within a specified period, and section 59(3) requires security in addition to the bond. The bond continues in force notwithstanding the transfer of the goods to another warehouse, and where the goods are transferred to another person the transferee executes his own bond and security. Section 71 fixes the only lawful exits — no warehoused goods shall be taken out of a warehouse except on clearance for home consumption or for export, or for removal to another warehouse, or as otherwise provided by the Act. Section 72 deals with the unlawful exit, letting the proper officer demand the full amount of duty chargeable together with all penalties, rent, interest and other charges, and, if the owner does not pay, detain and sell after notice a sufficient portion of his goods in the warehouse. Section 73 is the ending. When the whole of the goods covered by a bond executed under section 59 have been cleared for home consumption or exported or transferred or are otherwise duly accounted for, and when all amounts due on account of those goods have been paid, the proper officer shall cancel the bond as discharged in full and shall on demand deliver it, so cancelled, to the person who executed it or is entitled to receive it. The trigger is the goods and the money, never the calendar.

citation.ref: Sections 59(1), 59(2) and 59(3), 71, 72(1) and 72(2), and 73, read with sections 46, 61(2) and 68

concepts.subsection: Section 49 — Storing imported goods in a warehouse without warehousing them
concepts.statement: Section 49 exists for the importer who has entered his goods for home consumption and then cannot take them away. Where the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner is satisfied, on the importer's application, that imported goods entered for home consumption cannot be cleared within a reasonable time, the goods may pending clearance be permitted to be stored in a public warehouse for a period the section fixes, extendable by the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner. What makes the section examinable is its closing words — such goods shall not be deemed to be warehoused goods for the purposes of the Act, and the warehousing chapter therefore does not apply to them. Everything follows from that sentence. No bond under section 59 is taken, because there is nothing to bond. No interest under section 61(2) accrues, because interest there attaches to warehoused goods left beyond their free period. No manipulation of the goods under section 64 is available. And, most often tested, the rate of duty and tariff valuation stay where section 15(1)(a) put them — the date of presentation of the bill of entry for home consumption — instead of moving to section 15(1)(b), which fixes the rate for warehoused goods by the date on which the bill of entry for home consumption in respect of them is presented under section 68. The goods are physically in a warehouse and legally are not warehoused goods; a building does not change their status, an order under section 60 permitting deposit does. The importer pays rent and charges for the storage, but nothing about the levy moves while he waits.

citation.ref: Section 49 with its provisos, read with sections 15(1)(a), 15(1)(b), 46, 59, 60, 61(2) and 68

concepts.subsection: Sections 28-I and 28J — When a customs advance ruling cannot be given, and who it binds
concepts.statement: A customs advance ruling is a written decision on a question raised by an applicant in respect of goods before their importation or exportation, given by the Customs Authority for Advance Rulings constituted under section 28EA. An applicant is a person holding a valid Importer-exporter Code Number, a person exporting goods to India, or a person with a justifiable cause to the satisfaction of the Authority. Section 28H(2) fixes what may be asked — classification of goods, the applicability of a notification issued under section 25(1) having a bearing on the rate of duty, the principles to be adopted for determining value, the applicability of notifications in respect of duties under the Customs Act, the Customs Tariff Act or any other law where the duty is chargeable in the same manner as customs duty, the determination of origin of the goods under a trade agreement, and any other matter the Central Government notifies. Section 28-I(2) lets the Authority allow or reject the application by order, and its proviso is a bar rather than a discretion — the Authority shall not allow the application where the question raised in it is already pending in the applicant's case before any officer of customs, the Appellate Tribunal or any court, or where the same question has already been decided by the Appellate Tribunal or any court. The bar looks at the question, not at the consignment, so a future import does not escape it while the identical question is alive in the applicant's own earlier matter. No application is rejected without giving the applicant an opportunity of being heard, and the order must give reasons. Section 28J sets the reach of a ruling that is given — it is binding only on the applicant who sought it, in respect of the questions listed in section 28H(2), and on the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs and the customs authorities subordinate to him in respect of that applicant, and it stays binding unless there is a change in the law or the facts on which it was pronounced. Section 28K makes a ruling void from the start where the Authority finds it was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation of facts.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 28-I(2) with sections 28-I(4), 28E, 28EA, 28H(2), 28J(1), 28J(2) and 28K

concepts.subsection: Sections 68 and 71 — A duty-free shop is a warehouse, and duty falls when the goods leave it
concepts.statement: A duty-free shop at an international airport is not foreign territory and is not outside the Customs Act. It is a warehouse licensed under the warehousing chapter, and the goods on its shelves are warehoused goods on which duty has been deferred rather than remitted. That single fact answers most questions asked about it. Section 71 allows warehoused goods to leave a warehouse in only a few ways — cleared for home consumption, cleared for export, removed to another warehouse, or as otherwise provided by the Act — so the sale across the counter is not itself the taxable event; the exit route is. Where an arriving passenger buys at an arrival duty-free shop, the goods take the home-consumption exit, and section 68 governs it. A bill of entry for home consumption in respect of the warehoused goods is presented, the import duty and any charges are paid, and the proper officer makes an order for clearance. Section 15(1)(b) then fixes the rate of duty and tariff valuation by the date that bill of entry is presented, not by the date the shop imported the stock, so a rate change between the two dates counts. Where a departing passenger buys at a departure duty-free shop, the goods leave the country instead of entering it, so no clearance for home consumption occurs and no import duty falls due at all. The shop is the same, the customer is the difference, and the levy follows the exit the goods take rather than the contract of sale.

citation.ref: Sections 68 and 71, read with sections 15(1)(b), 12 and 61

concepts.subsection: Rule 10(1)(c) — Royalties and licence fees, and the condition-of-sale test
concepts.statement: Rule 10(1) of the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007 lists what is added to the price actually paid or payable when the transaction value is built up. Clause (c) adds royalties and licence fees related to the imported goods that the buyer is required to pay, directly or indirectly, as a condition of the sale of the goods being valued, to the extent that such royalties and fees are not already included in the price. Two tests have to be met together and candidates usually apply only one. The payment must be related to the imported goods, and it must be something the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale. A royalty the buyer could decline without losing the shipment fails the second test however closely it tracks the goods; a payment the supplier insists on before shipping meets it even though it is measured on later domestic sales. Two explanations to the clause then carve out what looks like it belongs. Charges for the right to reproduce the imported goods in India shall not be added to the price actually paid or payable. And payments made by the buyer for the right to distribute or resell the imported goods shall not be added if such payments are not a condition of the sale for export of the goods to India. Clause (d) beside it adds the value of any part of the proceeds of a subsequent resale, disposal or use of the goods that accrues directly or indirectly to the seller, and clause (e) sweeps up all other payments made as a condition of sale by the buyer to the seller, or by the buyer to a third party to satisfy an obligation of the seller, so far as they are not already in the price.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) with its two explanations, read with rules 10(1)(d), 10(1)(e) and 3, and section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

concepts.subsection: Sections 111, 112 and 125 — Confiscation, penalty, and when the fine must be offered
concepts.statement: Section 111 lists the goods brought from a place outside India that are liable to confiscation. Three of its clauses do most of the work in a case study. Clause (d) catches goods imported, or attempted to be imported, or brought within Indian customs waters for the purpose of being imported, contrary to any prohibition imposed by or under the Act or any other law for the time being in force. Clause (m) catches goods which do not correspond in respect of value or in any other particular with the entry made under the Act, or in the case of baggage with the declaration made under section 77. Clause (o) catches goods conditionally exempted from duty or from a prohibition where the condition is not observed, unless the non-observance was sanctioned by the proper officer. Section 112 attaches a personal penalty to the same conduct — on a person who does or omits to do an act that renders the goods liable to confiscation under section 111, or abets it, and on a person who acquires possession of or is in any way concerned in carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping, concealing, selling or purchasing, or otherwise dealing with, goods he knows or has reason to believe are liable to confiscation. Section 125 is where the two words that decide the answer sit. Whenever confiscation is authorised, the officer adjudging it may, in the case of goods whose importation or exportation is prohibited, and shall, in the case of any other goods, give the owner, or the person from whose possession the goods were seized, an option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation. The discretion belongs to the prohibited case; redemption of ordinary goods is not a favour the officer can withhold. A proviso caps the fine at the market price of the goods, less in the case of imported goods the duty chargeable on them. Section 125(2) adds that where a fine is imposed the owner is in addition liable to any duty and charges payable in respect of the goods, so redemption never replaces the duty.

citation.ref: Sections 111(d), 111(m) and 111(o), section 112, and sections 125(1) with its proviso and 125(2)

concepts.subsection: Sections 30, 31 and 32 — The arrival manifest, entry inwards, and what may be unloaded
concepts.statement: Before a single package comes ashore, three sections have to be satisfied and they apply to different conveyances. Section 29 requires a vessel or aircraft entering India from outside India to call or land only at a customs port or customs airport, except with the Board's permission or for accident, stress of weather or other unavoidable cause. Section 30(1) requires the person-in-charge of a vessel or aircraft carrying imported goods or export goods, or any other person the Central Government specifies, to deliver to the proper officer an arrival manifest or import manifest before the arrival of the vessel or aircraft, and in the case of a vehicle an import report after its arrival at the customs station; late delivery without sufficient cause draws a penalty. Section 30(3) requires the person delivering it to subscribe to a declaration as to the truth of its contents, and section 30(4) lets the proper officer permit an incorrect or incomplete manifest to be amended or supplemented where he is satisfied there was no fraudulent intention. Section 31 then adds a step that exists for one kind of conveyance only. The master of a vessel shall not permit the unloading of any imported goods until an order has been given by the proper officer granting entry inwards to that vessel, and no such order shall be given until an arrival manifest or import manifest has been delivered or the officer is satisfied there was sufficient cause for not delivering it. There is no entry inwards for an aircraft — the section speaks of the master of a vessel throughout. Section 31(3) excepts baggage accompanying a passenger or a member of the crew, mail bags, animals, perishable goods and hazardous goods, so those may be unloaded without waiting. Section 32 is the independent check on every conveyance — no imported goods shall be unloaded unless they are mentioned in the arrival manifest, import manifest or import report for that conveyance. Sections 33 and 34 confine unloading to approved places and to the supervision of a customs officer.

citation.ref: Sections 30(1), 30(3) and 30(4), 31(1), 31(2) and 31(3), and 32, read with sections 29, 33 and 34

concepts.subsection: Section 2(6) — Aggregate turnover, and what it counts
concepts.statement: Aggregate turnover is the measuring stick the whole Act reaches for — registration under section 22, eligibility for the composition levy, the e-invoicing obligation, the audit and annual return duties all read off it — and section 2(6) defines it once for all of them. It means the aggregate value of all taxable supplies, excluding the value of inward supplies on which tax is payable by a person on reverse charge basis, plus exempt supplies, plus exports of goods or services or both, plus inter-State supplies of persons having the same Permanent Account Number, to be computed on all India basis. Four things therefore go in and each of them catches candidates out in a different way. Exempt supplies count, so a person whose sales are largely exempt can still be pushed over the registration line by them. Exports count, though they carry no tax. Supplies made from a second State under the same PAN count, so the test is never registration-wise. And the figure is aggregate value, not taxable value, so it is read before any deduction. Two things stay out. The value of inward supplies on which the person himself pays tax under reverse charge is excluded — he is the recipient there, and his own purchases are not his turnover. And the taxes themselves are excluded: central tax, State tax, Union territory tax, integrated tax and cess are all stripped out of the figure. The explanations to the section add that the value of activities in Schedule III, and interest on deposits, loans and advances, do not enter the composition scheme's reading of it.

citation.ref: Section 2(6), read with sections 22 and 10

concepts.subsection: Article 246A — What GST replaced, and what it left standing
concepts.statement: GST needed a constitutional amendment before it could exist, because the old scheme split the taxing power — the Union taxed manufacture and services, the States taxed sale of goods, and neither could reach the other's field. The Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted Article 246A, which gives Parliament and every State legislature simultaneous power to make laws with respect to goods and services tax, with Parliament alone competent for inter-State supply under Article 269A. Central excise duty, additional duties of excise and customs, service tax, State value added tax, central sales tax, entry tax, octroi, luxury tax, entertainment tax levied by a State, and the several cesses and surcharges on supply were subsumed. What was left standing is the more useful half of the list. Basic customs duty survives untouched on imports and sits beside the integrated tax charged there. Stamp duty on instruments survives, being a duty on the document rather than a tax on supply. State excise and State VAT on alcoholic liquor for human consumption survive, because Article 366(12A) defines goods and services tax as a tax on the supply of goods or services or both except the supply of alcoholic liquor for human consumption — that supply is outside GST by definition and not merely exempt. Electricity duty and property tax survive. And five petroleum products — crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel — are inside the GST framework but not yet inside the levy, tax on them beginning only from a date the Council recommends.

citation.ref: Article 246A with Articles 269A and 366(12A), inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016

concepts.subsection: Article 279A — The GST Council, and how far its word goes
concepts.statement: Article 279A creates the Goods and Services Tax Council — the Union Finance Minister as Chairperson, the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance, and the Minister in charge of Finance or Taxation, or any other Minister, nominated by each State Government, who choose one of their number as Vice-Chairperson. Its function is to make recommendations to the Union and the States on the taxes to be subsumed, the goods and services to be exempted, model laws and principles of levy, the threshold below which supplies may be exempted, and rates including floor rates with bands. Half the total number of Members is the quorum. A decision is taken by a majority of not less than three fourths of the weighted votes of the members present and voting, the Central Government's vote weighing one third of the votes cast and all the State Governments' votes together weighing two thirds — so neither side can carry a decision alone. The word that matters is recommendations. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations have persuasive value and are not binding on the Union and the States, since Article 246A gives both simultaneous power to legislate and the Council is a forum for that dialogue rather than an authority above it. The practice is that recommendations are followed and notified; the law is that they are not commands.

citation.ref: Article 279A, sub-articles (1) to (9), read with Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd. (2022)

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 74 — Health care services, and where the exemption stops
concepts.statement: Health care services supplied by a clinical establishment, an authorised medical practitioner or para-medics are exempt, and so is transportation of a patient in an ambulance. The width of the exemption comes from the definition, and so does its limit. Health care services means any service by way of diagnosis or treatment or care for illness, injury, deformity, abnormality or pregnancy in any recognised system of medicines in India, and includes services by way of transportation of the patient to and from a clinical establishment. It does not include hair transplant, or cosmetic or plastic surgery — except where that surgery is undertaken to restore or to reconstruct anatomy or functions of the body affected by congenital defects, developmental abnormalities, injury or trauma. So the same operation performed by the same surgeon in the same hospital falls on either side of the line depending on why it is being done. A clinical establishment is a hospital, nursing home, clinic, sanatorium or any institution offering services requiring diagnosis or treatment, including a place established as an independent entity or part of an establishment for diagnosis or investigation. The exemption attaches to the service, not to the building, which is why a hospital's shop rentals, its canteen sales to visitors and its cosmetic work are all outside it while its ward and its operating theatre are inside.

citation.ref: Entry 74, read with the definitions of health care services and clinical establishment in paragraph 2 of the notification

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 66 — An educational institution, and the services bought in
concepts.statement: Entry 66 has two halves and candidates lose marks by reading only the first. Clause (a) exempts services supplied by an educational institution to its students, faculty and staff, and services by way of conduct of an entrance examination against a fee. An educational institution means an institution providing services by way of pre-school education and education up to higher secondary school or equivalent, or education as a part of a curriculum for obtaining a qualification recognised by any law for the time being in force, or education as a part of an approved vocational education course. So a degree college and a school are both educational institutions for what they supply to their own students. Clause (b) runs the other way — it exempts services supplied to an educational institution by way of transportation of students, faculty and staff, catering including any mid-day meals scheme sponsored by the Government, security or cleaning or house-keeping services performed in such institution, and services relating to admission to or conduct of examination. But clause (b) is cut down: for the first three of those, the exemption applies only where the institution provides pre-school education and education up to higher secondary school or equivalent. The inward leg therefore stops at the school gate. A bus operator, a caterer or a housekeeping agency serving a school is exempt; the same three serving a degree college are taxable, and the college takes credit if it has any taxable output to set it against. Examination-related services and online educational journals have their own, differently drawn, treatment.

citation.ref: Entry 66, clauses (a) and (b), read with the definition of educational institution in paragraph 2 of the notification

concepts.subsection: Renting a residential dwelling, and the reverse charge that follows registration
concepts.statement: Renting of a residential dwelling for use as residence has always been exempt, and the exemption used to turn on the building and the use alone. It no longer does. The entry now reads except where the recipient is a registered person, so the moment the tenant is registered under GST the supply leaves the exemption. Nothing about the flat has changed; the status of the tenant has. Having taken the supply out of exemption, the law then moves the liability: the notified entry under section 9(3) makes the registered recipient pay the tax on renting of a residential dwelling under reverse charge, which is how a landlord who is unregistered, and who may have no idea GST is involved, is left with nothing to do. The company or firm renting a flat for a director, a guest house or a staff hostel therefore self-invoices and pays in cash. One carve-out was added because the first version swept too wide — where the registered person is a proprietor renting the dwelling in his personal capacity, for use as his own residence, and on his own account rather than on the account of his business, the exemption survives. The test is the capacity in which the tenant takes the flat, not merely whether his name appears on a GST registration.

citation.ref: Entry 12 as amended, read with entry 5AA of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) and the proviso on renting in a personal capacity

concepts.subsection: Notification 12/2017 entry 1 — Charitable activities, and what a trust is still taxed on
concepts.statement: Entry 1 exempts services by an entity registered under section 12AA or 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 by way of charitable activities. Both limbs have to be satisfied and students routinely forget the second. Registration under the Income-tax Act qualifies the entity; it does not exempt everything the entity does. Charitable activities is a defined expression and the definition is a closed list — activities relating to public health by way of care or counselling of terminally ill persons or persons with severe physical or mental disability, of persons afflicted with HIV or AIDS, or of persons addicted to a dependence-forming substance, and public awareness of preventive health, family planning or prevention of HIV infection; advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga; advancement of educational programmes or skill development relating to abandoned, orphaned or homeless children, physically or mentally abused and traumatised persons, prisoners, or persons over the age of sixty-five years residing in a rural area; and preservation of environment including watershed, forests and wildlife. Anything else the trust supplies for a consideration is taxable in the ordinary way — commercial coaching, hall hire, publication sales, sponsorship. Separate entries deal with religious places and with religious ceremonies, and they have their own conditions rather than riding on this one.

citation.ref: Entry 1, read with the definition of charitable activities in paragraph 2 of the notification and section 12AB of the Income-tax Act, 1961

concepts.subsection: Section 77 and section 19 of the IGST Act — Tax paid under the wrong head
concepts.statement: Getting the place of supply wrong is the commonest mistake in GST and it is the one the law is gentlest about, because the mistake costs the exchequer nothing — the money was paid, only into the wrong pocket. Section 77(1) says a registered person who has paid central tax and State tax or Union territory tax on a transaction considered by him to be an intra-State supply, but which is subsequently held to be an inter-State supply, shall be refunded the amount of taxes so paid in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Section 77(2) adds that he shall not be required to pay any interest on the amount of integrated tax payable. Section 19 of the IGST Act carries the identical rule the other way for a person who paid integrated tax on what turns out to be an intra-State supply. Three things follow. The correct tax has to be paid — the section forgives interest, not tax. The wrong tax is refunded rather than adjusted, so a refund claim is made and the limitation for it runs from the date the correct-head tax is paid rather than from the original payment. And the relief does not depend on the mistake being innocent in any moral sense; it depends only on the supply having been treated one way and held to be the other.

citation.ref: Sections 77(1) and 77(2), read with section 19 of the IGST Act, 2017

concepts.subsection: Section 70 — Summons, and why the proceeding is a judicial one
concepts.statement: Section 70(1) gives the proper officer power to summon any person whose attendance he considers necessary either to give evidence or to produce a document or any other thing in any inquiry, in the same manner as provided in the case of a civil court. Two words carry the weight. Any person — the power is not confined to the registered person under investigation, and reaches a supplier, a customer, a transporter, a bank official or an employee, none of whom need be suspected of anything. And inquiry — the power exists during an inquiry and does not wait for a show cause notice or an assessment. Section 70(2) then provides that every such inquiry shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of the penal provisions on giving false evidence and on intentionally insulting or interrupting a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding. That deeming is the sanction behind the summons: a statement recorded under section 70 is evidence, and an untrue one is not a compliance lapse to be met with a penalty but an offence under the general criminal law. A summons is therefore a different instrument from the inspection, search and seizure powers of section 67 — it compels a person and a document rather than entering a place, needs no reason to believe an offence has occurred, and produces sworn testimony rather than seized goods.

citation.ref: Sections 70(1) and 70(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 122(1) — The penalty for a specified offence, and the floor beneath it
concepts.statement: Section 122(1) is the list of specified offences and it names twenty-one of them — supplying without an invoice, issuing an invoice without a supply, issuing an invoice using another registered person's identification number, collecting tax and failing to pay it over within three months, taking or utilising input tax credit without receiving the goods or services, obtaining a refund by fraud, falsifying records, failing to register when liable, obstructing an officer, transporting goods without the prescribed documents, and the rest. All twenty-one carry one penalty formula rather than a scale: an amount equivalent to the tax evaded, or the tax not deducted or short deducted, or the tax not collected or short collected, or the input tax credit availed of or passed on or distributed irregularly, or the refund claimed fraudulently, as the case may be — or the fixed sum the sub-section names, whichever is higher. The fixed sum is a floor, not a cap, and not an alternative the officer may pick. Sub-section (1A) reaches the person who retains the benefit of certain of those transactions and at whose instance they are conducted, and sub-section (2) deals separately with tax short paid or not paid otherwise than by fraud, and with the same conduct where fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression is present. Section 125 is the residual penalty and it applies only where no penalty is separately provided, so conduct on the section 122 list never reaches it.

citation.ref: Section 122(1), read with sections 122(1A), 122(2) and 125

concepts.subsection: Section 83 — Provisional attachment, and the year it lasts
concepts.statement: Section 83(1) lets the Commissioner, where proceedings under the specified chapters are pending and he is of the opinion that it is necessary so to do for the purpose of protecting the interest of the Government revenue, by order in writing attach provisionally any property including a bank account belonging to the taxable person or to a person who retains the benefit of certain transactions. Three limits sit inside that sentence. Proceedings must actually be pending — the power is ancillary and cannot be used to open an investigation. The opinion must be formed and recorded, and in Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh the Supreme Court called the power draconian and held that the formation of the opinion must rest on tangible material bearing a live link to the need to protect revenue, not on a mechanical recital. And the attachment must be of property belonging to the person against whom the proceedings run. Section 83(2) then supplies the clock: every such provisional attachment shall cease to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of the order. That lapse is automatic and needs no application, no order releasing it and no adjudication in the meantime. Rule 159(5) gives the affected person a separate remedy while it runs — an objection to the Commissioner within seven days that the property was not liable to attachment, with an opportunity of being heard.

citation.ref: Sections 83(1) and 83(2), read with rule 159 of the CGST Rules, 2017 and Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2021)

concepts.subsection: Section 85 — Selling the business, and the tax that follows it
concepts.statement: Chapter XVI attaches GST liability to people other than the person who incurred it, and section 85 is its widest provision. Where a taxable person liable to pay tax, interest or penalty transfers his business in whole or in part, by sale, gift, lease, leave and licence, hire or in any other manner whatsoever, the taxable person and the person to whom the business is so transferred shall, jointly and severally, be liable wholly or to the extent of such transfer to pay the tax, interest or penalty due from the taxable person up to the time of such transfer, whether such dues have been determined before the transfer but remain unpaid, or are determined afterwards. Two consequences follow that buyers regularly miss. A liability quantified two years after the sale, for a period before it, still lands on the buyer — the words are whether determined before or after. And a clause in the sale agreement allocating pre-transfer taxes to the seller is enforceable between the two of them and worth nothing against the department, which may proceed against either. Where the transferee carries on the business under a changed name, he must within the prescribed period apply for amendment of his registration. Sections 87 to 90 do the same work for other events — amalgamation, dissolution of a firm, liquidation of a company and partners' liability — and section 93 for the estate of a deceased person.

citation.ref: Section 85(1) and 85(2), read with sections 87 to 90

concepts.subsection: Sections 117 and 118 — When the appeal from the Tribunal skips the High Court
concepts.statement: An appeal lies to the High Court from every order passed by the State Bench or Area Benches of the Appellate Tribunal, but only where the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law. The memorandum states precisely that question, the Court formulates it if satisfied one exists, and the appeal is heard on the question so formulated — the Court does not re-open the facts. It is filed within one hundred and eighty days of the order being communicated, and the Court may admit a late appeal on being satisfied there was sufficient cause. A Bench of not less than two Judges hears it and decides by majority. Then comes the exception that examiners like. The proviso to section 117(1) takes out of the High Court's reach any order of the Appellate Tribunal relating to a matter where two or more States, or a State and the Centre, have a difference of views regarding the place of supply — because such a dispute is not one State's High Court's to settle. Section 118 sends that appeal directly to the Supreme Court, and also gives a direct appeal to the Supreme Court from any order of the Principal Bench of the Appellate Tribunal. So the route upward depends not on the amount or on the taxpayer, but on what the dispute is about.

citation.ref: Section 117(1) with its proviso and sections 117(2) to 117(5), read with section 118

concepts.subsection: Rule 86A — Blocking the credit ledger, and what blocking is not
concepts.statement: Rule 86A lets the Commissioner, or an officer authorised by him not below the rank of Assistant Commissioner, having reasons to believe that credit of input tax available in the electronic credit ledger has been fraudulently availed or is ineligible, disallow debit of an amount equivalent to such credit for discharging any liability or for claiming a refund of any unutilised amount. The grounds are listed — credit on an invoice issued by a supplier found non-existent or not conducting business from the registered place, credit on an invoice without receipt of the goods or services, credit on tax not paid to the Government, credit taken by a registered person found non-existent, and credit taken without an invoice or debit note. What the rule does is narrow, and the words say so: it disallows a debit. It does not determine a liability, reverse a credit or recover anything — a demand still needs a notice and an order under section 73 or 74A, with the hearing those carry. The reasons must be recorded in writing before the order, and the courts have repeatedly struck down blocking done on a borrowed instruction rather than the officer's own belief. Sub-rule (2) lets the same officer lift the restriction once satisfied the conditions no longer exist, and sub-rule (3) ends it anyway: the restriction ceases to have effect after the expiry of a period of one year from the date of imposing it.

concepts.subsection: Rules 3 to 9 — The order the customs valuation methods must be tried in
concepts.statement: Customs valuation is a ladder and the rungs must be taken in order. Rule 3(1) says the value of imported goods shall be the transaction value adjusted under rule 10, subject to rule 12 — the power to raise doubts about the truth or accuracy of the declared value and, after telling the importer the grounds and hearing him, to reject it. Rule 3(4) then provides that if the value cannot be determined under sub-rule (1), it shall be determined by proceeding sequentially through rules 4 to 9. Rule 4 is the value of identical goods sold for export to India at or about the same time, at the same commercial level and in substantially the same quantity. Rule 5 is the same for similar goods — not identical, but with like characteristics and component materials performing the same functions. Rule 7 is deductive value, working back from the unit price at which the imported goods or identical or similar goods are sold in India in the greatest aggregate quantity, less commissions, transport, insurance and duties. Rule 8 is computed value, built up from the cost of materials and fabrication, profit and general expenses. Rule 9 is the residual method, using reasonable means consistent with the principles of the rules and the data available in India. Rule 6 holds the sequence together and grants the one permitted departure from it: the value is determined by proceeding sequentially through rules 7 and 8, but at the request of the importer, and with the approval of the proper officer, the order of application of rules 7 and 8 may be reversed. Nothing else in the ladder may be skipped.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 3(4) with rule 6, read with rules 4, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 12

concepts.subsection: Sections 110 and 110A — Six months to issue the notice, and release in the meantime
concepts.statement: Section 110(1) lets a proper officer who has reason to believe that any goods are liable to confiscation seize them, and where it is not practicable to seize them, order that the owner shall not remove or deal with them without permission. Seizure is a holding step, not a punishment, and the law puts a clock on it. Section 110(2) provides that where no notice under section 124(a) is given within six months of the seizure of the goods, the goods shall be returned to the person from whose possession they were seized. The proviso lets the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Customs extend that period by a further six months, for reasons to be recorded in writing, and the person concerned must be informed before the original period expires. Miss both and the goods go back by operation of the sub-section, with no application needed. What returning the goods does not do is end the case: the department may still issue a notice and adjudicate confiscation and penalty later, it simply no longer holds the goods while it does. Documents and things seized are governed separately, and section 110A supplies the middle course throughout — pending the order of the adjudicating authority, goods, documents or things seized or bank accounts provisionally attached may be released to the owner on taking a bond, with such security and conditions as the adjudicating authority requires.

citation.ref: Sections 110(1) and 110(2) with the proviso, read with sections 110A and 124

concepts.subsection: Section 26A — Import duty back on goods that were not what was ordered
concepts.statement: Section 26A is the customs answer to a bad delivery. Where imported goods on which duty has been paid and which have been cleared for home consumption are found to be defective, or otherwise not in conformity with the specification agreed upon between the importer and the supplier, the duty is refunded — but the section fences the relief with conditions and each of them is a possible exam point. The goods must not have been worked, repaired or used after importation, except where such use was indispensable to discover the defect or to test whether the goods conform to the specification. The goods must be identified to the satisfaction of the Assistant or Deputy Commissioner as the goods that were imported. The importer must not claim drawback on them. And the goods must be exported, or the importer must relinquish his title to them and abandon them to customs, or they must be destroyed or rendered commercially valueless in the presence of the proper officer, within the period the section allows from the date of clearance, extendable on sufficient cause. The refund claim itself is filed within the further period prescribed. The section does not apply at all to perishable goods, to goods that have exceeded their shelf life or their recommended storage-before-use period, or to goods against which an offence appears to have been committed under the Act or any other law. Distinguish it from section 74, which is drawback on re-export of duty-paid goods generally, and from section 27, which refunds duty paid in excess of what was due.

citation.ref: Section 26A(1) with its provisos and section 26A(3)

concepts.subsection: Sections 128, 129A and 129DD — The three orders the Tribunal cannot hear
concepts.statement: A customs appeal has an ordinary route and an exception, and the exception is the examinable part. The ordinary route — any person aggrieved by a decision or order passed by an officer of customs lower in rank than the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner may appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) within sixty days of communication, extendable by a further thirty days on sufficient cause shown; from the Commissioner (Appeals), or from an order passed by a Principal Commissioner or Commissioner as adjudicating authority, an appeal lies to the Appellate Tribunal under section 129A. The exception is the first proviso to section 129A(1), which says no appeal shall lie to the Appellate Tribunal in respect of an order relating to any goods imported or exported as baggage, any goods loaded in a conveyance for importation into India but not unloaded at their place of destination or short-landed, or the payment of drawback as provided in Chapter X and the rules made under it. Those three go instead to the Central Government by revision application under section 129DD, filed within three months, and the Central Government's order is the end of that road but for a writ. Beyond the Tribunal, section 130 gives an appeal to the High Court on a substantial question of law, and section 130E an appeal to the Supreme Court — but any question relating to the rate of duty or to the value of goods for assessment goes to the Supreme Court and never to the High Court.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 129A(1), read with sections 128, 129DD, 130 and 130E

concepts.subsection: Social Welfare Surcharge — What it is charged on
concepts.statement: The Social Welfare Surcharge replaced the education cesses on imported goods and is levied by section 110 of the Finance Act, 2018 to finance education, health and social security. Its character decides every question asked about it: it is a surcharge on duty, not a duty on value. The surcharge is calculated at the prescribed rate on the aggregate of duties, taxes and cesses which are levied and collected by the Central Government under section 12 of the Customs Act, 1962 and any other law for the time being in force as an addition to, and in the same manner as, a duty of customs — so the assessable value never enters the computation, and where the basic customs duty is nil the surcharge on it is nil too. Three levies are expressly kept out of that base: the integrated tax charged on imports under section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, the goods and services tax compensation cess under section 3(9), and the safeguard, countervailing and anti-dumping duties under sections 8B, 9 and 9A of that Act. The surcharge is collected as a duty of customs, and all the machinery provisions of the Customs Act on refunds, exemptions, interest, recovery and penalties apply to it. Because it is not the integrated tax, it is not creditable — like the basic customs duty it rides on, it is a cost.

citation.ref: Section 110 — Social Welfare Surcharge on imported goods, read with sections 3(7) and 3(9) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975

concepts.subsection: Section 7 of the FTDR Act — The Importer-Exporter Code, and who does not need one
concepts.statement: Section 7 of the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 says that no person shall make any import or export except under an Importer-Exporter Code number granted by the Director General of Foreign Trade or an officer authorised by him. It is the licence to trade across the border and the first thing an exporter obtains, before any scheme, scrip or authorisation. The code is now the Permanent Account Number of the person, issued in the format of an IEC by the DGFT on an online application, so one entity holds one code across all its branches, and the details must be updated electronically every year even where nothing has changed — an IEC not updated is liable to be deactivated. Two classes of person are outside the requirement. A Ministry or department of the Central Government or of a State Government, and other categories the policy notifies, may import and export without one. And goods imported or exported for personal use, not connected with trade, manufacture or agriculture, need no code — which is what lets a traveller bring in a personal effect and a person import equipment for a family member without registering as a trader. Import and export by categories such as notified charitable institutions are similarly relieved. The code is a permission to trade and not a benefit: holding it confers no exemption and no duty concession by itself.

citation.ref: Section 7, read with the Importer-Exporter Code provisions of the Foreign Trade Policy and the exempt categories notified under them

concepts.subsection: Section 16 — Input tax credit conditions
concepts.statement: Input tax credit needs every section 16(2) condition together — a tax invoice, receipt of the goods or services, the detail appearing in GSTR-2B, the tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier, and the return filed. Holding a valid invoice while the supplier has not paid the tax defeats the credit.

citation.ref: Section 16(2)

concepts.subsection: Section 9(3) — Reverse charge
concepts.statement: For notified supplies — legal services from an advocate to a business entity among them — the recipient, not the supplier, is liable to pay the tax, and pays it in cash rather than through input tax credit.

citation.ref: Section 9(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 22 — Registration
concepts.statement: Registration becomes compulsory when aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh for a supplier of services. The ₹40 lakh limit is for suppliers exclusively of goods in eligible States, and special category States carry lower limits.

citation.ref: Section 22

concepts.subsection: Section 10 — Composition levy
concepts.statement: A composition taxpayer cannot make inter-State outward supplies of goods. The scheme trades a small turnover-based levy for staying local; crossing the State line with outward supplies forfeits eligibility.

citation.ref: Section 10(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs valuation
concepts.statement: Additions to the transaction value of imported goods include selling commissions, and cost of transport and insurance to the place of importation — but buying commission, paid to the importer's own agent for representing him abroad, is not added.

citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 16(4) — Time limit for input tax credit
concepts.statement: Input tax credit for an invoice cannot be taken after the thirtieth of November following the end of the financial year the invoice belongs to, or the filing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. A valid, eligible credit dies purely of lateness.

citation.ref: Section 16(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Place of supply of goods
concepts.statement: Where a supply involves movement of goods, the place of supply is the location where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Who arranges the transport does not decide it; where the goods end up does.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Time of supply — advances
concepts.statement: An advance received for a supply of services is taxable when received. For goods, suppliers other than composition taxpayers pay tax only on issue of the invoice — advances for goods were taken out of the tax net by notification. The same rupee of advance is taxed on one side of the goods-services line and not the other.

citation.ref: Section 12 and 13, with Notification 66/2017-CT

concepts.subsection: Section 15 — Value of supply
concepts.statement: A discount given after the supply reduces the taxable value only if it was agreed before or at the time of supply and can be linked to the specific invoices, and the recipient reverses the proportionate input tax credit. A goodwill discount invented after the event changes the price, not the tax.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(b)

concepts.subsection: Section 50 — Interest on delayed payment
concepts.statement: Interest on delayed payment of tax runs at 18 per cent, and on the portion paid through the electronic cash ledger it is charged only on that net cash amount where the return is filed late — the credit-covered portion carries no interest. Wrongly availed and utilised credit draws its own interest.

citation.ref: Section 50(1) proviso and 50(3)

concepts.subsection: Section 143 — Job work
concepts.statement: Inputs sent for job work must return, or be supplied from the job worker's premises, within one year; capital goods within three years. Miss the window and the original despatch is deemed a supply from the day the goods went out, with tax and interest reaching back to it.

citation.ref: Section 143(3) and 143(4)

concepts.subsection: IGST Act — Zero-rated supply
concepts.statement: Exports and supplies to SEZ units are zero-rated, not exempt: the output carries no tax, yet input tax credit survives. The exporter either supplies under a letter of undertaking without paying tax and claims refund of unutilised credit, or pays IGST and claims refund of the tax paid.

citation.ref: Section 16

concepts.subsection: Rule 138 — E-way bill
concepts.statement: An e-way bill is generated before movement of goods worth more than fifty thousand rupees in a consignment. The obligation attaches to the movement, not the sale — stock transfers, job work despatches and sales returns all need one, and some States set higher intra-State limits.

citation.ref: Rule 138

concepts.subsection: Section 129 — Detention of goods in transit
concepts.statement: Goods moved in contravention — typically without a valid e-way bill or invoice — are detained, and release requires a penalty of two hundred per cent of the tax payable where the owner comes forward. Detention is a transit consequence and runs independently of whether the tax on the supply itself was ever evaded.

citation.ref: Section 129(1)(a)

concepts.subsection: Schedule I — Supply without consideration
concepts.statement: Four transactions are supplies even without consideration — permanent transfer of business assets on which credit was taken, supplies between related or distinct persons in business, goods moved through agents who undertake to supply or receive on the principal's behalf, and imported services from a related person for business. Employer gifts to an employee stay out up to fifty thousand rupees a year.

citation.ref: Schedule I

concepts.subsection: Schedule III — Neither goods nor services
concepts.statement: Schedule III lists what GST cannot touch at all — an employee's services to the employer in the course of employment, sale of land and of completed buildings, actionable claims other than specified ones, funeral services, and duties of courts and MPs. These are not exempt supplies; they are not supplies, so they never enter aggregate turnover.

citation.ref: Schedule III

concepts.subsection: Section 54 — Refunds
concepts.statement: A refund claim is filed within two years from the relevant date, and the relevant date moves with the ground of the claim — export shipment dates for goods exported, the date payment lands for export of services, the judgment's date where tax was paid under a later-reversed demand. Miss the window and the money stays with the Government however good the ground was.

citation.ref: Section 54(1)

concepts.subsection: Section 10(2A) — Composition for service providers
concepts.statement: A supplier of services outside the restaurant category, ineligible for the ordinary composition scheme, may opt for the special scheme where aggregate turnover in the preceding year stayed within fifty lakh rupees, paying six per cent. The ordinary scheme's goods-centred gates do not decide this one.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A)

concepts.subsection: Section 17(5) — Blocked credits
concepts.statement: Input tax credit on motor vehicles for transporting persons with seating capacity up to thirteen (including the driver) is blocked — unless the vehicle is used for further supply of such vehicles, transporting passengers, or driving training. Vehicles above thirteen seats and goods-transport vehicles are outside the block, and services of insurance, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle they attach to.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a)

concepts.subsection: Section 13 — Time of supply of services
concepts.statement: For services, time of supply is the earlier of invoice and payment where the invoice issues within the thirty-day limit; where it does not, the earlier of the date the service is provided and the payment. The clock decides which tax period the liability lands in — issuing the invoice late does not push the liability later.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)

concepts.subsection: Customs — Duty drawback on re-export
concepts.statement: Section 74 refunds up to ninety-eight per cent of import duty when the imported goods themselves are re-exported within two years, identified as the same goods. Goods that were used before re-export get tapering rates by period of use. Section 75 is the other drawback — for duty on inputs consumed in manufacturing exported goods — and the two never apply to the same claim.

citation.ref: Section 74

concepts.subsection: IGST — Place of supply for immovable property services
