options.misconception: compares the receipt with a single share and ignores the ratio, so the receipt looks four times dearer than it is
options.why: One receipt is a claim on four shares, not one. The comparison has to be receipt against 4 × ₹800 = ₹3,200, which gives 3.75 per cent. Against a single share the figure is 3,320/800 − 1 = 315 per cent, and it measures nothing.

options.text: A premium of 3.61 per cent, the ₹120 gap against the ₹3,320 receipt price
options.misconception: divides the premium by the receipt's own price instead of by the value of the underlying shares the premium is measured against
options.why: 120 / 3,320 = 3.61 per cent answers a different question — what share of the receipt's price the gap is. The premium is measured against what the receipt is a claim on, ₹3,200, giving 3.75 per cent.

options.text: A premium of ₹120 per receipt, or 3.75 per cent over the underlying shares
options.why: Four underlying shares are worth 4 × 800 = ₹3,200. The receipt converts to 40 × 83 = ₹3,320. The gap is ₹120, and measured against the ₹3,200 the receipt is a claim on, that is 120 / 3,200 = 3.75 per cent — the receipt is the dearer side.

options.text: A discount of 3.75 per cent, since ₹3,200 is less than ₹3,320
options.misconception: computes the gap correctly but reads its direction backwards, calling the more expensive side the discounted one
options.why: The receipt costs ₹3,320 for what is worth ₹3,200 in Mumbai, so the receipt is dear, not cheap — a premium. Whoever pays more is paying the premium, and here that is the buyer of the receipt.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company's share trades at ₹800 on the domestic exchange. Its depository receipt trades abroad at $40.00, and one receipt represents four underlying shares. The spot rate is ₹83 per dollar.

items.stem: What is EPS after the buyback?

options.text: ₹11.11 — profit of ₹1,000 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.misconception: counts the benefit of the buyback, the reduced share count, but not its cost, the after-tax income the cash was earning
options.why: The cash did not leave without taking its earnings with it. ₹84 lakh of after-tax income goes when the ₹1,500 lakh goes, so the numerator is ₹916 lakh, not ₹1,000 lakh, and EPS is ₹10.18 rather than ₹11.11.

options.text: ₹9.78 — profit of ₹880 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.misconception: deducts the forgone interest gross of tax, forgetting that the company was only ever keeping 70 paise in the rupee of it
options.why: The gross ₹120 lakh was taxed at 30 per cent, so only ₹84 lakh ever reached profit after tax. Charging the full ₹120 lakh double-counts the tax and understates EPS: the right numerator is ₹916 lakh, giving ₹10.18.

options.text: ₹9.16 — profit of ₹916 lakh over 100 lakh shares
options.misconception: charges the cost of the buyback but leaves the share count untouched, which is the one thing a buyback certainly changes
options.why: Ten lakh shares have been cancelled, so 90 lakh remain. Dividing the correctly reduced profit by the old count shows only the cost and none of the benefit, turning a small rise into a fall.

options.text: ₹10.18 — profit of ₹916 lakh over 90 lakh shares
options.why: The ₹1,500 lakh of cash was earning 1,500 × 8% = ₹120 lakh before tax, or 120 × 0.7 = ₹84 lakh after tax, and that income is now gone. Profit falls to 1,000 − 84 = ₹916 lakh and the share count falls to 90 lakh, giving 916 / 90 = ₹10.18. The smaller share count outweighs the lost income, so EPS rises slightly.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company earns profit after tax of ₹1,000 lakh on 100 lakh shares, so EPS is ₹10. It buys back 10 lakh shares at ₹150 each, paying ₹1,500 lakh out of surplus cash that had been earning 8 per cent a year before tax. The tax rate is 30 per cent, and nothing else changes.

items.stem: On which yield should the investor price this bond, and what is it?

options.text: About 10.75 per cent, the same call working divided by the ₹1,000 face value
options.misconception: divides by face value instead of by the average of the price paid and the call price, which is the money actually tied up over the four years
options.why: 107.5 / 1,000 = 10.75 per cent. The investor did not pay face value; he paid ₹1,100 and expects ₹1,050 back, so the average investment over the period is ₹1,075. Using ₹1,000 flatters the yield because it understates what is at stake.

options.text: About 10.91 per cent, the current yield of ₹120 on a price of ₹1,100
options.misconception: uses current yield, which counts the coupon alone and never records the capital loss taken when the bond is called below the purchase price
options.why: 120 / 1,100 = 10.91 per cent is the current yield and it stops at the coupon. It never records that ₹1,100 paid today comes back as ₹1,050 on the call date — a capital loss of ₹50 spread over four years. Once that is in, the return is 10.00 per cent.

options.text: About 10.48 per cent, the yield to maturity over the full ten years
options.misconception: prices a premium bond on its yield to maturity and ignores the call feature, which is the issuer's right to end the bond early exactly when it is expensive to keep
options.why: The 10.48 per cent assumes the bond runs all ten years. The call option belongs to the issuer, not the investor, and it is used when refinancing is cheaper — which is what a price of ₹1,100 on a 12 per cent coupon is saying. Pricing on the yield to maturity here quotes a return the investor is unlikely ever to receive.

options.text: About 10.00 per cent, the yield to call
options.why: The approximate yield to call runs the ₹120 coupon against the fall from ₹1,100 to the call price of ₹1,050 over four years: [120 + (1,050 − 1,100)/4] ÷ [(1,050 + 1,100)/2] = 107.5 / 1,075 = 10.00 per cent. The approximate yield to maturity is [120 + (1,000 − 1,100)/10] ÷ 1,050 = 110 / 1,050 = 10.48 per cent. A bond standing at a premium is one the issuer can refinance more cheaply, so the call is the likely outcome and the yield to worst — the lower of the two — is the number to price on.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries a 12 per cent annual coupon and has 10 years left to maturity. It trades at ₹1,100. The issuer may redeem it at ₹1,050 at the end of year 4. Use the approximate yield formula — annual coupon plus the annual amortisation of the discount or premium, over the average of the price paid and the amount receivable.

items.stem: What is the conversion premium, and what is the debenture's floor value?

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹80, with a floor of ₹880
options.misconception: measures the premium against the straight bond value rather than the conversion value, so it reports the downside cushion instead of what conversion costs
options.why: 960 − 880 = ₹80 is the premium over the straight bond value, and it answers a different question — how far the price can fall before the bond floor catches it. The conversion premium is measured against what the shares fetch on conversion, ₹840, and it is ₹120.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹160, with a floor of ₹880
options.misconception: takes the ₹1,000 face value as the debenture's price, when the premium is measured from the market price actually paid
options.why: 1,000 − 840 = ₹160 uses face value where the market price belongs. The buyer gives up ₹960 today, not ₹1,000, so the conversion premium is ₹120. Face value matters at redemption; it is not what anyone pays now.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹120, with a floor of ₹840
options.misconception: takes the conversion value as the floor, when the floor is whichever of the conversion value and the straight bond value is higher — and here the bond value is
options.why: The premium is right and the floor is not. Conversion value of ₹840 acts as a floor only while it exceeds the straight bond value. Here the bond alone is worth ₹880, and that claim survives whatever the share does, so ₹880 is the floor.

options.text: A conversion premium of ₹120, or 14.29 per cent, with a floor of ₹880
options.why: The conversion value is 20 × ₹42 = ₹840, so the conversion premium is 960 − 840 = ₹120, which is 120 / 840 = 14.29 per cent over conversion value. The floor is the higher of the two lower bounds: the straight bond value of ₹880 stands above the conversion value of ₹840, so a holder who never converts still has an ₹880 claim and the debenture will not sensibly trade below it.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A convertible debenture of ₹1,000 face value converts into 20 equity shares. The share trades at ₹42. A non-convertible debenture of the same issuer, coupon and maturity would be worth ₹880. The convertible itself trades at ₹960.

items.stem: What happens when the warrants are exercised?

options.text: The company issues new shares and takes in ₹250 each, and the debentures stay outstanding
options.why: A detachable warrant is a claim on the company itself, so exercise brings fresh cash in at the exercise price and the company issues new shares to meet it. That is equity dilution — the existing holders' slice of the company shrinks. Because these warrants were detached, the borrowing is untouched: unlike a convertible debenture, nothing is extinguished and the debentures run on to maturity.

options.text: No new shares are created; the company buys shares in the market and delivers them, as an option writer would
options.misconception: confuses a company-issued warrant with an exchange-traded call option written by another investor, which creates no new shares because the writer is not the company
options.why: An exchange-traded call option is a contract between two outsiders and the company is not in it — the writer hands over existing shares and the share count never moves. A warrant is issued by the company, so meeting it means issuing new shares. That is the whole reason a warrant dilutes and a traded option does not.

options.text: Nothing changes for the debenture holder, since a warrant cannot be sold apart from the debenture it came with
options.misconception: misses that a detachable warrant is a security in its own right, separately listed and separately priced from the debenture it was attached to
options.why: These warrants are detachable and listed, so they have their own market price and their own buyers. A holder can sell the detachable warrant and keep the debenture, or sell the debenture and keep the warrant — from the day they are detached the two are separate securities.

options.text: The debentures are extinguished, the debt turning into the shares issued
options.misconception: treats a detachable warrant as a conversion right, when a warrant is exercised by paying cash and leaves the debt exactly where it was
options.why: That is what a convertible debenture does — the holder surrenders the debt and takes shares, and the borrowing disappears. A warrant is met by paying the exercise price in cash, so the company ends up with the new shares issued and the debentures still on its books.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A company issues debentures with detachable warrants attached. Each warrant entitles its holder to buy one share from the company at ₹250 within three years. The warrants are listed and trade separately from the debentures.

items.stem: What is the project's NPV once the abandonment option is allowed for, and what is that option worth?

options.text: NPV of about +₹3.80 lakh, with the option worth about ₹19.84 lakh
options.why: In the bad state, continuing is worth 40 / 1.1 = ₹36.36 lakh at the end of year 1, so the ₹80 lakh abandonment value is taken; in the good state, continuing is worth 150 / 1.1 = ₹136.36 lakh and the plant is kept. Expected value at the end of year 1 is 0.5 × 136.36 + 0.5 × 80 = ₹108.18 lakh, so NPV = −140 + (50 + 108.18)/1.1 = +₹3.80 lakh. The abandonment option is the gap from the static NPV of −₹16.03 lakh, that is ₹19.84 lakh — which is also 0.5 × (80 − 36.36) / 1.1 taken directly.

options.text: NPV of about −₹21.82 lakh, taking the ₹80 lakh at the end of year 1 in both states
options.misconception: exercises the abandonment option regardless of the state, surrendering a continuation worth ₹136.36 lakh in the good state for ₹80 lakh
options.why: −140 + (50 + 80)/1.1 = −₹21.82 lakh, worse than the static case. An abandonment option is exercised only where exercising pays: in the good state, continuing is worth ₹136.36 lakh against an abandonment value of ₹80 lakh, so the plant is kept and only the bad state is abandoned.

options.text: The option is worth about ₹43.64 lakh, being ₹80 lakh less the ₹36.36 lakh continuation value
options.misconception: prices the option on the bad state alone, forgetting both that the bad state occurs only half the time and that the gain lands a year away
options.why: ₹43.64 lakh is the gain in the bad state, at the end of year 1. It has to be weighted by the half chance of that state happening and brought back one year: 0.5 × 43.64 / 1.1 = ₹19.84 lakh. What an option is worth is what it is expected to pay in today's money, not what it pays in the state where it pays most.

options.text: NPV of about −₹16.03 lakh, so reject, on an expected year-2 cash flow of ₹95 lakh
options.misconception: discounts probability-weighted cash flows as though the manager had to sit through year 2 whatever happened, which prices the flexibility at exactly zero
options.why: 0.5 × 150 + 0.5 × 40 = ₹95 lakh, and −140 + 50/1.1 + 95/1.21 = −₹16.03 lakh. That is the static NPV, and it is the right answer only if the plant cannot be sold. The option to abandon is worth ₹19.84 lakh here, which turns the decision round.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A project costs ₹140 lakh now and runs two years. It yields ₹50 lakh at the end of year 1 whatever happens. Demand is then known: with equal probability year 2 brings ₹150 lakh or ₹40 lakh. At the end of year 1 the plant can be sold for ₹80 lakh, and that offer stands in either state. The discount rate is 10 per cent.

items.stem: What is the most the two can save between them by borrowing and swapping, and who borrows what?

options.text: 2.5 per cent, being the 2 per cent rupee gap plus the 0.5 per cent dollar gap
options.misconception: adds the two interest rate differentials instead of taking the difference between them, counting the same advantage twice over
options.why: 2.0 + 0.5 = 2.5 per cent adds the two interest rate differentials together. The swap can only harvest what remains after each party gives up its own edge in the currency it walks away from, and that is the difference between the spreads, 1.5 per cent, never their sum.

options.text: 0.5 per cent, the narrower of the two gaps
options.misconception: reads the saving as the smaller spread on its own, when the saving is the gap between the two spreads
options.why: 0.5 per cent is A's edge in dollars taken alone. The saving exists because A's edge is much wider in rupees than in dollars — 2.0 against 0.5 — and it is that gap of 1.5 per cent that borrowing-and-swapping converts into a saving for both parties.

options.text: 1.5 per cent in all, with A borrowing rupees and B borrowing dollars
options.why: A's edge over B is 2 per cent in rupees and 0.5 per cent in dollars, so its comparative advantage lies in rupees even though it holds an absolute advantage in both currencies. Each borrows where its edge is widest and moves into the currency it wants through a currency swap. The total gain — the quality spread differential — is the difference between the two spreads, 2.0 − 0.5 = 1.5 per cent, to be shared between them and any dealer in the middle.

options.text: Nothing, since A borrows more cheaply than B in both currencies and so has nothing to gain from B
options.misconception: confuses absolute advantage with comparative advantage; the gain comes from the two parties' spreads differing, not from either being cheaper overall
options.why: A holds an absolute advantage in both currencies and still gains. What matters is comparative advantage: A is relatively better at raising rupees, B relatively better at raising dollars, and each borrowing where it is relatively strong creates 1.5 per cent that existed nowhere before.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian company A can borrow rupees at 8 per cent and dollars at 6 per cent. An American company B can borrow rupees at 10 per cent and dollars at 6.5 per cent. A wants dollar funding and B wants rupee funding.

items.stem: What is the fund's net selectivity under Fama's decomposition?

options.text: 2.0 per cent
options.why: A fully diversified portfolio carrying this fund's total risk would have required 6 + (25/20) × (14 − 6) = 6 + 10 = 16 per cent. Net selectivity is what the manager earned above that: 18 − 16 = 2.0 per cent. Gross selectivity, measured against beta alone, is 18 − [6 + 1.1 × 8] = 3.2 per cent, and the 1.2 per cent between the two is the diversification cost — the extra return the fund had to earn purely for holding risk it need not have held.

options.text: 4.0 per cent
options.misconception: compares the fund's return with the market's raw return, charging nothing at all for the fund carrying more risk than the market
options.why: 18 − 14 = 4.0 per cent says only that the fund beat the market. It ran a standard deviation of 25 per cent against the market's 20 per cent, so more was required of it; the return demanded for that total risk is 16 per cent, and only the 2.0 per cent above it belongs to the manager.

options.text: 3.2 per cent
options.misconception: stops at the return required for systematic risk, which charges the manager for beta but not for the unsystematic risk he chose to carry
options.why: 6 + 1.1 × 8 = 14.8 per cent is the return required for systematic risk, and 18 − 14.8 = 3.2 per cent is gross selectivity — the same number as Jensen's alpha. Fama goes one step further and also charges the manager for imperfect diversification, which takes the figure down to 2.0 per cent.

options.text: 1.2 per cent
options.misconception: reports the diversification component on its own, which is a charge against the manager rather than a reward earned by him
options.why: 16 − 14.8 = 1.2 per cent is the diversification component — the extra return demanded because the fund is not fully diversified. It is deducted from gross selectivity of 3.2 per cent, leaving net selectivity of 2.0 per cent. It is a cost in the working, not the answer.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Over the year a fund returned 18 per cent with a standard deviation of 25 per cent. The market returned 14 per cent with a standard deviation of 20 per cent. The risk-free rate was 6 per cent. The fund's beta was 1.1.

items.stem: Which arrangement fits what he has asked for?

options.text: Bill discounting by his own bank
options.misconception: reads discounting as the same thing as forfaiting, when a discounting bank holds the drawer liable and works on short-dated paper
options.why: A bank discounting a bill keeps recourse against the drawer, so the exporter stays liable if the note is dishonoured, and such facilities are short-dated. Forfaiting is the without-recourse, medium-term version, and it is the bank's aval on the notes that makes a five-year instrument fundable that way at all.

options.text: Forfaiting
options.why: Forfaiting discounts medium- to long-term export receivables evidenced by negotiable instruments — bills of exchange or promissory notes — usually carrying an aval from the importer's bank, and it is always without recourse to the exporter. It is arranged deal by deal, pays over the full discounted value rather than a part advance, and brings no ledger service with it. Every feature he asked for is in it.

options.text: Factoring, since he is selling a receivable
options.misconception: treats any sale of a receivable as factoring, when factoring handles short-term trade debts as a continuing book and comes bundled with ledger work
options.why: Factoring buys short-term trade debts, usually the whole turnover rather than one deal, advances a part of each invoice rather than the whole, and normally includes sales ledger administration and collection. His receivable runs five years, is a single transaction, and he wants no ledger service at all.

options.text: Factoring with recourse
options.misconception: chooses the arrangement that leaves the default risk sitting with the exporter, which is the single thing he asked to be rid of
options.why: With recourse means the factor can come back on the exporter if the buyer does not pay, so the credit risk never leaves him. He asked for money without recourse; a recourse arrangement hands him cash and keeps the risk exactly where it was.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An exporter holds one large receivable of ₹15 crore from a foreign buyer, payable over five years and evidenced by promissory notes carrying the guarantee of the buyer's bank. He wants the cash now, wants no comeback on himself if the buyer fails to pay, and does not want anyone running his sales ledger.

items.stem: What cost of equity does that policy produce?

options.text: 15.5 per cent
options.misconception: adds both premiums to the risk-free rate without scaling by beta, so the project's own riskiness never enters the answer
options.why: 7 + 5.5 + 3 = 15.5 per cent forgets beta entirely. A beta of 1.2 says this business swings more than the market, so the equity risk premium is multiplied by 1.2 — and under the stated policy the country risk premium travels through beta with it, giving 17.2 per cent.

options.text: 16.6 per cent
options.misconception: adds the country premium as a flat constant outside beta, so every business in that country is charged the same country premium however exposed it is
options.why: 7 + 1.2 × 5.5 + 3 = 16.6 per cent is the flat-addition version. It is a defensible method in its own right, but it is not the one stated here: carrying the country risk premium through beta gives a cost of equity of 7 + 1.2 × 8.5 = 17.2 per cent, and the two differ by 0.2 times the country premium, that is 0.6 per cent.

options.text: 13.6 per cent
options.misconception: prices a developing-country subsidiary at a mature-market cost of equity, leaving country risk out of the number altogether
options.why: 7 + 1.2 × 5.5 = 13.6 per cent uses the mature-market equity risk premium alone. The 3 per cent sovereign spread is the market's own price for the extra risk of operating there, and dropping it values the subsidiary as though it stood in a mature market.

options.text: 17.2 per cent
options.why: Carrying the country risk premium through beta means it joins the equity risk premium before beta multiplies: 7 + 1.2 × (5.5 + 3) = 7 + 10.2 = 17.2 per cent as the cost of equity. A subsidiary more exposed than average to its market is then charged more than average for country risk too, which is precisely what the stated policy says should happen.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company is valuing a subsidiary in a developing country. It uses an Indian risk-free rate of 7 per cent, a mature-market equity risk premium of 5.5 per cent and a project beta of 1.2. That country's sovereign bonds yield 3 per cent more than comparable Indian government paper, and the company takes that 3 per cent as the country risk premium. Its stated policy is that a business's exposure to country risk moves with its exposure to market risk, so the country premium is carried through beta.

items.stem: What does the cotton effectively cost the mill?

options.misconception: reverses the sign of the futures result, adding the gain to the purchase cost when a long position gains as prices rise and that gain reduces what the buyer pays
options.why: 60,000 + 4,400 = ₹64,400 treats the futures leg as a loss. The mill bought at ₹56,000 and closed at ₹60,400, a gain of ₹4,400 a tonne. A long hedge is meant to gain exactly when the price the mill must pay goes up, so the gain comes off: ₹55,600.

options.misconception: assumes a futures hedge locks the entry price exactly, which holds only if the basis is unchanged when the hedge is lifted
options.why: A hedge does not lock the entry futures price; it locks that price plus whatever the basis turns out to be at the close. Here the closing basis is 60,000 − 60,400 = −₹400, so the mill pays 56,000 − 400 = ₹55,600. Had the basis stayed at its opening −₹1,000 it would have paid ₹55,000, so basis risk moved the outcome by ₹600 a tonne against it.

options.misconception: prices the purchase at the spot market and leaves the futures leg out of the effective cost entirely
options.why: 300 × 60,000 = ₹1,80,00,000 is what the cotton costs in the spot market, and it is what the mill would have faced with no hedge at all. The long futures position gained ₹13,20,000 as prices rose, and that gain belongs in the effective cost — it brings it down to ₹55,600 a tonne.

The cotton costs 300 × 60,000 = ₹1,80,00,000 in the physical market. The long hedge gains 300 × (60,400 − 56,000) = ₹13,20,000, bringing the effective cost to ₹1,66,80,000, which is ₹55,600 a tonne. The same figure falls out of the futures price at entry plus the closing basis: 56,000 + (60,000 − 60,400) = ₹55,600.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A spinning mill will buy 300 tonnes of cotton in three months. Cotton spot is ₹55,000 a tonne today and the three-month futures is ₹56,000. The mill buys 10 futures contracts of 30 tonnes each. Three months later, when it buys the cotton, spot is ₹60,000 and the futures it closes out stands at ₹60,400.

items.stem: What does a credit rating say, and what does it not say?

options.text: A rating once assigned holds good for the life of the instrument
options.misconception: ignores continuous surveillance and rating migration, when a grade is reviewed through the instrument's life and can fall, including to default grade
options.why: A rating is a live opinion, not a certificate issued once and filed. The agency keeps the issuer under surveillance and revises the grade as the finances change; rating migration to a lower grade, and in the worst case to default grade, happens to somebody every year.

options.text: It grades how likely that one instrument is to be serviced on time, is kept under review, and says nothing about whether the price is fair
options.why: A credit rating ranks default risk — the likelihood of interest and principal being paid on time on one specific instrument, which is exactly why the same company's bank facilities and commercial paper can be graded differently. The agency keeps it under surveillance, so rating migration up or down is ordinary. On price it is silent: whether the yield offered compensates for the risk is the investor's own judgement.

options.text: It is the agency's recommendation to buy the debentures at the yield offered
options.misconception: reads a rating as investment advice, when it grades default risk and is deliberately silent on whether the price compensates for that risk
options.why: A rating agency does not tell anybody what to buy. It grades default risk and stops there. A highly rated instrument at a thin yield can be a poor investment and a low-rated one at a rich yield a good one — the rating is one input into that judgement and never the judgement itself.

options.text: Since the company is rated, every instrument it issues carries the same rating
options.misconception: treats the rating as an attribute of the company rather than of the individual instrument, when tenure, security and structure all move the grade
options.why: The scenario itself shows otherwise — long-term bank facilities and commercial paper are graded differently on the same company. A credit rating attaches to an instrument: its tenure, its security, and where it stands in the queue if things go wrong. A secured long-term facility and unsecured short-dated paper are assessed separately.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: A company's long-term bank facilities carry a high rating while its commercial paper carries a different one. A retail investor, offered the company's debentures, asks what the rating tells him.

items.stem: What is the Z-score, and which zone does the company fall in?

options.text: 2.18, the distress zone, since it falls short of 2.99
options.misconception: collapses the three zones into two, reading everything below the safe boundary as a prediction of failure
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the reading is not. The model has three zones: above 2.99 is safe, below 1.81 is the distress zone, and 2.18 lies between them in the grey zone, where the model declines to call it either way.

options.text: 2.18, the grey zone
options.why: 1.2(0.20) + 1.4(0.15) + 3.3(0.10) + 0.6(0.50) + 1.0(1.10) = 0.24 + 0.21 + 0.33 + 0.30 + 1.10 = 2.18. That stands above the 1.81 boundary of the distress zone and below the 2.99 boundary of the safe zone, so the Z-score puts the company in the grey zone — not predicted to fail, not cleared either, and a case for watching rather than for a verdict.

options.text: 1.08, the distress zone
options.misconception: drops the X5 term, sales to total assets, whose weight of 1.0 makes it the largest single contributor here
options.why: 2.18 − 1.10 = 1.08 leaves out the asset turnover term. X5 contributes 1.10 of the 2.18 — more than the other four put together — so omitting it drives the Z-score down two zones. All five ratios go in, each at its own coefficient.

options.text: 2.05, the grey zone
options.misconception: adds the five ratios without their weights, which throws the model away; landing in the same zone here is coincidence, not a result
options.why: 0.20 + 0.15 + 0.10 + 0.50 + 1.10 = 2.05 is a plain total of the ratios. The coefficients are the model — a weight of 3.3 on EBIT to total assets against 0.6 on the market value term says profitability counts several times as heavily as the cover on liabilities. This total happens to land in the grey zone as well, which proves nothing: shift one ratio and the two answers part company.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A listed manufacturer is scored on Altman's five-variable model for public manufacturing companies, in the form given here — Z = 1.2X1 + 1.4X2 + 3.3X3 + 0.6X4 + 1.0X5, where X1 is working capital to total assets, X2 retained earnings to total assets, X3 EBIT to total assets, X4 market value of equity to book value of total liabilities, and X5 sales to total assets. Take the safe zone as Z above 2.99, the distress zone as Z below 1.81, and anything between the two as the grey zone. For this company X1 is 0.20, X2 is 0.15, X3 is 0.10, X4 is 0.50 and X5 is 1.10.

items.stem: What is the best estimate of the call's new price?

options.text: About ₹12.00
options.misconception: drops the one-half from the second-order term, doubling the gamma contribution
options.why: 8.00 + 3.00 + 0.04 × 25 = ₹12.00 uses the whole of gamma times the squared move. The second-order term carries a one-half in front of it, so the correct contribution is 0.5 × 0.04 × 25 = ₹0.50, not ₹1.00, and the estimate is ₹11.50.

options.text: About ₹11.50
options.why: The delta term gives 0.60 × 5 = ₹3.00 and the second-order term adds one-half of gamma times the square of the move, 0.5 × 0.04 × 25 = ₹0.50, so the estimate is 8.00 + 3.00 + 0.50 = ₹11.50. The same answer arrives another way: gamma says delta itself rises from 0.60 to 0.60 + 0.04 × 5 = 0.80 over the move, and the average delta of 0.70 applied to the ₹5 move gives ₹3.50 as well.

options.text: About ₹11.20
options.misconception: adds gamma to delta as though gamma were itself a rate of price change, when gamma is the rate at which delta changes
options.why: 8.00 + (0.60 + 0.04) × 5 = ₹11.20 treats gamma as a second delta. Delta answers how much the option moves per rupee; gamma answers how much delta moves per rupee, so it must be multiplied by the move twice over and then halved. Theta and vega are the other two of the family, measuring the loss to a passing day and the gain from rising volatility.

options.text: About ₹11.00
options.misconception: uses delta alone, which is a straight-line estimate of a curved relationship and always understates what a bought option gains on a move in its favour
options.why: 8.00 + 0.60 × 5 = ₹11.00 treats delta as fixed across the whole ₹5 move. It is not fixed — gamma of 0.04 says it climbs as the share climbs, so the true gain is larger. The straight-line estimate misses the curvature, and the gap widens with the square of the move.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹200. A call option on it is priced at ₹8.00, with a delta of 0.60 and a gamma of 0.04 per rupee. The share then rises to ₹205 in the same trading session, and volatility is unchanged.

items.stem: Between which share prices does this position lose money at expiry, and what is the most it can lose?

options.text: It loses between ₹480 and ₹520, and the most it can lose is ₹40
options.misconception: averages the two premiums instead of adding them, halving the move the share must make before the position pays
options.why: Taking (22 + 18) / 2 = ₹20 either side of the strike gives ₹480 and ₹520. The straddle cost ₹40 in total, not ₹20, so the share has to travel ₹40 from the strike before the position is whole. Averaging the premiums understates the move needed and makes the strategy look twice as easy as it is.

options.text: It loses between ₹460 and ₹540, and the most it can lose is ₹40
options.why: The long straddle costs 22 + 18 = ₹40, and that whole premium is paid whichever way the share goes. Above the strike only the call pays, so the break-even is 500 + 40 = ₹540; below it only the put pays, so the other break-even is 500 − 40 = ₹460. Between the two the position loses, and the worst case is the share finishing at exactly ₹500, where both options expire worthless and the entire ₹40 is gone.

options.text: It loses between ₹460 and ₹540, and the loss is unlimited
options.misconception: attaches the writer's unlimited risk to the buyer, when a bought option can never cost more than the premium paid for it
options.why: The break-even points are right and the loss is not. A buyer of a call or a put can abandon it, so the worst outcome is losing the ₹40 premium paid. Unlimited loss belongs to the writer of a straddle, who has sold both options and must perform however far the share travels.

options.text: It loses between ₹482 and ₹522, and the most it can lose is ₹40
options.misconception: charges each side only the premium of the option that finishes in the money, when both premiums are paid whatever the share does
options.why: 500 − 18 = ₹482 and 500 + 22 = ₹522 charge the put's premium below the strike and the call's above it. But the buyer paid for both options on day one, so at ₹522 the call is worth ₹22 and has merely repaid its own premium while the ₹18 put premium is still lost. Both break-even points are one full ₹40 away from the strike.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹500. An investor expecting a large move but unsure of its direction buys a three-month call at a strike of ₹500 for a premium of ₹22 and a three-month put at the same strike for a premium of ₹18.

items.stem: What is the swap worth to the company now?

options.text: An asset of about ₹1.87 crore
options.misconception: values the swap from the counterparty's side, reversing which leg is paid and which is received
options.why: The arithmetic is right and the direction is wrong. This company is the payer of fixed at 8 per cent against a floating receipt of 6 per cent, so it is out of pocket. The ₹1.87 crore is an asset to the receiver of fixed on the other side of the same contract, and a liability here.

options.text: Nil, since a swap has no value and the notional is never exchanged
options.misconception: carries the zero value at inception through the life of the swap, when the fixed rate is frozen and market rates are not
options.why: A swap is worth nothing at inception, because the fixed rate is set on that day to make it so. After that rates move and the fixed rate does not, and the swap becomes an asset to one side and a liability to the other. The notional principal is indeed never exchanged, but that is a separate point — it cancels between the two bonds and changes nothing about the value.

options.text: A liability of exactly ₹2.00 crore
options.misconception: takes the net difference at face value without discounting, when the payment is a year away
options.why: The ₹2 crore net outflow is right and its timing is ignored. It falls due in one year, and at a discount rate of 7 per cent its present value is 2 / 1.07 = ₹1.87 crore. Valuing a swap means valuing the future differences where they stand, not adding them up as though they were payable today.

options.text: A liability of about ₹1.87 crore
options.why: The company must pay fixed of ₹8 crore and will receive ₹6 crore, a net outflow of ₹2 crore in one year, whose present value is 2 / 1.07 = ₹1.87 crore — a liability. The two-bond method gives the same figure: the fixed bond is worth 108 / 1.07 = ₹100.93 crore and the floating bond 106 / 1.07 = ₹99.07 crore, and the notional principal of ₹100 crore inside each cancels, which is why it never has to be exchanged.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A company pays fixed and receives floating on an interest rate swap of ₹100 crore notional, settled annually. Exactly one payment is left, due in one year. The fixed rate is 8 per cent, so ₹8 crore is payable. The floating rate for this final year was fixed at the last reset at 6 per cent, so ₹6 crore is receivable. The one-year discount rate today is 7 per cent.

items.stem: What mix minimises the portfolio's risk, and what is that risk?

options.text: 100 per cent in A, giving a risk of 20 per cent
options.misconception: assumes the least risky single share must be the least risky holding, which is only true when the two shares are perfectly correlated
options.why: Holding A alone carries A's own 20 per cent. Because the correlation is zero, adding some of B introduces a risk that moves independently of A's, and the two partly cancel — the minimum variance portfolio reaches about 16.6 per cent, below either share on its own. Only at a correlation of exactly one would the safest share alone be the safest holding.

options.text: 50 per cent in each, giving a risk of about 18.0 per cent
options.misconception: splits the money equally, which ignores that the riskier share has to be held in a smaller amount before the total stops falling
options.why: An equal split gives 0.25 × 400 + 0.25 × 900 = 325, a standard deviation of about 18.0 per cent. Equal weighting gives the 30 per cent share as much room as the 20 per cent one, and the variance formula squares each weight, so cutting the riskier holding below half brings the total down to 16.6 per cent.

options.text: About 69.2 per cent in A and 30.8 per cent in B, giving a risk of about 16.6 per cent
options.why: With zero correlation the covariance term drops out, so the weight of A is B's variance over the sum of the variances, 900 / (400 + 900) = 0.692, leaving 0.308 in B. The minimum variance portfolio's variance is 0.692² × 400 + 0.308² × 900 = 191.7 + 85.2 = 276.9, so its standard deviation is about 16.6 per cent — below A's own 20 per cent, which is the diversification gain that any correlation under one makes available.

options.text: 60 per cent in A and 40 per cent in B, giving a risk of about 17.0 per cent
options.misconception: weights the two shares in inverse proportion to their standard deviations, when the formula works on variances and the covariance
options.why: Taking 30 / (20 + 30) = 0.6 for A weights by standard deviations rather than by variances. Its own risk gives it away: 0.6² × 400 + 0.4² × 900 = 144 + 144 = 288, a standard deviation of about 17.0 per cent, which is higher than the 16.6 per cent the true minimum reaches. A mix that can be beaten is not the minimum.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Two shares are available. A has a standard deviation of 20 per cent and B of 30 per cent, and the correlation between them is zero.

items.stem: How does an exchange traded fund actually differ?

options.text: Its units trade on the exchange all day at a market price, and creation and redemption in large lots keeps that price close to the fund's net asset value
options.why: An investor buys an exchange traded fund from another investor on the exchange, at whatever price is quoted at that moment, where an open-ended scheme is transacted with the fund itself at the day's net asset value. Authorised participants may create or redeem units in large creation unit lots, usually against the underlying basket of shares, so any gap between the market price and the underlying value is an arbitrage they close.

options.text: Its units are issued once at launch and the number in issue never changes, as with a closed-end fund
options.misconception: confuses an exchange traded fund with a closed-end fund, when units are created and cancelled continuously and that is what stops a discount persisting
options.why: A closed-end fund has a fixed number of units, which is why it can trade at a lasting discount — nobody can create or cancel units to close the gap. An exchange traded fund's count moves continuously as authorised participants create and redeem, and that is precisely what stops such a discount taking hold.

options.text: There is no difference that matters — units are bought from the fund at the day's closing net asset value either way
options.misconception: treats an exchange traded fund as an ordinary open-ended scheme, when a retail investor deals in the secondary market at a live price and not with the fund
options.why: A retail buyer of an exchange traded fund never deals with the fund. He buys on the exchange from another investor at a live market price that moves through the session, which is exactly what an open-ended scheme transacting once a day at net asset value cannot offer.

options.text: Because it is exchange traded, its price is set by demand for the units and has no fixed link to the value of the shares it holds
options.misconception: forgets the creation and redemption mechanism, which is the arbitrage that pins an exchange traded fund's price to the value of its holdings
options.why: Demand can push the price off the underlying value, but not far and not for long. When the price runs above the value of the shares held, an authorised participant creates new units against that basket and sells them; when it runs below, it redeems. That arbitrage is why the price tracks the holdings within a narrow band.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: An investor is told that an exchange traded fund tracking an index is bought the same way as an ordinary open-ended index fund.

items.stem: What return did the unit holder earn over the year?

options.text: 8.0 per cent
options.misconception: counts only the change in net asset value and drops the distributions, which is money the holder actually received
options.why: (43.20 − 40.00) / 40.00 = 8.0 per cent measures the appreciation alone. The ₹2.40 of distributions paid out during the year is return the holder banked, and leaving it out punishes a scheme for distributing — the very act that held the closing net asset value down.

options.text: 6.0 per cent
options.misconception: counts only the cash distributions received and ignores that the units themselves are worth more than they cost
options.why: (1.60 + 0.80) / 40.00 = 6.0 per cent is the distribution yield. The units also rose from ₹40.00 to ₹43.20, and that ₹3.20 is as real as the cash — it is realised the day they are sold. Both parts go into the holding period return, giving 14.0 per cent.

options.text: 14.0 per cent
options.why: The holding period return counts the rise in net asset value and everything taken out during the year, over what was invested at the start: (43.20 − 40.00 + 1.60 + 0.80) / 40.00 = 5.60 / 40.00 = 14.0 per cent. The dividend and the capital gains distribution belong in the numerator because they were paid out of the fund's own assets, which is why the closing figure is lower than it would otherwise be.

options.text: About 12.96 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the closing net asset value instead of the opening one, so the return is measured against money the holder never had to put in
options.why: 5.60 / 43.20 = 12.96 per cent divides the gain by the closing net asset value. The denominator has to be what was actually invested at the start, ₹40.00, since that is the money that was at work. Using the closing figure understates a rising fund's return and overstates a falling one's.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A unit holder bought units of a scheme at a net asset value of ₹40.00. A year later the net asset value is ₹43.20. During the year the scheme paid a dividend of ₹1.60 a unit and a capital gains distribution of ₹0.80 a unit, both taken in cash.

items.stem: What separates a pass through certificate from a pay through security?

options.text: A pay through structure can have only one class of paper, since all investors rank equally
options.misconception: misses that re-sequencing collections into tranches of different maturity and seniority is the main reason for choosing a pay through structure
options.why: Re-sequencing is the point of it. Because the special purpose vehicle keeps the pool and issues its own paper against it, it can carve the collections into tranches that mature at different dates and differ in seniority, which is exactly what a single pass through class cannot do.

options.text: A pass through certificate carries ownership of a share of the pool and hands on collections as they arrive; a pay through security is debt of the vehicle, which keeps the pool and re-sequences its collections
options.why: A pass through certificate sells an undivided ownership interest in the receivables themselves, so whatever the borrowers pay that month goes straight out to the holders in proportion — an early repayment reaches them early, and the timing risk is theirs. A pay through security is a debt obligation of the special purpose vehicle, which retains ownership of the pool and uses the collections to service paper it has re-sequenced into tranches of different maturity.

options.text: Under a pass through structure the vehicle absorbs early repayments and still pays holders on a fixed schedule
options.misconception: reverses where prepayment timing lands, when a pass through hands collections on as received and so passes the timing risk straight to the investor
options.why: Passing collections on as they arrive is the definition of the structure. When borrowers repay early that prepayment reaches pass through holders at once, and they must reinvest it at whatever rates then prevail. It is the pay through structure, holding the pool and paying a schedule of its own, that can absorb that timing.

options.text: Both are debt of the special purpose vehicle; only the frequency of payment differs
options.misconception: treats both instruments as borrowings, when a pass through transfers ownership of the receivables and creates no debt at all
options.why: Only the pay through security is debt of the special purpose vehicle. The holder of a pass through certificate owns a slice of the receivables and is not a lender to anybody — which is why his return rises and falls with what the pool actually collects rather than with a promised schedule.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An originator securitises a pool of housing loans. One tranche of investors is told they hold a proportionate interest in the pool itself; another is told they hold paper issued by the special purpose vehicle, repayable on a schedule the vehicle has set.

items.stem: How does a venture capital investor realise its money?

options.text: By the company repaying the investment with interest at the end of the agreed term
options.misconception: treats venture capital as a loan with a maturity, when it is equity or convertible preferred and carries no promise of repayment
options.why: A venture capital investment is not a loan. There is no maturity and no interest to be repaid; the fund holds equity, usually convertible preferred shares, and gets its money only when somebody buys those shares. That is why a failed startup returns nothing at all rather than a reduced repayment.

options.text: A buy-back by the promoters is not a real exit, because a company cannot purchase shares from its own investor
options.misconception: dismisses the buy-back route, when a negotiated purchase by the promoters or the company is a standard exit clause in a venture agreement
options.why: A promoter buy-back is one of the ordinary exit routes and is written into most venture agreements, often with a formula for the price. It matters most where a listing is out of reach and no trade buyer appears — it is the exit that does not depend on finding a stranger.

options.text: Through an initial public offering, which is the only route that returns the full value of a venture stake
options.misconception: treats one route as always best, when a listing needs scale, a receptive market and a company able to bear public reporting
options.why: An initial public offering is often the dearest exit and it is never guaranteed. It needs the company to be large enough to list, the market to be open when the fund needs it, and the business to carry the cost of being public. A trade sale to a strategic buyer can pay more, because the buyer is also paying for what the business is worth inside its own group.

options.text: By selling the stake — through an initial public offering, a trade sale, a secondary sale to another investor, or a buy-back by the promoters or the company
options.why: The fund holds equity, so the only way out is to sell what it holds. An initial public offering lists the company and lets the stake be sold into the market; a trade sale hands the whole company to a strategic buyer; a secondary sale passes the holding to another financial investor; and a promoter buy-back has the founders or the company purchase it back. Which route is available decides the price and the timing, so it is negotiated at entry.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A venture capital fund holds a 25 per cent stake in a company it backed four years ago. The fund's own life is running down and it must return money to its investors.

items.stem: What is the company's market value added?

options.text: ₹50 crore
options.why: Market capitalisation is 50 lakh × ₹180 = ₹90 crore, so the market value of the whole firm is 90 + 35 = ₹125 crore. Capital employed is share capital of ₹5 crore plus reserves of ₹35 crore plus debt of ₹35 crore, that is ₹75 crore. Market value added is the excess of one over the other, 125 − 75 = ₹50 crore — the market's verdict that this company is worth ₹50 crore more than the money put into it.

options.text: ₹90 crore
options.misconception: reports market capitalisation as though it were the value added, when what is added is the excess over the capital the company was given
options.why: ₹90 crore is the market capitalisation and nothing has been deducted from it. Market value added measures the gap between what the market says the company is worth and what its providers of capital put in; the ₹75 crore of capital employed has to come out, leaving ₹50 crore.

options.text: ₹85 crore
options.misconception: deducts only the paid-up share capital and treats reserves as though they were not capital, when retained profit is shareholders' money left in the business
options.why: 90 − 5 = ₹85 crore counts only the ₹5 crore of paid-up share capital as money the shareholders provided. The ₹35 crore of reserves is profit that belonged to them and was kept back instead of paid out, so it is as much capital employed as the original subscription, and the debt counts too.

options.text: ₹125 crore
options.misconception: stops at the total market value of the firm and never subtracts the capital employed at all
options.why: 90 + 35 = ₹125 crore is the market value of the firm, equity and debt together. That is the first half of the working. Market value added is what is left after the ₹75 crore of capital employed is taken off it, which is ₹50 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company has 50 lakh equity shares of ₹10 each, so its share capital is ₹5 crore, and its reserves stand at ₹35 crore. Its debt is ₹35 crore and trades at book value. The share price is ₹180.

items.stem: What synergy does the deal create, and what is the most A Ltd could pay without harming its own shareholders?

options.text: Synergy of ₹60 crore, being the premium over B Ltd's standalone value
options.misconception: reads the premium paid as the synergy created, when the premium only decides how the synergy is divided between the two sets of shareholders
options.why: 260 − 200 = ₹60 crore is the premium A Ltd chose to offer, not the value the merger creates. The synergy of ₹120 crore exists whatever price is agreed; the premium settles who gets it. Here B Ltd's shareholders take ₹60 crore of it and A Ltd's keep the other ₹60 crore.

options.text: Synergy of ₹320 crore, and a maximum price of ₹320 crore
options.misconception: measures synergy as the rise over the acquirer's own value, forgetting that the target's standalone value is also inside the combined figure
options.why: 1,120 − 800 = ₹320 crore treats everything above A Ltd's own worth as created by the merger. Most of it is simply B Ltd, whose standalone value was ₹200 crore before anyone thought of a deal. Taking that out leaves synergy of ₹120 crore, and it is a coincidence of these numbers that ₹320 crore is also the correct ceiling on the price.

options.text: Synergy of ₹120 crore, and a maximum price of ₹320 crore
options.why: Synergy is the combined value less the two standalone values: 1,120 − (800 + 200) = ₹120 crore. The maximum price is B Ltd's standalone value plus the whole of that synergy, 200 + 120 = ₹320 crore, because above it A Ltd hands over more than the deal creates. At the ₹260 crore actually offered, A Ltd pays a ₹60 crore premium and keeps ₹60 crore of the gain.

options.text: Synergy of ₹120 crore, and a maximum price of ₹120 crore
options.misconception: caps the price at the synergy alone, forgetting that the acquirer is also buying a business already worth ₹200 crore
options.why: The synergy is right and the ceiling is not. A Ltd is buying a company worth ₹200 crore on its own, and it may pay that plus everything the combination creates before it starts losing. The maximum price is 200 + 120 = ₹320 crore; a bid of ₹120 crore would simply be refused.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A Ltd is worth ₹800 crore on its own and B Ltd ₹200 crore on its own. Advisers value the combined company at ₹1,120 crore. A Ltd offers ₹260 crore in cash for the whole of B Ltd.

items.stem: What does the scheme actually achieve?

options.text: It rearranges the existing claims so the balance sheet shows realistic values and the accumulated losses are extinguished, without any cash entering the company from the exercise
options.why: A financial reconstruction moves value between the parties who already have claims. The capital reduction and the sacrifice by lenders and preference holders create a credit that the accumulated losses are written off against, and the assets come down to what they are worth. Not one rupee comes in from the exercise itself, which is why fresh money is almost always raised alongside it.

options.text: It cannot work unless the sacrifices are imposed on the creditors, since no creditor would agree to take less than he is owed
options.misconception: assumes a creditor compares the sacrifice with the full amount owed, when the real comparison is with what a liquidation would actually pay him
options.why: A creditor of a failing company is not choosing between the scheme and being paid in full. He is choosing between the scheme and a liquidation, where he would rank behind the secured lenders and take whatever the assets fetch in a forced sale. A sacrifice that leaves him better off than that is one he has reason to accept.

options.text: It brings cash into the company equal to the amount by which the share capital is written down
options.misconception: reads a capital reduction as a receipt, when writing capital down is a bookkeeping entry and no money moves
options.why: Writing down share capital reduces a figure on the liabilities side; it does not put anything on the assets side. The company's bank balance is exactly the same the morning after the scheme as the morning before. Cash comes only from a fresh issue or fresh borrowing arranged alongside the capital reduction.

options.text: Writing off the accumulated losses raises the company's profit for the year
options.misconception: confuses removing a past loss from the balance sheet with earning profit, when the year's trading result is untouched by the scheme
options.why: The accumulated losses are the sum of results already reported in past years, and clearing them against the capital reduction changes nothing about how the company traded this year. What the scheme buys is a balance sheet that can support fresh borrowing and, in time, a dividend — not a profit.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company with large accumulated losses puts a scheme to its members and creditors. Equity shares are to be written down, the preference shareholders are to give up arrears of dividend, the lenders are to accept less than they are owed, and the assets are to be brought to their realistic values.

items.stem: Which description is right?

options.text: The crown jewel defence means the target buys the bidder's most valuable division to weaken it
options.misconception: points the defence at the wrong company, when the crown jewel defence disposes of the target's own prized asset so there is less left worth bidding for
options.why: The crown jewel is the target's own best asset, and the defence is to sell it or grant somebody an option over it. Once it is gone or spoken for, the reason for the bid has gone with it. Buying something from the bidder is a different manoeuvre altogether and does nothing to make the target less attractive.

options.text: A white knight is the party financing the hostile bid, brought in to complete the purchase
options.misconception: reverses the role, when a white knight is a friendlier acquirer the target invites in to outbid the hostile one
options.why: A white knight is on the target's side. The board, unable to stop a sale, looks for an acquirer it prefers — one that will pay more, keep the management, or leave the business intact — and invites it to bid against the hostile one. The shareholders still sell; they sell to somebody else.

options.text: Greenmail is a payment the bidder makes to the target's board in return for dropping its objection
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the money, when greenmail is the target buying the raider's block back at a premium to make him go away
options.why: The money flows the other way. Greenmail is the target company purchasing the raider's own block of shares back from him at a premium to the market price, so he leaves with a profit and the bid disappears. It is the shareholders who did not sell who pay for it.

options.text: A poison pill lets every shareholder except the bidder buy new shares cheaply, so the bidder's stake is diluted and the offer becomes far dearer
options.why: The poison pill works by making the company more expensive to buy the moment a hostile bidder crosses a stated shareholding. Rights to subscribe cheaply are triggered for everyone except him, the new shares flood in, and his stake suffers dilution while the price of taking control climbs. The defence is designed never to be used — its purpose is to force the bidder to negotiate with the board.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A company learns that a rival has quietly built a large stake and intends a hostile offer. Its board reviews the defences described in the textbooks.

items.stem: What does the dollar loan actually cost in rupees, and which borrowing is cheaper?

options.text: 5.00 per cent, so the dollar loan is much cheaper
options.misconception: quotes the foreign coupon as the cost and ignores exchange risk altogether, which is the whole trap in foreign currency borrowing
options.why: 5 per cent is what the loan costs in dollars, and the company earns and reports in rupees. It has to buy 1.05 million dollars at ₹84 to discharge a loan it took at ₹80, and that exchange risk is a real cost of exactly the same kind as interest. Including it, the effective cost is 10.25 per cent.

options.text: 9.00 per cent, because interest rate parity makes the two borrowings cost the same
options.misconception: assumes parity binds the expected spot rate, when parity fixes the forward rate and the rate a company expects may sit above or below it
options.why: Interest rate parity would put the one-year forward rate at 80 × 1.09 / 1.05 = ₹83.05, and borrowing dollars with a forward cover at that rate would indeed cost 9 per cent. The company expects ₹84, which is worse than the forward, so on its own expectation the dollar loan costs 10.25 per cent. Parity fixes what can be contracted, not what people expect.

options.text: 10.00 per cent, so the rupee loan at 9 per cent is cheaper
options.misconception: adds the interest rate and the expected depreciation instead of compounding them, which leaves out the extra rupees needed to buy the interest itself
options.why: 5 + 5 = 10 per cent adds the coupon to the expected depreciation. The company must buy dollars at ₹84 for the interest as well as for the principal, and that cross term — 0.05 × 0.05 — is the missing 0.25 per cent. Compounding gives 1.05 × 1.05 − 1 = 10.25 per cent. The verdict happens to be the same here, but the number is not.

options.text: 10.25 per cent, so the rupee loan at 9 per cent is cheaper
options.why: The company receives 1 million × ₹80 = ₹8.00 crore today and must repay 1.05 million dollars at ₹84, that is ₹8.82 crore. The effective cost is 0.82 / 8.00 = 10.25 per cent, which is also 1.05 × 1.05 − 1. The expected depreciation compounds with the interest rather than adding to it, because the dearer dollars must be bought for the interest as well as for the principal, and at 10.25 per cent this foreign currency loan is dearer than the 9 per cent rupee alternative.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company can borrow rupees for one year at 9 per cent, or borrow US dollars for one year at 5 per cent. The spot rate is ₹80 to the dollar and the company expects it to be ₹84 to the dollar in a year. Take a borrowing of one million dollars.

items.stem: Which selection should the company make?

options.text: Projects B, C and D, since every one of them has a positive NPV
options.misconception: ignores the budget constraint, which is exactly what distinguishes capital rationing from an ordinary accept-or-reject decision
options.why: B, C and D together cost 55 + 45 + 40 = ₹140 lakh against a ceiling of ₹100 lakh. Taking every positive NPV project is the right rule when there is no budget constraint; capital rationing is the case where it is not, and the whole exercise is choosing which positive NPV projects to give up.

options.text: Project A alone, for a total NPV of ₹50 lakh
options.why: With indivisible projects the profitability index only shortlists; the decision is made on the highest total NPV among the combinations that fit. A on its own uses the whole ₹100 lakh for ₹50 lakh of NPV. The best that starting with B can reach is B and C, ₹55 lakh plus ₹45 lakh, for 30 + 18 = ₹48 lakh. Under capital rationing the ranking loses to the combination, and ₹50 lakh beats ₹48 lakh.

options.text: Projects B and D, for a total NPV of ₹47 lakh, taking the two highest indices that fit
options.misconception: ranks by index and stops at the second project, leaving ₹5 lakh of the budget idle and ₹3 lakh of NPV on the table
options.why: B at ₹55 lakh and D at ₹40 lakh come to ₹95 lakh for 30 + 17 = ₹47 lakh, with ₹5 lakh unspent. Idle budget is a symptom, not the fault itself — even the fuller combination of B and C reaches only ₹48 lakh, and A alone reaches ₹50 lakh. The test is the total NPV of the combination that the profitability index only shortlists, however tidily the money is used up.

options.text: Projects B and C, for a total NPV of ₹48 lakh, since B has the highest profitability index
options.misconception: applies index ranking to indivisible projects, which is valid only when a project can be taken in part and the last of the budget can always be filled
options.why: Ranking by profitability index puts B first at 1.55, and the ₹45 lakh then left over reaches only C at 1.40, giving 30 + 18 = ₹48 lakh. Index ranking is exact when projects are divisible, because any remaining budget buys a fraction of the next project. Here nothing can be taken in part, and A alone delivers ₹50 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company can spend at most ₹100 lakh this year. Four projects are available, none of which can be taken in part or postponed. Project A costs ₹100 lakh with an NPV of ₹50 lakh and a profitability index of 1.50. Project B costs ₹55 lakh with an NPV of ₹30 lakh and an index of 1.55. Project C costs ₹45 lakh with an NPV of ₹18 lakh and an index of 1.40. Project D costs ₹40 lakh with an NPV of ₹17 lakh and an index of 1.43.

items.stem: What one-year rate does the market imply for the second year?

options.text: 6.00 per cent
options.misconception: assumes today's one-year rate will still be the one-year rate next year, which the rising shape of the curve itself denies
options.why: If the second year also earned 6 per cent, two years of lending would return 1.06² = 1.1236 and the two-year spot rate would be 6 per cent, not 8. An upward-sloping curve is precisely a market saying the later year earns more, and the forward rate is how much more.

options.text: 8.00 per cent
options.misconception: reads the two-year spot rate as the rate for the second year, when it is the average return over both years together
options.why: The two-year spot rate of 8 per cent applies to both years together, and the first of them earns only 6 per cent. The second year must therefore earn more than 8 per cent to pull the average up — which is what the forward rate of about 10.04 per cent is.

options.text: About 10.04 per cent
options.why: The forward rate comes out of the two spot rates by compounding, not subtraction: 1.08² / 1.06 − 1 = 1.1664 / 1.06 − 1 = 10.04 per cent. Put in money, ₹100 lent for two years at the two-year spot rate grows to ₹116.64, while ₹100 lent for one year at 6 per cent gives ₹106 — so the second year must earn 116.64 / 106 = 1.1004 for the two routes to finish level.

options.text: 2.00 per cent
options.misconception: subtracts one spot rate from the other, when the two rates cover different lengths of time and must be compounded out
options.why: 8 − 6 = 2 per cent treats the rates as though they were amounts. They are returns over different periods — one over a year, one over two — so the shorter has to be compounded out of the longer by dividing the growth factors, 1.1664 / 1.06, giving about 10.04 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The one-year spot rate is 6 per cent and the two-year spot rate is 8 per cent, both annually compounded.

items.stem: What can the shape actually be taken to mean?

options.text: It always means the market expects interest rates to rise
options.misconception: takes the expectations theory as the only explanation of the shape, when a term premium produces the same upward slope with no change in rates expected
options.why: That is the expectations theory's reading and it is one of three. Liquidity preference says part of the slope is payment for tying money up rather than a forecast, and market segmentation says it can come from nothing more than heavy demand for short paper. A curve that has sloped up for most of recorded history cannot have been forecasting rising rates the whole time.

options.text: Liquidity preference explains it by long bonds being more liquid and so yielding less
options.misconception: inverts the premium, when the theory says the lender must be paid more for longer paper whose price swings further when rates change
options.why: Liquidity preference runs the other way. A long bond's price moves far more for a given change in rates, and the lender's money is committed for longer, so he demands extra yield to hold it. That extra is the term premium, and it pushes long yields up rather than down.

options.text: Market segmentation theory explains it by making the long rate the average of expected short rates
options.misconception: attaches the expectations theory's mechanism to market segmentation, which holds the opposite — that each maturity is priced by its own supply and demand
options.why: Market segmentation says the maturities are separate markets. Banks want short paper, insurers and pension funds want long paper, and each bucket's rate is set by who is buying and selling in it — the rates need not be linked by any average at all. Averaging expected short rates is the expectations theory.

options.text: Under the expectations theory it says short rates are expected to rise; under liquidity preference it may slope up on a term premium alone, with rates expected to stay flat
options.why: The expectations theory reads the long rate as the average of the short rates the market expects, so an upward slope is a forecast of rising rates. Liquidity preference adds that a lender parting with money for longer must be paid a term premium for the price risk he takes on, which tilts the curve upwards even when no change in rates is expected. The same shape supports both readings, which is why the curve alone settles nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: The yield curve slopes upwards — three-month paper yields less than one-year paper, which yields less than ten-year paper. Two analysts read the same curve and reach different conclusions.

items.stem: What spot rate does the international Fisher effect imply for a year from now?

options.text: ₹80.00, unchanged, since the exchange rate has nothing to do with interest rates
options.misconception: treats the interest difference as a free gain, when the expected currency movement is exactly what the effect says removes it
options.why: If the rate stayed at ₹80, a dollar investor could borrow at 4 per cent, lend at 12 per cent in rupees and pocket the 8 per cent interest difference for nothing. The international Fisher effect exists to describe why that is not expected to work — the rupee is expected to weaken to about ₹86.15 and give the difference back.

options.text: About ₹86.15 to the dollar
options.why: The international Fisher effect puts the expected spot rate at today's spot times one plus the home nominal interest rate over one plus the foreign one: 80 × 1.12 / 1.04 = ₹86.15. The currency of the higher nominal interest rate is expected to weaken by about the difference, so a lender who chases the 12 per cent rupee rate expects to hand the gain back on the exchange rate.

options.text: About ₹86.40 to the dollar
options.misconception: applies the interest difference as a simple percentage of the spot rate instead of taking the ratio of the two growth factors
options.why: 80 × 1.08 = ₹86.40 adds the 8 percentage point difference straight to the spot rate. The relationship is a ratio, not a difference: 1.12 / 1.04 = 1.0769, which is a 7.69 per cent movement and gives ₹86.15. The approximation is close at small differences and drifts as they widen.

options.text: About ₹74.29 to the dollar
options.misconception: puts the two rates the wrong way round, so the high interest currency is expected to strengthen — the reverse of what the effect states
options.why: 80 × 1.04 / 1.12 = ₹74.29 has the rupee appreciating. The international Fisher effect says the opposite: a high nominal interest rate carries high expected inflation inside it, and the currency of the higher rate is expected to weaken, not strengthen. The home rate goes on top of the fraction.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: One-year nominal interest rates are 12 per cent in India and 4 per cent in the United States. The spot rate is ₹80 to the dollar.

items.stem: What is the initial outlay on the replacement?

options.misconception: deducts the whole sale price and forgets the tax the sale itself triggers on the excess over written-down value
options.why: 12,00,000 − 5,00,000 = ₹7,00,000 assumes every rupee of the sale price stays with the company. It sold for ₹1,00,000 more than the written-down value, and 30 per cent of that excess goes in tax, so only ₹4,70,000 is left to set against the new machine.

options.misconception: treats the replacement as a fresh purchase, ignoring that disposing of the old machine funds part of the new one
options.why: ₹12,00,000 is the new machine's price with no credit for the old one. A replacement is an incremental decision — the company would not be selling this machine but for the replacement, so its net proceeds of ₹4,70,000 belong in the initial outlay, bringing it to ₹7,30,000.

The old machine brings in ₹5,00,000, out of which tax of 0.30 × (5,00,000 − 4,00,000) = ₹30,000 goes on the excess over its written-down value, so ₹4,70,000 is actually recovered. The initial outlay is therefore 12,00,000 − 4,70,000 = ₹7,30,000. Everything in a replacement decision is measured this way, on incremental cash flows — what changes because the old machine goes and the new one arrives.

options.misconception: sets off the old machine's book value instead of what it actually fetched, when book value is not cash and the buyer's cheque is
options.why: 12,00,000 − 4,00,000 = ₹8,00,000 uses the written-down value of ₹4,00,000. That book value is the tax records' view of the machine, not money. What reduces the outlay is the ₹5,00,000 the buyer pays, less the ₹30,000 of tax on the excess.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company is replacing a machine whose written-down value is ₹4,00,000. A buyer will pay ₹5,00,000 for it today. The new machine costs ₹12,00,000. Take it that the excess of the sale price over the written-down value is taxed at 30 per cent in the year of sale.

items.stem: What is the project's NPV today?

options.text: About ₹20 lakh
options.misconception: rolls the tree back correctly but never discounts the year-one expected value to today
options.why: 100 − 80 = ₹20 lakh treats ₹100 lakh arriving at the end of year 1 as though it were in hand today. At 10 per cent its present value is 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.91 lakh, so the NPV is ₹10.91 lakh. Rolling a decision tree back gives values at the node where they stand, and each still has to be discounted to today.

options.text: About ₹10.91 lakh
options.why: Roll the decision tree back from the far end. In a good market the second stage is worth 320 − 200 = ₹120 lakh, so that node is worth 40 + 120 = ₹160 lakh at the end of year 1. In a bad market the second stage is worth 150 − 200 = −₹50 lakh, so the company does not spend, and the node is worth ₹40 lakh. Weighting the two chance branches equally gives 0.5 × 160 + 0.5 × 40 = ₹100 lakh at the end of year 1, whose present value is 100 / 1.10 = ₹90.91 lakh, and the NPV is 90.91 − 80 = ₹10.91 lakh.

options.text: About ₹65.45 lakh
options.misconception: values the project on the favourable branch alone, ignoring the equal chance that the market turns out badly
options.why: 160 / 1.10 − 80 = ₹65.45 lakh plans on the good market arriving. It has only an even chance of doing so, and the bad branch is worth ₹40 lakh, not ₹160 lakh. The two must be weighted by their probabilities at the chance node before anything is discounted, which brings the year-1 figure to ₹100 lakh.

options.text: About minus ₹11.82 lakh
options.misconception: forces the second stage at both nodes, when the whole reason for staging is that the company may walk away after a bad result
options.why: Spending the ₹200 lakh in a bad market too gives 40 + 150 − 200 = −₹10 lakh at that node, so the expected value falls to 0.5 × 160 + 0.5 × (−10) = ₹75 lakh, a present value of 75 / 1.10 = ₹68.18 lakh and an NPV of −₹11.82 lakh. Nobody is compelled to spend after a bad result. At a decision node the better branch is taken and the other dropped, which is what makes the node worth ₹40 lakh rather than minus ₹10 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Advanced Capital Budgeting Decisions

items.scenario: A company spends ₹80 lakh today on the first stage of a project. That stage returns ₹40 lakh at the end of year 1 whatever happens. Also at the end of year 1 the market is revealed, with an equal chance of being good or bad. At that point, and only then, the company may spend a further ₹200 lakh on the second stage. In a good market the later flows from that second stage are worth ₹320 lakh measured at the end of year 1; in a bad market they are worth ₹150 lakh on the same basis. The discount rate is 10 per cent.

items.stem: What money rate should be used, and what is the project's NPV?

options.text: A money rate of 13.4 per cent, giving an NPV of about minus ₹7.03 lakh
options.misconception: uses the money rate on cash flows still stated in today's prices, so inflation is charged in the discount rate while never being credited to the receipts
options.why: Discounting the uninflated ₹50 lakh at 13.4 per cent gives 50 / 1.134 = ₹44.09 lakh and 50 / 1.285956 = ₹38.88 lakh, a total of ₹82.97 lakh and an NPV of minus ₹7.03 lakh. The money rate belongs with the money cash flows. Charging inflation in the denominator while leaving today's prices in the numerator penalises the project for a rise in prices it is never given credit for.

options.text: A money rate of 13.0 per cent, giving an NPV of about minus ₹0.37 lakh
options.misconception: adds the real rate and the inflation rate instead of compounding them, which leaves out the inflation earned on the real return itself
options.why: 8 + 5 = 13 per cent understates the rate, because inflation applies to the real return as well as to the principal. Compounding gives 1.08 × 1.05 − 1 = 13.4 per cent. At 13 per cent the inflated flows discount to 52.50 / 1.13 = ₹46.46 lakh and 55.125 / 1.2769 = ₹43.17 lakh, a total of ₹89.63 lakh and an NPV of minus ₹0.37 lakh — too kind by nearly half a lakh.

options.text: A money rate of 13.4 per cent, giving an NPV of about ₹5.87 lakh
