Its partnership deed, obtained from the public record, shows the managing director's son as a partner. The firm appears nowhere on management's related party list and nowhere in the related party note. The finance controller says the accounts department simply missed it. The audit senior proposes to have the disclosure added to the note and to move on.

items.stem: What does SA 501 require you to do?

options.text: Issue an unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph noting that a legal matter exists whose outcome could not be quantified
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter to carry a scope limitation, and emphasises a matter that is not disclosed in the financial statements at all
options.why: There is no disclosure in the financial statements to emphasise, and an Emphasis of Matter never signals that the auditor was blocked. The inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence goes into the opinion.

options.text: Accept the written representation, since management is the party that knows what claims exist and confidentiality is a legitimate reason to withhold correspondence
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation for direct communication with the entity's external legal counsel
options.why: A representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any matter it deals with, least of all one that management has an interest in keeping quiet. The standard names the external legal counsel precisely because the answer must come from outside management.

options.text: Modify the opinion — management's refusal, combined with alternative audit procedures that did not yield sufficient appropriate audit evidence, is an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence
options.why: SA 501 states the outcome plainly. Where management refuses permission to communicate with the external legal counsel and the auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by alternative procedures, the auditor modifies the opinion. Both limbs are made out here.

options.text: Write to the external legal counsel directly without management's permission, since the auditor's statutory right of access overrides the client's wish for confidentiality
options.misconception: bypasses the requirement that the letter of inquiry is prepared by management and sent by the auditor, and ignores the privilege binding the lawyer
options.why: The letter of inquiry is prepared by management and sent by the auditor for a reason — the lawyer's duty runs to his client, and without management's authority he cannot answer. A letter sent around management would go unanswered and would not cure anything.

citation.ref: para 10 and para 11

items.scenario: Reviewing legal expense accounts you find ₹1.4 crore paid during the year to a law firm that does not appear on the client's schedule of pending litigation. Management says the matter is confidential, refuses permission for you to write to or meet the company's external legal counsel, and offers instead a written representation that no material claim is outstanding. Your alternative procedures — board minutes, subsequent payments, inquiries of the company secretary — produce nothing about the matter. Overall materiality is ₹1 crore.

items.stem: What does SA 240 require of you?

options.text: Take it up with the chief financial officer, since SA 240 requires communication to the appropriate level of management and he is the officer responsible for the payments
options.misconception: communicates to the very person suspected, ignoring the rule that communication goes at least one level above those apparently involved
options.why: Telling the suspect first is how evidence disappears. The standard fixes the level expressly, and where the suspicion touches management it adds a separate channel to those charged with governance.

options.text: Withdraw from the engagement immediately, since exceptional circumstances have arisen that bring your ability to continue into question
options.misconception: treats withdrawal as the first step rather than as a matter to be considered after determining the applicable professional and legal responsibilities
options.why: The standard has the auditor determine the professional and legal responsibilities applicable, then consider whether withdrawal is appropriate and possible under law, and if he withdraws, discuss the reasons with management and those charged with governance. Walking out first skips all of it.

options.text: Say nothing outside the audit file, because disclosing information acquired in the course of a professional engagement without the client's consent is itself professional misconduct
options.misconception: reads professional confidentiality as absolute when the clause itself excepts a disclosure required by any law in force
options.why: The confidentiality clause excepts disclosure required by any law for the time being in force, and both SA 240 and section 143(12) sit inside that exception. Confidentiality protects the client's information, not the client's officers.

options.text: Communicate the matter to those charged with governance on a timely basis, the suspected fraud involving management, and to a level of management above the chief financial officer — then consider whether the circumstances bring your ability to continue the engagement into question, taking legal advice on any duty to report outside the entity
options.why: Communication to management goes at least one level above the persons who appear to be involved, so the chief financial officer is the wrong addressee. Where the suspected fraud involves management, SA 240 requires timely communication to those charged with governance as well, whatever management would prefer.

citation.ref: para 40 and para 41

items.scenario: You establish that the chief financial officer personally authorised ₹3 crore of payments to a vendor with no premises, no employees and no earlier trading history, and that the supporting purchase orders were raised after the payments. The chairman of the audit committee is the chief financial officer's brother-in-law. The managing director asks you to take the matter up with the chief financial officer alone, saying the board should not be troubled until the facts are settled.

items.stem: What do you do once the forty-five days have expired?

options.text: Forward your report to the Central Government in Form ADT-4, together with a note containing the details of the report earlier sent to the audit committee and not replied to
options.why: Rule 13 provides for exactly this case. Where the auditor gets no reply or observations within the stipulated forty-five days, he forwards his report to the Central Government with a note giving the details of the report earlier sent for which no reply was received. The report goes to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs in a sealed cover, in Form ADT-4.

options.text: Wait until the audit committee replies, because the report to the Central Government must carry the committee's observations and your comments on them
options.misconception: makes the reply a precondition to reporting, when the rule expressly provides for its absence
options.why: The reply travels with the report only if one arrives. Making it a precondition would let any company kill the report by staying silent, which is the reason the rule spells out the alternative.

options.text: Record the fraud in the Board's report with its nature, approximate amount and the parties involved, that being the route the rules prescribe
options.misconception: applies the below-one-crore route to a fraud above the threshold
options.why: Disclosure in the Board's report is what happens to frauds below one crore rupees, which go to the audit committee or the Board and no further. At ₹2.4 crore the report is owed to the Central Government.

options.text: Nothing further — the duty was discharged when you reported to the audit committee within two days, and its silence is its response
options.misconception: treats the intimation to the audit committee as the report to the Central Government rather than as the first step towards it
options.why: Above one crore rupees the report is owed to the Central Government. The audit committee stage exists to attach the company's side to it, not to absorb it — which is why the rule says what to do when nothing comes back.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) read with Rule 13(2) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: On 3 June you come to have reason to believe that the procurement head of an unlisted public company has defrauded it of ₹2.4 crore through a chain of inflated purchase invoices. On 4 June you report the matter to the audit committee, seeking its reply or observations within forty-five days. The forty-five days pass and no reply of any kind arrives. The company secretary tells you the file is closed because the committee chose not to respond.

items.stem: Which forum hears the case, and is counsel right about the worst outcome?

options.text: The Board of Discipline hears it, and counsel is right — removal for a period not exceeding three months is the outer limit
options.misconception: sends a Second Schedule charge to the forum that hears only First Schedule cases
options.why: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties sits in the Second Schedule, which takes the case out of the Board of Discipline entirely. The three-month cap belongs to the Board and travels no further.

options.text: The two charges are heard separately — the First Schedule charge by the Board of Discipline and the Second Schedule charge by the Disciplinary Committee
options.misconception: splits one case across two forums, when a case touching both Schedules goes whole to the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: The Act sends a case falling under both Schedules to the Disciplinary Committee as one case. Splitting it would put the same facts before two bodies and could produce two inconsistent findings on one audit.

options.text: The Disciplinary Committee hears it, because the case falls under both the Schedules, and counsel is wrong — that Committee may remove the member's name from the Register of Members permanently or for such period as it thinks fit
options.why: Routing follows the Schedule. A case under the First Schedule alone goes to the Board of Discipline; a case under the Second Schedule, or under both Schedules, goes to the Disciplinary Committee. Permanent removal is available only to the Disciplinary Committee, so the three-month ceiling counsel is relying on is the wrong forum's.

options.text: Neither — the Director (Discipline), having formed a prima facie opinion of guilt, may impose the punishment himself
options.misconception: treats the Director (Discipline)'s prima facie opinion as a finding of guilt and gives him a punishing power he does not have
options.why: A prima facie opinion decides only which forum the case goes to. Guilt is found, and punishment imposed, by the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee after the member has been given an opportunity of being heard.

citation.ref: Section 21A(3) and Section 21B(3), read with the routing under Section 21(3)

items.scenario: A complaint against a member in practice carries two charges. The first is that he accepted appointment as statutory auditor of a company without first communicating in writing with the retiring auditor — a clause of Part I of the First Schedule. The second is that he was grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties on the same audit — a clause of Part I of the Second Schedule. The Director (Discipline) forms a prima facie opinion that the member is guilty on both. The member's counsel argues that the worst outcome available is removal for three months.

items.stem: What does SA 260 require?

options.text: Reporting to the group financial controller was enough, since he is the officer who can fix the delays
options.misconception: treats a report to the very management that created the obstruction as a communication to those charged with governance
options.why: SA 260 directs the communication at those charged with governance. Management is a different body with a different role, and here it is the party whose conduct is the subject of the communication.

options.text: Nothing, because the evidence was ultimately obtained and the opinion is unmodified
options.misconception: makes the communication conditional on how the audit turned out rather than on the matter having arisen
options.why: A clean opinion says the financial statements are not materially misstated. It says nothing about a finance function that made the audit take seven extra weeks, which is exactly the kind of thing the body overseeing the financial reporting process is there to hear about.

options.text: Mention the difficulties orally at the closing meeting, since SA 260 leaves the form of every communication to the auditor's judgement
options.misconception: treats the form as unconstrained, when significant findings go in writing wherever oral communication would not be adequate
options.why: SA 260 does allow oral communication, but only where it would be adequate. Significant findings from the audit are communicated in writing when, in the auditor's professional judgement, oral communication would not be adequate — and a difficulty management itself created is precisely where a written record earns its place.

options.text: Communicate the difficulties to the audit committee as part of the significant findings from the audit, alongside your views on the significant qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices, the significant matters discussed with management and the written representations you are requesting
options.why: SA 260 names significant difficulties encountered during the audit as one of the significant findings that must reach those charged with governance, and the requirement is not written as an exception report — the difficulty itself is what governance oversees, whatever opinion came out at the end. The same list carries the auditor's views about significant qualitative aspects of the entity's accounting practices and the written representations the auditor is requesting.
keywords: significant difficulties encountered during the audit

citation.ref: para 16

items.scenario: Your team spent seven weeks waiting for a subsidiary's ledgers, was refused access to the treasury system until March, and was told the group financial controller had no time for the cut-off walkthrough. Every one of those obstacles was eventually overcome, and the opinion will be unmodified. The manager reported each delay to the group financial controller as it happened and proposes to say nothing about any of it to the audit committee, on the ground that the evidence was obtained in the end.

items.stem: What is missing from the letter?

options.text: Nothing — the description and the potential effects are the whole of the requirement, and what a recipient does with the letter is not the auditor's affair
options.misconception: reads the content requirement as ending at the description, treating the context statements as courtesy rather than requirement
options.why: The context statements sit in the requirement itself, not in the application guidance. SA 265 sets them out as the second limb of what the written communication shall include.

options.text: A restriction on use, stating that the letter is for the addressee alone and may not be relied upon by any other party
options.misconception: substitutes a restriction-on-use paragraph for the context the standard actually prescribes
options.why: A restriction on use is sensible practice and SA 265 does not require it. What the standard requires is the three statements about the purpose of the audit, the limited reason internal control was considered, and the limits of what is being reported.

options.text: An opinion on whether the four deficiencies, taken together, amount to a material weakness
options.misconception: imports internal financial controls reporting into a SA 265 letter, which carries no opinion at all
options.why: Reporting on internal financial controls with reference to financial statements is a separate requirement under section 143(3)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013, and it produces an opinion inside the auditor's report. A SA 265 communication to those charged with governance expresses no opinion on internal control.

options.text: The context statements SA 265 prescribes — that the purpose of the audit was to express an opinion on the financial statements, that internal control was considered only in order to design audit procedures appropriate in the circumstances, and that the deficiencies reported are limited to those identified during the audit
options.why: SA 265 requires the written communication to carry a description of the deficiencies and an explanation of their potential effects, together with sufficient information to enable those charged with governance and management to understand the context of the communication. Those statements exist precisely to stop a list of four deficiencies being read as an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control, which is how the chairman has just used it.
keywords: opinion on the effectiveness of internal control

citation.ref: para 11

items.scenario: You write to the audit committee describing four significant deficiencies in internal control and the amount each could expose. The letter contains nothing else — no explanation of why you looked at internal control, and no statement of what your list does and does not cover. The chairman forwards it to the company's lenders as "our auditor's assessment of the company's internal controls".

items.stem: What is wrong with that plan?

options.text: Only the period is a problem, and a bridging letter from the service organisation covering January to March closes it
options.misconception: treats an assertion by the service organisation as audit evidence about the operation of its own controls
options.why: A bridging letter is the service organisation saying that nothing changed. It is not evidence obtained by the auditor or by a service auditor, and it leaves the three controls at the client untouched in any case.

options.text: Refer to the service auditor's report in the Basis for Opinion section, so readers know part of the evidence came from another auditor
options.misconception: refers to the service auditor in a report carrying an unmodified opinion, and treats disclosure as a substitute for the missing work
options.why: SA 402 bars the user auditor from referring to the work of a service auditor in a report containing an unmodified opinion unless law or regulation requires it, and such a reference would not diminish the user auditor's own responsibility in any event. Naming the provider does not test a control the client was supposed to run.

options.text: Nothing — an unmodified type 2 report is evidence that the controls operated effectively throughout the period it covers, which is what reliance requires
options.misconception: reads the type 2 report as covering the whole control system, when the complementary user entity controls it names were never within its scope
options.why: It is evidence about the provider's controls and only those. The description names three controls the provider assumed the client would run, and nobody has yet looked at whether the client ran them.

options.text: Two things — the three controls the provider named sit at the client, so they must be understood and their operating effectiveness tested there; and the report stops at 31 December, so the time elapsed since the service auditor's tests and the three uncovered months must both be dealt with
options.why: The service auditor tested nothing at the user entity, so an unmodified type 2 report says nothing about whether the client authorised new joiners, reviewed the exception report or reconciled the charge. SA 402 requires the user auditor to determine whether the complementary user entity controls identified by the service organisation are relevant and, where they are, to obtain an understanding of whether the user entity has designed and implemented them and to test their operating effectiveness — and separately to evaluate the adequacy of the time period covered by the tests of controls and the time elapsed since those tests were performed.

citation.ref: para 8(a), with the type 2 report requirements on complementary user entity controls and on the time elapsed since the tests of controls

items.scenario: Your client outsources payroll. The provider gives you a type 2 report for 1 April to 31 December with an unmodified service auditor's opinion. Its description of the system lists three complementary user entity controls: the client must authorise every new joiner in the provider's portal, must review the monthly exception report, and must reconcile the payroll charge to the general ledger. The year end is 31 March. The manager proposes to rely on the type 2 report for the whole year and do no controls work at the client at all.

items.stem: Which reliance survives SA 330?

options.text: Both — neither control has changed and neither has reached its third audit
options.misconception: applies the three-year rotation to controls over a significant risk, which are carved out of it
options.why: The rotation rule is general; the carve-out for a significant risk is written into the same standard. Revenue recognition carries a presumed fraud risk under SA 240, and controls over a significant risk are tested in every period the auditor relies on them.

options.text: The bank reconciliation control only — it may be relied on without retesting this year, the change test having been satisfied; the revenue cut-off control must be tested this year because it addresses a significant risk
options.why: SA 330 lets unchanged controls be tested at least once in every third audit, so a control last tested two years ago can still be relied on once the auditor has obtained audit evidence about whether significant changes have occurred. That concession stops at a significant risk: where the auditor plans to rely on controls over a risk determined to be a significant risk, those controls are tested in the current period.
keywords: at least once in every third audit

options.text: Both, provided management confirms in writing that neither control has changed since it was last tested
options.misconception: substitutes a written representation for the evidence SA 330 requires to establish continuing relevance
options.why: Continuing relevance is established by audit evidence obtained through inquiry combined with observation or inspection, not by management's word. A written representation is never sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about the matter it deals with.
keywords: inquiry combined with observation or inspection

options.text: Neither — evidence about a control's operating effectiveness speaks only for the period in which it was obtained, so every control must be tested afresh each year
options.misconception: denies the rotation SA 330 permits and turns every audit into a full test of every control relied on
options.why: SA 330 expressly allows audit evidence obtained in previous audits to be used once the auditor has established its continuing relevance. Testing everything every year is not what the standard asks for and is not what the file has to show.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 15

items.scenario: Two controls are in question. The first is a three-way bank reconciliation over cash. The second is a management review control over revenue cut-off; you have assessed revenue recognition as a significant risk under the SA 240 presumption. Both were tested two years ago and found effective, and inquiry combined with observation shows that neither has changed since. The senior plans to rely on both this year without testing either, since neither has reached its third audit.

items.stem: What does SA 330 require?

options.text: Cover the remaining period with procedures that give a reasonable basis for extending the interim conclusion to the year end, and — the December error being one you did not expect — reassess the risk and reconsider the remaining-period work before performing it
options.why: SA 330 gives two routes across the remaining period: substantive procedures combined with tests of controls for the intervening period, or further substantive procedures only where the auditor determines that is sufficient. Either has to provide a reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions from the interim date to the period end. And where misstatements that the auditor did not expect are detected at an interim date, the auditor evaluates whether the related assessment of risk and the planned nature, timing and extent of the substantive procedures covering the remaining period need to be modified — a scan for unusual items is not that evaluation.
keywords: reasonable basis for extending the audit conclusions
misstatements that the auditor did not expect

options.text: Re-circularise the whole population at 31 March, since interim substantive testing may not be relied on once an unexpected misstatement has been found
options.misconception: converts a requirement to reassess into a bar on interim testing that SA 330 does not contain
options.why: SA 330 requires the auditor to evaluate whether the risk assessment and the remaining-period procedures need to be modified. It does not throw the interim work away, and redoing everything substitutes effort for the judgement the standard asks for.

options.text: Treat the ₹70 lakh as an anomaly, its cause being known and confined to September despatches, and carry on with the planned scan
options.misconception: reaches for the anomaly label to make an unexpected misstatement stop counting, when nothing here supplies the certainty that label needs
options.why: An anomaly under SA 530 needs a high degree of certainty, obtained by performing additional audit procedures, that the misstatement is not representative of the population — and even then the label removes it only from the projection, never from the evaluation. Nothing here has established any of that.

options.text: Nothing more — 92 per cent of the balance was confirmed, and external confirmation is the strongest evidence available for receivables
options.misconception: treats the strength of the interim evidence as covering a period it never touched
options.why: A confirmation dated 31 December says nothing about a balance at 31 March. The strength of a procedure does not extend its date, and the three months it does not reach are where the year's cut-off risk has just been shown to sit.

citation.ref: para 22 and para 23

items.scenario: Trade receivables were circularised at 31 December for a 31 March year end and 92 per cent by value was confirmed. During that same interim work you found ₹70 lakh of credit notes issued in December against September despatches, never accrued — an error nobody expected. Performance materiality is ₹60 lakh. The manager proposes to roll the December conclusion forward by scanning the January to March receivables ledger for unusual items.

items.stem: What has the manager skipped?

options.text: Reassessing materiality against the entity's actual results before evaluating the uncorrected misstatements, and obtaining an understanding of management's reasons for refusing to correct them
options.why: SA 450 requires the auditor, prior to evaluating the effect of uncorrected misstatements, to reassess materiality determined in accordance with SA 320 to confirm whether it remains appropriate in the context of the entity's actual financial results. At the same 5 per cent of an actual profit before tax of ₹7 crore the figure is ₹35 lakh, not ₹1.2 crore, and ₹65 lakh is then material. The standard separately requires the auditor to obtain an understanding of management's reasons for not making the corrections and to take that understanding into account.

options.text: Nothing — materiality is set at planning, and revising it once the results are known would be designing the audit around its own answer
options.misconception: treats planning materiality as fixed, when SA 320 requires revision as the audit progresses and SA 450 requires a reassessment before the final evaluation
options.why: Both standards say the opposite. SA 320 requires materiality to be revised where the auditor becomes aware of information that would have caused a different figure to be set initially, and SA 450 makes the reassessment a step before the evaluation. A figure built on a forecast that missed by ₹17 crore is not a figure to measure anything against.

options.text: Obtaining a written representation that management believes the effects of the uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, which would have settled the point
options.misconception: treats the representation about uncorrected misstatements as evidence that they are immaterial, when it records management's belief and nothing more
options.why: SA 450 does require that representation, with a summary of the items included in or attached to it, but a written representation is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own. Management's belief that ₹65 lakh does not matter is the very belief the auditor is testing.

options.text: Communicating the uncorrected misstatements to those charged with governance, which would have taken the decision out of the auditor's hands
options.misconception: treats the communication to those charged with governance as discharging the auditor's own evaluation
options.why: That communication is required, and it is not what was skipped — it accompanies the evaluation rather than replacing it. SA 450 leaves the determination of whether uncorrected misstatements are material, individually or in aggregate, with the auditor.

citation.ref: para 9 and para 10

items.scenario: At planning you set materiality for the financial statements as a whole at ₹1.2 crore, being 5 per cent of a forecast profit before tax of ₹24 crore. The audited profit before tax comes out at ₹7 crore after a bad year. Uncorrected misstatements total ₹65 lakh. Management declines to correct any of them, saying each is small and the effort is not worth it. The manager proposes an unmodified opinion because ₹65 lakh sits comfortably below ₹1.2 crore.

items.stem: How does SA 701 have the report set out?

options.text: Replace the qualification with a full key audit matter describing the ₹28 crore, which tells the reader everything a qualification would
options.misconception: treats a description in the auditor's report as an alternative to modifying the opinion, which is the substitution SA 701 names first
options.why: A key audit matter is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances require it. The ₹28 crore is a material misstatement in the financial statements, and a misstatement that is material but not pervasive is answered by a qualified opinion.

options.text: Describe both in the Key Audit Matters section, saying why each was of most significance and how each was addressed, and drop the separate going concern section as duplicative
options.misconception: uses the Key Audit Matters section to carry matters the reporting standards give their own sections, so a description stands where a modification is required
options.why: That is the substitution SA 701 forbids in terms. A reader who finds the ₹28 crore discussed among the key audit matters and nowhere else has been handed a description in place of a qualification.

options.text: Both are by their nature key audit matters, but neither is described in the Key Audit Matters section — the impairment goes in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, the uncertainty in a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to each
options.why: SA 701 says that communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion under SA 705 (Revised), and not a substitute for reporting under SA 570 (Revised) where a material uncertainty related to going concern exists. Such matters are by their nature key audit matters, but the standard directs that they shall not be described in the Key Audit Matters section, and that a reference to the relevant section is included there instead.
keywords: material uncertainty related to going concern

options.text: Put the impairment in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section and say nothing about it in the Key Audit Matters section, since one matter cannot sit in two places
options.misconception: drops the cross-reference SA 701 requires, leaving the Key Audit Matters section reading as though the qualification was not among the significant matters
options.why: The standard's answer is not silence but a reference. The Key Audit Matters section includes a reference to the Basis for Qualified Opinion section so that the reader is sent to where the most significant matter actually went.

citation.ref: para 4 and para 14

items.scenario: A listed company. You are qualifying the opinion because ₹28 crore of capital work in progress on an abandoned project is carried without impairment — material but not pervasive. Separately, a material uncertainty related to going concern exists and is adequately disclosed. The engagement partner wants both written up as key audit matters, "because they are plainly the two most significant matters in this audit", and wants no separate going concern section on the ground that the key audit matter description covers it.

items.stem: What does SA 705 require?

options.text: Express an unmodified opinion on the Indian operations alone, with an Other Matter paragraph stating that the overseas branches were not audited
options.misconception: carves the audited part out of the financial statements the opinion covers, and uses an Other Matter paragraph to record a limitation
options.why: The opinion covers the financial statements as a whole, and there is no separate set for the Indian operations. An Other Matter paragraph never signals that the auditor was blocked — an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence goes into the opinion.

options.text: Request management to remove the limitation, communicate the refusal to those charged with governance, attempt alternative procedures — and then withdraw from the audit, first telling those charged with governance about the misstatements you identified that would have given rise to a modification
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) routes a management-imposed limitation through the request, the communication to those charged with governance and the alternative procedures before any opinion is reached. Where the auditor is still unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence and the possible effects of undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive, the standard asks first whether withdrawal is practicable and possible under applicable law or regulation.

options.text: Disclaim an opinion at once, the possible effects of the inability to obtain evidence being both material and pervasive
options.misconception: reaches the disclaimer without taking the withdrawal step SA 705 puts ahead of it where withdrawal is practicable and possible
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion is what happens where withdrawal is not practicable or not possible under applicable law or regulation. Here it is both, and the standard puts withdrawal first — a disclaimer would leave a report in the world on 71 per cent of revenue nobody audited, in place of a refusal to give one.

options.text: Qualify the opinion, describing the three branches you were unable to audit in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.misconception: grades a limitation covering most of the entity as material but not pervasive
options.why: Pervasiveness asks whether the possible effects are confined to specific elements of the financial statements. Branches carrying 71 per cent of revenue and 64 per cent of assets are not a specific element — the possible effects represent a substantial proportion of the financial statements, so this is material and pervasive, not material but not pervasive.

citation.ref: para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: Two months into the audit of a listed company the managing director instructs you in writing not to visit the three overseas branches, not to correspond with their bankers and not to obtain their trial balances. Those branches carry 71 per cent of revenue and 64 per cent of assets. Your alternative procedures produce nothing you can rely on. The engagement letter signed in April gave you full access, and withdrawal is both practicable and possible under your terms of appointment and under the Act.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 570 require?

options.text: An adverse opinion, the going concern basis of accounting being inappropriate
options.why: SA 570 (Revised) is unconditional here: where the financial statements have been prepared using the going concern basis of accounting but in the auditor's judgement management's use of that basis is inappropriate, the auditor expresses an adverse opinion. Adequate disclosure answers a material uncertainty; it cannot answer a wrong basis of preparation, because every figure in the statements is measured on it.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the note
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where a modification is required, and where the standard gives going concern its own named section in any event
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed and never carries a going concern conclusion. SA 570 (Revised) gives going concern its own section where the basis is appropriate, and an adverse opinion where it is not.

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, the position being fully and accurately disclosed
options.misconception: applies the adequately-disclosed material uncertainty rule to a case where the going concern basis itself is inappropriate
options.why: That section belongs to a case where the going concern basis of accounting is still appropriate and a material uncertainty about it is adequately disclosed. Here there is no uncertainty left to disclose — the plant is gone, the licences are surrendered and the board has resolved to liquidate.

options.text: A qualified opinion, the misstatement being confined to the basis of preparation and the note telling the reader everything
options.misconception: treats a wrong basis of preparation as a matter confined to one element, when it runs through every figure in the statements
options.why: The basis of preparation is not one element. Assets carried at values that assume continued operations, liabilities classified as non-current and the absence of closure costs all follow from it, so the effects are pervasive to the financial statements — and a pervasive misstatement takes an adverse opinion.

citation.ref: para 21

items.scenario: A manufacturer's only plant was sold in February under a court-monitored order, its manufacturing licences have been surrendered, and the board resolved in March to apply for voluntary liquidation. The financial statements are nevertheless drawn up on a going concern basis, with a note describing the sale, the surrender and the resolution, and stating that management is exploring alternatives. You are satisfied the note is complete and accurate.

items.stem: On which, if either, may you express an unmodified opinion?

options.text: On both, each engagement being separate, the work complete, and neither report published with the disclaimer
options.misconception: applies the specific-element concession to a single financial statement, which SA 805 excludes by deeming it a major portion
options.why: Separate publication is one of three conditions and it is available only for a specific element. A single financial statement is deemed to constitute a major portion of the complete set, so the bar holds even where the two reports never travel together.

options.text: On both, provided each report carries an Other Matter paragraph stating that the opinion on the complete set was disclaimed
options.misconception: uses an Other Matter paragraph to license an opinion the standard prohibits
options.why: Disclosure does not create permission. SA 805 offers no Other Matter paragraph as an alternative to its three conditions, and a single financial statement stays barred however the report is worded.

options.text: On neither, since an unmodified opinion on any part of financial statements you have disclaimed an opinion on would contradict the disclaimer
options.misconception: reads the contradiction rule as absolute, when SA 805 opens a narrow route for a specific element audited separately
options.why: The contradiction bites where both opinions appear in the same auditor's report, or where the element is a major portion of the complete set. SA 805 sets out the conditions on which a specific element may still be reported on, and the secured borrowings schedule meets them.

options.text: On the schedule of secured borrowings only
options.why: SA 805 allows an unmodified opinion on a specific element after a disclaimer of opinion on the complete set only where three conditions all hold — the auditor is not prohibited by law or regulation, the report is not published together with the report containing the disclaimer, and the specific element does not constitute a major portion of the complete set. ₹60 crore of a ₹1,400 crore balance sheet is not a major portion. The statement of profit and loss is a single financial statement, which the standard deems to constitute a major portion, so it is barred.

citation.ref: para 18 and para 19

items.scenario: You disclaimed an opinion on a company's complete set of financial statements, having been unable to obtain evidence over an ₹800 crore related party receivable. A lender now engages you separately to audit and report on the company's schedule of secured borrowings — ₹60 crore against a balance sheet of ₹1,400 crore — and, on a second separate engagement, on the company's statement of profit and loss. Your work on both is complete and finds nothing wrong, and neither report would be published together with the disclaimer.

items.stem: Which of these amount to professional misconduct?

options.text: The second and the third
options.why: Clause 10 of Part I of the First Schedule bars fees based on a percentage of profits or contingent upon the findings or results of the employment, except as permitted by regulation. Regulation 192 permits a receiver or a liquidator to charge on a percentage of the realisation of the assets, which saves the first engagement. It permits a percentage of profits only for the auditor of a co-operative society, so an audit fee at 1 per cent of profit before tax in a private company is misconduct, and it nowhere permits a fee that rises with a tax demand being deleted.

options.text: The third only — a fee contingent on a result is misconduct, but a percentage of profits is merely a way of measuring a fee and falls outside the clause
options.misconception: separates a percentage-of-profits fee from a contingent fee, when Clause 10 names both
options.why: Clause 10 names two things: fees based on a percentage of profits, and fees contingent upon the findings or results of the employment. The first limb catches an audit fee set at 1 per cent of profit before tax whatever the second limb does.

options.text: All three, Clause 10 admitting no exception once a fee moves with an outcome
options.misconception: reads Clause 10 without the words "except as permitted under any regulations made under this Act", which sit in the clause itself
options.why: The exception is written into the clause. Regulation 192 names the permitted cases, and a liquidator's percentage of the realisation of the assets is the first of them.

options.text: The second only — a tax representation is advocacy rather than professional employment, so Clause 10 does not reach the third
options.misconception: reads "professional employment" as confined to audit and assurance, when it covers the whole of a member's practice
options.why: Clause 10 applies in respect of any professional employment. Appearing before an appellate authority is professional work of a member in practice, and a fee of 15 per cent of the demand deleted is contingent upon the results of that employment.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 10, read with Regulation 192 of the Chartered Accountants Regulations, 1988

items.scenario: A chartered accountant in practice accepts three engagements. First, as liquidator of a company in members' voluntary liquidation, at 2 per cent of the assets realised. Second, as statutory auditor of a private limited company, at a fee of 1 per cent of its profit before tax for the year. Third, representing a client before the Commissioner (Appeals) in an income tax matter, at 15 per cent of whatever demand is ultimately deleted.

items.stem: What is the position under clause 3(xix)?

options.text: Yes to both — a clean going concern conclusion under SA 570 answers clause 3(xix), and the two together tell the committee the company will meet its liabilities
options.misconception: collapses a CARO clause with its own named inputs into the SA 570 conclusion, and reads either as an assurance about the future
options.why: The two questions overlap but are not the same, and the clause makes the auditor state in terms that he neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance that all liabilities falling due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date will get discharged.
keywords: neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance
one year from the balance sheet date

options.text: The clause is answered on its own named inputs, and the report must also say that the reporting is based on facts up to the date of the audit report and carries no guarantee about the liabilities being discharged
options.why: Clause 3(xix) does not import the SA 570 conclusion. It asks whether the auditor is of the opinion that no material uncertainty exists as on the date of the audit report that the company is not capable of meeting its liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet as and when they fall due within a period of one year from the balance sheet date, and it names the inputs — the financial ratios, the ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, other information accompanying the financial statements, and the auditor's knowledge of the Board of Directors' and management's plans. The clause itself answers the committee's second question: the auditor neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance.
keywords: ageing and expected dates of realisation
neither gives any guarantee nor any assurance

options.text: The clause looks one year forward from the date of the audit report and covers every liability the company will incur in that period
options.misconception: shifts both the window and the population, when the clause fixes them at liabilities existing at the balance sheet date and falling due within one year of it
options.why: The clause is anchored twice to the balance sheet date. It reaches only the liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet, and the one-year period runs from the balance sheet date. Only the auditor's opinion is dated as on the date of the audit report.
keywords: liabilities existing at the date of the balance sheet

options.text: The clause cannot be reported clean where the current ratio is below one, a ratio below one being a material uncertainty in itself
options.misconception: turns one of the named inputs into the conclusion, skipping the plans and the expected dates of realisation the clause names alongside it
options.why: The financial ratios are one of four things the clause puts in front of the auditor. The ageing and expected dates of realisation of financial assets and payment of financial liabilities, the other information accompanying the financial statements and the auditor's knowledge of the Board of Directors' and management's plans — the enforceable support letter among them — go in beside the ratios.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xix)

items.scenario: You are satisfied the going concern basis is appropriate and that no Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section is needed, a promoter having given a binding and enforceable letter of support and having the means to honour it. The current ratio is 0.6 and ₹90 crore of borrowings fall due within eleven months of the balance sheet date. The audit committee asks whether clause 3(xix) can therefore be reported clean, and whether a clean answer means the company will survive the year.

items.stem: Is that right?

options.text: No — the first limb asks whether the internal audit system fits this company's size and nature whether or not section 138 applies, and the second limb separately asks whether the internal auditors' reports for the period were considered by you
options.why: The clause is not keyed to section 138. It asks whether the company has an internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature of its business, and a one-person function leaving eleven branches and the whole of procurement uncovered is not that. The second limb stands on its own: the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit have to be considered by the statutory auditor, and these ones name repeated irregularities.
keywords: internal audit system commensurate with the size and nature

options.text: No, and you must therefore adopt the internal auditor's procurement findings as audit evidence, he being inside the company and closer to the facts
options.misconception: treats internal audit findings as evidence the statutory auditor may take over, skipping the evaluation SA 610 requires before any of that work is used
options.why: SA 610 (Revised) has the auditor evaluate the internal audit function's objectivity, its level of competence, and whether it applies a systematic and disciplined approach, before using its work at all — and then evaluate the adequacy of the particular work used. Considering the reports under clause 3(xiv)(b) is not adopting their conclusions.

options.text: Yes — clause 3(xiv) reports on the internal audit that section 138 requires, so a company outside those classes reports the clause as not applicable
options.misconception: reads a CARO clause about the adequacy of a system as a compliance check on section 138
options.why: Section 138, read with Rule 13 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, decides who must appoint an internal auditor. Clause 3(xiv) asks a different question — whether the system this company actually has fits this company — and it is answered wherever CARO applies.

options.text: No, but only the first limb fails — the second is answered by the company having an internal auditor at all
options.misconception: reads the second limb as another applicability test rather than as a question about what the statutory auditor did
options.why: Clause 3(xiv)(b) asks whether the reports of the Internal Auditors for the period under audit were considered by the statutory auditor. It is a statement about the audit, and an appointment whose reports nobody read does not answer it.

citation.ref: paragraph 3(xiv)(a) and 3(xiv)(b)

items.scenario: An unlisted public company has paid-up share capital of ₹4 crore and turnover of ₹60 crore, and is outside the classes section 138 covers. Its internal audit function is one person, who covers head office cash and payroll and nothing else, leaving eleven branches and the whole of procurement untouched. His four quarterly reports name repeated procurement irregularities at two branches. The audit senior drafts clause 3(xiv) as "not applicable, the company not being covered by section 138".

items.stem: Is the manager right?

options.text: Half right — the inquiry is a duty and not a right, and nothing is reported where the inquiry is satisfied, but an adverse finding on the book-entry adjustments and on the family travel is stated in your report
options.why: The proviso to section 143(1) says the auditor shall inquire, so the six matters are a duty. What is not required is a positive statement in the auditor's report where the answers are satisfactory, which is why the first advance goes unreported. Where the inquiry produces an adverse finding — here on transactions represented merely by book entries, and on personal expenses charged to revenue account — the auditor states it.
keywords: personal expenses charged to revenue account

options.text: No — all six matters in the proviso must be positively answered in the auditor's report every year, whether the answers are satisfactory or adverse
options.misconception: turns a duty of inquiry into a standing reporting format, which section 143(1) does not create
options.why: Nothing in section 143(1) prescribes a form of words for the report. The auditor inquires into all six and reports only what is adverse, which is why a clean report is silent about them.

options.text: No, and the ₹40 lakh of family travel goes into the CARO report as a fraud on the company by its officers
options.misconception: routes a personal expense charged to revenue straight to the fraud clause without the reason to believe an offence of fraud that fraud reporting needs
options.why: Personal expenses charged to revenue account is a named matter of inquiry under the proviso to section 143(1), and an adverse finding is stated in the report. CARO 2020 clause 3(xi) reports a fraud by the company or on the company noticed or reported during the year, which is a different finding needing its own basis — as does a report under section 143(12).
keywords: personal expenses charged to revenue account

options.text: Yes — section 143(1) confers a right of access and a right to inquire, and everything the auditor must report is listed in section 143(3)
options.misconception: reads the proviso's "shall inquire" as an option, and treats section 143(3) as the whole of the auditor's reporting
options.why: The proviso is cast as a duty in the same words as the rest of the section. And section 143(3) is not exhaustive of the report — an adverse finding under section 143(1) belongs in it, as do the matters the Central Government orders under section 143(11).

citation.ref: Section 143(1), proviso clauses (b) and (e)

items.scenario: An unlisted company's books show ₹14 crore of advances against supplies to three parties, unsecured, on which no goods have moved in two years; ₹2.6 crore of inter-company adjustments passed entirely by journal entry with no cash movement either way; and ₹40 lakh of the managing director's family travel charged to sales promotion. Your inquiries satisfy you on the first. On the second and third they do not. The manager plans to report nothing under section 143(1), saying it creates a right of inquiry rather than a reporting obligation.

items.stem: What is wrong with what the company has done?

options.text: Only the hearing — the sequence is a matter of form, and the Central Government's approval cures the special resolution once it arrives
options.misconception: treats "previous approval" as an approval that may follow, when the word fixes the order
options.why: The section says previous approval, and Rule 7 counts the sixty days for the general meeting from receipt of that approval. An approval arriving afterwards approves nothing that had not already been done without it.

options.text: The company should have proceeded under section 140(2) instead, filing Form ADT-3 within thirty days
options.misconception: confuses removal by the company with resignation by the auditor, and hands the company a filing that belongs to the auditor
options.why: Section 140(2) is the auditor's own route out — he resigns and files a statement in Form ADT-3 with the company and the Registrar within thirty days. A company cannot resign on its auditor's behalf, and nothing about that route is available where the auditor has not resigned.

options.text: Nothing — an auditor holds office at the pleasure of the members, and a special resolution is the highest authority in the company
options.misconception: treats the members' resolution as sufficient, when section 140(1) deliberately puts a government approval and a hearing between the members and the auditor
options.why: The point of section 140(1) is that the auditor is not removable at will. The previous approval of the Central Government and the reasonable opportunity of being heard exist to protect an auditor who has qualified a report from the board he qualified it against.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

options.text: The order is reversed and a step is missing — the previous approval of the Central Government must come before the special resolution, with the general meeting held within sixty days of that approval, and the auditor must be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any action is taken
options.why: Section 140(1) permits removal before the expiry of the term only by a special resolution of the company after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and its proviso requires that the auditor concerned be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. Rule 7 puts the application in Form ADT-2 within thirty days of the Board resolution and the general meeting within sixty days of receipt of the approval, so a resolution passed on 8 July, before any application was even made, removes nobody.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with Rule 7(2) and Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company's board falls out with its auditor, appointed for five years at the 2024 annual general meeting, over a qualification. On 10 June the board resolves to remove him. On 8 July the company convenes an extraordinary general meeting, passes a special resolution removing him, and posts him the resolution that evening. On 20 July it applies to the Central Government in Form ADT-2, enclosing the special resolution as evidence of the members' wishes. The auditor was never asked for his views.

items.stem: Which clauses of Part I of the Second Schedule are engaged?

options.text: Clause 5 for the undisclosed guarantee, Clause 8 for the inventory, and Clause 6 for the understated payables
options.why: Clause 5 catches a member who fails to disclose a material fact known to him which is not disclosed in a financial statement but whose disclosure is necessary — the guarantee. Clause 8 catches a member who fails to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion — an inventory balance taken on management's schedule with no count and no alternative procedures. Clause 6 catches a member who fails to report a material misstatement known to him to appear in a financial statement — the ₹3 crore of unrecorded invoices sitting in his own working papers.
keywords: fails to disclose a material fact
fails to report a material misstatement

options.text: Clause 7 alone — the three failures together are gross negligence in the conduct of his professional duties, which covers all of them
options.misconception: collapses several specific clauses into the general negligence clause, when the Schedule names each failure in its own words
options.why: Clause 7 covers a member who does not exercise due diligence, or is grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties, and it may well be charged alongside. It does not displace the specific clauses, and a complaint resting on it alone leaves out the disclosure, evidence and reporting failures the Schedule describes separately.
keywords: grossly negligent in the conduct of his professional duties

options.text: Clause 5 and Clause 6 only — the inventory is a matter of audit quality answered by SA 501 rather than by the Schedule
options.misconception: treats a failure to obtain evidence as a standards matter outside the disciplinary Schedules, when Clause 8 names it in terms
options.why: Clause 8 names the failure to obtain sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion as professional misconduct in its own right. SA 501 says what should have been done about the inventory; the Second Schedule says what follows from not doing it.
keywords: sufficient information which is necessary for expression of an opinion

options.text: None — the member expressed his opinion in good faith, and Part I of the Second Schedule requires an intention to mislead before misconduct is made out
options.misconception: reads an intention requirement into clauses that turn on knowledge and on failure rather than on motive
options.why: The clauses are worded on what the member knew and what he failed to do. Clause 5 and Clause 6 both turn on a fact or a misstatement known to him, and Clause 8 does not ask about his state of mind at all.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clauses 5, 6 and 8

items.scenario: A member issues an unmodified opinion on a company's financial statements. Three things are later established. He knew of a ₹9 crore guarantee given to a promoter entity that appears nowhere in the notes. He accepted management's schedule for a ₹6 crore inventory balance without attending any count and without any alternative procedures, and said nothing about it. And he knew trade payables were understated by ₹3 crore through unrecorded purchase invoices that he had himself listed in his working papers.

items.stem: What does SA 210 require?

options.text: Agree, provided a fresh engagement letter records the new terms — SA 210 requires the new terms to be recorded and asks nothing beyond that
options.misconception: reads the recording requirement as the whole of the rule, skipping the test of whether there was any reasonable justification for the change
options.why: Recording the new terms is what happens after a change has been justified, not instead of justifying it. The standard puts the bar first: no agreement to a change where there is no reasonable justification for doing so. A letter documenting an unjustified downgrade documents the wrong thing very carefully.

options.text: Agree, since a misunderstanding as to the nature of the service originally requested is a reasonable justification and the managing partner plainly wanted a review all along
options.misconception: dresses a change sought after the evidence problem emerged as a misunderstanding that existed at the start
options.why: A misunderstanding as to the nature of the service originally requested is indeed a reasonable justification, and it is one that exists when the engagement begins. Here the terms were understood for five weeks and the request arrived only after the qualification was announced, so what produced it is the evidence, not any misunderstanding.
keywords: misunderstanding as to the nature of the service originally requested

options.text: Carry on under the existing engagement letter and issue the qualified opinion, since a client's request has no effect on terms already agreed
options.misconception: assumes the original engagement simply continues, when SA 210 provides for the case where management refuses to let it continue
options.why: Refusing the change is right; assuming the audit rolls on is not. SA 210 deals expressly with the auditor who is unable to agree to a change and is not permitted by management to continue the original audit engagement, and the answer there is withdrawal where possible under applicable law or regulation, together with the question of who else has to be told.
keywords: not permitted by management to continue

options.text: Refuse the change — a request made to make a qualification disappear is not a reasonable justification — and, if he will not let you continue the original engagement, withdraw where possible and determine whether the circumstances must be reported to those charged with governance, owners or regulators
options.why: SA 210 says the auditor shall not agree to a change in the terms of the audit engagement where there is no reasonable justification for doing so. A change sought because the auditor is unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over ₹52 crore of unbilled revenue is the paradigm case: the level of assurance is being lowered so that the qualification goes away, not because the entity's requirements changed. Where the auditor is unable to agree to the change and is not permitted by management to continue the original engagement, he withdraws where possible under applicable law or regulation and determines whether there is any obligation to report the circumstances to other parties, such as those charged with governance, owners or regulators.

citation.ref: para 14 and para 17

items.scenario: You are five weeks into the audit of a large partnership firm's financial statements — a contractual engagement, not one any statute requires. You have told the managing partner that you cannot obtain evidence over ₹52 crore of unbilled revenue and that the opinion will be qualified. He writes back asking you to convert the engagement into a limited review, saying the bank will take a review report and the fee can stay the same, and asking that you carry on under the existing engagement letter to save paperwork.

items.stem: What fails SA 220 (Revised) here?

options.text: Only the staffing — an article assistant should never have worked those areas, and once that is fixed the review and the dating are unobjectionable
options.misconception: reads the standard as barring junior staff from difficult areas, when what it requires is that their work be directed, supervised and reviewed by more experienced members
options.why: SA 220 (Revised) does not reserve difficult areas for senior staff. It requires that the work of less experienced engagement team members be directed, supervised and reviewed by more experienced engagement team members, and it separately bars dating the report before the engagement quality review is complete — so fixing the staffing alone answers neither.

options.text: Nothing — the engagement partner takes overall responsibility for quality, and a documented firm-wide review protocol is how that responsibility is discharged
options.misconception: treats a uniform firm protocol as discharging a responsibility the standard makes responsive to each engagement
options.why: Overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality is where SA 220 (Revised) starts, not where it stops. The standard asks that direction, supervision and review be responsive to the nature and circumstances of the engagement, so a protocol identical for a dormant company and for a goodwill impairment worked by an article assistant fails by never varying.
keywords: overall responsibility for managing and achieving quality
responsive to the nature and circumstances

options.text: Only the timing of the report — how work is reviewed is a matter for the firm's system of quality management under SQC 1, not for this engagement
options.misconception: pushes engagement-level direction, supervision and review up into the firm's system, when SA 220 places it on the engagement partner
options.why: SQC 1 governs the firm's system and SA 220 (Revised) governs this audit. The requirements on direction, supervision and review sit on the engagement partner for this engagement, and delegating the work never delegates the responsibility for quality on it.

options.text: Three things — the hardest judgements were worked by a less experienced team member without direction, supervision and review by more experienced ones; the partner reviewed no documentation on those judgements himself; and the report was dated before the engagement quality review was complete
options.why: SA 220 (Revised) requires direction, supervision and review to be planned and performed on the basis that the work of less experienced engagement team members is directed, supervised and reviewed by more experienced engagement team members, and it requires the engagement partner to review the audit documentation relating to significant matters and significant judgements, including difficult or contentious matters, and the conclusions reached. A flat manual that sends every file through the same review has stopped responding to the nature and circumstances of the engagement. And where an engagement quality review is required, the auditor's report is not dated until the partner is notified that it is complete.
keywords: nature and circumstances of the engagement

citation.ref: para 13, with the requirements on direction, supervision and review and on the completion of an engagement quality review before the auditor's report is dated

items.scenario: A firm's manual gives every audit file the same review: the manager reviews all working papers, the partner reviews the manager's memo and the draft report, and nothing else. On this engagement the goodwill impairment model, a disputed ₹22 crore tax position and the revenue cut-off conclusion were all worked and concluded by a first-year article assistant, and the manager's memo says "no exceptions". The partner signs the report the same evening the engagement quality reviewer receives the file.

items.stem: What does SA 299 (Revised) require?

options.text: A had to communicate the scrap sale to both B and C in writing before the audit was completed, and he is not bound by the majority — a joint auditor in disagreement expresses his own opinion in a separate audit report
options.why: SA 299 (Revised) makes coordination a written duty: a joint auditor who comes across matters relevant to the areas of responsibility of other joint auditors, or requiring discussion with or the application of judgement by them, communicates those matters to all the other joint auditors in writing prior to the completion of the audit — and a telephone call to one of the three is neither in writing nor to all of them. On the opinion the joint auditors are not a committee. A joint auditor is not bound by the views of the majority, and where he disagrees he expresses his opinion in a separate audit report.
keywords: in writing prior to the completion of the audit
not bound by the views of the majority

options.text: A's call to C discharged the coordination duty, C owning the related party listing and A's only obligation running to the auditor whose area the matter touched
options.misconception: narrows a communication owed to all the other joint auditors down to one of them, and drops the requirement that it be in writing
options.why: The requirement runs to all the other joint auditors, not to whichever one seems closest, and it is a communication in writing prior to the completion of the audit. B audits the south plants, where the same vendor may well appear, and an oral mention leaves nothing on any file.
keywords: in writing prior to the completion of the audit

options.text: A should press for a qualification, but responsibility for the missed related party is C's alone, the head office having been divided to him
options.misconception: uses the division of work to move a matter one joint auditor actually found onto the auditor in whose area it fell
options.why: Division fixes who performs the work, and each joint auditor is responsible for the work divided to him. It does not excuse a joint auditor who has himself come across a matter deserving the others' attention from communicating it, and it does not decide the opinion, which each joint auditor forms for himself.

options.text: A must sign the common report — joint auditors issue one report, and a dissent that splits it defeats the purpose of appointing joint auditors
options.misconception: makes the common report compulsory, when SA 299 provides for a separate report precisely where the joint auditors disagree
options.why: The common report is what joint auditors issue when they agree. SA 299 (Revised) provides for the other case in terms: where the joint auditors are in disagreement with regard to the opinion or any matters to be covered by the audit report, the dissenting joint auditor expresses his opinion in a separate audit report.

citation.ref: the coordination requirement to communicate in writing to all the other joint auditors prior to the completion of the audit, and the separate audit report on disagreement, read with the division of responsibility at para 13 and para 14

items.scenario: Three firms are joint auditors of a company and the work is divided by location: A takes the north plants, B the south plants, C the head office and the financial statements. Working at a north plant, A finds a ₹34 crore scrap sale routed through a vendor that C's related party listing does not carry, and mentions it to C on a telephone call. At the report stage B and C are satisfied with an unmodified opinion; A believes a qualification is required. B and C tell A that two out of three settles it and that he must sign the common report.

items.stem: Which of the three may the auditor rely on as it stands?

options.text: The invoice test — fifty items traced to despatch notes with no exceptions is sufficient appropriate audit evidence over receivables
options.misconception: reads sufficiency as curing a relevance failure, when a procedure that does not test the assertion answers nothing however many items it covers
options.why: Sufficiency is the measure of quantity and appropriateness the measure of quality, and quality begins with relevance. A test running from the recorded population outwards can never reach an unrecorded sale, so five hundred items would answer completeness no better than fifty.

options.text: The customer statements — they originated outside the entity, and evidence from an independent external source is the most reliable category there is
options.misconception: keeps the external-source generalisation while ignoring that the document reached the auditor as a photocopy and through the client's own hands
options.why: Evidence from independent sources outside the entity is more reliable, but that generalisation sits beside two others: evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly, and an original document is more reliable than a photocopy. A statement downloaded by the credit controller and handed over as a photocopy has lost both.

options.text: None of them — the invoice test is not relevant to completeness, the ageing report is information produced by the entity whose accuracy has not been tested, and a photocopy routed through the client is neither an original nor obtained directly by the auditor
options.why: Relevance is the connection between the procedure and the assertion. Selecting from the sales ledger and tracing outwards tests occurrence, because a sale never recorded is not in the population sampled from, so it cannot test completeness. Agreeing an ageing report's total to the trial balance says nothing about whether the buckets are right, and SA 500 requires the auditor using information produced by the entity to obtain audit evidence about the accuracy and completeness of the information and to evaluate whether it is sufficiently precise and detailed. And evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly, while an original document is more reliable than a photocopy.

options.text: The ageing report — it came out of the system rather than from a person, and a system-generated report needs no further testing
options.misconception: treats a report as reliable because a system printed it, when the report is still information produced by the entity
options.why: A report is information produced by the entity whether a clerk typed it or the system generated it. Its reliability turns on the controls over that system and on the parameters the report was run with, and SA 500 asks for audit evidence about its accuracy and completeness before it is used.

citation.ref: para 7 and para 9

items.scenario: To test whether trade receivables are complete, the senior selects fifty invoices from the sales ledger and traces each to a despatch note. To support the ageing, he takes the ageing report the client's system printed on 2 April, ties its grand total to the trial balance, and does nothing further with it. To confirm three large balances he accepts photocopies of customer statements that the client's credit controller downloaded from the customers' portals.

items.stem: What does SA 505 require?

options.text: Accept the documents offered — contracts, despatch records and the ledger are alternative procedures, and performing them deals with the refusal
options.misconception: stops at the alternative procedures and drops the inquiry into the reasons and the evaluation of what the refusal itself means
options.why: Alternative audit procedures are one of the three steps, not all of them. The refusal is itself audit evidence about the risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and here it sits on top of an undisclosed related party — which is exactly what the evaluation step exists to catch.

options.text: Send the requests anyway — the auditor controls the confirmation process, and management has no standing to withhold permission
options.misconception: reads control over the process as a power to override the entity's refusal, which SA 505 answers with a procedure instead
options.why: The auditor does control the external confirmation process — determining the information to be confirmed, selecting the confirming party, designing the requests and sending them. Control does not extend to writing to a customer over the entity's objection. SA 505 answers a refusal by inquiring, evaluating and performing alternative audit procedures, and by taking an unreasonable refusal to those charged with governance.

options.text: Inquire into the reasons and seek evidence as to their validity and reasonableness, evaluate what the refusal does to your risk assessment, perform alternative procedures — and, the brother's directorship making the refusal look unreasonable, communicate with those charged with governance and determine the implications for the opinion
options.why: SA 505 sets three steps on a refusal: inquire as to management's reasons for the refusal and seek audit evidence as to their validity and reasonableness; evaluate the implications of the refusal on the assessment of the relevant risks of material misstatement, including the risk of fraud, and on the nature, timing and extent of other audit procedures; and perform alternative audit procedures designed to obtain relevant and reliable audit evidence. Where the auditor concludes that the refusal is unreasonable, or the alternative procedures do not deliver, he communicates with those charged with governance and determines the implications for the audit and for the auditor's opinion.

options.text: Treat the refusal as a management-imposed limitation and disclaim an opinion at once, ₹47 crore being material
options.misconception: jumps from a refusal to a disclaimer, skipping the alternative procedures and the grading of the possible effects
