options.text: The write-back and the profit on sale come out of normalised earnings as non-recurring; the token salary and nominal rent are replaced with market cost because those arrangements end at completion; the unfunded gratuity is debt-like and goes into net debt; and the disputed demand is a hidden liability that feeds the indemnity, not an earnings adjustment
options.why: Normalised earnings strip out what will not recur — a provision write-back and a profit on the sale of surplus land are both non-recurring — and put in the costs the business will bear after completion, so a token salary and a nominal rent from a promoter-owned firm are replaced with market cost. Net debt collects everything debt-like against a debt-free cash-free price, and an unfunded gratuity obligation is exactly that. A disputed demand is a hidden liability whose size and likelihood drive the indemnity and the warranties, and running it through the earnings multiple would misprice it.

options.text: All four are earnings adjustments, since every one of them affects what the buyer will earn after completion
options.misconception: pushes balance-sheet items through the earnings multiple, which double-counts them against a price already settled debt-free and cash-free
options.why: An unfunded obligation and a disputed demand are amounts owed, not annual costs, and a price agreed on a multiple of earnings is settled separately against net debt. Running an obligation through the multiple values it several times over and then the buyer pays it again on completion.

options.text: The gratuity and the excise demand are contingent and are left out; only the write-back and the profit on sale are adjusted
options.misconception: treats an unfunded obligation as contingent, and drops the very items the price and the indemnity are meant to reflect
options.why: An unfunded gratuity obligation is not contingent — it exists and is unfunded, which is why it is debt-like and goes into net debt. And a disputed demand is left in the analysis with an assessment of its likely outcome, because it is what the indemnity is written for; a hidden liability that is left out is one the buyer pays for twice.

options.text: None may be adjusted, because the financial statements are audited and carry an unmodified opinion
options.misconception: confuses a due diligence with an audit of the financial statements, when the two answer different questions
options.why: An unmodified opinion says the financial statements give a true and fair view under the applicable framework. It does not say the reported profit is what a buyer will earn, and a due diligence exists precisely to work out what the buyer is buying. The adjustments are not corrections of the accounts.

citation.ref: Ch. Due Diligence, Investigation and Forensic Accounting — normalisation of earnings for non-recurring items and for arrangements ending at completion, the computation of net debt against a debt-free cash-free price, and the identification of hidden liabilities

items.scenario: You are doing a financial due diligence on a target the buyer will price at a multiple of earnings, settled on a debt-free, cash-free basis. The target's reported profit includes the write-back of a warranty provision no longer required and a profit on the sale of surplus land. The promoter draws a token salary and the factory is rented from a promoter-owned firm at a nominal rent, both of which end at completion. There is an unfunded gratuity obligation, and a disputed excise demand is under appeal.

items.stem: Which route is available, and on what basis?

options.text: An application to the Tribunal under section 213, which may order an investigation on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest one of the matters the section lists, after giving the applicant a reasonable opportunity of being heard; the Central Government then appoints the inspectors
options.why: Section 213 is the members' route. The Tribunal may order an investigation into a company's affairs on an application by the requisite number of members on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest that the business is being conducted with intent to defraud, or for a fraudulent or unlawful purpose, or that persons concerned in the management have been guilty of fraud or misfeasance, or that the members have not been given all the information with respect to the company's affairs which they might reasonably expect. The applicant is given a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and where the Tribunal so orders the Central Government appoints the inspectors.
keywords: the Central Government appoints the inspectors

options.text: An application to the Central Government under section 210, which orders an investigation where members ask for one
options.misconception: reads section 210 as available on a member's application, when it moves on a report, a special resolution or the public interest
options.why: Section 210 is the Central Government's own power, exercised where it is of the opinion that it is necessary — on the receipt of a report of the Registrar or an inspector under section 208, on the intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated, or in the public interest. A member's request is not one of those triggers; the members' route runs through the Tribunal.

options.text: A request to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office under section 212, which investigates fraud on a complaint by affected members
options.misconception: treats the SFIO route, which the Central Government alone assigns, as one a member may invoke directly
options.why: Under section 212 the Central Government assigns an investigation to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office by order, on a report of the Registrar or an inspector, on the intimation of a special resolution, in the public interest, or on the request of a Department of the Central Government or a State Government. A member cannot set it in motion by complaining to the office.

options.text: Ask the statutory auditor to investigate the diversion and to report his findings to them, the auditor having a right of access to all books under section 143(1)
options.misconception: turns the auditor of the financial statements into an investigator for a group of members, with a scope and an audience he does not have
options.why: The right of access under section 143(1) exists for the audit of the financial statements, and the auditor reports to the members as a body in his report, not privately to a group of them. An investigation into a company's affairs is ordered under sections 210 or 213 and conducted by inspectors appointed for it.

citation.ref: Section 213 — investigation ordered by the Tribunal on an application by the requisite number of members on being satisfied that the circumstances suggest the matters the section lists, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard — read against Section 210 and Section 212

items.scenario: A group of minority members of an unlisted company believes the promoters have diverted funds to a related concern and that the members have been refused information about the company's affairs that they might reasonably expect. They hold well above the shareholding the law requires for such an application. They want an investigation ordered and ask what route is open to them.

items.stem: How do you deal with both?

options.text: The Other Matter paragraph stays — it states the number of components you did not audit and the quantum they represent and that your opinion on those amounts is based solely on the other auditors' reports, and it qualifies nothing; but a component matter material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole requires you to modify your own opinion, an Other Matter paragraph never being a substitute for a modification
options.why: The Other Matter paragraph is a disclosure of division, not a disclaimer: it gives the number of components and the total assets, total revenues and net cash flows they represent, and states that the opinion in so far as it relates to those amounts is based solely on the reports of the other auditors. It does not qualify the opinion and it does not reduce the parent auditor's responsibility. And where the matter is material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole the opinion is modified under SA 705 (Revised); an Other Matter paragraph is never a substitute for a modification.
keywords: based solely on the reports of the other auditors
material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole
never a substitute for a modification

options.text: Keep the paragraph and use it for the component qualification as well, leaving the opinion unmodified — the qualification is the component auditor's opinion and not yours
options.misconception: uses an Other Matter paragraph to carry a matter that requires a modification, on the footing that another auditor's qualification is not the parent auditor's concern
options.why: The parent's auditor signs one opinion on the consolidated financial statements and he alone is responsible for it. Once he has evaluated the matter as material to those statements as a whole, his own opinion is wrong if it is unmodified, and describing the component auditor's qualification in a paragraph does not change what his opinion says.
keywords: material to those statements as a whole

options.text: Use an Emphasis of Matter paragraph for both — it draws attention to the division of work and to the component qualification without modifying the opinion
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter where a modification is required, and for a matter that is not even presented or disclosed in the financial statements
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter appropriately presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding, and it is not used where the matter requires a modification of the opinion. The division of audit work is not disclosed in the financial statements at all, and the component qualification requires a modification.

options.text: Drop the Other Matter paragraph as management asks and modify the opinion for the component qualification, since the modification tells the reader everything the paragraph would have
options.misconception: treats the disclosure of the division of work as optional once the opinion carries a modification
options.why: The two do different jobs. The modification says what is wrong with the consolidated financial statements; the Other Matter paragraph says how much of them the parent's auditor did not audit himself and that his opinion on those amounts rests on other auditors' reports. A reader needs both, and management's dislike of the paragraph is not a reason to remove it.

citation.source: Guidance Note on Audit of Consolidated Financial Statements
citation.ref: the Other Matter paragraph stating the number of components not audited by the parent's auditor, the quantum they represent, and that his opinion on those amounts is based solely on the reports of the other auditors, read with SA 706 (Revised) paras 8 and 10 and SA 705 (Revised)

items.scenario: You are the parent's auditor on consolidated financial statements covering twelve subsidiaries, three of them audited by other auditors whose reports have been furnished to you. Management asks you to drop your draft Other Matter paragraph, saying it reads like a qualification and dilutes a clean opinion. Separately, one of those three component auditors has qualified his opinion on a matter you have evaluated as material to the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and your manager proposes to describe that qualification inside the same Other Matter paragraph and leave your opinion unmodified.

items.stem: Is that correct under section 177?

options.text: No, but the only addition needed is the auditor's appointment; related party transactions and inter-corporate loans go to the Board under sections 188 and 186
options.misconception: treats the Board's separate approval under other sections as removing the audit committee's own approval and scrutiny under section 177(4)
options.why: The Board's powers under those sections and the audit committee's terms of reference under section 177(4) run together, not instead of each other. Section 177(4) puts approval of related party transactions and scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments in the committee's terms of reference, so a transaction entered into without the committee's approval is an identified non-compliance with law however the Board dealt with it.

options.text: No — section 177(4) expressly includes in the committee's terms of reference the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors, the approval of related party transactions, and the scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, alongside examination of the financial statement
options.why: Section 177(4) requires the Board to specify the terms of reference in writing and lists what they include: the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors; review and monitoring of the auditor's independence and performance and of the effectiveness of the audit process; examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report on it; approval of related party transactions; scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments; valuation of undertakings or assets; evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems; and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers.

options.text: Yes — the audit committee's statutory role is confined to the financial statement and the auditors' report, the rest being the Board's own powers
options.misconception: reads one item in the section's list as the whole of it
options.why: Examination of the financial statement and the auditors' report is one item on the list in section 177(4), not the list. The section puts seven other matters in the terms of reference, and the Board specifies them in writing rather than choosing among them.

options.text: Yes for an unlisted company, but for a listed company the terms of reference are set by the SEBI Listing Regulations and section 177 does not apply
options.misconception: treats the listing regulations as displacing the Act for a listed company, when the two apply together
options.why: Section 177 applies to every company required to constitute an audit committee, listed or not, and the SEBI Listing Regulations apply in addition to it for a listed entity — they do not replace the Act. A listed company answers to both, and the stricter requirement governs where they differ.

citation.ref: Section 177(4) — the terms of reference of the audit committee, including the recommendation for appointment, remuneration and terms of appointment of the auditors, approval of related party transactions, and scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments — read with Section 177(5) and Section 177(7)

items.scenario: The Board of a listed company hands its audit committee written terms of reference limited to examining the financial statement and the auditors' report on it. The chairman explains that the auditor's appointment and remuneration, the approval of related party transactions and the scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments are Board matters and are not for the committee.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Both are wrong — the proviso to section 148(3) bars the auditor appointed under section 139 from being appointed to conduct the audit of cost records, and a reservation touching the absorption of overheads into inventory is audit evidence about the financial statements he is reporting on
options.why: The proviso to section 148(3) provides in terms that the auditor appointed under section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, so the proposed appointment is not open whatever the convenience. And a reservation about the absorption of overheads goes to the carrying amount of inventory in the financial statements, so it is audit evidence the statutory auditor evaluates and, if it indicates a misstatement, deals with in his own report.

options.text: The appointment is barred, but the reservation may be disregarded because the cost audit report goes to the Board and is furnished to the Central Government, not to the statutory auditor
options.misconception: treats the destination of the cost audit report as removing what it says from the statutory auditor's evidence
options.why: Where a report goes decides who must receive it, not what it is worth as evidence. The statutory auditor has a right of access to the company's books and records under section 143(1), the cost audit report is available to him, and a reservation about overhead absorption bears directly on the inventory figure he is reporting on.

options.text: Both are acceptable — cost audit is in addition to the audit under section 143, so the two are separate exercises and neither constrains the other
options.misconception: reads "in addition to" as "unrelated to", and misses the express bar in the section
options.why: Cost audit is indeed in addition to the audit under section 143, and that says nothing about who may conduct it or about what its findings are worth to the statutory auditor. Section 148(3) contains an express bar on the auditor appointed under section 139 taking it, and a reservation about inventory costing is evidence about a figure in the financial statements.

options.text: The appointment is open, because section 144's list of services an auditor may not render does not include cost audit; only the treatment of the reservation is wrong
options.misconception: looks for the bar in section 144 and, not finding it there, concludes there is none, when section 148(3) contains it
options.why: Section 144's list does not include cost audit, and that is exactly why this answer is attractive and wrong. The bar is in the proviso to section 148(3), which says that the auditor appointed under section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records. A prohibition is not absent because it sits in a different section.

citation.ref: the proviso to Section 148(3) that the auditor appointed under Section 139 shall not be appointed for conducting the audit of cost records, and Section 148(6) on furnishing the cost audit report with full information and explanation on every reservation or qualification in it, read with Section 144

items.scenario: A manufacturing company whose cost records the Central Government has directed to be audited proposes to appoint its statutory audit firm, appointed under section 139, to conduct the cost audit as well, since that firm knows the books. In the previous year's cost audit report the cost auditor recorded a reservation on the basis on which overheads were absorbed into inventory. The statutory auditor proposes to disregard it as a cost matter that does not concern him.

items.stem: What is wrong with that?

options.text: Both halves — SQC 1 applies to the firm in respect of all its audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements, and the engagement quality control review is one part of one of six elements, the others being leadership responsibilities, ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance, human resources and monitoring
options.why: SQC 1's scope is stated in the standard itself: it applies to a firm in respect of all its audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements, not to listed company audits alone. And the system it requires has six elements — leadership responsibilities for quality within the firm, ethical requirements including independence, acceptance and continuance of client relationships and specific engagements, human resources, engagement performance, and monitoring — with the engagement quality control review sitting inside engagement performance.
keywords: all its audits and reviews of historical financial information

options.text: The partner is right about scope but wrong about the elements — SQC 1 covers audit engagements only, so the firm's other assurance work is outside its system
options.misconception: narrows the standard's scope to audits, when it expressly reaches other assurance and related services engagements
options.why: SQC 1 reaches other assurance and related services engagements as well as audits and reviews of historical financial information, so a firm cannot run a quality control system over its audit work and leave its other assurance work outside it. Acceptance and continuance, independence and monitoring apply across everything the firm does.
keywords: other assurance and related services engagements

options.text: The partner is wrong, but only because SQC 1 has been replaced by the quality management standards, which apply to every firm and require a risk-based approach
options.misconception: applies quality management standards the Council deferred in March 2026, when SQC 1 remains the standard in force
options.why: The quality management standards that would have replaced SQC 1 were deferred by the Council in March 2026 and have not taken effect, so SQC 1 is the standard in force for Indian firms and its six elements are what a firm's system is tested against. Answering from the deferred standards gets the right criticism for a reason that does not yet exist in law.
keywords: deferred by the Council in March 2026
SQC 1 is the standard in force

options.text: Nothing — SQC 1 expresses its requirement for an engagement quality control review for audits of listed entities, so listed company audits are its scope
options.misconception: reads one requirement inside one element as defining the scope of the whole standard
options.why: The engagement quality control review is required for audits of the financial statements of listed entities, and that is a requirement about when a review is compulsory, not about which engagements the standard covers. The standard's own scope reaches all the firm's audits and reviews of historical financial information and its other assurance and related services engagements.

citation.ref: the scope of SQC 1 over all a firm's audits and reviews of historical financial information and other assurance and related services engagements, and the six elements of a system of quality control, with the engagement quality control review sitting within engagement performance

items.scenario: The senior partner of a four-partner firm tells you that SQC 1 applies only to audits of listed companies, and that his firm's system of quality control consists of the engagement quality control review the partners perform on one another's reports before signing.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: Governance in ESG means the entity's compliance with environmental law, so the Governance pillar is a subset of the Environment pillar
options.misconception: collapses two of the three pillars into one by reading Governance as environmental compliance
options.why: Governance is the internal system of practices, controls and procedures the entity adopts to govern itself, make effective investment decisions, comply with the law and meet the needs of all stakeholders, and it carries board diversity, executive pay, business ethics, anti-competitive practices, corruption and tax transparency. Environmental compliance sits under the Environment pillar; the two are separate pillars, not one inside the other.

options.text: ESG names the three pillars of sustainability — Environment, Social and Governance — and the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2015 by all United Nations member states as a call for action by developed and developing countries alike
options.why: Sustainable development applied to a business rests on three pillars, and those pillars are exactly what the letters stand for: Environment, Social and Governance. Environment covers climate policy, energy, waste, pollution and natural resources; Social covers relationships with people and communities across the value chain; Governance is the internal system of practices, controls and procedures by which the entity governs itself. Separately, in 2015 the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals were adopted by all United Nations member states as a blueprint addressed to countries, developed and developing alike.

options.text: ESG has four pillars — Economic, Environment, Social and Governance — the fourth having been added by the Brundtland report
options.misconception: invents a fourth pillar and credits it to the report that defined sustainable development
options.why: There are three pillars, not four. The Brundtland report is where sustainable development is defined as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs; it does not add an Economic pillar to ESG. Economic impacts are reported under the Global Reporting Initiative's disclosures, which is a reporting framework and not a fourth pillar.

options.text: ESG names the three pillars of sustainability, and the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2011 by the member countries of the OECD as targets binding on listed companies
options.misconception: attaches the goals to the wrong body and the wrong year, and turns a call to countries into an obligation on companies
options.why: The Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2015 by all United Nations member states, not by a smaller group of countries in 2011, and they are a universal call for action to countries rather than a set of targets binding on any listed company. A company contributes to them; the goals are not addressed to it.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the three pillars of Environment, Social and Governance, and the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals adopted in 2015 by all United Nations member states

items.scenario: A trainee reading a listed company's sustainability section asks you to settle two things before he starts: what the three letters in ESG actually stand for, and where the Sustainable Development Goals came from.

items.stem: Which list is the six capitals of Integrated Reporting?

options.text: Financial and manufactured capital only, the other four being reported under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report rather than in an integrated report
options.misconception: splits the capitals between two reports, when the whole point of an integrated report is that it carries all six
options.why: An integrated report carries all six capitals; that is what makes it integrated and what lets it answer how the organisation creates value over the short, medium and long term. A company already reporting on this basis may cross-reference those disclosures to the ones the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report seeks, which is the opposite of splitting them between two documents.

options.text: Financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and intellectual capital
options.why: Integrated Reporting tracks six capitals. Financial capital is the pool of funds available for producing goods or services. Manufactured capital is the human-created, production-oriented equipment, buildings and infrastructure. Natural capital is water, land, minerals, forests, biodiversity and ecosystem health. Human capital is people's skills, experience and motivation to innovate. Social capital is the institutions and relationships built with communities, customers, suppliers and partners, including the social licence to operate. Intellectual capital is the key element in future earning potential, tied to research and development and innovation.

options.text: Financial, physical, environmental, employee, community and reputational capital
options.misconception: renames the capitals from memory instead of using the framework's own six
options.why: The framework's names are fixed and are examined as fixed: financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and intellectual. "Physical", "environmental", "employee", "community" and "reputational" are plausible paraphrases, but reputational standing is part of social capital and nothing in the framework is called environmental capital.

options.text: Financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and political capital
options.misconception: swaps out the one capital that carries future earning potential for a category the framework does not use
options.why: The sixth capital is intellectual capital — the key element in an organisation's future earning potential, linked to investment in research and development, innovation, human resources and external relationships, and what determines competitive advantage. There is no political capital in the framework.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — Integrated Reporting and its six capitals: financial, manufactured, natural, human, social and intellectual

items.scenario: A listed company has been preparing an integrated report voluntarily for several years and cross-references those disclosures to what its Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report asks for. A colleague asks which stores of value an integrated report tracks.

items.stem: Under which principle do these disclosures belong, and how are the nine principles arranged?

options.text: Under Principle 1, ethics, transparency and accountability, which is where an anti-bribery policy and the machinery for bribery and corruption complaints are disclosed; the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct are split two in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance
options.why: Principle 1 is ethics, transparency and accountability — business decisions open to disclosure, policies and procedures keeping ethics uncompromised, and a proactive response to those who violate the principles. An anti-bribery policy, the internal control mechanism behind it and the machinery for bribery and corruption complaints are the standard disclosures under it. The nine principles are split two in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance, and they interlock rather than standing apart.
keywords: two in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance

options.text: Under Principle 9, providing value to consumers responsibly, because a bribery complaint is a consumer grievance
options.misconception: reads a corruption complaint as a consumer complaint and lands on the principle about products
options.why: Principle 9 is about reducing the negative impacts of products and services on consumers, the environment and society, not restricting freedom of choice or fair competition, disclosing adverse impacts accurately, and respecting the customer's right to privacy when handling customer data. A bribery or corruption complaint is not a consumer grievance about a product.

options.text: Under whichever principle the company selects, since the nine principles are not allocated to the three ESG pillars and Section C leaves the mapping to the reporting entity
options.misconception: treats a fixed structure as a matter of preference, when the principles and their pillar allocation are both fixed
options.why: The nine principles are fixed by the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, and their allocation to the three pillars is stated — two in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance. Section C asks for principle-wise performance disclosures against those principles, so the mapping is not the entity's to choose.

options.text: Under Principle 8, inclusive growth and equitable development, since bribery damages the communities in which the entity operates
options.misconception: routes a disclosure by the harm it eventually causes rather than by the principle whose subject it is
options.why: Principle 8 is about identifying and addressing the impacts of the entity's activities on the social, cultural and economic life of people — land acquisition, business-induced displacement, products for marginalised communities, and CSR aligned to local development priorities. Integrity in the conduct of business is the subject of Principle 1, whatever the downstream harm of failing at it.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct, Principle 1 on ethics, transparency and accountability and the anti-bribery disclosures made under it, and their split of two in Environment, three in Social and four in Governance

items.scenario: A listed company is completing Section C of its Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report. It has to disclose its anti-bribery policy, the internal control mechanism behind it, and the machinery for dealing with bribery and corruption complaints. The finance team has put these disclosures under the principle on inclusive growth, on the reasoning that corruption harms communities.

items.stem: Which body's work is being described, and by whom was it created?

options.text: The Global Reporting Initiative, created by the Financial Stability Board, whose standards are used by ninety-three per cent of the world's largest two hundred and fifty corporations
options.misconception: keeps the right creator against the wrong framework, and misses that the Global Reporting Initiative is deliberately not sector-specific
options.why: The Global Reporting Initiative is an independent international organisation based in Amsterdam, not a creation of the Financial Stability Board, and its whole design is to work across a wide range of organisations reporting economic, environmental and social impacts to all their stakeholders. The share of the world's largest corporations reporting through it is a fact about its reach, not about any focus on financial firms.

options.text: The International Sustainability Standards Board, created in 2015 by the IFRS Foundation Trustees to serve banks and insurers
options.misconception: dates the standard-setting board from the year the Task Force was created and narrows its audience to one sector
options.why: The IFRS Foundation Trustees announced the creation of the International Sustainability Standards Board on 3 November 2021, not in 2015, and its purpose is a comprehensive global baseline of sustainability-related disclosure standards for investors and other capital market participants generally, not a framework for one sector.

options.text: The Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures, created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board, which unlike the Global Reporting Initiative is targeted at companies that predominantly handle financial-related interests such as banks and insurance firms
options.why: The Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures was created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board with the goal of helping companies create consistent climate-related disclosures, and it is targeted at companies that predominantly handle financial-related interests, such as banks and insurance firms. The Global Reporting Initiative, by contrast, works across a wide range of organisations. The Task Force's recommendations are also what the International Sustainability Standards Board's proposed climate standard was built on.
keywords: Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures

options.text: The Carbon Disclosure Project, which captures data on greenhouse gas emissions, water, forests and the supply chain and is therefore the framework for financial firms
options.misconception: picks the body that collects environmental performance data and reads its investor audience as a sectoral focus
options.why: The Carbon Disclosure Project captures environmental performance data — greenhouse gas emissions, water, forests and the supply chain — and reports on climate change, forests and water security to investors, buyers and other stakeholders. Its audience includes investors, but it is not a framework aimed at entities that handle financial-related interests, and it is not the body that set out to produce consistent climate-related disclosures for such firms.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures created in 2015 by the Financial Stability Board, read against the Global Reporting Initiative, the Carbon Disclosure Project and the International Sustainability Standards Board announced on 3 November 2021

items.scenario: A bank asks you which international framework it should look at for producing consistent climate-related disclosures. It notes that the framework it wants is one aimed at organisations that predominantly handle financial-related interests rather than at every kind of entity.

items.stem: What are the Social Audit Standards?

options.text: A series of assurance standards for reporting on an entity's sustainability information, replacing SSAE 3000 for social matters
options.misconception: files the social audit series under the assurance-on-sustainability-information ground that SSAE 3000 already occupies
options.why: SSAE 3000 is the umbrella standard for assurance engagements on an entity's sustainability information and remains so. The Social Audit Standards are a different thing entirely: they govern impact assessment engagements of social enterprises, not assurance on a company's sustainability report, and they replace nothing.

options.text: Standards on Internal Audit applying to the internal audit of an entity's corporate social responsibility spending
options.misconception: reads "social" as corporate social responsibility inside a company and lands in the internal audit series
options.why: The Standards on Internal Audit are a separate series governing internal audit engagements within an entity. The Social Audit Standards address a Social Auditor assessing the impact of a Social Enterprise's work in fields such as hunger and poverty, health care, education, gender equality and disaster management — an external impact assessment, not internal audit of a spending head.

options.text: A series numbered SAS 100 to SAS 1600, issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, guiding the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise and setting the minimum requirements for conducting the social impact assessment
options.why: The Social Audit Standards run from SAS 100 to SAS 1600 and were issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India. Each guides the Social Auditor in an independent impact assessment engagement of a Social Enterprise working in a particular field, and sets out the audit steps and procedures for the social impact assessment. Each states the minimum requirements to be followed, and any additional requirement established by law or regulation is followed as well.

options.text: Standards issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India prescribing the format of the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report
options.misconception: credits the standards to the regulator that mandated the reporting rather than to the Institute's board that wrote them
options.why: The Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report format comes from the Securities and Exchange Board of India. The Social Audit Standards come from the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, and they deal with social impact assessment, not with the format of a listed entity's report.

citation.ref: Ch. Sustainable Development Goals and ESG Assurance — the Social Audit Standards SAS 100 to SAS 1600 issued by the Sustainability Reporting Standards Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India for independent impact assessment engagements of Social Enterprises

items.scenario: A social enterprise working on safe drinking water and sanitation needs an independent assessment of the impact of its programmes. The engagement partner asks which body's standards govern such an assignment and what they are for.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require of you?

options.text: Accept, and set the extent of the examination procedures by the fee agreed and the time available, the standard leaving the nature, timing and extent of procedures unregulated
options.misconception: treats the scope of work as a commercial variable, when the standard lists the matters that must set it
options.why: The nature, timing and extent of the examination procedures are set by named considerations: the knowledge from previous engagements, management's competence to prepare such information, the likelihood of material misstatement, the extent to which the information is affected by management's judgement, the sources of information and the reliability of the underlying data, the stability of the entity's business, and the team's experience with the business and with reporting on prospective financial information.

options.text: Consider before acceptance the intended use of the information, whether its distribution is general or limited, whether the assumptions are best-estimate or hypothetical, the elements to be included and the period covered; and, on the capacity point, require that every significant implication of the assumption be carried through the information before it can be reported on
options.why: The five acceptance considerations are the intended use of the information, whether it is for general or limited distribution, the nature of the assumptions — whether best-estimate or hypothetical — the elements to be included, and the period covered. And where hypothetical assumptions are used, all their significant implications must have been taken into account: if sales are assumed to grow beyond current plant capacity, the information must include the necessary investment in the additional capacity or the cost of an alternative such as subcontracting production.

options.text: Decline the engagement outright, because prospective financial information prepared by an employee rather than by a professional accountant cannot be examined
options.misconception: invents a bar on who may prepare the information, when management's responsibility for preparing it is the standard's own premise
options.why: Management is responsible for the preparation and presentation of prospective financial information, including identifying and disclosing it, explaining the basis of the forecast and the underlying assumptions. Who inside the entity drafted it is not a ground for refusal. The grounds for refusing are assumptions that are clearly unrealistic, or a belief that the information will be inappropriate for its intended use.

options.text: Accept the engagement and express an opinion on whether the projected sales and profits will be achieved over the seven years, since that is what the bankers want to know
options.misconception: promises the one opinion an examination of prospective financial information can never give
options.why: Prospective financial information relates to events and actions that have not yet occurred and might not occur, and the evidence supporting the assumptions is itself future-oriented and speculative. An opinion as to whether the results shown will be achieved cannot be expressed, however the report is to be used.

citation.ref: the matters considered before accepting an engagement to examine prospective financial information, the matters determining the nature, timing and extent of the examination procedures, and the requirement that every significant implication of a hypothetical assumption be carried through the prospective financial information

items.scenario: A company asks you to examine a seven-year projection for a new plant, prepared by its finance executive, which is to be given to its bankers to support a loan application. The projection assumes sales growing to twice the plant's designed capacity in year four, and the working papers contain no provision for additional capacity and no cost of subcontracting.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require on presentation and disclosure here?

options.text: Inadequate disclosure of the consequences of a highly sensitive assumption is a matter for the engagement file and never affects the opinion, which deals only with arithmetic on the stated assumptions
options.misconception: separates disclosure from the opinion, when inadequate presentation and disclosure is one of the grounds for modifying it
options.why: Where the auditor believes the presentation and disclosure of the prospective financial information are not adequate — the example the standard gives is a failure to disclose adequately the consequences of highly sensitive assumptions — he expresses a qualified or an adverse opinion, or withdraws from the engagement. Disclosure is part of what the opinion covers, not a file note.

options.text: The assumptions need not be marked as best-estimate or hypothetical so long as they are listed, since the report itself states which kind of prospective financial information it covers
options.misconception: leaves the reader of the notes to infer from the report's title what each individual assumption is
options.why: The assumptions must be adequately disclosed in the notes to the prospective financial information, and it must be clear whether they represent management's best-estimates or are hypothetical. A single set can mix the two, so a label on the document does not settle what any particular assumption is.

options.text: The basis of establishing the points in the range must be clearly indicated and the range must not be selected in a biased or misleading manner, and where an assumption is material and subject to a high degree of uncertainty, that uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of the results must be adequately disclosed
options.why: Where results are expressed in terms of a range, the basis of establishing the points in the range must be clearly indicated and the range must not be selected in a biased or misleading manner. And where assumptions are made in areas that are material and subject to a high degree of uncertainty, that uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of the results must be adequately disclosed, because a reader shown two end points and no method cannot tell how far the number really moves.
keywords: basis of establishing the points in the range

options.text: Nothing further, provided the two end points are arithmetically correct on the assumptions used, since a range already discloses the uncertainty by its width
options.misconception: treats the existence of a range as a substitute for disclosing how the range was built and how sensitive the result is
options.why: A range whose end points were chosen without a disclosed basis tells the reader nothing about the method, and it can be selected to flatter. That is precisely why the standard requires the basis of establishing the points to be indicated and forbids a biased or misleading range, and why sensitivity is disclosed separately from the width of the range.

citation.ref: the assessment of presentation and disclosure — the basis of establishing points in a range and the bar on a biased or misleading range, the disclosure of uncertainty and the resulting sensitivity of results, and the marking of assumptions as best-estimate or hypothetical

items.scenario: A forecast you are examining expresses profit before tax as a range. The notes give the two end points of the range but say nothing about how they were arrived at, and one assumption — a commodity price that drives most of the margin — is material and highly uncertain, with no disclosure of that uncertainty or of how far the result moves with it.

items.stem: What does SAE 3400 require you to do?

options.text: Express a qualified opinion, since only one assumption out of many is affected and the effect is material but not pervasive
options.misconception: imports the material-but-not-pervasive grid from a report on historical financial statements into a fault that goes to the foundation
options.why: SAE 3400 does not scale the response to how many assumptions failed. Where a significant assumption does not provide a reasonable basis, the response prescribed is an adverse opinion setting out the reasons, or withdrawal. The qualified-or-adverse choice belongs to the separate case of presentation and disclosure that is not adequate.

options.text: Express an adverse opinion setting out the reasons in the report, or withdraw from the engagement
options.why: Where the auditor believes that one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis for prospective financial information prepared on best-estimate assumptions, the answer is an adverse opinion setting out the reasons in the report, or withdrawal from the engagement. The assumptions are the whole foundation of the information, so information built on a foundation that does not hold cannot be partly relied on and a qualification does not meet the case.
keywords: adverse opinion setting out the reasons

options.text: Issue the report unmodified with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph drawing attention to the renewal assumption, the assumption being disclosed in the notes
options.misconception: uses a paragraph that describes a matter to deal with a matter that requires a modification
options.why: A paragraph drawing attention to a matter is not an opinion about it. Where the auditor believes a significant assumption does not provide a reasonable basis, the required response is an adverse opinion or withdrawal; disclosure of the assumption in the notes does not cure a foundation the auditor has concluded does not hold.

options.text: Disclaim the opinion, since the achievability of the renewal cannot be verified and no evidence about a future event can ever be conclusive
options.misconception: treats the future-oriented nature of all such evidence as a scope limitation, when the standard reserves a disclaimer for procedures actually precluded
options.why: A disclaimer is considered where the examination is affected by conditions that preclude the application of one or more procedures the auditor considers necessary in the circumstances. Evidence about assumptions is future-oriented in every such engagement; that is the premise of the standard, not a scope limitation, and here the auditor was able to perform his procedures and reached a conclusion.

citation.ref: the modification of the report on an examination of prospective financial information — an adverse opinion setting out the reasons or withdrawal where one or more significant assumptions do not provide a reasonable basis, a qualified or adverse opinion or withdrawal where the presentation and disclosure are not adequate, and withdrawal or a disclaimer where conditions preclude a necessary procedure

items.scenario: You are examining a forecast prepared on best-estimate assumptions. One assumption drives most of the projected profit: that a single customer, whose current contract expires in four months, will renew for five years at a higher price. There is no correspondence, no negotiation record and no history of such a renewal. You conclude the assumption does not provide a reasonable basis for the forecast, and management will not change it or the forecast.

items.stem: What does SAE 3402 require?

options.text: Report the deviations in the separate section or attachment describing the tests of controls, stating which controls were tested, whether the items tested were all of the population or a selection, the extent of testing including the sample size, and the number and nature of the deviations — even though you concluded the control objective was achieved
options.why: A type 2 report includes a separate section after the opinion, or an attachment, describing the tests of controls performed and their results, stating which controls were tested, whether the items tested represent all or a selection of the population, and the nature of the tests in enough detail for user auditors to judge the effect on their risk assessments. Where deviations are identified, the extent of testing including the sample size and the number and nature of the deviations are given, and the service auditor reports deviations even where he concluded the related control objective was achieved.
keywords: number and nature of the deviations

options.text: Modify the opinion, because a deviation found in testing means the controls tested did not operate effectively
options.misconception: converts every deviation into a failure of operating effectiveness, skipping the evaluation the service auditor has already performed
options.why: The opinion is modified where the controls tested did not operate effectively in all material respects, and that is a conclusion the service auditor reaches after evaluating the deviations, not an automatic consequence of finding one. Here he concluded the related control objective was achieved, so the deviations are reported and the opinion is not modified for them.

options.text: Report the deviations, but in a covering letter to the service organisation rather than in the report, since the report is a public document
options.misconception: treats a report addressed to a defined readership as a public one and moves the findings out of the readers' reach
options.why: The report is not a public document: it states that it and, in a type 2 report, the description of tests of controls are intended only for user entities and their auditors, who have sufficient understanding to consider it alongside information about controls the user entities operate themselves. Those are precisely the people the deviations must reach.

options.text: Omit the three items, since a deviation that did not prevent the control objective from being achieved is not a finding and reporting it would mislead the user auditors
options.misconception: lets the service auditor's own conclusion about the objective decide what the user auditor is allowed to see
options.why: The standard settles this in terms: deviations are reported even where the service auditor has concluded, on the basis of the tests performed, that the related control objective was achieved. The user auditor is entitled to see the population the deviation came from and to reach his own conclusion about what it means for his entity's risk assessment.

citation.ref: the separate section or attachment to a type 2 report describing the tests of controls and their results, the disclosure of the extent of testing including the sample size and the number and nature of deviations, the rule that deviations are reported even where the service auditor concluded the related control objective was achieved, and the restriction of the report to user entities and their auditors

items.scenario: You are the service auditor issuing a type 2 report on a payroll processing organisation. You tested the authorisation control over master-data changes on a sample of twenty-five changes and found three where the approval was obtained after the change was made. Considering the compensating review performed at month end, you conclude the related control objective was nonetheless achieved. The service organisation's management asks you to leave the three items out of the report, since the objective was met and listing them will alarm user auditors.

items.stem: What does SAE 3420 require you to do?

options.text: Issue an unmodified opinion with an Emphasis of Matter paragraph describing the adjustment, since the regulation forbids a modified opinion and the paragraph puts the reader on notice
options.misconception: uses an Emphasis of Matter paragraph as a way round a modification the practitioner has already concluded is required
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph is available only where the practitioner has obtained sufficient appropriate evidence that the matter does not affect whether the pro forma financial information has been compiled in all material respects on the basis of the applicable criteria. Here the adjustment does affect exactly that, so the paragraph is not open to him and the regulation is not a licence to issue an opinion he does not hold.

options.text: Issue the report without an opinion, describing the disagreement, since the regulation prevents a modified opinion from being published
options.misconception: answers a legal restriction on publication by withholding the opinion the engagement exists to give
options.why: A reasonable assurance engagement under this standard exists to express an opinion on whether the pro forma financial information has been compiled, in all material respects, on the basis of the applicable criteria. The prescribed route where publication of a modification is precluded is discussion with the responsible party and then withdrawal or legal advice, not a report carrying no opinion.

options.text: Discuss the matter with the responsible party, and where it does not agree to make the necessary changes, withdraw from the engagement or consider seeking legal advice
options.why: Where the relevant law or regulation precludes publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion and the practitioner nonetheless concludes that a modified opinion is appropriate, he discusses the matter with the responsible party. If the responsible party does not agree to make the necessary changes, the practitioner shall withdraw from the engagement or consider seeking legal advice. He does not soften the opinion so that the prospectus can be published.
keywords: discusses the matter with the responsible party

options.text: Recompile the pro forma financial information yourself on a factually supportable basis and report on your own compilation
options.misconception: takes over the responsible party's job, which is the one thing this engagement rules out
options.why: The practitioner has no responsibility to compile the pro forma financial information; that responsibility rests with the responsible party, and the practitioner's sole responsibility is to report on whether it has been compiled, in all material respects, by the responsible party on the basis of the applicable criteria. Compiling it himself would destroy the engagement.

citation.ref: the course where law or regulation precludes publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion — discussion with the responsible party and, failing agreement to make the necessary changes, withdrawal from the engagement or seeking legal advice — and the conditions on an Emphasis of Matter paragraph

items.scenario: You are reporting under SAE 3420 on pro forma financial information in a prospectus. One pro forma adjustment is not factually supportable and you conclude a modified opinion is appropriate. The relevant regulation precludes the publication of a prospectus containing a modified opinion on the compilation of pro forma financial information. The responsible party will not change the adjustment or the disclosure, and asks you to issue an unmodified opinion with a paragraph drawing attention to the adjustment instead.

items.stem: How do you deal with this?

options.text: The company must prepare consolidated financial statements, because section 129(3) applies to every company that has one or more subsidiaries and the Rules provide no exemption from it
options.misconception: reads the section without the exemption in the Rules and so requires a consolidation the law does not
options.why: Section 129(3) does require a company having one or more subsidiaries, including an associate company and a joint venture, to prepare consolidated financial statements — but the Companies (Accounts) Rules carry an exemption where three conditions hold together, and this company meets all three. Reciting the section alone reaches the wrong answer.

options.text: The directors are right about the subsidiary acquired during the year, because control intended to be temporary is excluded from consolidation, so that subsidiary would be left out in any case
options.misconception: revives an exemption for temporary control that the applicable framework does not contain
options.why: There is no exemption for temporary control, or for operation under severe long-term restrictions on the transfer of funds. Consolidation of an investee begins from the date the investor obtains control and ceases when the investor loses control, so a subsidiary acquired during the year and sold in the next is consolidated for both years in which it was controlled.

options.text: The company is not required to prepare consolidated financial statements, because all three conditions hold together — a wholly-owned subsidiary, securities not listed and not in the process of listing, and an ultimate holding company filing compliant consolidated financial statements with the Registrar; the temporary-control argument is separately wrong, because no such exemption exists
options.why: The exemption is cumulative: the company must be a wholly-owned subsidiary, or a partially-owned subsidiary whose other members do not object after written intimation with proof of delivery; its securities must not be listed and not in the process of listing in India or outside India; and its ultimate or any intermediate holding company must file consolidated financial statements with the Registrar which comply with the applicable accounting standards. All three hold here. There is no exemption for temporary control: consolidation begins from the date control is obtained and ceases when it is lost.

options.text: The company is exempt on the strength of being a wholly-owned subsidiary alone, so the listing status of its securities and what its holding company files are beside the point
options.misconception: takes one limb of a cumulative test as if it were sufficient on its own
options.why: Being a wholly-owned subsidiary is one of three conditions, not the whole test. The securities must also not be listed and not be in the process of being listed on any stock exchange in India or outside India, and the ultimate or any intermediate holding company must file consolidated financial statements with the Registrar complying with the applicable accounting standards.

citation.ref: Section 129(3) on the preparation of consolidated financial statements, the three cumulative conditions in the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 on which a company need not prepare them, and the absence under Ind AS 110 of any exemption for temporary control

items.scenario: An unlisted Indian company is a wholly-owned subsidiary of another Indian company. Its securities are not listed and are not in the process of being listed anywhere in India or abroad. Its ultimate holding company files consolidated financial statements with the Registrar which comply with the applicable accounting standards. The company itself has two subsidiaries of its own and has not prepared consolidated financial statements. Separately, its directors say that even if it were required to consolidate, one of its subsidiaries was acquired in the year and is to be sold next year, so control there is temporary.

items.stem: What is required?

options.text: Report under clause 3(xxi) alone, indicating the details of the companies whose CARO reports carry qualifications or adverse remarks together with the paragraph numbers of those reports containing them
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) is the only clause of the Order that operates on a report on consolidated financial statements. Under it the auditor reports whether there have been any qualifications or adverse remarks by the respective auditors in the CARO reports of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements, and indicates the details of those companies together with the paragraph numbers of the CARO reports containing them.

options.text: Modify the opinion on the consolidated financial statements, since four component CARO reports carry qualifications
options.misconception: reads a signposting clause as a trigger for a modification of the group opinion
options.why: Clause 3(xxi) is a signpost and not an opinion. A qualification or adverse remark in a component's CARO report is evaluated separately for whether it says anything material about the consolidated financial statements as a whole, and a matter material only at the component does not travel up into the group opinion.
keywords: material about the consolidated financial statements

options.text: Prepare a separate clause-by-clause CARO 2020 report covering the parent and all subsidiaries incorporated in India
options.misconception: re-runs the whole Order at group level, when only one clause reaches the consolidated statements
options.why: The Order attaches to the auditor's report on standalone financial statements. On consolidated financial statements only clause 3(xxi) operates, and it asks for a pointer to qualifications and adverse remarks already made by the component auditors, not for the twenty other clauses to be answered again for the group.

options.text: Supplement the CARO report on the standalone financial statements with additional information in respect of all subsidiaries incorporated in India
options.misconception: attaches group information to the standalone report instead of reporting where the Order actually requires it
options.why: The standalone CARO report answers the Order for the standalone financial statements of the company it belongs to. The consolidated position is dealt with in the report on the consolidated financial statements, under clause 3(xxi), and moving the information into the standalone report leaves the reader of the consolidated statements with nothing.

citation.ref: Clause 3(xxi) — the details of the companies included in the consolidated financial statements whose CARO reports carry qualifications or adverse remarks, and the paragraph numbers of those reports containing them, this being the only clause of the Order applying to the auditor's report on consolidated financial statements

items.scenario: You are finalising the auditor's report on the consolidated financial statements of a company with eight subsidiaries incorporated in India, audited by other auditors whose reports have been furnished to you. Four of those CARO reports carry qualifications or adverse remarks. Your manager asks how CARO 2020 is to be dealt with in the report on the consolidated financial statements.

items.stem: Which set of representations is the one SA 580 and the guidance on consolidated financial statements point to?

options.text: No written representations are needed where every component has been audited, since the component auditors' reports already cover the same ground
options.misconception: assumes component audits answer questions that only exist at the group level
options.why: A component auditor reports on that component's own financial statements. He says nothing about whether every component has been included in the consolidation, about the group's reportable segments, or about the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments — which are exactly the matters the parent's management is asked to confirm.

options.text: A representation that the consolidation is arithmetically accurate, which discharges the auditor's work on the consolidation adjustments
options.misconception: treats a representation as evidence that removes the need for the procedures it describes
options.why: A written representation is audit evidence, but it is not sufficient appropriate audit evidence on its own about any of the matters it deals with. It does not relieve the auditor of the procedures on the completeness of components, on the consolidation adjustments or on related parties that he would otherwise perform.

options.text: A representation from each component's management that its own financial statements are free from material misstatement, in place of representations from the parent
options.misconception: pushes the representation down to the components and leaves the group-level matters unrepresented
options.why: The written representations in an audit of consolidated financial statements are obtained from the management of the parent, because it is the parent's management that is responsible for preparing and presenting those statements — for identifying components, obtaining their financial information, making the consolidation adjustments and harmonising accounting policies.

options.text: Completeness of the components included in the consolidated financial statements; identification of reportable segments for segmental reporting; identification of related parties and related party transactions for reporting; and the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments, including the elimination of intra-group transactions
options.why: Those four are the standard examples of representations obtained from the parent's management on matters material to the consolidated financial statements, alongside the acknowledgement of its responsibility for a true and fair presentation and its approval of those statements. The completeness of the components is the one the auditor can least easily establish alone, because a component left out of the consolidation leaves no trace inside it.
keywords: matters material to the consolidated financial statements

citation.ref: Ch. Group Audits — written representations from the parent's management on the completeness of components, the identification of reportable segments, the identification of related parties and related party transactions, and the appropriateness and completeness of the permanent and current period consolidation adjustments including the elimination of intra-group transactions, read with SA 580

items.scenario: You are completing the audit of a group's consolidated financial statements and are drafting the written representations to be obtained from the parent's management on matters material to those statements.

items.stem: Which statement is correct?

options.text: He is appointed by the Central Government and holds office at its pleasure, his reports being submitted to the Ministry of Finance
options.misconception: makes a constitutional authority an appointee of the executive whose accounts he audits
options.why: The appointment is by the President under Article 148, and removal is possible only by a special procedure on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity — not at anyone's pleasure. His audit reports go to the President or the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly, not to a ministry.

options.text: The form in which the accounts of the Union and the States are kept is prescribed by Parliament by statute, the Comptroller and Auditor General having no say in it
options.misconception: moves the power over the form of the accounts to the legislature and drops his advisory role
options.why: Article 150 provides that the President prescribes the form in which the accounts of the Union and the States shall be kept, and he does so on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor General. The advice is part of the office's constitutional position, not an omission from it.

options.text: His duties and powers are settled by the Constitution alone, no statute having been made under Article 149
options.misconception: stops at the Constitution and misses the statute that actually defines the duties and powers
options.why: Article 149 provides that he shall perform such duties and exercise such powers as may be prescribed by or under any law made by Parliament, and the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 is that law, defining his functions and powers in detail and fixing his tenure.

options.text: He is appointed by the President under Article 148 and may be removed only by a special procedure on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity; under the 1971 Act he holds office for six years or up to the age of sixty-five, whichever is earlier; and under Article 151 his reports are laid before Parliament or the State Legislature
options.why: Article 148 provides for appointment by the President and for a special procedure for removal, only on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity, with salary and conditions of service determined by Parliament. The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 provides a term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier. Article 151 requires his reports to be submitted to the President or the Governor, who causes them to be laid before Parliament or the State Legislative Assembly.
keywords: six years or up to the age of sixty-five

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — Articles 148 to 151 of the Constitution and the term of six years or up to the age of sixty-five years, whichever is earlier, under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971

items.scenario: A trainee asks what protects the independence of the Comptroller and Auditor General, given that the Government whose accounts he audits is also the executive he works alongside.

items.stem: Which committee is this, and what marks it out?

options.text: An Audit Board, constituted by the Comptroller and Auditor General with experts in the relevant disciplines to conduct comprehensive audit appraisals
options.misconception: confuses the C&AG's own appraisal machinery with a committee of the legislature
options.why: An Audit Board is part of the Comptroller and Auditor General's own machinery for comprehensive audit appraisals of public sector enterprises: it associates experts, discusses findings with the enterprise and its ministry, has no separate legal entity and works under his supervision and control. It is not a committee of Parliament, and Parliament's committees are where the reports land afterwards.

options.text: The Public Accounts Committee, whose duty is to satisfy itself that the moneys were disbursed legally on the purpose to which they were applied and that the expenditure was authorised
options.misconception: names the committee whose subject is the regularity of expenditure when the question describes an appraisal of commercial performance
options.why: The Public Accounts Committee satisfies itself that moneys were disbursed legally on the service or purpose to which they were applied, that the expenditure incurred was authorised, and that re-appropriation was made in accordance with the provisions made. That is the regularity of spending, not whether an undertaking is run on prudent commercial practices.

options.text: The Estimates Committee, which reports what economies and improvements in efficiency may be effected and may suggest alternative policies
options.misconception: picks the committee that works on the estimates before the money is spent rather than on the working of an undertaking
options.why: The Estimates Committee examines the estimates to report what economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform may be effected consistently with the policy underlying them, to suggest alternative policies, and to suggest the form in which the estimates shall be presented. It does not comment on a policy approved by Parliament, and its subject is the estimates, not the appraisal of a public undertaking's performance.

options.text: The Committee on Public Undertakings, which exercises over public sector undertakings the same financial control the Public Accounts Committee exercises over Government departments, and whose examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of the undertaking's performance
options.why: The Committee on Public Undertakings examines the reports and accounts of public undertakings, examines the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General on them, and examines their autonomy and efficiency and whether they are being managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices. It exercises the same financial control over public sector undertakings that the Public Accounts Committee exercises over the functioning of Government departments, and its examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of performance.

citation.ref: Ch. Overview of Audit of Public Sector Undertakings — the Committee on Public Undertakings, the Public Accounts Committee and the Estimates Committee and their respective functions, and the Audit Boards constituted by the Comptroller and Auditor General for comprehensive appraisals

items.scenario: A committee of Parliament has taken up a public sector power company. It is examining the company's reports and accounts, the Comptroller and Auditor General's reports on it, and whether the undertaking is being managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices. Its examination is taking the form of a comprehensive appraisal of the company's performance, including its policies and its programmes.

items.stem: How is this engagement classified?

options.text: As no assurance engagement at all, since there is no assertion by the entity for the auditor to test
options.misconception: treats an entity assertion as a precondition of every assurance engagement, which direct reporting engagements exist to disprove
options.why: A public sector audit has three parties — the auditor, the responsible party and the intended users — and it does not require the responsible party to have made an assertion first. In a direct reporting engagement the auditor measures the subject matter against the criteria himself, and it is a full engagement with the same elements as any other.

options.text: As a financial audit, since every audit conducted for the Comptroller and Auditor General is an attestation engagement on financial information
options.misconception: collapses the three types of public sector audit into the one that is always an attestation engagement
options.why: Financial audit expresses an opinion on financial statements and is always an attestation engagement, but the audit of public enterprises is not restricted to financial and compliance audit; it extends to performance, which examines the economy, efficiency and effectiveness with which the entity operates and fulfils its objectives.

options.text: As a direct reporting engagement, in which the auditor himself measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria; performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements, while financial audits are always attestation engagements because they rest on financial information presented by the responsible party
options.why: In a direct reporting engagement it is the auditor who measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria. In an attestation engagement the responsible party measures the subject matter against the criteria and presents the subject matter information, and the auditor gathers evidence to express a conclusion on it. Financial audits are always attestation engagements, and performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements — which is why a performance audit reports findings and recommendations rather than an opinion.
