options.text: On the third only, since it is the one being actively dealt with
options.misconception: inverts the rule; held-for-sale classification is the single case that stops the charge
options.why: Once an asset is classified as held for sale it is measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell and is not depreciated. It is precisely the machine that has stopped, and the two still in the business that carry on.

options.text: On the first two for the whole year; only the third stops, and it stops on 1 December 2025
options.why: Depreciation of an asset begins when it is available for use and ceases at the earlier of the date the asset is classified as held for sale under Ind AS 105 and the date it is derecognised. Nothing else stops the clock — depreciation does not cease when the asset becomes idle or is retired from active use, unless the asset is fully depreciated. Machines 1 and 2 are neither classified as held for sale nor derecognised, so the charge runs on for the full year. The one qualification is a usage method of depreciation, where the charge can fall to zero while there is no production, and none of these is on a usage method.

citation.ref: para 55, read with the useful life factors in para 56 and the disclosure of idle and retired assets in para 79

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company holds three machines, each with carrying amount left and each depreciated on the straight-line method. Machine 1 has stood idle for eight months while the plant waits for the order book to recover; it is not for sale. Machine 2 was retired from active use in January 2026 and is being kept as a source of spare parts; it does not meet the held-for-sale criteria. Machine 3 was classified as held for sale on 1 December 2025. The accountant has stopped depreciating all three.

items.stem: What is capitalised as an intangible asset at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹1.20 crore — everything spent after the criteria were met is development expenditure on the asset
options.misconception: capitalises the whole window and ignores the exclusions the standard names by name
options.why: Meeting the criteria opens the door; it does not admit every rupee that follows through it. Training, pre-performance inefficiencies and unattributable overhead are excluded by name, whichever side of the date they fall.

options.text: ₹87 lakh, and the ₹80 lakh already taken to profit or loss stays there
options.why: The cost of an internally generated intangible asset is the sum of the expenditure incurred from the date the recognition criteria are first met, and expenditure previously recognised as an expense shall not be reinstated, however clearly the project has since succeeded. So the ₹80 lakh spent before 1 September stays in profit or loss. Three things are then named as not being components of the cost: selling, administrative and other general overhead expenditure unless it can be directly attributed to preparing the asset for use; identified inefficiencies and initial operating losses incurred before the asset achieves planned performance; and expenditure on training staff to operate the asset. Taking ₹15 lakh, ₹10 lakh and ₹8 lakh out of ₹1.20 crore leaves ₹87 lakh.

options.text: ₹1.02 crore — the training readies the asset for use and so is directly attributable, leaving only the inefficiencies and the overhead to come out
options.misconception: treats staff training as a cost of readying the asset, when Ind AS 38 names it as an exclusion
options.why: Training builds the skill of the people, and the entity does not control that skill the way it controls the asset. The standard settles the argument by listing training as an exclusion rather than leaving it to the directly-attributable test.

options.text: ₹2 crore — the ₹1.20 crore and the ₹80 lakh together, since the project has now met the criteria and the earlier spending built the same asset
options.misconception: reinstates expenditure already recognised as an expense, which the standard prohibits outright
options.why: The prohibition is absolute and deliberate: it stops an entity from deciding, once a project succeeds, that its earlier failures were assets all along. The cut-off is the date the criteria were first demonstrated, and here that is 1 September.

citation.ref: para 65, 66 and 71

items.scenario: A company began developing a new engine on 1 April 2025 and expensed the ₹80 lakh spent over the first five months, because it could not then demonstrate technical feasibility or a market. On 1 September 2025 all six criteria were met. Between that date and 31 March 2026 it spent ₹1.20 crore more, of which ₹15 lakh was training the production staff to operate the new engine line, ₹10 lakh was scrap and rework from teething problems before the line reached planned performance, and ₹8 lakh was a share of head-office administration that cannot be directly attributed to preparing the asset for use.

items.stem: What rate does the lessee discount the lease payments at?

options.text: The 9 per cent at which the parent borrows, because that is what the group actually finances the lease at
options.misconception: substitutes the group's cost of funds for the lessee entity's own
options.why: The definition names the lessee, and the lessee's own credit profile is one of the things the rate is meant to reflect. A subsidiary borrowing behind a stronger parent would otherwise report a liability at a rate it could never obtain on its own covenant.

options.text: The rate implicit in the lease, estimated from the property's fair value and an assumed residual value, because the incremental borrowing rate may be used only where no estimate at all is possible
options.misconception: reads "readily determined" as "capable of being estimated", which would make the fallback almost unreachable
options.why: The implicit rate depends on the lessor's initial direct costs and its residual value assumption, which a lessee usually cannot see. The standard's test is whether the rate can be readily determined, not whether a lessee could build a guess at it from outside.

options.text: The 11 per cent property yield, since it is the observable market rate for exactly this kind of asset
options.misconception: takes an observable yield as the answer rather than as a starting point needing adjustment
options.why: Observable rates such as a property yield can be used as a starting point, then adjusted for the credit profile of the lessee, the borrowing currency and the length of the lease term. Unadjusted, a property yield prices the building over its whole life, not a five-year right to use it.

options.text: Its own incremental borrowing rate — the 12 per cent quote, adjusted to a borrowing of a similar amount in the currency the rent is payable in
options.why: Where the interest rate implicit in the lease cannot be readily determined, the lessee discounts at its incremental borrowing rate: the rate it would have to pay to borrow, over a similar term and with a similar security, the funds necessary to obtain an asset of a similar value to the right-of-use asset, in a similar economic environment. A similar term means the five-year lease term, not the life of the building, and a similar value means the right-of-use asset and not the underlying property. The rate is the lessee's own, so a parent's cost of funds is not it. Because the payments are made in a foreign currency, the rate is determined on a borrowing of a similar amount in that currency.

citation.ref: para 26, read with the definition of the lessee's incremental borrowing rate in Appendix A

items.scenario: A retailer takes a five-year lease of a shop. The lessor will not disclose its initial direct costs or the residual value it has assumed, so the interest rate implicit in the lease cannot be readily determined. Three rates are on the table: 9 per cent, at which the retailer's overseas parent borrows; 11 per cent, the observable yield on shop property in that city; and 12 per cent, which the retailer's own bank quotes it for a five-year secured loan of about the value of the right-of-use asset. The rent is payable in a foreign currency.

items.stem: What may the company build into the provision at the reporting date?

options.text: The cost reduction from applying the existing method with more experience, and the higher standard the new legislation will demand — but not the hoped-for new technique and not the ₹2 crore land gain
options.why: Future events that may affect the amount required to settle an obligation are reflected in the provision where there is sufficient objective evidence that they will occur. Expected cost reductions from applying an existing technology with increased experience qualify; the development of a completely new technology does not, unless evidence supports it. The effect of possible new legislation is taken into account when there is sufficient objective evidence that the legislation is virtually certain to be enacted, and a bill through the legislature awaiting only its notification is that. Gains on the expected disposal of assets are not taken into account at all, even where the disposal is closely linked to the event giving rise to the provision — the land gain is dealt with under Ind AS 16 when it happens.

options.text: The new technique and the land gain, but not the new legislation, which binds nobody until it is notified in the gazette
options.misconception: waits for enactment when the test is virtual certainty of enactment, and lets in a technology with no evidence behind it
options.why: The two are exactly the wrong way round. A bill through the legislature awaiting only notification is the standard's own example of virtual certainty, while a technique nobody has invented is the example it gives of what may not be assumed.

options.text: All four — the two cost reductions, the new standard and the land sale — because the best estimate must use every piece of information available
options.misconception: treats "best estimate" as licence to net a future asset gain against a liability
options.why: The best estimate is of the expenditure required to settle the obligation, and the land gain is not part of that expenditure. Netting it would show a smaller liability than the entity has, and would recognise a gain on an asset it has not yet sold.

options.text: Nothing beyond today's cost at today's legal standard, because a provision measures the obligation as it stands at the reporting date
options.misconception: freezes the estimate at present conditions, when the standard expressly asks for future events supported by evidence
options.why: The obligation exists now but will be settled in fifteen years, and it is the future settlement that is being measured. Ignoring evidenced future changes in cost would make every long-dated provision wrong in a predictable direction.

citation.ref: para 48 to 50 for future events and para 51 and 52 for expected disposals

items.scenario: A chemical works has a legal obligation to clean up its site at the end of the plant's fifteen-year life. Its engineers expect the existing cleaning method to get cheaper as the crew gains experience with it. Its research team hopes an entirely new technique will be invented that would halve the cost, though nothing of the kind exists yet. A bill requiring a higher clean-up standard has passed the state legislature and only the gazette notification is awaited. The company also expects to sell the site's land for ₹2 crore once the clean-up is finished.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 37 require the generator to do?

options.text: Provide the whole ₹2,30,000 contract price, because the contract as a whole is loss-making
options.misconception: provides for the gross cost of the contract rather than for the excess of unavoidable cost over expected benefit
options.why: A provision is for the loss, not for the commitment. The gas still has value to the company, and the amount to be recognised is what the contract costs over and above the benefits expected under it.

options.text: Write down the dedicated plant for impairment first, then provide for whatever loss is left — and where a provision is needed, measure it at ₹50,000, the lower of fulfilling and the penalty
options.why: Before a separate provision for an onerous contract is established, the entity recognises any impairment loss that has occurred on assets used in fulfilling that contract, in accordance with Ind AS 36. Only to the extent a loss remains after those assets have been written down is a provision recorded; otherwise the same shortfall is counted twice. The unavoidable costs under the contract reflect the least net cost of exiting it, which is the lower of the cost of fulfilling it and any compensation or penalties arising from failure to fulfil it — so ₹50,000 and not ₹55,000. Both the incremental costs of fulfilling and an allocation of costs that relate directly to the contract go into that fulfilment figure.
keywords: lower of the cost of fulfilling

options.text: Provide ₹55,000 for the onerous contract now, and test the plant for impairment separately as part of the ordinary year-end review
options.misconception: reverses the order the standard fixes, and takes the more expensive of the two exit routes
options.why: The sequence is not housekeeping. Providing first and impairing afterwards charges the same economic loss twice, once as a provision and once as a write-down. And the measure is the least net cost of getting out, so the ₹50,000 route governs, not the ₹55,000 one.

options.text: Provide nothing, since the loss arises on the electricity and expected future operating losses are never provided for
options.misconception: uses the bar on future operating losses to escape a contract whose own unavoidable costs exceed its benefits
options.why: The bar on future operating losses covers losses an entity expects from continuing to trade, which it can stop making. A signed contract it cannot get out of for less than ₹50,000 is a present obligation, and the two rules sit side by side in the same standard without contradicting each other.

citation.ref: para 66 to 69, read with the definition of an onerous contract in para 10

items.scenario: A generator has a contract to buy one million units of gas at ₹23 a unit, a contract price of ₹2,30,000. All of the gas goes into electricity made on plant dedicated to this contract, and the electricity now sells at a loss so that the operation as a whole is loss-making. Working out its position, the company finds that fulfilling the contract and selling the gas on to a third party would leave it ₹50,000 worse off, while paying to exit the purchase contract would cost a penalty of ₹55,000.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 109 permit, and where does each amount end up?

options.text: An irrevocable election on initial recognition for the supplier stake, presenting its fair value changes in other comprehensive income, with dividends still in profit or loss and the cumulative gain never recycled on sale
options.why: Every investment in an equity instrument is measured at fair value, and the business model and cash flow tests decide nothing here — an equity instrument's returns are not solely payments of principal and interest, so amortised cost is unavailable. For an equity investment that is not held for trading, Ind AS 109 allows an irrevocable election at initial recognition, made instrument by instrument, to present subsequent fair value changes in other comprehensive income. Dividends on it are still recognised in profit or loss. On disposal the cumulative amount is not reclassified to profit or loss, although it may be transferred between reserves within equity. The trading block cannot take the election at all.
keywords: not reclassified to profit or loss

options.text: The supplier stake must be measured at amortised cost, because the manufacturer holds it to collect the dividends it produces
options.misconception: applies the hold-to-collect business model to an equity instrument, whose cash flows can never be solely payments of principal and interest
options.why: Amortised cost needs both tests to pass, and the cash flow test asks whether the contractual terms give rise on specified dates to payments of principal and interest on a principal amount outstanding. An equity share has no principal and no contractual interest, so it fails before the business model is even reached.

options.text: The election may be made for the supplier stake now and revoked later if the shares begin to be actively traded
options.misconception: treats the election as revisable, when the standard makes it irrevocable and the reclassification rule reaches only debt
options.why: Financial assets are reclassified only when the entity changes the business model for managing them, and that rule reaches debt instruments. The equity election is irrevocable by its own terms, which is what stops an entity choosing after the event where a gain should appear.

options.text: Both holdings may go to fair value through other comprehensive income, and in each case the cumulative gain is recycled to profit or loss on sale
options.misconception: carries the recycling rule for debt instruments at fair value through other comprehensive income across to the equity election, where it does not run
options.why: The two fair value through other comprehensive income routes behave differently on disposal. A debt instrument in that category recycles; an equity instrument under the election does not, and that is the price of keeping the movements out of profit or loss in the first place. A holding acquired to be sold within weeks is held for trading and cannot take the election either way.

citation.ref: para 4.1.4 and 5.7.5, read with para 5.7.1(b) for dividends and para B5.7.1

items.scenario: A manufacturer buys 19 per cent of the equity shares of an unlisted supplier for long-term strategic reasons and exercises no significant influence over it. It holds separately a block of listed shares bought to be sold within weeks. On initial recognition of the supplier stake the finance head wants the fair value movements kept out of profit or loss so that reported results are not swung by them. Dividends are received each year, and the stake is eventually sold at a large gain.

items.stem: On what amount is interest revenue computed for each loan?

options.text: On the net amount for all three, since accruing interest on more than the lender expects to collect overstates income
options.misconception: moves interest to the net figure from the start, which the standard reserves for credit-impaired assets
options.why: A twelve-month allowance on a performing loan is a statistical expectation across a portfolio, not a judgement that this borrower will not pay. Netting it against the interest base would understate the yield on every performing loan the lender holds.

options.text: On the ₹100 crore gross carrying amount for both P and Q, and on ₹70 crore for R
options.why: Two things change as an asset deteriorates and they do not change at the same point. The loss allowance moves from twelve-month to lifetime expected credit losses as soon as credit risk has increased significantly, so Q already carries a lifetime allowance. Interest revenue, though, stays on the gross carrying amount — the amortised cost before adjusting for any loss allowance — through both that stage and the one before it. It moves to the amortised cost, net of the allowance, only once the asset is credit-impaired. A borrower entering financial reorganisation is evidence of exactly that, so R's interest runs on ₹100 crore less the ₹30 crore allowance.

options.text: On the gross amount for P only; Q moves to the net amount when it passes 30 days past due, and R with it
options.misconception: attaches the interest switch to the significant-increase trigger rather than to credit impairment
options.why: The 30-days-past-due presumption is about the size of the allowance, moving it to lifetime expected credit losses. It says nothing about the interest base, which changes one stage later.

options.text: On the gross ₹100 crore for all three, because interest is a contractual entitlement and does not depend on the allowance
options.misconception: never makes the switch at credit impairment, so income keeps accruing on money the lender has concluded it will not collect
options.why: The contractual entitlement survives, but the standard stops recognising revenue on the part of it the lender has already written down. Otherwise a loan to a company in reorganisation would keep producing income at full rate while its allowance grew.

citation.ref: para 5.4.1 and 5.5.3, read with the definition of a credit-impaired financial asset in Appendix A

items.scenario: A lender carries three loans at amortised cost, all outside the simplified approach and each with a gross carrying amount of ₹100 crore. Loan P is performing and its credit risk has not increased significantly since initial recognition. Loan Q is 45 days past due and the lender has not rebutted the presumption that credit risk has increased significantly. Loan R's borrower has entered financial reorganisation. The loss allowances carried are ₹1 crore on P, ₹9 crore on Q and ₹30 crore on R.

items.stem: What reaches profit or loss from the two conversions?

options.text: A gain on the conversion at maturity equal to the equity component released, and nothing on the inducement
options.misconception: recognises income on a conversion, which would let an entity report profit by issuing its own shares
options.why: Transactions in an entity's own equity instruments do not produce profit. Recognising the equity component as a gain would credit the statement of profit and loss with the shareholders' own money.

options.text: ₹3 crore as a loss, and on the maturity conversion the difference between the liability's carrying amount and the market value of the shares issued
options.misconception: measures the shares issued at market value, when on conversion the liability's carrying amount simply becomes equity
options.why: If the shares were measured at market value on conversion, the issuer would report a loss every time its share price had risen — the opposite of the economics. The liability's carrying amount is transferred, and no measurement of the shares is needed.

options.text: Nothing from the conversion at maturity, and a ₹3 crore loss from the inducement
options.why: On conversion of a convertible instrument at maturity the entity derecognises the liability component and recognises it as equity, while the original equity component simply stays in equity, though it may be moved from one line within equity to another. There is no gain or loss on conversion at maturity. Where the entity instead amends the terms to induce early conversion, the difference at the amendment date between the fair value of the consideration the holder receives under the revised terms and the fair value of what it would have received under the original terms is recognised as a loss in profit or loss — the ₹3 crore here.
keywords: no gain or loss on conversion at maturity

options.text: Nothing at all — a conversion is a movement within equity in both cases, so profit or loss is untouched
options.misconception: extends the maturity rule to an inducement, where the entity has given away value to buy an early conversion
options.why: At maturity the holder receives what the original contract promised, so nothing has been paid for anything. An inducement is a fresh transfer of value made to get a result the original terms did not give, and the standard charges it as a loss for that reason.

citation.ref: para AG32 for conversion at maturity and para AG35 for an induced early conversion

items.scenario: Three years ago a company issued convertible debentures and split the proceeds on issue into a liability component and an equity component. Two things happen in the year ended 31 March 2026. Holders of half the debentures convert at maturity on the original terms. To clear the other half early, the company amends the terms to offer a more favourable conversion ratio, and those holders convert too; the extra shares handed over are worth ₹3 crore more than the shares they would have received under the original terms.

items.stem: How are the tax effects presented and measured?

options.text: The revaluation's tax in other comprehensive income, the issue costs' tax in profit or loss, and the ₹40 crore discounted
options.misconception: applies the follow-the-item rule to other comprehensive income but not to equity, when the standard treats both the same way
options.why: The rule names both destinations in the same breath: outside profit or loss means either other comprehensive income or directly in equity, and the tax goes wherever the underlying item went. Share issue costs go to equity, so their tax relief does too.

options.text: No tax is recognised on either transaction until the building is sold and the deferred tax liability becomes payable
options.misconception: waits for realisation, which is the opposite of the temporary difference approach
options.why: Deferred tax exists precisely to recognise the future tax consequence of something that has already happened. Waiting for the cash would leave the balance sheet showing a revalued asset with no trace of the tax that will be paid when it is recovered.

options.text: All of the tax through tax expense in the statement of profit and loss, with the ₹40 crore discounted to present value
options.misconception: routes every tax effect through profit or loss and imports discounting, which Ind AS 12 forbids for deferred tax
options.why: Putting the revaluation's tax through profit or loss would show a tax charge with no matching income anywhere near it. And the bar on discounting is absolute, not a matter of materiality — the standard rules it out rather than permitting it where scheduling happens to be possible.

options.text: The deferred tax on the revaluation in other comprehensive income and the tax relief on the issue costs directly in equity, with no deferred tax balance discounted
options.why: Tax follows the item it relates to. Tax on a transaction recognised in other comprehensive income is itself recognised in other comprehensive income, and tax on a transaction recognised directly in equity is recognised directly in equity — which is why the revaluation's deferred tax never reaches the statement of profit and loss. Deferred tax assets and liabilities shall not be discounted, however distant the reversal, because reliably scheduling the reversal of every temporary difference would be impracticable and entities that did and did not schedule would stop being comparable. Where the split between profit or loss and items outside it is genuinely hard to determine, a reasonable pro rata allocation is used.

citation.ref: para 61A and 62 for tax recognised outside profit or loss, read with the bar on discounting in para 53 and 54

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a company revalues a building upward and takes the gain to other comprehensive income. In the same year it issues equity shares and charges the transaction costs of the issue directly against equity. It also carries a deferred tax liability of ₹40 crore that will not reverse for eight years, and its tax adviser suggests that so distant a liability should be shown at present value.

items.stem: What does Appendix C to Ind AS 12 require?

options.text: Group the three claims, because Appendix C requires uncertainties settled in one assessment to be considered together
options.misconception: turns a judgement into a rule, and takes the procedure of the assessment as the test
options.why: The entity decides whether to consider each uncertain tax treatment separately or together with one or more others on the basis of which approach better predicts the resolution. That they happen to be dealt with in one assessment order is not that test.

options.text: Reverse the claim in full, because a treatment that is not probable of acceptance is disallowed
options.misconception: jumps from "not probable" to full reversal, when the effect is measured rather than assumed
options.why: Failing the probable test opens the measurement question; it does not answer it. The effect is reflected using the most likely amount or the expected value, and either can land well short of the whole claim where a partial allowance is a real outcome.

options.text: Assume the authority examines what it has a right to examine with full knowledge of everything related, and — acceptance not being probable at 40 per cent — reflect the effect of the uncertainty
options.why: Appendix C takes detection risk out of the question. In assessing whether and how an uncertain tax treatment affects taxable profit, tax bases, unused tax losses, unused tax credits and tax rates, an entity shall assume that a taxation authority will examine amounts it has a right to examine and have full knowledge of all related information when making those examinations. So neither the low chance of being picked up nor the department's ignorance of an internal file may be relied on. Where the entity concludes it is not probable that the authority will accept the treatment, it reflects the effect of the uncertainty using either the most likely amount or the expected value, whichever better predicts the resolution. Whether uncertainties are looked at separately or together is a separate judgement, made on the same better-prediction test.
keywords: full knowledge of all related information

options.text: Nothing need be recognised, because the chance that the department both finds the claim and rejects it is well under half
options.misconception: multiplies in a detection risk that the appendix instructs the entity to assume away
options.why: Compounding the probability of examination with the probability of rejection is exactly the reasoning the appendix was written to stop. The assumption of full examination with full knowledge is made whatever the entity thinks the department will actually do.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 6 to 11

items.scenario: A company has claimed a deduction its tax counsel rates at a 40 per cent chance of being upheld. The finance head argues that the claim sits in a schedule the department has never queried in eight years and is unlikely to be picked up, and that even if it were, the department would not have the internal file that undermines it. He also wants the claim grouped with two unrelated uncertain claims, on the ground that all three will be settled in the same assessment.

items.stem: Is he right?

options.text: Yes — an entity that borrows in a currency and reports in it is operating in it, so the change runs from 1 April 2025
options.misconception: promotes the two secondary indicators above the primary ones
options.why: Both of the facts relied on are named in the standard as supporting evidence, to be used where the primary indicators are mixed. Here they are not mixed: prices and costs are both in rupees, and that settles it.

options.text: No — the primary indicators still point to the rupee, the currency of the borrowing and of the retained receipts is only supporting evidence, and choosing a presentation currency changes nothing
options.why: Functional currency is the currency of the primary economic environment in which the entity operates, normally the one in which it primarily generates and expends cash. The primary indicators are the currency that mainly influences sales prices for its goods and services and the currency that mainly influences the labour, material and other costs of providing them — rupees on both counts here. The currency in which funds from financing activities are generated and the currency in which receipts from operating activities are usually retained are secondary indicators that may provide supporting evidence, and priority goes to the primary ones. Presentation currency is simply the currency in which the financial statements are presented and may differ from the functional currency, so electing to report in dollars is not a change at all.

options.text: Yes, but the change runs from the date the bond was issued rather than from the start of the year, and is applied prospectively from that date
options.misconception: applies the timing rule correctly to a change that has not happened
options.why: A change in functional currency is indeed applied prospectively from the date of the change, translating all items at the rate on that date. But the trigger is a change in the underlying transactions, events and conditions, and issuing a bond has not changed what the company sells, where, or in what currency it pays for it.

options.text: No, because a functional currency once determined can never change
options.misconception: makes the currency permanent, when it changes whenever the underlying conditions do
options.why: It is not a policy choice, but it is not fixed forever either. Where the transactions, events and conditions relevant to it genuinely change — a company that moves its production and its market abroad — the functional currency changes with them.

citation.ref: para 9 to 11 and 13, read with para 35 and 36 for presentation currency

items.scenario: An Indian company sells almost everything it makes in India, prices in rupees, and pays for its labour and materials in rupees. During 2025-26 it raises a large dollar-denominated bond and keeps the proceeds in a dollar account, and it decides to present its financial statements in dollars so that its new overseas lenders can read them. The finance head concludes that the functional currency has changed to the dollar with effect from 1 April 2025.

items.stem: How are these tax cash flows classified in the statement of cash flows?

options.text: The whole ₹5,30,000 in operating activities, because income tax is by nature an operating cash flow
options.misconception: takes the default for an absolute rule, when the standard names an exception it expects to be used where the trace is practicable
options.why: Operating is where tax goes when nobody can say which transaction produced it. Here somebody can: the ₹30,000 is the tax on a specific building sale, and the standard directs it to the activity that sale belongs to.

options.text: The whole ₹5,30,000 in investing activities, since it was paid in advance and is an asset until the assessment
options.misconception: classifies by what the payment is called rather than by the transaction that gave rise to it
options.why: The label on the challan decides nothing. The classification follows the underlying transaction, which for ₹5,00,000 of it is the ordinary trading of the year.

options.text: ₹5,00,000 in operating and ₹30,000 in financing, because tax on a capital gain is a cost of the capital the company has raised
options.misconception: confuses selling an asset with raising capital; a building sale is an investing transaction
options.why: Financing covers changes in the size and composition of the entity's contributed equity and borrowings. Selling a factory building is the disposal of a long-term asset, which is investing, and its tax follows it there.

options.text: ₹5,00,000 in operating activities and ₹30,000 in investing activities, with the total taxes paid disclosed
options.why: Cash flows arising from taxes on income shall be separately disclosed and shall be classified as cash flows from operating activities unless they can be specifically identified with financing and investing activities. Tax arises on transactions across all three categories, but the tax cash flow is often impracticable to trace to one of them and may fall in a different period from the transaction it relates to, which is why operating is the default. Here the ₹30,000 is specifically identified with the sale of a building, an investing transaction, so it is classified as investing. When taxes paid are allocated over more than one class of activity, the total amount of taxes paid is disclosed.

citation.ref: para 35 and 36

items.scenario: X Ltd, which is not a financial institution, paid ₹5,30,000 of advance tax during the year ended 31 March 2026. Of that, ₹30,000 is identified as the tax on the long-term capital gain from selling a factory building. The remaining ₹5,00,000 cannot be traced to any particular transaction.

items.stem: How does the company compute the tax expense for the first quarter?

options.text: One rate for everything — total expected tax over total expected income — applied to each quarter's pre-tax income
options.misconception: reaches for the blended rate the standard allows only where separate rates are impracticable
options.why: Blending the capital gain's rate into the business income's rate would charge the first quarter for a gain it has not made. The standard permits that shortcut only as a reasonable approximation, and here the split is straightforward.

options.text: No tax expense in the first quarter, because the capital gain that changes the rate has not yet arisen and the annual rate is not yet known
options.misconception: defers the charge until the year's picture is complete, which is the opposite of the year-to-date approach
options.why: The rate is an estimate re-estimated on a year-to-date basis as the year unfolds, and a significant change in that estimate is disclosed. Not knowing the final figure is the ordinary condition of interim reporting, not a reason to report no tax at all.

options.text: A separate estimated average annual rate for each category of income and, so far as practicable, for each jurisdiction — so ₹7,00,000 at the 38 per cent business-income rate, ₹2,66,000
options.why: Interim income tax expense is accrued using the estimated average annual effective income tax rate applied to the interim period's pre-tax income, and that rate blends the progressive structure expected for the full year. But the standard asks for more precision where it can be had. To the extent practicable a separate rate is determined for each taxing jurisdiction and applied individually to that jurisdiction's interim pre-tax income; and where different rates apply to different categories of income, such as capital gains, a separate rate is applied to each category so far as practicable. The business income of ₹25,00,000 bears ₹1,50,000 at 30 per cent and ₹8,00,000 at 40 per cent, ₹9,50,000 in all, which is 38 per cent of ₹25,00,000. A weighted average across jurisdictions or categories is used only where it is a reasonable approximation.
keywords: estimated average annual effective income tax rate

options.text: The actual tax on the quarter's own income, computed as though the quarter were a tax year in itself
options.misconception: treats the interim period as a discrete period for tax, when income tax is assessed annually
options.why: A quarter is part of a year, not a small year. Taxing it discretely would put the whole of a progressive structure's lower slab into the first quarter and none of it into the fourth.

citation.ref: para 30(c), read with Appendix B para B12 to B14

items.scenario: For the year ending 31 March 2026 a company expects pre-tax income of ₹33,00,000, of which ₹8,00,000 is a long-term capital gain taxed at a different rate from its business income. Under the rates given to it, business income up to ₹5,00,000 bears 30 per cent and the balance bears 40 per cent. It also runs a branch in another country with its own tax regime. In the first quarter it earns ₹7,00,000 of business income and no capital gain.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 24 require instead?

options.text: Disclose the ₹12 crore incurred for the provision of key management personnel services by the management entity; the breakdown of what M Ltd pays its own people is not required
options.why: Where an entity obtains key management personnel services from another entity — a management entity — it is not required to apply the compensation requirements to the amounts paid or payable by the management entity to that entity's own employees or directors. What it must give instead are the amounts it incurred for the provision of key management personnel services provided by a separate management entity: ₹12 crore, and not split into the short-term, post-employment, other long-term, termination and share-based categories. The management entity is itself a related party of the company, and its transactions with the company are disclosed in that character.

options.text: Disclose both figures in full, since the relief reaches only the ₹1.5 crore of share-based payment made in M Ltd's own shares
options.misconception: invents a partial relief; what the management entity pays its own people is outside the requirement altogether
options.why: The relief is drawn round the payer, not round the type of payment. Everything the management entity pays or owes its own employees and directors falls outside the company's compensation disclosure, share-based awards included.

options.text: Disclose the ₹9 crore in its five categories, because the four officers are the company's key management personnel whoever writes their cheques
options.misconception: keeps the category breakdown in a case where the standard has expressly lifted it
options.why: The relief exists because the company usually cannot see how a management entity divides what it pays its own staff, and would be disclosing a figure it cannot verify. The amount it can verify, and must give, is what it paid the management entity.

options.text: Disclose nothing at all, because the four are not employees of the company and no related party relationship arises
options.misconception: severs the relationship; an entity that provides key management personnel services is a related party of the reporting entity
options.why: Being a related party does not require an employment contract. A management entity supplying the people who run the company is squarely within the definition, and the amounts it charges are disclosed for that reason.

citation.ref: para 17A and 18A, read with the compensation categories in para 17

items.scenario: A listed company employs nobody at the top itself. Its chief executive, chief financial officer and two other senior officers are supplied under contract by M Ltd, a separate management entity, for a fee of ₹12 crore for the year. M Ltd pays those four ₹9 crore between them, of which ₹1.5 crore is an award in M Ltd's own shares. The company's accountant proposes to disclose the ₹9 crore split into the five compensation categories and to say nothing about the ₹12 crore.

items.stem: What cumulative expense has the company recognised by 31 March 2027?

options.text: The charge for all 50 executives, because a failed market condition means the count is never revised
options.misconception: confuses which condition is trued up through the count — the service condition always is
options.why: Two different mechanisms are at work. The market condition is fixed in the fair value and never revisited; the service condition is revisited through the number of instruments expected to vest and then the number that did. The five who left take their options with them.

options.text: Nothing, and any charge already taken is reversed, because the options never vested
options.misconception: applies the no-cumulative-charge rule for a failed vesting condition to a market condition, where it does not run
options.why: The rule that nothing is recognised where an award fails to vest is expressly made subject to the market condition requirement. Its purpose is to reverse charges for services the entity did not get; here it got three years of service from 45 people.

options.text: The full charge for the 45 executives who served the three years — 45,000 options at ₹90 — even though the share price target was missed
options.why: A share price target is a market condition, and market conditions are taken into account when estimating the grant date fair value of the equity instruments granted. Because the probability of reaching ₹500 is already inside the ₹90, it is never trued up afterwards. The entity recognises the goods or services received from a counterparty who satisfies all the other vesting conditions irrespective of whether that market condition is satisfied. The service requirement is a vesting condition other than a market condition, so it is trued up the other way — through the number of instruments — and the count settles at the 45 who stayed.
keywords: irrespective of whether that market condition is satisfied

options.text: The charge for 45 executives, remeasured to the option's fair value at 31 March 2027 now that the target has been missed
options.misconception: remeasures an equity-settled award after grant date, which the standard never permits
options.why: Grant date fair value for an equity-settled award is fixed on the day it is set, whatever the share price then does. Remeasuring is what a cash-settled award requires, because that one is a liability.

citation.ref: para 19, 20 and 21, read with the definition of a market condition in Appendix A

items.scenario: On 1 April 2024 a company granted 1,000 share options to each of 50 executives. They vest on 31 March 2027 only if the executive is still in service on that date and the company's share price has reached ₹500 by then. The grant date fair value was ₹90 an option, set by a model that already built in the probability of the ₹500 target being reached. By 31 March 2027, 45 of the 50 executives are still in service, and the share price has stalled at ₹410.

items.stem: How much of the three reaches profit or loss for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹50 lakh — the ₹10 lakh and the ₹40 lakh in full — while the ₹2 crore is deferred or netted against the plant
options.why: A government grant that becomes receivable as compensation for expenses or losses already incurred, or for the purpose of giving immediate financial support to the entity with no future related costs, is recognised in profit or loss of the period in which it becomes receivable, with disclosure to ensure that its effect is clearly understood. The vaccine reimbursement and the workforce support are both of that kind, so ₹50 lakh goes straight through. A grant related to an asset is different: it is presented in the balance sheet by setting the grant up as deferred income released over the plant's life, or by deducting it in arriving at the carrying amount of the asset. Neither presentation puts ₹2 crore into this year's profit.

options.text: ₹2.50 crore — all three, because a grant with no unfulfilled condition is income as soon as it is received
options.misconception: makes receipt the recognition event, when an asset grant is recognised over the periods the related costs are recognised
options.why: Receipt of a grant is not even conclusive that its conditions have been met. The plant grant is tied to an asset with a three-year build and a long life, and it is released over that life rather than banked on arrival.

options.text: Nothing — no grant reaches profit or loss until the entity has incurred the expenditure the grant is matched against
options.misconception: applies matching to grants that by definition have no future related costs to be matched against
options.why: Matching works where there are future costs to match. For a reimbursement of research already done, or support with nothing required in return, there is nothing left to wait for, so the standard recognises it when it becomes receivable.

options.text: ₹40 lakh only — the ₹10 lakh relates to an earlier year and goes to retained earnings as a prior period adjustment
options.misconception: treats a grant for past expenses as the correction of an error
options.why: Nothing was wrong in 2023-24; the research was properly expensed and no grant was then receivable. The standard puts such a grant in the period it becomes receivable, with disclosure so that the reader can see why the year's profit moved.

citation.ref: para 20 and 21, read with the recognition condition in para 7 and the presentation of asset grants in para 24 and 26

items.scenario: A pharmaceutical company receives three government payments in the year ended 31 March 2026. ₹10 lakh reimburses research it carried out in 2023-24 on a vaccine, with no conditions attached to it. ₹40 lakh is described as immediate financial support to keep a loss-making unit's workforce employed, and requires nothing of the company in future. ₹2 crore is towards a new plant it will build over the next three years.

items.stem: What does the Code of Ethics require of him?

options.text: He may accept, and the paragraph he plans to put in the report about the limits of his experience satisfies the principle
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for competence, which the Code nowhere permits
options.why: A fundamental principle is complied with, not disclosed around. Telling the reader that the work may be below standard does not make it competent, and a member who genuinely cannot reach the level required should decline or bring in someone who can.

options.text: He may accept and delegate as planned, since the principle binds the member's own work and not what articled assistants do
options.misconception: detaches the member from work carried out under his own authority
options.why: The Code closes that gap in terms: the member shall take reasonable steps to ensure that those working under his authority have appropriate training and supervision. Work signed in his name is his work however many hands touched it.

options.text: He may take the work if he attains the knowledge and skill it needs and acts diligently, but he must take reasonable steps to see that those working under his authority have training and supervision
options.why: Professional competence and due care asks two things of a member: to attain and maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level required to ensure that a client receives competent professional service, based on current technical and professional standards and relevant legislation; and to act diligently and in accordance with applicable technical and professional standards. Competence can be attained, so the principle does not shut a member out of an area he has not worked in before. Diligence is the responsibility to act in accordance with the requirements of the assignment, carefully, thoroughly and on a timely basis. And in complying with the principle a Chartered Accountant shall take reasonable steps to ensure that those working in a professional capacity under his authority have appropriate training and supervision — which leaving two assistants unreviewed until the report is drafted does not.

options.text: He must refuse the engagement, because competence means having done that kind of work before
options.misconception: reads competence as prior experience, when the principle speaks of attaining the level required
options.why: Every member did each kind of work for the first time once. The principle asks whether he will reach the required level before the client relies on his output, not whether he has a history of it, and continuing professional development exists precisely to make that possible.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — professional competence and due care

items.scenario: A member in practice is offered his first valuation engagement under Ind AS 113. He has never done one. He plans to accept it, read up on the standard over the coming weeks, hand most of the fieldwork to two articled assistants, and look at their files only when the report is drafted. He intends to add a paragraph to the report noting that valuation is not his usual area of work.

items.stem: When is the opening Ind AS balance sheet drawn up, and what happens in it?

options.text: At 1 April 2025 — recognise the derivative, derecognise the ₹4 crore, reclassify the building as investment property and remeasure the investments, with the ₹6 crore taken directly to retained earnings or another appropriate category of equity
options.why: The date of transition to Ind AS is the beginning of the earliest period for which the entity presents full comparative information, so a company adopting from 1 April 2026 with one comparative year draws its opening balance sheet at 1 April 2025. In it the entity shall recognise all assets and liabilities whose recognition is required by Ind AS; not recognise items as assets or liabilities if Ind AS do not permit such recognition; reclassify items recognised under previous GAAP as one type of asset, liability or component of equity that are a different type under Ind AS; and apply Ind AS in measuring all recognised assets and liabilities. Those adjustments arise from transactions and events before the date of transition, so they are recognised directly in retained earnings, or another category of equity where that is appropriate, and never in profit or loss.

options.text: At 1 April 2026, since that is when the first Ind AS reporting period begins, with the four adjustments running through that year's profit or loss
options.misconception: places the opening balance sheet at the start of the reporting period rather than of the comparative period, and routes transition differences through profit
options.why: The comparative year must itself be presented under Ind AS, which is impossible unless the restatement starts at its beginning. And running the differences through profit would show a year's earnings made up of accounting changes rather than of trading.

options.text: At 1 April 2025, but only the measurement difference on the investments is adjusted; recognition and classification as they stood under previous GAAP are carried forward
options.misconception: keeps one of the four steps of the general principle, which is a set rather than a menu
options.why: The four steps are cumulative and each catches a different failure. Carrying forward previous GAAP recognition would leave the derivative off the balance sheet and the ₹4 crore on it, and carrying forward its classification would leave a let-out building inside property, plant and equipment.

options.text: At 1 April 2025, but with all four adjustments recognised in the comparative year's profit or loss so that a reader can see the movement
options.misconception: puts transition differences into the comparative year's performance, when they belong to periods before it
options.why: The differences accumulated over every year the entity applied previous GAAP, not over the comparative year alone. Reconciliations between previous GAAP and Ind AS are the disclosure that makes the movement visible; the profit or loss is not.

citation.ref: para 6, 7, 10 and 11, read with the definition of the date of transition in Appendix A

items.scenario: A company adopts Ind AS from 1 April 2026 and will present one year of comparatives. Under previous GAAP it never recognised the derivative it holds, it carries ₹4 crore of deferred revenue expenditure that Ind AS does not permit as an asset, it presents a building let out on an operating lease within property, plant and equipment, and it holds certain investments at the lower of cost and fair value where Ind AS requires fair value. The four differences net to a ₹6 crore credit.

items.stem: What do the three observations show about how Ind AS is put together?

options.text: The blank paragraphs are a printing fault in the notified text, since a standard cannot have gaps in its numbering
options.misconception: reads a deliberate carve-out as a typographical accident
options.why: The gap is the point. Keeping the number empty is how the reader is told that the international standard has something there and India does not, and each such gap carries a note sending the reader to the appendix that explains the difference. Renumbering to close the gap would hide every carve-out the framework has made.

options.text: Ind AS renumber the standards from scratch, which is why the numbers no longer line up with IFRS and IAS
options.misconception: thinks the Indian numbering is independent, when it mirrors the international series
options.why: The numbering mirrors the international series on purpose. An IAS keeps its number — IAS 1 becomes Ind AS 1 — and an IFRS is given a new hundred series, so IFRS 1 becomes Ind AS 101. The alignment is what makes a paragraph-by-paragraph comparison possible in the first place.

options.text: Ind AS keep the IFRS and IAS paragraph numbers, so a paragraph India has not taken across is left blank with a note pointing to the standard's Comparison with IFRS appendix; interpretations are carried as an appendix to the standard they interpret; and Appendix C to Ind AS 103 was developed here with nothing corresponding to it internationally
options.why: Ind AS follow the structure of IFRS and IAS and deliberately retain their paragraph numbers, so that a reader can look straight across at the international text and see what changed. Where India has not adopted a paragraph, the number is kept blank with a note referring to that standard's Comparison with IFRS appendix, which is exactly what the empty paragraphs 60 to 65 of Ind AS 40 are — the fair value model's transfer rules left out. IFRIC and SIC interpretations are not issued as separate documents here; they are included as an appendix to the relevant standard. And Appendix C to Ind AS 103 was written in India with no corresponding international interpretation behind it, which is a carve-in rather than a carve-out.

options.text: Interpretations are not part of Ind AS, so an entity may follow an IFRIC only where a separate Indian interpretation has been issued
options.misconception: treats an interpretation carried as an appendix as though it were outside the standard
options.why: An appendix to a notified Ind AS is part of that standard and is mandatory in the same way its paragraphs are. Printing an interpretation inside the standard rather than beside it changes where the reader finds it, not whether it binds.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Introduction to Ind AS — how Ind AS are numbered and structured, carve-outs and carve-ins

items.scenario: A student reading the notified text of Ind AS beside the international standards notices three things. Paragraphs 60 to 65 of Ind AS 40 are printed with nothing in them. The interpretations he expected to find as separate IFRIC and SIC documents are printed instead as appendices inside the standards they interpret. And Ind AS 103 carries an Appendix C for which he can find no IFRIC or SIC anywhere in the international material.

items.stem: How should the two incidents be classified, and is the IT head right?

options.text: Both are malware attacks, and both are answered by network security measures such as firewalls
options.misconception: collapses two different threat types into malware and reaches for the one control the IT head already had
options.why: Only the first involves malicious software at all; the second is a person copying a file he was entitled to open. Calling both malware leads straight to the wrong remedy, which is the practical cost of misclassifying an incident — the fix is chosen from the label.

options.text: The first is a supply chain attack and the second an insider threat; the IT head is wrong on both, because neither is stopped by a perimeter measure or by password strength — access control, employee training and incident response planning are what these two call for
options.why: A supply chain attack compromises third-party software or hardware to gain access to a system or network, which is precisely what a poisoned vendor update is. An insider threat is malicious action by an employee or other insider who already has access to sensitive data. A firewall guards the boundary and a password proves who you are; the first attack came in through a channel the company had already decided to trust, and the second was carried out by someone whose password worked exactly as intended. The measures that bite here are access control limited to what each person needs and reviewed as roles change, employee training, and an incident response plan setting out how an attack is detected, contained and mitigated.

options.text: Only the first is a cybersecurity incident; the second is a human resources matter and falls outside the company's cybersecurity framework
options.misconception: puts the insider outside the security perimeter because he was an employee
options.why: Insider threats are listed among the common cybersecurity threats for exactly this reason. Someone with legitimate access can take more, faster and more quietly than an outsider, and treating it as a staffing problem leaves the access controls and the monitoring untouched for the next person.

options.text: The first is a denial of service attack and the second a phishing attack
options.misconception: reaches for the two best known threat names without matching either to what happened
options.why: A denial of service attack overwhelms a system or network with traffic to disrupt operations, and nothing here was overwhelmed. Phishing tricks a user into clicking a malicious link or handing over information, and the executive was tricked by nobody. Both labels are real threats and neither describes these facts.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — common cybersecurity threats and proactive measures

items.scenario: A listed company suffers two incidents in one quarter. In the first, a routine update pushed by the vendor of its payroll software carried malicious code, which reached the company's servers through the vendor's own trusted channel. In the second, a finance executive with legitimate access to the customer master copied it to a personal drive in the week before he resigned. The IT head tells the audit committee that both were failures of the firewall and that a stricter password policy would have prevented both.

items.stem: What drawbacks does automation bring, and how are they answered?

options.text: The right answer to the job losses is to stop expanding the automation, since a process that costs employment cannot be said to have improved the reporting
options.misconception: treats retraining and stopping as the same choice, when the material names only the first
options.why: The material answers the job risk with appropriate training so the workforce stays current with the technology, and points at the opportunity it opens — accountants freed from routine activity for work needing judgement and skill. Freezing the automation gives up the accuracy, the timeliness and the cost saving to solve a problem training already solves.

options.text: The main drawback is that bots cannot be given access to the subsidiary systems, so the data must still be extracted by hand before the bots can work on it
options.misconception: invents a technical limit the technology does not have
options.why: Extracting and consolidating data from subsidiary systems is one of the things bots do directly, by mimicking the way a person interacts with those systems. The drawbacks are the human and security ones, not an inability to reach the data.

options.text: A standing need for ongoing training and education to keep up with the technology, a heightened risk of data breaches and cyber-attacks against financial data, and the potential loss of jobs — which is met by training the workforce onto the technology rather than by slowing the automation down
options.why: Automation is not free of cost once the licence is paid. It creates a need for ongoing training and education, because the staff who supervise the bots have to keep up with what the bots do. It widens the surface for data breaches and cyber-attacks, because financial data now moves between systems without a person looking at it. And it carries the potential loss of jobs, which the material answers by retraining the workforce so that people move to the work the bots cannot do rather than out of the organisation.

options.text: None worth naming — automation removes human error, so the residual risk after implementation is lower than it was before on every measure
options.misconception: reads the accuracy benefit as though it settled every other risk as well
options.why: Accuracy and speed are real gains and they are not the whole account. A bot repeats what it was told to do, including a mistake, at machine speed and without hesitating, and the data it moves is a target. The gains and the drawbacks sit side by side and are managed separately.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — challenges in the automation process

items.scenario: A year after putting bots to work on its consolidation, a group's board asks the finance head what the automation has cost it beyond licence fees. Two of the three people who used to do the consolidation manually have been moved to other work, one has left, and the internal auditor has raised the question of what happens if the consolidation data is reached by an attacker.

items.stem: Which of the three does the Code of Ethics allow?

options.text: None of the three — an accountant leaving a firm may take neither information nor technique, since both were acquired in the course of the engagement
options.misconception: extends the duty over the accountant's own skill, which the Code expressly leaves with him
options.why: The Code says in terms that on changing employment or acquiring a new client the accountant is entitled to use prior experience. A rule that took his expertise as well as the client's information would make every engagement the last one an accountant could accept in that industry.

options.text: The first and the third — the duty runs to disclosures made in a professional capacity, and a private remark to a relative is not one
options.misconception: draws the line at the setting rather than at the information
options.why: The Code puts the social setting at the top of the list rather than outside it, because that is where the disclosure is easiest to make without meaning to. The information does not become less confidential because it was said over dinner, and a relative is under no duty at all once he has heard it.

options.text: The first and the second — once the engagement has ended the accountant may use anything he lawfully came by while it was running
options.misconception: reads the end of the engagement as the end of the duty
options.why: The duty survives the relationship. If it did not, every client would be handing over its commercial position on a timer, and the free flow of information from client to accountant that confidentiality exists to protect would stop at once. Ending the engagement changes who the accountant works for, not what he may repeat.

options.text: Only the first — an accountant is entitled to use prior experience on changing employment, but the duty of confidentiality continues after the relationship has ended, and the Code names disclosure in a social environment and to a close family member as a specific danger to be alert to
options.why: The Code separates the two things a departing accountant carries. He is entitled to use prior experience — the skill and judgement he built — and that is the costing technique. He shall not use or disclose any confidential information acquired or received as a result of a professional or employment relationship, and that duty continues even after the end of the relationship, which disposes of the price list. And the first thing the principle asks of him is to be alert to the possibility of inadvertent disclosure, including in a social environment and particularly to a close business associate or an immediate or a close family member, which disposes of the dinner.
keywords: after the end of the relationship

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — confidentiality after the relationship ends

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant resigns from a firm and joins a company that competes with one of the firm's audit clients. Before he starts he proposes three things. He will use the costing technique he became expert in while at the firm. He will take with him a copy of that client's supplier price list, on the view that the engagement is over and the duty went with it. And at a family dinner he will mention that the client is about to open a second plant, since his brother-in-law is only family and will not tell anyone.

items.stem: How is each measured at 31 March 2027?

options.text: Both at cost less accumulated depreciation and impairment, the goats moving to cost now that their market has become unreliable
options.misconception: lets the presumption be rebutted after initial recognition, in the direction the standard closes off
options.why: The rebuttal runs one way only. The presumption can be rebutted only on initial recognition, and an entity that has previously measured a biological asset at fair value less costs to sell continues to measure it that way until disposal. A thinning market makes the measurement harder, and Ind AS 113 has the machinery for that; it does not reopen the basis.

options.text: The timber at fair value less costs to sell, having been at cost less any accumulated depreciation and any accumulated impairment losses while the presumption was rebutted; and the goats still at fair value less costs to sell, because the presumption may be rebutted only on initial recognition
options.why: Ind AS 41 presumes that fair value can be measured reliably for a biological asset. The presumption is rebutted only where quoted market prices are not available and the alternative fair value measurements are determined to be clearly unreliable, and in that case the asset is measured at its cost less any accumulated depreciation and any accumulated impairment losses. That is the timber's position from 2025. Once the fair value of such an asset becomes reliably measurable, the entity measures it at fair value less costs to sell, so the auction market moves the timber across in 2027. The rebuttal is available only on initial recognition, so an entity that has previously measured an asset at fair value less costs to sell goes on doing so until disposal — the goats never go back to cost, however thin their market becomes.

options.text: The timber stays at cost, because a measurement basis chosen on initial recognition is an accounting policy the company must apply consistently until the asset is disposed of
options.misconception: treats the cost measurement as a policy choice rather than as relief that lapses when fair value becomes measurable
options.why: It was never a choice. Cost applies only while fair value cannot be measured reliably, and the standard says that once fair value becomes reliably measurable the entity shall measure the asset at fair value less costs to sell. Consistency governs a choice between permitted treatments; here only one treatment is permitted at a time and which one it is depends on the market.

options.text: Both at fair value less costs to sell for the whole period, with the 2025 and 2026 figures restated, since fair value has turned out to be measurable after all
options.misconception: applies the later measurability retrospectively, when the change is made from the date fair value becomes measurable
options.why: Nothing in Ind AS 41 restates a period in which fair value genuinely could not be measured reliably. The company applies fair value less costs to sell once it can, and the earlier years stand as they were prepared on the information then available.

citation.ref: para 30 and 31, with the measurement requirements in para 12 and 13

items.scenario: A plantation company grows a hybrid timber species newly introduced to India. At 31 March 2025, when the first block was planted, there were no quoted market prices for it and the company determined that the alternative fair value measurements available were clearly unreliable. By 31 March 2027 an auction market for the species has opened and prices are quoted weekly. The same company also runs a goat herd, measured at fair value less costs to sell since it was bought, for which the local market has since become thin and prices erratic.

items.stem: Is he right, and what must the financial statements say?

options.text: Yes for the year ended 31 March 2026, with the basis of preparation changing only in the year in which the closure actually happens
options.misconception: postpones the change of basis to the closure date, when the assessment is made at the time the statements are prepared
options.why: The assessment is made when the financial statements are prepared, on the information then available. Management's post-year-end assessment is what governs, and once it indicates the entity is not a going concern, the financial statements in respect of which that assessment is being made are not prepared on the going concern basis. Waiting for the closure would put two more sets of accounts in front of readers on a basis management already knows is wrong.

options.text: Yes — the going concern basis holds, with the intended closure disclosed as a material uncertainty in the notes
options.misconception: reaches for the material uncertainty disclosure, which belongs to a company that is still a going concern
options.why: A material uncertainty is disclosed where events or conditions may cast significant doubt and the outcome is still open. Nothing is uncertain here: the board has resolved to close and there is no realistic alternative. Disclosing a settled intention as a doubt would tell the reader the opposite of what management knows.

options.text: No, and the only requirement is to state that the going concern basis has not been used; the basis actually adopted is a matter for management and needs no explanation
options.misconception: gives half the disclosure, leaving the reader with a negative and no way to read the numbers
options.why: Saying what a set of accounts is not prepared on tells the reader nothing about how to read the figures. The entity discloses the basis on which the financial statements have been prepared as well as the reason the entity is not regarded as a going concern, so that the reader knows what the amounts mean.

options.text: No — the twelve months is a minimum horizon and not a cut-off, so a company that intends to cease operations beyond it cannot use the going concern basis; the statements disclose the basis on which they have been prepared and the reason the company is not regarded as a going concern
options.why: Management assesses the entity's ability to continue as a going concern taking into account all available information about the future, covering at least twelve months from the end of the reporting period. That period is a minimum requirement, not a window beyond which management may stop looking, and the standard's own example is an entity intending to cease operations eighteen months after the reporting date, which cannot use the going concern basis. Where the financial statements are not prepared on a going concern basis, the entity discloses that fact, the basis on which they have been prepared, and the reason the entity is not regarded as a going concern.
keywords: basis on which they have been prepared
reason the entity is not regarded as a going concern

citation.ref: para 25, with the assessment period in para 26

items.scenario: In February 2026 a company's board resolved to wind up its operations, with the last plant to close in December 2027 — twenty-one months after the year end of 31 March 2026. There is no realistic alternative; the decision follows the loss of the group's only market. The chief financial officer proposes to prepare the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 on the going concern basis, on the ground that the company will certainly still be trading throughout the twelve months following the reporting date.

items.stem: What does the company recognise at 31 March 2026 in respect of the division?

options.text: A restructuring provision for the whole plan, the public announcement on 15 March having raised a valid expectation in those affected
options.misconception: applies the general constructive obligation test to a sale, for which the standard sets a separate and later trigger
options.why: Announcement is the trigger for a restructuring the entity can carry out on its own. A sale needs a counterparty, and the standard says separately that no obligation arises for the sale of an operation until there is a binding sale agreement. Provisioning on the announcement would book a liability the company can still walk away from, and would have to walk away from if the buyer refused.

options.text: A provision measured at the expected loss on sale of the division, since the ₹300 crore of assets will not be recovered in full
options.misconception: turns an expected loss on assets into a provision, when a shortfall against carrying amount is an impairment
options.why: A shortfall between what assets are worth and what they are carried at is written off the assets, not provided for as a liability. That is why the standard sends the assets of an operation to be sold to Ind AS 36 for review. A provision would double-count the same loss once the assets were written down.

options.text: No provision for the sale of the division, because there is no binding sale agreement, but the division's assets are reviewed for impairment under Ind AS 36; the plant closure is a separate part of the restructuring and does carry a constructive obligation
options.why: No obligation arises for the sale of an operation until the entity is committed to the sale, which means there is a binding sale agreement. Even after a decision to sell has been taken and announced publicly, the entity is not committed until a purchaser has been identified and an agreement is binding, because until then it can change its mind, and will have to take another course if no buyer can be found on acceptable terms. Where the sale of an operation is envisaged as part of a restructuring, the assets of the operation are reviewed for impairment under Ind AS 36. A sale being only part of the restructuring, a constructive obligation can still arise for the other parts before any binding sale agreement exists, which is the position of the plant that has been announced and started.

options.text: No provision for either part, because at the reporting date the company had signed nothing and could still reverse the whole plan
options.misconception: extends the binding-agreement rule from the sale to the closure, where nothing is being agreed with anybody
options.why: The closure is not a transaction with a counterparty. The company announced it to those affected and has begun dismantling, which is implementation, so the valid expectation exists and a constructive obligation with it. The binding-agreement rule exists because a sale depends on someone else agreeing; a closure depends only on the entity.

citation.ref: para 78 and 79, read with the restructuring recognition conditions in para 72

items.scenario: On 10 March 2026 a company's board resolved on a restructuring with two parts.
