The larger division is to be sold as a going concern; the decision was announced publicly on 15 March, letters went to the division's employees on the same day, and negotiations with a single interested buyer were well advanced at 31 March 2026, but no agreement had been signed. The smaller plant is to be shut outright; that closure was announced on 15 March too, and dismantling began on 25 March 2026. The division's assets stand at ₹300 crore.

items.stem: How are the remaining assets measured at 31 March 2026?

options.text: All three cease to be classified as held for sale, because the disposal group as a whole no longer meets the criteria
options.misconception: lets the group's failure carry away assets that individually still qualify
options.why: The standard splits the question. What fails is the group, and each remaining non-current asset is then tested in its own right — those that individually meet the criteria stay classified and are measured individually, and only those that do not come out. The factory and the warehouse are each actively marketed and each meets every criterion.

options.text: The trademarks alone are remeasured, and the rest of the group is left exactly as it stood because the company has not changed its intention about any of it
options.misconception: reads the withdrawal of the buyer as no change, when the highly probable test is about the sale and not about the intention
options.why: Intending to sell is not the test. The sale must be highly probable, and a buyer who has withdrawn from a group nobody else is bidding for defeats that for the group even though management would still be glad to sell. The assets it does not defeat are the two still being actively marketed on their own.

options.text: All three go on being measured as a single disposal group, since the group was properly classified when the plan was adopted and only the trademarks have been removed
options.misconception: keeps the group alive because the original classification was valid, when the test is applied again after the removal
options.why: The classification is not a status the group keeps once earned. After an item is taken out, the remaining assets and liabilities continue to be measured as a group only if what is left still meets the criteria, and here the buyer has gone and it does not. Measuring three assets on different paths as one group would apply a single fair value less costs to sell to a collection nobody is buying.

options.text: The factory and the warehouse are measured individually, each at the lower of its carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell at that date; the delivery fleet ceases to be classified as held for sale and is measured under the rule for an asset that stops being so classified
options.why: Where an entity removes an individual asset or liability from a disposal group classified as held for sale, the remaining assets and liabilities go on being measured as a group only if the group still meets the classification criteria. Where it does not, the remaining non-current assets that individually meet the criteria are measured individually at the lower of their carrying amounts and fair values less costs to sell at that date, and any non-current assets that do not meet the criteria cease to be classified as held for sale. Losing the buyer breaks the group, so the factory and the warehouse stand on their own feet and the fleet comes back into use.
keywords: fair values less costs to sell
cease to be classified as held for sale

citation.ref: para 29, read with the measurement on ceasing to be classified in para 27

items.scenario: A company classified the whole of its leisure equipment operation as a disposal group held for sale in June 2025 — a factory, a warehouse, a delivery fleet and a portfolio of trademarks. In January 2026 it decided to keep the trademarks and go on licensing them for royalty income, and took them out of the disposal group. The buyer, who had wanted the operation whole, then withdrew, and at 31 March 2026 what is left no longer meets the held-for-sale criteria as a group. The factory and the warehouse are each still being actively marketed and each individually meets every criterion; the delivery fleet is not for sale at all and will go on being used.

items.stem: How are the two dealt with in the financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: The mines are not a discontinued operation either, since a discontinued operation must have been disposed of or be classified as held for sale
options.misconception: reads abandonment out of the discontinued operation definition altogether
options.why: The material addresses abandonment directly: an abandoned disposal group that meets the criteria for a discontinued operation must still make the discontinued operation disclosures. The point of the presentation is to tell the reader which part of the result will not recur, and a major line of business that has been shut will not recur whether it was sold or closed.

options.text: The mines become a discontinued operation from February 2026 when the decision was taken, and the plastics plant is treated as abandoned from January 2026, with depreciation stopping on both
options.misconception: dates abandonment from the decision and treats a mothballed plant as abandoned
options.why: A decision is not an abandonment; the operation is a discontinued one once it actually ceases to be used, which is why the coal mines qualify in the year the work stopped. And an asset that is being maintained in working condition for a return to use is neither abandoned nor held for sale, so its depreciation does not stop — it goes on being consumed over the life across which it will be recovered.

options.text: The mines cannot be classified as held for sale, because their carrying amount will be recovered principally through continuing use rather than through sale, but they are presented as a discontinued operation now that work has stopped; the plastics plant is neither abandoned nor held for sale, so depreciation on it continues
options.why: Non-current assets to be abandoned do not qualify to be classified as held for sale, because their carrying amount will be recovered principally through continuing use in the entity's operations rather than through sale. That is true of assets used to the end of their economic life and of assets to be closed rather than sold. But where a disposal group to be abandoned meets the criteria to be a discontinued operation, the discontinued operation disclosures must still be given, and a separate major line of business at which all work has stopped during the year does meet them. Assets temporarily taken out of use are not accounted for as abandoned at all, so the plastics plant stays where it is and depreciation on it continues.

options.text: Both are classified as held for sale and measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell, since neither will go on generating revenue
options.misconception: classifies as held for sale whatever has stopped earning, when the test is how the carrying amount will be recovered
options.why: Held for sale asks a single question — will the carrying amount be recovered principally through a sale transaction rather than through continuing use. Nobody is buying the mines and the plastics plant is being kept for the company's own use, so neither answers it. Ceasing to earn is not the test, which is why an idle asset is not automatically written down to a selling price.

citation.ref: para 13 on assets to be abandoned, read with the definition of a discontinued operation in Appendix A

items.scenario: In February 2026 a company decided to abandon all of its coal mines, which are a separate major line of business. All work at the mines stopped during the year ended 31 March 2026; the mines are not for sale and will simply be closed. Separately, the company stopped running one of its plastics plants in January 2026 because demand had fallen. That plant is being maintained in working condition and is expected to be brought back into use when demand recovers.

items.stem: What does the investor recognise in each of the two years?

options.text: A liability of ₹90 lakh should have been recognised at 31 March 2025, so both years' profits are recognised in full and released against it
options.misconception: recognises a liability for unrecognised losses where no obligation exists
options.why: A liability is recognised only to the extent the investor has incurred legal or constructive obligations or made payments on behalf of the associate. This investor has guaranteed nothing and paid nothing, so there is no obligation to record. Booking one would put the associate's losses on the investor's balance sheet as though it had promised to meet them.

options.text: Nothing for the year ended 31 March 2026, and ₹20 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2027
options.why: Once the interest is reduced to nil, further losses are provided for and a liability recognised only to the extent the entity has incurred legal or constructive obligations or made payments on behalf of the associate, which is why ₹90 lakh went unrecognised. If the associate subsequently reports profits, the entity resumes recognising its share of those profits only after its share of the profits equals the share of losses not recognised. The ₹40 lakh of 2026 is absorbed in full and ₹50 lakh of the shortfall remains; of the ₹70 lakh of 2027, ₹50 lakh clears the rest and ₹20 lakh is recognised.

options.text: ₹40 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹70 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2027, the unrecognised losses having lapsed when they were not recognised
options.misconception: treats losses that were never put on the balance sheet as though they had been written off for good
options.why: They were not written off; they were held back. The equity method is a running measure of the investor's share of the associate's net assets, and letting the profits through while the matching losses are forgotten would carry the investment back above what the share is actually worth. The standard keeps a memorandum record precisely so the two meet.

options.text: ₹22.50 lakh and ₹52.50 lakh — the investor's 25 per cent share of the ₹90 lakh shortfall is made good first and the rest is recognised
options.misconception: applies the ownership percentage a second time to a figure that is already the investor's share
options.why: The ₹90 lakh is already the investor's own share of the losses, not the associate's total, and so are the ₹40 lakh and the ₹70 lakh. Taking a quarter of a share gives a sixteenth of the associate, which is not what the investor owns.

citation.ref: para 38 and 39

items.scenario: An investor holds 25 per cent of an associate. By 31 March 2025 its share of the associate's losses had reduced the carrying amount of every part of its interest to nil, and a further ₹90 lakh of its share of losses went unrecognised. The investor has guaranteed nothing, has incurred no legal or constructive obligation on the associate's behalf and has made no payments for it. The associate returns to profit: the investor's share is ₹40 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2026 and ₹70 lakh for the year ended 31 March 2027.

items.stem: How much of each loss does X Ltd recognise?

options.text: 60 per cent of each — ₹12 lakh and ₹15 lakh — since gains and losses alike are recognised only to the extent of unrelated investors' interests
options.misconception: applies the unrelated-investors restriction to losses that evidence a real fall in value
options.why: The restriction exists to stop an investor booking profit on a sale to itself. A loss that evidences a reduction in net realisable value or an impairment is not that; the asset is genuinely worth less, and the standard sets it apart for exactly this reason. Restricting it would leave part of a real fall in value unrecorded by anyone.

options.text: The whole ₹20 lakh and the whole ₹25 lakh, both losses being recognised in full
options.misconception: reads the full-recognition rule as covering the upstream leg too
options.why: Full recognition is written for downstream transactions, where the investor is the seller of the asset that has fallen in value. For an upstream transaction the investor recognises its share in those losses, because the asset was the associate's and the associate has already taken the loss in full through its own profit. Taking all of it would count the other 60 per cent that belongs to the associate's other owners.

options.text: Nothing on either, because both transactions were at market value and no unrealised profit therefore arises
options.misconception: looks only for unrealised profit and misses that the standard also governs losses
options.why: The absence of an unrealised gain is not the end of the question. Ind AS 28 deals separately with transactions that provide evidence of a reduction in net realisable value or of an impairment, and both of these do. Selling inventory carried at ₹100 lakh for ₹80 lakh is a real ₹20 lakh loss for X Ltd however fair the price was.

options.text: The whole ₹20 lakh on the sale to Y Ltd, and 40 per cent of the ₹25 lakh on the purchase from Y Ltd — ₹10 lakh, reaching X Ltd through its ₹80 lakh share of Y Ltd's profit
options.why: The rule that restricts gains to unrelated investors' interests does not run in the same way for losses that tell you an asset is worth less. When downstream transactions provide evidence of a reduction in the net realisable value of the assets to be sold or contributed, or of an impairment loss of those assets, those losses shall be recognised in full by the investor — so the whole ₹20 lakh comes off X Ltd's own profit. When upstream transactions provide evidence of such a reduction or impairment in the assets to be purchased, the investor recognises its share in those losses, and the ₹25 lakh already sits inside Y Ltd's ₹200 lakh so 40 per cent of it reaches X Ltd through the equity method.

citation.ref: para 29, read with para 28

items.scenario: X Ltd holds 40 per cent of Y Ltd, an associate it equity accounts. During the year ended 31 March 2026 X Ltd sold inventory to Y Ltd for ₹80 lakh; its carrying amount in X Ltd's books was ₹100 lakh and ₹80 lakh was its market value, so the sale is evidence of a fall in the net realisable value of that inventory. In the same year X Ltd bought a machine from Y Ltd for ₹60 lakh; the machine's carrying amount in Y Ltd's books was ₹85 lakh and the sale is evidence of an impairment loss on it. Y Ltd's profit for the year, after that ₹25 lakh loss, was ₹200 lakh.

items.stem: How much of what each employee shareholder receives is consideration for the acquired business?

options.text: ₹1 crore for each of the three, because all three sold the same one-third stake and the consideration must be the same for the same thing sold
options.misconception: equalises the price across shareholders, when the difference is what tells you part of the payment is not for shares
options.why: The difference in what each receives is evidence rather than a problem to be smoothed away. The non-employee gets ₹1 crore for a third of the company; the employees get ₹60 lakh for a third of the company plus a great deal more for staying. Forcing them to be equal would put two years of somebody's salary into goodwill.

options.text: The whole ₹60 lakh and the additional payment, at its acquisition-date fair value, because a payment measured on the acquired business's own earnings is by its nature consideration for that business
options.misconception: takes the earnings formula as decisive and ignores the employment condition attached to it
options.why: Both remuneration and contingent consideration can be measured on earnings, so the formula settles nothing. What separates them is who has to do what to earn the money, and this payment requires the shareholder to keep working. The standard names that condition first among its indicators.

options.text: Only the ₹60 lakh is consideration, and the additional payment is disclosed as a contingent liability until the two years are served
options.misconception: gets the classification right and then defers the expense that follows from it
options.why: Calling it remuneration decides where it goes, not whether it goes anywhere. Compensation for post-combination services is recognised as an expense over the period the services are rendered under the Ind AS that governs employee benefits. A contingent liability is a possible obligation from a past event, and these services have not been rendered yet.

options.text: Only the ₹60 lakh — the additional payment is remuneration for post-combination services, because it is automatically forfeited if the employment terminates
options.why: Ind AS 103 gives the forfeiture condition as the indicator that settles this. A contingent consideration arrangement in which the payments are automatically forfeited if employment terminates is remuneration for post-combination services, and an arrangement in which the contingent payments are not affected by termination of employment may indicate that they are additional consideration instead. Here the whole of the additional payment goes if the employee leaves, so it is compensation for the two years he serves and is accounted for under the other Ind AS, not as part of the consideration transferred. Only the ₹60 lakh is exchanged for the business.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B55(a), read with the consideration transferred in para 37

items.scenario: ABC Ltd acquires all the shares of XYZ Ltd from its three shareholders, who held equal stakes. Two of them were senior employees of XYZ Ltd and will stay on after the acquisition; the third was not an employee. Each of the two employee shareholders receives ₹60 lakh on completion plus an additional payment of between ₹1.5 crore and ₹2 crore based on a multiple of earnings over the next two years, and that additional payment is forfeited in full if he leaves XYZ Ltd's employment at any time in those two years. The non-employee shareholder receives ₹1 crore and nothing more. The salaries the two employees draw are reasonable remuneration for their services.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 7 require instead?

options.text: Two separately presented investing amounts — a ₹260 lakh outflow and a ₹220 lakh inflow — because the cash flow effects of losing control are not deducted from those of obtaining control, with aggregate disclosure of the total consideration, the portion consisting of cash and cash equivalents, the cash and cash equivalents in each business, and the other assets and liabilities by major category
options.why: The aggregate cash flows arising from obtaining or losing control of subsidiaries or other businesses are presented separately and classified as investing activities, and the standard says in terms that the cash flow effects of losing control are not deducted from those of obtaining control. Each is reported net of the cash and cash equivalents acquired or disposed of as part of the transaction, which gives ₹300 lakh less ₹40 lakh and ₹250 lakh less ₹30 lakh. Alongside, the entity discloses in aggregate for both the total consideration paid or received, the portion of it consisting of cash and cash equivalents, the amount of cash and cash equivalents in the businesses over which control was obtained or lost, and the amount of the assets and liabilities other than cash summarised by each major category.
keywords: not deducted from those of obtaining control

options.text: The ₹260 lakh in investing activities and the ₹220 lakh in financing activities, a disposal of shares in a subsidiary being a transaction with owners
options.misconception: applies the financing classification for an ownership change to a transaction that loses control
options.why: Financing is where cash flows go when the parent's ownership interest changes without losing control, because those are equity transactions with the group's own co-owners. Losing control is not one — the group has parted with a business — so it is an investing flow, presented separately.

options.text: A single net investing figure of ₹40 lakh, since both are changes in the composition of the group and the standard requires them to be aggregated
options.misconception: reads the word aggregate as permission to net an acquisition against a disposal
options.why: Aggregate means each side is added up across the transactions of its own kind, not that the two sides are set against each other. The separate presentation exists so that the reader can see how much cash went into buying businesses and how much came back from selling them, which a single net figure destroys — a busy year of both would look like a quiet one.

options.text: A ₹300 lakh outflow and a ₹250 lakh inflow, the cash held by the subsidiaries being part of the group's own cash and not a deduction
options.misconception: presents the gross consideration and forgets that cash came with the business
options.why: The cash inside A Ltd became the group's cash on the same day the ₹300 lakh left it, so the group parted with ₹260 lakh net to acquire the business. Reporting the gross figure would show an outflow larger than the group actually suffered and would double-count the ₹40 lakh, which also appears in the closing cash balance.

citation.ref: para 39, 40 and 42, read with para 42A and 42B

items.scenario: During the year ended 31 March 2026 P Ltd obtained control of A Ltd, paying ₹300 lakh in cash; A Ltd held ₹40 lakh of cash and cash equivalents on that date. In the same year P Ltd lost control of B Ltd, receiving ₹250 lakh in cash; B Ltd held ₹30 lakh of cash and cash equivalents on the date control passed. The finance manager proposes to show a single net investing outflow of ₹40 lakh and to add no further note, on the ground that both transactions are acquisitions and disposals of subsidiaries and the reader can see the net effect.

items.stem: What must the company disclose for credit risk beyond the expected credit loss note?

options.text: The maximum exposure to credit risk, measured after deducting the collateral held over the dealers' stock, since collateral is what the exposure actually reduces to
options.misconception: nets the collateral into the exposure figure the standard asks to be given before it
options.why: The exposure is disclosed without taking account of any collateral held or other credit enhancements, and the collateral is then described separately along with its financial effect. Netting the two would hide both the size of the risk and the quality of what stands behind it, and would make companies with worthless collateral look like companies with good collateral.

options.text: Nothing further — the expected credit loss allowance is the credit risk disclosure, and an instrument measured at fair value through profit or loss already carries its credit risk in its carrying amount
options.misconception: treats the impairment note as the whole of credit risk disclosure and the fair value as a substitute for exposure information
options.why: Fair value tells the reader what the instrument is worth, not how much the entity stands to lose if every counterparty defaults, and a guarantee given may have a small or nil carrying amount while exposing the company to its full face value. The standard therefore asks separately for the amount that best represents the maximum exposure for instruments outside the impairment requirements.

options.text: For the instruments outside the Ind AS 109 impairment requirements, the amount that best represents its maximum exposure to credit risk without taking account of any collateral held or other credit enhancements, and a description of the collateral held as security and other credit enhancements together with their financial effect — with the first of those not required where the carrying amount itself best represents the exposure
options.why: Ind AS 107 splits credit risk disclosure in two. Where the impairment requirements of Ind AS 109 are applied, the expected credit loss information carries the weight. For all financial instruments to which those requirements are not applied — the dealer loans at fair value through profit or loss and the guarantees — the entity discloses by class the amount that best represents its maximum exposure to credit risk at the end of the reporting period without taking account of any collateral held or other credit enhancements, and a description of collateral held as security and other credit enhancements and their financial effect, such as a quantification of the extent to which they mitigate the risk. The first disclosure is not required for instruments whose carrying amount best represents that exposure.

options.text: A maturity analysis of the guarantees showing their remaining contractual maturities, which is the credit risk disclosure for a guarantee given
options.misconception: gives the liquidity risk disclosure in answer to a credit risk question
options.why: The maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities, into which an issued financial guarantee enters, is the liquidity risk disclosure — it tells the reader when cash might have to leave. Credit risk asks a different question, which is how much the company loses if the people who owe it money do not pay.

citation.ref: para 35K and 36, read with the collateral disclosures in para 15

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company holds ₹500 crore of trade receivables, on which it applies the impairment requirements of Ind AS 109 and discloses the expected credit loss allowance. It also holds ₹150 crore of dealer loans measured at fair value through profit or loss, to which the impairment requirements do not apply and which are secured by a charge over the dealers' stock, and it has given ₹200 crore of financial guarantees on behalf of a joint venture. The chief financial officer says the expected credit loss note on the receivables discharges the company's credit risk disclosure for everything.

items.stem: What must the company disclose?

options.text: Only the 11 per cent customer, with its name and the amount each segment earned from it; the products-and-services disclosure is indeed unnecessary because the entity reports three segments
options.misconception: treats any segment disclosure as satisfying the entity-wide requirement, and over-discloses on the customer
options.why: The entity-wide disclosures are given where the reportable segment information does not already provide them, and geographic segments do not provide a product split. On the customer, the entity discloses that the threshold is crossed, the total revenue from each such customer and the identity of the segment or segments reporting the revenue — it need not disclose the customer's name, nor the amount each segment reports from that customer.

options.text: Only the products-and-services split; the three related companies are separate legal persons contracting separately, so none of them reaches 10 per cent
options.misconception: counts legal persons where the standard counts a group under common control
options.why: A group of entities known to the reporting entity to be under common control is considered a single customer, because the concentration of risk the disclosure exists to reveal sits with whoever controls the buying, not with the entity that signs. Judgement is required for a government and the entities it controls, where the extent of economic integration matters, but an ordinary commercial group is caught.

options.text: Revenue from external customers for each product and service or each group of similar products and services, because segments organised by geography do not already give it, unless the information is not available and the cost to develop it would be excessive, in which case that fact is disclosed; and reliance on both customers, because a group of entities known to be under common control is treated as a single customer
options.why: The entity-wide disclosures exist for the case where the segments do not happen to answer the question. Reportable segments built on geography say nothing about how much revenue comes from cement as against paints, so the entity reports the revenues from external customers for each product and service, or each group of similar products and services — unless the necessary information is not available and the cost to develop it would be excessive, and then that fact itself is disclosed. On customers, revenues from transactions with a single external customer of 10 per cent or more of an entity's revenues must be disclosed, and a group of entities known to the reporting entity to be under common control is considered a single customer, so 6 plus 6 plus 6 is 18 per cent and crosses the threshold.
keywords: group of similar products and services
cost to develop it would be excessive

options.text: Both customers, but the products-and-services disclosure only if the company chooses to re-organise its segments around products
options.misconception: makes an entity-wide disclosure depend on how the entity is managed, which is the one thing it is designed not to depend on
options.why: Entity-wide disclosures are required of every entity within the standard's scope, including one with a single reportable segment, precisely so that the information does not disappear because of how management happens to organise itself. Reorganising the segments is not on offer as an alternative to disclosing.

citation.ref: para 32, 33 and 34

items.scenario: A company's three reportable segments are North, South and West, organised on geography because that is how the chief operating decision maker runs it. Within each segment it sells cement, paints and logistics services, which are essentially different from one another. Revenue from one customer is 11 per cent of total revenue. Revenue also comes from three separate companies at 6 per cent each, and the company knows all three to be under the common control of one group. The finance head says the products-and-services disclosure is unnecessary because the company already reports segments, and that no single one of the three related companies crosses the threshold.

items.stem: What diluted per-share amounts does the company report?

options.text: ₹2.50 for continuing operations, a loss of ₹3.00 for the discontinued operation and an overall diluted loss per share of ₹0.50 — the options are included even though the overall loss per share falls from ₹0.60 to ₹0.50
options.why: An entity that reports a discontinued operation uses income from continuing operations, adjusted for preference dividends and similar adjustments, as the control number in deciding whether potential ordinary shares are dilutive. The same number of potential ordinary shares used in computing the diluted per-share amount of income from continuing operations is then used in computing every other reported diluted per-share amount, even where the effect is antidilutive against the respective basic amount. Continuing operations fall from ₹3.00 to ₹2.50 on 12,00,000 shares, so the options are dilutive and go in everywhere: ₹36,00,000 over 12,00,000 is a ₹3.00 loss, and ₹6,00,000 over 12,00,000 is a ₹0.50 loss.
keywords: same number of potential ordinary shares

options.text: The options are excluded altogether, because including them reduces the overall loss per share from ₹0.60 to ₹0.50 and is therefore antidilutive
options.misconception: tests dilution against the overall result, when the control number is the result from continuing operations
options.why: Testing against the bottom line lets a one-off discontinued loss decide how the recurring business is presented, and would flip the answer from year to year on facts that have nothing to do with the options. That is why the standard fixes the control number as profit or loss from continuing operations attributable to the ordinary equity holders of the parent, and here that number is diluted.

options.text: No diluted amounts are reported at all, because the company has made an overall loss and diluted earnings per share is not presented in a loss year
options.misconception: believes a loss suspends diluted reporting, when it changes only which potential shares are dilutive
options.why: A loss does not switch the diluted presentation off. It usually means potential ordinary shares are antidilutive against the control number and are excluded, which is a different matter from not presenting the figure. Here the control number is a profit and is diluted, so the options are included and the diluted amounts are reported.

options.text: ₹2.50 for continuing operations, with the discontinued operation and the overall figure left on 10,00,000 shares at a loss of ₹3.60 and ₹0.60
options.misconception: uses two different share counts in one set of diluted figures
options.why: The whole point of the control number is that one denominator governs the set. The same number of potential ordinary shares used for continuing operations is used in computing all other reported diluted per-share amounts, so that the three figures still add up and the reader can trace one to another. Mixing counts would leave a set of numbers that does not reconcile.

citation.ref: para 41 and 42, applied to an entity reporting a discontinued operation

items.scenario: For the year ended 31 March 2026 a company reports income from continuing operations of ₹30,00,000 and a loss from discontinued operations of ₹36,00,000, giving a net loss of ₹6,00,000. The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding is 10,00,000, and its outstanding stock options would add 2,00,000 incremental shares. Basic figures are therefore ₹3.00 for continuing operations, a loss of ₹3.60 for the discontinued operation and an overall loss per share of ₹0.60.

items.stem: How is each scheme accounted for?

options.text: P Ltd's as cash-settled; Q Ltd's as equity-settled, with the whole ₹90 lakh debited to equity because a settlement of an equity-settled award never touches profit or loss
options.misconception: puts the entire payment through equity and misses the cap at the fair value of the instruments
options.why: A repurchase of equity is a transaction with owners only up to what the equity is worth. The payment is deducted from equity to the extent of the fair value of the equity instruments repurchased, measured at the repurchase date, and any excess over that is recognised as an expense. Putting the whole ₹90 lakh through equity would let the company pay ₹15 lakh more than the award was worth without that ever reaching the year's result.

options.text: Both as cash-settled, since in the event both were settled in cash and the accounting must follow what actually happened
options.misconception: decides the classification with hindsight, when it is made from the obligation the entity has at the time
options.why: The classification is made on whether a present obligation to settle in cash exists, judged as the services are received, not on what the entity later chose to do. Q Ltd could have issued shares and had said nothing to suggest it would not, so it had no such obligation; its later decision to pay is a repurchase of the equity it had already granted.

options.text: P Ltd's as cash-settled, because past practice and a stated policy give it a present obligation to settle in cash; Q Ltd's as equity-settled, with the cash settlement treated as the repurchase of an equity interest — ₹75 lakh debited to equity and the ₹15 lakh excess recognised in profit or loss
options.why: Where the entity has the choice of settlement, the whole award is treated as cash-settled or as equity-settled depending on whether the entity has a present obligation to settle in cash. That obligation is taken to exist where there is no commercial substance to issuing equity — a restriction on issuing new share capital, for instance — or where there is a past practice or stated policy of settling in cash, which is P Ltd exactly. Q Ltd has neither, so equity-settled accounting was right; and where equity-settled accounting has been applied but the settlement is made in cash, it is accounted for as the repurchase of an equity interest, debiting the amount previously credited to equity and recognising in profit or loss the excess paid over the fair value of the equity instruments that would otherwise have been issued.
keywords: present obligation to settle in cash

options.text: Both as equity-settled, because the entity's freedom to choose means no liability has been incurred in either case
options.misconception: reads a contractual right to choose as conclusive, when practice and policy can create the obligation anyway
options.why: A right to settle in shares is worth nothing if the entity has told everybody it will pay cash and has done so six times running. The standard looks for a present obligation however it arises, and a past practice or a stated policy of cash settlement creates one just as a restriction on issuing capital would.

citation.ref: para 41, 42 and 43, read with the repurchase rule in para 29

items.scenario: Two companies each grant share options under which the entity, not the employee, chooses whether to settle in cash or by issuing shares. P Ltd has settled every one of its six previous schemes of this kind in cash and has told employees it will do so again. Q Ltd has always settled in shares, is under no restriction on issuing new capital and has stated no policy, so it accounted for its scheme as equity-settled and credited ₹75 lakh to equity over the vesting period. On settlement Q Ltd nonetheless paid ₹90 lakh in cash; the fair value of the equity instruments that would otherwise have been issued was ₹75 lakh on that date.

items.stem: What does the company recognise on the cancellation?

options.text: ₹16,46,667 charged at once as an acceleration of vesting, plus ₹90,000 of expense — ₹16,20,000 of the payment being a deduction from equity at the ₹90 fair value on the repurchase date and only the ₹5 an option excess reaching profit or loss
options.why: A grant cancelled or settled during the vesting period, otherwise than by forfeiture when the vesting conditions are not satisfied, is accounted for as an acceleration of vesting, so the amount that would otherwise have been recognised over the remainder of the vesting period is recognised immediately. On 9 directors the total grant date charge is 9 times 2,000 times ₹130, or ₹23,40,000, of which ₹6,93,333 has been taken, leaving ₹16,46,667. Any payment made on the cancellation is accounted for as the repurchase of an equity interest, that is as a deduction from equity, except to the extent that the payment exceeds the fair value of the equity instruments granted measured at the repurchase date — 9 times 2,000 times ₹90 is ₹16,20,000 deducted from equity, and the remaining ₹90,000 is an expense.

options.text: ₹16,46,667 as an acceleration of vesting, with the whole ₹17,10,000 payment recognised as an expense of the year
options.misconception: expenses the entire settlement payment instead of treating it first as a repurchase of equity
options.why: The payment buys back an equity interest the employees already hold, and a transaction with holders in that capacity is a deduction from equity. Only what is paid over and above the fair value of those instruments at the repurchase date is an expense — ₹5 an option here, not ₹95.

options.text: A credit reversing the ₹6,93,333 already charged, since the options will now never vest and no shares will ever be issued
options.misconception: treats a cancellation like a failed service condition, which is the one case the rule expressly excludes
options.why: Reversal is what happens when a vesting condition fails, because the entity never received the services it was paying for. Here the directors gave the service and the company chose to end the scheme, so it must recognise immediately what it would otherwise have spread. Letting a cancellation claw the charge back would let any board erase its option cost by cancelling in the last year.

options.text: ₹16,46,667 as an acceleration of vesting, with the whole ₹17,10,000 payment deducted from equity
options.misconception: puts the entire payment through equity and ignores the cap at the fair value on the repurchase date
options.why: The deduction from equity is capped at what the instruments were worth on the day they were bought back, which is ₹90 an option. Paying ₹95 for something worth ₹90 is a cost of ending the scheme early, and the ₹90,000 that represents is an expense of the period rather than a distribution to owners.

citation.ref: para 28(a) and 28(b)

items.scenario: On 1 April 2024 a company granted 2,000 share options to each of its 10 directors, vesting on 31 March 2027 subject to three years' service. The grant date fair value was ₹130 an option and at the end of the first year 8 directors were expected to remain, so ₹6,93,333 was charged for the year ended 31 March 2025. During the year ended 31 March 2026 the board cancelled the scheme outright. Nine directors were then in employment; the fair value of an option at the date of cancellation was ₹90 and the company agreed to pay each of the nine ₹95 an option, a total of ₹17,10,000. The cancellation is not a forfeiture — the service condition had not failed.

items.stem: Which positions are presented net in the balance sheet?

options.text: The first only — gross settlement through a clearing house qualifies, but a right of set-off can never run against a party other than the counterparty
options.misconception: treats the different-counterparties rule as absolute, when a three-party agreement is the recognised exception
options.why: The general case is indeed that amounts owed to and by different parties are not offset. The standard sets out the exception in terms: in unusual circumstances a debtor may have a legal right to apply an amount due from a third party against the amount due to a creditor, where an agreement between the three parties clearly establishes the right of set-off. That agreement exists here and is enforceable in every state the criteria name.

options.text: The third only — settlement through a clearing house is settlement in full on both sides, so nothing is being settled net
options.misconception: reads the criterion as requiring literal net settlement, when an equivalent outcome suffices
options.why: The criterion is met where the outcome is in effect equivalent to net settlement, and a single settlement cycle with margining that leaves credit and liquidity risk insignificant is exactly the arrangement contemplated. Insisting on a single net payment would make the presentation turn on a plumbing detail rather than on the exposure the entity actually carries.

options.text: The first and the third — the clearing house cycle is in effect equivalent to net settlement, and a three-party agreement can create the legal right of set-off; the synthetic instrument's two legs are presented gross
options.why: The intention limb is satisfied not only by settling net but where the entity can settle in a manner whose outcome is in effect equivalent to net settlement, which happens if and only if the gross settlement mechanism has features that eliminate or result in insignificant credit and liquidity risk and that process receivables and payables in a single settlement process or cycle — the first position exactly. In unusual circumstances a debtor may have a legal right to apply an amount due from a third party against an amount due to a creditor, provided there is an agreement between the three parties clearly establishing that right, which is the third. Offsetting is inappropriate where several instruments emulate a single one — a synthetic instrument — because each leg is a separate right or obligation, transferable and settleable on its own and exposed to its own risks.

options.text: All three — each pair has the same economic effect as a single net position, and substance governs presentation
options.misconception: reasons from economic substance past the two criteria the standard sets
options.why: Substance is what the two criteria are for, and the synthetic instrument fails them. Each of the borrowing and the swap is a contractual right or obligation with its own terms, each may be transferred or settled separately, and each is exposed to risks the other is not. Netting them would hide a ₹200 lakh borrowing behind a ₹12 lakh derivative.

citation.ref: para 42 and 48, with para 45 and 49(a)

items.scenario: A company holds three positions at 31 March 2026. The first is a ₹80 lakh receivable and a ₹80 lakh payable with the same counterparty, settled gross through a clearing house that processes receivables and payables in a single settlement cycle on the same day, with margining that leaves credit and liquidity risk insignificant; a legally enforceable right of set-off exists. The second is a ₹200 lakh floating rate borrowing combined with an interest rate swap under which the company receives floating and pays fixed, together synthesising a fixed rate borrowing; the swap is an asset of ₹12 lakh and no right of set-off exists between the two. The third is a ₹50 lakh receivable from X and a ₹50 lakh payable to Y, with a written agreement between the company, X and Y establishing the company's right to set the two off, enforceable in the normal course of business and on default and insolvency, and the company intends to settle net.

items.stem: What are the cash-generating units here, and what does the transfer pricing do to the measurement?

options.text: X and Y together are one cash-generating unit, because sixty per cent of X's output goes to Y and X's cash inflows therefore depend on demand for Y's products
options.misconception: treats the internal share of the output as decisive, when the existence of an active market is what settles independence
options.why: That reasoning is right where there is no active market for the intermediate product, because then X's inflows really do depend on demand for Y's. Here X can sell the same product to outsiders, so the inflows it would generate are largely independent of Y whatever proportion currently goes internally. The market, not the current routing of the goods, is the test.

options.text: X and Y are separate units, and the value in use of each is measured on the internal transfer prices actually charged, since those are the prices at which the transactions really occur
options.misconception: measures value in use on prices the entity sets for itself
options.why: Internal transfer prices here do not reflect market prices — they are set to pass all margins to X and are above the market. Measuring on them would overstate X's recoverable amount and understate Y's by the same amount, so that an impairment in one unit could be hidden by the pricing policy. The budgets are adjusted to what the goods would fetch at arm's length.

options.text: Neither is a cash-generating unit, because the two plants are managed together and the smallest group generating independent inflows is the entity as a whole
options.misconception: goes to the entity level, which is the answer for the case where no active market exists
options.why: Being managed together matters when the recoverable amount of one plant cannot be assessed independently of the other, which is the no-active-market case. Here it can. Testing at the entity level would let a profitable business absorb an impairment in a plant that is failing on its own terms, which is the outcome the cash-generating unit exists to prevent.

options.text: X and Y are each a separate cash-generating unit, because an active market exists for X's output even though part of that output is used internally; and in determining value in use for both, the budgets are adjusted to management's best estimate of future prices achievable in arm's length transactions for the output used internally
options.why: Where an active market exists for the output produced by an asset or group of assets, that asset or group is identified as a cash-generating unit even if some or all of the output is used internally, because the entity could sell the output on that market and so generate cash inflows largely independent of the rest of the entity. X could sell to outsiders what it sells to Y, so X is a unit; Y sells eighty per cent of its production outside, so Y is one too. Because the internal transfer prices do not reflect market prices for X's output, the entity adjusts the financial budgets and forecasts of both units to management's best estimate of the future prices that could be achieved in arm's length transactions for those of X's products that are used internally.

citation.ref: para 70, read with para 6 and the value in use requirements in para 30

items.scenario: Plant X makes an intermediate product. Sixty per cent of X's output goes to plant Y of the same entity at a transfer price that passes all margins to X, and the other forty per cent is sold to outside customers. Y uses the intermediate product as a significant raw material and sells eighty per cent of its own final production outside the entity. An active market exists for X's intermediate product, and the internal transfer prices X charges Y are higher than the prices in that market.

items.stem: On what basis is each measured?

options.text: The machine at its current use, in combination with the other assets and liabilities as installed or otherwise configured for use; and the customer relationships together with the right to future updates, because the valuation premise is the one market participants would adopt
options.why: Highest and best use is judged from the perspective of market participants, and an entity's current use of a non-financial asset is presumed to be its highest and best use unless market or other factors suggest otherwise. Nothing suggests otherwise for a lightly customised machine that will go on doing the same job, so its highest and best use is its current use. The valuation premise then asks whether the maximum value comes from the asset in combination with other assets and liabilities or on a standalone basis, and where the combination is the one market participants would use, the asset is measured on that basis. The same premise takes the customer relationships and the update right together, since the relationships would have little value without them.

options.text: The machine at the value it would have if converted to the highest-value use physically and legally available to it, whatever A Ltd intends
options.misconception: hunts for an alternative use where the standard presumes the current one
options.why: Highest and best use does reach past the entity's own intentions, and it is still bounded. An alternative use must be physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible, and the current use is presumed to be the highest and best use unless market or other factors suggest otherwise. There is no evidence of any such factor here.

options.text: The customer relationships on their own, at the price a market participant would pay for them separately, since the update right is a distinct intangible with its own fair value
options.misconception: separates two assets whose value is jointly determined because each is separately identifiable
options.why: Being separately identifiable and being separately valuable are different things. The valuation premise asks where the maximum value lies, and the relationships would have little or no value without the free updates that come with them, so market participants would value them together. Splitting them would produce two numbers neither of which anyone would pay.

options.text: The machine at the price a market participant would pay for it standing alone, uninstalled, since fair value is an exit price and an exit means the asset leaves on its own
options.misconception: forces a standalone premise on an asset whose value comes from being installed
options.why: An exit price is what a market participant would pay, and a market participant here would pay for a machine that is installed and configured for use in a line. The valuation premise follows the value, not the physical act of removal. Measuring it uninstalled would price it as scrap plus freight and lose the very thing the buyer of B Ltd was paying for.

citation.ref: para 27, 29 and 31, read with the highest and best use requirements in para 27 to 30

items.scenario: A Ltd obtains control of B Ltd and must fair value two of the assets acquired. The first is a machine B Ltd bought from an outside vendor and then customised, though not extensively, for its own production line; A Ltd will keep using it on that line, and a market participant would get most value from it installed and configured alongside the other assets of the line. There is no evidence that the machine's current use is not its highest and best use. The second is a customer relationship intangible that comes with a contractual right for those customers to receive all future technology updates free, a right that is itself a separate intangible and without which the relationships would be worth little.

items.stem: How does the lessee account for the modification?

options.text: As a separate lease — a new right-of-use asset and lease liability are recognised for the 3,000 square metres at the end of the second quarter of year six, and the accounting for the original 2,000 square metres is not touched
options.why: A lease modification is accounted for as a separate lease where both conditions are met: the modification increases the scope of the lease by adding the right to use one or more underlying assets, and the consideration for the lease increases by an amount commensurate with the stand-alone price for that increase in scope, adjusted for the circumstances of the particular contract. Both hold here — a new underlying asset in the shape of the additional space, at the market rate less a discount that reflects costs the lessor genuinely avoids. The lessee therefore applies the ordinary initial recognition and measurement requirements at the commencement date of the new lease, which is when the space becomes available, and makes no adjustment at all to the original lease.

options.text: As a partial termination in reverse — the right-of-use asset and the liability are grossed up in proportion to the increase in floor area, and any difference goes to profit or loss
options.misconception: borrows the proportionate mechanics of a decrease in scope and runs them backwards
options.why: The proportionate adjustment and the gain or loss belong to a decrease in scope, where the lessee is giving back a right it has already recognised and must derecognise part of both balances. An increase in scope at a commensurate price gives up nothing and gains a new asset, so nothing is derecognised and no difference arises to take to profit or loss.

options.text: Nothing until the end of the second quarter of year six, and then a remeasurement of the single combined lease, since the two spaces are in the same building under one amended contract
options.misconception: lets one legal contract decide the accounting, when the test is the right of use added and the price paid for it
options.why: One document can contain two leases. The conditions look at whether an additional right to use an underlying asset has been granted and whether the price paid for it is commensurate with its stand-alone price, not at how many contracts were signed. Both spaces sitting in the same building and the same amendment changes neither answer.

options.text: As a single modified lease — the liability is remeasured at a revised discount rate for the whole 5,000 square metres and the right-of-use asset adjusted by the same amount
options.misconception: applies the not-a-separate-lease treatment to a modification that meets both separate-lease conditions
options.why: Remeasuring at a revised discount rate against the right-of-use asset is what happens to every modification that is not a separate lease — an increase in scope priced below the stand-alone price, a decrease in scope, a change in the term. It is the residual treatment, reached only when the two separate-lease conditions are not both met, and here they are.

citation.ref: para 44, read with para 45 and 46

items.scenario: A lessee holds a ten-year lease of 2,000 square metres of office space. At the beginning of year six the lessee and the lessor agree to amend the lease for its remaining five years to add another 3,000 square metres in the same building. The additional space becomes available for the lessee's use at the end of the second quarter of year six. The increase in total consideration matches the current market rate for the new 3,000 square metres, adjusted only for a discount reflecting costs the lessor does not incur because it is not letting the space to a new tenant, such as marketing costs.

items.stem: What deferred tax does the acquirer recognise on the two?

options.text: A deferred tax liability on the goodwill, which increases goodwill by the same amount, and none on the standalone asset
options.misconception: recognises the goodwill liability and grosses goodwill up, which is the circularity the prohibition exists to stop
options.why: Grossing goodwill up creates a larger temporary difference, which demands a larger liability, which grosses goodwill up again. The figure never settles, and the whole increase would be an asset the acquirer did not buy. That is why the standard closes the door on initial recognition rather than working the circle to a limit.

options.text: None on the goodwill, and a deferred tax liability on the standalone asset, since it plainly has a carrying amount and a nil tax base
options.misconception: applies the general rule to an asset the initial recognition exception takes out of it
options.why: A taxable temporary difference plainly exists; the exception is what stops it being recognised. Recognising deferred tax on the initial recognition of such an asset would mean grossing up the asset itself or putting an expense through profit or loss on the day of purchase, and the standard says the entity does neither, and does not recognise subsequent changes in that unrecognised difference either.

options.text: None on either — the standard prohibits recognising the deferred tax liability that would arise on the initial recognition of goodwill, and the initial recognition exception covers an asset bought in a transaction that is not a business combination and affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit
options.why: Goodwill with a nil tax base carries a taxable temporary difference equal to its whole carrying amount, and recognising the deferred tax liability on it would increase goodwill, which would increase the temporary difference, which would increase the liability again — a circular computation, since goodwill is measured as a residual. The standard therefore forbids it on the initial recognition of goodwill. The second asset falls in the other exception: no deferred tax is recognised on the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and at the time of the transaction affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit.
keywords: neither accounting profit nor taxable profit

options.text: A deferred tax liability on both, since a difference between carrying amount and tax base always produces deferred tax where the rate is known
options.misconception: reads the general rule as having no exceptions
options.why: The general rule has two named exceptions and both are in play here. Applying it everywhere would make goodwill a self-inflating number and would put a tax charge on the purchase of an ordinary asset in the year it was bought, neither of which reports anything a reader could use.

citation.ref: para 15(a) and 15(b), read with para 21

items.scenario: An acquirer pays ₹100 crore for a subsidiary whose identifiable net assets have an acquisition date fair value of ₹65 crore, so goodwill of ₹35 crore is recognised. The tax authority allows no deduction for that goodwill at any time, including on a later disposal of the underlying business, so its tax base is nil. In the same year, and in a transaction that is not a business combination, the acquirer buys a standalone asset for ₹40 crore which attracts no tax allowance of any kind; at the time of the purchase the transaction affects neither accounting profit nor taxable profit, and it is not a leasing or decommissioning transaction giving rise to equal taxable and deductible temporary differences.

items.stem: What does the company do about the ₹80 lakh at 31 March 2026?

options.text: Recognise a liability when the obligation arises, to the extent the contributions payable will not be available as a refund or as a reduction in future contributions after they are paid into the plan; the liability increases the defined benefit liability so that no gain or loss is expected
options.why: The company's general point is ordinarily right — a requirement to contribute does not affect the measurement, because once paid the contributions become plan assets and the additional net liability is nil. The Appendix to Ind AS 19 identifies the case where that breaks down. Where an entity has an obligation under a minimum funding requirement to pay contributions covering an existing shortfall for services already received, it must ask whether those contributions will be available as a refund or as a reduction in future contributions after they are paid in. To the extent they will not, a liability is recognised when the obligation arises, and it increases the defined benefit liability so that no gain or loss is expected when the money is actually paid.
keywords: no gain or loss is expected

options.text: Nothing at 31 March 2026, because the asset ceiling applies only where the plan is in surplus and this plan is in deficit
options.misconception: reads the whole Appendix as being about the ceiling, when it also asks when a funding requirement creates a liability
options.why: The ceiling limits a surplus, and there is no surplus here. The Appendix addresses three issues, and the third is when a minimum funding requirement might give rise to a liability — which does not depend on the plan being in surplus at all. A deficit plan whose contributions are irrecoverable is exactly the case it was written for.

options.text: Nothing — the company is right, because a contribution becomes a plan asset on payment and so leaves the net defined benefit liability unchanged
options.misconception: applies the general position to the one case the Appendix carves out of it
options.why: The reasoning holds only while the money remains the company's in some form once it is in the plan, whether as a refund it can draw or as contributions it will not have to make later. Here the rules allow no refund and the actuary has found no reduction in future contributions, so the ₹80 lakh leaves the company and never comes back in any shape. That is a cost the company is already committed to, and it belongs on the balance sheet now.

options.text: Disclose the ₹80 lakh as a contractual commitment, since it is a future contribution and Ind AS 19 requires disclosure of expected contributions for the next annual period
options.misconception: answers a recognition question with the disclosure that sits beside it
options.why: Expected contributions for the next annual reporting period are indeed disclosed, and that disclosure exists alongside the recognition rule rather than instead of it. Where the contributions payable to meet an existing shortfall will not be available afterwards, the Appendix requires a liability to be recognised, and a note cannot stand in for an amount the standard says goes on the face of the statements.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para 23 and 24, read with the asset ceiling in para 64

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company's defined benefit plan is in deficit on the Ind AS 19 measurement. A statutory minimum funding requirement obliges the company to pay ₹80 lakh of contributions during the year to 31 March 2027 to make good a shortfall for past service measured on the minimum funding basis. The plan rules permit no refund to the company in any circumstances, and the actuary determines that once these ₹80 lakh are in the plan they will not reduce the contributions the company must make for future service either. The company's view is that a contribution can never affect the measurement of a defined benefit liability, because the money becomes a plan asset the moment it is paid.

items.stem: When does the maker recognise revenue on the spare parts?

options.text: Never on a bill-and-hold basis, since revenue on goods always waits for delivery
options.misconception: reads the standard as forbidding revenue before delivery, when it sets out the terms on which such revenue is recognised
options.why: The standard devotes a section of Appendix B to these arrangements precisely because they can support revenue. The discipline is in the four criteria, which stop a seller from invoicing goods it has not finished and calling the difference revenue.

options.text: On the date the four criteria for a bill-and-hold arrangement are met, even though the parts never leave the maker's warehouse
options.why: A customer can obtain control of a product that stays in the seller's physical possession, because it can direct the use of and obtain substantially all the remaining benefits from it while choosing not to take delivery. For a bill-and-hold arrangement, four criteria must be met on top of the ordinary indicators — the reason for the arrangement must be substantive, the product must be identified separately as belonging to the customer, the product must currently be ready for physical transfer, and the entity cannot have the ability to use the product or to direct it to another customer. All four hold here. The storage that follows is a separate custodial service.
keywords: identified separately as belonging to the customer

options.text: On despatch to the customer's own store, because control follows physical possession
options.misconception: treats physical possession as the whole test of control, when it is one indicator among several
options.why: Physical possession is an indicator of the transfer of control, not the definition of it. If it were the definition, no consignment would ever be excluded and no bill-and-hold arrangement would ever be recognised. The question is who can direct the use of the parts and take their benefits, and on these facts that is the customer.

options.text: On the invoice date, the customer having been billed and having taken the risk of loss
options.misconception: takes billing and risk of loss as sufficient, skipping the three criteria that ask whether the goods exist, are set aside and are beyond the seller's use
options.why: Invoicing and risk of loss are the easiest facts for a seller to arrange and the least probative. A maker could bill for parts still on the line and shift the risk by a clause. The other three criteria are what make the arrangement substantive.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B79 to B82, read with the indicators of transfer of control in para 38

items.scenario: A machine tool maker finishes a batch of spare parts a customer ordered. The customer asks the maker to keep them because its own store is full. The parts are labelled with the customer's name and kept on a rack set aside for that customer, they are ready to be shipped the moment the customer calls for them, and the maker cannot use them or divert them to anyone else. The customer has been invoiced and has accepted the risk of loss while the parts sit in the warehouse.

items.stem: What revenue does the contractor recognise for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹25,00,000, being ₹20,00,000 of costs incurred over ₹40,00,000 of total expected costs, applied to the whole transaction price
options.misconception: leaves the uninstalled lifts inside the measure of progress, so a purchase order manufactures half a project's revenue
options.why: Half of ₹50,00,000 is the ₹25,00,000 here, and it says the contractor is halfway through a refurbishment on which it has laid one-fifth of the service work. Buying a lift is not progress towards refurbishing a building. That mismatch between cost and progress is exactly what the adjustment to the input method exists to correct.

options.text: Nil on the lifts until they are installed, so ₹7,00,000 for the year
options.misconception: withholds revenue on goods the customer already controls, on the ground that the contractor has not yet used them
options.why: Control of the lifts passed on delivery to the site. The adjustment does not defer their revenue; it strips out their margin, recognising revenue equal to cost so that buying them neither creates nor destroys profit.

options.text: ₹22,00,000 — ₹15,00,000 for the lifts at cost with no margin, plus 20 per cent of the remaining ₹35,00,000 of the transaction price
options.why: Where a cost incurred is not proportionate to the entity's progress, the input method is adjusted and revenue is recognised only to the extent of that cost incurred. The four conditions for that adjustment all hold — the lifts are not a distinct performance obligation, the customer takes control of them well before receiving the service, their cost is significant against total expected costs, and the contractor merely procures them. So the lifts are excluded from the measure of progress, which becomes ₹5,00,000 over ₹25,00,000, or 20 per cent. Twenty per cent of the ₹35,00,000 attributable to the service is ₹7,00,000, and the lifts add ₹15,00,000 of revenue equal to their cost.
keywords: only to the extent of that cost incurred

options.text: ₹6,25,000, being ₹5,00,000 over ₹40,00,000 applied to the whole transaction price
options.misconception: strips the lifts out of the numerator of the progress fraction but leaves their cost in the denominator, and gives them no revenue at all
options.why: This excludes the lifts twice over. Once their cost is taken out of the measure of progress, the ₹15,00,000 of expected lift cost comes out of the denominator too, leaving ₹5,00,000 over ₹25,00,000. And the lifts still carry revenue equal to their cost, because the customer controls them.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B19, read with para 39 to 41

items.scenario: A contractor refurbishes a building under a single performance obligation satisfied over time. The transaction price is ₹50,00,000. Expected costs are ₹15,00,000 for lifts bought in from a third party and ₹25,00,000 for construction services, ₹40,00,000 in all. The lifts are delivered to the site six months before they will be installed, the customer obtains control of them on delivery, the contractor modifies nothing about them, and they are not a distinct performance obligation. By 31 March 2026 the lifts have been delivered and ₹5,00,000 of the other costs have been incurred. The contractor measures progress by a cost-to-cost input method.

items.stem: What revenue should the retailer report on each jacket sold?

options.text: Either ₹3,000 or ₹1,200, provided the basis is disclosed and applied consistently
options.misconception: turns a facts-driven determination into a presentation policy
options.why: Nothing offers an option here. The capacity in which an entity acts is a conclusion drawn from the facts, and two retailers with identical facts must report identically — which is the whole point of having indicators rather than a preference.

options.text: ₹3,000, because gross presentation is required whenever the entity issues the invoice to the customer in its own name
options.misconception: promotes invoicing into the test, which would make every agent a principal
options.why: The number is right and the reason would produce the wrong answer everywhere else. Agents routinely invoice and collect in their own name; the travel portal that only arranges a hotel room does exactly that. Invoicing is not among the indicators the standard lists.

options.text: ₹1,200, its margin, because the manufacturer made the jackets and the retailer only sells them
options.misconception: reads who produced the goods as deciding the capacity, when the test is who controls them immediately before transfer
options.why: Almost nothing a retailer sells was made by the retailer, and if manufacture decided the question no shop would report gross revenue. The standard asks about control of the specified good before it reaches the customer, and here the shop bought, stored, priced and risked it.

options.text: ₹3,000 — it is the principal, so it reports the gross amount of consideration
options.why: The indicators all point one way. The retailer is primarily responsible for fulfilling the promise, it carries the inventory risk on unsold jackets and on returns, and it has discretion in establishing the price. Together those show that it obtains control of the jackets before they are transferred to the customer, which makes it the principal, and a principal recognises revenue in the gross amount of consideration to which it expects to be entitled.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B34A, B35 and B37, with the gross presentation in para B35B

items.scenario: A specialty retailer buys 5,000 winter jackets outright from a manufacturer at ₹1,800 each, takes them into its own warehouse, and sets its own shelf price of ₹3,000. It cannot return unsold stock, it handles every return and defect claim itself, and it bears the loss on whatever is left at the end of the season. It reports only its ₹1,200 margin per jacket as revenue, arguing that all it really does is put the maker's coat on a shopper's back.

items.stem: Which method of estimating variable consideration fits each contract?

options.text: The expected value for both, as the controller proposes, because it uses more of the available information
options.misconception: treats the more elaborate method as always the better predictor, when the standard picks the method that fits the shape of the outcomes
options.why: A probability-weighted figure on an all-or-nothing bonus produces an amount the contract can never pay — a number between nil and ₹5 crore that no outcome delivers. More arithmetic is not a better prediction when the arithmetic describes an impossible result.

options.text: The most likely amount for the commissioning bonus and the expected value for the volume rebate
options.why: An entity estimates variable consideration using either the expected value or the most likely amount, whichever it expects to better predict the consideration to which it will be entitled. The expected value, being the sum of probability-weighted amounts across a range of possible outcomes, suits an entity with a large number of contracts with similar characteristics, which the 4,000 rebate contracts are. The most likely amount, being the single most likely outcome, suits a contract with only two possible outcomes, which the all-or-nothing bonus is. The selection is not a free choice.

options.text: The most likely amount for both, since each contract in the end settles at one figure
options.misconception: reads the eventual single settlement as the test, when the choice turns on how many outcomes the contract can produce
options.why: Every contract settles at one figure eventually; that says nothing about how to estimate it today. Across 4,000 rebate contracts the single most likely tier ignores the whole distribution the company has years of data on.

options.text: Either method for either contract, provided the choice is applied consistently and disclosed
options.misconception: turns the selection into an accounting policy election
options.why: Consistency is required within a contract once a method is chosen, and that is a constraint, not a permission. The method itself is selected on the facts of each contract, and different types of variable consideration inside one contract may even take different methods.

citation.ref: para 53, read with para 54 and 55

items.scenario: A company has two contracts on hand. Under the first it will receive a single ₹5 crore bonus if a plant is commissioned by a fixed date and nothing at all if it is not, and there are no other outcomes. Under the second it supplies goods to 4,000 retailers under a volume rebate that settles at nil, 2 per cent, 5 per cent or 8 per cent depending on each retailer's purchases for the year, and the company has several years of data on how that population behaves. The financial controller wants the probability-weighted figure used for both, calling it the more scientific method.

items.stem: How are these items classified at 31 March 2026?

options.text: The inventories are current, but the trade payable is non-current because it falls due in fifteen months
options.misconception: keeps the operating-cycle limb for assets and drops it for liabilities
options.why: The liability test carries the same limb. A payable settled within the entity's normal operating cycle is current even if it is due more than twelve months after the reporting period, and showing the barley as working capital while its own supplier is long-term misstates the working capital position.

options.text: Everything but the overdraft is non-current, since a 26-month operating cycle is not clearly identifiable and the cycle defaults to twelve months
options.misconception: overrides a stated operating cycle with the twelve-month default, which applies only where the cycle cannot be identified
options.why: The default is a fallback for entities whose cycle cannot be pinned down. Here the cycle is stated as clearly identifiable at 26 months, so it governs, and a distiller's ageing period is the textbook case of a cycle longer than a year.

options.text: Only the bottled whisky and the overdraft are current; the barley and the spirit sit more than twelve months from cash and are non-current
options.misconception: applies the twelve-month test to items the operating-cycle limb has already made current
options.why: The two limbs are alternatives, not a sequence. An item that fails the twelve-month test can still be current on the operating-cycle test, which is why raw materials in a long process are shown as working capital rather than as long-term assets.

options.text: All three inventories and the fifteen-month trade payable are current, and the overdraft is current as well
options.why: An asset is current when the entity expects to realise it in its normal operating cycle, even where realisation is not expected within twelve months after the reporting period, so the barley, the spirit in barrels and the bottled whisky are all current. The same operating-cycle limb makes a trade payable current when it is settled in that cycle, whatever its due date, so the fifteen-month payable is current too. The overdraft is current on a different ground — no right to defer settlement for at least twelve months exists at the reporting date.
keywords: twelve months after the reporting period

citation.ref: para 66 and 68 for assets, para 69 and 70 for liabilities

items.scenario: A distiller ages whisky for 24 months before it can be sold, and its normal operating cycle is clearly identifiable at 26 months. At 31 March 2026 it holds barley and yeast, part-distilled spirit in barrels, and bottled whisky ready for sale, none of which will turn into cash within twelve months.
