options.misconception: stops the capital market line at the market portfolio, forgetting that it continues beyond it for anyone willing to borrow
options.why: The market portfolio is the best holding of risky assets, and it is not the end of the line. Combining it with lending gives points below it and combining it with borrowing gives points above it, up to 16 per cent at a standard deviation of 25 per cent.

options.text: 16 per cent, by putting 125 per cent of his money in the market portfolio and borrowing the other 25 per cent at the risk-free rate
options.why: The capital market line runs from the risk-free rate through the market portfolio and onwards: expected return is 6 + [(14 − 6)/20] × 25 = 6 + 0.4 × 25 = 16 per cent. The slope of 0.4 is the reward per unit of risk. A standard deviation of 25 against the market's 20 means holding 25/20 = 1.25 times his own money in the market, and the extra 0.25 is borrowed — a borrowing portfolio. Checking it, 1.25 × 14 − 0.25 × 6 = 16 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: The risk-free rate is 6 per cent. The market portfolio is expected to return 14 per cent with a standard deviation of 20 per cent. An investor is willing to carry a standard deviation of 25 per cent and wants the best return the capital market line offers at that level of risk.

items.stem: What is the combined company's earnings per share?

options.text: ₹4.00, unchanged
options.misconception: sets the exchange ratio on the two earnings per share figures when the offer is stated in terms of market prices
options.why: On earnings per share the ratio would be 3.00 / 4.00 = 0.75, meaning 7.5 lakh new shares and 110 / 27.5 = ₹4.00 — no change at all, which is what swapping on earnings always produces. The deal here is struck on market prices, and the market rates B Ltd's earnings below A Ltd's, so only 5 lakh shares are issued.

options.misconception: puts the combined earnings over the acquirer's own share count, forgetting that shares had to be issued to pay for the target
options.why: 110 / 20 = ₹5.50 counts B Ltd's earnings and none of the cost of getting them. The consideration was 5 lakh new shares, and they dilute the earnings across 25 lakh shares, not 20.

The exchange ratio on market prices is 30 / 60 = 0.5, so B Ltd's 10 lakh shareholders receive 5 lakh new shares in A Ltd. Combined earnings are 80 + 30 = ₹110 lakh over 20 + 5 = 25 lakh shares, giving an earnings per share of ₹4.40 against A Ltd's own ₹4.00 before the deal. The rise is arithmetic: B Ltd's earnings were bought on a multiple of 10 while A Ltd's own shares trade on 15.

options.text: About ₹3.67
options.misconception: adds the target's own share count to the acquirer's instead of the number of shares actually issued in exchange for them
options.why: 110 / 30 = ₹3.67 assumes B Ltd's 10 lakh shares carry over one for one. They are cancelled and replaced at the agreed ratio of 0.5, which is 5 lakh A Ltd shares, so the combined count is 25 lakh.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A Ltd has 20 lakh shares, earnings of ₹80 lakh and a market price of ₹60 a share. B Ltd has 10 lakh shares, earnings of ₹30 lakh and a market price of ₹30 a share. A Ltd will absorb B Ltd and the shares are to be exchanged on the basis of the two market prices. Earnings are simply added, with no synergy.

items.stem: What is the most the acquirer can pay for the target?

options.text: ₹215 crore
options.why: The savings are worth 25 × (1 − 0.28) = ₹18 crore a year after tax, and in perpetuity at 12 per cent that is 18 / 0.12 = ₹150 crore. The integration cost of ₹25 crore is a cost of the acquisition and comes off, leaving net synergy of ₹125 crore. The ceiling is the target's own standalone value plus that net synergy: 90 + 125 = ₹215 crore.

options.text: About ₹273 crore
options.misconception: capitalises the savings before tax, valuing money the taxman will take
options.why: 25 / 0.12 = ₹208.33 crore, less ₹25 crore and plus ₹90 crore, gives ₹273 crore. Only ₹18 crore of each year's ₹25 crore stays in the business; the other ₹7 crore is extra tax on the higher profit the saving creates. Capitalising the pre-tax figure overstates the ceiling by nearly ₹60 crore.

options.text: ₹90 crore
options.misconception: refuses any premium at all, when the synergy is precisely the fund a premium can be paid out of
options.why: Paying the standalone value and not a rupee more would leave the acquirer with the whole ₹125 crore of net synergy, and no seller would accept it. The ceiling is not where the acquirer's gain is largest but where it runs out, and that is at ₹215 crore.

options.text: ₹240 crore
options.misconception: capitalises the savings and never deducts what it costs to achieve them, when the integration spend is as much a part of the deal as the price
options.why: 90 + 150 = ₹240 crore treats the ₹150 crore of savings as free. Somebody has to pay the ₹25 crore of integration cost, and it is the acquirer, out of the same pocket as the purchase price. Net of it the synergy is ₹125 crore and the ceiling is ₹215 crore.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A target is worth ₹90 crore as an independent company. The acquirer expects the merger to produce cost savings of ₹25 crore a year before tax, for ever. Integrating the two businesses will cost ₹25 crore, payable at once. The tax rate is 28 per cent and the relevant cost of capital is 12 per cent.

items.stem: What money multiple does the sponsor earn on exit?

options.text: 3.25 times
options.misconception: credits the whole exit enterprise value to the sponsor, forgetting that the lenders are repaid before the equity sees anything
options.why: 780 / 240 = 3.25 times skips the debt. ₹360 crore is still owed on the day of sale and the lenders take it off the top; only the ₹420 crore beneath it belongs to the sponsor.

options.text: 2.50 times
options.misconception: values the exit at the multiple the sponsor paid on entry, so the deal is credited with growth it achieved and spared the fall in the multiple it did not control
options.why: 120 × 8.0 = ₹960 crore less ₹360 crore gives ₹600 crore and 2.50 times. The exit multiple is set by whoever is buying, and here it is 6.5, not 8.0. That contraction costs the sponsor ₹180 crore of enterprise value and three-quarters of a turn of return.

options.text: About 0.98 times
options.misconception: applies the change in enterprise value to the sponsor's stake in proportion, which is the arithmetic of an ungeared holding
options.why: Enterprise value did fall from ₹800 crore to ₹780 crore, and 780 / 800 gives 0.975. But the sponsor never owned the enterprise — it owned a ₹240 crore slice sitting beneath ₹560 crore of debt, and that slice grows as the debt above it shrinks. That is the whole point of leverage, and it works in the sponsor's favour here.

options.text: 1.75 times
options.why: Exit enterprise value is 120 × 6.5 = ₹780 crore, and the debt still outstanding comes off first: 780 − 360 = ₹420 crore of equity. Against the ₹240 crore put in that is 420 / 240 = 1.75 times. The ₹200 crore of debt repaid and the 20 per cent EBITDA growth together outweighed the fall in the exit multiple from 8.0 to 6.5, but only just.

citation.ref: Ch. Mergers, Acquisitions and Corporate Restructuring

items.scenario: A sponsor buys a company at 8.0 times an EBITDA of ₹100 crore, so ₹800 crore, funded with ₹560 crore of debt and ₹240 crore of its own equity. Five years later EBITDA is ₹120 crore, debt outstanding is ₹360 crore, and buyers are only willing to pay 6.5 times EBITDA.

items.stem: What one-year rupee interest rate is consistent with the international Fisher effect?

options.text: About 0.72 per cent
options.misconception: divides by the expected rate instead of multiplying, which has the rupee strengthening when the quoted numbers say it weakens
options.why: 1.045 × 80/83 = 1.0072 puts the ratio upside down. Going from ₹80 to ₹83 a dollar means more rupees per dollar, which is a weaker rupee, so the multiplier is 83/80 and the rupee rate has to be the higher of the two, not the lower.

options.text: 4.50 per cent, the same as the dollar rate
options.misconception: assumes the two currencies must pay the same nominal rate, when it is the expected currency movement that equalises them and not the rates themselves
options.why: If both paid 4.5 per cent while the rupee was expected to fall to ₹83, no rupee investor would lend in rupees. What the effect equalises is the return after the expected exchange movement, and that needs a rupee rate of about 8.42 per cent.

options.text: About 8.42 per cent
options.why: The international Fisher effect says one plus the rupee rate equals one plus the dollar rate times the expected change in the rate of exchange: 1.045 × 83/80 = 1.045 × 1.0375 = 1.0842, so about 8.42 per cent. Put in money, a dollar investor with ₹80 could earn 4.5 per cent at home, and for the two routes to leave him equally well off the rupee must pay enough to cover both that and the ₹3 the rupee is expected to lose.

options.text: 8.25 per cent
options.misconception: adds the expected depreciation to the foreign interest rate instead of compounding them, leaving out the depreciation suffered on the interest itself
options.why: 83/80 is a fall of 3.75 per cent and 4.5 + 3.75 = 8.25 per cent. The rupee weakens on the interest as well as on the principal, so the two multiply: 1.045 × 1.0375 = 1.0842. The approximation is close at these numbers and drifts as the rates widen.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: The spot rate is ₹80 to the dollar and the market expects it to be ₹83 to the dollar in a year. The one-year nominal interest rate in the United States is 4.5 per cent.

items.stem: What does leading and lagging tell the company to do?

options.text: Lag the payable and lead the receivable, the standard action when the home currency is expected to strengthen
options.misconception: reads a single direction for the rupee when it is expected to move differently against the two currencies in the question
options.why: The rupee is not simply strengthening. It is expected to weaken against the dollar and strengthen against the euro, and each exposure is judged against its own currency. Lagging the dollar payable is the one action here that loses money on both counts.

options.text: Delay both, to keep the money inside the business for as long as possible
options.misconception: treats leading and lagging as a cash-management preference rather than a view on currencies, so it gives the same answer whatever the rates are expected to do
options.why: Holding cash longer is worth something, and it is not what this tool is for. Lagging the dollar payable means buying dollars after they have become dearer, and lagging the euro receivable means converting euros after they have become cheaper — losing on both sides to gain three months of float.

options.text: Lead the payable and lag the receivable, because payables are always settled early and receivables collected late
options.misconception: applies a fixed rule by the type of item, when the rule depends entirely on which way the currency in question is expected to move
options.why: Half right by accident. If the euro were expected to strengthen against the rupee the receivable should indeed be lagged — but here the rupee is expected to strengthen against the euro, so waiting costs money. There is no rule about payables and receivables, only about currencies.

options.text: Settle the dollar payable early and press for the euro receivable early — lead both
options.why: Leading means paying or collecting before the due date and lagging means after it, and the choice turns on which way the currency is expected to move. Dollars are expected to cost more rupees in three months, so the payable is settled now while they are cheap. Euros are expected to fetch fewer rupees in three months, so the receivable is collected now while it is worth more. Both point the same way here, which is why reading the currency rather than the type of item is the whole skill.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian company has a payable of one million dollars and a receivable of one million euros, both due in three months. It expects the rupee to weaken against the dollar over those three months and to strengthen against the euro. Both counterparties are group companies and will accept early settlement.

items.stem: What is the effective annual cost of this borrowing in rupees?

options.text: About 3.41 per cent
options.misconception: counts the currency movement but treats the front-end fee as an expense outside the loan, when it reduces the money the borrower ever had the use of
options.why: 1.06 × 80/82 − 1 = 3.41 per cent is the cost of a dollar loan with no fee. Here ₹16.4 lakh was taken off the top, so the company services a one million dollar loan on 990,000 dollars of money. Dividing by what was received rather than by what was signed for gives 4.46 per cent.

options.text: About 4.46 per cent
options.why: The company actually receives 990,000 × ₹82 = ₹8,11,80,000. In a year it must repay 1.06 million dollars at ₹80, which is ₹8,48,00,000. The cost is 36,20,000 / 8,11,80,000 = about 4.46 per cent. The strengthening rupee cuts the cost well below the 6 per cent coupon, and the front-end fee claws part of that saving back by shrinking what was received.

options.text: About 3.56 per cent
options.misconception: subtracts the expected currency gain from the coupon instead of compounding the two, and drops the front-end fee as well
options.why: ₹82 to ₹80 is a fall of 2.44 per cent, and 6 − 2.44 = 3.56 per cent. The rupee gain applies to the interest as well as to the principal, so the two compound rather than subtract, and the fee has still to come out. Both corrections together give 4.46 per cent.

options.text: 6.00 per cent
options.misconception: quotes the foreign coupon as the cost, ignoring both the movement in the exchange rate and the fee deducted at drawdown
options.why: 6 per cent is what the loan costs in dollars. The company earns and reports in rupees, and in rupees it borrowed ₹8.12 crore and will repay ₹8.48 crore. That works out at 4.46 per cent, and the difference is a real gain, not a presentation.

citation.ref: Ch. International Financial Management

items.scenario: An Indian company borrows one million dollars for one year at 6 per cent interest. A front-end fee of 1 per cent of the loan is deducted at drawdown, so only 990,000 dollars are received. The spot rate is ₹82 to the dollar and the company expects ₹80 to the dollar in a year.

items.stem: What is the result on the futures position?

options.text: A gain of ₹7,50,000
options.misconception: applies the three-month fraction twice, once to the interest period and once again to the whole position
options.why: 30,00,000 × 3/12 = ₹7,50,000 scales an answer that has already been scaled. The 3/12 belongs inside the value of one contract and nowhere else; after that the twenty contracts are simply added up.

options.text: A loss of ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: forgets that the price is quoted as one hundred minus the rate, so it reads a rise in rates as a rise in the futures price and puts the seller on the losing side
options.why: Rates rose, and because the quote is 100 minus the rate the price fell from 94.00 to 92.80. Somebody who sold at 94.00 buys back at 92.80 and gains. That is exactly why a borrower sells: the futures gain arrives at the same moment the borrowing becomes dearer.

options.misconception: applies the rate change to the notional principal for a full year, when the contract prices only three months of interest
options.why: 20 × 5,00,00,000 × 0.0120 = ₹1.20 crore charges a whole year of interest on the notional. These contracts settle a three-month period, so the move is multiplied by 3/12 and each contract is worth ₹1,50,000, not ₹6,00,000.

options.text: A gain of ₹30,00,000
options.why: The price moved 1.20, which is 120 basis points, and the treasurer is short, so the fall is a gain. Each contract is worth 5,00,00,000 × 0.0120 × 3/12 = ₹1,50,000, because the contract covers only a three-month interest period however large the notional principal is. Twenty contracts give ₹30,00,000, which is set against the extra interest the treasurer now pays on the actual borrowing.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer sells 20 interest rate futures contracts at a price of 94.00. Each contract has a notional principal of ₹5 crore and covers a three-month interest period, and the price is quoted as one hundred minus the rate. At settlement the reference rate is 7.20 per cent, so the futures price is 92.80.

items.stem: At what index level would the trader first face a margin call?

options.misconception: has the direction of the loss the wrong way round, treating a seller of futures as somebody who loses when the index falls
options.why: 22,000 − 1,100 = 20,900 is where a buyer would be called. This trader sold, so a falling index credits the account and a rising one debits it. The danger is above, at 23,100.

options.misconception: counts the lot size of one contract when two are open, so it doubles the number of points the cushion can absorb
options.why: 55,000 / 25 = 2,200 points prices the move on a single lot. Two contracts are open, so every index point moves ₹50 through the account, not ₹25, and the cushion runs out in half the distance — 1,100 points.

options.misconception: measures the fall against the whole initial margin, when the call is triggered as soon as the balance drops through the maintenance level
options.why: 2,20,000 / 50 = 4,400 points is where the account would be emptied altogether. The maintenance margin exists precisely so that nobody gets that far: the call comes at ₹1,65,000, which is ₹55,000 or 1,100 points below the start.

A short position loses when the index rises. The cushion is the initial margin less the maintenance margin, 2,20,000 − 1,65,000 = ₹55,000, and each index point costs 2 × 25 = ₹50. So 55,000 / 50 = 1,100 points may be lost before the balance touches the maintenance line, which puts the trigger at 22,000 + 1,100 = 23,100. Once it is breached the call restores the full initial margin, not merely the shortfall.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A trader sells 2 index futures contracts at 22,000, with a lot size of 25 units per contract. The initial margin on the two contracts together is ₹2,20,000 and the maintenance margin is ₹1,65,000. Nothing else moves in the account.

items.stem: What is the best estimate of the option's price after those five days?

options.text: About ₹14.54
options.misconception: counts the gain from rising volatility and forgets that five days of life have been consumed as well
options.why: 14.00 + 0.54 = ₹14.54 leaves out theta. Every day that passes takes ₹0.06 off a long option whatever else is happening, and five of them have gone: ₹0.30. Both effects apply at once, leaving ₹14.24.

options.text: About ₹13.70
options.misconception: counts the time decay and treats vega as irrelevant because the share price did not move, when vega prices expected future movement and not past movement
options.why: 14.00 − 0.30 = ₹13.70 is the price if nothing but the calendar changed. Volatility did change, from 24 to 27, and an option is worth more when the market expects a wider range of outcomes — whether or not anything has happened yet. That adds ₹0.54.

options.text: About ₹14.24
options.why: Theta takes 5 × 0.06 = ₹0.30 out for the five days that have passed, and vega puts 3 × 0.18 = ₹0.54 back for the three percentage points volatility has risen. The net change is plus ₹0.24, so the estimate is ₹14.24. The share never moved, which is what makes this a clean reading of the two: a bought option can gain on a still day if the market's view of future movement widens enough.

options.text: About ₹13.16
options.misconception: treats a rise in volatility as a loss to the option holder, which is the writer's position and not the buyer's
options.why: 14.00 − 0.30 − 0.54 = ₹13.16 subtracts the vega effect. Rising volatility helps the buyer of either a call or a put, because the option's downside is capped at the premium while its upside is not. It is the writer who loses when volatility climbs.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A call option is priced at ₹14.00. Its theta is minus 0.06 a day and its vega is 0.18 for each percentage point of volatility. Over the next five days the share price does not move, but implied volatility rises from 24 per cent to 27 per cent.

items.stem: What annual return did the unit holder earn?

options.text: 16.0 per cent
options.why: The holding period return is (27.50 − 25.00 + 0.50) / 25.00 = 3.00 / 25.00 = 12.0 per cent for the nine months. Stated on an annual basis that is 12.0 × 12/9 = 16.0 per cent, because the money was at work for three quarters of a year and a yearly figure has to cover four quarters.

options.text: 9.0 per cent
options.misconception: multiplies by nine twelfths instead of twelve ninths, scaling a part-year return down when it should be scaled up
options.why: 12.0 × 9/12 = 9.0 per cent shrinks a return the holder earned in less than a year. The fraction goes the other way: a year is twelve ninths of nine months, so the annual figure is 12.0 × 12/9 = 16.0 per cent.

options.text: About 13.3 per cent
options.misconception: annualises the change in net asset value alone and leaves the dividend out, when the cash paid out is part of what the holder earned
options.why: (27.50 − 25.00) / 25.00 = 10.0 per cent, annualised to 13.3 per cent, counts the price rise and forgets the ₹0.50 taken in cash. That ₹0.50 came out of the fund's own assets and is exactly why the closing figure is not higher still.

options.text: 12.0 per cent
options.misconception: reports the nine-month return as though it were an annual one, so a shorter holding is quietly compared with a longer one
options.why: 12.0 per cent is what the holder earned in nine months, and it is the right first step. Left there it understates the scheme, because anyone comparing it with a fund that took a year to earn 12 per cent would rank the two the same when this one was a quarter faster.

citation.ref: Ch. Mutual Funds

items.scenario: A unit holder bought units of a scheme at a net asset value of ₹25.00 and sold them exactly nine months later at ₹27.50. During those nine months the scheme paid a dividend of ₹0.50 a unit, taken in cash. Returns are to be stated on a simple annual basis.

items.stem: What is the share worth today?

options.text: About ₹59.21
options.misconception: discounts the capitalised value for four years because the first dividend falls in year four, when the formula already places that value one year ahead of the dividend it uses
options.why: 100 / 1.6890 = ₹59.21 charges one year of discounting twice. Dividing a dividend by the required return less growth produces a value as at the end of the year before that dividend — year three here — so three years of discounting is the whole of it.

options.text: About ₹67.50
options.why: Capitalising the ₹8 dividend gives 8 / (0.14 − 0.06) = ₹100, and that figure stands one year before the dividend inside it — at the end of year three. Discounting three years back, 100 / 1.4815 = ₹67.50. Nothing else is added, because there is no dividend in years one to three to discount.

options.misconception: stops at the capitalised figure and never brings it back to today, quoting a value that stands three years out as if it were a price now
options.why: ₹100 is what the share will be worth at the end of year three, when the first dividend is one year away. Money three years out is not money today; at 14 per cent it is worth 100 / 1.4815 = ₹67.50.

options.text: About ₹71.55
options.misconception: grows the ₹8 by another year before capitalising it, when ₹8 is already the first dividend of the growing phase
options.why: 8 × 1.06 / 0.08 = ₹106, discounted three years, gives ₹71.55. The growth rate applies from the first dividend onwards, so ₹8 goes into the formula as it stands. Growing it once more assumes a dividend in year three that the company has said it will not pay.

citation.ref: Ch. Business Valuation

items.scenario: A company will pay no dividend at all for the next three years while it builds capacity. Its first dividend, of ₹8 a share, will be paid at the end of year four, and dividends will grow at 6 per cent a year for ever after that. The required return is 14 per cent. Take 1.14 cubed as 1.4815 and 1.14 to the fourth as 1.6890.

items.stem: What is the investor's position?

options.text: The total interest he ever collects can come to less than the ₹40 crore he paid, so he can lose money even holding to the end
options.why: Interest is charged on principal that is still outstanding. When borrowers repay early the principal disappears and the interest stops with it, so the strip's cash flows do not merely arrive later — some of them never arrive at all. That is what makes an Interest Only strip unusual: an ordinary bond held to maturity returns its face value, and this instrument carries no such promise.

options.text: The strip gains, because a lower discount rate raises the present value of every future payment
options.misconception: applies the ordinary bond rule that prices rise when rates fall, missing that the strip's own cash flows shrink at the same time
options.why: Falling rates do lift the value of a fixed stream. This stream is not fixed: the same fall in rates is what sends borrowers off to refinance, and the interest they would have paid is cancelled. The loss of cash flow outweighs the gentler discounting.

options.text: His loss is limited, since the principal still outstanding is returned to him at the end
options.misconception: reads a principal claim into an instrument that was defined by having none
options.why: The strip pays interest and nothing else — the principal goes to the Principal Only holder by construction. There is no redemption amount to fall back on, which is why these instruments are described as highly volatile and are the least preferred by investors.

options.text: He is unaffected, because early repayment of principal is the Principal Only holder's concern and the interest schedule is fixed
options.misconception: assumes the strip has a fixed payment schedule, when the schedule is whatever the borrowers choose to do
options.why: The schedule is not fixed on either strip. Prepayment shortens the life of the whole pool, and the two halves feel it in opposite ways — the Principal Only holder gets his money sooner and gains, while the Interest Only holder simply stops being paid.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An investor pays ₹40 crore for the Interest Only strip on a pool of housing loans. Market interest rates then fall sharply and a large part of the pool is repaid early by borrowers refinancing elsewhere.

items.stem: Is the fund asking for this at the right point?

options.text: No — the exit plan is the sixth stage and belongs at the end of the holding period, once the state of the market is actually known
options.misconception: reads the order of the list as the order in which each matter is decided, when the exit is settled at the outset and only carried out at the end
options.why: What happens at the end is the exit itself. What happens at the beginning is the agreement about it — which routes are open and on what terms. Leaving that to be argued six years later is how a fund ends up locked into a company it cannot leave.

options.text: No — the six stages end at post investment activity, and an exit plan is a commercial preference rather than a stage of the process
options.misconception: drops a stage from the list, treating the exit as something outside the process when it is the sixth stage of it
options.why: The exit plan is the sixth and last of the named stages, not an optional extra. A venture fund exists to put money in and take it out again within a set life, so how it leaves is structural to the investment rather than a matter of taste.

options.text: No — this is post investment activity, which starts the moment the term sheet is signed
options.misconception: starts post investment activity at signature rather than at investment, and misplaces the exit discussion into it
options.why: Post investment activity begins once the money is actually in, and it is where the fund puts its nominee on the board and monitors the milestones. Nothing has been invested here; terms are still being agreed, which is deal structuring.

options.text: Yes — the exit plan is named last among the six stages, but the fund settles it at the time of investing, because that is when it has the leverage to insist
options.why: The six stages are deal origination, screening, due diligence, deal structuring, post investment activity and exit plan. The list names the stages; it does not say every one of them is decided only when its turn arrives. The exit plan is spelled out at the time of investing, while the founder still needs the money — afterwards the fund is a minority holder asking a favour.

citation.ref: Ch. Startup Finance

items.scenario: A venture fund has finished checking a founder's claims and is now settling terms. Before it signs, it requires the promoter to set out in writing how the fund will eventually get its money back out of the company — even though the fund expects to stay invested for six years or more.

items.stem: What is the arbitrage-free futures price?

options.misconception: charges the interest on the money tied up but forgets that holding the stock also pays a dividend, so it prices the futures as if the two positions earned the same
options.why: 220 + 8.25 = ₹228.25 counts only the cost of carrying the stock. A person who buys the stock instead of the futures receives ₹2.50 that the futures holder never sees, and that receipt reduces the premium the futures can fairly command, bringing the fair price to ₹225.75.

The cost-of-carry model is futures price equals spot price plus carrying cost less returns. The carrying cost for three months is 220 × 0.15 × 0.25 = ₹8.25, and the ₹2.50 dividend is a return the stockholder collects and the futures holder does not, so it comes off: 220 + 8.25 − 2.50 = ₹225.75. That is the theoretical minimum price at which the contract can trade without opening an arbitrage.

options.misconception: adds the dividend to the carrying cost instead of deducting it, treating a receipt as though it were another expense of holding the stock
options.why: 220 + 8.25 + 2.50 = ₹230.75 puts the dividend on the wrong side. The formula is spot plus carrying cost less returns, and a dividend is a return. Adding it makes holding the stock look dearer than it is and pushes the fair futures price ₹5 too high.

options.misconception: applies a full year of interest to a three-month contract, ignoring that the carrying cost runs only for the life of the contract
options.why: 220 × 0.15 = ₹33 is a year's interest, giving 220 + 33 − 2.50 = ₹250.50. The contract runs three months, so the rate is pro-rated by 0.25, which is ₹8.25. Charging four times the carry puts the futures ₹24.75 above where arbitrage would hold it.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A stock trades at ₹220 on 31 December. Three-month futures on it are available. Money is borrowed and lent at 15 per cent a year. The company will pay a dividend of ₹2.50 a share before the futures contract expires, and the holder of the stock — not the holder of the futures — will receive it.

items.stem: What does the fund do in the futures market?

options.text: Sell 96 contracts
options.misconception: uses the target beta itself as the hedge ratio instead of the difference between the target and the beta the portfolio already has
options.why: 0.8 × ₹12 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 96 contracts hedges an exposure of 0.8, leaving an effective beta of 1.2 − 0.8 = 0.4 — half of what was asked for. The calculation works on the gap between where the portfolio is and where it is wanted, which is 0.4.

options.text: Sell 144 contracts
options.misconception: computes a full hedge when only part of the beta is to be removed, which leaves the portfolio short of the market rather than lightly exposed to it
options.why: 1.2 × ₹12 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 144 contracts takes the beta all the way to zero. The fund asked for 0.8, not nought, so only the 0.4 of beta it wants to shed is hedged. Selling 144 would leave it hoping the market falls.

options.text: Buy 48 contracts
options.misconception: gets the number right and the direction backwards, so the trade raises the portfolio's market sensitivity instead of lowering it
options.why: Long futures add market exposure. Buying 48 contracts takes the effective beta from 1.2 up to 1.6, moving away from the 0.8 target rather than towards it. Lowering a beta means selling futures; raising one means buying them.

options.text: Sell 48 contracts
options.why: The number of contracts is the change in beta wanted, times the portfolio value, divided by the contract value. (0.8 − 1.2) × ₹12 crore = −₹4.8 crore of market exposure to shed, and ₹4.8 crore ÷ ₹10 lakh = 48 contracts. The sign is negative, so they are sold.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A fund holds a ₹12 crore equity portfolio with a beta of 1.2. It does not want to come out of the market; it wants the portfolio to behave as though its beta were 0.8. Index futures trade at 20,000 with a lot size of 50, so one contract is worth ₹10 lakh.

items.stem: What is that put worth?

options.misconception: rearranges the identity with the wrong signs, adding the share and subtracting the present value of the strike instead of the other way round
options.why: 150 + 12 − 148.15 = ₹13.85 is the identity turned inside out. Parity says call minus put equals share minus present value of strike, so the share is subtracted from the put's side, not added to it: −150 + 12 + 148.15 = ₹10.15.

Put-call parity in the study material's form is value of put = minus value of share, plus value of call, plus present value of the exercise price. The present value of the exercise price is 160 ÷ 1.08 = ₹148.15, so the put is −150 + 12 + 148.15 = ₹10.15. The identity holds whatever the share's volatility, because it is enforced by arbitrage rather than by a valuation model.
keywords: present value of the exercise price

options.misconception: puts the strike into the identity at its face amount instead of its present value, ignoring that the strike is paid a year from now and not today
options.why: −150 + 12 + 160 = ₹22.00 uses the undiscounted strike. The parity portfolio lends only ₹148.15 today so that it grows to ₹160 by expiry. The ₹11.85 of interest between the two is the whole difference between ₹22.00 and ₹10.15.

options.misconception: assumes a call and a put on the same share, strike and expiry must cost the same, when they are equal only where the share price equals the present value of the strike
options.why: The two premiums are equal only in the special case where the share stands exactly at the present value of the strike. Here the share is ₹150 and that present value is ₹148.15, so the call is dearer by exactly ₹1.85 and the put is ₹10.15.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹150 and pays no dividend. A one-year European call at a strike of ₹160 costs ₹12. The one-year risk-free rate is 8 per cent. A European put on the same share, at the same strike and expiry, is not quoted anywhere.

items.stem: What is the one-step binomial value of the put?

options.misconception: computes the expected payoff correctly and then quotes it as the price, forgetting that the payoff arrives one period from now
options.why: ₹6.67 is what the put is expected to be worth at the end of the period, not what it is worth today. Dividing by the risk-free growth factor of 1.10 brings it back to ₹6.06, and the 61 paise is the interest on the money over the period.

options.misconception: prices the option on what exercising it today would fetch, when an option's value comes from what it may be worth at expiry and not from its intrinsic value now
options.why: The share is at ₹100 and the strike is ₹100, so exercising today gains nothing. That is the intrinsic value, not the price. There is a real chance the share falls to ₹80, and what the put is worth today is the discounted value of that chance, ₹6.06.

With u = 1.25 and d = 0.80, the risk-neutral probability is p = (1.10 − 0.80) ÷ (1.25 − 0.80) = 0.30 ÷ 0.45 = 0.6667. The put pays nothing at ₹125 and 100 − 80 = ₹20 at ₹80, so the expected payoff is 0.3333 × 20 = ₹6.67, and discounting that at 1.10 gives ₹6.06.

options.misconception: values the call rather than the put, taking the payoff on the up move where a put pays on the down move
options.why: 0.6667 × (125 − 100) ÷ 1.10 = ₹15.15 is the call. Check the pair against put-call parity: call minus put should equal share minus the discounted strike, 100 − 100 ÷ 1.10 = ₹9.09, and 15.15 − 6.06 = ₹9.09. The two are consistent, and only ₹6.06 answers what was asked.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trading at ₹100 will move in one period to either ₹125 or ₹80. The risk-free growth factor for the period is 1.10. A European put on the share has a strike of ₹100.

items.stem: How many puts does it buy, and why is that not 20,000?

options.text: 8,000 puts
options.misconception: multiplies the shares by the delta where the sizing divides, which is the arithmetic for hedging an option position with shares run backwards
options.why: 20,000 × 0.4 = 8,000 is the calculation for the opposite problem — how many shares hedge a written option. Here the options are the hedging instrument, so the share exposure is divided by each option's delta: 20,000 ÷ 0.4 = 50,000.

options.text: 50,000 puts
options.why: The shares carry a position delta of plus 20,000, one for each share held. Each put contributes minus 0.4, so the number needed is 20,000 ÷ 0.4 = 50,000. A put's delta is negative, which is what makes it a hedge for a long holding, and it is smaller than one in size, which is why the hedge needs more puts than there are shares.

options.text: 33,333 puts
options.misconception: divides by one minus the size of the delta, a figure that belongs to no hedge at all
options.why: 20,000 ÷ 0.6 = 33,333 uses 0.6 where 0.4 belongs. The hedge ratio is the delta itself, so the divisor is 0.4 and the answer is 50,000. At 33,333 puts the position still loses about ₹6,667 on a ₹1 fall.

options.text: 20,000 puts
options.misconception: matches one option to one share, ignoring that each put offsets only 0.4 of a share's move
options.why: On a ₹1 fall the shares lose ₹20,000 while 20,000 puts gain only 0.4 × 20,000 = ₹8,000. Three-fifths of the exposure would still be open. It takes 50,000 puts for the two sides to cancel.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A fund holds 20,000 shares of a company and wants protection against a small fall without selling them. It will buy put options on the same share, each option covering one share. The puts have a delta of minus 0.4.

items.stem: Over what range does this position make money, and how bad can each of its two sides get?

options.text: It makes money outside the range ₹460 to ₹540, and the most it can lose is the ₹40 received
options.misconception: describes the buyer's position rather than the writer's, so it hands the writer the buyer's profit region and the buyer's capped loss
options.why: Making money outside the range and losing at most the premium is the position of whoever bought this straddle. The writer took the ₹40 in and makes money when the share stays inside the range; his loss is the buyer's gain, and it is not capped.

options.text: It makes money between ₹460 and ₹540; above ₹540 the loss has no ceiling, while below ₹460 it stops at ₹460 a share
options.why: The break-even points are the same ₹460 and ₹540 as for the buyer, because a written straddle is the buyer's position seen from the other side — the two are mirror images and what one loses the other makes. Above ₹540 the written call's loss grows rupee for rupee with the share and nothing stops it. Below ₹460 the written put's loss also grows, but a share cannot fall below zero, so the worst case there is ₹500 of intrinsic value less the ₹40 received, that is ₹460.

options.text: It makes money between ₹482 and ₹522, and the most it can make is ₹40
options.misconception: charges each side only the premium of the option that finishes in the money, when the writer received both premiums whatever the share does
options.why: 500 − 18 = ₹482 and 500 + 22 = ₹522 apply one premium on each side. The writer took in ₹40 on day one and keeps it whichever way the share moves, so the cushion either side of the strike is the full ₹40 and the break-evens are ₹460 and ₹540.

options.text: It makes money between ₹460 and ₹540, and the loss has no ceiling in either direction
options.misconception: reads a written put as carrying unlimited loss like a written call, when a share price cannot go below zero and so that side is bounded
options.why: The break-evens are right and the downside is not. A call's loss is unbounded because a share can rise without limit. A put's loss stops where the share stops, at zero, so the most that side can cost is ₹500 of intrinsic value less the ₹40 premium — ₹460 a share. Large, and finite.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: A share trades at ₹500. A trader who expects it to stay where it is writes a three-month call at a strike of ₹500 for a premium of ₹22 and writes a three-month put at the same strike for a premium of ₹18. He receives ₹40 on day one.

items.stem: What does the position make?

options.text: A profit of ₹45
options.why: The bought call finishes 1,080 − 1,000 = ₹80 in the money. The written call struck at ₹1,100 finishes out of the money and expires worthless, so nothing is owed on it. The net premium paid on day one was 60 − 25 = ₹35, and 80 − 35 = ₹45. The maximum gain of ₹65 has not been reached, because the share has not passed the higher strike where the ceiling begins.

options.text: A profit of ₹80
options.misconception: reports the bought call's intrinsic value as the profit, charging none of the premium the position cost to put on
options.why: ₹80 is what the bought call is worth at expiry, not what the position made. ₹35 of net premium went out on day one and has to be recovered before anything is profit, which leaves ₹45.

options.text: A profit of ₹65
options.misconception: assumes the position is already at its cap, when the cap applies only from the higher strike upward and the share is ₹20 short of it
options.why: ₹65 is the most this spread can make and it is reached only at or above ₹1,100. At ₹1,080 the bought call is worth ₹80 rather than ₹100, so the profit is 80 − 35 = ₹45. The last ₹20 of the share's climb would have been worth another ₹20 to the position.

options.text: A profit of ₹20
options.misconception: charges the full ₹60 premium of the bought call and never credits the ₹25 received on the call that was sold
options.why: 80 − 60 = ₹20 treats the spread as costing ₹60. The ₹25 received on the written call is real money that came in on day one, so the position cost ₹35 net and the profit is ₹45. Ignoring that credit understates every figure in the strategy.

citation.ref: Ch. Derivatives Analysis and Valuation

items.scenario: An investor built a bull call spread on a share: bought a three-month call at a strike of ₹1,000 for a premium of ₹60, and sold a three-month call on the same share and expiry at a strike of ₹1,100 for a premium of ₹25. At expiry the share finishes at ₹1,080.

items.stem: How does the money market hedge run, and roughly what rate does it lock in?

options.text: ₹87.36 per dollar
options.misconception: grosses the spot rate up for the rupee borrowing but forgets that the dollars bought today sit on deposit and earn interest over the same six months
options.why: 84 × 1.04 = ₹87.36 charges the rupee interest and credits nothing for the dollar deposit. Because the dollars earn 2 per cent over the half year, fewer of them need to be bought today, and the effective rate is 84 × 1.04 ÷ 1.02 = ₹85.65.

options.text: ₹82.35 per dollar
options.misconception: credits the interest the dollars earn but never charges the cost of the rupees borrowed to buy them, taking only the half of the calculation that helps
options.why: 84 ÷ 1.02 = ₹82.35 is what the dollars cost today once the deposit interest is allowed for. Those rupees are borrowed at 8 per cent, so six months of interest has to be added back, bringing the locked rate to ₹85.65.

options.text: Borrow dollars now, convert at spot, and invest the proceeds in rupees — locking roughly ₹85.65 per dollar
options.misconception: runs the exporter's version of the hedge on an importer's exposure, building a dollar liability where the importer already has one
options.why: Borrowing dollars manufactures a dollar debt. The importer already owes dollars; what the hedge must build is a dollar asset maturing when the payment falls due. The rate quoted happens to be right because interest rate parity fixes it either way, but the trade described leaves the exposure doubled rather than covered.

options.text: Borrow rupees now, convert at spot, and place the dollars on deposit — locking roughly ₹85.65 per dollar
options.why: The dollar deposit has to grow to exactly $5,00,000 in six months, so 5,00,000 ÷ 1.02 = $4,90,196 goes in today. At ₹84 that costs ₹4,11,76,470, which is borrowed in rupees and repaid six months later with 4 per cent for the half year, as ₹4,28,23,529. Divided by the $5,00,000 it settles, that is about ₹85.65 a dollar — the same figure as 84 × 1.04 ÷ 1.02.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An importer must pay $5,00,000 in six months. The spot rate is ₹84 per dollar. Dollar deposits earn 4 per cent a year and rupee borrowing costs 8 per cent a year. The importer will not use the forward market.

items.stem: What cross rate does the bank quote?

options.why: On its bid the bank buys sterling and pays rupees, so it buys the pound at 1.2500 dollars and sells those dollars at 83.20: 1.2500 × 83.20 = ₹104.00. On its offer it takes the other side of each leg, 1.2520 × 83.30 = ₹104.29. Chaining two quotes always widens the spread, because the bank takes the worse half of both.

options.text: ₹104.15, quoted both ways
options.misconception: works the cross from the mid rates and hands the customer a quote with no spread in it, which is not a price any dealer makes
options.why: 83.25 × 1.2510 = ₹104.15 is the mid cross. It is a useful reference number and it is not a quote — a dealer who buys and sells at the same price earns nothing on either side and loses on both legs of his own cover.

options.misconception: pairs each bid with the other quote's offer, which narrows the chained spread when chaining can only widen it
options.why: 1.2500 × 83.30 = ₹104.13 and 1.2520 × 83.20 = ₹104.17 mix the sides. A six-pip spread and a ten-paisa spread cannot combine into a four-paisa one; the bank would be quoting a tighter cross than either market it covers in, and a customer could deal both ways against it and take the difference.

options.misconception: divides the rupee quote by the sterling quote instead of multiplying, which is the arithmetic for a cross whose two quotes share a base currency
options.why: 83.20 ÷ 1.2520 = ₹66.45 and 83.30 ÷ 1.2500 = ₹66.64. Division is what you use when both quotes are against the same base. Here the dollar is the base in one and the counter in the other, so the two chain by multiplication and the pound is worth about ₹104, not ₹66.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A Mumbai bank quotes USD/INR at 83.20 / 83.30 and is quoted GBP/USD at 1.2500 / 1.2520 by its London correspondent. In each pair the first figure is the bid and the second the offer. A customer asks the bank for a two-way GBP/INR quote.

items.stem: What rate does relative purchasing power parity say today's should be, and what does the gap mean?

options.text: ₹49.50, so the market is close enough and there is no real movement to speak of
options.misconception: applies Indian inflation alone and forgets that American prices rose too, so the whole 10 per cent is charged to the rupee instead of only the 8 point gap
options.why: 45.00 × 1.10 = ₹49.50 assumes US prices stood still. They rose 2 per cent, so the rate moves on the ratio 1.10 ÷ 1.02, which is ₹48.53. Getting the parity rate wrong by ₹0.97 hides two-thirds of the real movement the comparison exists to expose.

options.text: ₹41.73, so the dollar has depreciated in real terms
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, putting foreign inflation on top, which makes the currency with the faster inflation strengthen — the opposite of what the theory says
options.why: 45.00 × 1.02 ÷ 1.10 = ₹41.73 is the formula upside down. A currency whose prices rise 10 per cent against another's 2 per cent buys less, so the rupee must weaken and the parity rate must sit above ₹45.00, not below it.

options.text: ₹48.53, and the ₹1.47 gap is a real appreciation of the rupee of 3.27 per cent
options.misconception: computes the parity rate correctly and then names the wrong currency as the one that gained, reading a rise in a direct quote as strength in the home currency
options.why: The parity rate is right. In a direct quote of rupees per dollar, a higher number means more rupees are needed for one dollar, so the dollar is the currency that gained. The rupee has depreciated in real terms by that same ₹1.47.

options.text: ₹48.53, and the ₹1.47 gap is a real appreciation of the dollar of 3.27 per cent
options.why: The same formula runs forward from last year: 45.00 × 1.10 ÷ 1.02 = ₹48.53. The market is at ₹50.00, so the dollar buys ₹1.47 more than inflation on its own explains. Measured against the ₹45.00 it started from, that is 1.47 ÷ 45.00 = 3.27 per cent of real appreciation, and it is explained by factors other than inflation.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: A year ago the exchange rate was ₹45.00 per US dollar. Over the year that has passed, inflation was 10 per cent in India and 2 per cent in the United States. Today the rate stands at ₹50.00 per dollar.

items.stem: Which exposure is this, and does any cash move because of it?

options.text: Transaction exposure, because dollar amounts had to be converted into rupees
options.misconception: reads an accounting conversion as a settlement, when transaction exposure needs an amount actually received or paid across currencies
options.why: Transaction exposure arises on a receivable, a payable or a committed amount that is settled at a rate different from the one assumed. Nothing here was settled; the dollars stayed in the subsidiary and only the reporting arithmetic changed.

options.text: No exposure at all, since the subsidiary's business is unchanged and no money was lost
options.misconception: treats an exposure as real only when it moves cash, when a translation effect changes reported net worth, gearing and any covenant written on them
options.why: It costs no cash and it is still an exposure. The consolidated figures are what lenders read covenants against and what shareholders judge the group by, and a rate move can breach a gearing covenant without a single rupee changing hands.

options.text: Translation exposure, and no cash moves — the change is in the arithmetic of consolidation
options.why: Translation exposure is the parent's restatement of a foreign subsidiary's accounts into the reporting currency. Nothing in the subsidiary's trading changed and no amount was settled at a worse rate, so no cash flow arises from it — what changed is the rupee number the consolidation reports.

options.text: Economic exposure, because the group is worth less in rupees than it was
options.misconception: applies economic exposure to a balance sheet restatement, when it is about future operating cash flows and competitive position
options.why: Economic exposure is the effect of a rate move on the present value of future operating cash flows — harm that reaches a company through its prices, its customers and its rivals. This subsidiary's customers and margins are unchanged; only the closing rate used to restate it moved.

citation.ref: Ch. Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

items.scenario: An Indian parent owns a US subsidiary whose assets and liabilities are all in dollars. This year the subsidiary traded exactly as before — same customers, same margins, same dollar profit — and settled nothing across a border. The rupee strengthened against the dollar, and the group's consolidated balance sheet now shows a smaller rupee figure for the subsidiary's net assets than last year.

items.stem: What is the settlement amount, and who pays whom?

options.text: The seller pays the buyer about ₹7,34,394
options.why: The formula is notional times the excess of the reference rate over the forward rate times the day fraction, the whole divided by one plus the reference rate for that same fraction. The gross difference is ₹20 crore × 0.015 × 90/360 = ₹7,50,000. Because an FRA settles at the start of the borrowing period rather than at its end, that figure is discounted at the actual rate now prevailing: 7,50,000 ÷ (1 + 0.085 × 0.25) = ₹7,34,394. The market fixed above the agreed rate, so the seller owes the buyer.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer about ₹7,37,101
options.misconception: discounts the difference at the agreed contract rate instead of the actual rate now prevailing, when it is the rate the market is offering that the money can be put to work at
options.why: 7,50,000 ÷ (1 + 0.07 × 0.25) = ₹7,37,101 uses the contract rate. The study material is explicit that the differential is discounted at the post-change actual rate, because that is what the buyer earns on the money over the period he now holds it early. At 8.5 per cent the answer is ₹7,34,394.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer ₹30,00,000
options.misconception: applies the rate difference to the notional for a whole year, when a 3x6 contract fixes a rate for a three-month period only
options.why: ₹20 crore × 0.015 = ₹30,00,000 is a year of the difference. A 3x6 FRA covers the three months beginning three months from now, so the day fraction of 90/360 applies and the gross figure is ₹7,50,000 before discounting.

options.text: The seller pays the buyer ₹7,50,000
options.misconception: settles the gross interest difference without discounting it, forgetting that the money changes hands at the start of the period while the extra interest it compensates for is suffered at the end
options.why: ₹7,50,000 is what the extra 1.5 per cent costs over the three months, but it is a cost borne at the end of the period. The FRA pays at the beginning, so the amount is brought back by one quarter's interest, giving ₹7,34,394. Paying the full figure early would over-compensate the buyer.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A treasurer buys a 3x6 forward rate agreement on a notional of ₹20 crore at an agreed forward rate of 7 per cent. On the settlement date the three-month reference rate fixes at 8.5 per cent. The day count is 90 days over a 360-day year.

items.stem: How much is there in total for the two of them to share through a swap, and where does it come from?

options.text: 1.0 per cent a year in total
options.why: A's advantage over B in the fixed market is 11.5 − 10 = 1.5 per cent; in the floating market it is only 1.0 − 0.5 = 0.5 per cent. The quality spread differential, 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 per cent, is the whole surplus available. It exists because A's advantage is larger in the market it does not want, so each borrows where its own edge is greatest and they swap the streams.

options.text: 2.0 per cent a year
options.misconception: adds the two market gaps instead of subtracting them, counting the same company's advantage twice over
options.why: 1.5 + 0.5 = 2.0 per cent adds an advantage A has in one market to an advantage A has in the other. Both belong to the same company; the swap can only monetise the amount by which one exceeds the other, which is 1.0 per cent.

options.text: 0.5 per cent a year
options.misconception: takes the gap in the floating market alone, which is the smaller of the two advantages rather than the difference between them
options.why: 0.5 per cent is A's edge in the floating market — the market A actually wants, and therefore the edge it could have used with no counterparty at all. What the swap is worth is the difference between the two edges, 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 per cent.

options.text: 1.5 per cent a year
options.misconception: takes A's advantage in the fixed market as the gain, when that advantage is partly matched in the floating market and only the excess can be shared
options.why: 1.5 per cent is how much cheaper A borrows fixed than B does. B is not helpless in the floating market either — it is only 0.5 per cent behind there — so 0.5 of the 1.5 is available to A without any swap at all. Only the 1.0 per cent difference between the two gaps is created by the swap.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: Company A can borrow fixed at 10 per cent or floating at MIBOR plus 0.5 per cent. Company B can borrow fixed at 11.5 per cent or floating at MIBOR plus 1 per cent. A wants floating-rate debt and B wants fixed-rate debt.

items.stem: What does the cap pay after each of those two resets?

options.text: Nothing after either reset — a cap limits the rate charged on the loan rather than paying cash
options.misconception: assumes a cap attaches to the loan and rewrites its interest rate, when it is a separate contract with a separate counterparty that settles in cash
options.why: The lender is not a party to the cap. The borrower still pays the lender at 10.5 per cent and separately receives ₹37.5 lakh from the cap seller, and it is the two together that hold the effective cost at 9 per cent.

options.text: ₹1.5 crore after the first reset, and nothing after the second
options.misconception: applies the rate difference for a whole year to a contract that resets and pays quarterly
options.why: ₹100 crore × 0.015 = ₹1.5 crore is a year of the excess. The reset covers 90 days, so the day fraction of 90/360 applies and the payment is ₹37.5 lakh. The annual figure would be reached only if the benchmark stayed at 10.5 per cent through all four quarters.

options.text: ₹37.5 lakh after the first reset, and ₹50 lakh paid away after the second
options.misconception: treats a bought cap as a swap that settles in both directions, when the buyer paid a premium precisely so that he owes nothing when rates fall
options.why: ₹100 crore × (0.090 − 0.070) × 90/360 = ₹50 lakh is what a swap struck at 9 per cent would cost the borrower at 7 per cent. A cap is an option and is exercised only when it helps; the premium paid up front is the whole of what its buyer ever gives up.

options.text: ₹37.5 lakh after the first reset, and nothing after the second
options.why: The cap pays the notional times the excess of the actual rate over the cap rate times the day fraction: ₹100 crore × (0.105 − 0.090) × 90/360 = ₹37.5 lakh, paid on the payment date at the end of that period. At 7 per cent the benchmark is below the strike, and a cap is an option, so the payment is the greater of nought and the difference — which is nothing.

citation.ref: Ch. Interest Rate Risk Management

items.scenario: A borrower buys an interest rate cap on a notional of ₹100 crore with a cap rate of 9 per cent, reset quarterly on a 90-day over 360-day basis. At the first reset the benchmark fixes at 10.5 per cent. At the next reset it fixes at 7 per cent.

items.stem: What are its Macaulay duration and its modified duration?

options.text: Both are 2 years
options.misconception: reads duration off the maturity, which is true only of a zero-coupon bond because only there does every rupee arrive at the end
options.why: A coupon-bearing bond's duration is always less than its maturity, because ₹100 comes back at the end of year one and does not wait for redemption. That early rupee pulls the weighted average down to 1.909 years, and modified duration is lower again at 1.736.

options.text: Macaulay 1.5 years
options.misconception: averages the two years without weighting them by the present value arriving in each, so a ₹100 coupon counts as heavily as a ₹1,100 redemption
options.why: (1 + 2) ÷ 2 = 1.5 years gives the two years equal billing. Ninety-one per cent of the bond's value arrives in year two, and the weights have to reflect that, which pulls the answer to 1.909 years — far closer to two than to one.

options.text: Macaulay 1.909 years, modified 1.736
options.why: Macaulay duration is the weighted average time at which the money comes back. The year-one cash flow of ₹100 has a present value of ₹90.91 and the year-two cash flow of ₹1,100 has a present value of ₹909.09, so weighting each year by its share of the ₹1,000 price gives (1 × 90.91 + 2 × 909.09) ÷ 1,000 = 1.909 years. Modified duration divides that by one plus the yield, 1.909 ÷ 1.10 = 1.736, and it is the figure that estimates the percentage price move per one per cent change in yield.

options.text: Macaulay 1.736 years, modified 1.909
options.misconception: swaps the two, when modified duration is Macaulay divided by one plus the yield and so is always the smaller of the pair
options.why: The two figures are right and they are the wrong way round. Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by 1.10, so it can only be smaller. The Macaulay figure is 1.909 years and the modified figure is 1.736.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value carries a 10 per cent annual coupon and has exactly two years left to maturity. Its yield to maturity is 10 per cent, so it trades at ₹1,000. The discount factors at 10 per cent are 0.9091 for year one and 0.8264 for year two.

items.stem: In what proportions should the fund hold them, and what does that achieve?

options.text: 40 per cent in P and 60 per cent in Q
options.why: A portfolio's duration is the weighted average of the durations of what it holds, so w × 2 + (1 − w) × 7 = 5 gives 7 − 5w = 5 and w = 0.4. At a portfolio duration of five years, matching the horizon, the price loss and the reinvestment gain from a rate move cancel on the date the money is needed, which is what immunisation means.

options.text: All of it in Bond Q, whose 7-year duration is the nearer of the two to the horizon
options.misconception: picks the single closest bond instead of blending, when a mix can hit the horizon exactly and one bond alone cannot
options.why: Bond Q is nearer — two years out against Bond P's three — and near is not matched. A portfolio of duration seven against a five-year liability loses more on a rate rise than the extra reinvestment income makes up. Blending the two hits five exactly.

options.text: 50 per cent in each
options.misconception: assumes the midpoint of two durations must be the answer, when the target of five is not the midpoint of two and seven
options.why: 0.5 × 2 + 0.5 × 7 = 4.5 years. An equal split lands halfway between the two durations, which is 4.5 and not 5. The target sits three-fifths of the way from 2 towards 7, so the weight on Q is 0.6.

options.text: 60 per cent in P and 40 per cent in Q
options.misconception: reports the weights the wrong way round, giving a portfolio duration a year short of the horizon
options.why: 0.6 × 2 + 0.4 × 7 = 4.0 years, a year short of five. A portfolio whose duration is below its horizon is exposed to rates falling, because the reinvestment income it was counting on does not arrive. Reading which weight belongs to which bond is half the calculation.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A fund must pay a fixed sum in exactly five years. Only two bonds are available: Bond P, whose duration is 2 years, and Bond Q, whose duration is 7 years.

items.stem: What does the convexity-adjusted estimate give on the fall, and what does the pair of answers show?

options.text: ₹1,136 — a 13.6 per cent gain, larger than the 10.4 per cent loss an equal rise causes
options.why: The duration term is plus 6 × 0.02 = 12 per cent and the convexity term is 0.5 × 80 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 1.6 per cent. The convexity term is added on a fall exactly as it is added on a rise, because it turns on the square of the yield change and a square is positive either way. That is the asymmetry a bondholder is paying for: 13.6 per cent up against 10.4 per cent down, on moves of the same size.

options.text: ₹1,152 — a 15.2 per cent gain
options.misconception: drops the one-half, doubling a correction that comes from the second-order term of the expansion the estimate is built on
options.why: Using 80 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 3.2 per cent instead of half of it gives 15.2 per cent and ₹1,152. The one-half belongs to the second-order term and does not go away; with it the estimate is ₹1,136.

options.text: ₹1,104 — a 10.4 per cent gain, the same size as the loss on an equal rise
options.misconception: subtracts the convexity correction on a fall, in the belief that it is added only on a rise, which makes the price response symmetric when convexity is exactly what breaks the symmetry
options.why: 12 − 1.6 = 10.4 per cent gives ₹1,104 and makes the gain and the loss mirror each other. The correction carries the square of the yield change, so it is positive whichever way the yield went, and it is always added. The right answer is 12 + 1.6 = 13.6 per cent.

options.text: ₹1,120 — a 12 per cent gain, the duration estimate with convexity left out
options.misconception: uses the straight-line duration estimate alone, which understates the gain on a fall just as it overstates the loss on a rise
options.why: Plus 6 × 0.02 = 12 per cent gives ₹1,120. The straight line is the same in both directions and the real price curve is not. Leaving the 1.6 per cent correction out costs ₹16 of estimated value here, and far more on a larger move.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond priced at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 6 years and a convexity of 80. Its yield falls by 200 basis points. On an equal rise of 200 basis points the convexity-adjusted estimate is a fall of 10.4 per cent.

items.stem: What is the effective annual yield, and why is it not 10 per cent?

options.text: 10.00 per cent
options.misconception: reads the coupon rate as the return actually earned, treating a bond that pays twice a year as though the whole ₹100 arrived at the year end
options.why: 10 per cent would be right if the ₹100 came once, at the end of the year. It comes as ₹50 after six months and ₹50 after twelve, and the first ₹50 can be put to work for the remaining half year. That is what lifts the effective figure to 10.25 per cent.

options.text: 10.38 per cent
options.misconception: compounds four times a year when the bond pays twice, applying quarterly mechanics to a half-yearly instrument
options.why: 1.025 to the fourth power, less one, is 10.38 per cent — the effective rate for a bond paying ₹25 every quarter. This one pays ₹50 every six months, so the rate per period is 5 per cent and there are two periods, giving 10.25 per cent. More frequent payment would indeed be worth more; it is not what the terms say.

options.text: 10.25 per cent
options.why: At par the yield for each half-yearly period is the coupon over the price, 50 ÷ 1,000 = 5 per cent. Two such periods compound inside the year: 1.05 × 1.05 − 1 = 0.1025, so the effective annual yield is 10.25 per cent. The 10 per cent on the certificate is a nominal rate quoted per annum, and the extra 25 basis points is what the first half-year's ₹50 earns over the rest of the year.

options.text: 5.00 per cent
options.misconception: quotes the rate per period as though it were the annual figure, halving a return instead of compounding it
options.why: 5 per cent is what the bond yields over six months, not over a year. Two of those periods make a year, and compounding rather than merely adding them gives 1.05 × 1.05 − 1 = 10.25 per cent.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Valuation

items.scenario: A bond of ₹1,000 face value pays interest at 10 per cent a year in two half-yearly instalments of ₹50 each. It is quoted at par, ₹1,000. An investor reads the coupon and says his return is 10 per cent a year.

items.stem: What are the weights, and what is that portfolio's standard deviation?

options.text: 50 per cent in each, with a standard deviation of about 11.18 per cent
options.misconception: assumes an equal split must be the least risky one, when the weights that minimise variance tilt towards the less volatile asset
options.why: 0.25 × 0.01 + 0.25 × 0.04 = 0.0125, whose square root is 11.18 per cent — worse than holding Asset A alone. An equal split gives the twice-as-volatile asset equal billing, and variance punishes that heavily because it works on the square of each weight.

options.text: 100 per cent in A, with a standard deviation of 10 per cent
options.misconception: assumes the least risky portfolio must be entirely the least risky asset, missing that a small holding of an uncorrelated asset lowers total risk
options.why: 10 per cent is beatable. Because the two assets are uncorrelated, 20 per cent of B partly offsets A's own swings, and the combination comes to 8.94 per cent. That a mix can be safer than either of its components is the whole point of diversification.

options.text: 20 per cent in A and 80 per cent in B, with a standard deviation of about 16.12 per cent
options.misconception: reports the weights swapped, loading the portfolio into the riskier asset when the minimising weight belongs to the safer one
options.why: 0.04 × 0.01 + 0.64 × 0.04 = 0.026, whose square root is 16.12 per cent. The formula puts B's variance in the numerator of A's weight precisely so that the asset with the larger variance receives the smaller share. Read the other way it maximises risk instead of minimising it.

options.text: 80 per cent in A and 20 per cent in B, with a standard deviation of about 8.94 per cent
options.why: At zero correlation the minimum variance weight in A is B's variance over the sum of the two variances: 0.04 ÷ (0.01 + 0.04) = 0.8. Variance is then 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.01 + 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.04 = 0.0064 + 0.0016 = 0.008, and the square root of that is 8.94 per cent. Note where it lands — below Asset A's own 10 per cent, so the safest mix is less risky than the safer asset held alone.

citation.ref: Ch. Portfolio Management

items.scenario: Asset A has a standard deviation of 10 per cent and Asset B one of 20 per cent. The correlation between them is zero. An investor wants the least risky combination of just these two, without regard to return.

items.stem: Which form of efficiency does this market reach, and which does it fail?

options.text: It satisfies only the weak form
options.misconception: stops at the lowest level and ignores the finding on published accounts, which is precisely the semi-strong test being met
options.why: The weak form covers past prices and volumes. Published annual results are other public information, which is the semi-strong level, and the study found that they too paid nothing. The market therefore reaches semi-strong, one rung above weak.

options.text: It fails all three forms, since somebody is beating the market
options.misconception: treats any profitable trading as proof of inefficiency at every level, when each level is defined against a stated set of information
options.why: Efficiency is always tested against a named information set. Insiders profiting says only that private information is not yet in the price. Two of the three tests were passed here, and passing the semi-strong one necessarily means passing the weak one beneath it.

options.text: It satisfies the semi-strong form and fails the strong form
options.why: The strong form says price reflects all information, private as well as public, so not even an insider could earn an abnormal return. Directors dealing on unpublished information are earning exactly that, so the strong form fails. Charts paying nothing is the weak form holding, and published results paying nothing is the semi-strong form holding — and because the levels nest, the higher of the two that holds is the market's grade.

options.text: It satisfies the strong form, since prices did move once the insiders traded
options.misconception: reads price movement after a trade as evidence of efficiency, when the test is whether anyone could earn an abnormal return from the information beforehand
options.why: Prices moving after insiders buy is the market slowly discovering what they already knew. Strong form efficiency would mean the price had moved before they could act, leaving them nothing to earn. They earned a consistent premium, so it had not.

citation.ref: Ch. Security Analysis

items.scenario: A study of one market finds three things. Trading rules built on past prices and volumes earn nothing above the market once risk is allowed for. Trading on published annual results earns nothing either. But directors dealing in their own companies' shares before an announcement is made public earn a consistent abnormal return.

items.stem: Which of the four is the financial risk?

options.text: All four, since every one of them costs the company money
options.misconception: sorts risks by whether they hurt the accounts rather than by where they come from, which would make every risk a financial risk and empty the classification of meaning
options.why: Every risk on any list ends up in the accounts somewhere; that is not what the heading means. The chapter separates strategic, compliance, operational and financial risk by their source, so that each can be owned by whoever is in a position to act on it.

options.text: The customer's default alone — the other three are operational, compliance and strategic risk in turn
options.why: Financial risk is an unexpected change in financial conditions, and a customer failing to honour its obligation is counter party risk, one of its categories. The mis-keyed payment is operational risk, which is people and process inside the company. The missed filing is compliance risk. Losing in a market the board chose to enter is strategic risk.

options.text: The missed filing and the customer default, since both end in a demand for money
options.misconception: pulls compliance risk under financial risk because a penalty is payable, when the penalty is the consequence and the source is a rule that was not followed
options.why: A missed filing is compliance risk — the failure to meet a requirement of law or regulation. What it costs is not what classifies it. Only the customer's default is financial risk here.

options.text: The mis-keyed payment, since it is a payment and money left the company
options.misconception: files a risk under the department where it happens to land rather than under what caused it
options.why: A clerk keying the wrong figure is a failure of process and control inside the company, which is operational risk however large the amount. The financial risk in this list is the customer's default, because it is an outside party failing to honour what it owes.

citation.ref: Ch. Risk Management

items.scenario: Four things go wrong at a manufacturer in one month. A clerk keys a supplier payment as ₹50 lakh instead of ₹5 lakh. A new environmental notification requires a filing that nobody made. The expansion into a new market that the board chose last year is losing badly to a bigger rival. And a customer defaults on a ₹2 crore bill.

items.stem: What are the borrowers called in this structure, and what is the NBFC now doing?

options.text: The borrowers are the investors, since it is their instalments that pay the securities
options.misconception: confuses who supplies the cash flow with who buys the paper, which are opposite ends of the same structure
options.why: The investors are the people who bought the securities the SPV issued, and they receive the money. The borrowers pay it in. They are the obligors, and their instalments are the asset the securities are backed by.

options.text: The borrowers are the obligors, and the NBFC is acting as the servicer — an administrative role sub-contracted back to it, which does not undo the sale
options.why: The obligors are the parties who owe the money, and their payments are the root of the whole securitisation, which is why the pool is assessed on their credit quality. The servicer collects what is due from the obligors, passes it to the SPV and follows up on defaults; the chapter notes that this administration is generally sub-contracted back to the originator or an associate of it.

options.text: The NBFC still owns the receivables, since it is still the one collecting them
options.misconception: reads possession of the collection process as ownership of the asset, when the true sale transferred both legal and beneficial interest to the SPV
options.why: The true sale moved legal as well as beneficial interest to the SPV, which is what takes the assets off the NBFC's balance sheet and puts them beyond its own creditors. Who physically collects the money is an administrative arrangement, and the SPV can replace the servicer without the sale being affected.

options.text: The NBFC is the credit enhancer, because the collections are still coming through it
options.misconception: reads a collection agency's work as a guarantee of payment, when enhancement is a separate and separately sized commitment
options.why: Credit enhancement is a stated commitment — over-collateralisation, a cash collateral account, or a third party's support — that absorbs losses up to a capped amount. Collecting and forwarding instalments is servicing and carries no such promise; the NBFC bears nothing if a borrower stops paying.

citation.ref: Ch. Securitization

items.scenario: An NBFC sells its car-loan receivables to an SPV in a true sale. The borrowers go on paying their instalments at the NBFC's branches exactly as before, and the NBFC forwards every collection to the SPV for a fee. It also chases anyone who falls behind, and takes legal action where it has to.

items.stem: Which stage of venture capital funding is this?

options.text: The second round
options.misconception: places a profitable company in the stage meant for one that is selling product but has not yet reached profit
options.why: The second round is working capital for early-stage companies that are selling product but are not yet profitable. This company turned profitable already, so it has passed that stage and sits at the third round.

options.text: The third round, also called mezzanine financing
options.why: The third round is expansion money for a newly profitable company, and it is the stage the study material also names mezzanine financing.
