Its due date under section 139(1) for assessment year 2026-27 is 31 October 2026. It furnishes its return under section 139(4B) on 20 December 2026.

items.stem: What is the officer to do with the application?

options.text: Grant the certificate, the permanent account number being a matter for the deductor's quarterly statement and not a condition of the certificate
options.misconception: treats the permanent account number as a reporting detail rather than the express condition section 206AA(4) makes it
options.why: The number is needed in the statement of deduction as well, and that is a separate requirement. Section 206AA(4) puts it on the application itself as a condition of the certificate.

options.text: Refuse the certificate, section 197 being open only to a person other than a company or a firm
options.misconception: imports the restriction on the self-declaration under section 197A into section 197 itself
options.why: Section 197 is open to any person receiving income on which tax is deductible under the sections it lists, a company included. It is section 197A that confines its declarations to persons other than a company or a firm.

options.text: Grant the certificate at the higher rate section 206AA prescribes for a deductee without one
options.misconception: mixes the rate section 206AA sets for a deductee with the bar the same section places on the certificate
options.why: A certificate under section 197 exists to bring a rate down. One issued at the section 206AA rate would give the applicant nothing, and the section does not contemplate it.

options.text: Refuse the certificate, a missing permanent account number being fatal to the application
options.why: Section 206AA(4) provides that no certificate under section 197 shall be granted unless the application made under that section contains the permanent account number of the applicant. The officer has no discretion to look past its absence, however sound the estimate is.
keywords: no certificate under section 197 shall be granted

citation.ref: Section 206AA(4), read with Section 197(1), Section 197A(1) and Rule 28 (Form 13)

items.scenario: A contractor working on thin margins applies to the Assessing Officer in Form 13 for a certificate under section 197 authorising his customers to deduct tax at a lower rate. The application sets out his estimated income for the year and his existing tax liabilities in full, and the officer is satisfied that the estimate is honest. The permanent account number field on the application is blank, the contractor having applied for one that has not yet been allotted.

items.stem: At what rate and for what period does interest run under section 201(1A)?

options.text: At one per cent for every month or part of a month, from 7 June 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.misconception: uses the failure-to-deduct rate and starts the period at the due date for payment
options.why: One per cent is the rate section 201(1A)(i) sets for a failure to deduct, and that clause runs from the date the tax was deductible to the date it is deducted. Once the tax has been deducted, clause (ii) governs and both the rate and the starting point change.

options.text: At one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month, from 7 June 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.misconception: takes the right rate but starts the period at the due date for payment instead of at the date of deduction
options.why: The clause names the date of deduction as the starting point. The company held the Government's money from 12 May 2025, and the interest is computed for the whole of that time.

options.text: No interest, the tax having been paid before the end of the financial year
options.misconception: treats payment within the year as compliance, which section 201(1A) does not
options.why: Section 201(1A) has no end-of-year grace. Interest runs for every month or part of a month of the delay, however and whenever the delay ends.

options.text: At one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month, from 12 May 2025 to 20 January 2026
options.why: Section 201(1A)(ii) governs tax that has been deducted but not paid. Interest runs at one and one-half per cent for every month or part of a month on the amount of such tax, from the date on which it was deducted to the date on which it is actually paid. The date on which payment fell due does not start the clock.
keywords: from the date on which it was deducted

citation.ref: Section 201(1A)(ii), read with Section 201(1A)(i) and Section 201(1)

items.scenario: Halcyon Media Ltd deducted ₹2,00,000 of tax under section 194J from a payment it made on 12 May 2025. The tax was due to be paid to the credit of the Central Government by 7 June 2025. The company in fact paid it on 20 January 2026.

items.stem: Was the Transfer Pricing Officer entitled to take up the loan?

options.text: Yes — a transaction that comes to his notice during the proceedings before him is treated as though it had been referred to him
options.why: Section 92CA(2A) provides that where any other international transaction comes to the notice of the Transfer Pricing Officer during the course of the proceedings before him, the provisions of the Chapter apply as if that transaction were one referred to him under sub-section (1). No fresh reference from the Assessing Officer is needed.

options.text: No — his jurisdiction is confined to the transactions the Assessing Officer actually referred, so the loan needed a fresh reference
options.misconception: reads section 92CA(1) as the whole of the Transfer Pricing Officer's jurisdiction, missing sub-section (2A)
options.why: That was the position before sub-section (2A) was inserted, and it is the reason the sub-section exists. A transaction the Assessing Officer never spotted is exactly the case it was written for.

options.text: No, because the loan was reported in the section 92E report and a reported transaction cannot be taken up without the assessee's consent
options.misconception: invents a consent requirement and inverts the effect of reporting
options.why: Reporting a transaction does not immunise it. A transaction not reported under section 92E is dealt with by a separate sub-section, and a reported one sits squarely inside sub-section (2A).

options.text: Yes, but only if the Principal Commissioner approves the widening of the reference
options.misconception: carries the approval condition attached to the Assessing Officer's reference over to the Transfer Pricing Officer's own power
options.why: The previous approval of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner is a condition of the reference the Assessing Officer makes under section 92CA(1). Sub-section (2A) operates on its own once the transaction comes to the Transfer Pricing Officer's notice.

citation.ref: Section 92CA(2A), read with Section 92CA(1), Section 92CA(2B) and Section 92CA(3)

items.scenario: With the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner, the Assessing Officer refers one international transaction — a royalty paid to the German parent — to the Transfer Pricing Officer. While examining the royalty, the Transfer Pricing Officer notices a second international transaction, an interest-free loan to a fellow subsidiary. That loan was reported in the company's section 92E report but was never referred to him. He determines its arm's length price as well, and the company objects that he had no jurisdiction over it.

items.stem: Who is right, and whom does the agreement bind?

options.text: The officer, because an advance pricing agreement binds the taxpayer alone and never the revenue
options.misconception: makes the agreement one-sided, which section 92CC(5) does not
options.why: The sub-section binds the person and the authorities together. An agreement binding one side only would be worth nothing to the taxpayer who applied for it.

options.text: The company — the agreement binds the Board alone, an Assessing Officer being no party to it
options.misconception: reads the agreement as a private contract between the Board and the company, binding nobody else
options.why: Section 92CC(5) reaches the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the authorities subordinate to him, so the Assessing Officer is bound while the agreement stands. It is the change in law that releases him, not any want of privity.

options.text: The company — an advance pricing agreement binds both sides for its full term, whatever happens afterwards
options.misconception: treats the agreement as immune to a change in the very law it was written under
options.why: The certainty an agreement buys is certainty about the application of the law as it stood when the agreement was made. Section 92CC(6) says so in terms.

options.text: The officer — the agreement ceases to bind on a change in law, and while it stands it binds the company and the tax authorities alike on that transaction
options.why: Section 92CC(5) binds the person in whose case the agreement is entered into, only in respect of the transaction it covers, and binds the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner and the authorities subordinate to him in respect of that person and that transaction. Section 92CC(6) then provides that the agreement shall not be binding if there is a change in law or facts having a bearing on it.

citation.ref: Sections 92CC(5) and 92CC(6), read with Section 92CC(1) and Section 92CD(1)

items.scenario: An advance pricing agreement is entered into with Vasant Systems Ltd covering the arm's length price of a management fee paid to its parent, for five consecutive previous years. In the third of those years Parliament amends the very provision on which the agreed method rests. The Assessing Officer for that year says the agreement no longer binds him. The company says an agreement is an agreement and both sides are held to it for its full term.

items.stem: Does section 9A still keep the manager's activity from creating a business connection in India?

options.text: Yes, provided he gives up the salaried post before the end of the previous year
options.misconception: invents a cure by later resignation that the section does not provide
options.why: The conditions describe the arrangement under which the activity was actually carried on during the year. Nothing in section 9A lets a condition be satisfied afterwards for the months during which it was broken.

options.text: No, and the consequence is that the fund becomes resident in India for the year
options.misconception: overstates the consequence, confusing the loss of the section 9A protection with a finding on residence
options.why: Losing section 9A means the two deemings in sections 9A(1) and 9A(2) are not available, so the manager's activity may create a business connection and the place of control may be examined. Residence still has to be decided under section 6(3) on its own facts.

options.text: No — the manager must not be an employee of the fund, and his salaried post breaks that condition
options.why: Section 9A(1) gives its protection only where the fund management activity is carried out through an eligible fund manager, and section 9A(4)(a) opens that definition with the requirement that the manager is not an employee of the eligible investment fund or a connected person of the fund. A man on the fund's payroll fails it, and the conditions that are met cannot supply the one that is not.

options.text: Yes — the employment is beside the point, section 9A caring only that the manager is registered and paid at arm's length
options.misconception: keeps the conditions most often quoted and drops the independence condition that opens the definition
options.why: Registration and arm's length remuneration are two of the conditions in section 9A(4). The first of them is independence from the fund, and a definition fails on any one of its limbs.

citation.ref: Section 9A(4)(a), read with Sections 9A(1), 9A(2) and 9A(3) and Section 6(3)

items.scenario: Meridian Offshore Fund appoints Mr Sridhar, based in Mumbai, as its fund manager. He is registered with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, acts in the ordinary course of his business, is paid at arm's length for the activity, and neither he nor his connected persons are entitled to more than the share of the fund's profits that section 9A(4) permits. He is also on the fund's own payroll as its whole-time head of research and draws a salary from it. Every condition in section 9A(3) is satisfied.

items.stem: What does the Act say on the officer's proposal and on Mr Bhalla's question?

options.text: The complaint may be filed only at the instance of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and the offence may be compounded either before or after proceedings are instituted
options.why: Section 279(1) says a person shall not be proceeded against for an offence under section 276CC except at the instance of the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, so the Assessing Officer cannot launch the prosecution on his own. Section 279(2) allows the offence to be compounded by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner, and says it may be done either before or after the institution of proceedings.

options.text: Neither sanction nor compounding arises, an offence under section 276CC being a matter for the criminal court alone
options.misconception: treats the offence as one the Act sets in motion by itself
options.why: The Act creates the offence and also says who may set it in motion and who may compound it. The criminal court tries the complaint; it does not initiate one.

options.text: The complaint needs the Principal Commissioner's sanction, but compounding is possible only before the complaint is filed
options.misconception: states the sanction requirement correctly and then halves the compounding power
options.why: The sanction half of this is right. Section 279(2) then allows compounding either before or after the institution of proceedings, so the filing of the complaint is not a cut-off.

options.text: The Assessing Officer may file the complaint himself, and once it is filed the offence can no longer be compounded
options.misconception: skips the sanction requirement and denies a compounding power the Act expressly gives after institution
options.why: The sanction of a senior authority stands between an officer's satisfaction and a criminal court. And compounding survives the filing of the complaint, the sub-section saying so in terms.

citation.ref: Sections 279(1) and 279(2), read with Section 276CC and Section 278E

items.scenario: The Assessing Officer is satisfied that Mr Bhalla wilfully failed to furnish his return for assessment year 2023-24 and that the case falls outside the proviso to section 276CC. He proposes to file a complaint in the criminal court himself, without troubling anyone above him. Mr Bhalla, hearing of it, wants to know whether the matter can still be settled without a trial.

items.stem: For what period does interest under section 244A run on this refund?

options.text: From 18 September 2025 to 14 July 2026
options.why: Section 244A(1)(b) covers a refund of any amount other than those the earlier clauses name, and gives interest at one-half per cent for every month or part of a month from the date of payment of the tax or penalty to the date on which the refund is granted. The tax was paid on 18 September 2025 and refunded on 14 July 2026.
keywords: date on which the refund is granted

options.text: From 2 May 2026 to 14 July 2026
options.misconception: treats the appellate order as the event that creates the refund and so starts the interest
options.why: The appellate order establishes that the money should never have been collected. Section 244A therefore compensates from the date it was collected, not from the date the mistake was found.

options.text: From 1 April 2026 to 14 July 2026
options.misconception: applies the starting point clause (a) sets for advance tax and tax deducted at source to a payment made against a notice of demand
options.why: The first of April is the starting point in clause (a), which deals with refunds out of advance tax and tax collected or deducted at source. Tax paid against a notice of demand is refunded with interest from the day it was paid.

options.text: No interest is payable, the refund arising from an appellate order rather than from the assessment
options.misconception: reads section 244A as confined to refunds thrown up by the assessment itself
options.why: Section 244A applies to any amount becoming due to an assessee under the Act, and a refund following an appellate order is squarely within it.

citation.ref: Section 244A(1)(b), read with Section 244A(1)(a) and Section 244A(2)

items.scenario: A demand of ₹5,00,000 was raised on Ms Fernandes by a notice under section 156 following her assessment, and she paid the whole of it on 18 September 2025. None of it was advance tax, tax deducted at source or self-assessment tax. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition by an order dated 2 May 2026, and the refund of ₹5,00,000 was granted to her on 14 July 2026.

items.stem: What is his aggregate turnover, and what is his turnover in the State of Gujarat?

options.text: ₹39 lakh for both figures, turnover in a State meaning aggregate turnover under another name
options.misconception: treats turnover in State as a synonym rather than the narrower measure it is
options.why: Section 2(112) measures the turnover of supplies made from a particular State by a taxable person. It is used where a rule has to work State by State, and it can equal the all-India figure only where the person supplies from one State and no other.

options.text: ₹36 lakh, exempt supplies belonging to turnover in a State but not to aggregate turnover
options.misconception: swaps the two definitions, dropping exempt supplies out of the wider one
options.why: Both definitions take in exempt supplies. Section 2(6) names them in terms, and section 2(112) is built on the same idea narrowed to one State. Neither definition leaves them out, which is why a person selling mostly exempt goods can still be pulled over a line.

options.text: ₹25 lakh, each registration being a distinct person whose turnover is computed on its own
options.misconception: reads section 25 as splitting the definition, when distinct persons still share one PAN
options.why: Section 25(4) makes separately registered establishments distinct persons for the charge, and section 2(6) still measures across everything under the same Permanent Account Number. The two provisions work together, and the second is not undone by the first.

options.text: Aggregate turnover ₹39 lakh, computed for the whole PAN; turnover in Gujarat ₹14 lakh
options.why: Section 2(6) computes aggregate turnover on an all India basis for persons having the same Permanent Account Number, so the two registrations are added together — ₹22 lakh plus ₹3 lakh plus ₹14 lakh. Section 2(112) defines turnover in State separately, as the turnover of supplies made from that State alone, which is ₹14 lakh. Being distinct persons changes who files a return; it does not split the definition.

citation.ref: Sections 2(6) and 2(112), read with section 25(4)

items.scenario: A person holds one Permanent Account Number and two registrations, one in Maharashtra and one in Gujarat. Supplies made from Maharashtra for the year are taxable ₹22 lakh and exempt ₹3 lakh. Supplies made from Gujarat are taxable ₹14 lakh. There is nothing else. He argues that the two registrations are distinct persons under section 25, so each State's figure stands alone.

items.stem: How do the four lines classify?

options.text: Only the liquor is exempt; the rice is taxable, a nil rate being a rate like any other
options.misconception: separates a nil rate from exemption when section 2(47) puts them in the same definition
options.why: A nil rate is a rate, but the very first words of section 2(47) name a supply attracting nil rate of tax as an exempt supply. Nil rated and exempt part company when a rate is being quoted and travel together when credit is being worked out.

options.text: Rice and land are exempt supplies; liquor and the export are outside GST altogether
options.misconception: puts land inside the definition and pushes a zero-rated export outside the Act
options.why: Land is kept out by Schedule III, so it never becomes an exempt supply. The export is squarely inside the Act — section 16 of the IGST Act makes it a zero-rated supply, which is a taxable supply carrying a rate of zero rather than an escape from the levy.

options.text: All four are exempt supplies, none of them carrying any tax
options.misconception: uses the absence of tax as the test, when the definition works through nil rate, exemption and non-taxability
options.why: Tax can be absent for more than one reason. Land escapes because it is not a supply, and the export escapes because it is zero-rated with credit. Neither of those is an exemption, and calling them one costs the company the credit on its exports.

options.text: Rice exempt; liquor a non-taxable supply and so exempt as well; land not a supply at all; the export a taxable supply that is zero-rated
options.why: Section 2(47) defines an exempt supply as one attracting nil rate of tax or wholly exempt under section 11, and it includes a non-taxable supply. Alcoholic liquor for human consumption sits outside the charge, so it is swept in that way. The sale of land is neither a supply of goods nor a supply of services under Schedule III, so the definition never reaches it. The export is taxable at a rate of zero with the credit chain left intact.

citation.ref: Sections 2(47) and 2(78), read with Schedule III and section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: Four lines sit in one company's accounts for the year — sale of fresh unbranded rice, which bears a nil rate; sale of alcoholic liquor for human consumption; sale of a plot of land it had held for years; and export of software services. The accountant must mark each one.

items.stem: Which movement is a supply even though nothing was received for it?

options.text: The movement to the warehouse operator, possession having passed to him
options.misconception: uses transfer of possession as the test, which describes a bailment rather than the agency entry
options.why: Possession passes in a bailment too, and a bailment is not what entry 3 is about. The entry turns on who undertakes to supply the goods onward to the customer, and on these facts that is the consignment agent and not the warehouse.

options.text: Both, goods having left the manufacturer's premises without consideration in each case
options.misconception: makes the movement of the goods the test, when entry 3 asks who undertakes to supply them onward
options.why: Goods moving is not enough, or every despatch to a transporter would be taxed. Entry 3 needs the person receiving them to have undertaken to supply them on the principal's behalf, and a warehouse operator storing goods for a fee has undertaken nothing of the kind.

options.text: The movement to the consignment agent
options.why: Entry 3 of Schedule I treats a supply of goods by a principal to his agent as a supply made without consideration where the agent undertakes to supply such goods on behalf of the principal. Raising the invoice in his own name is what shows the consignment agent has undertaken that. The warehouse operator raises no invoice and supplies nothing onward, so he is a bailee holding goods for a fee and the movement to him is not a supply.

options.text: Neither, because entry 3 needs the agent to have paid something for the goods
options.misconception: puts a consideration back into an entry whose whole purpose is to deem a supply without one
options.why: Schedule I is the list of activities treated as a supply even if made without consideration. Requiring a payment would leave entry 3 with no work at all to do, since an agent who paid for the goods would be an ordinary buyer.

citation.ref: Entry 3 of Schedule I, read with section 7(1)(c) and Circular No. 57/31/2018-GST

items.scenario: A manufacturer moves goods to two places and receives nothing for either movement. The first lot goes to a consignment agent who stores the goods and sells them to customers under invoices he raises in his own name. The second lot goes to a public warehouse operator who holds the goods for a storage fee and hands them over to customers against invoices the manufacturer raises.

items.stem: What does the law require of him?

options.text: He may supply on his Rajasthan registration, the goods being his own and moved to his own stall
options.misconception: treats a registration in one State as covering supplies made from another
options.why: Registration under section 25(1) is State-wise. Supplies made from the Mumbai stall are made in Maharashtra and need a registration obtained there, whatever registrations the person holds elsewhere.

options.text: Nothing — his turnover is below the threshold and a ten-day stall is too small to matter
options.misconception: applies the section 22 threshold to a category section 24 places outside it
options.why: Section 24 opens with words overriding the threshold, and a casual taxable person is on its list. The ₹6 lakh gives him no protection at all once he starts supplying from the stall.

options.text: Registration in Maharashtra as a casual taxable person whatever his turnover, applied for before the fair begins
options.why: Section 24(ii) makes registration compulsory for a casual taxable person notwithstanding the threshold in section 22, and section 2(20) describes such a person as one who occasionally supplies in a State where he has no fixed place of business. The proviso to section 25(1) requires him to apply at least five days prior to the commencement of business.

options.text: A regular Maharashtra registration, the casual category being open only to a person unregistered everywhere
options.misconception: makes the casual category depend on being unregistered elsewhere rather than on having no fixed place of business in that State
options.why: Section 2(20) asks one question — whether the person has a fixed place of business in the State where he is supplying. His existing Rajasthan registration neither helps him nor disqualifies him from registering as a casual taxable person in Maharashtra.

citation.ref: Sections 24(ii) and 2(20), read with section 25(1) and its proviso

items.scenario: A Jaipur furniture maker with a turnover of ₹6 lakh takes a stall at a ten-day trade fair in Mumbai and will sell from it. He has no fixed place of business anywhere in Maharashtra. He is registered in Rajasthan.

items.stem: How does section 23 treat him?

options.text: Not an agriculturist at all, since he uses hired labour rather than working the land himself
options.misconception: narrows section 2(7), which expressly covers hired labour under personal supervision
options.why: Section 2(7) covers cultivation of land by the person's own labour, by the labour of his family, and by servants on wages or by hired labour under his personal supervision or that of a family member. Hiring help does not take him out of the definition.

options.text: Outside registration altogether, an agriculturist being relieved for everything he supplies
options.misconception: attaches the relief to the person when the clause attaches it to a described supply
options.why: The clause reads to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of land. It relieves a kind of supply, so any other business the same man carries on is looked at separately and on its own facts.

options.text: Outside registration for both lines, produce being produce and the neighbours' crops agricultural too
options.misconception: attaches the relief to the nature of the goods rather than to who cultivated them
options.why: The words are produce out of cultivation of land, meaning cultivation by the agriculturist himself. That the goods are agricultural does not carry the relief across to a trader who bought them from somebody else.

options.text: Outside registration for his own produce, but the trading in other farmers' produce stands on its own footing
options.why: Section 23(1)(b) relieves an agriculturist, to the extent of supply of produce out of cultivation of land. Section 2(7) covers an individual or a Hindu Undivided Family who undertakes cultivation of land, including by hired labour under personal supervision, so he qualifies as one. The words to the extent of confine the relief to what he grew, and buying a neighbour's crop and reselling it is not produce out of cultivation of land by him.

citation.ref: Sections 23(1)(b) and 2(7)

items.scenario: A man cultivates his own land using hired labour working under his personal supervision, and sells the crop. In the same year he also buys produce from neighbouring farmers and sells it on at a margin. He holds no registration and says section 23 covers everything he does.

items.stem: What must he still file, and by when?

options.text: A final return, within three months of the date of cancellation or the date of the order, whichever is later
options.why: Section 45 requires every registered person whose registration is cancelled to furnish a final return within three months of the date of cancellation or the date of the order of cancellation, whichever is later. The order of 20 May 2026 is the later of the two dates here, so the three months are counted from it and not from 31 March 2026.

options.text: Nothing — cancellation ends the duty to file, returns hanging on the registration
options.misconception: reads cancellation as ending every filing duty, when section 45 creates one that arises because of it
options.why: Section 45 is written for this exact person. The obligation it creates comes into existence on cancellation, so it cannot be escaped by pointing at the cancellation as the reason for not filing.

options.text: The annual return for the year, which serves as the final return for a person leaving the system
options.misconception: substitutes the annual return under section 44 for the separate final return under section 45
options.why: They are different returns under different sections. The annual return under section 44 is filed by a registered person for a financial year; the final return under section 45 is filed once, by a person whose registration has been cancelled.

options.text: A final return, within three months of the date of cancellation, the date of the order being irrelevant
options.misconception: takes the first of the two dates section 45 names instead of the later of them
options.why: The section names both dates and then says whichever is later. Where the cancellation takes effect from a date earlier than the order, as here, it is the order that starts the three months running.

citation.ref: Section 45, read with sections 29 and 44

items.scenario: A registered person applies for cancellation because he has closed his business. The order of cancellation is passed on 20 May 2026 and the cancellation is given effect from 31 March 2026. He assumes that once the registration is gone he has nothing further to file.

items.stem: What happens to the input tax credit?

options.text: Both credits go — clause (h) names destruction and writing off alongside gifts
options.why: Section 17(5)(h) blocks input tax credit in respect of goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or disposed of by way of gift or free samples. Destruction by flood and a write-off in the books are two of the five events listed there, so both credits must go. An insurance settlement is money received from an insurer and does not enter the clause at all.

options.text: Only the destroyed goods lose the credit; a write-off is a book entry and the goods are still there
options.misconception: treats writing off as reversible bookkeeping when the clause names it as an event in its own right
options.why: The clause says written off, without asking whether the goods survived the entry. Once the person has written them off in his books the credit goes, and what he does with the goods afterwards is a separate question with its own answer.

options.text: Both credits stand, the insurance settlement having made the company whole
options.misconception: makes the credit turn on whether the loss was made good, which clause (h) never asks
options.why: Clause (h) asks what became of the goods, not who ended up bearing the cost. Insurance is a contract with an insurer and has no place in the input tax credit computation on either side.

options.text: Neither goes, clause (h) being aimed at gifts and free samples, and a casualty is not a giving away
options.misconception: reads clause (h) as though it named only voluntary disposals
options.why: The clause lists five events and only two of them are voluntary. Goods lost, stolen or destroyed sit inside it as squarely as goods given away, which is why an ordinary stock loss carries a credit reversal with it.

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(h), read with section 16(1)

items.scenario: A manufacturer's godown floods. Finished goods that had carried input tax credit on their inputs are destroyed. In the same year the company writes off in its books a quantity of slow-moving raw material which is still physically lying in stock. An insurance settlement is received for the flood loss.

items.stem: What does section 49 permit?

options.text: Any credit may pay any liability, all three being taxes under one system collected together
options.misconception: treats the three heads as a single pool, which section 49(5) keeps deliberately apart
options.why: The three are levied by different statutes and the money is shared between different governments. Section 49(5) sets out head by head what each credit may be used for, and the central and the State heads never meet.

options.text: Central tax credit may pay State tax so long as the integrated tax credit has been exhausted first
options.misconception: reads the ordering rule in section 49A as if it also lifted the bar between the central and State heads
options.why: Section 49A governs the order in which credits are taken up, not what each of them may pay. Exhausting the integrated tax credit first does not unlock a set-off that section 49(5) never permitted in the first place.

options.text: The order of utilisation is the taxpayer's to choose, rule 88A having made section 49A optional
options.misconception: reads rule 88A as removing the ordering rule when it only relaxes it inside the integrated tax credit
options.why: Rule 88A lets integrated tax credit be applied towards central tax and State tax in any order and in any proportion once the integrated tax liability is met. The requirement to exhaust that credit before touching the other two survives untouched.

options.text: Integrated tax credit must be used up first and may go against any head; central tax credit can never be set against State tax
options.why: Section 49A requires the credit of integrated tax to be utilised fully towards integrated tax, central tax and State tax before central tax credit or State tax credit may be used at all. Section 49(5) then allows central tax credit against central tax and integrated tax only, and State tax credit against State tax and integrated tax only, so the cross set-off he proposes is barred and some cash will have to be paid.

citation.ref: Sections 49(5), 49A and 49B, read with rule 88A of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: For one month a registered person owes integrated tax ₹1 lakh, central tax ₹1 lakh and State tax ₹1 lakh. His electronic credit ledger holds integrated tax credit ₹1.5 lakh, central tax credit ₹1 lakh and State tax credit ₹0.2 lakh. To avoid paying anything in cash he proposes to set his central tax credit against the State tax liability.

items.stem: What must he pay, and what becomes of that balance?

options.text: Nothing at all, the credit having been validly taken when the goods were bought and the option operating only from April
options.misconception: treats a valid original credit as immune to a later change of status
options.why: Section 18(4) exists because the goods will now be used to make supplies taxed under the composition levy, where no credit is allowed. What triggers the payment is the change of status, not any defect in the credit when it was taken.

options.text: An amount equal to the credit on the stock and on the capital goods worked out as on 31 March 2027, and the balance left in the ledger lapses
options.why: Section 18(4) requires a registered person who opts to pay tax under section 10 to pay an amount equivalent to the credit of input tax on inputs held in stock, on inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock, and on capital goods, on the day immediately preceding the date of exercising the option. Rule 44 works the capital goods figure out on the remaining useful life. The sub-section then says that after the payment any balance of input tax credit lying in the electronic credit ledger shall lapse.

options.text: Nothing on the capital goods, section 18(4) reaching only inputs held in stock
options.misconception: reads section 18(4) as narrower than it is and drops its capital goods limb
options.why: Section 18(4) names inputs held in stock, inputs contained in semi-finished or finished goods held in stock, and capital goods, in the same breath. The amount on the capital goods is computed on their remaining useful life under rule 44.

options.text: The same amount, but the balance left in the credit ledger is refunded to him in cash
options.misconception: turns a lapse into a refund
options.why: The sub-section says the balance shall lapse, in those words. There is no refund of a credit balance on entering the composition levy, and that loss is part of the price of the option.

citation.ref: Section 18(4), read with section 10 and rule 44 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person paying tax under section 9 opts into the composition levy with effect from 1 April 2027. On 31 March 2027 he holds inputs in stock, inputs contained in finished goods in stock, and capital goods on which credit was taken two years earlier. After making the payment the law requires, a balance is still left in his electronic credit ledger.

items.stem: What is payable on each?

options.text: ₹30,000 on the lathe and ₹10,000 on the moulds, transaction value being the measure for any scrap sale
options.misconception: stretches the proviso for tooling to cover every disposal made as scrap
options.why: The proviso names refractory bricks, moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures, and nothing else. A lathe is none of those, so the comparison in the main sub-section governs it and ₹1 lakh falls due.

options.text: ₹1 lakh on the lathe and ₹2 lakh on the moulds and dies, the same comparison applying to both
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 18(6) to goods its proviso takes out of it
options.why: The proviso exists for exactly this case. Worn tooling sold as scrap fetches very little, and the general comparison would claw back nearly the whole original credit on a sale worth a fraction of it.

options.text: ₹1 lakh on the lathe and ₹10,000 on the moulds and dies
options.why: Section 18(6) requires the higher of the reduced credit and the tax on the transaction value, which for the lathe is ₹1 lakh against ₹30,000. The proviso to that sub-section carves out refractory bricks, moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures supplied as scrap, on which the taxable person may pay tax on the transaction value alone, so the tooling attracts ₹10,000.

options.text: Nothing on either, scrap being waste on which the buyer accounts for tax under reverse charge
options.misconception: invents a reverse charge for scrap that displaces the supplier's own liability under section 18(6)
options.why: Section 18(6) puts the amount on the person disposing of the capital goods, and nothing the buyer does answers it. The sub-section is about clawing a credit back, not about who collects tax on the sale.

citation.ref: Section 18(6) with its proviso

items.scenario: A foundry sells two things as scrap in one month. The first is a lathe on which credit of ₹5 lakh was taken four years ago; reducing that credit by the prescribed percentage points leaves ₹1 lakh, and tax on its transaction value is ₹30,000. The second is a set of worn-out moulds and dies on which credit of ₹2 lakh was taken, and tax on their transaction value is ₹10,000.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The lathe became a deemed supply on 1 September 2029, the day the department raised the point
options.misconception: dates the deemed supply from its discovery rather than from the day the goods left
options.why: The section deems the supply to have been made on the day the capital goods were sent out, not on the day the default was noticed. That backdating is what makes interest run from the earlier date rather than from the audit.

options.text: The lathe became a deemed supply when three years passed; the moulds are outside the time limit altogether
options.why: Section 19(6) deems capital goods sent to a job worker and not received back within three years to have been supplied to him on the day they were sent out, so the lathe crossed that line on 1 July 2029. Section 19(7) takes moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures, and tools sent to a job worker outside that rule entirely, so no period runs against them at all.

options.text: Neither became a deemed supply, capital goods carrying no time limit under section 19
options.misconception: confuses the exclusion for tooling with a general freedom for all capital goods
options.why: Capital goods carry a three-year limit under section 19(6). It is longer than the one year running on inputs, but it is still a limit, and the lathe went past it by two months.

options.text: Both became deemed supplies on 1 July 2029, three years having run against each
options.misconception: applies the three-year rule to goods section 19(7) expressly excludes from it
options.why: Section 19(7) names moulds and dies, jigs and fixtures, and tools, and says the sub-sections fixing the period do not apply to them. Such tooling often stays with the job worker for its whole working life, which is why the exclusion is there.

citation.ref: Sections 19(6) and 19(7), read with section 143

items.scenario: A principal sends a computer-controlled lathe to a job worker on 1 July 2026 and, the same day, a set of moulds made specially for that job worker to use on the principal's components. Neither comes back. On 1 September 2029 the department says both have become deemed supplies.

items.stem: What value may the Delhi office adopt?

options.text: ₹90,000, the option belonging to the recipient depot rather than to the Delhi office
options.misconception: gives the option to the wrong party
options.why: The words are that the value shall, at the option of the supplier, be an amount equivalent to ninety per cent of the price charged by the recipient. The recipient has no say in whether the proviso is used.

options.text: Whatever the Delhi office writes on the invoice, the two being distinct persons under one PAN
options.misconception: reaches for the second proviso, which needs a recipient eligible for full input tax credit
options.why: The second proviso deems the invoice value to be the open market value only where the recipient is eligible for full input tax credit. This depot is not, so that deeming is shut and the earlier measures in the rule have to be worked through.

options.text: ₹90,000, at the supplier's option
options.why: The first proviso to rule 28 gives the supplier an option, where the goods are intended for further supply as such by the recipient, to take the value at ninety per cent of the price charged for the supply of goods of like kind and quality by the recipient to a customer not being a related person. The second proviso cannot help here, because the depot is not eligible for full input tax credit.

options.text: ₹1,00,000, the price the depot will charge, that being the best evidence of open market value
options.misconception: adopts the recipient's onward price itself when the proviso allows ninety per cent of it
options.why: The proviso does not take the onward price. It allows ninety per cent of that price, and it is an option the supplier may exercise rather than a value pressed on him.

citation.ref: Rule 28, first proviso

items.scenario: A company in Delhi transfers goods to its own separately registered depot in Haryana. The depot will sell those goods on, as they are, to customers who are not related persons, at ₹1,00,000. The depot also makes exempt outward supplies of its own and is therefore not eligible for full input tax credit. No open market value for the transfer itself can be found.

items.stem: What does section 31(3) let him do about those supplies?

options.text: Nothing — supplies made before the certificate arrived fall outside the registration and carry no tax
options.misconception: dates liability from the certificate when the registration takes effect from the earlier date
options.why: The certificate was issued with effect from 1 June 2026, so those supplies were made by a registered person. Section 31(3)(a) exists precisely to paper over the gap between the two dates.

options.text: Issue credit notes under section 34 cancelling the old bills, and fresh invoices in their place
options.misconception: reaches for machinery meant for a change in the value or tax of a supply already invoiced with tax
options.why: A credit note under section 34 is issued where the taxable value or the tax charged in an invoice exceeds what is due, or where goods are returned. The original bills charged no tax at all, and the Act's answer for that period is the revised invoice.

options.text: Issue revised invoices at any time up to the filing of the annual return for the year
options.misconception: borrows the outer limit for correcting a return and applies it to the revised invoice
options.why: The revised invoice carries a limit of its own — one month from the date of issue of the certificate of registration. The annual return deadline governs other corrections and has nothing to do with this document.

options.text: Issue revised invoices against them, within one month from the date of issue of the certificate
options.why: Section 31(3)(a) lets a registered person issue a revised invoice against an invoice already issued during the period beginning with the effective date of registration and ending with the date of issuance of the certificate of registration. It has to be done within one month from the date the certificate was issued, and it is what lets the tax on those supplies be charged and the recipient take credit of it.

citation.ref: Section 31(3)(a), read with section 2(66) and rule 53 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A supplier becomes liable to register on 1 June 2026 and applies within the time allowed. The certificate of registration is issued to him on 20 June 2026, with effect from 1 June 2026. In between he made taxable supplies and issued ordinary bills carrying no tax, having no registration number to print on them.

items.stem: What is the effect of filing that return?

options.text: Only the Appellate Authority can set the order aside; a return filed afterwards has no effect on it
options.misconception: sends to appeal a matter the section resolves by itself
options.why: No appeal is needed. Section 62(2) operates on its own once a valid return is furnished inside the period allowed, and the order is deemed withdrawn without anybody having to set it aside.

options.text: The order stands, and the tax assessed on best judgement is payable in addition to the tax in the return
options.misconception: reads a best judgement order as final once passed, when section 62(2) provides for its withdrawal
options.why: The order is a device for making the return come in, not a second charge. Section 62(2) withdraws it the moment a valid return is furnished inside the period allowed, and no tax is paid twice over.

options.text: The assessment order is deemed withdrawn, but interest and late fee go on running
options.why: Section 62(2) says that where the registered person furnishes a valid return within the period allowed after service of the assessment order, the said assessment order shall be deemed to have been withdrawn. The same sub-section keeps alive the liability to pay interest under section 50 and to pay a late fee under section 47, so the return undoes the order without undoing the consequences of filing late.

options.text: The order is withdrawn and the interest and late fee fall away with it
options.misconception: lets the withdrawal carry off consequences the sub-section expressly preserves
options.why: The sub-section withdraws the order and then says in terms that the liability for interest under section 50 or for late fee under section 47 shall continue. He is put back where a late filer stands, not where a timely one stands.

citation.ref: Section 62(2), read with sections 46, 47 and 50

items.scenario: A registered person does not file his return for a month. A notice under section 46 is served on him and he still does not file. The proper officer passes a best judgement assessment order under section 62 on 10 June 2026. The person then furnishes a valid return, inside the period section 62(2) allows.

items.stem: Under which provision or provisions must the demand be raised?

options.text: Section 73 for FY 2023-24 and section 74A for FY 2024-25
options.why: Section 73(12) confines section 73 to a determination of tax pertaining to a period up to FY 2023-24, and section 74A governs a determination pertaining to FY 2024-25 onward. A single investigation does not merge the two periods, so the earlier year is demanded under section 73 and the later year under section 74A, each with its own machinery.

options.text: Section 73 for both years, the shortfall being bona fide and section 73 being the non-fraud provision
options.misconception: keeps using the old non-fraud section past the financial year at which it stops
options.why: Honesty decides the penalty inside section 74A; it no longer decides which section applies. For FY 2024-25 the non-fraud outcome is reached within section 74A, because section 73 has run out by then.

options.text: Section 74A for both years, the notice being issued after section 74A came into force
options.misconception: dates the section by when the notice issues rather than by the year the tax pertains to
options.why: The test written into these sections is the period the tax pertains to, not the date the notice goes out. FY 2023-24 stays with section 73 however late the department reaches it.

options.text: Section 74 for FY 2023-24 and section 74A for FY 2024-25, an error repeated over two years showing suppression
options.misconception: infers suppression from repetition, when it is an ingredient to be established on evidence
options.why: Fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression has to be shown, and a bona fide error made twice is still a bona fide error. Section 74 was not open on these facts even for the year it still covers.

citation.ref: Sections 73(12) and 74A, read with section 74(12)

items.scenario: One investigation into a company turns up short payment of tax in two financial years — ₹4 lakh in FY 2023-24 and ₹7 lakh in FY 2024-25. In each year the shortfall is a bona fide error and nothing was suppressed. The department wants to raise a single notice covering both years.

items.stem: Is the department's application in time, and how is it treated?

options.text: Yes, but only because the Appellate Authority may condone any delay for sufficient cause
options.misconception: leans on condonation where none was needed, and treats the condonation power as open-ended
options.why: The application was in time and needed no condonation. In any event the power in section 107(4) is to allow a further period of one month where sufficient cause is shown, which is a bounded extension rather than an open one.

options.text: No — a Commissioner reviewing a subordinate's order must revise it himself and cannot go to the Appellate Authority
options.misconception: confuses the review-and-appeal route in section 107(2) with the separate revisional power in section 108
options.why: Section 108 gives the Revisional Authority a power over an order passed by a subordinate officer. Section 107(2) is a different route in which the Commissioner alters nothing himself and instead directs an officer to take the matter to the Appellate Authority.

options.text: Yes — the Commissioner has six months, and the application is dealt with as an appeal would be
options.why: Section 107(1) gives an aggrieved person three months from communication of the order, but section 107(2) gives the Commissioner six months to call for and examine the record of a subordinate's proceeding and direct an officer to apply to the Appellate Authority. 20 August 2026 is inside six months of 5 March 2026. Section 107(3) then says such an application shall be dealt with as if it were an appeal made against the decision.
keywords: call for and examine the record
as if it were an appeal

options.text: No — the three months in section 107(1) governs every appellant, the department included
options.misconception: applies the taxpayer's period to a review application the statute gives its own longer one
options.why: The two sub-sections carry different clocks on purpose. Three months belongs to the person aggrieved by the order, and the longer period belongs to the Commissioner reviewing his own subordinate's work.

citation.ref: Sections 107(2), 107(3) and 107(4), read with sections 107(1) and 108

items.scenario: An adjudication order is passed by a Deputy Commissioner on 5 March 2026 and communicated the same day. The Commissioner examines the record and, on 20 August 2026, directs a subordinate officer to apply to the Appellate Authority against that order. The taxpayer objects that the department is out of time, the appeal period being three months.

items.stem: What can be done, and with what effect?

options.text: The department may take the confirmed ruling on further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal
options.misconception: assumes an appeal exists above the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling
options.why: The advance ruling route stops at the Appellate Authority. Nothing goes on from it to the Appellate Tribunal, and that is exactly why section 104 has to carry the remedy for a ruling obtained dishonestly.

options.text: Either Authority may declare the ruling void from the beginning, after hearing him
options.why: Section 104(1) lets the Authority or the Appellate Authority declare a ruling void ab initio where it finds that the ruling was obtained by fraud or suppression of material facts or misrepresentation of facts. The applicant must be given an opportunity of being heard first, and once the declaration is made all the provisions of the Act apply to him as if the advance ruling had never been made.

options.text: The ruling may be declared void, but only from the date of the declaration, everything before it standing
options.misconception: treats the declaration as prospective when the section makes the ruling void from the beginning
options.why: The words are void ab initio. All the provisions of the Act apply to the applicant as if the advance ruling had never been made, and the period between the ruling and the declaration is left out of account when limitation is computed.

options.text: Nothing — a ruling confirmed on appeal is final and the machinery cannot reopen it
options.misconception: reads finality on appeal as protecting a ruling obtained by suppression
options.why: Finality answers a difference of view, not a concealment. Section 104 exists so that a ruling procured by suppression can be set at nought whichever of the two authorities gave it.

citation.ref: Section 104, read with sections 100, 101 and 103

items.scenario: An applicant obtains an advance ruling in his favour, and the Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling confirms it on appeal. The department later finds that the applicant had suppressed a material fact about the contract when he made his application. It wants the ruling undone.

items.stem: What value is adopted?

options.text: Rule 5 cannot be used, goods that are merely interchangeable not being similar goods
options.misconception: applies the identical-goods test to the similar-goods rule
options.why: Identical goods must be the same in all respects. Similar goods need only have like characteristics and like component materials, perform the same functions and be commercially interchangeable, which is what these tiles are.

options.text: ₹85.67 per square metre, the average of the three comparison values
options.misconception: averages the comparison values when the rule names the lowest of them
options.why: The valuation rules never average. Where more than one transaction value of identical or of similar goods is found, the lowest such value is to be used, and that instruction sits in both rule 4 and rule 5.

options.text: ₹80 per square metre, under the similar goods rule
options.why: With no identical goods available, rule 4 fails and rule 5 takes over for similar goods — goods which, although not alike in all respects, have like characteristics and like component materials which let them perform the same functions and be commercially interchangeable. Where more than one such value is found, the rule directs that the lowest of them shall be used, so ₹80 is the value.

options.text: ₹92 per square metre, the highest being the safest measure of what the goods would fetch
options.misconception: reads valuation as a revenue-maximising exercise rather than as a rule-bound one
options.why: Valuation is not a bargaining position. The rule picks the lowest of the values found, which protects the importer against one unrepresentative comparison deciding his duty.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 5 with the definition of similar goods in rule 2, read with rules 3(4) and 4

items.scenario: The declared transaction value of a consignment of ceramic tiles is rejected under rule 12, on grounds put to the importer and after hearing him. No import of identical goods can be found. The officer does find three earlier imports of goods that are commercially interchangeable with the tiles, from the same country, at about the same time and in comparable quantities, at ₹80, ₹85 and ₹92 per square metre.

items.stem: Is the royalty added to the transaction value of the components?

options.text: Yes, rule 10 catching every payment that leaves India in connection with an import
options.misconception: invents a catch-all where rule 10 lists specific additions and rule 10(4) closes the list
options.why: Rule 10 is a list of named additions, and rule 10(4) says no addition shall be made to the price actually paid or payable except as provided for in that rule. A remittance abroad is not by itself a reason to load the transaction value.

options.text: No, neither limb of the clause is satisfied
options.why: Rule 10(1)(c) has two limbs and both must hold. The royalty must be related to the imported goods being valued, and the buyer must be required to pay it, directly or indirectly, as a condition of the sale of those goods. A trademark fee for the finished product assembled in India relates to what is made here, and the supplier ships regardless, so nothing is added.

options.text: No, but only because the royalty goes to a third party rather than to the seller of the components
options.misconception: makes the identity of the payee decisive, when the clause reaches payments to third parties too
options.why: The clause is not confined to payments made to the seller. A royalty paid to a third party can still be added where it relates to the imported goods and is required as a condition of their sale. This one fails on the substance, not on who was paid.

options.text: Yes, because any royalty paid abroad on goods made using imported components is added
options.misconception: treats a connection with the business as enough when the rule wants a link to the goods valued and a condition of sale
options.why: The rule is narrower than that. It asks whether the payment relates to the goods being valued and whether it is a condition of their sale, and a fee for a mark applied to Indian output answers neither question.

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(1)(c) with its explanations, read with rule 10(4) and section 14(1) of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: An Indian company imports components from an unrelated foreign supplier at a price the two of them settled. Separately it pays a running royalty to a third company abroad for the use of a trademark on the finished product it assembles in India. The component supplier ships whether or not the trademark agreement exists, and the two contracts are unconnected.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: Nothing can be demanded, the two-year period for a notice having run out
options.misconception: applies the ordinary limitation to a case the Act gives a longer period
options.why: Two years is the period for an ordinary short-levy under section 28(1)(a). The moment collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts is in issue, section 28(4) gives the department five years from the relevant date.

options.text: The matter is closed, section 28(2) barring a notice once duty and interest are paid voluntarily
options.misconception: uses the ordinary short-levy relief in a case the Act routes through a different sub-section
options.why: Section 28(2) belongs to an ordinary short-levy under section 28(1). Where collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression is alleged, the pre-notice route is section 28(5), and it asks for more than duty and interest.

options.text: A notice must issue in every suppression case, payment before notice counting for nothing
options.misconception: denies a pre-notice route that section 28(5) expressly provides
options.why: Section 28(5) exists precisely for a payment made before a notice in a collusion or suppression case. What it asks for is the full package, and where that is paid the proper officer issues no notice for the amount so paid.

options.text: The notice period here is five years, and duty with interest alone does not close the matter
options.why: Section 28(4) allows a notice within five years of the relevant date where the short-levy is by reason of collusion, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts, so three years is comfortably inside it. The relief for paying before a notice in such a case sits in section 28(5), and it is available only where the duty, the interest and the penalty that sub-section prescribes are all paid and the officer is informed in writing.

citation.ref: Sections 28(4) and 28(5), read with sections 28(1), 28(2) and 28AA

items.scenario: An investigation shows that an importer suppressed the true description of goods across several consignments, and duty was short-levied. Three years after the relevant date, before any notice reaches him, he pays the differential duty with interest and writes to the proper officer asking that the matter be treated as closed.

items.stem: What is he entitled to?

options.text: Neither, the department being entitled to hold everything while its investigation runs
options.misconception: ignores the express consequence section 110(2) attaches to the six months
options.why: Section 110(2) is unconditional on this point. Where no notice under section 124 is given within six months, extended at most by a further six months for reasons recorded in writing, the goods go back whatever stage the investigation has reached.

options.text: Both, the six months in section 110(2) applying to everything seized under section 110
options.misconception: carries the goods clock across to documents, which are seized under a different sub-section with no period
options.why: Section 110(2) speaks of goods seized under sub-section (1) and of returning those goods. Documents are seized under sub-section (3), and the Act sets no time limit on how long they may be held.

options.text: The goods back; the documents may be kept, and his right over them is to copy them
options.why: Section 110(2) fixes six months for goods and requires their return where no notice under section 124 is given in that time. Section 110(3) is a separate power to seize documents or things useful for or relevant to any proceeding, and it carries no such period. Section 110(4) gives the person from whose custody they were seized the right to make copies of them or take extracts from them in the presence of an officer of customs.
keywords: in the presence of an officer

options.text: Both, and once returned the documents may not be used against him in any proceeding
options.misconception: turns the return of seized material into a bar on using it in evidence
options.why: Nothing in section 110 makes returned material inadmissible. The department may take its own copies, and the case proceeds on the record whether or not the originals are still held.

citation.ref: Sections 110(2), 110(3) and 110(4), read with section 124

items.scenario: During a search the officers seize a consignment of goods and also a set of the importer's ledgers and contracts. Eight months later no notice under section 124 has been issued and no extension has been granted. The importer demands the goods and the documents back, saying one period of six months governs everything that was seized.

items.stem: What does section 59 require of him?

options.text: No bond at all, a warehouse being a bonded place where duty is simply deferred
options.misconception: assumes the licensing of the warehouse removes the need for a bond from the importer
options.why: Licensing a warehouse and bonding the goods are different things. Section 59 requires the importer himself to execute a bond for the goods he enters for warehousing, whatever the standing of the warehouse he sends them to.

options.text: A bond for ₹30 lakh, covering the duty, the interest and any fines and penalties on the goods
options.why: Section 59(1) requires the importer of goods entered for warehousing to execute a bond in a sum equal to thrice the amount of the duty assessed on those goods, binding himself to comply with the conditions of the Act and to pay, on or before the date specified in a notice of demand, all duties and interest payable together with any penalties and fines incurred.
keywords: thrice the amount of the duty

options.text: A bond for ₹10 lakh, equal to the duty assessed, a bond securing the duty and nothing more
options.misconception: reads the bond as security for the duty alone when the section fixes its sum at three times that
options.why: The bond answers for more than the duty. It reaches interest, fines and penalties as well, and the statute fixes its amount at three times the duty assessed rather than leaving it to be argued case by case.

options.text: A bond for ₹30 lakh, but it answers only for the duty, so a penalty must be secured separately
options.misconception: gets the sum right and then narrows what the bond covers
options.why: The bond binds the importer to pay the duties and interest and, in addition, any penalties and fines incurred in respect of the goods. Its coverage is wide, which is the reason its sum is set so far above the duty.

citation.ref: Section 59(1), read with sections 60, 71 and 73

items.scenario: Goods assessed to duty of ₹10 lakh are to be deposited in a warehouse. The importer offers to execute a bond for ₹10 lakh, saying a bond cannot sensibly be larger than the money at stake.

items.stem: On which of these is the importer liable to duty?

options.text: On none of them, section 13 relieving the importer of duty on any pilferage at the port
options.misconception: reads section 13 as a general relief for theft and misses both its window and its proviso
options.why: The section is bounded at both ends. It runs from unloading to the order for clearance or for warehousing, and it stops working the moment the goods come back into the importer's hands.

options.text: On the second and the third
options.why: Section 13 relieves the importer of duty on goods pilfered after unloading and before the proper officer makes an order for clearance for home consumption or an order permitting deposit in a warehouse. A pilferage after that order falls outside the section. Its proviso adds that where the pilfered goods are restored to the importer he becomes liable to duty on them, which brings the charge back in the third case.
keywords: before the proper officer makes an order

options.text: On the second only, a restoration merely putting the importer back where he already was
options.misconception: overlooks the proviso, which makes restored goods dutiable
options.why: The proviso says the importer becomes liable to duty where the pilfered goods are restored to him. He is not back where he started, because he now has both the relief and the goods, and the section will not allow him to keep both.

options.text: On all three, the importer being the person who imported the goods whatever became of them
options.misconception: ignores section 13 altogether
options.why: Section 13 was written to displace that outcome for a pilferage inside the window. The importer pays nothing on those goods, and section 45(3) makes the custodian answerable for the duty instead.

citation.ref: Section 13 with its proviso, read with sections 23 and 45(3)

items.scenario: Three things happen at a port. Part of a consignment is pilfered from the custodian's shed after unloading and before any order for clearance is made. Part of a second consignment is pilfered a day after the order for clearance for home consumption was made but before the goods were removed. The goods pilfered in the first case are later traced and restored to the importer.

items.stem: What is it entitled to?

options.text: ₹19.6 lakh, identity of the goods and the time limit being the only conditions section 74 imposes
options.misconception: applies the unused-goods rate to goods that have been used
options.why: Identity and the time limit are conditions, not the whole of the section. The rate itself turns on whether the goods were used after importation, and a lower one is prescribed where they were.

options.text: Nothing, drawback under section 74 being lost the moment the goods are put to use in India
options.misconception: reads use as disqualifying when section 74(2) exists to give used goods a reduced rate
options.why: Use cuts the drawback down; it does not wipe it out. Section 74(2) is the sub-section written for goods used after importation, and it directs a lower rate rather than none at all.

options.text: ₹15 lakh, but only if the machine was manufactured in India before it was exported
options.misconception: imports a condition from the manufacture-based drawback in section 75
options.why: Manufacture belongs to section 75, which gives drawback on imported materials used in goods made here. Section 74 asks only that the goods going out be the goods that came in, identified as such.

options.text: ₹15 lakh
options.why: Section 74(1) gives ninety-eight per cent only where the goods are re-exported without having been used after importation. Section 74(2) covers goods used after importation and lets the Central Government fix drawback at a lower rate, having regard to the duration of the use. At the seventy-five per cent prescribed for this period, ₹20 lakh yields ₹15 lakh.

citation.ref: Sections 74(1) and 74(2)

items.scenario: A company imported a machine and paid ₹20 lakh in duty. It ran the machine in its plant for eight months and then re-exported it, identified by the customs authorities as the machine that was imported. For goods used for more than six months but not more than nine months, the notification made under section 74(2) prescribes drawback at seventy-five per cent of the duty paid. The company claims ninety-eight per cent.

items.stem: Who pays the tax on each month's security bill?

options.text: Each agency charges tax on its own bill, section 9(3) covering only legal, transport and Government services
options.misconception: treats the notified list as closed at the entries most often quoted
options.why: The notification runs to many entries and security services is one of them. An advocate's fee and a goods transport agency's freight are simply the two that appear most often in question papers.

options.text: The manufacturer pays under reverse charge on both, and may discharge either liability out of its credit ledger
options.misconception: gets the coverage wrong and then pays a reverse-charge liability from the wrong ledger
options.why: Two errors sit on top of each other. May is outside the entry altogether, and a liability that does arise under section 9(3) is payable in cash — the credit ledger discharges output tax on a person's own supplies, not the tax he owes as a recipient.

options.text: The manufacturer pays under reverse charge on both, security being a notified service whoever supplies it
options.misconception: reads the entry as naming a service when it names a service supplied by a described person to a described person
options.why: Every entry under section 9(3) has three parts — the service, the supplier and the recipient — and all three have to fit before the liability moves. Reading only the service column is what makes a body corporate's bill look like a reverse-charge bill.

options.text: The manufacturer pays under reverse charge on April's bill; the May bill carries tax charged by the agency itself
options.why: Entry 14 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate) notifies security services, meaning the supply of security personnel, under section 9(3) only where the supplier is any person other than a body corporate and the recipient is a registered person. The proprietary agency fits, so the manufacturer self-assesses on April. A private limited company is a body corporate, so the entry does not reach May and the agency charges forward.

citation.ref: Section 9(3) with entry 14 of Notification No. 13/2017-Central Tax (Rate), read with section 49(4) and rule 86(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered manufacturing company buys security guards for its factory gate. In April it uses a proprietary security agency run by an individual. In May, unhappy with the service, it moves to a private limited company that supplies the same guards. Neither agency is under the composition levy, and the manufacturer is registered in the ordinary way.

items.stem: What follows from the shortfall?

options.text: The promoter himself pays tax on the shortfall under reverse charge, being a notified class of person on a notified supply
options.why: What survives of section 9(4) after the 2019 substitution is a power to notify, and the live notification names promoters in real estate as the notified class of person and the shortfall in registered procurement as the notified supply. Both halves fit here, so the promoter pays under reverse charge on the amount by which his registered purchases fell short.

options.text: The promoter loses input tax credit on the whole project, the shortfall being a breach of a condition of credit
options.misconception: turns a reverse-charge liability into a disallowance of credit, which the notification does not impose
options.why: The consequence written into the scheme is that the promoter pays the tax himself on the shortfall. Credit stands or falls on section 16 and section 17, and the shortfall is not one of the things either of them denies.

options.text: The unregistered contractors must take registration and charge tax, section 9(4) applying only where the supplier could have registered
options.misconception: puts the consequence on the supplier when the whole point of a reverse charge is that the recipient answers for it
options.why: Nothing in section 9(4) obliges the supplier to do anything. It shifts the liability to the recipient precisely because the supplier is outside the net, and an unregistered contractor below the threshold stays outside it.

options.text: Nothing is payable, section 9(4) having been rendered inoperative for every registered person from 1 February 2019
options.misconception: reads the substitution as a repeal when it replaced a general charge with a targeted one
options.why: The substitution narrowed the sub-section; it did not empty it. Tax under it now falls on a notified class of registered persons on notified supplies, and the promoter's shortfall is exactly the case the Government notified.

citation.ref: Section 9(4), as substituted with effect from 1 February 2019, read with Notification No. 07/2019-Central Tax (Rate)

items.scenario: A promoter builds a residential project. Take it as given that the notification issued under section 9(4) requires him to buy at least eighty per cent of the value of his inputs and input services for the project from registered suppliers. For the financial year just closed he bought only seventy per cent from registered suppliers, the rest from small unregistered local contractors.

items.stem: Which of the two is a works contract?

options.text: Only the warehouse job, a works contract reaching immovable property alone
options.why: Section 2(119) defines a works contract as a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods is involved in the execution of such contract. The warehouse is immovable property; a skid-mounted generator that travels between sites is not.

options.text: Only the generator job, the warehouse work being construction of immovable property and so outside the levy
options.misconception: confuses a works contract on immovable property with the sale of a completed building that Schedule III keeps out
options.why: What Schedule III keeps outside GST is the sale of a building after completion, not the work of building or repairing it. A contractor's service on immovable property is taxable, and Schedule II calls it a supply of services.

options.text: Neither, a works contract requiring new construction rather than repair of something already built
options.misconception: confines the definition to fresh construction when it lists repair, maintenance and renovation among the covered activities
options.why: The list in section 2(119) runs from building at one end to repair, maintenance, renovation and alteration at the other. Mending a roof is squarely inside it.

options.text: Both, each being a job of repair in which the contractor supplies the materials
options.misconception: takes the transfer of goods during a service as the whole definition and drops the immovable-property limb
options.why: Supplying materials while doing the work is one of two conditions. The definition names immovable property in terms, and a contract to repair a machine that can be lifted onto a lorry fails on it however much steel is consumed.

citation.ref: Section 2(119), read with paragraph 6(a) of Schedule II and paragraph 5 of Schedule III
