Where payment is made by any other mode, the invoice must instead carry a cross-reference of that payment. Both of the chain's counters are inside one of the two.

citation.ref: Rule 46 with Notification No. 14/2020-Central Tax and its provisos on compliance, read with rule 48(4)

items.scenario: A retail chain above the notified turnover shows the payment code on a screen at the till. Some customers scan it and pay; some pay by card at the same counter. In both cases the printed invoice handed over carries a cross-reference of the payment made. The chain's auditor says every one of those invoices is defective because the code itself is not printed on the paper.

items.stem: What can the department do about the ruling?

options.text: Nothing, unless the company first applies for a fresh ruling on the correct composition
options.misconception: puts the initiative on the applicant when section 104 gives the power to the Authority
options.why: The power to declare a ruling void sits with the Authority or the Appellate Authority and is exercised on their own finding. It waits on no application from the person who obtained the ruling.

options.text: Nothing — a ruling binds the jurisdictional officer under section 103 until the law changes, and the law has not changed
options.misconception: treats section 103's binding force as absolute, when section 104 removes the ruling itself in a fraud case
options.why: Section 103 binds an officer to a ruling that stands. Section 104 is about whether it stands at all, and a ruling obtained on false facts can be taken away from underneath the binding rule.

options.text: Nothing for the past, but the ruling ceases to bind from the date the misstatement is discovered
options.misconception: gives the declaration prospective effect, when the words of section 104 are void ab initio
options.why: Void ab initio means void from the beginning. A prospective cessation would leave the benefit of the fraud with the applicant for two years, which is the opposite of what the section does.

options.text: Declare it void ab initio, so it is treated as if it had never been made and the intervening period is open to demand
options.why: Section 104 lets the Authority or the Appellate Authority declare a ruling void ab initio where it finds the ruling was obtained by fraud or suppression of material facts or misrepresentation of facts. All the provisions of the Act then apply to the applicant as if the ruling had never been made, after he is given an opportunity of being heard.
keywords: as if the ruling had never been made

citation.ref: Section 104, read with sections 103(1) and 103(2)

items.scenario: A company obtained an advance ruling in its own favour on the classification of a product, describing the product's composition in its application. Two years later the department finds that the composition stated in the application was not the composition of the product the company actually makes, and that the difference was known to the company when it applied.

items.stem: What did the department leave out, and what was it entitled to do?

options.text: The findings, the reasons for them and his rights and obligations had to be communicated within thirty days in FORM GST ADT-02; the demand itself is properly raised under section 74A
options.why: Section 65(6) requires the proper officer, on conclusion of the audit, to inform the registered person within thirty days of the findings, the reasons for those findings, and his rights and obligations, and the communication goes in FORM GST ADT-02. Where the audit shows tax unpaid, short paid, wrongly refunded or credit wrongly availed, the officer may then proceed under section 74A, so the demand route is right even though the intimation was skipped.

options.text: Nothing was left out — an audit report is an internal document and the taxpayer sees the case for the first time in the notice
options.misconception: treats the audit findings as internal when the section requires them to be communicated
options.why: The section makes the communication a step in the audit itself, not a courtesy. The taxpayer is told the findings and the reasons before any demand is framed.

options.text: The findings had to be communicated, and because they were not, no demand can be raised on them at all
options.misconception: turns a procedural default into a complete bar on the demand
options.why: The intimation is required and its omission is a defect the taxpayer can press. It does not take away the power to determine tax on what the audit found.

options.text: The findings had to be communicated within thirty days, and the demand should have gone under section 73 as no fraud is alleged
options.misconception: reaches for section 73, which stops at FY 2023-24, instead of section 74A
options.why: Sections 73 and 74 govern up to FY 2023-24. From FY 2024-25 onwards section 74A is the single demand provision whether or not fraud is alleged, and section 65(6) sends the officer to it.

citation.ref: Section 65(6), read with rule 101 of the CGST Rules, 2017, FORM GST ADT-02 and section 74A

items.scenario: An audit under section 65 is completed on 10 August 2026. The audit team's working papers show that credit of ₹14 lakh was wrongly availed. Nothing is communicated to the registered person, and in December 2026 he receives a notice determining that amount, the first he hears of the finding.

items.stem: What must happen before the material is used?

options.text: The company must be given an opportunity of being heard on the material gathered in the special audit and proposed to be used against it
options.why: Section 66(4) guarantees the registered person an opportunity of being heard in respect of any material gathered on the basis of the special audit and proposed to be used in any proceedings under the Act. Material the company has never seen cannot become the basis of a determination until that hearing is given.

options.text: The report must first be sent to the Commissioner for approval, his prior approval being needed at every stage of a special audit
options.misconception: repeats the prior approval required for directing the audit and attaches it to the use of the report
options.why: The Commissioner's prior approval is a condition of the direction under section 66(1). The condition on using the material is the hearing in section 66(4).

options.text: The company must first be allowed to appoint its own accountant to answer the report, the special audit being one-sided
options.misconception: invents a right of counter-audit where the section gives a right to be heard
options.why: The accountant is nominated by the Commissioner and paid by him, and the company neither picks nor pays. What it gets is a hearing on the material, not an audit of its own.

options.text: Nothing more — the report of an accountant nominated by the Commissioner is evidence in itself and the company's remedy is an appeal
options.misconception: treats the report as self-proving and postpones the hearing to the appellate stage the section brings forward
options.why: The section puts the hearing before the material is used, not after the demand. Sending the taxpayer to appeal instead is what section 66(4) was written to prevent.

citation.ref: Section 66(4), read with sections 66(1), 66(2) and rule 102 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A special audit under section 66 is directed and the nominated cost accountant submits his report, which relies on costing working papers the accountant obtained from the company's overseas parent. The officer proposes to determine tax on the strength of that material. The company has never seen the working papers.

items.stem: Can he?

options.text: The transfer order is appealable but the prosecution sanction is not, an internal reallocation of work affecting his rights
options.misconception: keeps one of the two listed matters appealable because it feels administrative rather than penal
options.why: Both appear on the same list. Section 121 names the transfer of proceedings first and the sanction of prosecution third, and gives neither a different treatment.

options.text: Neither is appealable — both are on the list in section 121, and his remedy against an arbitrary order of either kind is a writ, not an appeal
options.why: Section 121 shuts out an appeal against an order directing the transfer of proceedings from one officer to another, and against an order sanctioning prosecution under the Act. Both are steps in the administration of a case rather than determinations of liability. The bar is on an appeal and not on every remedy, so a writ to the High Court remains available.

options.text: Both are appealable, since section 107 lets any person aggrieved by any decision or order appeal to the Appellate Authority
options.misconception: reads section 107(1) without section 121, which opens with words overriding every other provision
options.why: Section 121 begins notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any provision of the Act. The wide words in section 107(1) do not survive it for the matters section 121 lists.

options.text: Neither is appealable, and neither can be revised either, but only because the Revisional Authority has no power over a Commissioner's own order
options.misconception: explains the revisional bar by rank when it comes from section 108(1) being made subject to section 121
options.why: It is true that neither can be revised, and the reason is that section 108(1) opens subject to the provisions of section 121. Rank has nothing to do with it.

citation.ref: Section 121 clauses (a) and (c), read with sections 107(1) and 108(1)

items.scenario: A taxpayer receives two communications on the same day. One is an order of the Commissioner transferring his case from the officer who had been hearing it to another officer in a different range. The other is an order sanctioning prosecution against him under the Act. He wants to appeal against both to the Appellate Authority.

items.stem: May he revise it on 1 June 2026?

options.text: Yes — no appeal has been filed, and the only bar in section 108(2) is an order that has been the subject of an appeal
options.misconception: reads clause (a) of section 108(2) as the whole of the sub-section, when it shuts four doors
options.why: The appeal bar is the first of four. Clause (b) adds a floor and a ceiling in time, clause (c) shuts out an order already taken for revision, and clause (d) an order itself passed in revision.

options.text: No, and he can never revise it, because a revision may only follow an appellate order
options.misconception: makes an appeal a precondition of revision, when revision is the department's look at an order nobody has appealed
options.why: Revision exists precisely for the unappealed order. What clause (b) does is make the Authority wait for the appeal window to close first.

options.text: No — he must wait until the section 107(2) period has expired, so not before 1 September 2026, and in any event not after three years from the order
options.why: Section 108(2)(b) puts two limits on the same power. The Revisional Authority shall not exercise it where the period specified under section 107(2) has not yet expired — that period is the department's own window to direct an appeal, six months on the given facts — or where more than three years have expired after the order sought to be revised was passed. A revision on 1 June 2026 falls inside the first bar.

options.text: Yes, provided he first stays the operation of the order, which cures the timing objection
options.misconception: uses the power to stay, which section 108(1) gives, as if it lifted the bar in section 108(2)
options.why: Staying the order is part of how a revision is conducted once it may be begun. It says nothing about whether it may be begun, which clause (b) decides.

citation.ref: Section 108(2)(b), read with sections 108(1), 108(2)(a) and 107(2)

items.scenario: An adjudicating officer passes an order on 1 March 2026 and it is communicated the same day. Nobody appeals. On 1 June 2026 the Revisional Authority, having read the file, considers the order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of revenue and proposes to revise it at once. Take as given that the period specified in section 107(2) is six months from communication.

items.stem: What is the position on limitation and on who hears the appeal?

options.text: The appeal is in time, since limitation runs from the date the Tribunal passed the order and not from communication, and a single Judge may hear it
options.misconception: starts the clock at the order rather than at communication, and drops the requirement of a two-Judge Bench
options.why: Limitation runs from the date the order is communicated to the person. And the appeal is heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges, so the composition is wrong as well.

options.text: The appeal does not lie to the High Court at all, an order of a State Bench of the Tribunal going directly to the Supreme Court
options.misconception: extends the direct-to-Supreme-Court route, which is for the Principal Bench and for place-of-supply differences, to an ordinary State Bench order
options.why: A direct appeal to the Supreme Court lies from an order of the Principal Bench, and from an order relating to a difference of views on the place of supply. An ordinary valuation dispute decided by a State Bench goes to the High Court on a substantial question of law.

options.text: The appeal is barred outright, the one hundred and eighty days being an absolute limit the High Court cannot relax
options.misconception: reads the period without the express power to admit a late appeal on sufficient cause
options.why: The section gives the period and, in the same breath, the power to admit an appeal filed after it where the Court is satisfied there was sufficient cause. An absolute reading takes that power away.

options.text: The appeal is late against the one hundred and eighty days allowed, but the Court may admit it on sufficient cause; and once admitted it is heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges
options.why: An appeal to the High Court is filed within one hundred and eighty days of the order being communicated, and the Court may admit an appeal after that period on being satisfied there was sufficient cause for not filing it in time. Counsel's illness is the kind of cause the Court weighs. The appeal is then heard by a Bench of not less than two Judges, which decides by majority, so a single Judge cannot dispose of it.

citation.ref: Sections 117(2), 117(3) and 117(5), read with section 117(1) and section 118

items.scenario: A State Bench of the Appellate Tribunal decides an ordinary valuation dispute, with no difference of views between States about the place of supply. The order is communicated to the taxpayer on 1 April 2026. He files an appeal to the High Court on 1 December 2026, explaining that his counsel was ill for four months. A single Judge takes up the admission.

items.stem: Can it rectify without hearing him?

options.text: No — where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice must be followed, and this one cuts his refund
options.why: The third proviso to section 161 says that where the rectification adversely affects any person, the principles of natural justice shall be followed by the authority carrying it out. A transposed digit is indeed an error apparent on the face of record and is within the section, but reducing a refund from ₹9,00,000 to ₹90,000 plainly affects him adversely, so he must be heard first.

options.text: No, and the order cannot be rectified at all — a change in the amount of a refund is a review, which section 161 does not permit
options.misconception: calls an arithmetical correction a review, when the section is written for exactly this kind of slip
options.why: Section 161 will not reopen a debatable question or a fresh appreciation of evidence. A transposed digit is neither; it is the clerical or arithmetical error the section exists to put right.

options.text: Yes, provided the correction is made within six months, because the six-month limit is the only condition the section imposes
options.misconception: treats the first proviso's time limit as the section's only condition and overlooks the safeguard in the third
options.why: Time is one condition and natural justice is another. Being inside six months does not excuse an unheard rectification that takes money away.

options.text: Yes — an error apparent on the face of record is corrected on the record itself and no hearing is contemplated by the section
options.misconception: reads the power in section 161 without the third proviso that conditions its exercise
options.why: The section corrects the record and the third proviso decides when the person must be heard first. Whether the error is obvious is a different question from whether the correction hurts him.

citation.ref: Section 161 with its third proviso, read with its first and second provisos

items.scenario: An order allowed a refund of ₹9,00,000. Two months later the authority notices that a figure in its own computation was transposed and that the correct refund is ₹90,000. It proposes to rectify the order under section 161 and issue a corrected one, without hearing the taxpayer, on the footing that a transposed digit needs no argument.

items.stem: How is the lathe's sale valued, and what happens to the shortfall?

options.text: The lathe carries no taxable value at all, and the negative margin is simply ignored — the other machine is still taxed on its full ₹1,00,000 margin
options.why: Rule 32(5) values the supply at selling price less purchase price, and a negative margin is ignored. So the lathe bears no value and no tax, and the shortfall does not travel: it is not a loss to be set against the margin on any other supply, so the other machine is taxed on its own ₹1,00,000.

options.text: The lathe is taxed on its full selling price of ₹5,20,000, the margin scheme being unavailable where the dealer sells at a loss
options.misconception: reads a loss as disqualifying the supply from the scheme, when the rule provides for it by ignoring the negative margin
options.why: Nothing about a loss puts the supply outside rule 32(5). The conditions are that the goods are second-hand, sold as such after at most minor processing that does not change their nature, and that no input tax credit was taken.

options.text: The lathe is outside the scheme because cleaning and testing is processing, so the whole ₹5,20,000 is taxable
options.misconception: treats any work on the goods as processing that changes their nature, which the rule allows so long as the nature is unchanged
options.why: The rule tolerates minor processing that does not change the nature of the goods. Cleaning and testing a lathe leaves it the same lathe.

options.text: The lathe carries a negative value of ₹80,000, which reduces the other machine's margin to ₹20,000
options.misconception: pools the margins across supplies, when the rule values each supply on its own
options.why: The rule fixes a value for the supply in front of it. There is no pooling of margins across a dealer's stock and no net margin for the month.

citation.ref: Rule 32(5) with its proviso on the negative margin

items.scenario: A dealer in second-hand machinery buys a lathe from an unregistered owner for ₹6,00,000, takes no input tax credit, cleans and tests it without altering its nature, and sells it for ₹5,20,000 because the market has moved against him. He asks whether the ₹80,000 shortfall can be set against the margin on another machine sold the same month for a ₹1,00,000 margin.

items.stem: May the principal supply the goods directly from the job worker's premises?

options.text: No, and no declaration can help — goods can only ever be supplied from a place named on the principal's own registration at the time the inputs were sent out
options.misconception: treats the additional place of business as impossible to add, when declaring it is exactly the route the proviso offers
options.why: The declaration is the way through, not a closed door. Once the job worker's premises is on the principal's registration as an additional place of business, the supply may go from there.

options.text: Yes, freely — section 143 permits supply from the job worker's premises within the one year and asks nothing further
options.misconception: reads the permission in section 143(1)(b) without the proviso that conditions it
options.why: The one year is the time limit and the proviso is the condition. Both have to be satisfied, and the time limit alone does not open the job worker's shed as a despatch point.

options.text: Yes, because the job worker being unregistered means the premises is treated as the principal's own by default
options.misconception: inverts the proviso, which excuses the declaration where the job worker is registered and requires it where he is not
options.why: Registration of the job worker is what removes the need to declare. An unregistered job worker is the case in which the declaration is required.

options.text: Not as things stand — he must first declare the job worker's premises as his own additional place of business, the job worker being unregistered and the goods not notified
options.why: Section 143(1)(b) lets the principal supply the goods from the place of business of a job worker, but its proviso stops him unless he declares that place as his additional place of business. The proviso excepts two cases only — where the job worker is registered under section 25, or where the principal supplies goods of a class notified by the Commissioner — and neither applies here.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(b) with its proviso, read with sections 143(3) and 25

items.scenario: A principal in Nashik sends inputs to a job worker in Aurangabad and, well inside the one year, finds a buyer who wants the finished goods shipped straight from the job worker's shed. The job worker is not registered under GST, and the principal has not declared the shed as anything on his own registration certificate. The goods he makes are not of any class notified by the Commissioner.

items.stem: Until when must those records be kept?

options.text: Until 31 December 2029 — seventy-two months are counted from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year, not from the end of the year itself
options.why: Section 36 requires the accounts and records to be retained for seventy-two months from the due date of furnishing the annual return for the year they relate to. On the given date of 31 December 2023, seventy-two months run to 31 December 2029, so nothing may be cleared out in the early part of that year.

options.text: Until 31 December 2029, but only for the accounts, invoices and other documents being free to go after five years
options.misconception: splits the retention obligation between records and documents, which section 36 does not do
options.why: Section 36 speaks of the accounts and records required by section 35, and holds them all for one period. There is no shorter clock for the underlying documents.

options.text: Until 31 March 2029 — seventy-two months from the end of the financial year 2022-23
options.misconception: counts from the close of the financial year, which is the anchor the section does not use
options.why: The end of the year is the natural place to start counting and it is not the one section 36 names. The section anchors the period to the due date of the annual return, which falls later.

options.text: Until 31 December 2028 — sixty months from the due date of the annual return
options.misconception: substitutes a sixty-month period for the seventy-two months the section prescribes
options.why: Section 36 fixes seventy-two months. Sixty is the period the earlier indirect tax laws used and it has no place here.

citation.ref: Section 36, read with sections 35(1) and 44

items.scenario: A registered person is clearing out storage in 2029 and wants to know when his records for the financial year 2022-23 may go. Take as given that the annual return for 2022-23 was due to be furnished on 31 December 2023. No appeal, revision, other proceeding or investigation touches that year.

items.stem: Are they right?

options.text: The transporter is right and the godown owner is not, storage being a supply of service while transport of the goods of others is not
options.misconception: decides the obligation by whether the person makes a taxable supply, when section 35(2) turns on what he handles
options.why: Section 35(2) names the transporter and the owner or operator of a warehouse or godown side by side. Whether either makes a taxable supply is not what the sub-section asks.

options.text: Both are right, because an unregistered person can be asked for records only through a notice under section 71 to enter and inspect
options.misconception: confuses the power to access premises with the standing duty section 35(2) imposes to keep the records in the first place
options.why: Access to a place of business is a separate power. Section 35(2) imposes the duty to maintain the records, and that duty exists before any officer asks to see them.

options.text: No — section 35(2) reaches every owner or operator of a warehouse or godown and every transporter, whether or not he is registered
options.why: Section 35(1) is indeed written for a registered person, but section 35(2) reaches beyond registration. Every owner or operator of a warehouse, godown or other place used for storage of goods, and every transporter, must maintain records of the consigner, the consignee and other prescribed particulars of the goods, irrespective of whether he is registered under the Act.

options.text: Yes — nobody outside registration owes an obligation under Chapter VIII, and the department must approach the registered supplier instead
options.misconception: reads the whole of section 35 as applying to registered persons, when sub-section (2) is written for unregistered ones
options.why: The sub-section exists because goods pass through hands that are not registered, and the trail would break there. It says in terms that it applies whether or not the person is registered.

citation.ref: Section 35(2), read with section 35(1) and rule 58 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A transport company and the owner of a godown are both asked by the department for records of the consignors, the consignees and the goods handled over a period. Neither is registered under GST — the transporter because his own turnover is small, the godown owner because he only rents out space and makes no taxable supply. Both reply that section 35 is written for registered persons and does not reach them.

items.stem: What is the place of supply?

options.text: Delhi, because every meeting was held there and the drawings were handed over there
options.misconception: applies a performance test to a service that section 12(2) governs by the recipient's location
options.why: Where a service is physically performed decides the place of supply only for the services specified in sections 12(3) to 12(14). This service is not among them, so the general rule governs and where the work happened is irrelevant.

options.text: Delhi, the supplier's location, an unregistered recipient having no location the section can use
options.misconception: goes straight to the supplier's location, which section 12(2)(b) reaches only where no address is on record
options.why: The supplier's location is the last step of section 12(2)(b), not the first. It is used only in other cases, meaning where no address of the recipient exists on record, and here one plainly does.

options.text: Punjab, but the architect charges central tax and State tax, both parties being inside India
options.misconception: gets the place of supply right and then misreads what makes a supply inter-State
options.why: A supply is inter-State under section 7 of the IGST Act where the supplier's location and the place of supply are in different States. Delhi against Punjab makes this inter-State, so integrated tax is charged.

options.text: Punjab, being the address on record of the unregistered recipient
options.why: Section 12(2)(b) fixes the place of supply for an unregistered recipient at the location of the recipient where the address on record exists. Ludhiana is the address on record, so the place of supply is Punjab, and the supplier's own location is reached only in other cases, meaning where no such address exists.

citation.ref: Section 12(2)(b), read with section 12(2)(a) and section 7 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An architect registered in Delhi designs a house for an individual who is not registered under GST. The client's address in the architect's records is in Ludhiana, Punjab. The client visits the Delhi office for every meeting, and the drawings are handed over there. The service is not one of those listed in sections 12(3) to 12(14).

items.stem: Where is the place of supply of this service?

options.text: India, the location of the supplier, no clause of section 13 fitting a service delivered electronically
options.misconception: falls back to the supplier's location, which section 13 uses only for the specific services in section 13(8)
options.why: Section 13 sends the place of supply to the supplier's location only for the services listed in section 13(8), such as banking services to account holders, intermediary services and short-term hiring of means of transport. An electronic delivery is covered by the proviso instead.

options.text: Singapore, the location of the recipient under the general rule in section 13(2)
options.misconception: applies the general rule where a specific clause of section 13(3) governs
options.why: Section 13(2) opens by excepting the services specified in the sub-sections that follow it. A service on goods made physically available to the supplier is specified in section 13(3)(a), so the general rule never reaches it.

options.text: Sri Lanka, where the mill stands at the time the service is supplied
options.why: The first proviso to section 13(3)(a) says that where the services are supplied from a remote location by way of electronic means, the place of supply shall be the location where goods are situated at the time of supply of services. The mill is in Sri Lanka, so that is the place of supply and it lies outside India.
keywords: remote location by way of electronic means

options.text: India, the service having been actually performed by engineers sitting in India
options.misconception: applies the main limb of section 13(3)(a) when its first proviso displaces the performance test for a remote electronic supply
options.why: The main limb of section 13(3)(a) does look at where the service is actually performed, and the first proviso exists to take remote electronic supplies out of it. Once the work is done over a link, the goods and not the engineers fix the place.

citation.ref: First proviso to section 13(3)(a), read with sections 13(2) and 13(8) of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: An Indian engineering firm is engaged by a company in Singapore to diagnose and re-configure the control software of a rolling mill. The mill stands at the Singapore company's plant in Sri Lanka. The firm's engineers never leave India and do the whole job over a secure link. The machine is never brought to India.

items.stem: Which fact fixes the place of supply on the manufacturer's leg?

options.text: That the movement of the goods terminated at the Kerala customer's premises
options.misconception: applies the general movement rule in section 10(1)(a) when clause (b) displaces it for a third-party delivery
options.why: Section 10(1)(a) fixes the place of supply where the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient, and on those words the manufacturer's leg would end in Kerala. Clause (b) is written for precisely this pattern and takes it out of clause (a).

options.text: That the manufacturer and the trader are registered in different States
options.misconception: confuses the test that makes a supply inter-State with the test that fixes the place of supply
options.why: Comparing the two States is what section 7 of the IGST Act does after the place of supply is known. It cannot fix the place of supply itself, and running the comparison first puts the answer before the question.

options.text: That the Karnataka trader instructed the delivery, his own place of business being deemed the place of supply
options.why: Section 10(1)(b) deems the third person who gives the instruction to have received the goods, and fixes the place of supply as the principal place of business of that third person. The trader instructed the delivery, so the manufacturer's leg lands in Karnataka however far the goods actually travelled.

options.text: That the e-way bill for the journey was raised showing a Karnataka party
options.misconception: mistakes a document recording movement for the provision that decides chargeability
options.why: An e-way bill records the physical journey. It has no part in fixing a place of supply, and a supply carries the same tax whether the document was raised correctly or not at all.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(b), read with sections 10(1)(a) and 7 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A Kerala manufacturer despatches goods to a customer in Kerala on the written instruction of a trader registered in Karnataka, who has bought them and sold them on. Both invoices in the chain correctly carry integrated tax. The manufacturer's accountant accepts the answer but cannot say what produced it.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the imported goods?

options.text: Vietnam, the location of the supplier
options.misconception: inverts section 11, which puts an export outside India and an import at the importer
options.why: Section 11 has two limbs and they point opposite ways — an import to the location of the importer, an export to the location outside India. Reading the import limb as the supplier's country uses the export limb by mistake.

options.text: Haryana, the location of the importer
options.why: Section 11(a) says the place of supply of goods imported into India shall be the location of the importer. The importer is registered in Haryana, so that is the place of supply, and section 7(2) then makes the import an inter-State supply on which integrated tax is levied.

options.text: Maharashtra, where the goods were landed and the bill of entry was filed
options.misconception: uses the port of clearance, which section 11 never makes the test
options.why: Section 11 gives one answer for every import, and it is the importer and not the port. Where the vessel berths decides which customs house works the consignment and nothing about the place of supply.

options.text: Maharashtra, the movement of the goods terminating there for delivery under section 10(1)(a)
options.misconception: applies section 10 to a cross-border supply that section 11 governs on its own
options.why: Section 10 works supplies within India. A supply of goods imported into India is taken out of it by section 11, which is written as a separate provision for exactly this case.

citation.ref: Section 11(a), read with sections 7(2) and 10(1)(a) of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A company registered only in Haryana imports a consignment of components from a supplier in Vietnam. The vessel berths at Nhava Sheva in Maharashtra, the bill of entry is filed there, and the goods are cleared and trucked to the company's Haryana plant.

items.stem: What is the time of supply?

options.text: 15 July 2026, the date the client paid
options.misconception: picks one of the two dates in section 13(2)(b) instead of the earlier of them
options.why: Payment is one of the two candidates in clause (b), not the answer. The clause takes whichever comes first, and provision of the service on 10 May comes first.

options.text: 30 June 2026, the date of the invoice
options.misconception: uses the invoice date under section 13(2)(a), which is available only where the invoice was issued within the prescribed period
options.why: Section 13(2)(a) offers the invoice date only where the invoice is issued within the period prescribed under section 31. A late invoice takes the supplier out of clause (a) altogether, and the invoice date stops being a candidate at all.

options.text: 9 June 2026, the thirty-first day after the service was completed
options.misconception: turns the invoicing deadline in rule 47 into a time of supply, which no limb of section 13 does
options.why: Rule 47 sets the outer date for issuing the invoice. Missing it moves the supplier from clause (a) to clause (b) of section 13(2); it does not create a time of supply of its own on the day the window shut.

options.text: 10 May 2026, the date the service was provided
options.why: Section 13(2)(b) applies where the invoice is not issued within the period prescribed under section 31, and it takes the date of provision of service or the date of receipt of payment, whichever is earlier. The service was provided on 10 May and the payment came in July, so 10 May governs.

citation.ref: Section 13(2)(b), read with sections 13(2)(a) and 31(2) and rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A consultant completes an assignment on 10 May 2026. He issues his invoice on 30 June 2026, well outside the period rule 47 allows, and the client pays him on 15 July 2026. No advance was taken and no part payment was made before completion.

items.stem: May the credit still be taken?

options.text: No — the window shut on 5 September 2026, when the annual return was furnished
options.why: Section 16(4) allows credit until the thirtieth day of November following the end of the financial year to which the invoice relates or the furnishing of the relevant annual return, whichever is earlier. Filing that return early on 5 September 2026 is the earlier of the two, so the door closed then.
keywords: furnishing of the relevant annual return

options.text: Yes, until 30 November 2026, that being the statutory cut-off for a 2025-26 invoice
options.misconception: treats the November date as a fixed deadline and drops the second limb of section 16(4)
options.why: The November date is one of two limits and the sub-section takes whichever is earlier. An annual return furnished before it pulls the cut-off forward, which is exactly what happened here.

options.text: Yes — section 16(5) reopens the time limit for a credit that was always eligible
options.misconception: applies a relaxation written only for invoices of the financial years 2017-18 to 2020-21
options.why: Section 16(5) is a narrow retrospective relaxation for invoices and debit notes of the financial years 2017-18 to 2020-21. It says nothing about a 2025-26 invoice and reopens nothing here.

options.text: No, but the lapsed credit can be recovered as a refund of unutilised credit under section 54(3)
options.misconception: sends a time-barred credit down the refund route, which opens only for zero-rated supplies and the inverted duty structure
options.why: Section 54(3) refunds unutilised credit in two cases only — zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and accumulation from an inverted duty structure. A credit that died of lateness is neither, and it is simply gone.

citation.ref: Section 16(4), read with section 44 and section 16(5)

items.scenario: A company files its annual return for the financial year 2025-26 early, on 5 September 2026. In October 2026 its accountant finds an eligible input tax credit of ₹3 lakh on a supplier's invoice dated 20 August 2025 that was never taken. Every condition in section 16(2) is satisfied.

items.stem: What does rule 37 require the company to do?

options.text: Nothing — the rule does not reach a supply on which the recipient pays the tax himself
options.why: Rule 37(1) opens by excepting the supplies on which tax is payable on reverse charge basis from the 180-day requirement. The reason is structural — the recipient has already paid the tax to the Government himself, so no supplier's tax is being withheld and no reversal arises however long the fee stays unpaid.

options.text: Nothing, and nothing else either — credit on a reverse-charge supply carries no conditions at all
options.misconception: over-reads one exception into a general exemption from section 16(2)
options.why: The exception is narrow. Every other condition in section 16(2) still binds a reverse-charge supply — the self-invoice, receipt of the service, the tax being paid to the Government and the return being furnished.

options.text: Reverse the credit now and take it back when the fee is paid, subject to the time limit in section 16(4)
options.misconception: applies the rule to a reverse-charge supply and then applies section 16(4) to a re-availment that rule 37(4) frees from it
options.why: Two errors sit on top of each other. The reversal never arises on a reverse-charge supply, and even where it does, rule 37(4) lets the credit be taken back on payment and says the section 16(4) time limit shall not apply to that re-availment.

options.text: Add the whole credit to its output tax liability, with interest, the bill being wholly unpaid
options.misconception: applies the 180-day reversal to a supply the rule expressly takes out of it
options.why: That would be the answer on an ordinary forward-charge supply left wholly unpaid. Here the exception in rule 37(1) applies first, and a reversal computed on a supply outside the rule overstates the liability by the whole amount.

citation.ref: Rules 37(1) and 37(4), read with the second proviso to section 16(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered company received legal services from an advocate in March 2026. Tax on those services is payable by the company itself under reverse charge, and it paid that tax and took the credit. A fee dispute means the advocate's bill is still unpaid more than 180 days after the date of the invoice.

items.stem: Which machines enter the common credit pool?

options.text: Only the third — the export machine takes its credit in full and the exempt machine takes none
options.why: Rule 43 sorts capital goods before it spreads anything. A machine used exclusively for exempt supplies has its input tax not credited to the electronic credit ledger at all, and one used exclusively for taxable supplies is credited in full. Zero-rated supplies count as taxable for this purpose, so the export machine is credited in full and only the machine on common use joins the pool.
keywords: not credited to the electronic credit ledger

options.text: The first and the third, an export being a supply made without tax and so an exempt supply for rule 43
options.misconception: treats a zero-rated supply as an exempt supply, when section 16 of the IGST Act allows credit on it
options.why: A zero-rated supply carries no tax and still carries full credit — that is what zero-rating means, and section 16 of the IGST Act says so in terms. Folding it into exempt supplies would strip an exporter of the very credit the refund machinery then returns to him.

options.text: The second and the third, the exempt machine's credit entering the pool so that it can be reversed month by month
options.misconception: routes a wholly ineligible credit through the apportionment instead of keeping it out of the ledger
options.why: A machine used only for exempt supplies never gets its credit into the ledger, so there is nothing sitting there to reverse in instalments. Putting it in the pool would credit a slice of it every month and take back only the exempt share of that slice.

options.text: All three, rule 43 apportioning every capital good the manufacturer owns
options.misconception: skips the exclusive-use sorting and puts the whole capital block into the formula
options.why: The formula runs on common credit only. Rule 43 first separates the machines used exclusively one way or the other, and a manufacturer who apportions everything both denies himself the export machine's credit and claims part of the exempt machine's.

citation.ref: Rule 43(1), clauses (a), (b) and (c), read with section 17(2) of the CGST Act, 2017 and section 16 of the IGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A manufacturer buys three machines in the same month. The first is used only to make goods exported under a letter of undertaking. The second is used only to make an exempt product. The third runs both lines. He asks which of them feed the common capital goods credit that rule 43 then spreads over the useful life.

items.stem: What becomes of the ₹12,000 difference?

options.text: Nothing — the twelve monthly reversals are final once the returns for those months are filed
options.misconception: reads the monthly reversal as final when rule 42 requires the computation to be made again for the year
options.why: The monthly reversal is provisional by design, because a single month's ratio is a poor guess at the year's. Rule 42 exists to correct it once the real exempt and total turnover for the year are known.

options.text: He applies for a refund of ₹12,000 in cash under section 54
options.misconception: treats an over-reversal as a refund claim when rule 42 restores it as credit in the ledger
options.why: Rule 42 restores the amount as credit, not as money. Section 54 refunds unutilised credit only for zero-rated supplies and for an inverted duty structure, and an over-reversal is neither of those.

options.text: He claims it back with interest, on the same footing as a shortfall carries interest
options.misconception: makes the interest run both ways when rule 42 attaches it only to the amount added back
options.why: The rule is deliberately one-sided. Interest is charged where the true-up shows too little was reversed, because the Government was short of tax for those periods. Nothing in rule 42 pays interest to the taxpayer on the opposite result.

options.text: He claims it back as credit, and no interest is paid to him on it
options.why: Rule 42(2) requires the reversal to be computed again for the whole financial year. Where the annual figure falls short of what was reversed month by month, the excess is claimed back as input tax credit in a return. Interest runs only the other way, on an amount added to output tax liability where the annual figure turns out to be higher.
keywords: claimed back as input tax credit

citation.ref: Rule 42(2), clauses (a) and (b), read with section 17(2) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A trader reversed common credit month by month through the year, using each month's own ratio of exempt turnover to total turnover, and reversed ₹52,000 in all. The computation done again for the whole financial year, on the year's actual figures, shows that the correct reversal is ₹40,000.

items.stem: What input tax credit may the school take?

options.text: Credit on the car and its servicing, but not on the general insurance, which clause (b) blocks
options.misconception: pulls motor insurance into clause (b), which covers life insurance and health insurance
options.why: Clause (b) names life insurance and health insurance. General insurance on a motor vehicle is dealt with by clause (ab), and that is the clause carrying the proviso which saves it here.

options.text: Credit on the car alone — clause (ab) blocks insurance, servicing, repair and maintenance of motor vehicles
options.misconception: reads clause (ab) without its proviso, which releases the attached services wherever the vehicle itself escapes the block
options.why: Clause (ab) does block those services, and its proviso restores them where the vehicle is used for the purposes specified in clause (a). The services follow the vehicle, and they follow it in both directions.

options.text: No credit at all, the car seating fewer than thirteen persons
options.misconception: applies the seating test and ignores the three saving uses written into clause (a)
options.why: Seating capacity opens the block; it does not close the question. Clause (a) then excepts further supply of such vehicles, transportation of passengers, and driving training, and a driving school sits inside the third exception.

options.text: Credit on the car, its insurance and its servicing
options.why: Section 17(5)(a) blocks a motor vehicle for transportation of persons with approved seating capacity of not more than thirteen persons, except where it is used for one of three taxable supplies, the third being imparting training on driving such motor vehicles. The proviso to section 17(5)(ab) then lets the general insurance, servicing, repair and maintenance follow the vehicle out of the block.
keywords: imparting training on driving such motor vehicles

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(a) with its exceptions and section 17(5)(ab) with its proviso, read with section 17(5)(b)

items.scenario: A driving school buys a five-seater hatchback and uses it for nothing but teaching pupils to drive. It also pays for the car's general insurance and for its periodic servicing at the dealership.

items.stem: Whose credit survives section 17(5)?

options.text: Neither — clause (c) blocks every works contract service for construction of immovable property
options.misconception: reads clause (c) without the exception written into it
options.why: The exception is part of the clause, not a concession sitting outside it. Without it the tax would stack at every level of a construction chain, which is the cascading the exception was written to stop.

options.text: The main contractor's, but only so far as he does not capitalise the sub-contractor's bill in his own books
options.misconception: applies the capitalisation words, which widen construction for a person building on his own account, to a contractor supplying the service onward
options.why: The reference to capitalisation sits in the Explanation that widens construction to take in reconstruction, renovation, additions, alterations and repairs. It says what counts as construction; it is not a second condition on the exception in clause (c).

options.text: Both — the shed will be used for the client's taxable manufacture, which satisfies section 16(1) for everyone in the chain
options.misconception: treats business use as an answer to a block that applies even where the property is used in business
options.why: Business use is the entry condition in section 16(1), and section 17(5) then blocks the listed items notwithstanding it. Clause (d) says so in terms, applying even where the goods or services are used in the course or furtherance of business.

options.text: The main contractor's, on the sub-contractor's bill; the client's credit on the main contractor's bill is blocked
options.why: Clause (c) blocks works contract services for construction of immovable property, except where they are an input service for further supply of works contract service. The sub-contractor's service is exactly that in the main contractor's hands. The client is building for himself and supplies no works contract onward, so clause (c) catches him.
keywords: input service for further supply of works contract service

citation.ref: Section 17(5)(c) with its exception, read with section 17(5)(d) and the Explanation defining construction

items.scenario: A client engages a main contractor to build a factory shed. The main contractor sub-contracts the whole of the civil work, and the sub-contractor bills him a works contract service with tax. The main contractor in turn bills the client a works contract service with tax. The shed will be used entirely for the client's taxable manufacture.

items.stem: May he choose that order?

options.text: No, and worse — once rule 86B applies he may not use the credit ledger at all for that period
options.misconception: reads a proportional cap as a total bar on the ledger
options.why: Rule 86B leaves the great bulk of the liability payable from credit and requires only a small proportion in cash. Treating it as a total bar would in effect make such a person pay his whole output tax twice over.

options.text: Yes — rule 86B overrides section 49(5) for anyone it applies to
options.misconception: treats a cap on quantity as a rewrite of the order of utilisation
options.why: A restriction on how much may be paid from the ledger and a rule on which credit is spent first answer different questions. Rule 86B was written to force some cash into the system, not to hand the taxpayer a free choice of heads.

options.text: No — rule 86B caps how much of the liability may come out of the credit ledger and leaves the order of utilisation untouched
options.why: Rule 86B restricts the proportion of output tax liability a person above its threshold may discharge from the electronic credit ledger, and it says nothing about sequence. Section 49B with rule 88A still requires the integrated tax credit to be exhausted first, before central tax or State tax credit may be used at all.

options.text: Yes — rule 88A already lets credit be used in any order and in any proportion
options.misconception: reads rule 88A's freedom as general when it applies only to the balance of the integrated tax credit
options.why: Rule 88A gives a choice at one point only. Integrated tax credit goes to integrated tax first, and the balance may then go towards central tax and State tax in any order and in any proportion. Nothing in it lets the central tax credit jump the queue.

citation.ref: Rule 86B, read with rule 88A and sections 49(5) and 49B of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A registered person to whom rule 86B applies has a large balance of integrated tax credit and a smaller balance of central tax credit. Knowing that rule 86B will force him to pay part of his output liability in cash whatever he does, he proposes to spend the central tax credit first and keep the integrated tax credit for later months.

items.stem: Does the ₹40,000 enter the value of supply?

options.text: Yes, under section 15(2)(b), the supplier having been liable to pay it and the buyer having borne it
options.why: Section 15(2)(b) includes any amount that the supplier is liable to pay in relation to the supply but which has been incurred by the recipient and is not included in the price actually paid or payable for the goods. The contract put the freight on the supplier, so the buyer's direct payment is the supplier's liability discharged by another hand.
keywords: liable to pay in relation to the supply

options.text: Yes, under section 15(2)(c), freight being an incidental expense charged by the supplier to the recipient
options.misconception: picks the clause for expenses the supplier charges when the supplier charged nothing at all
options.why: Clause (c) catches incidental expenses, including commission and packing, charged by the supplier to the recipient. The supplier here charged nothing for freight, so clause (b) and not clause (c) is what brings the amount in.

options.text: No, because the buyer paid the transporter and nothing for freight ever reached the supplier
options.misconception: looks at who paid the money rather than who was liable to pay it
options.why: Who wrote the cheque is not the test. Clause (b) is written for the very case where the recipient pays, and it asks one question — was the supplier liable. Here he was, by the terms of the contract.

options.text: No — freight borne separately by the buyer is outside the value, being his own cost of getting the goods home
options.misconception: invents an exclusion for separately borne freight, when the only route out is the pure agent rule and its conditions are absent
options.why: An amount leaves the value only where rule 33 makes the supplier a pure agent of the recipient, which needs the recipient's authorisation and separate disclosure and is the reverse of this situation. Nothing here removes a liability the supplier had contracted to bear.

citation.ref: Section 15(2)(b), read with sections 15(2)(c) and 15(1) and rule 33 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A machine is sold for ₹8,00,000 on terms that put the cost of delivering it to the buyer's site on the supplier. For his own convenience the buyer engages the transporter himself, pays him ₹40,000 directly, and remits the supplier ₹7,60,000. The supplier's invoice shows ₹8,00,000 and no freight line at all.

items.stem: What is the value of the supply?

options.text: ₹50,000, the transaction value under section 15(1), the parties being unrelated
options.misconception: stops at the unrelated-parties limb and forgets that section 15(1) also needs price to be the sole consideration
options.why: Section 15(1) gives transaction value only where the parties are not related and the price is the sole consideration for the supply. A machine came with the money, so the second limb fails and section 15(4) sends the valuation into the rules.

options.text: ₹80,000, under clause (b) of rule 27
options.why: Rule 27 works down in order. Clause (a) is the open market value, which cannot be found here. Clause (b) is the sum total of consideration in money and such further amount in money as is equivalent to the consideration not in money, if such amount is known at the time of supply. It is known and recorded, so the ladder stops at ₹50,000 plus ₹30,000.
keywords: known at the time of supply

options.text: The value of a supply of like kind and quality, under clause (c) of rule 27
options.misconception: reaches a lower rung of the ladder while a higher one is still available
options.why: Rule 27's clauses are a sequence, not a menu. The like kind and quality limb is reached only where the money equivalent of the non-monetary consideration is not known at the time of supply, and here it is known and written into the contract.

options.text: One hundred and ten per cent of the printer's cost of provision, under rule 30
options.misconception: jumps to the bottom of the ladder when an earlier clause of rule 27 answers the question
options.why: Rule 30 is reached through the last clause of rule 27, after every earlier clause has failed. It is a cost-based estimate for when nothing better exists, and here a known money equivalent exists.

citation.ref: Rule 27, clauses (a) to (d), read with rule 30 and sections 15(1) and 15(4) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A printer supplies stationery to an unrelated customer for ₹50,000 in cash together with a used binding machine. The parties agree, at the time of supply, that the machine is worth ₹30,000, and that figure is written into the contract. No open market value can be found for the printer's supply.

items.stem: What denominator does rule 35 actually use for each head?

options.text: One hundred and eighteen for both heads
options.why: Rule 35 divides by one hundred plus the sum of the tax rates in per cent that apply to the supply, and multiplies by the rate for the head being worked out. On this intra-State supply the sum of the tax rates is eighteen, so the denominator is one hundred and eighteen for the central tax and the same again for the State tax.

options.text: One hundred, the marked price being the taxable value
options.misconception: treats a tax-inclusive price as a taxable value, which is the error rule 35 exists to prevent
options.why: A price marked as including all taxes already contains the tax. Applying the rate to it charges tax on tax, and rule 35 supplies its formula precisely so that the tax is backed out first.

options.text: One hundred and nine for each head, each head bearing only its own nine per cent
options.misconception: builds the denominator from one rate when the rule uses the sum of all the applicable rates
options.why: Both taxes are inside the marked price, so both have to come out of it before a taxable value is left. Dividing by one hundred and nine strips only one of them and leaves the other sitting in the value.

options.text: One hundred and eighteen for the central tax and one hundred and nine for the State tax
options.misconception: uses the sum of the rates for one head and a single rate for the other, when the same denominator serves both
options.why: The denominator does not change with the head. Only the numerator does, and on this supply it is nine for each of the two heads.

citation.ref: Rule 35, read with section 15(1) of the CGST Act, 2017

items.scenario: A retailer marks an intra-State supply at a single price stated to include all taxes. The applicable rate is eighteen per cent, nine central and nine State. His accountant proposes to work out the central tax as the marked price multiplied by nine and divided by one hundred and nine, reasoning that only nine per cent of central tax sits inside the price for that head.

items.stem: Does the discount reduce the value of supply?

options.text: No — tax is charged on the price before the discount, the discount being a matter between the parties
options.misconception: treats value as the gross price when section 15(3) removes a recorded discount from value altogether
options.why: Section 15(3) says the value of the supply shall not include any discount which is given as it describes. A recorded discount is not a side arrangement; it is taken out of the value by the statute itself.

options.text: No — every discount needs a prior written agreement and a proportionate reversal of credit by the recipient
options.misconception: applies the conditions in clause (b) to a discount that clause (a) already covers
options.why: Those conditions guard the clause dealing with a discount given after the supply has been made. A discount already on the face of the invoice never needs them, because the tax was charged on the net figure in the first place.

options.text: Yes — a discount recorded in the invoice for that supply is excluded by section 15(3)(a), and nothing more is needed
options.why: Section 15(3)(a) excludes any discount given before or at the time of the supply if such discount has been duly recorded in the invoice issued in respect of such supply. It asks for one thing and it is satisfied here. The prior agreement, the invoice linkage and the recipient's credit reversal belong to clause (b), which is written for a different kind of discount.
keywords: before or at the time of the supply

options.text: Yes, but a credit note under section 34 must also be issued for the discount
options.misconception: requires a credit note where nothing was over-charged and there is nothing to reduce
options.why: Section 34 corrects an invoice on which the taxable value or the tax charged exceeds what is payable. Here the invoice was right when it was issued, so there is no excess for a credit note to undo.

citation.ref: Section 15(3)(a), read with section 15(3)(b) and section 34(1)

items.scenario: A wholesaler gives a dealer a ten per cent trade discount and shows it on the face of the tax invoice, charging tax on the net figure. There is no written agreement made before the supply, no invoice-wise linkage exercise, no credit note, and the dealer reverses nothing.

items.stem: What does the CGST Act make of that return?

options.text: It is valid to the extent of the ₹3,00,000 paid, the balance standing as an ordinary arrear
options.misconception: splits one return into a valid part and an invalid part, which section 2(117) does not permit
options.why: The definition admits no fractions — the self-assessed tax is either paid in full or it is not. The balance is indeed recoverable, but under section 75(12) as unpaid self-assessed tax, not as the residue of a partly valid return.

options.text: It is a valid return, validity turning on the return having been furnished by the due date
options.misconception: reads validity as timeliness when section 2(117) makes it payment in full
options.why: Timeliness decides the late fee and the interest. Section 2(117) attaches the word valid to one thing only, which is whether the tax the person assessed on himself has actually been paid.

options.text: It is no return at all, so section 39(10) bars him from furnishing the return for July 2026
options.misconception: treats a return short of tax as unfurnished, when section 39(10) bars only a period whose return has not been furnished
options.why: Section 39(10) bars a return for a tax period where the return for any previous tax period has not been furnished. This one was furnished. It is invalid, which is a different defect with different consequences.

options.text: It has been furnished, but it is not a valid return, and the ₹2,00,000 is recoverable without a fresh notice
options.why: Section 2(117) defines a valid return as a return furnished under section 39(1) on which the self-assessed tax has been paid in full, and payment in part fails that definition. Section 75(12) then lets self-assessed tax that remains unpaid be recovered under section 79 without going through a demand under section 73 or section 74A.

citation.ref: Section 2(117), read with sections 39(1), 39(7), 39(10) and 75(12)

items.scenario: A supplier furnished FORM GSTR-3B for June 2026 on time. It declares output tax of ₹5,00,000, but he debited only ₹3,00,000 and left ₹2,00,000 of the self-assessed tax unpaid. Nothing is in dispute — he simply did not have the cash.

items.stem: From which date do the two years in section 54(1) run?

options.text: 30 April 2026, when the service was completed
options.misconception: uses completion of the service, which the Explanation never makes a relevant date for exported services
options.why: Completion is the fact the Explanation uses to choose between its two dates, not a date it offers. It tells you to look at the payment; it does not put the clock on the day the work ended.

options.text: 10 May 2026, the date of the invoice
options.misconception: uses the invoice limb, which the Explanation reserves for payment received in advance of the invoice
options.why: The invoice date is the relevant date only where payment for the services had been received in advance prior to the date of issue of the invoice. That is the other half of the same clause, and it does not describe these facts.

options.text: 20 August 2026, the date the payment in convertible foreign exchange was received
options.why: For services exported out of India the Explanation to section 54 offers two relevant dates and picks between them on one fact. Where the supply of services had been completed prior to the receipt of such payment, the relevant date is the date of receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange. The work finished in April and the money came in August, so August governs.
keywords: completed prior to the receipt of such payment

options.text: 31 March 2027, the end of the financial year in which the export was made
options.misconception: borrows a financial-year starting point that section 54 does not use for any ground of claim
options.why: The Explanation lists a relevant date for each ground of claim and none of them is the close of a financial year. Reading one in would hand every exporter several extra months the section never gave.

citation.ref: Section 54(1), read with the definition of relevant date in the Explanation to section 54 for services exported out of India

items.scenario: A consultancy exports a service under a letter of undertaking, without payment of tax. The work is finished on 30 April 2026, the invoice is issued on 10 May 2026, and the payment arrives in convertible foreign exchange on 20 August 2026. No advance was taken.

items.stem: Does section 54(3) allow the refund?

options.text: Yes, because export duty is a customs levy and section 54(3) is concerned only with goods and services tax
options.misconception: reads the bar as needing the export duty to be a GST levy, when it turns on the goods being subjected to export duty at all
options.why: The proviso asks one question — are the goods exported subjected to export duty. It does not ask which statute imposes it. The policy is that goods the country taxes on the way out do not also get their input credit back.

options.text: Yes — a zero-rated supply made without payment of tax is the first of the two gates, and that settles it
options.misconception: stops at the enabling proviso and never reads the proviso that follows it
options.why: The enabling proviso says which cases may claim; the provisos after it carve cases back out. Reading only the first turns a two-stage test into a one-stage one and gives the wrong answer whenever the carve-out bites.

options.text: No, because unutilised input tax credit is never refundable and can only be carried forward
options.misconception: denies both the gates that the first proviso to section 54(3) opens
options.why: Unutilised credit is refundable in two cases — zero-rated supplies made without payment of tax, and accumulation because the rate on inputs is higher than the rate on output supplies. The claim fails here on the export duty, not because no such refund exists.

options.text: No — a later proviso denies refund of unutilised credit where the goods exported are subjected to export duty
options.why: The first proviso to section 54(3) opens two gates, and a zero-rated supply made without payment of tax is one of them. The second proviso then shuts this case again — no refund of unutilised input tax credit shall be allowed where the goods exported out of India are subjected to export duty. Passing the first proviso is not the end of the enquiry.

citation.ref: Second proviso to section 54(3), read with the first proviso to section 54(3)

items.scenario: An exporter ships a mineral out of India under a letter of undertaking, without payment of integrated tax. The mineral is one on which export duty is leviable, and he pays that duty. He then applies for refund of the input tax credit accumulated on his inputs.

items.stem: What may the proper officer do about the provisional ninety per cent?

options.text: Nothing but sanction ninety per cent within seven days, the timeline being unconditional
options.misconception: reads rule 91 as it stood before the risk evaluation was written into rule 91(2)
options.why: The seven days still run, but the provisional route is no longer automatic. The amended rule 91(2) makes it turn on the risk evaluation and gives the officer an express power to step out of it with recorded reasons.

options.text: Decline the provisional sanction for reasons recorded in writing, such a claim being otherwise eligible for it
options.why: Rule 91(2), as amended with effect from 1 October 2025, ties the provisional sanction to the system's identification and evaluation of risk and lets the proper officer decline that route in a given case for reasons to be recorded in writing. The same amendment extended the ninety per cent route to a claim arising from the inverted duty structure, so eligibility is not the obstacle here — the risk flag is.
keywords: reasons to be recorded in writing

options.text: Refuse outright — the provisional route is confined to refunds arising from zero-rated supplies
options.misconception: describes the position before 1 October 2025, when the ninety per cent route was extended to inverted duty claims
options.why: That was true until 1 October 2025. From that date the provisional sanction covers a claim arising from an inverted rate structure as well, so the manufacturer is inside the route even though he can be taken out of it on risk.

options.text: Decline, but only with the previous approval of the Commissioner
options.misconception: adds an approval the rule does not require, when what it asks for is reasons in writing
options.why: Rule 91(2) puts the decision with the proper officer and disciplines it by requiring his reasons on the file. Nothing in it sends the question up to the Commissioner.

citation.ref: Section 54(6) with rule 91(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017, as amended with effect from 1 October 2025

items.scenario: A manufacturer claims a refund of credit accumulated because the tax on his inputs is higher than the tax on his output. The claim is acknowledged in June 2026. The system's own risk evaluation flags his application.

items.stem: Which rate of exchange converts the invoice into rupees for assessment?

options.text: The rate notified by the Reserve Bank of India on the date of the supplier's invoice
options.misconception: takes the wrong authority and the wrong date together
options.why: Two things are wrong at once. The Explanation to section 14 points at the Board and not at the central bank, and the date is fixed by presentation of the bill of entry, not by the supplier's invoice.

options.text: The notified rate in force on 25 May 2026, the date of entry inwards
options.misconception: carries the entry-inwards date from section 15, which fixes the rate of duty, into section 14, which fixes the rate of exchange
options.why: Entry inwards matters under the proviso to section 15(1)(a), where a bill of entry presented ahead of the vessel is deemed presented on that date for the rate of duty. Section 14 has its own date for conversion and does not borrow that deeming.

options.text: The notified rate in force on 20 May 2026, the day the bill of entry was presented
options.why: The proviso to section 14(1) dealing with conversion says the price shall be calculated with reference to the rate of exchange as in force on the date on which a bill of entry is presented under section 46. The Explanation to section 14 makes the rate of exchange the one determined by the Board, so the bank's own rate never enters the assessment.

options.text: The rate the importer's bank actually applied on 10 June 2026
options.misconception: uses the commercial rate at which the money moved instead of the notified rate on a fixed date
options.why: What the importer paid his bank is a fact about his banking, and using it would make two identical consignments bear different duty. Assessment uses one published rate on one fixed date.

citation.ref: Section 14(1) with the proviso fixing the rate of exchange and the Explanation to section 14, read with section 46 and the proviso to section 15(1)(a)

items.scenario: An importer's invoice is in United States dollars. He presents the bill of entry on 20 May 2026, the vessel is granted entry inwards on 25 May 2026, and he remits the supplier on 10 June 2026. The rate notified by the Board moved between those dates, and his bank gave him a different rate again on the day of remittance.

items.stem: Why does rule 10(2) produce a higher value for A?

options.text: Because insurance rises to 1.125 per cent of the free on board value once the transport cost is undocumented
options.misconception: ties the two fallbacks together when each is triggered separately by its own cost being unascertainable
options.why: The two substitutes are independent. Insurance goes to 1.125 per cent of the free on board value only where the insurance cost itself cannot be ascertained, and both importers here have the same documented premium.

options.text: It should not — the officer must accept the freight A states, a declaration being enough to ascertain the cost
options.misconception: treats a bare declaration as ascertainment when the rule asks for the cost to be ascertainable
options.why: If a statement were enough the fallback would never operate, because every importer can state a figure. The rule works on evidence of what was paid, and where that is missing it supplies its own number.

options.text: Because rule 10(2) adds a landing charge of one per cent wherever the transport cost is not documented
options.misconception: revives the flat landing charge that was deleted from rule 10(2) with effect from 26 September 2017
options.why: The one per cent notional loading was removed on 26 September 2017 and is added to nothing today. It was never conditional on documentation in any event; while it lasted it applied to every consignment alike.

options.text: Because an undocumented transport cost is taken at twenty per cent of the free on board value, whatever was in fact paid
options.why: Rule 10(2) uses a documented figure as it stands and supplies a substitute only where the cost of transport cannot be ascertained — twenty per cent of the free on board value. The substitute is a rule of evidence rather than a measure of what happened, so it can sit well above the freight actually paid.
keywords: twenty per cent of the free on board value

citation.source: Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007
citation.ref: Rule 10(2) with its provisos, as amended by Notification 91/2017-Customs (N.T.) dated 26 September 2017

items.scenario: Two importers land identical consignments on the same day at the same free on board value, shipped on the same vessel at the same freight and covered by the same insurer at the same premium. Importer A's assessable value comes out higher than importer B's. The only difference between them is that B produced documentary evidence of the transport cost he paid and A could not.

items.stem: What is he liable for after the relinquishment?

options.text: Nothing at all, the relinquishment wiping out the rent and the interest along with the duty
options.misconception: over-reads a relief that covers duty only and is conditional on the other charges being paid
options.why: The relief is granted upon payment of those charges — they are the price of walking away, not part of what is forgiven. The warehouse keeper's rent and the interest already accrued stay his.

options.text: Rent, interest, other charges and penalties on the goods, but not the duty on them
options.why: The proviso to section 68 lets the owner relinquish his title to warehoused goods at any time before an order for clearance for home consumption has been made, upon payment of the rent, interest, other charges and penalties payable in respect of the goods, and says that upon such relinquishment he shall not be liable to pay duty on them.
keywords: not be liable to pay duty

options.text: The full duty, unless he re-exports the goods under section 69 instead
options.misconception: treats re-export as the only exit from a warehouse when relinquishment before a clearance order is a separate one
options.why: Section 69 is one exit and it needs a buyer abroad and a shipping bill. Relinquishment under the proviso to section 68 is another, and it is the one open to an importer with no market at either end.

options.text: The full duty, relinquishment changing the ownership of the goods and not the liability to duty
options.misconception: reads the levy as surviving a relinquishment that the proviso to section 68 expressly relieves
options.why: The proviso was written for the importer who no longer wants the goods and would otherwise be taxed on something he will never take. Its closing words remove the duty, and that is the whole point of it.

citation.ref: The provisos to section 68, read with sections 61 and 69 of the Customs Act, 1962

items.scenario: An importer warehoused a consignment months ago and the market for it has collapsed. No order for clearance for home consumption has been made, and no offence appears to have been committed in respect of the goods. He writes to the department relinquishing his title to them. Warehouse rent and interest have accrued in the meantime.

items.stem: How is the import duty on the warehoused goods contained in that scrap dealt with?

options.text: Charged on all the scrap, waste never being exported and so never earning the remission
