The board says nothing has happened, because section 164 lists neither absence from meetings nor a shareholding requirement.

items.stem: Where is the counsel wrong?

options.text: Only on the creditor — the reliefs are correctly stated, because once a resolution has been passed the members' remedy is confined to damages against the directors
options.misconception: limits section 245 to compensation and ignores the declaratory and restraining orders in it
options.why: Damages under section 245(1)(g) are the last of the orders, not the only one. The section was drafted to let a class stop something as well as be paid for it, which is why declaring the resolution void and restraining the directors from acting on it are both on the list.

options.text: On the reliefs and on the creditor — section 245(1) lets the Tribunal declare void a resolution altering the memorandum or articles where it was passed by suppression of material facts and restrain the company and its directors from acting on it, but the application may be made only by members or depositors or any class of them, so the supplier has no standing
options.why: Section 245(1) is not confined to damages. Its list of orders begins with restraining the company from committing an act ultra vires the memorandum or articles, and includes declaring a resolution altering the memorandum or articles void where the resolution was passed by suppression of material facts or obtained by mis-statement, and restraining the company and its directors from acting on such a resolution. Who may ask is the other half of the section, and it names the requisite number of members or depositors, or any class of them. A trade creditor is neither, so he cannot join.

options.text: On nothing — the members' only route against a resolution passed by suppression of facts is an application for oppression and mismanagement under sections 241 and 244
options.misconception: sends a class action down the oppression route the Act keeps separate from it
options.why: Sections 241 and 244 give a remedy for affairs conducted in a manner prejudicial or oppressive, and they run against the company and its management. Section 245 is a separate remedy with its own list of orders and its own class of applicants, and the members here may use it.

options.text: Only on the reliefs — the supplier may join, because a class action is open to any class of persons whose interests are prejudiced by the conduct of the company's affairs
options.misconception: reads "any class of them" as opening the section to persons other than members and depositors
options.why: The words "or any class of them" attach to the members and the depositors already named; they widen how those two groups may come, not who may come. A creditor's remedy lies elsewhere — in his own suit, or under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 — and not in section 245.

citation.ref: Section 245(1), contrasted with sections 241 and 244

items.scenario: An unlisted public company passed a special resolution altering the objects clause of its memorandum, having kept from the members a material fact about the promoter's interest in the new business. A group of members well above the number the Rules require, joined by a trade supplier the company owes money to, wants the Tribunal to declare the resolution void and to stop the directors acting on it. The company's counsel says a class action lies only for damages after the loss has been suffered, that a resolution already passed cannot be touched, and that a creditor stands in the same shoes as a member.

items.stem: What is the correct position on the two questions?

options.text: The managing director is right about the valuation, which belongs to the Board under section 179, and the committee's remit is confined to the financial statements and the auditors
options.misconception: reads the committee's terms of reference as ending at the accounts
options.why: Section 177(4) reaches well past the accounts — scrutiny of inter-corporate loans and investments, valuation of undertakings or assets of the company wherever it is necessary, evaluation of internal financial controls and risk management systems, and monitoring the end use of funds raised through public offers are all in the list.

options.text: The recommendation does not bind the Board and nothing need be said about it anywhere, the committee's views being internal to the company
options.misconception: leaves out the disclosure section 177(8) requires when a recommendation is refused
options.why: Section 177(8) is the whole answer to a Board that departs from its audit committee. The Board's report must disclose the composition of the committee and, where a recommendation has not been accepted, that fact with the reasons, so the members read the disagreement before they vote.

options.text: The recommendation does not bind the Board, but section 177(8) requires the Board's report to disclose that a recommendation of the audit committee was not accepted and the reasons for it; and the valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary, is inside the committee's terms of reference under section 177(4)
options.why: Section 139(1) makes the appointment of the auditor an act of the members at the annual general meeting on the Board's proposal, so the audit committee recommends and does not decide. What the Act does instead is make the disagreement visible: section 177(8) requires the Board's report to disclose the composition of the audit committee and, where the Board has not accepted any recommendation of the committee, to disclose that along with the reasons for it. Section 177(4) then lists the committee's terms of reference and valuation of undertakings or assets of the company, wherever it is necessary, is one of them.

options.text: The recommendation binds the Board, because section 177(4) puts the recommendation for appointment and remuneration of auditors in the committee's hands
options.misconception: turns a power to recommend into a power to appoint
options.why: Section 177(4) gives the committee the recommendation and section 139(1) gives the members the appointment. The Act deals with a Board that overrides the committee by making it say so in its report under section 177(8), not by taking the decision away from it.

citation.ref: Sections 177(4) and 177(8), read with section 139(1)

items.scenario: A listed company's audit committee, properly constituted, recommends against proposing the existing audit firm for reappointment, giving its reasons in writing. The Board disagrees and puts the firm to the members at the annual general meeting anyway. Separately, the Board proposes to have an undertaking of the company valued for a possible sale, and the managing director tells the committee that a valuation is a Board matter with which it has no concern. The company secretary advises that the committee's recommendation binds the Board and that the valuation is indeed outside its remit.

items.stem: What does section 90 require the company itself to do?

options.text: It must apply to the Tribunal at once for an order restricting the shares, the empty register being enough on its own
options.misconception: skips the notice and the reply period the section places before any application
options.why: The application is the last step and not the first. Section 90(7) allows it only where the person noticed under section 90(5) fails to give the information within the thirty days section 90(6) allows, or gives information that is not satisfactory, and it must then be made within fifteen days of the expiry of that period.

options.text: It must go and find him — section 90(4A) puts the company under a duty to take steps to identify a significant beneficial owner, section 90(5) lets it give notice in Form BEN-4, the recipient has thirty days to reply, and on no reply or an unsatisfactory one the company must apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days for an order restricting the shares
options.why: Section 90(4A) requires every company to take necessary steps to identify an individual who is a significant beneficial owner in relation to it and to require him to comply with the section, so the duty does not wait on a declaration. Section 90(5) lets the company give notice in Form BEN-4 to any person it knows or has reasonable cause to believe to be a significant beneficial owner or to have knowledge of one. Section 90(6) gives that person thirty days to give the information. Where no information is given or the information given is not satisfactory, section 90(7) requires the company to apply to the Tribunal within fifteen days of the expiry of that period for an order restricting the shares, which the Tribunal passes within sixty days under section 90(8).

options.text: It must report the body corporate to the Registrar, who then investigates and identifies the individual behind it
options.misconception: hands the company's own enquiry to the Registrar
options.why: The Registrar is not the enquiring authority here. Section 90 puts the enquiry on the company — identify under sub-section (4A), notice under sub-section (5), reply under sub-section (6) — and the forum for an unanswered notice is the Tribunal under sub-section (7), not the Registrar.

options.text: Nothing until a declaration is filed — the obligation in section 90(1) is on the individual, and the company's part is to file Form BEN-2 once it has a declaration to file
options.misconception: reads the company's role as passive, which section 90(4A) was inserted to end
options.why: Section 90(1) does put a declaration on the individual and the company does file Form BEN-2 once it has one. Section 90(4A) was inserted afterwards precisely because that left a company free to know nothing, and it now requires the company to take necessary steps to identify the individual itself.

citation.ref: Sections 90(4A), 90(5), 90(6), 90(7) and 90(8), read with Rule 2(1)(h) of the Companies (Significant Beneficial Owners) Rules, 2018

items.scenario: An unlisted public company's register of members shows a body corporate holding eighteen per cent of its equity. The company's directors know that the body corporate is controlled by an individual, but nobody has declared anything and the register of significant beneficial owners is empty. The company secretary says the company's duty begins only when a declaration in Form BEN-1 arrives, and that until an individual comes forward there is nothing the company can do.

items.stem: What does section 197 permit?

options.text: The excess is his unless the company sues for it, and a special resolution at any later general meeting can put the matter beyond doubt
options.misconception: treats the excess as the director's money and the waiver as available without a time limit
options.why: Section 197(9) makes him hold the sum in trust for the company until he refunds it, so it is the company's money in his hands. Section 197(10) then puts a two-year limit on any waiver, measured from the date the sum becomes refundable, and a resolution outside that window cannot waive anything.

options.text: The company may waive recovery by an ordinary resolution, a waiver being a matter of ordinary business once the excess has been disclosed in the accounts
options.misconception: downgrades the special resolution section 197(10) requires
options.why: Section 197(10) names a special resolution and nothing less. The excess arose because the limits themselves may be exceeded only on a special resolution, so letting a simple majority forgive it afterwards would undo the section.

options.text: He must refund it and holds it in trust for the company until he does; the company may waive recovery only by a special resolution passed within two years from the date the sum became refundable, and because a default to a public financial institution is running, that lender's prior approval must be obtained before the members are asked
options.why: Section 197(9) says a director who draws remuneration in excess of the limits shall refund the sum to the company and, until it is refunded, hold it in trust for the company, so the money is the company's from the start and not his. Section 197(10) forbids the company to waive recovery unless approved by special resolution within two years from the date the sum becomes refundable, which puts the outer date at 30 September 2028 and makes a September 2028 meeting the last chance. Its proviso requires that where the company has defaulted in payment of dues to any bank or public financial institution or non-convertible debenture holder or other secured creditor, the prior approval of that creditor be obtained before the shareholders are asked.

options.text: The lender's approval is irrelevant, and Central Government approval is what section 197 requires before any excess remuneration may be retained
options.misconception: revives the Central Government approval abolished in 2018 and drops the lender's prior approval
options.why: Central Government approval for remuneration beyond the section 197 limits was removed by the 2017 amendment with effect from 2018, and what replaced it is the members' special resolution. The proviso to section 197(10) then adds the lender, requiring the prior approval of the bank, public financial institution, non-convertible debenture holder or other secured creditor whose dues are in default.

citation.ref: Sections 197(9) and 197(10) with its proviso, read with section 197(1)

items.scenario: A public company's managing director drew remuneration for 2025-26 that exceeded the limit section 197 allows, and no special resolution was passed at any time. The excess became refundable on 30 September 2026. The company has defaulted in repaying a term loan to a public financial institution, and that default is continuing. The Board wants to let the managing director keep the excess and proposes to put a special resolution to the members at the annual general meeting in September 2028, taking the view that the money is his until the members say otherwise and that the lender has no say in the company's remuneration decisions.

items.stem: Is the finance head right on either point?

options.text: On neither — Rule 4(3) exempts all three from cost audit on those facts and not on which Table the industry sits in, and the exemption is from the audit alone, the duty to maintain cost records under Rule 3 continuing unaffected
options.why: Rule 4(3) of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 exempts from the requirement of cost audit a company whose revenue from exports in foreign exchange exceeds seventy-five per cent of its total revenue, a company operating from a special economic zone, and a company engaged in the generation of electricity for captive consumption through a captive generating plant. Each of the three answers one of those descriptions on its own facts. The Tables decide coverage and thresholds, not exemption, and Rule 3 keeps the cost records requirement running for a covered company whether or not its accounts are audited.

options.text: Right on the records but wrong on the Tables — the three exemptions apply across both Tables, and a company exempt from cost audit is relieved of maintaining cost records as well
options.misconception: reads an exemption from the audit as an exemption from the records
options.why: Rule 4 is headed by the audit and Rule 3 by the records, and the exemption in Rule 4(3) is expressed as an exemption from the requirement of cost audit. A covered company continues to include the particulars of cost in its books under section 148(1) and Rule 3.

options.text: Right on the Tables but wrong on the records — the export exemption applies only to a company in the non-regulated sector, because a regulated industry is audited on public interest grounds
options.misconception: attaches a sector condition to an exemption Rule 4(3) writes without one
options.why: Rule 4(3) names three descriptions of company and attaches no sector condition to any of them. The regulated and non-regulated split in the Tables governs which industries are covered and at what turnover, and it stops there.

options.text: On both — Table A companies are in the regulated sector and can never be exempt, while a Table B company that is exempt from cost audit keeps no cost records
options.misconception: makes the exemption turn on the Table and treats records and audit as one duty
options.why: Rule 4(3) is written by reference to what the company does with its revenue and where it operates, and it applies across both Tables. Rule 3 imposes the record-keeping duty separately, and nothing in Rule 4(3) touches it — a company exempt from the audit still writes the records the audit would have examined.

citation.ref: Rule 4(3) of the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014, read with Rule 3 of those Rules and sections 148(1) and 148(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Three companies sit in industries listed in the Tables to the Companies (Cost Records and Audit) Rules, 2014 and each crosses the turnover threshold for cost audit. The first earns eighty per cent of its total revenue from exports in foreign exchange. The second operates wholly from a special economic zone. The third generates electricity solely for its own captive consumption. Their common finance head says the exemption depends entirely on whether the industry sits in Table A or Table B, and that in any case a company exempt from cost audit need keep no cost records either.

items.stem: What has the plan missed?

options.text: Three things — a notice of the proposed scheme inviting objections or suggestions from the Registrar, the Official Liquidator and persons affected by the scheme, within thirty days; a declaration of solvency filed by each company with the Registrar; and the cancellation of the shares the transferee holds in the transferor, which it may not keep in its own name
options.why: Section 233(1)(a) requires a notice of the proposed scheme inviting objections or suggestions from the Registrar and Official Liquidators where the registered offices of the companies are situated, and from persons affected by the scheme, within thirty days. Section 233(1)(b) requires each of the companies to file a declaration of solvency with the Registrar before convening the meeting. Section 233(11) then says the transferee company shall not on merger or amalgamation hold any shares in its own name or in the name of any trust, and all such shares shall be cancelled or extinguished, so treasury shares are not an outcome the section allows.

options.text: Only the notice — a declaration of solvency is required only in a members' voluntary winding up, and a transferee may hold shares in the transferor as an investment once the merger is registered
options.misconception: borrows the winding-up context for the declaration and ignores section 233(11)
options.why: Section 233(1)(b) writes the declaration of solvency into the merger itself, in the prescribed form and filed with the Registrar. Section 233(11) is equally express that the transferee shall not hold shares in its own name or in the name of any trust and that all such shares shall be cancelled or extinguished.

options.text: Nothing — with more than ninety per cent of total shares and nine-tenths in value of creditors, section 233 asks for nothing more from anybody outside the two companies
options.misconception: treats the two approval thresholds as the whole of section 233
options.why: The thresholds are only sub-clauses (c) and (d). Sub-clause (a) puts the scheme in front of the Registrar, the Official Liquidator and persons affected by it for thirty days, and sub-clause (b) requires a declaration of solvency, both before the approvals are taken.

options.text: Only the shares — the notice and the declaration of solvency belong to a scheme under section 232 before the Tribunal, and section 233 exists to dispense with them
options.misconception: assumes the fast track dispenses with every formality rather than with the Tribunal
options.why: What section 233 dispenses with is the Tribunal, not the scrutiny. The notice under section 233(1)(a) and the declaration of solvency under section 233(1)(b) are the fast track's own requirements, and objections raised on that notice are what can send the scheme to the Tribunal under section 233(5).

items.scenario: A holding company proposes to absorb its wholly owned subsidiary under section 233. It has the members' approval by more than ninety per cent of the total number of shares and written approval from creditors representing more than nine-tenths in value. It has told nobody outside the two companies, has filed no declaration of solvency, and proposes on the merger to keep the shares it holds in the subsidiary alive in its own name so that they can be sold later. Its lawyers say the whole point of the fast track is that nobody outside the companies has to be consulted.

items.stem: How should the two objections be dealt with?

options.text: Both fail — section 5(7) makes a person to whom a financial debt has been legally assigned or transferred a financial creditor in his own right, and the acknowledgement in the signed balance sheet starts a fresh three-year period, so the application filed on 1 June 2026 is in time
options.why: Section 5(7) defines a financial creditor as any person to whom a financial debt is owed and includes a person to whom such debt has been legally assigned or transferred, so the assignee stands exactly where the bank stood. On limitation, section 238A applies the Limitation Act, 1963 to proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority; the three-year period under Article 137 runs from the date of default, but section 18 of that Act starts it afresh on an acknowledgement of liability made in writing and signed before the period expires, and an entry in a signed balance sheet can be such an acknowledgement. Three years from 15 July 2024 had not run out on 1 June 2026.

options.text: Both succeed — an assignee has bought a claim rather than disbursed money for the time value of money, and limitation runs from the default and cannot be restarted under the Code
options.misconception: reads the disbursement test as personal to the original lender and treats section 238A as excluding acknowledgement
options.why: The disbursement test in section 5(8) describes the debt, not the holder of it, and section 5(7) says in terms that an assignee is a financial creditor. Section 238A brings in the whole Limitation Act, 1963 and not merely its periods, so section 18 on acknowledgement applies along with Article 137.

options.text: The assignment objection fails but the limitation objection succeeds, because section 238A allows no acknowledgement to extend a period that runs from the date of default
options.misconception: applies the limitation period without the section that restarts it
options.why: Section 238A makes the provisions of the Limitation Act, 1963 apply as far as may be, and section 18 of that Act is one of them. An acknowledgement of liability signed before the period expires starts a fresh period from the date of the acknowledgement.

options.text: The limitation objection fails but the assignment objection succeeds, so the asset reconstruction company must first have the assignment confirmed by a civil court before it can apply
options.misconception: adds a confirmation step the Code does not require of an assignee
options.why: Section 5(7) needs no confirmation from anybody. A person to whom the debt has been legally assigned or transferred is a financial creditor for the purposes of the Code, and he applies under section 7 in that character.

citation.ref: Sections 5(7), 5(8) and 238A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, read with Article 137 and section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963

items.scenario: A bank's term loan to a manufacturing company fell into default on 1 March 2022, in an amount well above the sum notified under section 4. On 1 October 2023 the bank assigned the debt to an asset reconstruction company for value. The corporate debtor's audited balance sheet for the year ended 31 March 2024, signed on 15 July 2024, records the loan as payable. The asset reconstruction company files an application under section 7 on 1 June 2026. The corporate debtor resists on two grounds — that only the original lender who parted with the money is a financial creditor, and that the claim is time-barred because more than three years have gone by since the default.

items.stem: How do these three claims rank against the ₹9 crore?

options.text: The government's ₹10 crore ranks ahead of the ₹15 crore shortfall, statutory dues having priority over a private debt under the general law
options.misconception: imports a Crown priority the Code's ranking has displaced
options.why: Section 53(1) opens by overriding anything to the contrary in any other law, and inside it the government dues for the two years preceding the liquidation commencement date rank equally with the unpaid balance of a secured creditor that enforced its own security. Neither is ahead of the other.

options.text: The ₹15 crore shortfall ranks with the relinquishing secured creditors alongside the workmen in clause (b), because a secured creditor keeps its rank whether it relinquishes or enforces
options.misconception: gives the enforcing secured creditor the rank the Code reserves for one that relinquishes
options.why: The choice under section 52 is the whole point of the ranking. A secured creditor that relinquishes its security into the estate is put with the workmen in section 53(1)(b); one that enforces its own security keeps what it realises and takes any shortfall down to section 53(1)(e), alongside the government.

options.text: All ₹6 crore of workmen's dues rank ahead, then the ₹15 crore shortfall, then the government dues, because workmen come first in the waterfall whatever the period they relate to
options.misconception: ignores the twenty-four month window that defines the workmen's dues in clause (b)
options.why: Clause (b) is not "workmen's dues"; it is workmen's dues for the period of twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date. Anything older is a debt of the company like any other and joins the residual class in section 53(1)(f).

options.text: The ₹4 crore of recent workmen's dues is paid first; the ₹15 crore shortfall of the enforcing secured creditor ranks with the ₹10 crore of government dues below it and shares what is left rateably; and the ₹2 crore of older workmen's dues drops below both of them
options.why: Section 53(1)(b) covers workmen's dues for the period of twenty-four months preceding the liquidation commencement date, and that is where the ₹4 crore sits. A secured creditor that declines to relinquish and realises its security under section 52 is dealt with by section 53(1)(e), which ranks any amount unpaid to it following the enforcement equally with government dues for the two years preceding that date, so the ₹15 crore and the ₹10 crore share what survives the workmen. Workmen's dues falling outside the twenty-four month window are not in clause (b) at all and fall into the residual class in section 53(1)(f), behind both.

citation.ref: Sections 53(1)(b), 53(1)(e) and 53(1)(f), read with section 52

items.scenario: A company is in liquidation under the Code. A secured creditor owed ₹50 crore chose not to relinquish its security and realised ₹35 crore by enforcing it, leaving ₹15 crore unpaid. Workmen are owed ₹6 crore in all, of which ₹4 crore relates to the twenty-four months before the liquidation commencement date and ₹2 crore to earlier periods. Government dues for the two years preceding that date are ₹10 crore. The liquidator has ₹9 crore in the estate after paying process and liquidation costs in full.

items.stem: Is the bidder eligible?

options.text: Yes, and for the committee's reason — section 29A(c) looks only at the account of the resolution applicant itself and of the corporate debtor, so an account of a different company is irrelevant
options.misconception: reads clause (c) without Explanation I, which extends it to connected persons
options.why: Clause (c) is expressly extended by Explanation I, which is what makes section 29A a promoter test rather than a company test. It reaches the person in management or control of the applicant and the holding, subsidiary, associate and related party of that person, so a sister company's account is squarely in.

options.text: Yes, because section 240A switches off clause (c) wherever the resolution applicant is the promoter of the business rather than an outside investor
options.misconception: reads section 240A as a promoter relaxation when it is an MSME relaxation
options.why: Section 240A switches off clauses (c) and (h) only where the corporate debtor is a micro, small or medium enterprise, and this corporate debtor is not one. Nothing in the Code relaxes section 29A because the bidder happens to be a promoter.

options.text: No, and nothing can be done — once an account connected to the applicant has been a non-performing asset for over a year, clause (c) is an absolute bar and no payment cures it
options.misconception: applies clause (c) without the proviso that lets the applicant clear the account
options.why: The first proviso to clause (c) exists to let a bidder buy his way back to eligibility. Paying all overdue amounts with interest and charges on the non-performing asset accounts before the plan is submitted lifts the disqualification, and the timing of the payment is what matters.

options.text: Not on the committee's reasoning — section 29A(c) reaches a connected person, and Explanation I brings in the person in management or control of the resolution applicant and the companies he controls; but the proviso to clause (c) makes the bidder eligible if it pays all the overdue amounts with interest and charges before submitting the plan, which it proposes to do
options.why: Section 29A(c) disqualifies a person, or any other person acting jointly or in concert with him, whose account or an account of a corporate debtor under his management or control has been classified as a non-performing asset with at least one year gone from the classification to the insolvency commencement date, and Explanation I defines a connected person to include the person who is or shall be in management or control of the business of the corporate debtor during the implementation of the plan and the holding, subsidiary, associate or related party of such a person. The promoter's second company is caught that way. The first proviso to clause (c) is the cure: the person is eligible if he makes payment of all overdue amounts with interest and charges relating to the non-performing asset accounts before submission of the resolution plan.
keywords: before submission of the resolution plan

citation.ref: Section 29A(c) with its first proviso and Explanation I, read with sections 30(4) and 240A

items.scenario: A bidder company wants to submit a resolution plan for a corporate debtor that is not a micro, small or medium enterprise. The bidder's own accounts have never been irregular. Its promoter, who controls it and would control the corporate debtor while the plan was implemented, also controls a second company whose account was classified as a non-performing asset four years before the insolvency commencement date and remains overdue. Before submitting the plan the bidder offers to pay every overdue amount on that account with interest and charges. The committee of creditors says the bidder is clean because the bad account is neither its own nor the corporate debtor's.

items.stem: Are these preferential transactions?

options.text: Neither is — the supplier payment falls inside the exclusion for a transfer made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of both the corporate debtor and the transferee, and the mortgage secured new value advanced at the same time rather than an antecedent debt
options.why: Section 43(3)(a) takes out of the section a transfer made in the ordinary course of the business or financial affairs of the corporate debtor or the transferee, and the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain read that "or" as "and", so a payment that is ordinary for both sides is excluded — which this one is. The mortgage fails the section at its foundation: section 43(2) requires the transfer to be for the benefit of a creditor on account of an antecedent debt, and money advanced on the same day is not antecedent. Section 43(3)(b) says the same thing from the other side by excluding a transfer creating a security interest in property acquired by the corporate debtor to the extent that the security interest secures new value.

options.text: Both are — once a transfer inside the look-back puts a creditor in a better position than he would have been in under section 53, section 43 catches it
options.misconception: applies the better-position test without the antecedent debt requirement or the exclusions
options.why: The better-position test in section 43(2)(b) is the last of several conditions, not the first. The transfer must also be to a creditor, surety or guarantor on account of an antecedent debt, and it must survive the exclusions in section 43(3), and both transactions fail the section before the comparison with section 53 is reached.

options.text: Only the supplier payment is, because an ordinary trade payment prefers one unsecured creditor over the others, while a bank's registered charge is beyond challenge
options.misconception: reverses the two exclusions, treating registration rather than new value as what saves the mortgage
options.why: Registration is a condition of the exclusion, not the reason for it — what saves the mortgage is that it secures new value rather than an antecedent debt. And the supplier payment is protected by section 43(3)(a) precisely because it was ordinary for both sides.

options.text: Only the mortgage is, because a security interest granted while the company was sliding into insolvency prefers a secured creditor over every unsecured one
options.misconception: treats the effect of a security interest as decisive and ignores section 43(3)(b)
options.why: Section 43(3)(b) was written for exactly this transaction — a security interest in property the corporate debtor acquired, to the extent it secures new value given at the time of or after the security agreement and used to acquire that property. The effect on unsecured creditors is not the test where the exclusion applies.

citation.ref: Sections 43(2), 43(3)(a) and 43(3)(b), read with section 43(4) and section 44

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process commences on 1 July 2026. Two transactions from March 2026 are put to the resolution professional, and both are well inside the one-year look-back. The first is a payment of ₹3 crore to a raw-material supplier on the sixty-day credit terms the two have used for years, made in the ordinary way of business on both sides. The second is a mortgage the corporate debtor gave a bank over a machine, the bank having advanced the purchase money for that machine on the same day under a security agreement signed then, with the charge registered within thirty days of the debtor receiving the machine. The resolution professional says both are preferences because each left one creditor better off than the rest.

items.stem: What are the limits on the two orders?

options.text: The third party is protected, but only because the transfer is outside the two-year relevant period in section 46(1), and section 51 is limited to restoration
options.misconception: applies the section 45 look-back to a section 49 application and understates section 51
options.why: The relevant period in section 46(1) governs an application about an undervalued transaction under section 45. Section 49 is deliberately outside it, and what protects the purchaser is the good-faith limit written into section 49 itself.

options.text: The section 49 order cannot prejudice an interest in property acquired in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances, so the third party keeps the plot; and section 51 lets the Authority do far more than restore — set aside the whole or part of the debt, modify the terms, order repayment of amounts received, and require any security to be released
options.why: Section 49 has no relevant period, which is what makes it reach an old transfer, but it has its own limit: an order under it shall not affect any interest in property which was acquired from a person other than the corporate debtor in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances. A purchaser who paid full value and knew nothing answers that description. Section 51 then lists the orders for an extortionate credit transaction and restoration is only the first — the Authority may also set aside the whole or part of any debt created by the transaction, modify its terms, require any party to repay amounts received, and require any security interest created as part of it to be relinquished.
keywords: without notice of the relevant circumstances

options.text: The third party loses the plot because a transferee takes no better title than his transferor, but the section 51 point is right and only restoration is available
options.misconception: applies the general rule on title where the Code has written an express protection
options.why: The general rule would indeed follow the property, which is why the Code wrote an exception to it. The order under section 49 must not prejudice an interest acquired in good faith, for value and without notice, and section 51 in any event allows setting aside the debt, modifying the terms, ordering repayment and releasing a security.

options.text: Neither has a limit — section 49 carries no relevant period and therefore no defence, and section 51 confines the Authority to restoring the position
options.misconception: reads the absence of a look-back period as the absence of any protection, and reads section 51 too narrowly
options.why: Section 49 trades a look-back period for a good-faith defence: the order shall not prejudice an interest acquired in good faith, for value and without notice of the relevant circumstances. Section 51 is a menu of five kinds of order, of which restoring the position is one.

citation.ref: Sections 49 and 51, read with sections 45(2), 46(1) and 50(1)

items.scenario: Two questions come before the Adjudicating Authority in one liquidation. First, an application under section 49 concerns a plot the corporate debtor transferred at a gross undervalue to keep it away from a decree-holder; the original transferee has since sold the plot to a third party who paid full market value, knew nothing of the corporate debtor's affairs, and bought before any application was made. Second, the liquidator has established an extortionate credit transaction and asks what the Authority may do about it beyond putting the parties back where they were. The lender argues that section 49 sets aside the transfer wherever it can be traced, and that the only order available for an extortionate transaction is restoration.

items.stem: What are the thresholds?

options.text: Sixty-six per cent for all three, the committee being a single body that votes on one standard
options.misconception: applies the higher threshold to every decision instead of only the ones the Code names
options.why: The Code sets one general threshold and then raises it for named matters. Section 21(8) is the general rule at fifty-one per cent, and sixty-six per cent applies where section 28(3) or section 30(4) says so, which is to the listed actions and to the resolution plan.

options.text: Fifty-one per cent for all three, since section 21(8) is the general provision on how the committee decides and no other provision displaces it
options.misconception: applies the general threshold where two specific provisions raise it
options.why: Section 21(8) itself opens by saying it applies save as otherwise provided in the Code, and section 28(3) and section 30(4) are two such provisions. Both require sixty-six per cent, one for the actions listed in section 28(1) and the other for a resolution plan.

options.text: Seventy-five per cent for the resolution plan, sixty-six per cent for the security interest and fifty-one per cent for the administrative matter
options.misconception: uses the seventy-five per cent threshold the Code carried before the 2018 amendment
options.why: Seventy-five per cent was the original threshold and it was reduced to sixty-six per cent by the 2018 amendment, which also created the fifty-one per cent general rule. Section 30(4) now reads sixty-six per cent, the same as section 28(3).

options.text: Sixty-six per cent for the resolution plan and sixty-six per cent for the security interest, but fifty-one per cent for the administrative matter
options.why: Section 30(4) requires the committee to approve a resolution plan by a vote of not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors. Creating a security interest over the assets of the corporate debtor is one of the actions listed in section 28(1), and section 28(3) requires the prior approval of the committee by a vote of sixty-six per cent for any of them. Everything else runs on section 21(8), under which the committee takes its decisions by a vote of not less than fifty-one per cent of the voting share, so an ordinary administrative matter carries at fifty-one per cent.

items.scenario: A committee of creditors has three matters before it at one meeting. It must approve a resolution plan. It must decide whether to let the resolution professional create a security interest over the corporate debtor's assets to support a fresh facility. And it must settle an ordinary administrative matter, the scale of expenses the resolution professional may incur. The resolution professional tells the committee that every decision it takes needs sixty-six per cent of the voting share.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The staff are discharged but the liquidator may sue, because the deemed discharge in section 33(7) is absolute and only the bar on proceedings has an exception
options.misconception: takes the exception out of section 33(7) while keeping the proviso to section 33(5)
options.why: Both provisions carry a qualification and section 33(7)'s is the more important of the two here. It excepts the case where the business is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator, which is exactly what he has decided to do.

options.text: The deemed discharge does not operate, because section 33(7) excepts the case where the business is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator; and the liquidator may sue, because the proviso to section 33(5) lets a proceeding be instituted by the liquidator on behalf of the corporate debtor with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority
options.why: Section 33(7) deems the liquidation order to be a notice of discharge to the officers, employees and workmen of the corporate debtor, except where the business of the corporate debtor is continued during the liquidation process by the liquidator — and the plant is running, so the exception applies and the letters are wrong. Section 33(5) does bar the institution of a suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, but its proviso allows a suit or other legal proceeding to be instituted by the liquidator on behalf of the corporate debtor with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority, so the ₹4 crore is recoverable.
keywords: prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority

options.text: The staff are not discharged and the liquidator may sue without asking anybody, section 33(5) applying only to proceedings against the corporate debtor
options.misconception: reads the bar as one-directional and drops the requirement of prior approval
options.why: Section 33(5) bars a suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, in both directions. What the proviso gives the liquidator is not freedom but a route, and the route runs through the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority.

options.text: Both the human resources head and the former managing director are right — the order discharges the staff and shuts the company out of court altogether
options.misconception: reads section 33(7) and section 33(5) without the exception and the proviso inside them
options.why: Section 33(7) carries its own exception for a business continued by the liquidator, and section 33(5) carries its own proviso letting the liquidator sue with the Adjudicating Authority's prior approval. A liquidator who could neither keep staff nor sue a debtor could not sell an undertaking as a going concern at all.

citation.ref: Sections 33(5) with its proviso and 33(7), read with sections 34(1) and 35(1)(e)

items.scenario: A liquidation order is passed on 1 September 2026 and the resolution professional continues as liquidator. He decides to keep the plant running so that the undertaking can be sold whole, and it runs without a break. On the strength of the order the human resources head issues termination letters to every workman and officer, saying the Code has discharged them all automatically. The liquidator separately wants to sue a customer who owes the company ₹4 crore, and the former managing director tells him section 33(5) bars any proceeding by or against the company, so the receivable must simply be written off.

items.stem: What has the company got wrong under the Regulations?

options.text: Two things — Regulation 17(1C) required the members' approval at the next general meeting or within three months of the appointment, whichever is earlier, so 20 September was too late; and Regulation 17(2) allows a maximum gap of one hundred and twenty days between two board meetings, which the gap from 5 November 2026 to 20 March 2027 exceeds
options.why: Regulation 17(1C) requires the listed entity to ensure the approval of shareholders for the appointment of a person on the board of directors at the next general meeting or within a time period of three months from the date of appointment, whichever is earlier. Three months from 1 April 2026 is 1 July 2026, which comes first, so an approval in September is out of time however section 161(1) would have read on its own. Regulation 17(2) requires the board to meet at least four times a year with a maximum time gap of one hundred and twenty days between any two meetings, and 5 November 2026 to 20 March 2027 is a longer gap than that.

options.text: Only the appointment — four board meetings in a financial year satisfy Regulation 17(2), which counts meetings rather than the intervals between them
options.misconception: counts the meetings and ignores the maximum gap the Regulation also imposes
options.why: Regulation 17(2) imposes two conditions in one sentence — at least four meetings in a year and a maximum gap of one hundred and twenty days between any two of them. Four meetings bunched at the ends of the year fail the second even while they satisfy the first.

options.text: Only the meeting gap — the appointment is in order because a general meeting held within the same financial year satisfies Regulation 17(1C)
options.misconception: keeps the general meeting limb of Regulation 17(1C) and drops the three-month limb
options.why: Regulation 17(1C) says the next general meeting or three months from the date of appointment, whichever is earlier. Where the general meeting is more than three months away, the three months governs, and here it expired on 1 July 2026.

options.text: Nothing — section 161(1) governs an additional director's tenure and four meetings were held, so both the Act and the Regulations are satisfied
options.misconception: answers a Regulation question out of the Companies Act, where the Regulation is stricter
options.why: A listed entity has to satisfy both, and where they differ the stricter one decides. Regulation 17(1C) shortens the approval window to the earlier of the next general meeting and three months, and Regulation 17(2) polices the gap between meetings as well as their number.

citation.ref: Regulations 17(1C) and 17(2), read with sections 161(1) and 173(1) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A listed company's board appoints an additional director on 1 April 2026 and proposes to put his appointment to the members at the annual general meeting on 20 September 2026, relying on section 161(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, under which an additional director holds office up to the date of the next annual general meeting. The board met four times during 2026-27 — on 1 April 2026, 15 July 2026, 5 November 2026 and 20 March 2027. The company secretary certifies that the company has complied with both the Act and the Regulations.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: A special resolution is still needed, because Regulation 24(5) admits of no exception once the holding falls to fifty per cent or less
options.misconception: applies Regulation 24(5) without the carve-out for a court or tribunal approved scheme
options.why: The carve-out is written into the Regulation. Where the transaction is under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, or under a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Code, the special resolution is not required and a disclosure to the exchanges within one day of the approval takes its place.

options.text: No special resolution is needed, and the managing director is right about the audit committee, whose remit under the Regulations stops at the listed entity's own accounts
options.misconception: confines the audit committee to the listed entity and ignores Regulation 24(2)
options.why: Regulation 24 is built to follow the money down into the group. Regulation 24(2) requires the audit committee of the listed entity to review the financial statements and in particular the investments made by the unlisted subsidiary, and Regulations 24(3) and 24(4) bring the subsidiary's minutes and significant transactions up to the listed board.

options.text: No special resolution and no disclosure either, a scheme sanctioned by the Tribunal being a matter of public record from which the exchanges take their own notice
options.misconception: reads the carve-out as removing the disclosure along with the approval
options.why: The carve-out replaces one obligation with another. The listed entity is relieved of the special resolution but must disclose the event to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval, so the market learns of it on the entity's own initiative.

options.text: No special resolution is needed, because the requirement is carved out where the transaction is under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, but the event must be disclosed to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval; and the parent's audit committee is required to review the financial statements and in particular the investments made by the unlisted subsidiary
options.why: Regulation 24(5) requires a special resolution before a listed entity disposes of shares in a material subsidiary so as to reduce its holding to fifty per cent or less or to cease to exercise control, and Regulation 24(6) does the same for a sale of more than twenty per cent of the subsidiary's assets. Both are carved out where the transaction is made under a scheme of arrangement duly approved by a court or tribunal, or under a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, in which case the event is disclosed to the stock exchanges within one day of the approval. Regulation 24(2) separately requires the audit committee of the listed entity to review the financial statements, and in particular the investments made, of the unlisted subsidiary.

citation.ref: Regulations 24(2), 24(5) and 24(6), read with Regulations 24(3) and 24(4)

items.scenario: A listed parent has an unlisted Indian subsidiary that is material within the meaning of the Regulations. Under a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the Tribunal, the parent's holding in that subsidiary will fall from a hundred per cent to forty per cent. The parent's company secretary asks whether a special resolution of the parent's shareholders is still needed, and what if anything must be told to the stock exchanges. The managing director separately tells the parent's audit committee that it has no business reviewing an unlisted subsidiary's investments, those being the subsidiary board's affair.

items.stem: What is wrong with this quarter's submission?

options.text: Only the coverage point — the audit committee's role is advisory and the board may approve results it has not seen, and the chief financial officer is right that a review and an audit give the same assurance
options.misconception: makes the audit committee's review optional and equates two different levels of assurance
options.why: Regulation 33(2) makes the audit committee's review a step in the process and not a courtesy. And the two engagements differ by design — a limited review under SRE 2410 expresses a conclusion in the negative form, while an audit expresses an opinion under SA 700 (Revised) on the strength of reasonable assurance.

options.text: Nothing — the results were filed in time, and coverage and committee review are annual requirements that do not apply to a quarter
options.misconception: treats the consolidation coverage and the audit committee review as annual-only duties
options.why: The eighty per cent coverage rule is written for the quarterly consolidated results in terms, and Regulation 33(2) requires board approval after audit committee review of the financial results, quarterly as well as annual. Neither waits for the year end.

options.text: Only the audit committee point — the coverage is satisfied because the entity reviewed more than half of its consolidated revenue and more than half of its consolidated assets
options.misconception: reads the coverage test as a simple majority instead of the eighty per cent the Regulation sets
options.why: The test is at least eighty per cent of each of consolidated revenue, assets and profits, taken separately. Sixty per cent of revenue and fifty-five per cent of assets both fall short, and failing any one of the three limbs is enough.

options.text: Two things and a misunderstanding — at least eighty per cent of each of consolidated revenue, assets and profits must have been audited or subjected to limited review, and sixty and fifty-five per cent fall short; the results had to be approved by the board after review by the audit committee; and a limited review is a lower level of assurance than an audit, not the same one
options.why: For quarterly consolidated results a listed entity must ensure that at least eighty per cent of each of the consolidated revenue, assets and profits respectively has been subjected to audit or, in case of unaudited results, subjected to limited review. Regulation 33(2) requires the financial results to be approved by the board of directors after being placed before and reviewed by the audit committee, and it draws no distinction between a quarter and a year. A limited review under SRE 2410 consists of inquiry and analytical procedures and ends in a negative-form conclusion that nothing has come to the practitioner's attention, which is not the reasonable assurance behind an opinion under SA 700 (Revised).

citation.ref: Regulations 33(2) and 33(3), read with SRE 2410 and SA 700 (Revised)

items.scenario: A listed entity with six subsidiaries submits its quarterly consolidated financial results within the time allowed. Components making up sixty per cent of consolidated revenue and fifty-five per cent of consolidated assets were subjected to limited review; the rest are unreviewed management figures. The results were approved by the board of directors, but the audit committee did not see them first, because the chief financial officer took the view that the committee reviews only annual accounts. He adds that a limited review gives the same assurance as an audit, so the coverage cannot matter.

items.stem: Who may proceed and who may not?

options.text: All three may proceed — the first two are persons resident in India and the third is receiving property from a relative, which the Rules permit
options.misconception: treats residence as answering every question and reads the relative gift rule without its exclusions
options.why: Residence answers the German national's case and no more. The nationality bar operates whatever the person's residential status, and the gift permission for an Overseas Citizen of India covers immovable property other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property — which is precisely what is being given here.

options.text: The German national may buy, having become a person resident in India from the day he came here for employment; the Chinese national needs the Reserve Bank's prior permission whatever his residential status; and the Overseas Citizen of India may not take the farm house by gift at all, a farm house reaching him only by inheritance from a person resident in India
options.why: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 includes a person who has come to or stays in India for taking up employment, so the German national is a person resident in India from his arrival and may acquire immovable property here. The Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 separately require the prior approval of the Reserve Bank for the acquisition of immovable property by a citizen of Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, China, Iran, Nepal, Bhutan, Macau, Hong Kong or the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, whatever his residential status. Those Rules let an Overseas Citizen of India acquire any immovable property other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property, and allow such property to come to him only by inheritance from a person resident in India, so a gift of a farm house is outside the permission.
keywords: prior approval of the Reserve Bank

options.text: The German national must wait until he has spent more than one hundred and eighty-two days in India, the Chinese national may buy freely as a long-standing resident, and the Overseas Citizen of India may take the gift
options.misconception: reduces section 2(v) to the day count and drops the nationality bar and the farm house exclusion
options.why: Section 2(v) opens with the day count and then overrides it, including a person who has come to India for employment from the day he arrives. The nationality bar in the Rules is expressly independent of residential status, and a farm house may reach an Overseas Citizen of India only by inheritance from a person resident in India.

options.text: None may proceed — a foreign national needs the Reserve Bank's prior approval to acquire immovable property in India in every case
options.misconception: applies the prior-approval requirement to every foreign national instead of to a person resident outside India and the listed nationalities
options.why: The prior approval requirement attaches to a person resident outside India who is neither a Non-Resident Indian nor an Overseas Citizen of India, and separately to the listed nationalities whatever their residence. A German national who has become a person resident in India under section 2(v) is in neither category.

citation.ref: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, read with the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019

items.scenario: Three people want to buy property in India. A German national arrived on 1 May 2026 on a five-year employment contract with an Indian company and now lives in Bengaluru; he wants to buy a flat there. A Chinese national has lived and worked in India for nine unbroken years and is plainly a person resident in India by any day count; he wants to buy a flat in Pune. An Overseas Citizen of India living in Toronto wants to accept a farm house in Coimbatore as a gift from his brother, who is a person resident in India. Their common adviser says all three may go ahead, because residence is settled by counting days and each of the first two is resident while the third is taking property from a relative.

items.stem: Where is the chief financial officer wrong?

options.text: On neither — nine months is the period for every exporter and Rule 96A gives one year from the invoice for the money to arrive in every case
options.misconception: applies the general nine-month period and the services limb of Rule 96A to a warehouse export of goods
options.why: Regulation 9(1) itself carves out goods exported to a warehouse established outside India and gives them fifteen months from the date of shipment, because the goods are sold after they arrive. Rule 96A puts its one-year receipt-of-payment condition on services; for goods it measures the export of the goods themselves.

options.text: Only on the exchange period — fifteen months applies, but the letter of undertaking has indeed failed, because payment for any export under a letter of undertaking must be received within one year of the invoice
options.misconception: carries the services condition in Rule 96A across to an export of goods
options.why: Rule 96A has two limbs and they measure different things. For goods the undertaking is that the goods be exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months from the date of issue of the export invoice; the one-year receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange is the condition for a supply of services.

options.text: On both — goods exported to a warehouse established outside India carry fifteen months from the date of shipment, so the exchange obligation ran to 10 July 2027 and was met; and for goods the condition attached to the letter of undertaking is that the goods leave India within the period the rule allows from the invoice, so when the money arrived does not bear on it
options.why: Regulation 9(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 gives all exporters nine months from the date of export, but gives goods exported to a warehouse established outside India fifteen months from the date of shipment, and money received on 1 June 2027 is inside fifteen months from 10 April 2026. Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 puts the one-year condition on the receipt of payment only for a supply of services; for goods the undertaking is that the goods are exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months from the date of issue of the export invoice, which happened on 10 April 2026. For goods the tax clock measures the shipment and the exchange clock measures the money.

options.text: Only on the letter of undertaking — the tax position is safe, but fifteen months applies only where the Reserve Bank has granted an extension on an application, and none was made here
options.misconception: turns a period the Regulation itself gives into a discretionary extension
options.why: The fifteen months is written into Regulation 9(1) for goods exported to a warehouse established outside India and needs no application to anybody. An extension is a separate facility, and it is not what is being relied on here.

citation.ref: Regulation 9(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, read with section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017

items.scenario: An exporter ships goods out of India on 10 April 2026 to its own warehouse established in the Netherlands, from which the goods are sold as buyers are found. The export invoice is dated 5 April 2026 and the shipment goes under a letter of undertaking without payment of integrated tax. The money reaches India on 1 June 2027. The chief financial officer says the exchange obligation was breached on 10 January 2027, nine months from shipment, and that the letter of undertaking has also failed because the payment came in more than a year after the invoice.

items.stem: Is stopping the analysis at section 9B correct?

options.text: Yes — once section 9B taxes the land, section 45(4) does not apply again to the same reconstitution
options.misconception: treats the two sections as alternatives rather than cumulative charges
options.why: The sections tax different components of the same event: 9B taxes the asset transfer, 45(4) taxes the excess over the capital account. Both can apply to a single reconstitution without double-taxing the same rupee.

options.text: No — but the liability falls on partner A personally, not on the firm
options.misconception: shifts the charge to the retiring partner
options.why: Both section 9B and section 45(4) tax the entity — the firm, AOP or BOI — not the partner receiving the assets. The partner's own capital gains, if any, arise separately on disposal of what was received.

options.text: No — section 45(4) must also be tested, taxing any excess of money plus the fair market value of assets received by A over A's capital account balance, as the firm's capital gains
options.why: The two sections operate in sequence on the same event: 9B taxes the deemed transfer of the capital asset at fair market value; 45(4) separately catches any excess consideration — in cash or assets — over the partner's capital account, taxable as capital gains for the firm. Skipping 45(4) misses this second charge.

options.text: No — but section 45(4) only applies when the firm dissolves entirely, not on a partner's retirement
options.misconception: narrows reconstitution to dissolution only
options.why: Reconstitution covers a change in the constitution of the firm — including a partner's retirement, admission, or change in profit-sharing ratio — not only a full dissolution.

citation.ref: Sections 9B and 45(4)

items.scenario: A partnership firm has three partners. On reconstitution, partner A retires and receives a plot of land — a capital asset that had never appeared on the firm's books — plus a cash payment. The firm's accountant reports the land's fair market value as the firm's income under section 9B and stops there, treating the cash payment as a settlement outside the Act.

items.stem: Is the "no capital gains ever" claim correct?

options.text: No — section 47 only shields transfers between individuals and their HUF, not between companies
options.misconception: confuses the HUF-partition clause of section 47 with the subsidiary-holding company clause
options.why: Section 47 lists several independent transactions; the HUF partition clause and the wholly-owned subsidiary clause are separate limbs, and this transfer squarely fits its own limb.

options.text: Yes — section 47 permanently exempts all intra-group transfers between an Indian company and its subsidiary, in either direction, without conditions
options.misconception: drops the wholly-owned and continuing-holding conditions
options.why: The exemption needs the parent to hold the entire share capital of the subsidiary, and needs that holding to continue — it is not a blanket exemption for any group transfer.

options.text: No — the transfer is exempt only if the subsidiary is a foreign company
options.misconception: inverts the actual condition, which requires an Indian holding company
options.why: The clause requires the holding company to be an Indian company; a foreign parent does not qualify under this limb of section 47.

options.text: No — section 47 only defers the gain; if the parent later transfers the asset otherwise than within a similar wholly-owned structure, or ceases to hold the entire share capital, the exemption can be withdrawn under section 47A
options.why: Section 47 keeps the transfer outside section 45's charge at the time it happens, but section 47A claws the exemption back if the parent-subsidiary shareholding condition breaks or the asset leaves the group within the specified period — the tax is deferred, not cancelled.

citation.ref: Section 47

items.scenario: A wholly-owned subsidiary transfers a capital asset to its holding company, a 100 per cent Indian parent, for no separate consideration, as part of an internal restructuring. The subsidiary's tax team argues no capital gains tax applies to this transfer at all, ever.

items.stem: Can he claim the exemption despite the gain being short-term?

options.text: No — section 54B, like section 54, applies only to long-term capital gains
options.misconception: imports the long-term-only condition from section 54 into section 54B
options.why: Several capital gains exemptions apply only to long-term gains, but 54B is a deliberate exception — its use condition, not a holding-period condition, does the gatekeeping.

options.text: No — the new land must be purchased before the sale, not after
options.misconception: reverses the reinvestment window
options.why: The window runs from the date of transfer — reinvestment within two years afterward qualifies; the section does not require a purchase in advance of the sale.

options.text: Yes, but only up to fifty lakh rupees of reinvestment
options.misconception: imports the section 54EC monetary cap into section 54B
options.why: Section 54B carries no such ceiling; the entire capital gain can be exempted if the new agricultural land's cost covers it. The fifty lakh cap belongs to the bonds under section 54EC.

options.text: Yes — section 54B exempts both short-term and long-term gains on qualifying agricultural land; the two-year test attaches to agricultural use before the transfer, not to how long the land itself was held
options.why: Section 54B is unusual among the capital gains exemptions in reaching short-term gains too. What it insists on is that the land was used for agriculture by the assessee or a parent in the two years before transfer — a condition met here regardless of how briefly he owned the land.

citation.ref: Section 54B

items.scenario: An individual sells agricultural land that he personally cultivated for the three years before the sale, earning a short-term capital gain because he had held the land itself for only fourteen months. He buys another agricultural plot within a year of the sale and claims exemption under section 54B.

items.stem: Can the company, not being an individual or HUF, claim exemption under section 54D?

options.text: No — only individuals and HUFs can claim capital gains exemptions on compulsory acquisition
options.misconception: generalises the individual/HUF restriction from other sections to all compulsory-acquisition relief
options.why: That restriction belongs to specific sections such as 54 and 54B. Section 54D was drafted for industrial undertakings precisely because companies, not just individuals, run them.

options.text: Yes — section 54D is open to any assessee, including a company, unlike sections 54 and 54B which are restricted to individuals or HUFs
options.why: Section 54D's own words name no restriction on the class of assessee. It answers a different problem — compulsory loss of an industrial undertaking's premises — and is available to whichever assessee, individual or company, runs that undertaking.

options.text: No — the three-year reinvestment window has already expired since the company built the shed after two years, which falls outside the window
options.misconception: misreads a reinvestment made within the window as falling outside it
options.why: Building the replacement within two years of receiving compensation is comfortably inside the three-year window the section allows; the exemption is not lost.

options.text: Yes, but only if the new asset is also compulsorily acquired land
options.misconception: invents a mirror-image acquisition condition for the replacement asset
options.why: The section requires the new land or building to be for shifting or re-establishing the undertaking; it does not require the replacement itself to come from a compulsory acquisition.

citation.ref: Section 54D

items.scenario: A private limited company runs a factory on land that the state government compulsorily acquires for a highway. The company had used this land for its factory for the preceding four years. Compensation is received in March, and the company builds a replacement factory shed within two years of receiving it.

items.stem: Can the company still claim the section 80-IA deduction?

options.text: No — section 80AC requires the specific deductions it names to be claimed in a return filed by the section 139(1) due date; a belated return under 139(4), however timely otherwise, does not qualify
options.why: Section 80AC's condition is not merely that a return exists before assessment — it names the 139(1) due date specifically. A belated return filed under 139(4) fails this condition even though it is otherwise a valid return.

options.text: Yes — any return filed before the assessment is completed satisfies Chapter VI-A's requirements
options.misconception: substitutes a general before-assessment test for section 80AC's specific due-date test
options.why: That general idea describes ordinary computation, not the stricter gate section 80AC places in front of the named profit-linked deductions.

options.text: No — because Chapter VI-A deductions are never available to companies
options.misconception: invents a blanket bar on companies claiming Chapter VI-A deductions
options.why: Nothing in Chapter VI-A excludes companies as a class; several deductions, including profit-linked ones under sections 80-IA and similar, are squarely aimed at companies running eligible undertakings.

options.text: Yes, because Chapter VI-A deductions can never exceed gross total income and are otherwise unconditional
options.misconception: confuses the ceiling on the amount of deduction with the separate timing condition on claiming it
options.why: The gross-total-income ceiling limits how much can be deducted; it says nothing about when the return must be filed, which is a distinct condition under section 80AC.

citation.ref: Section 80AC read with Chapter VI-A (Sections 80C to 80U)

items.scenario: A company eligible for a deduction under section 80-IA misses the due date under section 139(1) but files its return two months later, within the period allowed for a belated return under section 139(4), still before the assessment is completed.

items.stem: Is the disallowance under section 40A(2) sustainable?

options.text: No — but only because the brother is not a "relative" as the section defines it
options.misconception: misreads the definition of relative, which does include a sibling of a person with substantial interest
options.why: The disallowance fails for want of evidence of excess, not because the relationship falls outside the definition — a sibling is squarely within it.

options.text: No — the section disallows only the excess over fair market value or legitimate business need, and the relationship alone, without a finding that the amount is unreasonable, cannot support disallowing the whole payment
options.why: Section 40A(2) is not a bar on related-party dealing; it is a check on overpayment. The Assessing Officer must show the amount paid is excessive against a comparable benchmark — here, the company's own dealings with unrelated consultants at the same rate undercut any such finding.

options.text: Yes, since section 40A(2) applies automatically whenever a company deals with a director's family member
options.misconception: skips the substantial-interest condition the section actually requires
options.why: The section targets persons having a substantial interest in the business, and their relatives — a director's family member qualifies only if that condition is independently met, and even then, only the excess is disallowed.

options.text: Yes — payments to a relative of a person with substantial interest are disallowed in full, regardless of reasonableness
options.misconception: treats section 40A(2) as an absolute bar rather than a reasonableness test
options.why: The section only ever disallows the excess portion; a payment shown to be at arm's length, as here, survives it entirely.

citation.ref: Section 40A(2)

items.scenario: A company pays consultancy fees to a firm in which the company's managing director's brother is a partner. The fee matches what the company pays unrelated consultants for comparable work. The Assessing Officer disallows the entire fee, citing only the related-party relationship as the reason.

items.stem: Does the voucher-splitting protect the deduction?

options.text: No — but because cash payments to suppliers are disallowed in full regardless of amount
options.misconception: drops the threshold entirely, as if any cash payment triggers disallowance
options.why: The section only bites once the daily aggregate to one person crosses the prescribed limit; cash payments below it are deductible in the ordinary way.

options.text: No — section 40A(3) tests the aggregate of payments to one person in a day, not each voucher separately; splitting one day's payment across vouchers does not take it outside the section
options.why: The section looks at total cash paid to a single person on a single day. Two ₹9,000 payments to the same supplier on the same day add up to ₹18,000, which is what gets tested — the paperwork split changes nothing.

options.text: Yes — the section applies voucher by voucher, so each payment under the limit escapes disallowance
options.misconception: reads the limit as applying per voucher rather than per day per payee
options.why: That reading would defeat the section's purpose by inviting exactly this kind of splitting, which is why the aggregation is by payee and by day, not by voucher.

options.text: Yes, provided the trader can prove the supplier's identity and the genuineness of the purchase
options.misconception: imports a genuineness defence the section does not recognise
options.why: Genuineness and the payee's identity are irrelevant to section 40A(3) — the disallowance turns solely on the mode and aggregate amount of payment, not on whether the transaction was real.

citation.ref: Section 40A(3) and (3A)

items.scenario: A trader pays a supplier ₹18,000 in cash in a single day for goods purchased, splitting it as two separate cash payments of ₹9,000 each recorded in two different vouchers to keep each voucher under the disallowance limit. He claims the full deduction, arguing no single voucher crossed the threshold.

items.stem: On which of these can additional depreciation be claimed, and at what rate for the year?

options.text: Only the new plant and machinery qualifies, and even that draws half the normal additional depreciation rate because it was used for less than 180 days
options.why: Additional depreciation is for new plant and machinery used in manufacturing or power generation — the trucks fail as road transport vehicles and the used machinery fails as second-hand. What survives, the new plant, is still caught by the general half-rate rule for assets used under 180 days in the year of acquisition.

options.text: None of the three qualifies, because additional depreciation is available only in the year following installation, not the year of acquisition itself
options.misconception: invents a one-year lag before additional depreciation can be claimed
