It is section 70(3) that restricts a long-term loss to a long-term gain; section 70(2) lets a short-term loss go against income in respect of any capital asset.

options.text: Total income ₹3,00,000, with a short-term capital loss of ₹3,00,000 carried forward
options.why: The long-term loss of ₹5,00,000 goes against the long-term gain of ₹6,00,000 under section 70(3), leaving ₹1,00,000. The short-term loss of ₹4,00,000 may go against any capital gain under section 70(2), so ₹1,00,000 of it absorbs that balance and ₹3,00,000 is left. Section 71(3) forbids setting it against house property, so total income is the ₹3,00,000 of house property and the ₹3,00,000 of short-term loss is carried forward under section 74.

options.text: Total income ₹3,00,000, and the ₹3,00,000 of short-term capital loss lapses, only a long-term capital loss being capable of carry forward
options.misconception: invents a restriction on carry forward, when section 74 carries both kinds and the asymmetry lies only in how a carried loss may later be used
options.why: Section 74 carries a capital loss of either kind for eight assessment years immediately succeeding, and Mr Pratap has filed in time so section 80 is satisfied. What differs is the use — a carried short-term loss may go against any capital gain, a carried long-term loss only against a long-term gain.

citation.ref: Sections 70(2), 70(3), 71(3) and 74, read with Section 80 and Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Mr Pratap has four figures for previous year 2025-26. A long-term capital gain of ₹6,00,000 on the sale of a plot. A long-term capital loss of ₹5,00,000 on the sale of unlisted shares. A short-term capital loss of ₹4,00,000 on the sale of listed shares. And income from house property of ₹3,00,000. He files his return within the due date under section 139(1).

items.stem: Which of the three changes can stand?

options.text: The first two; the disallowance of the legal fees cannot be made under section 143(1) at all
options.why: Section 143(1)(a)(i) covers an arithmetical error in the return, and clause (v) allows a deduction under the heading covering section 80-IA to be disallowed where the return is furnished beyond the due date under section 139(1). A view that a payment is excessive is a question of fact outside the closed list, and the first proviso independently bars any adjustment made without an intimation to the assessee.

options.text: None — section 143(1) produces only an acknowledgement of the return and no adjustment survives without a notice under section 143(2)
options.misconception: confuses an intimation with an acknowledgement of filing
options.why: An acknowledgement records that the return was received. An intimation under section 143(1) computes the total income and the tax, interest and fee, and where a sum is payable it is deemed to be a notice of demand under section 156.

options.text: All three, the requirement of a prior intimation being a formality that does not invalidate the adjustment
options.misconception: reads the first proviso as directory, when it is a condition on making any adjustment at all
options.why: The proviso says no such adjustments shall be made unless an intimation is given to the assessee in writing or in electronic mode, and the second proviso requires the response to be considered. Even with an intimation, an opinion about excessiveness is not one of the five adjustments the clause permits.

options.text: Only the correction of the arithmetical error
options.misconception: misses clause (v), which lets the lateness of the return defeat a section 80-IA claim at the processing stage itself
options.why: Processing is not confined to arithmetic. Clause (v) permits disallowance of a deduction claimed under section 10AA or under the deductions-in-respect-of-certain-incomes heading of Chapter VI-A, which is where section 80-IA sits, when the return is furnished late.

citation.ref: Section 143(1)(a) clauses (i) and (v) with its first and second provisos, read with Section 156

items.scenario: Quill Ltd furnishes its return for assessment year 2026-27 on 15 December 2026, well after the due date under section 139(1). Processing under section 143(1) produces three changes. One, the totalling of the disallowances in the computation is corrected, the return having added them wrongly. Two, the deduction claimed under section 80-IA is disallowed because the return was furnished after the due date. Three, ₹5,00,000 of legal fees is disallowed because the officer considers the payment excessive for the work done. No prior communication of any proposed adjustment was sent before the third change.

items.stem: Which of the four steps is beyond his powers?

options.text: The third — accounts of a year eight years before the previous year
options.why: The second proviso to section 142(1) says the Assessing Officer shall not require the production of any accounts relating to a period more than three years prior to the previous year. The three preceding years in step two are inside that limit, and eight years back is outside it. Nothing else in the section extends the reach.
keywords: three years prior to the previous year

options.text: The fourth — a special audit cannot be directed without the assessee's consent
options.misconception: substitutes the assessee's consent for the approval and the hearing the section actually requires
options.why: Section 142(2A) needs the previous approval of the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner or Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, and its proviso needs a reasonable opportunity of being heard for the assessee. Consent appears nowhere, and since 1 June 2007 the cost of the audit is borne by the Central Government under section 142(2D).

options.text: The first — once the time under section 139(1) has gone, a return can be compelled only by a notice under section 148
options.misconception: treats section 148 as the only route to a late return, when section 142(1)(i) is written for exactly this case
options.why: Section 142(1)(i) lets the Assessing Officer require a return from a person who has not made one within the time allowed under section 139(1). No escapement of income need be alleged and no approval of a specified authority is involved, which is what distinguishes it from a reassessment notice.

options.text: The second — section 142(1) reaches only the previous year under assessment
options.misconception: reads the proviso as a bar on every earlier year, when it fixes the limit at three years back
options.why: The proviso is permissive up to its limit and restrictive beyond it. Accounts of the three years preceding the previous year may be required; it is only anything earlier that cannot.

citation.ref: Section 142(1)(i) and (ii) with its provisos, and Sections 142(2A) and 142(2D)

items.scenario: Mr Rehman has furnished no return for assessment year 2026-27 and the time under section 139(1) has expired. The Assessing Officer proposes four steps. One, to serve a notice requiring him to furnish a return. Two, to require production of his accounts for the three years preceding previous year 2025-26. Three, to require production of his accounts for a year eight years before previous year 2025-26. Four, having regard to the multiplicity of transactions and the specialised nature of his business, to direct him to get his accounts audited by a nominated accountant.

items.stem: Is the assessment valid on the ground that no show cause notice was issued?

options.text: No — a show cause notice is mandatory before every best judgement assessment
options.misconception: reads the first proviso alone and stops before the second, which excuses the notice in exactly this case
options.why: The requirement is real and it has an express exception sitting immediately below it. Where a section 142(1) notice has already gone out, the second proviso dispenses with the separate show cause notice, and the assessment stands.

options.text: No — an assessment under section 144 requires the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner
options.misconception: imports the approval requirement from section 153D, which governs a search assessment
options.why: Section 144 contains no approval requirement at all. It is section 153D that forbids an order in a search assessment by an officer below the rank of Joint Commissioner without that officer's prior approval, and section 144A that lets a Joint Commissioner issue directions.

options.text: No — section 144 may be used only where no return has been filed at all, and a failure to comply with a notice is met by a penalty under section 272A alone
options.misconception: reduces section 144 to one of its four triggers, when failure to comply with a section 142(1) notice is a trigger in its own right
options.why: Section 144(1) lists four failures and failure to comply with all the terms of a notice under section 142(1) is the second of them. A penalty may follow as well, but it runs alongside the best judgement assessment and not instead of it.

options.text: Yes — the second proviso to section 144(1) removes the show cause requirement where a notice under section 142(1) has already been issued
options.why: The first proviso does require an opportunity by way of a show cause notice, but the second proviso to section 144(1) says it shall not be necessary to give such opportunity in a case where a notice under section 142(1) has been issued prior to the making of the assessment. That notice went on 4 August 2026 and was ignored, so the firm has already been asked once.

citation.ref: Section 144(1) with its first and second provisos, read with Sections 142(1) and 153D

items.scenario: Sable Traders was served a notice under section 142(1) on 4 August 2026 requiring it to furnish a return and produce its accounts for assessment year 2026-27. It did neither and answered nothing. On 20 November 2026 the Assessing Officer completed a best judgement assessment under section 144, estimating the income from the bank statements and the deduction-at-source records he had gathered. He did not issue any separate notice asking the firm to show cause why the assessment should not be completed to the best of his judgement.

items.stem: What is wrong with the notice?

options.text: Nothing — section 148A applies only where a search has been carried out, and this is an ordinary information case
options.misconception: reverses the exclusion; search cases are the ones taken out of section 148A, not the only ones put into it
options.why: Section 148A is written for the ordinary information case and expressly excludes a case where a search is initiated or books are requisitioned, which goes down the block assessment route in section 158BA instead. Mr Tanmay's case is the one the section was built for.

options.text: Only the missing approval — section 148A merely enables an enquiry, which the Assessing Officer is free to skip
options.misconception: treats the section 148A stage as optional, when section 148 makes it a condition of issuing the notice
options.why: Section 148 requires the procedure in section 148A to be followed before a notice may issue, and section 148A(3) requires an order deciding whether it is a fit case. Skipping the stage is not a procedural lapse to be cured later; the notice has no foundation without it.

options.text: Both the missing pre-notice stage and the missing approval — section 148A requires a show cause notice with the information relied on and consideration of the reply before any notice under section 148, and section 151 requires the prior approval of the specified authority
options.why: Section 148 permits a notice only where there is information suggesting escapement, only after the procedure in section 148A — which requires a show cause notice with the information put to the assessee, and his reply considered — has been followed, and only with the prior approval of the specified authority under section 151. Neither condition was met, and each on its own is enough to defeat the notice.

options.text: Nothing — Mr Tanmay's remedy is to file the return, ask for the reasons recorded and object before the Assessing Officer, who must dispose of the objections by a speaking order
options.misconception: describes the practice built on GKN Driveshafts, which section 148A replaced from 1 April 2021
options.why: That was the sequence when reassessment ran on the officer's recorded reasons, and the objection came after the notice. Section 148A moved the hearing to before the notice and put it in the statute, so there is nothing left to object to afterwards in that fashion.

citation.ref: Section 148 with its provisos and Section 148A, read with Sections 151 and 158BA

items.scenario: For assessment year 2022-23 the Assessing Officer receives information from a reporting entity suggesting that ₹18,00,000 of Mr Tanmay's income has escaped assessment. No search was carried out and no books were requisitioned. On 12 May 2025 the officer issues a notice under section 148 requiring a return. He sends no communication of any kind before it, and he obtains no approval from the specified authority. Mr Tanmay objects to the notice.

items.stem: What can the officer do?

options.text: Neither — section 154 may be exercised only by the authority on its own motion, so an application by the assessee is not maintainable
options.misconception: denies the assessee's right to apply, which section 154(2)(b) expressly gives
options.why: Section 154(2)(b) allows an amendment on an application made by the assessee, and section 154(8) then requires the authority to pass an order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is received. The power is not one-sided.

options.text: Nothing — the application is out of time, four years having run from the end of assessment year 2021-22
options.misconception: measures the section 154(7) period from the assessment year instead of from the financial year in which the order was passed
options.why: Counting from the end of assessment year 2021-22 would have closed the door on 31 March 2026. The sub-section is worded on the order, not the year assessed, which is why an order passed late in the cycle carries the power well beyond the assessment year.

options.text: The application is in time, and only the totalling error may be rectified
options.why: Section 154(7) allows an amendment within four years from the end of the financial year in which the order sought to be amended was passed. The order of 20 September 2023 falls in financial year 2023-24, so the period runs to 31 March 2028 and August 2026 is well inside it. The totalling error is a mistake apparent from the record; a point on which two High Courts differ is a debatable question of law and T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers puts it outside the section.

options.text: Both may be rectified, section 154 reaching any mistake of fact or of law
options.misconception: drops the word apparent, which is what confines the section
options.why: Section 154 reaches a mistake apparent from the record. Where two High Courts have reached opposite conclusions the point plainly needs argument, and a conclusion that requires argument to establish is by definition not apparent.

citation.ref: Sections 154(1), 154(2)(b), 154(7) and 154(8), read with T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers (1971) 82 ITR 50 (SC)

items.scenario: An assessment order under section 143(3) for assessment year 2021-22 was passed on 20 September 2023. In August 2026 the assessee applies under section 154 for two rectifications. One, the order adds up the disallowances wrongly, understating the total by ₹1,00,000 in the assessee's disfavour. Two, the officer refused a deduction on a question on which two High Courts have taken directly opposite views and no Supreme Court decision exists.

items.stem: What may the Principal Commissioner do?

options.text: Nothing — section 264 reaches only an order that is erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue
options.misconception: describes section 263, which is the revenue's revision, and applies its test to the assessee's
options.why: Erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue are the words of section 263(1), and that power is exercised only by the Commissioner on his own motion. Section 264 has no such requirement and may never end in an order prejudicial to the assessee.

options.text: Nothing — a claim never made in the return cannot be entertained in revision any more than it could have been in the assessment
options.misconception: extends the Goetze (India) rule from the Assessing Officer to the revisional authority
options.why: Goetze (India) itself recorded that it did not affect the powers of the appellate or revisional authorities. Section 264 is written in the widest terms and a claim omitted by oversight is one of the commonest reasons for using it.

options.text: He may revise the order and allow the deduction, even though it was never claimed in the return
options.why: Section 264(1) lets him pass such order as he thinks fit, not being an order prejudicial to the assessee, so relief is exactly what the section is for. The restriction in Goetze (India) that a fresh claim must come by a revised return binds the Assessing Officer and not the revisional authority. The application is within one year of communication under section 264(3), and section 264(4) no longer bars it because the appeal time has expired unused.
keywords: not being an order prejudicial to the assessee

options.text: Nothing — an order under section 143(3) is appealable, and section 264(4) bars revision of any appealable order
options.misconception: reads section 264(4) as barring revision of anything that could have been appealed, when the bar is tied to the appeal time and to an appeal actually filed
options.why: Section 264(4) bars revision while the time for an appeal has not expired and the right has not been waived, and where the order has been made the subject of an appeal. Mr Uday filed no appeal and the time has gone, so neither limb of the bar operates.

citation.ref: Sections 264(1), 264(3) and 264(4), read with Section 263(1) and Goetze (India) Ltd v. Commissioner of Income Tax (2006) 284 ITR 323 (SC)

items.scenario: An assessment under section 143(3) on Mr Uday was completed on 15 June 2025 and served on him on 20 June 2025. He then discovers that he was entitled to a deduction he never claimed, having overlooked it when preparing the return, so it appears nowhere in the return and nowhere in the assessment. He filed no appeal, and the time for an appeal to the Commissioner (Appeals) has now expired. In April 2026 he applies to the Principal Commissioner under section 264.

items.stem: What is the position on a further appeal?

options.text: The remedy is an application to the Tribunal under section 254(2), which can correct any error in the appreciation of evidence
options.misconception: treats section 254(2) as a rehearing, when it reaches only a mistake apparent from the record
options.why: Section 254(2) lets the Tribunal amend its order to rectify a mistake apparent from the record, which is the same narrow idea as section 154. A disagreement about how evidence was weighed needs argument, so it is not apparent and the Tribunal cannot rehear itself.

options.text: An appeal lies to the High Court as of right, section 260A(1) giving an appeal from every order passed in appeal by the Tribunal
options.misconception: reads the opening words of section 260A(1) and stops before the condition attached to them
options.why: The sub-section reads that an appeal shall lie from every such order if the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law. Section 260A(3) then requires the High Court itself to formulate that question, which is the filter the words as of right would remove.

options.text: The remedy is an appeal to the Supreme Court under section 261, which is free to reappraise the evidence
options.misconception: treats section 261 as a route around the High Court, when it lies only from a High Court judgment on a section 260A appeal
options.why: Section 261 gives an appeal to the Supreme Court from any judgment of the High Court delivered on an appeal made under section 260A, and only where the High Court certifies the case to be a fit one. There is no direct step from the Tribunal to the Supreme Court.

options.text: No appeal lies on that ground — section 260A admits an appeal only where the High Court is satisfied that the case involves a substantial question of law, and a re-weighing of evidence is not one
options.why: The Tribunal is the final fact-finding authority, and an appeal to the High Court under section 260A lies only on a substantial question of law. A finding reached on all the material stands unless it is perverse, meaning it rests on no evidence or on irrelevant material, and Vidur Ltd accepts that everything was considered. Arguing that the weight given to a document was wrong is an argument about facts, so no substantial question of law arises.

citation.ref: Sections 260A(1), 260A(3) and 261, read with Section 254(2)

items.scenario: The Appellate Tribunal dismisses Vidur Ltd's appeal. On the evidence before it — the supplier's statement, the transport documents and the bank trail — it holds that a purchase of ₹90,00,000 was not genuine. The company accepts that the Tribunal considered all the material but says it weighed the transport documents too lightly and the supplier's statement too heavily, and wants to take the matter further.

items.stem: What credit is he entitled to in assessment year 2026-27?

options.text: The whole ₹1,00,000 in assessment year 2026-27, credit following the year in which the tax was deducted and appears in Form 26AS
options.misconception: ties credit to the year of deduction, when section 199(3) and Rule 37BA(3) tie it to the year in which the income is assessable
options.why: Form 26AS records when the tax was deposited, not when the income is taxed. Credit follows the income, which is why an advance spread over two years takes its credit over the same two years.

options.text: ₹40,000, with the remaining ₹60,000 in assessment year 2027-28
options.why: Rule 37BA(3) gives credit for the assessment year for which the income is assessable, and where the income is assessable over more than one year, credit is allowed across those years in the same proportion in which the income is assessable. ₹4,00,000 of ₹10,00,000 is offered this year, which is two fifths, so two fifths of ₹1,00,000 is ₹40,000 now and ₹60,000 next year.

options.text: The whole ₹1,00,000 in assessment year 2026-27, and the whole ₹10,00,000 must be offered there as well, credit and income being inseparable
options.misconception: forces the income into the year of deduction to match the credit, when the rule works the other way round
options.why: The year in which income is assessable is settled by the method of accounting and the terms of the contract, not by when a payer chose to deduct. Rule 37BA(3) then follows that answer; it does not dictate it.

options.text: Nothing in assessment year 2026-27, the whole ₹1,00,000 falling in assessment year 2027-28 when the last of the income is offered
options.misconception: postpones the whole credit to the final year, when the rule apportions it as the income is offered
options.why: Rule 37BA(3)(ii) apportions rather than defers. Withholding all credit until the contract ends would leave Mr Wasim paying tax twice on the ₹4,00,000 he has offered this year.

citation.ref: Sections 199(1) and 199(3), read with Rule 37BA(3) of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: Mr Wasim, a consulting engineer who keeps his accounts on the mercantile basis, receives ₹10,00,000 in March 2026 as an advance under a two-year contract. The payer deducts ₹1,00,000 of tax on it and deposits it, and the deduction appears in Mr Wasim's Form 26AS for assessment year 2026-27. Applying his method of accounting, Mr Wasim offers ₹4,00,000 of the advance as income of previous year 2025-26 and will offer the remaining ₹6,00,000 in previous year 2026-27. He claims the whole ₹1,00,000 of credit in assessment year 2026-27.

items.stem: How much tax must Vega Ltd deduct?

options.text: Nil, because Mr Yash has declared that his income will be below the taxable limit
options.misconception: treats section 206AA as a rule about the payee's liability, when it fixes the payer's duty
options.why: Section 206AA(2) says a declaration under section 197A is not valid unless it carries the permanent account number, so this one is worthless. Deducting nothing leaves Vega Ltd an assessee in default under section 201(1), with interest under section 201(1A) and disallowance under section 40(a)(ia).

Section 206AA(1) requires deduction at the highest of the rate specified in the relevant provision, the rates in force and twenty per cent. Twenty per cent beats the 10 per cent section 194J rate, so 20 per cent of ₹8,00,000 is ₹1,60,000. Section 206AA(2) also makes the declaration invalid for want of the number, so it changes nothing.

options.misconception: reads section 206AA as reaching only a non-resident payee, when sub-section (7) is what takes certain non-residents out of it
options.why: Deducting at the ordinary 10 per cent gives ₹80,000. Section 206AA applies to every deductee who fails to furnish the number, and it is sub-section (7) that carves certain payments to a non-resident or a foreign company out where Rule 37BC is satisfied. A resident is squarely inside the section.

options.misconception: deducts on the excess over the section 194J threshold, when the threshold decides whether to deduct and not what to deduct on
options.why: Taking ₹8,00,000 less the ₹50,000 threshold and applying 20 per cent gives ₹1,50,000. The ₹50,000 figure in section 194J is a trigger; once the payments in that category cross it, deduction is on the whole sum credited or paid.

citation.ref: Sections 206AA(1), 206AA(2) and 206AA(7), read with Section 194J and Sections 201(1) and 201(1A)

items.scenario: Vega Ltd pays ₹8,00,000 of professional fees to Mr Yash, a resident consultant, during previous year 2025-26. Tax on a payment of this description is deductible under section 194J, and the rate specified there for it is 10 per cent. Mr Yash has a permanent account number but declines to give it to Vega Ltd, saying his income for the year will be below the taxable limit; he gives a declaration to that effect instead, without quoting the number.

items.stem: Which of the four give Zenith GmbH a permanent establishment in India?

options.text: The Pune building site and the Chennai employee
options.why: The Pune site ran fourteen months against the twelve the treaty's construction clause names, so it is a permanent establishment under Article 5(3). The Chennai employee habitually concludes contracts in Zenith's name, which is the agency permanent establishment in Article 5(5) and needs no premises at all.

options.text: The Pune building site alone
options.misconception: reads the whole of Article 5 as requiring a fixed place of business
options.why: Article 5(1) does turn on a fixed place, but Article 5(5) is a separate and independent route. A person acting on behalf of the enterprise who habitually concludes contracts in its name creates a permanent establishment whether or not the enterprise has any premises here.

options.text: All four, any fixed place or person in India being a permanent establishment
options.misconception: ignores the two exclusions, which take out a preparatory or auxiliary place and an agent of independent status
options.why: Article 5(4) takes out a place maintained solely for storage, display or delivery of goods, which is what the Mumbai warehouse is. Article 5(6) takes out an agent of independent status acting in the ordinary course of his own business, which is what the Delhi broker is.

options.text: The Chennai employee alone, a building site never amounting to a fixed place of business
options.misconception: applies the fixed place test to a building site, when the treaty gives it a clause and a time period of its own
options.why: Article 5(3) exists precisely because a site is temporary and would be argued about under Article 5(1). It settles the question with a period, and fourteen months is past the twelve this treaty names.

citation.ref: Article 5(3), 5(4), 5(5) and 5(6) of India's double taxation avoidance agreements on the OECD and UN Model pattern, read with Article 7

items.scenario: Zenith GmbH, a German company, is entitled to a treaty with India whose Article 5 follows the usual pattern and whose construction clause creates a permanent establishment where a building site lasts more than twelve months. During previous year 2025-26 it has four things in India. A warehouse in Mumbai used solely to store its goods and deliver them to Indian customers. A building site in Pune that ran for fourteen months. A broker in Delhi who acts for many principals in the ordinary course of his own brokerage business and takes orders for Zenith among others. An employee posted in Chennai who habitually concludes contracts in Zenith's name.

items.stem: What transfer pricing adjustment arises under Rule 10CA?

options.text: An adjustment of ₹2,00,000
options.misconception: adjusts to the nearer edge of the range instead of to the median, which Rule 10CA(5) names
options.why: Taking the lower edge of 9 per cent gives ₹9,00,000 and an adjustment of ₹2,00,000. Rule 10CA(5) does not push the price to the boundary; it says that where the transaction price is outside the range, the arm's length price shall be taken to be the median of the dataset.

options.text: No adjustment, the declared margin of 7 per cent lying inside the spread of the comparables
options.misconception: treats the whole dataset as the arm's length range instead of the band from the thirty-fifth to the sixty-fifth percentile
options.why: The comparables run from 6 to 18 per cent, and 7 per cent is inside that spread. The range Rule 10CA builds is a narrow central band, not the full data, and 7 per cent falls below its lower limit of 9 per cent.

options.text: An adjustment of ₹4,62,500
options.misconception: uses the arithmetic mean of the comparables when a dataset of six or more entries requires the range
options.why: The eight margins add to 93, so their arithmetic mean is 11.625 per cent, giving ₹11,62,500 and an adjustment of ₹4,62,500. The arithmetic mean under section 92C(2) governs only where the dataset has fewer than six entries; with eight, Rule 10CA displaces it.

options.text: An adjustment of ₹4,50,000
options.why: With six or more entries and the transactional net margin method, Rule 10CA(4) requires the arm's length range. Eight data points times 0.35 is 2.8, which is not a whole number, so the 35th percentile is the third point, 9 per cent; eight times 0.65 is 5.2, so the sixty-fifth percentile is the sixth point, 14 per cent. The declared margin of 7 per cent lies below that range, so under Rule 10CA(5) the arm's length price is the median. Eight times 0.5 is 4, a whole number, so the median is the average of the fourth and fifth points, 11.5 per cent. On an operating cost of ₹1,00,00,000 that is an arm's length operating profit of ₹11,50,000 against ₹7,00,000 declared, so the adjustment is ₹4,50,000.

citation.ref: Rule 10CA(4), Rule 10CA(5) and Rule 10CA(7), read with Section 92C(1) and Section 92C(2)

items.scenario: Meridian Components Pvt Ltd manufactures on contract for its foreign parent and is remunerated on a cost plus basis. The transactional net margin method is the most appropriate method, with operating profit on operating cost as the profit level indicator. Its operating cost for previous year 2025-26 is ₹1,00,00,000 and its declared operating profit is ₹7,00,000. The dataset of comparable uncontrolled companies has eight entries, whose margins arranged in ascending order are 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15 and 18 per cent.

items.stem: What follows under section 92CE?

options.text: A further ₹4,00,00,000 is added to the total income of the same previous year as the secondary adjustment
options.misconception: taxes the primary adjustment twice, when the secondary adjustment charges only the interest on the money left abroad
options.why: The primary adjustment has already raised the total income by ₹4,00,00,000. Section 92CE(2) does not repeat it; it looks at the cash that never came and charges imputed interest on it for as long as it stays away.

options.text: Nothing, because a secondary adjustment arises only where the assessee makes the primary adjustment himself in his return of income
options.misconception: reads section 92CE(1) as covering only a suo motu adjustment, when it names five triggers
options.why: The suo motu adjustment is the first of five. Section 92CE(1)(b) covers an adjustment made by the Assessing Officer and accepted by the assessee, which is exactly this case, and the remaining clauses cover an advance pricing agreement, the safe harbour rules and a mutual agreement procedure.

options.text: The ₹4,00,00,000 is deemed to be a dividend paid to the parent, on which tax must be deducted under section 195
options.misconception: applies the constructive dividend model some other countries use, when India's secondary adjustment is a deemed advance
options.why: A deemed dividend is one way a country can reach money left abroad, and it is not the way section 92CE(2) chose. The money is treated as an advance from the Indian company, and what is charged is interest on it, not a dividend in the parent's hands.

options.text: The unrepatriated money is deemed to be an advance made by the Indian company to its parent, and interest on that advance is charged as its income until the money is repatriated
options.why: Section 92CE(2) says the excess money available with the associated enterprise, if not repatriated to India within the time prescribed, shall be deemed to be an advance made by the assessee to that enterprise, with interest on it computed in the prescribed manner. The company may instead pay the one-time additional tax under section 92CE(2A), after which no further interest is imputed.

citation.ref: Sections 92CE(1)(b), 92CE(2) and 92CE(2A), read with Rule 10CB of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: The Assessing Officer makes a primary adjustment of ₹4,00,00,000 to the income of Larkspur India Pvt Ltd on the price at which it sold components to its foreign parent. The company accepts the adjustment and does not appeal. The parent does not send the ₹4,00,00,000 to India, and the time prescribed for repatriation passes.

items.stem: Which statement about the safe harbour scheme is correct?

options.text: Safe harbour and an advance pricing agreement are the same machinery, the first being the version available to smaller taxpayers
options.misconception: collapses two different mechanisms, one negotiated with the Board and one already notified in the Rules
options.why: An advance pricing agreement under section 92CC is negotiated between the Board and one taxpayer for a stated set of transactions and can be rolled back under section 92CD. Safe harbour is a set of margins already notified in the Rules, open to anybody who fits the description and negotiated with nobody.

options.text: The Transfer Pricing Officer may apply the safe harbour margins to any assessee he considers eligible, whether or not that assessee has asked for them
options.misconception: turns safe harbour into a power of the officer, when it is an option the assessee exercises
options.why: Section 92CB is written around the price declared by the assessee, and the rules require him to exercise the option himself in Form 3CEFA. What the officer may do is hold the option invalid, with an appeal against that to the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner.

options.text: The income-tax authorities accept the transfer price the company has declared, and no determination of the arm's length price is made for that transaction
options.why: The Explanation to section 92CB defines safe harbour as circumstances in which the income-tax authorities shall accept the transfer price declared by the assessee. Where the option is validly exercised the declared price is taken as it stands, so the transaction does not go on to a determination under section 92C or section 92CA.

options.text: A price fixed under the safe harbour rules can never give rise to a secondary adjustment
options.misconception: assumes safe harbour closes the file, when section 92CE(1)(d) names it as a trigger
options.why: Section 92CE(1)(d) lists an adjustment made as per the safe harbour rules under section 92CB as one of the five primary adjustments that carry a secondary adjustment. Safe harbour settles the price; it does not settle where the money is.

citation.ref: Section 92CB(1) with its Explanation, read with Rule 10TE of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 and Sections 92CC and 92CE(1)(d)

items.scenario: Corvus Software Services Pvt Ltd provides software development services to its foreign parent. It falls within the description of an eligible assessee and an eligible international transaction in the safe harbour rules, and it exercises the option in Form 3CEFA for previous year 2025-26 at the margin those rules specify. The option is held valid.

items.stem: What is the effect of section 9A?

options.text: The manager's ₹9,00,000 fee is also outside the charge, since taxing it would undo the purpose of the section
options.misconception: extends relief given to the fund to the manager, when the section requires the manager to be paid at arm's length precisely so that a real Indian profit is declared
options.why: Section 9A(4) requires the remuneration paid by the fund to the manager to be at arm's length for the activity carried out. That condition exists so that a real profit is declared and charged in India; the section never touches the manager's own liability.

options.text: It applies to any offshore fund whose manager is in India, no conditions having to be met
options.misconception: ignores the two lists of conditions in sections 9A(3) and 9A(4)
options.why: Section 9A(3) sets conditions on the fund — non-residence, a treaty or notified country, no business carried on or controlled in India, and the corpus, membership and participation tests — and section 9A(4) sets conditions on the manager. Fail one and the relief goes.

options.text: The whole income of the fund is exempt from tax in India, section 9A being an exemption for offshore funds managed from India
options.misconception: reads a provision that removes a deeming as one that grants an exemption
options.why: Section 9A sits in the chapter on the scope of income, not in section 10. It takes away two consequences of the manager sitting in India and leaves every other charge standing, which is why the Indian-source interest is still taxed.

options.text: The manager's activity creates neither a business connection nor Indian residence for the fund, but the fund's Indian-source interest remains chargeable and the manager's ₹9,00,000 fee is taxed in India
options.why: Section 9A(1) says the fund management activity carried out through an eligible fund manager shall not constitute a business connection in India of the fund, and section 9A(2) says the fund shall not be said to be resident in India merely because the manager is situated here. Both remove a deeming and neither grants an exemption, so interest sourced here under section 9(1)(v) is still charged and the ₹9,00,000 fee is the manager's own Indian income.

citation.ref: Sections 9A(1), 9A(2), 9A(3) and 9A(4), read with Sections 9(1)(i) and 9(1)(v)

items.scenario: Blue Harbour Fund is a non-resident investment fund. It appoints an Indian company in Mumbai as its fund manager, and every condition in section 9A(3) and section 9A(4) is satisfied, including the requirement that the manager be paid at arm's length. The manager earns a management fee of ₹9,00,000 for previous year 2025-26. The fund separately earns interest on a loan it made to an Indian borrower who uses the money in his business in India.

items.stem: What does section 115JH do for that year?

options.text: It applies to every foreign company that has any income arising in India
options.misconception: ignores the two conditions in the opening words of section 115JH(1)
options.why: The section is written for one situation only, and both limbs must be met: the foreign company is said to be resident in India in the previous year, and it was not resident in India in any of the preceding previous years. A non-resident foreign company with Indian income is nowhere near it.

options.text: It is the minimum alternate tax provision applied to foreign companies
options.misconception: confuses section 115JH with section 115JB, whose numbering it sits beside
options.why: Minimum alternate tax on book profit is section 115JB. Section 115JH shares the chapter and nothing else — it is a transition provision, and it charges no tax of its own.

options.text: It lets the Central Government notify exceptions, modifications and adaptations to the way the Act applies to such a company, on matters such as unabsorbed depreciation, set off and carry forward of losses, and collection and recovery
options.why: Section 115JH(1) applies where a foreign company is said to be resident in India in a previous year and was not resident in any preceding previous year. It then makes the provisions on computation of total income, unabsorbed depreciation, set off and carry forward of losses, collection and recovery and avoidance of tax apply with such exceptions, modifications and adaptations as the Central Government may notify.
keywords: not resident in any preceding previous year

options.text: It exempts the company from tax in India for the year in which it first becomes resident
options.misconception: reads a transition provision as a holiday from the charge
options.why: Section 115JH exempts nothing. It eases the mechanics of applying an Act the company has never been inside — it has no written down value, no brought forward loss and no unabsorbed depreciation computed under this Act — and leaves the charge exactly where it was.

citation.ref: Sections 115JH(1) and 115JH(3), read with Section 6(3) and Section 32(2)

items.scenario: Halden Trading GmbH is a company incorporated in Germany. For previous year 2025-26 its place of effective management is found to be in India, so it is resident in India under section 6(3). It was not resident in India in any earlier previous year.

items.stem: What are its profits under section 44BBA?

options.misconception: uses the outbound limb alone and drops inbound carriage altogether
options.why: ₹20,00,000 plus ₹8,00,000 is ₹28,00,000, and five per cent is ₹1,40,000. The section has two limbs, and the second one exists precisely to catch carriage from a place outside India where the money is received here.

The first limb takes the amount paid or payable, whether in or out of India, for carriage from any place in India, which is ₹20,00,000 plus ₹8,00,000. The second limb takes the amount received in India for carriage from a place outside India, which is ₹12,00,000. The ₹6,00,000 was received outside India for an inbound carriage and answers neither limb. The aggregate is ₹40,00,000 and five per cent of it is ₹2,00,000.
keywords: paid or payable, whether in or out of India

options.misconception: adds every receipt, when the second limb reaches an inbound carriage only where the money is received in India
options.why: All four amounts come to ₹46,00,000 and five per cent of that is ₹2,30,000. The ₹6,00,000 is the odd one out — the carriage began outside India, so the first limb cannot reach it, and the money was received outside India, so the second limb cannot either.

options.misconception: requires receipt in India under both limbs, when the first says paid or payable whether in or out of India
options.why: Counting only what was received in India gives ₹20,00,000 plus ₹12,00,000, or ₹32,00,000, and five per cent is ₹1,60,000. That drops the ₹8,00,000 payable in Dubai for a carriage from Chennai, which the first limb catches wherever the money was paid.

citation.ref: Sections 44BBA(1), 44BBA(2)(a) and 44BBA(2)(b)

items.scenario: Skyward Air Inc, a non-resident, is engaged in the business of operation of aircraft. Section 44BBA deems five per cent of the aggregate of the amounts specified in that section to be its profits. In previous year 2025-26 four amounts arise. ₹20,00,000 received in Mumbai for carriage of passengers from Mumbai to Dubai. ₹8,00,000 payable to it in Dubai for carriage of goods from Chennai to Dubai. ₹12,00,000 received in its Mumbai bank account for carriage of passengers from Dubai to Mumbai. ₹6,00,000 received in Dubai for carriage of passengers from Dubai to Mumbai.

items.stem: What are its profits under section 44BB?

options.why: Clause (a) takes the amount paid or payable, whether in or out of India, for plant used in the extraction of mineral oils in India, which is the ₹90,00,000 for the Gujarat field however it was paid. Clause (b) takes the amount received in India for such use outside India, which is the ₹30,00,000. The ₹20,00,000 was payable outside India for use outside India and falls in neither clause. The aggregate is ₹1,20,00,000 and ten per cent is ₹12,00,000.

options.misconception: requires receipt in India under both clauses, when clause (a) says paid or payable whether in or out of India
options.why: Ten per cent of the ₹30,00,000 received in India is ₹3,00,000. That treats the ₹90,00,000 as outside the section because it was paid in London, when clause (a) is indifferent to where the money was paid and asks only where the mineral oil work was done.

options.misconception: aggregates all three amounts, ignoring that clause (b) reaches work done outside India only where the money is received in India
options.why: All three come to ₹1,40,00,000, of which ten per cent is ₹14,00,000. The ₹20,00,000 has no Indian connecting factor at all — the rigs were used in Oman and the money was payable in London — so section 44BB does not reach it.

options.misconception: uses clause (a) alone, treating any work done outside India as outside the section
options.why: Ten per cent of ₹90,00,000 is ₹9,00,000. Clause (b) exists for exactly the case dropped here — services or plant used outside India where the money is received in India — and the ₹30,00,000 landed in the Mumbai account.

citation.ref: Sections 44BB(1), 44BB(2)(a) and 44BB(2)(b), read with Section 44BB(3)

items.scenario: Oceanic Drilling Ltd, a non-resident company, hires out drilling rigs used in the extraction of mineral oils. Section 44BB deems ten per cent of the aggregate of the amounts specified in that section to be its profits. In previous year 2025-26 three amounts arise. ₹90,00,000 paid to it in London by an Indian operator, for rigs used at a field in Gujarat. ₹30,00,000 received in its Mumbai bank account from a foreign operator, for rigs used at a field in Oman. ₹20,00,000 payable to it in London by a foreign operator, for rigs used at a field in Oman. It keeps no books under section 44AA and claims no lower profits.

items.stem: Which payment is not royalty under Explanation 2 to section 9(1)(vi)?

options.text: The hire of the scientific testing equipment
options.misconception: treats equipment hire as a rental outside the royalty definition
options.why: Explanation 2 includes consideration for the use or right to use any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment, excluding only the amounts referred to in section 44BB. Hiring testing equipment is the paradigm case of that clause.

options.text: The payment for the standard accounting software
options.misconception: applies the treaty answer to the question the Act asks, when the two are decided by different definitions
options.why: Under the Act, Explanation 4 says the transfer of all or any rights includes and has always included a right to use computer software, including by licence, irrespective of the medium, so the payment is royalty. Whether the treaty says the same is a separate question decided by section 90(2), and Engineering Analysis held that the sale of a copyrighted article rather than the copyright is not royalty on the narrower treaty wording.

options.text: The payment for satellite transponder capacity
options.misconception: argues that no secret process is involved, when Explanation 6 removed secrecy from the test
options.why: Explanation 6 to section 9(1)(vi) says process includes transmission by satellite, cable, optic fibre or any similar technology, whether or not it is secret. That Explanation was inserted to settle exactly this argument.

options.text: The payment to the foreign studio for the cinematographic film
options.why: The copyright limb of Explanation 2 covers consideration for the transfer of rights in a copyright, literary, artistic or scientific work including films or video tapes for use in connection with television, and then carves out in terms the consideration for the sale, distribution or exhibition of cinematographic films. A film bought outright for exhibition in cinemas falls squarely inside that exclusion.

citation.ref: Explanation 2 clause (v), Explanation 4 and Explanation 6 to Section 9(1)(vi), read with Section 90(2)

items.scenario: Trident Media Ltd, an Indian company, makes four payments to non-residents in previous year 2025-26. One, for the right to use a standard accounting software product it downloads, with no right to reproduce it or to exploit the copyright commercially. Two, for the hire of scientific testing equipment brought to its Pune plant. Three, to a foreign studio for buying a cinematographic film outright for exhibition in Indian cinemas. Four, to a satellite operator for transponder capacity used to carry its channel.

items.stem: Which section governs each of them?

options.text: Section 115AC governs Mr Farouk, and section 115ACA governs Ms Gita only if she is a shareholder rather than an employee
options.misconception: inverts the condition, when employment is what section 115ACA requires
options.why: Employment is the qualifying fact, not a disqualifying one. Section 115ACA is written for receipts issued under an employees' stock option scheme to a resident individual who is or was an employee of the issuing company or its subsidiary.

options.text: Both are governed by section 115AC, section 115ACA being the machinery provision for it
options.misconception: treats the two sections as one regime with a shared computation section
options.why: They are two separate charging provisions with two separate classes of assessee. Section 115ACA is not machinery for section 115AC; it has its own conditions, and a resident employee cannot be brought inside section 115AC at all.

options.text: Section 115AC governs Mr Farouk and section 115ACA governs Ms Gita
options.why: Section 115AC is written for a non-resident holding notified bonds or global depository receipts of an Indian company. Section 115ACA is written for an individual resident in India who is or was an employee of an Indian company engaged in a specified knowledge based industry or service, holding receipts issued under an employees' stock option scheme and purchased in foreign currency.

options.text: Both are governed by section 115ACA, which covers every holder of a global depository receipt
options.misconception: reads section 115ACA as attaching to the instrument rather than to the holder
options.why: The instrument is not the test in either section. Section 115ACA requires a resident individual who is or was an employee, and Mr Farouk is neither resident nor an employee, so he falls outside it and inside section 115AC.

citation.ref: Section 115AC(1) and Section 115ACA(1) with its Explanation

items.scenario: Two people hold global depository receipts of Indian companies, both purchased in foreign currency. Mr Farouk is a non-resident who bought receipts of an Indian company issued under a scheme notified by the Central Government. Ms Gita is resident in India and is an employee of an Indian software company; her receipts were issued to her under that company's employees' stock option scheme.

items.stem: On which of the two must tax be deducted under section 196D?

options.text: On the ₹18,00,000 of income in respect of the securities only
options.why: Section 196D(1) requires deduction from income in respect of securities referred to in section 115AD(1)(a), which is the ₹18,00,000. Section 196D(2) then says in terms that no deduction shall be made from any income by way of capital gains arising from the transfer of those securities, so the ₹25,00,000 gain carries no deduction and is charged in the assessment instead.

options.text: On neither, a Foreign Institutional Investor being outside the deduction chapter altogether
options.misconception: treats a special collection section as an exemption from collection
options.why: Sections 196A to 196D are collection sections for particular non-residents, not exemptions from collection. Section 196D(1) plainly requires deduction from the income in respect of the securities.

options.text: On the ₹25,00,000 capital gain only
options.misconception: reverses the two sub-sections of section 196D
options.why: It is the other way round. Sub-section (1) is the charge to deduct, and it is aimed at the income in respect of the securities; sub-section (2) is the exclusion, and it is aimed at the capital gains.

options.text: On both amounts
options.misconception: assumes every stream reaching a Foreign Institutional Investor is deducted from
options.why: Section 196D(2) is an express carve-out for capital gains on the transfer of those securities. Parliament wrote it because a deductor cannot know the investor's cost of acquisition, so the gain is left to be charged when the return is assessed.

citation.ref: Sections 196D(1) and 196D(2), read with Section 115AD(1)(a)

items.scenario: Northgate Capital is a Foreign Institutional Investor. During previous year 2025-26 it earns ₹18,00,000 of income in respect of securities referred to in section 115AD(1)(a), and it also makes a short-term capital gain of ₹25,00,000 on selling some of those securities on an Indian stock exchange.

items.stem: How may the claim be dealt with?

options.text: The benefit is denied only where obtaining it was the sole purpose of the arrangement
options.misconception: raises the bar to a sole or dominant purpose, when Article 7 says one of the principal purposes
options.why: The wording is one of the principal purposes, which is deliberately lower than sole or even dominant. An arrangement with genuine commercial reasons alongside the treaty benefit can still fail the test.

options.text: The benefit must be granted, a valid tax residency certificate being conclusive proof of entitlement to treaty relief
options.misconception: reads section 90(4) as making the certificate sufficient, when it makes it necessary
options.why: Section 90(4) says a non-resident shall not be entitled to claim treaty relief unless he obtains a tax residency certificate. That is a condition of making the claim, and section 90(5) lets the authorities call for such other documents as may be prescribed besides.

options.text: Only Chapter X-A can deny it, the Multilateral Instrument being an agreement between governments with no effect on an assessee
options.misconception: treats the Convention as sitting outside the treaty, when it modifies the treaty's own text
options.why: The Convention works by modifying covered tax agreements, so once both countries have listed the treaty and their positions match, its terms are applied as part of that treaty. The taxpayer is claiming under the treaty as so modified.

options.text: The benefit may be denied under the principal purpose test in Article 7 of the Multilateral Instrument, which is read into the treaty itself, without Chapter X-A being invoked at all
options.why: Article 7 denies a benefit where it is reasonable to conclude, having regard to all relevant facts and circumstances, that obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, unless granting it would accord with the object and purpose of the relevant provisions. The Convention modifies a covered tax agreement, so the test is part of the treaty India applies and works without the domestic rule in Chapter X-A being invoked.

citation.source: Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting
citation.ref: Article 7(1) of the Convention, read with Sections 90(2A), 90(4) and 90(5) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: Orion Holdings is incorporated in a country whose treaty with India is a covered tax agreement modified by the Multilateral Instrument. It was set up three weeks before it acquired shares in an Indian company from its own group parent, has no employees, no premises of its own and no board that meets anywhere but at the parent's office, and its only asset is those shares. It now sells them, claims the treaty benefit on the capital gain, and produces a valid tax residency certificate.

items.stem: What comes into Mr Pranav's total income from the firm?

options.text: Nil, everything received from a firm being exempt in a partner's hands once the firm has paid tax on its income
options.misconception: extends the reason behind section 10(2A) to receipts the firm has already deducted in computing that income
options.why: Section 10(2A) exists to stop the same profit being taxed twice, and the firm's profit was arrived at after deducting the ₹5,00,000 and the ₹6,00,000 under section 40(b). Those sums were never taxed in the firm's hands, which is exactly why section 28(v) taxes them in his.

options.misconception: treats remuneration and interest as part of the exempt share, when section 28(v) charges them separately
options.why: The share and the payments are two different things. Section 10(2A) covers the share in the firm's total income, while section 28(v) charges interest, salary, bonus, commission or remuneration received by a partner from the firm as his own business income.

options.misconception: adds the share of profit back, treating section 10(2A) as a relief to be claimed rather than an exclusion from total income
options.why: ₹12,00,000 plus ₹5,00,000 plus ₹6,00,000 is ₹23,00,000. Section 10 opens by saying that income falling within its clauses shall not be included in computing total income, so the share never enters the computation and there is nothing to take out of it later.

His 30 per cent share works out to ₹12,00,000 of the firm's total income, and section 10(2A) keeps that outside his total income altogether — it is an exclusion, not a deduction he claims. What remains is the ₹5,00,000 of remuneration and the ₹6,00,000 of interest, which section 28(v) charges as his business income to the extent they were allowed to the firm under section 40(b), giving ₹11,00,000.

citation.ref: Section 10(2A) with its Explanation, read with Section 28(v) and Section 40(b)

items.scenario: Mehra & Sons is a firm assessed as a firm, and its total income for previous year 2025-26 is ₹40,00,000. Mr Pranav is a partner whose share of the profits under the deed is 30 per cent. During the year the firm also paid him remuneration of ₹5,00,000 and interest on his capital of ₹6,00,000, both of which were allowed to the firm under section 40(b).

items.stem: Which of the four is not a use of the trust's income or property for the benefit of a specified person under section 13(2)?

options.text: The interest-free unsecured loan to the managing trustee's son
options.misconception: assumes a relative of a trustee is not himself a specified person
options.why: Section 13(3) brings in a relative of a trustee as a specified person in his own right, and section 13(2)(a) catches money lent to such a person without either adequate security or adequate interest. This loan has neither.

options.text: The ₹3,00,000 of shares in the company in which the founder holds 40 per cent
options.misconception: reads an investment as neutral because the trust paid a market price for the shares
options.why: Section 13(2)(h) catches funds invested for any period in a concern in which a specified person has a substantial interest, and a 40 per cent holding is well past that. Equity shares are also outside the modes permitted by section 11(5), so section 13(1)(d) bites as well.

options.text: The room in the trust's building used by the founder rent free
options.misconception: treats a non-cash benefit as outside the sub-section
options.why: Section 13(2)(b) covers land, building or other property of the trust made available for the use of a specified person without charging adequate rent or other compensation. The founder is named first in the section 13(3) list.

options.text: The salary paid to the founder's daughter
options.why: Section 13(2)(c) catches an amount paid to a specified person for services rendered to the trust only to the extent it is in excess of what may reasonably be paid for those services. The daughter works full time and is paid the trust's own rate for that grade, so nothing is in excess and the clause is not attracted.
keywords: in excess of what may reasonably be paid

citation.ref: Sections 13(2)(a), 13(2)(b), 13(2)(c) and 13(2)(h) with Section 13(3), read with Sections 13(1)(c), 13(1)(d) and 11(5)

items.scenario: The Anandi Charitable Trust is registered under section 12AB. During previous year 2025-26 it lends ₹5,00,000 to the son of its managing trustee, without security and without interest. It pays ₹40,000 a month to the founder's daughter, who works full time as its accountant, this being the rate the trust pays other accountants of the same grade. It lets the founder use a room in its building rent free. And it holds ₹3,00,000 of equity shares in a company in which the founder holds 40 per cent of the voting power.

items.stem: Which stream is not exempt under section 13A?

options.text: The rent from the building
options.misconception: assumes a political party can hold no property that produces exempt income
options.why: Income chargeable under the head income from house property is the first of the four heads section 13A names, so rent from a building the party owns and lets out is exempt on the plain words of the section.

options.text: The interest on the bank deposits
options.misconception: treats interest as a commercial receipt outside the exemption
options.why: Bank interest is chargeable under the head income from other sources, and section 13A names that head expressly. The source of the money makes no difference; the head does.

options.text: The profits of the printing press
options.why: Section 13A exempts four things and business income is not among them — income chargeable under the head income from house property, income chargeable under the head income from other sources, income by way of capital gains, and income by way of voluntary contributions. Profits of a printing press run commercially fall under profits and gains of business or profession, and are charged.

options.text: The voluntary contributions
options.misconception: confuses the conditions attached to contributions with the exemption of them
options.why: Income by way of voluntary contributions received from any person is the fourth item section 13A exempts. What the section attaches to contributions are conditions — a record of each one above the specified amount, and no donation above two thousand rupees in cash — and the scenario says every condition is met.

citation.ref: Section 13A with clauses (a) to (d) and its provisos, read with Section 139(4B)

items.scenario: A political party registered under section 29A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 has four streams of income in previous year 2025-26 — rent from a building it owns and lets out, interest on its bank deposits, voluntary contributions from its members, and the profits of a printing press it runs commercially for outside customers. Every condition in section 13A is satisfied.

items.stem: How much head office expenditure is allowed?

options.misconception: sets off the brought forward loss before computing adjusted total income, which the Explanation expressly forbids
options.why: ₹80,00,000 less ₹30,00,000 is ₹50,00,000, and five per cent of that is ₹2,50,000. The Explanation lists the brought forward loss under section 72(1) among the things adjusted total income is computed without giving effect to, so it is added straight back.

options.misconception: allows the whole amount attributable to India and ignores the ceiling in section 44C
options.why: Section 44C is a ceiling, not a tracing rule. It allows the lower of the percentage of adjusted total income and the amount attributable, and here the percentage figure of ₹4,00,000 is the lower of the two.

The Explanation to section 44C computes adjusted total income without giving effect to the head office allowance itself and without giving effect to the brought forward loss under section 72(1), so the base stays at ₹80,00,000. Five per cent of that is ₹4,00,000, and the section allows the lower of that figure and the ₹6,00,000 actually attributable.

options.misconception: deducts the head office expenditure itself before computing the base, when adjusted total income is computed before that very allowance
options.why: ₹80,00,000 less ₹6,00,000 is ₹74,00,000, and five per cent is ₹3,70,000. The Explanation says adjusted total income is computed without giving effect to the allowance referred to in the section, so the expenditure cannot be taken out of the base used to limit it.

citation.ref: Section 44C with its clauses and the Explanation defining adjusted total income, read with Section 72(1)

items.scenario: Rhineland Bank, a non-resident, runs a branch in India. For previous year 2025-26 its total income computed under the Act, before any allowance for head office expenditure and before setting off any brought forward loss, is ₹80,00,000. It has a brought forward business loss of ₹30,00,000 under section 72(1). Head office expenditure attributable to the Indian business is ₹6,00,000. Section 44C caps the allowance at five per cent of the adjusted total income.

items.stem: How is the ₹90,00,000 loss dealt with?

options.text: ₹70,00,000 is set off against the trading profit under section 70(1) and ₹20,00,000 is carried forward
options.misconception: applies the ordinary intra-head set-off, when section 73A overrides it for a specified business
options.why: Section 70(1) is the general rule for setting one business loss against another business profit, and section 73A is the special rule that displaces it here. A specified business loss is ring-fenced and can only meet a specified business profit.

options.text: The loss is carried forward but only for eight assessment years
options.misconception: imports the eight-year limit that governs a business loss under section 72
options.why: Section 72 carries a business loss for eight assessment years, and section 73A(2) is written without any such limit. The carry forward continues year after year until a specified business profit absorbs it.

options.text: No loss arises at all, the capital expenditure having already been written off in full under section 35AD
options.misconception: treats the section 35AD deduction as something other than a charge against profits
options.why: The deduction under section 35AD(1) is what produces the loss in the first place — a hundred per cent write-off of capital cost in year one almost always exceeds the year's revenue. Section 73A exists precisely because that loss is real.

options.text: None of it can be set off this year, and the whole ₹90,00,000 is carried forward with no limit on the number of years
options.why: Section 73A(1) says a loss computed in respect of a specified business shall not be set off except against the profits of any other specified business, and the company has none, so the ₹70,00,000 trading profit is out of reach. Section 73A(2) then carries the whole ₹90,00,000 forward to be set off against the profits of any specified business in a later year, and it puts no limit on the number of years.

citation.ref: Sections 73A(1) and 73A(2), read with Section 35AD(1) and Section 70(1)

items.scenario: Sundar Cold Chain Ltd commissions a cold chain facility, a specified business under section 35AD, in previous year 2025-26 and claims the deduction for its capital expenditure. After that deduction the specified business shows a loss of ₹90,00,000 for the year. The company also runs a trading business which earns a profit of ₹70,00,000 in the same year, and it operates no other specified business.

items.stem: What is the actual cost of the machine under section 43(1)?

options.misconception: keeps the cash-paid installation charge in the cost, ignoring the proviso to section 43(1)
options.why: Adding the ₹60,000 back gives ₹48,50,000. The proviso denies actual cost treatment to expenditure for acquisition of an asset where the payment or aggregate of payments to a person in a day, otherwise than by an account payee cheque or draft or through a bank account or a prescribed electronic mode, exceeds ₹10,000.

options.misconception: capitalises the interest for the period after the asset was first put to use
options.why: Adding the ₹90,000 gives ₹48,80,000. Explanation 8 says interest for any period after the asset is first put to use shall not be included and shall never be deemed to have been included in the actual cost; it is a revenue deduction under section 36(1)(iii) instead.

Start with ₹50,00,000 plus ₹2,00,000 of installation. The proviso to section 43(1) keeps out expenditure where the payment to a person in a day otherwise than through a banking channel exceeds ₹10,000, so the ₹60,000 cash payment comes off, leaving ₹51,40,000. Explanation 10 removes the ₹5,00,000 subsidy relatable to the cost, leaving ₹46,40,000. Interest up to the date the asset is first put to use is added, giving ₹47,90,000, while Explanation 8 keeps the ₹90,000 of later interest out.

options.misconception: ignores the subsidy received against the cost of the asset
options.why: Leaving the ₹5,00,000 in gives ₹52,90,000. Explanation 10 says that where a portion of the cost has been met by a government or any other person in the form of a subsidy, grant or reimbursement, so much of the cost as is relatable to it shall not be included.

citation.ref: Section 43(1) with its proviso and Explanations 8 and 10, read with Section 36(1)(iii)

items.scenario: Vasant Textiles Ltd buys a machine during previous year 2025-26. The invoice price is ₹50,00,000, paid by account payee cheque. Installation charges are ₹2,00,000, of which ₹1,40,000 was paid by cheque and ₹60,000 was paid in cash to one contractor on a single day. A State Government subsidy of ₹5,00,000 is received specifically against the cost of this machine. Interest on the loan taken to buy it is ₹1,50,000 for the period up to the date the machine was first put to use and ₹90,000 for the period after that date.

items.stem: What must Mr Verma show to escape liability under section 179?

options.text: That the non-recovery cannot be attributed to any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part in relation to the affairs of the company
options.why: Section 179(1) makes every person who was a director of a private company at any time during the relevant previous year jointly and severally liable where the tax cannot be recovered from the company, unless he proves that the non-recovery cannot be attributed to any gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty on his part. The burden sits on him, and he was a director throughout previous year 2022-23.
keywords: gross neglect, misfeasance or breach of duty

options.text: Nothing, since the liability is absolute once recovery from the company has failed
options.misconception: reads the sub-section as a strict charge, when it carries its own express escape
options.why: Section 179(1) itself says "unless he proves" and then sets out the defence. Failure of recovery from the company opens the door to the director; it does not close it behind him.

options.text: That he had resigned before the demand was raised
options.misconception: uses the date of the demand as the test, when the section looks at the previous year in which the income arose
options.why: The section fixes liability on a person who was a director at any time during the relevant previous year. Mr Verma held office through the whole of previous year 2022-23, so resigning in June 2024 takes him nowhere.

options.text: That the company was a public company, section 179 applying to a director of any company
options.misconception: widens the section beyond a private company, when its opening words confine it to one
options.why: Section 179(1) is written for a private company alone, and there is no counterpart for a public company. Section 167C carries the same rule across to the partners of a limited liability partnership.

citation.ref: Section 179(1) with its Explanation, read with Section 167C

items.scenario: Tax of ₹18,00,000 is due from Kalyani Traders Pvt Ltd, a private company, in respect of its income of previous year 2022-23. The company has no assets and the tax cannot be recovered from it. Mr Verma was a director of the company throughout previous year 2022-23 and resigned in June 2024, before the demand was raised.

items.stem: Which of these is void as against the revenue's claim under section 281?

options.text: The gift of the flat to his brother
options.why: Section 281(1) names gift among the modes of transfer it reaches, and the flat is a building, which the Explanation includes in assets. Neither limb of the proviso saves it — a gift is not made for adequate consideration, and no previous permission of the Assessing Officer was taken.
keywords: previous permission of the Assessing Officer

options.text: The sale of the plot at market value to a buyer who knew nothing of the proceedings
options.misconception: applies the section to every transfer during the pendency, ignoring the first limb of the proviso
options.why: The proviso saves a transfer made for adequate consideration and without notice of the pendency of the proceeding or of the tax payable. Full market value and a buyer with no knowledge is exactly the case it protects.

options.text: None of them, section 281 reaching only a transfer made after the assessment order has been passed
options.misconception: starts the window at the assessment order, when the sub-section opens it during the pendency of the proceeding
options.why: Section 281(1) covers a transfer made during the pendency of any proceeding as well as after its completion, and runs until a notice under Rule 2 of the Second Schedule is served. All three transfers here fall inside that window; what separates them is the proviso and the Explanation.

options.text: The sale of cloth out of the shop's stock
options.misconception: overlooks the narrow definition of assets in the Explanation to section 281
options.why: The Explanation defines assets as land, building, machinery, plant, shares, securities and fixed deposits in banks, and only to the extent they do not form part of the stock-in-trade of the business. Cloth sold from the shop is stock-in-trade and outside the section.

citation.ref: Section 281(1) with its proviso and the Explanation to Section 281, read with Rule 2 of the Second Schedule

items.scenario: Assessment proceedings against Mr Bakshi, a cloth trader, are pending, and no notice under Rule 2 of the Second Schedule has been served. During that time he does three things. He gifts a flat worth ₹60,00,000 to his brother, without asking the Assessing Officer. He sells a plot of land for its full market value of ₹45,00,000 to a buyer who has no knowledge of the proceedings. And he sells ₹9,00,000 of cloth out of his shop's stock in the ordinary course of trade.

items.stem: What follows for Ashwin Chemicals Ltd?

options.text: The two are deemed to be associated enterprises and the payment a deemed international transaction, the deduction is refused unless the prescribed documents and information are maintained and furnished, and tax is deducted at a floor of thirty per cent
options.why: Section 94A(2) deems all the parties to a transaction with a person located in a notified jurisdictional area to be associated enterprises and the transaction to be an international transaction, so transfer pricing applies whatever the shareholding. Section 94A(3) refuses the deduction unless the prescribed documents and information are maintained and furnished, and section 94A(5) requires deduction at the highest of the rate in the relevant provision, the rates in force, and thirty per cent.

options.text: The ₹70,00,000 is disallowed outright, and no documentation can restore the deduction
options.misconception: reads section 94A(3) as an absolute disallowance rather than a conditional one
options.why: Section 94A(3) is written as an unless. The deduction comes back where the assessee maintains and furnishes the prescribed documents and information, and for a payment to a financial institution where he furnishes the authorisation letting the authorities seek information.

options.text: Nothing under section 94A, since the two are not in fact associated enterprises within section 92A
options.misconception: looks for a real relationship when section 94A(2) creates a deemed one
options.why: Section 94A(2) is a deeming provision and does not ask whether anybody holds a share in anybody. Location in a notified jurisdictional area is the whole trigger, which is what makes the section work against parties who are strangers on paper.

options.text: Tax must be deducted at twenty per cent, the floor in section 206AA, Marcato SA having no permanent account number
options.misconception: applies the missing-PAN floor when section 94A(5) sets a higher floor of its own
options.why: Section 206AA answers a different question — what happens when a deductee furnishes no permanent account number — and sets a floor of twenty per cent. Section 94A(5) sets its own floor of thirty per cent for a payment to a person located in a notified jurisdictional area, and it is the higher of the two.

citation.ref: Sections 94A(1), 94A(2), 94A(3) and 94A(5), read with Sections 92A and 206AA

items.scenario: Ashwin Chemicals Ltd pays ₹70,00,000 during previous year 2025-26 to Marcato SA, a company located in a country the Central Government has specified as a notified jurisdictional area under section 94A(1). Ashwin Chemicals holds no shares in Marcato SA and the two are not associated enterprises under section 92A on any ordinary test. Ashwin Chemicals has furnished Marcato SA's permanent account number to nobody, because Marcato SA has none.

items.stem: Is he entitled to the section 54 exemption?

options.text: No, but he can claim it under section 54F instead
options.misconception: swaps in the section that runs in the opposite direction
options.why: Section 54F exempts gains on assets other than a residential house when the proceeds buy a residential house. Here the sale was residential and the purchase was not — the wrong way round for both sections.

options.text: Yes, because the amount invested exceeds the capital gain
options.misconception: reads the quantum condition and skips the nature-of-asset condition
