options.why: The deed is the first gate; the statutory formula is the second. Remuneration beyond the formula is disallowed however solemnly the deed promises it.

citation.ref: Section 40(b) (Finance Act 2024) with 194T

items.scenario: For FY 2025-26 a firm's book profit is ₹20 lakh, and its deed authorises remuneration of ₹15 lakh to its two working partners, which the firm pays and claims. The accountant computes the deductible ceiling using the limits he memorised years ago: ₹1.5 lakh or 90 per cent on the first ₹3 lakh, and 60 per cent beyond.

items.stem: How do the write-off and the later recovery fare?

options.text: The write-off deducts on the book entry alone — irrecoverability need not be proved — and the ₹30 lakh is income of the year it arrives
options.why: Since the 1989 amendment the condition is that the debt is written off as irrecoverable in the accounts, not established as such — the Supreme Court settled that the officer cannot demand proof the debt died. The balancing safeguard is section 41(4): what returns is taxed when it returns, so the ₹30 lakh lands in the recovery year's income.

options.text: The disallowance stands — a live customer means a live debt
options.misconception: applies the pre-1989 establish-it-first test
options.why: That evidentiary battle is what the amendment ended. Commercial judgment recorded in the books carries the deduction; the recovery rule protects the revenue if the judgment proves pessimistic.

options.text: The write-off deducts, and the ₹30 lakh recovery is a tax-free windfall
options.misconception: takes the deduction and forgets its mirror
options.why: Section 41(4) exists precisely for this sequence. A deduction taken and cash later received without tax would make pessimistic write-offs a planning device.

options.text: The write-off deducts only after filing a recovery suit that fails
options.misconception: adds a litigation condition the section dropped
options.why: Requiring futile suits was the old regime's waste. The books' write-off is the statutory event; suing a hopeless debtor is commerce, not a tax condition.

citation.ref: Section 36(1)(vii) with 41(4)

items.scenario: A manufacturer writes off ₹90 lakh owed by a struggling customer, passing the entry before year-end. The assessing officer disallows it: the customer is still in business, recovery suits were never filed, and the debt might yet be paid. Two years later the customer, recovering, pays ₹30 lakh of the written-off amount.

items.stem: How does ICDS treat the two claims?

options.text: The contract loss deducts as prudence, the MTM waits as speculation
options.misconception: lets one anticipated loss through on sentiment
options.why: Prudence is the accounting reason for the provision — and anticipation of losses is exactly what the construction ICDS declines to import into tax.

options.text: Both wait — expected contract losses are not anticipated under ICDS, and speculative MTM losses are generally not deductible until settlement
options.why: Section 145(2)'s standards govern the computation whatever the books say: ICDS on construction contracts recognises losses as incurred by the percentage of completion, refusing the upfront ₹15 crore that Ind AS prudence demands; and ICDS I's general rule denies marked-to-market losses except where a specific ICDS allows them. The books stay Ind AS; the return adjusts both items out and reverses them over time.

options.text: Both deduct — audited accounts bind the assessing officer
options.misconception: promotes book profits into taxable profits
options.why: The computation standards exist precisely to detach tax from accounting prudence. Book-tax differences of this kind are the daily work of the computation.

options.text: Neither deducts ever — ICDS disallows provisions permanently
options.misconception: reads a timing standard as a prohibition
options.why: ICDS moves recognition, it does not extinguish it. The contract loss deducts as completion progresses, and the forward loss on settlement — later, not never.

citation.ref: Section 145(2) with ICDS I-X

items.scenario: A construction company's Ind AS accounts recognise a ₹15 crore provision for the expected total loss on an onerous contract in year one of three, and also book a ₹4 crore mark-to-market loss on open forward contracts held for a speculative position. The tax computation claims both, the CFO reasoning that audited Ind AS accounts are the last word for tax too.

items.stem: What does section 115BBC actually charge each?

options.text: Neither — donations to registered trusts are exempt income
options.misconception: lets registration absorb the anonymous-donation charge
options.why: Sections 11-12 exempt applied income; 115BBC carves anonymous receipts out of that comfort for secular trusts. Registration is the precondition of the regime, not immunity from this section.

options.text: The hospital pays 30 per cent on ₹55 lakh — the cushion of ₹25 lakh spares the rest — and the temple pays nothing under this section
options.why: The hospital's cushion is the higher of ₹1 lakh or 5 per cent of total donations (₹25 lakh), so ₹55 lakh of the anonymous ₹80 lakh bears the flat 30 per cent. The temple stands wholly outside: religious institutions' anonymous offerings are the section's express exception, Parliament recognising that hundi donations are anonymous by devotion, not design.

options.text: Both pay 30 per cent on their full anonymous receipts
options.misconception: misses both the cushion and the religious exception
options.why: The section's two mercies are its most examinable features. Charging the temple's hundi would tax a practice as old as the temples.

options.text: The hospital on ₹55 lakh, the temple on whatever exceeds its own ₹16 lakh cushion
options.misconception: gives the temple a cushion it does not need
options.why: The cushion mechanics never reach the temple — wholly religious institutions are excluded from the section before any computation begins.

citation.ref: Section 115BBC

items.scenario: A charitable hospital trust receives ₹5 crore of donations in the year, of which ₹80 lakh arrived in collection boxes with no donor records. Separately, a temple trust — wholly religious — counts ₹3 crore of anonymous hundi offerings. Both fear the 30 per cent anonymous-donation levy on their unrecorded receipts.

items.stem: What does section 35D actually allow?

options.text: ₹1.6 crore a year for five years — the full ₹8 crore amortised
options.misconception: spreads the whole spend and skips the five per cent cap
options.why: The cap is the section's binding constraint here: only ₹5 crore enters the amortisation at all. Instalments divide the capped pool, not the invoice total.

options.text: Nothing — preliminary expenses are permanently capital
options.misconception: states the pre-35D common law as the whole answer
options.why: That harsh default is real, and section 35D is its legislated exception for the listed expenses. Denying the ₹5 crore ignores the section outright.

options.text: ₹1 crore a year for five years — the pool caps at ₹5 crore (five per cent of the project), and the excess ₹3 crore earns nothing
options.why: Pre-commencement expenditure is capital in nature and undeducible but for this section, which rations its mercy twice: the qualifying pool cannot exceed five per cent of project cost — ₹5 crore here — and even that spreads over five equal instalments from commencement. The ₹3 crore beyond the cap simply perishes; neither this section nor section 37 rescues pre-business spending.

options.text: ₹8 crore in year one — expenses of starting up deduct when business starts
options.misconception: converts capital pre-commencement spending into revenue
options.why: Before the business exists there is no business to deduct against, which is the very gap 35D fills — on its own instalment and cap terms, not on the claimant's.

citation.ref: Section 35D

items.scenario: Before commencing its ₹100 crore plant, a company spends ₹8 crore on feasibility studies, project reports and incorporation-related legal work — all within the specified list. In year one of operations the CFO claims the entire ₹8 crore, calling it revenue expenditure of setting up.

items.stem: Which of the three arrangements does Clause 1 permit?

options.text: Mr Iyer's and Mr Rao's — Mr Rao has completed articleship and works under Verma's supervision, which is what the clause is aimed at
options.misconception: reads supervision and training as a substitute for membership, when the clause asks only whether the person is a chartered accountant in practice
options.why: Nothing in Clause 1 turns on how well supervised the person is. It asks whether he is a chartered accountant in practice, and a semi-qualified assistant is not, however capable he is and however closely Verma watches the Nashik desk.

options.text: All three, provided Verma signs every report himself and the three men only meet clients and prepare files
options.misconception: confuses Clause 1, which is about practising in the member's name, with Clause 12, which is about who may sign
options.why: Clause 12 is the clause about signing, and Verma keeping the pen would answer that one. Clause 1 is about a different mischief — a person holding himself out to the public as practising in the member's name — and meeting clients in the firm's name at a desk in another town is exactly that.

options.text: Only Mr Iyer's — he alone satisfies both conditions, being a chartered accountant in practice and employed by Verma
options.why: Clause 1 permits a member to allow another person to practise in his name only where that person is also a chartered accountant in practice and is in partnership with or employed by him. Both conditions have to hold at once. Mr Iyer holds a certificate of practice and is employed, so he passes both. Mr Rao is not a member at all. Mr Sen is a member but, holding no certificate of practice, he is not a chartered accountant in practice, so his employment answers only the second condition and the first defeats him.
keywords: in partnership with or employed by him

options.text: Mr Iyer's and Mr Sen's — both are members of the Institute and both are on Verma's payroll
options.misconception: treats membership of the Institute as the same thing as being in practice, and so ignores the certificate of practice
options.why: Membership and practice are two different states. A member who has not taken out a certificate of practice is not a chartered accountant in practice, and the clause names the second, not the first. Mr Sen's employment satisfies half the test and the missing half is the half that matters.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 1

items.scenario: CA Verma runs a sole practice. To cover three towns he makes three arrangements. Mr Rao, who cleared the Intermediate examination and completed articleship but is not a member, runs the Nashik desk in the firm's name and meets clients there. Mr Iyer is a chartered accountant who holds a certificate of practice and is Verma's salaried employee; he works in the firm's name at Pune. Mr Sen is a chartered accountant employed by Verma who has never taken out a certificate of practice; he works in the firm's name at Nagpur.

items.stem: Which of the three breaches Clause 5, and does any other clause come into it?

options.text: Only Mr Khanna's arrangement, and only under Clause 2 — Clause 5 is about advertising, not about agents
options.misconception: collapses Clause 5 into the advertising and solicitation clauses, missing that it polices who brought the work in
options.why: Advertising is Clause 7 and solicitation is Clause 6. Clause 5 is a separate provision about how the business was secured, and its first limb names the person who is not an employee or a partner. Charging only under Clause 2 answers where the money went and leaves the procurement itself unanswered.

options.text: Mr Khanna's arrangement and the manager's calls — any canvassing for work is business secured by means not open to a chartered accountant
options.misconception: reads the second limb so widely that it swallows the first limb's careful exclusion of the member's own employees and partners
options.why: The clause's own words exclude an employee of such chartered accountant. A firm's salaried manager speaking to the firm's existing clients is the firm speaking, and reading the second limb to catch that would make the first limb's exclusion meaningless.
keywords: an employee of such chartered accountant

options.text: Only Mr Khanna's arrangement — and it breaches Clause 2 as well, because the share of fees also went to a non-member
options.why: Clause 5 catches a member who secures professional business through the services of a person who is not an employee of such chartered accountant or who is not his partner. Mr Khanna is neither, so the first limb is breached the moment he brings work in. The salaried manager is an employee, which is precisely the person the clause leaves alone, and responding to a tender is expressly outside the solicitation bar in Clause 6. The commission is a second, separate wrong — Clause 2 forbids paying any share of professional fees to a person who is not a member of the Institute — so one arrangement breaches two clauses, one about how the work was secured and one about where the fee went.

options.text: All three — a tender response is soliciting work from the public, however the tender was worded
options.misconception: forgets the proviso that lets a member respond to tenders and enquiries issued by users of professional services
options.why: The solicitation clause carries a proviso permitting a member to respond to tenders or enquiries issued by users of professional services and to secure work as a consequence. A bank that floats a tender has invited the offer, so the member is answering rather than soliciting.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 5, read with Clauses 2 and 6

items.scenario: A practising firm signs three arrangements in one year. It retains Mr Khanna, a business development consultant who is neither a partner nor an employee, on a monthly retainer plus two per cent of the fees of every certification engagement he introduces. It asks its own salaried manager, an employee of the firm, to call on existing clients about the firm's new transfer pricing practice. And it responds to a tender floated by a public sector bank for concurrent audit and is selected.

items.stem: Where does Bose stand?

options.text: Not guilty — whether the company complied with the Companies Act is the company's own affair and its officers' liability, not the incoming auditor's
options.misconception: treats compliance with the appointment provisions as owed only by the company, when Clause 9 makes the incoming auditor's failure to ascertain it his own misconduct
options.why: The company's default is the company's, but Clause 9 creates a duty on the member — to ascertain from the company, before accepting, whether the requirements have been duly complied with. His misconduct is not the removal; it is accepting without asking.

options.text: Not guilty — he communicated with the outgoing auditor in writing and received a clear reply, which is the whole of the incoming auditor's duty
options.misconception: treats Clause 8 as the only pre-acceptance duty, so a clean reply from the outgoing auditor is read as clearance for the appointment itself
options.why: Clause 8 is about a conversation between two professionals. Clause 9 is about the lawfulness of the appointment, and the outgoing auditor's silence cannot cure a removal that never went through section 140(1). Two duties, and he performed one.

options.text: Guilty under Clause 9 — writing to the outgoing auditor discharged Clause 8 and nothing else, and Clause 9 required him to ascertain that the requirements for the appointment had been duly complied with
options.why: Clause 8 and Clause 9 are two separate duties on the same appointment, and satisfying one says nothing about the other. Clause 8 asks for a letter to the outgoing auditor; Clause 9 asks the incoming auditor to ascertain from the company whether the requirements governing the appointment have been duly complied with. A removal before the expiry of the term needs a special resolution and the previous approval of the Central Government under section 140(1), and Bose never asked whether either existed. The letter he did write is therefore beside the point.

options.text: Guilty under Clause 8 as well, because a removal in dispute means the outgoing auditor's no-objection was needed before acceptance
options.misconception: converts the communication required by Clause 8 into a permission the outgoing auditor can withhold
options.why: Clause 8 requires communication in writing and nothing more; an outgoing auditor has never been able to veto his successor. Bose wrote, so Clause 8 is answered, and adding a second charge here would punish him for a duty that does not exist.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 9, read with section 140(1) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A company's board tells CA Bose that the existing auditor has been removed with immediate effect and offers him the appointment. Bose writes to the outgoing auditor, who replies that he has nothing to add, and Bose accepts. It emerges later that the removal was before the expiry of the auditor's term and that the company obtained neither the previous approval of the Central Government nor the special resolution of the members. Bose says he did everything the profession asked of him.

items.stem: Which signatures may lawfully be given on the firm's behalf?

options.text: The fellow partner's and the manager's — the manager is a chartered accountant employed by the firm, which is what the clause requires
options.misconception: reads the clause as though employment by the firm were enough, when its second limb excludes a member who is not a partner
options.why: Employment is enough under Clause 1, which governs practising in the member's name. It is not enough here, because Clause 12 names a member not being his partner as a person who may not sign. The two clauses draw their lines in different places on purpose.

options.text: All three — a certificate of net worth is not a balance sheet, a profit and loss account or a report, so the articled assistant's signature is outside the clause
options.misconception: reads the list of documents narrowly and forgets that a member may not allow a non-member to sign for the firm at all
options.why: The clause names a balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements, and a net worth certificate is a report on financial information issued in the firm's name. Reading the list as a loophole for certificates would let the least qualified person in the office sign the documents the public relies on most.

options.text: Only the fellow partner's — Clause 12 bars a member who is not his partner as firmly as it bars a non-member
options.why: Clause 12 makes it misconduct to allow a person not being a member of the Institute in practice, or a member not being his partner, to sign on his behalf or on behalf of his firm, any balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements. The manager is a member, but he is not a partner, so the second limb catches him. The articled assistant is not a member at all. Only the fellow partner is inside both limbs, and the absent partner's email and the client's resolution change nothing, because authority to sign is not something either of them can confer.
keywords: balance sheet, profit and loss account, report or financial statements

options.text: The fellow partner's and the manager's, because the written authority and the client's board resolution together supply the authority
options.misconception: assumes signing authority can be delegated by agreement, when the clause fixes who may sign regardless of what anyone consents to
options.why: Neither an absent partner nor a client can widen the class of people Clause 12 allows. A resolution recording that the client is content proves only that the client is content. The prohibition runs against the member who allows the signature, not against the client who receives it.

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part I, Clause 12

items.scenario: The signing partner of a firm is abroad when three documents fall due. He emails written authority for his manager, a chartered accountant in whole-time employment with the firm, to sign the audit report of a company; he asks his fellow partner to sign the audit report of a second company; and he asks an articled assistant to sign a net worth certificate. The client of the first company also passes a board resolution recording that it accepts the manager's signature.

items.stem: Which heads of misconduct do the three facts attract, and before which forum?

options.text: All three — Clause 1 for acting as a fellow, Clause 2 for not supplying the information called for, and Clause 3 for false information in a tender, all in Part III of the First Schedule, and so all before the Board of Discipline
options.why: Part III of the First Schedule binds every member. Clause 1 catches a member who, not being a fellow of the Institute, acts as a fellow of the Institute, which is what "FCA" on an associate's letterhead does. Clause 2 catches a member who does not supply the information called for by the Director (Discipline), and the merits of the complaint are no answer to it. Clause 3 catches false information given while responding to tenders. All three sit in the First Schedule, so the case goes before the Board of Discipline.

options.text: Only the silence, since a letterhead is a private matter between the member and his stationer and a tender is a commercial negotiation
options.misconception: treats representations made to clients and to tendering authorities as outside the disciplinary code because no audit opinion was involved
options.why: Part III applies to a member whether in practice or not and is not confined to audit work. Holding out as a fellow and overstating a firm's standing to a tendering authority are both representations the public relies on, and both are named in the Schedule.

options.text: All three, but before the Disciplinary Committee, because giving false information knowingly is a Second Schedule matter
options.misconception: assumes that dishonesty always routes a case to the heavier forum, when the routing follows the Schedule the clause sits in
options.why: Knowledge does move some charges to the Second Schedule, but only where a Second Schedule clause covers the facts. False information in a tender is named in Clause 3 of Part III of the First Schedule, so the routing follows that Schedule and the Board of Discipline hears it.

options.text: The letterhead under Clause 7 of Part I, the tender under Clause 3 of Part III, and nothing for the silence
options.misconception: files the false fellowship under the designation clause and treats silence towards the Institute's own machinery as no misconduct at all
options.why: Clause 7 of Part I is about advertising attainments and about designations other than chartered accountant; claiming a grade of membership the member does not hold is dealt with by Clause 1 of Part III. And silence is expressly misconduct — the clause names not supplying the information called for as the wrong itself.
keywords: not supplying the information called for

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part III, Clauses 1, 2 and 3

items.scenario: CA Menon is an associate of the Institute. His letterhead reads "CA S. Menon, FCA". The Director (Discipline), examining a complaint against him, writes three times asking for the working papers of one engagement; Menon does not reply, saying privately that the complaint is malicious and he will answer when it reaches a hearing. In the same year he bids for a government empanelment and states in the tender that his firm has four partners and eleven years of standing, knowing it has two partners and six.

items.stem: Which head does each fall under, and which forum hears it?

options.text: All three go before the Disciplinary Committee, because other misconduct is the graver charge and the Board of Discipline handles only clause-by-clause professional misconduct
options.misconception: treats other misconduct as a single grave head, when it is split across the two Schedules and routed like anything else
options.why: Other misconduct is not one head but two, and the routing works exactly as it does for professional misconduct. A matter under First Schedule Part IV goes before the Board of Discipline; only Second Schedule Part III reaches the Disciplinary Committee.

options.text: A and B are other misconduct under First Schedule Part IV and go before the Board of Discipline; C is other misconduct under Second Schedule Part III and goes before the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: First Schedule Part IV covers a conviction for an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and, separately, an action that in the opinion of the Council brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute, whether or not related to professional work. A's three-month offence and B's disrepute both land there, so the Board of Discipline hears them. C's offence is punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months, which is Second Schedule Part III, so the Disciplinary Committee hears it. The dividing line is the term the offence carries, not the sentence awarded.

options.text: A and C are other misconduct; B is not, because a conviction by a court is what the head requires
options.misconception: reads both limbs of First Schedule Part IV as needing a court's finding, when the second limb turns only on the opinion of the Council
options.why: Part IV has two limbs and only the first needs a conviction. The second asks whether, in the opinion of the Council, the member brings disrepute to the profession or the Institute, and a member acquitted or never charged can still fall within it.

options.text: None of them — the Schedules punish professional misconduct, and nothing here arose out of professional work
options.misconception: assumes the Schedules reach only work done as a chartered accountant, missing that other misconduct is a separate head that expressly need not relate to professional work
options.why: Other misconduct exists precisely for conduct outside the practice. First Schedule Part IV says in terms that the action may be one whether or not related to his professional work, and a conviction under either Schedule needs no connection with an engagement.
keywords: whether or not related to his professional work

citation.ref: First Schedule, Part IV, and Second Schedule, Part III

items.scenario: Three members come before the Institute in the same month. A is convicted by a magistrate of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of up to three months and is let off with a fine. B is not convicted of anything, but a widely reported brawl at a housing society meeting leads the Council to form the opinion that his conduct has brought disrepute to the profession. C is convicted of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of two years. None of the three facts arose out of professional work.

items.stem: Which clause is the cleanest charge, and why does the partner's review not save it?

options.text: Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule alone — the failure is gross negligence, and Clause 2 is about disclosure of information
options.misconception: reaches for the negligence clause and misremembers Clause 2 of the Second Schedule as the confidentiality provision
options.why: Confidentiality is Clause 1 of that Part, not Clause 2. Gross negligence may well be present too, but Clause 2 fits these facts precisely, because it asks the one question the scenario answers — whose hands made the examination.

options.text: No clause is breached, because the firm used an expert's work and satisfied itself about the expert's competence and the relevance of the findings
options.misconception: borrows the auditor's use of an expert, which applies to a field outside accounting and auditing, to justify outsourcing the accounting examination itself
options.why: Using an expert covers expertise in a field other than accounting and auditing — a valuer, an actuary, a geologist. An examination of financial statements and the related records is the member's own field, and Clause 2 names exactly who may perform it.

options.text: No clause is breached, provided the consultancy worked under the firm's written supervision and its files were retained by the firm
options.misconception: treats supervision and file custody as making outside workers into employees in his firm
options.why: Supervision does not change who the workers are. The clause permits an employee in his firm, and a contracted consultancy is not that however closely it is instructed or however completely its papers end up in the firm's cabinet.

options.text: Clause 2 of Part I of the Second Schedule — the examination was made by none of the four permitted persons, and reading a summary is not making the examination
options.why: Clause 2 forbids certifying or submitting, in his name or the name of his firm, a report of an examination of financial statements unless the examination of such statements and the related records has been made by him or by a partner or an employee in his firm or by another chartered accountant in practice. The outside consultancy is none of those four. The partner's questions may show diligence, but the clause asks who made the examination, and on these facts nobody inside the permitted circle did.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 2

items.scenario: A firm is asked to certify a company's claim for an export incentive, which requires an examination of the financial statements and the related shipping and costing records. To meet the deadline the firm engages an outside consultancy of commerce graduates, none of them members of the Institute and none employed by the firm, to carry out the entire examination. The engagement partner reads their summary memorandum, asks two questions, and signs the certificate in the firm's name.

items.stem: Has the firm breached Clause 3 of Part I of the Second Schedule?

options.text: No — the assumptions genuinely were reasonable and the file proves it, so there was nothing false in the presentation
options.misconception: tests the clause by the quality of the underlying work rather than by the belief the wording invites
options.why: The clause does not ask whether the work was good. It asks whether the name was used in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and a firm with an immaculate file can still lend its name to a sentence that promises the future.
keywords: vouches for the accuracy of the forecast

options.text: Yes — a chartered accountant may not associate his name with projected figures at all, whatever words are used
options.misconception: turns a rule about how the name is used into a ban on working with prospective financial information
options.why: Members report on prospective financial information regularly and properly. What Clause 3 controls is the manner of the association, so a report on whether the assumptions provide a reasonable basis, with a plain warning that actual results are likely to differ, is permitted work.

options.text: Yes — the words used lead the reader to believe the firm vouches for the accuracy of the forecast, and careful work on the assumptions does not answer that
options.why: Clause 3 is breached where the member permits his name or the firm's name to be used in connection with an estimate of earnings contingent upon future transactions in a manner which may lead to the belief that he vouches for the accuracy of the forecast. "Examined and certified" says exactly that to an ordinary reader. The clause tests the impression the document creates, so the quality of the file behind it is beside the point; a report saying the assumptions provide a reasonable basis for the projection and that actual results will differ would have created no such impression.
keywords: vouches for the accuracy of the forecast

options.text: No — the breach would only arise once the projections proved wrong, and even then the fault would lie with the company that lost the contract
options.misconception: judges the clause by the outcome, when the wrong is complete at the moment the name is lent
options.why: The breach of Clause 3 was complete when the presentation went out. Projections that happened to come true would have made the firm lucky, not compliant, and the loss of a customer contract is the ordinary reason forecasts move.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 3

items.scenario: A company circulates an investor presentation carrying three years of projected profits. On the page facing the numbers is the line "Profit projections examined and certified by M/s Kulkarni & Co., Chartered Accountants", with the firm's name and logo. The engagement partner had in fact reviewed each assumption, found them supportable, and holds a file that shows it. The projections later prove far too optimistic because a customer contract was lost.

items.stem: How is he answered?

options.text: None of the three is misconduct — Council guidelines are advisory, and only the Schedules themselves create misconduct
options.misconception: treats the guidelines as sitting outside the Schedules, when a clause of the Second Schedule expressly pulls them inside
options.why: The guidelines do sit outside the Schedules, and that is why Clause 1 of Part II exists: it makes contravention of any guidelines issued by the Council a misconduct in itself. The argument answers the wrong question.

options.text: Each of the three contravenes guidelines issued by the Council and so is professional misconduct under Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule, which puts the case before the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: Clause 1 of Second Schedule Part II makes it professional misconduct to contravene any of the provisions of the Act or the regulations made thereunder or any guidelines issued by the Council. That single sentence converts every Council guideline into a disciplinary obligation, so the bar on accepting an audit where the previous auditor's undisputed fee is unpaid, the ceiling on tax audit assignments and the requirement to maintain proper books of account all bite. Because the clause sits in the Second Schedule, the case goes before the Disciplinary Committee, which is the forum that can remove a name permanently.

options.text: Only the unpaid fee point, because it prejudices another member; a ceiling and a cash book harm nobody
options.misconception: asks whether anyone was harmed, when the clause asks only whether a guideline was contravened
options.why: Harm is not an ingredient. Clause 1 is breached by the contravention itself, and the ceiling on assignments and the requirement to keep books exist to protect the quality and the accountability of the work rather than any one identifiable victim.

options.text: All three are misconduct, but under the First Schedule, because they concern how a member conducts his practice, so the Board of Discipline hears them
options.misconception: routes by subject matter rather than by the Schedule the clause sits in
options.why: Routing follows the clause, not the topic. The clause that catches a breach of a Council guideline is Clause 1 of Second Schedule Part II, so the case goes to the Disciplinary Committee even though the facts are about the everyday running of a practice.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 1, read with the Council General Guidelines issued under the Act

items.scenario: A practising member does three things in one year. He accepts the statutory audit of a company knowing that the previous auditor's undisputed audit fee for the last statutory audit remains unpaid and the company is not a sick unit. He accepts tax audit assignments under section 44AB beyond the number the Council's guidelines permit. And he keeps no cash book and no ledger for his own practice. He argues that Council guidelines are recommendations, not law, and that in any case none of this hurt a client.

items.stem: Where does each disclosure stand?

options.text: Sharing the old employer's costing sheets is misconduct under Clause 2 of Part II of the Second Schedule; producing the summoned records is within the exception for a disclosure required by any law for the time being in force
options.why: Clause 2 of Second Schedule Part II makes it professional misconduct for a member, being an employee, to disclose confidential information acquired in the course of his employment except as and when required by any law for the time being in force or except as permitted by the employer. Costing sheets learnt at the old employer are exactly that information, the duty does not end with the job, and the absence of a secrecy agreement is irrelevant because the obligation comes from the Schedule and not from a contract. The summons falls in the first exception, and the current employer's instruction cannot override a statute.
keywords: required by any law for the time being in force

options.text: Sharing the costing sheets is permitted because his new employer, as the person he now serves, has effectively given permission
options.misconception: reads the employer's permission as coming from whoever employs him now, when the permission must come from the employer whose information it is
options.why: The exception in Clause 2 is permission from the employer whose information is being disclosed. The new board is the audience, not the owner of the information, so its enthusiasm is not the permission the clause has in mind.

options.text: Neither is misconduct — he signed no confidentiality agreement with the old employer, and an employee must follow his current employer's instruction on a summons
options.misconception: sources the duty in the contract of employment rather than in the Schedule, and treats an employer's instruction as capable of defeating a statutory demand
options.why: The duty is statutory, so a missing agreement changes nothing. And the exception is worded as a disclosure required by any law for the time being in force, which means the law compels production whatever the employer prefers.
keywords: required by any law for the time being in force

options.text: Both are governed by Clause 1 of Part I of the Second Schedule, which protects information acquired in the course of a professional engagement
options.misconception: applies the confidentiality clause written for a member in practice and his client to a member who is an employee
options.why: Clause 1 of Part I speaks of information acquired in the course of a professional engagement and of the client's consent. Pillai had no client; he had an employer. The clause built for that situation is Clause 2 of Part II, and the door out of it is a disclosure permitted by the employer.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clause 2

items.scenario: CA Pillai leaves a manufacturing company, where he was finance controller, to join a competitor as chief financial officer. In his first month he shares his old employer's product-wise costing sheets with his new board, saying the old employer never asked him to sign anything about secrecy. In the same month a summons issued under a tax statute requires him to produce his current employer's records, and the current employer tells him not to comply.

items.stem: Under which clauses does each fall?

options.text: Both fall under Clause 4, since a knowingly false return is itself a form of dishonesty equivalent to embezzlement
options.misconception: merges two separate clauses because both involve dishonesty, losing the distinct ingredient each one requires
options.why: Clause 4 requires moneys received in his professional capacity to be defalcated or embezzled, and a false return involves no money at all. Two wrongs need two charges, and Clause 3 is the one that fits the filing.

options.text: The return falls under Clause 2 of Part III of the First Schedule and the money under Clause 10 of Part I of the Second Schedule
options.misconception: picks the lighter neighbour of each clause — silence towards the Institute instead of a knowing falsehood, and a custody failure instead of taking the money
options.why: Clause 2 of Part III punishes not supplying the information called for, and this member supplied it; what he did was supply particulars knowing them to be false, which is Clause 3 of Part II. And Clause 10 of Part I punishes failing to keep client moneys separate, which survives repayment — but here there was no repayment and the money went to his own purchase, which is Clause 4.
keywords: not supplying the information called for

options.text: The return falls under Clause 3 and the money under Clause 4, both in Part II of the Second Schedule, so both go before the Disciplinary Committee
options.why: Clause 3 of Second Schedule Part II catches a member who includes in any information, statement, return or form to be submitted to the Institute any particulars knowing them to be false, which is what the return did. Clause 4 catches a member who defalcates or embezzles moneys received in his professional capacity, and money taken for a personal purchase and never repaid is taken, not merely misplaced. Both clauses sit in the Second Schedule, so the Disciplinary Committee hears both.

options.text: Neither is professional misconduct, because a filing with the Institute is administrative and the money dispute is a civil claim the client can pursue in court
options.misconception: assumes a disciplinary charge needs a professional engagement and an unremedied client loss, when both clauses stand on their own words
options.why: Clause 3 names a return submitted to the Institute in terms, so a filing with the Institute is the very thing it governs. And a civil remedy running alongside a disciplinary charge has never displaced it — the client may sue and the Disciplinary Committee may still act.

citation.ref: Second Schedule, Part II, Clauses 3 and 4

items.scenario: Two complaints reach the Institute about the same member. The first is that a return he filed with the Institute about the paid assistants in his firm carried particulars he knew to be false. The second is that a client gave him money to pay the client's advance tax and he used it for a personal property purchase and never repaid it. He says the return was a clerical matter and that the money question is merely a failure to keep a separate bank account.

items.stem: Which of the three offices comply with section 27?

options.text: The Indore second office and the Bhopal room — a member's own residence is never a second office
options.misconception: decides what counts as an office by the type of address rather than by how the place is held out to clients
options.why: A residence stays private only while it stays private. Once the firm's name board is up and clients are received there on appointed days, it is held out as an office and section 27 treats it as one.

options.text: The Indore second office and the Guwahati office — Guwahati is answered by the partner's quarterly visit, since the section asks for charge, not for daily presence
options.misconception: treats occasional supervision from another city as separate charge, when the member in charge is expected to be actually in charge of that office
options.why: Separate charge means a member of the Institute who is genuinely in charge of that office, ordinarily a partner or a member in whole-time employment attending it. A visit once a quarter leaves the office in the hands of people the Institute cannot hold answerable for the work done there.

options.text: Only the Indore second office, and even that fails, because section 27 admits no exemption and every office needs its own member
options.misconception: reads the section without the Council's general exemptions, so a second office in the same building is condemned along with the rest
options.why: The section's requirement is real but the Council's exemptions are equally real: where the second office is in the same premises, or in the same city, or within the distance from a city's municipal limits that the guidelines prescribe, both offices may be under the same charge.

options.text: Only the Indore second office — it is in the same premises, which the Council's exemptions cover; the Guwahati office and the Bhopal room each need a member in separate charge
options.why: Section 27 requires that where a chartered accountant in practice or a firm has more than one office in India, each one of such offices shall be in the separate charge of a member of the Institute. The Council's exemptions relieve that requirement where the second office is in the same premises as the first, which covers another floor of the same building. Guwahati has no member in charge at all, and semi-qualified staff with a quarterly visit are not a member in separate charge. The Bhopal room carries the firm's name board and is held out as a place clients may come to, which makes it an office however few days it opens.
keywords: separate charge of a member of the Institute

citation.ref: Section 27, read with the Council's general exemptions from separate charge of a second office

items.scenario: A firm has its head office in Indore. It opens a second office on another floor of the same building. It opens a third office in Guwahati, staffed by two semi-qualified assistants and visited by a partner once a quarter, with no member in charge there. And a partner keeps a room at his residence in Bhopal with the firm's name board outside, where he meets clients on Saturdays; no member is in charge of it separately.

items.stem: What are the answers under section 22G?

options.text: It can enhance the penalty, it can remit the case for further enquiry, and it cannot pass any such order without giving the parties concerned an opportunity of being heard
options.why: Section 22G lets the Appellate Authority confirm, modify or set aside the order; impose any penalty, or set aside, reduce or enhance the penalty imposed; remit the case to the Board of Discipline or the Disciplinary Committee for such further enquiry as it considers proper; or pass such other order as it thinks fit. So an appeal is not a one-way door — the Authority may enhance the penalty. It may also remit the case rather than decide it. And the proviso requires that the parties concerned be given an opportunity of being heard before any order is passed.

options.text: It can only confirm or reduce the penalty, since no appellate body may put an appellant in a worse position than the order he challenged
options.misconception: imports a general no-worse-off principle that section 22G's express power to enhance the penalty displaces
options.why: The section says what it says, and among the powers it lists is the power to set aside, reduce or enhance the penalty imposed. A member advised to appeal has to be told that the Authority may enhance the penalty, because the statute puts that squarely within its powers.

options.text: It rehears the complaint from the beginning, taking evidence afresh, because an appeal against a disciplinary order is a fresh trial
options.misconception: treats the appeal as a retrial, when the Authority acts on the record and may remit the case where more enquiry is needed
options.why: The Authority calls for the records and revises the order, and where more enquiry is genuinely required its route is to remit the case to the forum below rather than to conduct the enquiry itself.

options.text: The appeal lies not to the Appellate Authority but to the High Court, the Authority being constituted only for orders of the Board of Discipline
options.misconception: confines the Authority to First Schedule matters, when section 22G covers orders of both disciplinary forums
options.why: The Authority hears appeals against penalties imposed by the Board of Discipline and by the Disciplinary Committee alike. It is constituted under section 22A with a Chairperson who is or has been a judge of a High Court, which is the source of the confusion, but the appeal itself lies to the Authority.

citation.ref: Sections 22A and 22G, with the proviso to section 22G

items.scenario: The Disciplinary Committee holds a member guilty under the Second Schedule and removes his name from the Register of Members for six months. His counsel advises an appeal to the Appellate Authority, and the member asks three questions: can the Authority make the punishment heavier, can it send the matter back for more enquiry rather than deciding it, and can it act on the papers without hearing him.

items.stem: Which of the three may the firm do?

options.text: All three, provided the firm applies safeguards — an engagement quality review and a separate team for the non-audit work
options.misconception: assumes every independence problem can be reduced to an acceptable level by safeguards, when assuming a management responsibility is one of the places the Code simply prohibits
options.why: Safeguards work on threats that can be brought to an acceptable level. Assuming a management responsibility is not one of them; the Code prohibits it outright, so a separate team and a reviewer are answering a question the Code never asks here.

options.text: The first and the third — running a bank account for a short unpaid period is an administrative convenience rather than a decision-making role
options.misconception: measures a management responsibility by the fee and the duration rather than by whether the firm is controlling the client's resources
options.why: Controlling or managing bank accounts or investments is named as a management responsibility, and what makes it one is the control over the client's resources, not how long it lasts or whether anyone was billed for it.

options.text: None of the three, because section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013 bars an auditor from rendering any service to the company it audits
options.misconception: reads section 144 as a total bar on services, when it lists particular services and leaves permitted work to be approved by the board or the audit committee
options.why: Section 144 names specified services that a company auditor may not render and leaves other services to be approved by the Board of Directors or the audit committee. It is a second gate on top of the Code, not a prohibition on speaking to the client at all.

options.text: Only the first — advice and options are permitted if management decides; deciding which recommendations to implement and operating a bank account are management responsibilities and no safeguard makes them acceptable
options.why: Providing advice and recommendations to assist management is not assuming a management responsibility, so the redesign advice is permitted provided the board decides. Deciding which recommendations of the firm to implement, and controlling or managing bank accounts, are both named as management responsibilities, and a firm shall not assume a management responsibility for an audit client — there is no safeguard for it, so the absence of a fee and the shortness of the period change nothing. What the firm must be satisfied about throughout is that client management makes all judgements and decisions that are properly management's.

citation.ref: the prohibition on a firm assuming a management responsibility for an audit client, read with section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: An audit client asks its audit firm for three things during the year. First, to advise on redesigning the credit approval process and to present options to the board. Second, to decide which of the firm's control recommendations will be implemented and in what order, because the board says the firm knows best. Third, to operate the company's treasury bank account for two months, without fee, while a new controller is recruited.

items.stem: What does the Code require?

options.text: Nothing yet — section 139(2) fixes the term, and while the firm's term runs the same partner may continue to sign
options.misconception: treats the statutory rotation of the firm as covering the field, so the Code's separate requirement about the individual is never reached
options.why: Two rules run at once and each has to be satisfied. Section 139(2) governs the appointment of the firm; the Code governs how long an individual may serve as a key audit partner on a public interest entity. Complying with the first says nothing about the second.

options.text: The individual must rotate off and serve the cooling-off period the Code specifies, and during it he may not consult with the team on technical or industry-specific issues on that engagement
options.why: Long association creates a familiarity threat and a self-interest threat, and for a public interest entity the Code stops evaluating and prescribes: an individual may not act as a key audit partner beyond the consecutive years specified and must then serve a cooling-off period. The rule has teeth precisely because of what it forbids during that period — being a member of the engagement team, providing quality control for the engagement, consulting on technical or industry-specific issues, or otherwise directly influencing the outcome. The firm's proposal is that last thing wearing a different title. And section 139(2) rotates the firm and the individual auditor as a matter of company law; it does not answer the Code's requirement about the individual on the engagement.

options.text: Nothing more than a safeguard — an appropriate reviewer who was not a member of the engagement team should review the work, which addresses the familiarity threat
options.misconception: applies the evaluate-and-address route to a public interest entity, where the Code replaces judgement with a fixed rotation and cooling-off requirement
options.why: Reviewing the work is one of the ways a firm addresses the familiarity threat where the Code leaves the matter to evaluation. For a public interest entity it does not, because the rotation and the cooling-off period are stated requirements rather than options.

options.text: He may stay on as technical consultant, since the prohibition is on signing the report and he would no longer sign it
options.misconception: reads the requirement as being about the signature rather than about influence over the engagement's outcome
options.why: The cooling-off provisions name consulting with the engagement team on technical or industry-specific issues as one of the things the individual may not do, alongside anything else that directly influences the outcome of the engagement. Handing over the pen while keeping the judgement is the arrangement the rule was written against.

citation.ref: the long association provisions on rotation and cooling-off of key audit partners for a public interest entity, read with section 139(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: The same engagement partner has signed the audit report of a listed company for many more consecutive years than the Code permits for a public interest entity. The firm's position is that section 139(2) rotates the audit firm, that the firm's own term has not expired, and that nothing therefore needs to change. When pressed, the firm offers to move the partner off the signature but keep him as the technical consultant to the team on the same audit, since he knows the client best.

items.stem: What does the Code require the firm to do?

options.text: Nothing on the fees — outstanding fees and the size of a client are commercial facts, and independence is about interests and relationships rather than about money owed
options.misconception: keeps fee matters outside independence, when the Code treats fee dependency and overdue fees as sources of threats in their own right
options.why: Money owed is exactly a relationship. Fees still outstanding when the report is issued create a self-interest threat, and the firm is required to consider whether the overdue fees are equivalent to a loan to the client, which is as much an independence question as a shareholding would be.

options.text: Treat all three facts as threats — a self-interest threat from the dependency, a self-interest threat from fees that may be equivalent to a loan, and an intimidation threat from the hint about the panel — disclose the fee position to those charged with governance and discuss the action to be taken, and put the work through a reviewer who is not a member of the engagement team
options.why: The Code deals with each of these separately and here they arrive together. A large proportion of the firm's total fees from one client creates a self-interest threat and an intimidation threat. Fees unpaid before the current year's report is issued create a self-interest threat, and the firm must determine whether the overdue fees are equivalent to a loan to the client. A remark about reviewing the panel while an accounting question is open is pressure. For a public interest entity above the specified proportion for two consecutive years the firm must disclose that fact to those charged with governance and discuss which action it will take, and having an appropriate reviewer who is not a member of the engagement team review the work is one of the actions the Code names.

options.text: Resign immediately, because a self-interest threat of this size admits of no safeguard, exactly as with a management responsibility
options.misconception: borrows the outright prohibition that applies to assuming a management responsibility and applies it to fee threats, which the Code asks the firm to evaluate and address
options.why: The Code does prohibit some things outright, but fee dependency is not among them. Here it asks for evaluation and for named actions — reducing the dependency, an appropriate reviewer who is not a member of the engagement team, an independent quality review, disclosure to those charged with governance — with withdrawal as the answer only if the threat cannot be brought to an acceptable level.

options.text: Disclose the fee dependency in the audit report, so that readers of the financial statements can weigh the opinion for themselves
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure to the public for the evaluation and action the Code requires, and disclosure to the wrong audience at that
options.why: The disclosure the Code calls for goes to those charged with governance, not to the readers of the report, and it is a step in addressing the threat rather than a way of living with it. Telling the public that the auditor depends on the client does not make the auditor independent.

citation.ref: the fees provisions on fee dependency, on disclosure to those charged with governance for a public interest entity, and on overdue fees

items.scenario: A firm's largest client, a listed company, has for two consecutive years produced a share of the firm's total fees well above the proportion at which the Code requires the matter to be taken up. Last year's audit fee is still unpaid on the date the current year's audit report is due. In a meeting about a disputed inventory write-down, the finance director observes that the board is "reviewing the audit panel" this year.

items.stem: How does the Code treat each?

options.text: All three may be accepted provided they are disclosed to those charged with governance and recorded in a gifts register
options.misconception: treats recording and disclosure as a safeguard for an inducement the Code bars outright
options.why: A register tells people what happened; it does not change what may be accepted. An inducement offered with intent to improperly influence behaviour is prohibited outright, and hospitality that is not trivial and inconsequential is not made acceptable by being written down.

options.text: Value alone settles all three — the diary and the tickets are small and may be accepted, the resort stay is large and may not
options.misconception: applies the trivial-value test to an inducement offered with intent to improperly influence, where value has stopped being the question
options.why: Value decides the ordinary case. It stops deciding once there is intent to improperly influence behaviour, because the Code prohibits such an inducement outright and does not ask what it cost. Cheap tickets attached to a request about the write-down are worse than an expensive gift sent to everybody.

options.text: None may be accepted, because a member of an audit team may take nothing at all from an audit client
options.misconception: hardens the rule into an absolute prohibition, dropping the exception for a gift whose value is trivial and inconsequential
options.why: The rule has an exception written into it — gifts and hospitality from an audit client may be accepted where the value is trivial and inconsequential. A Diwali diary sent to every supplier is the example that exception exists for.

options.text: The diary may be accepted as trivial and inconsequential; the resort stay is not trivial, so the framework applies and it should be declined; the tickets are prohibited outright, whatever their value, because of the intent behind them
options.why: A firm or an audit team member shall not accept gifts and hospitality from an audit client unless the value is trivial and inconsequential, which a branded diary sent to everyone is. A week at the group's resort for the family, timed just before the audit, is not trivial, and applying the conceptual framework to its value, timing and cumulative effect points to declining it. The tickets come with a note tying them to an open accounting question, so they are offered with intent to improperly influence the behaviour of the recipient, and that is prohibited outright whatever the value.

citation.ref: the inducements provisions, and the rule that gifts and hospitality from an audit client may be accepted only where the value is trivial and inconsequential

items.scenario: The managing director of an audit client sends the engagement partner three things in one quarter. A branded diary and pen at Diwali, of the kind sent to every supplier. A week's stay for the partner's family at the group's resort, arriving a fortnight before the year-end audit begins. And two tickets to a cricket final, with a note saying he hopes the inventory write-down "can be looked at again".

items.stem: How is B's valuation engagement to be treated?

options.text: B is independent of A, because separate partners, separate profits and separate deeds mean two separate practices, so the valuation raises nothing for A
options.misconception: tests for a network by legal structure and profit sharing, when a common brand name or shared professional resources is enough on its own
options.why: Each limb of the definition stands alone. A structure that uses a common brand name is a network even where the profits never mix, because the public and the client see one practice. Separate deeds are not the answer to a question the definition never asked.

options.text: B is not a network firm, because a network requires common ownership, control or management, and there is none here
options.misconception: reads one limb of the definition as the whole test, so a brand-sharing structure escapes
options.why: Common ownership, control or management is one route into the definition and there are others — profit or cost sharing, common quality control policies and procedures, a common business strategy, a common brand name, or a significant part of professional resources shared. Any one of them makes a network.

options.text: B is a network firm merely because the two firms refer work to one another, and that alone would have settled it even without the brand and the shared specialists
options.misconception: widens the definition to catch co-operation that has no profit sharing, common control, brand or shared resources behind it
options.why: Referring work to one another, sharing an immaterial cost, or joining for a single engagement does not by itself create a network. What settles this case is the common brand name and the shared pool of specialists, not the referrals.

options.text: B is a network firm, so the independence requirements that apply to A's audit client apply to B as well, and the valuation is treated as though A had performed it — a self-review threat, and a service caught by section 144 besides
options.why: A network is a larger structure aimed at co-operation that, among other things, uses a common brand name or shares a significant part of professional resources. B does both, which makes it a network firm whatever the partnership deeds say. The consequence is the point of the definition: the independence requirements for an audit client of the firm apply to the network firm too, so B valuing the intangible that A audits creates a self-review threat in A's audit, and a valuation service for the audited company is separately caught by section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013.

citation.ref: the definition of a network and a network firm, read with section 144 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: Firm A audits a listed company. Firm B practises in another city under the same brand name, shares A's website and letterhead design, and draws on a common pool of specialists that both firms fund. B has its own partners, its own profits and its own client list, and the two partnership deeds are entirely separate. The audit client has retained B to value the very intangible asset that A audits.

items.stem: How does section 141(3)(g) actually work here?

options.text: P may take the listed company, since his employment is with a bank that has nothing to do with this client and the disqualification is about conflicts of interest
options.misconception: reads full-time employment elsewhere as a conflict-of-interest test tied to the particular client, when the section disqualifies on the employment itself
options.why: The disqualification for a person who is in full-time employment elsewhere is absolute and says nothing about who the employer is. It exists because a full-time job leaves no time for the responsibility, not because the employer might be connected to the audit client.

options.text: All three offers count towards the ceiling; the exclusions apply only to the appointment of a first auditor and not to the running count
options.misconception: forgets that the section's own proviso takes certain classes of company out of the count entirely
options.why: The exclusions sit in the section itself and apply to the count generally. One person companies, dormant companies, small companies and private companies below the prescribed paid-up share capital are outside it, which is what makes the ceiling workable for firms serving many small clients.

options.text: The dormant company and the small-capital private company do not enter the count at all; the listed company does, and it may be taken only in the name of a partner who is himself within the limit — so neither P nor Q may hold it
options.why: Section 141(3)(g) disqualifies a person in full-time employment elsewhere, and a person or a partner of a firm already holding appointment as auditor of more than the specified number of companies. The count leaves out one person companies, dormant companies, small companies and private companies having paid-up share capital below the prescribed amount, so two of the three offers never touch it. The ceiling attaches to each partner individually rather than to the firm, so P is out because he is in full-time employment elsewhere and Q is out because he has reached the limit, while R or S may hold the listed company.

options.text: The managing partner is right — the limit applies to the firm as a whole, so four partners give the firm four times the headroom and any of them may sign any of the three
options.misconception: treats the ceiling as belonging to the firm, when the section applies it to the person or partner holding the appointment
options.why: The words are a person or a partner of a firm holding appointment as its auditor, so the test runs partner by partner. A firm cannot create headroom by rotating whose name goes on the report, and a partner in more than one firm adds all his appointments together.

citation.ref: Section 141(3)(g) with its proviso, read with section 139(1)

items.scenario: A firm has four partners. Partner P is in full-time employment with a bank. Partner Q already holds appointments equal to the specified number of companies. Partners R and S hold far fewer. The firm is offered three audits at once — a dormant company, a private company whose paid-up share capital is below the amount the section prescribes, and a listed company. The managing partner says the ceiling belongs to the firm, so with four partners there is plenty of room and any partner may sign.

items.stem: Which of the three are problems, and what is the answer to each?

options.text: All three, and the only possible answer to each is that the firm must resign the audit
options.misconception: reaches for withdrawal where the Code provides a targeted answer for two of the three situations
options.why: Resignation is the last answer, not the first. The tax partner declines to become a director or officer of the audit client, the retired partner's arrangement is unwound so that no significant connection remains, and the manager leaves the engagement team with his work reviewed. The audit survives all three.

options.text: Only the tax partner's directorship — the manager has not joined yet, and a retired partner is outside the firm and no longer its concern
options.misconception: dates the threat from the day the person changes employer, when the threat begins with the offer and continues while a material connection with the firm remains
options.why: A manager who has accepted the client's offer is auditing his future employer, which is why he must leave the engagement team at once. And a retired partner is not outside the firm while payments material to the firm still run to him — the Code asks whether any significant connection remains, not whether his name is on the door.

options.text: Only the manager's move, because Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule saves a directorship simpliciter, so both the retired and the serving partner may take board seats
options.misconception: stops reading Clause 11's proviso before its exception, which withdraws the saving where the member or a partner is interested in the company as its auditor
options.why: Clause 11's proviso protects an ordinary board seat only so far — it withdraws the protection where the member or any of his partners is interested in the company as an auditor, which is precisely this company. And the Code adds its own bar on a partner serving as a director or officer of an audit client.
keywords: director or officer of an audit client

options.text: All three — the tax partner may not serve as a director or officer of an audit client at all; the retired partner's material continuing share is a significant connection with the firm; and the manager must come off the team at once, with his work reviewed
options.why: A partner or employee of the firm shall not serve as a director or officer of an audit client, so the tax partner's offer fails outright. A former partner joining the client's board creates a familiarity threat, or an intimidation threat, at an unacceptable level unless he has no significant connection remaining with the firm, and a continuing profit share that is material to the firm is exactly such a connection. The manager who has accepted a position with the client can no longer be objective about the numbers he is auditing, so the answer is to remove him from the engagement team immediately and have an appropriate reviewer review the work he has already done.
keywords: director or officer of an audit client

citation.ref: the provisions on serving as a director or officer of an audit client, on recent service with an audit client and on employment with an audit client, read with Clause 11 of Part I of the First Schedule to the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949

items.scenario: Three movements happen around one audit. The audit manager on the current engagement accepts the client's offer to become its chief financial officer next month, and wants to finish the audit first. A partner who retired from the firm last year, and who still receives a continuing share of the firm's profits that is material to the firm, joins the client's board. And the firm's tax partner is offered, and would like to accept, a directorship in the same audit client.

items.stem: Where do you stand under Clause 8?

options.text: Not guilty — he communicated, and the outgoing auditor raised no objection
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring communication in any form
options.why: Form is the substance here. A telephone call leaves nothing to show what was asked or answered, which is why the clause specifies writing.

options.text: Guilty, because the fee dispute meant he needed the outgoing auditor's consent
options.misconception: converts communication into permission
options.why: No consent is ever required — an outgoing auditor cannot veto a successor. Unpaid fees are a fact to weigh, not a bar. The failure is only the missing writing.

options.text: Guilty — the communication must be in writing, and a phone call is not that
options.why: The clause's words are "without first communicating with him in writing". The conversation happened and even produced no objection, but the safeguard the clause builds — a record that the incoming auditor asked and what he was told — exists only on paper. Oral communication, however cordial, is the misconduct.

options.text: Not guilty if he now sends a letter confirming the earlier call
options.misconception: backdates a safeguard that must come before acceptance
options.why: The clause says "first" — the writing must precede acceptance. A confirming letter after the appointment records the breach; it does not repair it.

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 8

items.scenario: A company removes its auditor and approaches you. You telephone the outgoing auditor, who says he has no objection but warns you the client disputes his fees. You accept the audit the next day, and a month later the outgoing auditor complains to the Institute that you never wrote to him.

items.stem: What may you tell the competitor client, and what must you give the tax officer?

options.text: Tell the competitor only what it could eventually learn from public filings
options.misconception: discloses early and calls it harmless
options.why: A pending negotiation is not public, and its value lies in the timing. What might become public later is still confidential now, and now is when you would be telling it.

options.text: Both — a firm owes each client the benefit of everything the firm knows
options.misconception: treats the firm's knowledge as a pooled asset of its clients
options.why: The information belongs to the engagement it came from. Pooling it is the precise disclosure the clause forbids, and would end professional confidence between auditor and client.

options.text: Nothing to the competitor; the summoned papers to the officer — legal compulsion is the exception, another client's interest is not
options.why: Clause 1 permits disclosure only with the client's consent or where law requires it. A statutory summons is the law requiring it. The competitor's commercial appetite is nothing at all — serving two clients does not merge their entitlement to what you learned from each.

options.text: Neither — auditor confidentiality is absolute, like privilege, and beats the summons
options.misconception: promotes a professional duty into a legal privilege
options.why: The clause itself carves out disclosure required by law. Defying a valid summons is not loyalty; it is contempt with a confidentiality label.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 1

items.scenario: During an audit you discover your client is negotiating to buy a supplier. Another client of your firm competes with that supplier and would dearly want to know. Separately, an income-tax summons under section 131 requires you to produce the client's working papers.

items.stem: Does the disclosure save the engagement?

options.text: No — the clause bars the opinion itself where the firm or any partner has substantial interest, and disclosure is no cure
options.why: Clause 4 reaches "he, his firm, or a partner in his firm". One partner's 30 per cent poisons every signature the firm can produce, and the clause prohibits expressing the opinion — a prominent confession of the conflict still expresses it. Independence questions of this kind are answered by declining.

options.text: No, but the firm may accept if the partner undertakes to sell the shares within the year
options.misconception: audits first, becomes independent later
options.why: Independence is tested when the opinion is given. A promise to divest afterwards means the opinion was expressed while the interest stood — which is the whole offence.

options.text: Yes, provided the interested partner takes no part in the audit work
options.misconception: builds an information wall the clause does not recognise
options.why: The prohibition follows the interest, not the staffing chart. The firm profits from the fee and the partner from the company; no allocation of files changes either.

options.text: Yes — transparency lets the reader discount the opinion appropriately
options.misconception: substitutes disclosure for independence
options.why: Disclosure manages many things; this clause is not one of them. An opinion from an interested firm is worthless even when labelled, because the reader cannot un-know the auditor wanted a particular answer.

citation.ref: Second Schedule Part I, Clause 4

items.scenario: A two-partner firm is offered the audit of a private company in which one partner holds 30 per cent of the shares. The other partner proposes to sign the report personally, disclosing the shareholding prominently in the audit report so readers can weigh it.

items.stem: Is he guilty under Clause 7?

options.text: Yes — certifying without examination is gross negligence, and honesty is no defence to it
options.why: Clause 7 punishes the absence of due diligence, not the presence of dishonesty. A certificate tells the world the certifier verified; signing on the manager's say-so means he verified nothing. Good faith and a small fee measure his intentions, not his diligence.

options.text: No — reliance on management representations is an accepted audit technique
options.misconception: stretches a corroborating tool into a substitute for evidence
options.why: Representations support evidence; they never replace it. Where a certificate rests on nothing but the interested party's own statement, the technique has become the abdication.

options.text: No — without fraudulent intent there can be no professional misconduct
options.misconception: imports a mens rea requirement the clause deliberately omits
options.why: The Second Schedule separates dishonesty offences from negligence offences precisely so that careless certification is punishable on its own. Clause 7 is the negligence limb.
