options.why: Para B63 opens with the words notwithstanding the requirements in paragraphs 56 to 59, which are the variable consideration and constraint paragraphs, and then says a sales-based or usage-based royalty promised in exchange for a licence of intellectual property is recognised only when the later of the subsequent sale or usage occurring and the satisfaction of the performance obligation happens. No estimate is made at inception.

options.text: Both are rights to use recognised in full on 1 October 2025, because the licences were granted and the customers could start using them that day
options.misconception: ignores the entity's continuing activities on the brand, which B58 and B59A make decisive
options.why: Para B59A says an entity's activities significantly affect the intellectual property where the customer's ability to obtain benefit is substantially derived from or dependent upon them, and it names a brand as the example. The clothing maker is exposed to the group's marketing and sponsorship, so the three criteria in para B58 are met and para B60 spreads the brand revenue over the five years.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, B59A, B60, B61 and B63

items.scenario: A media group signs two contracts on 1 October 2025, each licence being a separate performance obligation. Under the first it licenses its sports brand to a clothing maker for five years; the group runs a continuous marketing and sponsorship programme that the licensee expects and on which the value of the brand plainly depends, and the licensee is exposed to how well that programme goes. Under the second it licenses a completed feature film to a streaming service for three years; the film is finished and the group will do nothing further to it. The film licence carries a royalty of two per cent of the streaming service's subscription revenue.

items.stem: How does the company account for the ₹105 lakh?

options.text: Treat both warranties as performance obligations and allocate the ₹105 lakh across three of them, giving the one-year warranty its own slice of revenue
options.misconception: makes an assurance-type warranty a performance obligation, when B30 sends it to Ind AS 37
options.why: Para B30 is the test the one-year warranty fails: if a customer does not have the option to purchase a warranty separately, the entity accounts for it under Ind AS 37 unless the warranty, or part of it, provides a service in addition to the assurance that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications. This one promises performance to specification and nothing more, so it is a cost provision and not revenue deferred.

options.text: Allocate ₹100 lakh to the machine at its stand-alone selling price and the residual ₹5 lakh to the extended warranty
options.misconception: uses a residual approach where an observable stand-alone selling price exists, and so drops the ₹7 lakh discount entirely onto one obligation
options.why: Para 76 allocates the transaction price in proportion to the stand-alone selling prices of all the performance obligations, and para 81 requires a discount to be allocated proportionately to all of them unless the para 82 criteria for allocating it to only some are met. The extended warranty has an observable stand-alone selling price of ₹12 lakh, so the residual approach in para 79(c) is not available and the ₹7 lakh discount is shared.

options.text: Allocate ₹93.75 lakh to the machine, recognised on delivery, and ₹11.25 lakh to the extended warranty, recognised across the three years, with the one-year warranty provided for under Ind AS 37
options.why: Para B29 says that if a customer has the option to purchase a warranty separately, the warranty is a distinct service and is accounted for as a performance obligation, which the extended warranty is. Para B30 sends a warranty the customer cannot buy separately, and which only assures that the product complies with agreed-upon specifications, to Ind AS 37 as a provision. Para 74 and para 76 then allocate the transaction price on a relative stand-alone selling price basis and para 81 spreads the discount proportionately, so ₹105 lakh times ₹100 lakh over ₹112 lakh is ₹93.75 lakh and ₹105 lakh times ₹12 lakh over ₹112 lakh is ₹11.25 lakh.
keywords: option to purchase a warranty separately

options.text: Recognise the whole ₹105 lakh on delivery of the machine and provide for both warranties under Ind AS 37, since a warranty is a cost of selling a machine rather than a thing sold
options.misconception: sends a separately purchasable warranty to Ind AS 37, which B29 makes a distinct service
options.why: Para B29 is explicit that where the warranty is priced or negotiated separately the entity promises a service in addition to the product, so the warranty is a distinct service and a performance obligation with a share of the transaction price allocated to it. Booking the whole ₹105 lakh on delivery would recognise three years of servicing revenue on day one.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B29 and B30, with para 74, 76 and 81

items.scenario: A machine tool maker sells a machine with a one-year warranty that it will perform to the agreed specifications. That warranty is not priced separately and no customer can decline it. The company also sells a three-year extended warranty covering wear and consumables, which any customer may buy on its own for ₹12 lakh. A customer buys one machine and the extended warranty together for ₹105 lakh. The stand-alone selling price of the machine is ₹100 lakh and of the extended warranty ₹12 lakh. The machine is delivered on 1 April 2025.

items.stem: How does the company, as intermediate lessor, classify and account for the two subleases?

options.text: The office sublease is a finance lease, tested against the right-of-use asset from the head lease rather than the building, so the right-of-use asset is derecognised and a net investment recognised, discounted at the head lease rate adjusted for initial direct costs; the warehouse sublease is an operating lease
options.why: Para B58(b) classifies a sublease by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, rather than by reference to the underlying asset, and eighteen of the nineteen remaining years is substantially all of that right-of-use asset. Para B58(a) makes a sublease an operating lease where the head lease is a short-term lease the entity has accounted for applying para 6, which is the warehouse. Para 68 lets an intermediate lessor that cannot readily determine the interest rate implicit in the sublease use the discount rate used for the head lease, adjusted for any initial direct costs associated with the sublease, to measure the net investment.

options.text: The office sublease is an operating lease, because eighteen years is nowhere near the fifty-year economic life of the building, so the company keeps its right-of-use asset and recognises sublease income on a straight-line basis
options.misconception: classifies the sublease against the underlying asset, which B58(b) expressly refuses
options.why: Para B58(b) says the sublease shall be classified by reference to the right-of-use asset arising from the head lease, rather than by reference to the underlying asset, giving the item of property, plant or equipment that is the subject of the lease as the example of what not to use. What the intermediate lessor holds is nineteen years of use, not the building, and it has passed on eighteen of them.

options.text: Both subleases are finance leases, since in each case the sublease covers most of what remains of the head lease
options.misconception: applies the general B58(b) test to a sublease of a short-term head lease, which B58(a) settles first
options.why: Para B58(a) comes first and admits no comparison: if the head lease is a short-term lease that the entity, as a lessee, has accounted for applying paragraph 6, the sublease shall be classified as an operating lease. Having taken the recognition exemption the company has no right-of-use asset on the warehouse to measure the sublease against.

options.text: The office sublease is a finance lease but the company keeps the head lease right-of-use asset on its balance sheet alongside the net investment, since it remains liable to the head lessor
options.misconception: confuses the continuing head lease liability with the right-of-use asset, which is what the sublease transfers
options.why: The head lease liability does stay, because the sublease does not release the intermediate lessor from anything owed to the head lessor. What goes is the asset: on a finance sublease the intermediate lessor has passed substantially all the risks and rewards of the right-of-use asset to the sublessee and recognises a net investment in the sublease in its place. Holding both would count the same right of use twice.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B58, with para 68

items.scenario: A company holds two head leases as lessee. The first is a twenty-year lease of an office building whose economic life is fifty years; nineteen years of the head lease term remain and the company subleases the whole building to a third party for eighteen of those nineteen years. The second is a nine-month lease of a warehouse, on which the company took the short-term lease recognition exemption; it subleases the warehouse for six months. The rate implicit in the office sublease cannot be readily determined.

items.stem: What additional current tax liability does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹10.5 crore, using the expected value of the deduction of ₹58 crore
options.why: Para 9 asks whether it is probable the taxation authority will accept the treatment and para 11 governs where it is not. Para 11(b) uses the expected value, being the sum of the probability-weighted amounts in a range of possible outcomes, where the outcomes are neither binary nor concentrated on one value, which describes a 25, 45 and 30 per cent spread. One hundred at a quarter, sixty at forty-five per cent and twenty at thirty per cent is ₹58 crore, so ₹42 crore is disallowed and the tax on it at 25 per cent is ₹10.5 crore.

options.text: ₹10 crore, using the most likely amount of the deduction of ₹60 crore
options.misconception: uses the most likely amount where the range of outcomes calls for the expected value under para 11(b)
options.why: Para 11(a) offers the most likely amount, the single most likely amount in a range of possible outcomes, and says it may better predict the resolution of the uncertainty if the possible outcomes are binary or are concentrated on one value. Three outcomes spread at 25, 45 and 30 per cent are neither, so para 11(b)'s expected value is the method that better predicts the resolution, and it gives ₹58 crore rather than ₹60 crore.

options.text: ₹25 crore, disallowing the whole ₹100 crore claim because acceptance is not probable
options.misconception: reads a failure of the probable test as a total disallowance, when para 11 measures the effect of the uncertainty rather than assuming the worst
options.why: Para 11 says that where acceptance is not probable the entity shall reflect the effect of uncertainty by using either the most likely amount or the expected value. Neither method produces a full disallowance on these facts, since a 25 per cent chance of full allowance and a 45 per cent chance of ₹60 crore both carry weight. Para 11 is a measurement rule, not a switch between all and nothing.

options.text: Nothing, because no notice has been issued and the company thinks the claim will not be picked up for scrutiny
options.misconception: builds the chance of not being detected into the measurement, which para 8 forbids
options.why: Para 8 requires the entity to assume that a taxation authority will examine amounts it has a right to examine and have full knowledge of all related information when making those examinations. Detection risk is deliberately assumed away, so the odds of the claim going unnoticed cannot reduce the liability, and the absence of a notice is not a reason to recognise nothing.

citation.ref: Appendix C, para 8, 9 and 11

items.scenario: A company claimed a deduction of ₹100 crore in its return for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its tax counsel advises that it is not probable the assessing officer will accept the claim in full. The possible outcomes are a full allowance of ₹100 crore with a 25 per cent probability, an allowance of ₹60 crore with a 45 per cent probability, and an allowance of ₹20 crore with a 30 per cent probability. The applicable tax rate is 25 per cent. No notice has yet been issued and the company believes the claim is unlikely to be picked up for scrutiny.

items.stem: What can the undertaking leave out and what must it still give?

options.text: It may leave out everything about related parties, key management personnel compensation included, because the whole of Ind AS 24 gives way to the government-related exemption
options.misconception: reads para 25 as a blanket exemption from the Standard rather than from paragraph 18 alone
options.why: Para 25 exempts the entity from the disclosure requirements of paragraph 18 and names no other paragraph. Key management personnel compensation sits in paragraph 17 and the parent and ultimate controlling party disclosure sits in paragraph 13; neither is touched, and para 26 adds requirements rather than removing them.

options.text: It must give the full paragraph 18 detail for every transaction with every other government-controlled entity, since the exemption covers only transactions with the government itself
options.misconception: reads para 25 as reaching only the government, when para 25(b) covers fellow entities under the same government
options.why: Para 25(b) extends the exemption to another entity that is a related party because the same government has control or joint control of, or significant influence over, both the reporting entity and the other entity. That limb exists precisely because a state-owned entity would otherwise have to catalogue its dealings with every other state-owned entity in the country.

options.text: It may use the exemption and give nothing in its place, the relief in para 25 being unconditional
options.misconception: takes the exemption without the substitute disclosures para 26 makes the price of it
options.why: Para 26 opens with the words if a reporting entity applies the exemption in paragraph 25, it shall disclose the following, and then lists the name of the government, the nature of the relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction and an indication of the extent of the others. Para 27 adds that the level of detail turns on the closeness of the relationship, the size of the transaction and whether it was carried out on non-market terms.

options.text: It may leave out the paragraph 18 detail for the power and coal transactions, but must name the government and the nature of its relationship, give the nature and amount of the ₹4,000 crore power purchase as an individually significant transaction and an indication of the extent of the ₹150 crore of coal purchases, and must still disclose the ₹9 crore of key management personnel compensation and the relationship with its subsidiary
options.why: Para 25 exempts a reporting entity from the disclosure requirements of paragraph 18 in relation to transactions and outstanding balances with a government that has control, joint control or significant influence over it and with another entity that is a related party because the same government controls, jointly controls or significantly influences both. Para 26 replaces those with the name of the government and the nature of its relationship, the nature and amount of each individually significant transaction, and for the rest a qualitative or quantitative indication of their extent. The exemption reaches paragraph 18 and nothing else, so key management personnel compensation and the parent and subsidiary relationships stand.

citation.ref: para 25, 26 and 27

items.scenario: A central public sector undertaking is controlled by the Government of India. During the year ended 31 March 2026 it bought power worth ₹4,000 crore from another central public sector undertaking under the same government, bought coal worth ₹150 crore in aggregate from four others, paid its key management personnel ₹9 crore, and has a wholly owned subsidiary of its own. It wishes to use the relief Ind AS 24 offers to government-related entities.

items.stem: How is the ₹1,000 lakh split on initial recognition?

options.text: A financial liability of ₹711.80 lakh, being the present value of the redemption amount, and an equity component of ₹288.20 lakh
options.misconception: leaves the present value of the coupon stream out of the liability component
options.why: The liability component is the fair value of a similar liability without the conversion option, and a similar liability pays interest as well as principal. Para 32 measures it as the whole of that instrument's cash flows discounted at the market rate, so the ₹192.14 lakh present value of the ₹80 lakh coupons belongs in the liability. Dropping it overstates the equity component threefold.
keywords: fair value of a similar liability

options.text: A financial liability of ₹1,000 lakh and no equity component, since the company is obliged to redeem at par if the holders do not convert
options.misconception: classifies the whole convertible as a liability, missing the conversion option that para 29 identifies as equity
options.why: Para 28 requires the issuer of a non-derivative financial instrument to evaluate its terms to determine whether it contains both a liability and an equity component and to classify them separately. Para 29 gives a bond convertible by the holder into a fixed number of ordinary shares as the example of a compound financial instrument, the option to convert being an equity instrument because it will be settled in a fixed number of the entity's own shares. The redemption obligation is the liability component, not the whole.

options.text: An equity component of ₹150 lakh valued directly by an option pricing model and a financial liability of ₹850 lakh taken as the balance
options.misconception: measures the equity component first and leaves the liability as the residual, reversing the order para 31 fixes
options.why: Para 31 puts the residual on the equity side and only there: the equity component is assigned the residual amount after deducting from the fair value of the instrument as a whole the amount separately determined for the liability component. Valuing the option first would make the liability depend on an option model rather than on the fair value of a similar liability, and para 32 says the liability is determined first.

options.text: A financial liability of ₹903.94 lakh and an equity component of ₹96.06 lakh
options.why: Para 32 says the issuer of a bond convertible into ordinary shares first determines the carrying amount of the liability component by measuring the fair value of a similar liability that does not have an associated equity component. Eighty lakh of annual interest times the 2.4018 annuity factor is ₹192.14 lakh and ₹1,000 lakh times 0.7118 is ₹711.80 lakh, giving a liability of ₹903.94 lakh. Para 31 then assigns the equity component the residual amount after deducting the liability from the fair value of the instrument as a whole, which is ₹96.06 lakh, and records that no gain or loss arises from initially recognising the components separately.
keywords: fair value of a similar liability

citation.ref: para 28, 29, 31 and 32

items.scenario: On 1 April 2025 a company issues debentures with a face value of ₹1,000 lakh at par. They carry interest of 8 per cent payable annually in arrears and are redeemable at par in three years. Each debenture may be converted at the holder's option, at maturity, into a fixed number of the company's own equity shares. The market rate of interest for a similar debenture without a conversion option is 12 per cent. The three-year annuity factor at 12 per cent is 2.4018 and the present value factor for the third year at 12 per cent is 0.7118.

items.stem: What does the company disclose for liquidity and market risk?

options.text: A maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities at ₹2,340 crore of contractual undiscounted cash flows, the ₹300 crore of guarantees entering at their maximum amount in the earliest time band, a separate analysis for derivative financial liabilities, a description of how liquidity risk is managed, and a sensitivity analysis showing the effect on profit or loss and equity of changes reasonably possible at 31 March 2026, with a statement that the year-end exposure is unrepresentative
options.why: Para 39(a) and (b) require maturity analyses for non-derivative and for derivative financial liabilities showing the remaining contractual maturities, and para B11D says the contractual amounts disclosed are the contractual undiscounted cash flows, which differ from the balance sheet figure because that is based on discounted cash flows. Para B11C(c) allocates the maximum amount of an issued financial guarantee contract to the earliest period in which the guarantee could be called. Para 39(c) adds the description of how liquidity risk is managed, para 40 requires the sensitivity analysis for each type of market risk against changes reasonably possible at the reporting date, and para 42 requires the entity to say so where the year-end exposure makes that analysis unrepresentative.

options.text: The same maturity analysis but leaving out the ₹300 crore of financial guarantees, none of which the company expects to be called
options.misconception: applies an expected-outflow filter to issued financial guarantee contracts, which B11C(c) does not permit
options.why: Para 39(a) names issued financial guarantee contracts inside the maturity analysis of non-derivative financial liabilities, and para B11C(c) says that for issued financial guarantee contracts the maximum amount of the guarantee is allocated to the earliest period in which the guarantee could be called. Expectation is not the test; the worst-case timing and amount are, because that is what liquidity risk means.

options.text: A maturity analysis built on the ₹2,000 crore carrying amount of the borrowings, since that is the figure the balance sheet and the rest of the note are reconciled to
options.misconception: uses balance sheet carrying amounts in the maturity analysis where B11D requires contractual undiscounted cash flows
options.why: Para B11D says the contractual amounts disclosed in the maturity analyses required by paragraph 39(a) and (b) are the contractual undiscounted cash flows, and it adds that such undiscounted cash flows differ from the amount included in the balance sheet because the amount in the balance sheet is based on discounted cash flows. A liquidity table is about what has to be paid and when, so the ₹340 crore of future interest cannot be left out.

options.text: A sensitivity analysis run on the largest floating-rate exposure the company carried at any point in the year, since the year-end figure understates the risk
options.misconception: substitutes a peak exposure for the reporting date exposure, when para 40 fixes the date and para 42 handles the distortion by disclosure
options.why: Para 40(a) requires a sensitivity analysis for each type of market risk to which the entity is exposed at the end of the reporting period, showing how profit or loss and equity would have been affected by changes in the relevant risk variable that were reasonably possible at that date. Where the year-end exposure does not reflect the exposure during the year, para 42 requires the entity to disclose that fact and the reason, rather than to change the base of the analysis.

citation.ref: para 39, 40 and 42, with Appendix B, para B11C and B11D

items.scenario: A non-banking finance company is preparing its financial instruments note for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its borrowings of ₹2,000 crore carrying amount will require ₹2,340 crore of contractual payments including future interest. It has issued financial guarantees of ₹300 crore for a group company, none of which it expects to be called, callable on demand. It has floating-rate borrowings whose exposure at 31 March 2026 was smaller than at any point during the year.

items.stem: What may the parent do in its separate financial statements?

options.text: It cannot equity account anything; it must carry all three subsidiaries either at cost or under Ind AS 109, applying one of those consistently to that category, and it recognises the whole ₹20 crore dividend in profit or loss when its right to receive it was established
options.why: Para 10 gives two routes when an entity prepares separate financial statements — at cost, or in accordance with Ind AS 109 — and requires the entity to apply the same accounting for each category of investments. The Comparison with IAS 27, item 2, records that IAS 27's option to use the equity method in separate financial statements is not given in Ind AS 27, as the equity method is not a measurement basis like cost and fair value but is a manner of consolidation. Para 12 recognises a dividend from a subsidiary in profit or loss when the right to receive the dividend is established, drawing no line at pre-acquisition profits.

options.text: It may pick freely between cost and Ind AS 109 for each individual investment, so long as it says which it has used for which
options.misconception: reads the choice as available investment by investment, when para 10 fixes it for each category
options.why: Para 10 ends with the sentence that the entity shall apply the same accounting for each category of investments. Subsidiaries are one category, associates another and joint ventures a third, so the parent may treat the three categories differently but cannot carry one subsidiary at cost and another under Ind AS 109. Disclosure does not cure an inconsistency the Standard forbids.

options.text: It recognises ₹8 crore of the dividend in profit or loss and credits the ₹12 crore declared out of pre-acquisition profits against the carrying amount of the investment
options.misconception: applies the pre-acquisition and post-acquisition dividend split of the old standard, which Ind AS 27 para 12 does not carry
options.why: Para 12 says an entity shall recognise a dividend from a subsidiary, a joint venture or an associate in profit or loss in its separate financial statements when its right to receive the dividend is established, and it makes no exception for pre-acquisition profits. What a large dividend out of pre-acquisition reserves does trigger is an impairment indicator on the investment under Ind AS 36, which is a separate test with a separate answer.

options.text: It may equity account the subsidiaries, since the equity method is one of three options for separate financial statements
options.misconception: carries the IAS 27 equity method option into Ind AS 27, where it was deliberately not adopted
options.why: IAS 27 has three options and Ind AS 27 has two. Para 10 lists at cost and in accordance with Ind AS 109, and stops. The Comparison with IAS 27 explains the departure: the equity method is a manner of consolidation rather than a measurement basis, so allowing it in separate financial statements would produce something that is neither one set of statements nor the other.

citation.ref: para 10 and 12, with the Comparison with IAS 27, item 2

items.scenario: A listed parent prepares consolidated financial statements and, as the Companies Act requires, separate financial statements as well. In the separate financial statements it wants to equity account its three subsidiaries, carry its two associates at cost and measure its one joint venture at fair value through profit or loss. One subsidiary paid it a dividend of ₹20 crore during the year ended 31 March 2026, of which ₹12 crore was declared out of profits the subsidiary had earned before the parent bought it.

items.stem: How does the subsidiary's position enter the consolidated financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: The restatement is made but the gain or loss on the net monetary position is recognised in other comprehensive income alongside the exchange differences on translating the subsidiary
options.misconception: treats the monetary gain as part of the translation reserve, when para 9 puts it in profit or loss
options.why: Para 9 says the gain or loss on the net monetary position shall be included in profit or loss and separately disclosed. It is not an exchange difference and does not arise from translating anything; it is what the subsidiary made or lost by holding money while the price level moved, measured in its own currency before any translation into rupees happens at all.

options.text: The same restatement, but the cash, trade receivables and borrowings are restated by the general price index as well, so that every balance is brought to the same date
options.misconception: restates monetary items, which para 12 excludes because they already sit in the current measuring unit
options.why: Para 12 says monetary items are not restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the end of the reporting period, and defines them as money held and items to be received or paid in money. Restating them would double-count the inflation and would destroy the gain or loss on the net monetary position, which is the whole measurement of what holding money through inflation has cost.

options.text: The subsidiary's financial statements are restated into the measuring unit current at 31 March 2026, comparatives included, before translation; the plant is restated by the general price index while the cash, receivables and borrowings are not; every item of the statement of profit and loss is restated; and the gain or loss on the net monetary position goes to profit or loss and is separately disclosed, the restatement running from 1 April 2025
options.why: Para 8 requires the financial statements of an entity whose functional currency is that of a hyperinflationary economy to be stated in terms of the measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period, with the corresponding figures for the previous period stated the same way. Para 11 restates balance sheet amounts not already in that unit by applying a general price index and para 12 leaves monetary items alone because they are already expressed in the current monetary unit. Para 26 restates all items in the statement of profit and loss, para 9 puts the gain or loss on the net monetary position in profit or loss and requires it to be separately disclosed, and para 4 applies the Standard from the beginning of the reporting period in which the hyperinflation is identified.

options.text: The restatement runs only from December 2025, when the parent concluded that the economy had become hyperinflationary, so the first eight months of the year are carried unrestated
options.misconception: starts the restatement on the date of the conclusion rather than at the beginning of the reporting period
options.why: Para 4 says this Standard applies to the financial statements of any entity from the beginning of the reporting period in which it identifies the existence of hyperinflation in the country in whose currency it reports. Identifying it in December 2025 pulls the whole year from 1 April 2025 into the restatement, and para 8 requires the comparatives to be stated in the same measuring unit current at the end of the reporting period as well.

items.scenario: An Indian parent has a subsidiary in a country whose general price index rose by 18 per cent, 34 per cent and 41 per cent in the three years to 31 March 2026, so that cumulative inflation over the three years is a little above 100 per cent. Wages and prices there are index-linked and the population holds its savings in a foreign currency. The parent concludes in December 2025 that the economy has become hyperinflationary. The subsidiary's balance sheet holds cash and trade receivables in local currency, plant carried at historical cost, and local currency borrowings.

items.stem: How does the company account for the block at 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹415 crore is recognised as an exploration and evaluation asset, the development drilling being spent on the same block under the same policy
options.misconception: brings development expenditure inside the exploration and evaluation asset, which para 10 excludes
options.why: Para 10 says expenditures related to the development of mineral resources shall not be recognised as exploration and evaluation assets, and points to the Framework and to Ind AS 38 for the recognition of assets arising from development. The ₹200 crore was spent after technical feasibility and commercial viability were demonstrable, so it is development expenditure and is dealt with outside this Standard.

options.text: ₹215 crore is recognised as an exploration and evaluation asset at cost, the ₹200 crore of development drilling is not, and on 1 January 2026 the ₹215 crore is tested for impairment before it stops being classified as an exploration and evaluation asset, having been allocated to a unit no larger than the operating segment
options.why: Para 8 measures exploration and evaluation assets at cost and para 9 lets the entity set a policy on which expenditures qualify, weighing how far the expenditure can be associated with finding specific mineral resources, which covers the ₹80 crore of rights, the ₹15 crore of studies and the ₹120 crore of exploratory drilling. Para 10 keeps expenditures related to the development of mineral resources out. Para 17 says an exploration and evaluation asset shall no longer be classified as such when the technical feasibility and commercial viability of extracting a mineral resource are demonstrable, and that such assets shall be assessed for impairment, and any impairment loss recognised, before reclassification. Para 21 caps the unit at an operating segment.

options.text: ₹215 crore is recognised and tested for impairment against the company as a single cash-generating unit, since exploration success in one block funds the others
options.misconception: tests at an entity-wide level, when para 21 caps the unit at an operating segment
options.why: Para 21 lets an entity set its own policy for allocating exploration and evaluation assets to cash-generating units or groups of units, but adds that each unit or group to which such an asset is allocated shall not be larger than an operating segment determined in accordance with Ind AS 108. Testing the whole company as one unit would let a producing field's headroom hide a dry hole.

options.text: ₹215 crore is reclassified out of exploration and evaluation assets on 1 January 2026 and the impairment test is left to the annual review at 31 March 2026, by which time it sits with the developed field
options.misconception: reclassifies before testing, when para 17 fixes the order the other way round
options.why: Para 17 puts the test first in terms: exploration and evaluation assets shall be assessed for impairment, and any impairment loss recognised, before reclassification. The order matters because para 19 and para 20 give exploration and evaluation assets their own impairment triggers in place of paragraphs 8 to 17 of Ind AS 36, and those triggers stop applying the moment the asset is reclassified.

items.scenario: An oil company's accounting policy recognises exploration and evaluation expenditure as an asset to the extent it can be associated with finding specific mineral resources. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it spent ₹80 crore acquiring rights to explore a block, ₹15 crore on topographical and geological studies of it, and ₹120 crore on exploratory drilling there. On 1 January 2026 the technical feasibility and commercial viability of extracting oil from the block became demonstrable, and the company then spent ₹200 crore on development drilling. The block is one of six fields inside a single operating segment.

items.stem: What does the company recognise and do about the ₹4 crore?

options.text: Recognise the ₹4 crore as a liability and transfer all of it to a Fund specified in Schedule VII by 30 September 2026, since six months is the outer limit the section allows
options.misconception: applies the six-month Schedule VII route to money earmarked for an ongoing project, losing the three-year window section 135(6) gives it
options.why: The third proviso to section 135(5) applies only unless the unspent amount relates to any ongoing project referred to in sub-section (6). The ₹3 crore does relate to one, so it goes to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account within thirty days and stays available for the school building for three financial years. Sending it to a Schedule VII Fund would put the money beyond the project it was earmarked for.

options.text: Recognise the ₹4 crore as a liability at 31 March 2026, transfer the ₹3 crore to a separate Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account with a scheduled bank by 30 April 2026 to be spent within three financial years, and transfer the ₹1 crore to a Fund specified in Schedule VII by 30 September 2026
options.why: Section 135(6) requires an amount remaining unspent pursuant to an ongoing project to be transferred within thirty days from the end of the financial year to a special account in a scheduled bank called the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account for that financial year, and to be spent within three financial years of the transfer, failing which it goes to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within thirty days of the completion of the third financial year. The third proviso to section 135(5) sends unspent amounts that do not relate to an ongoing project to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year. Both transfers are statutory obligations at 31 March 2026, so a liability of ₹4 crore is recognised then and not when the cash moves.

options.text: Recognise the ₹4 crore as a liability and transfer the whole of it to the Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account by 30 April 2026, the account being the destination for everything left unspent
options.misconception: sends the non-ongoing shortfall down the ongoing project pipe, when the third proviso to section 135(5) routes it to Schedule VII
options.why: The Unspent Corporate Social Responsibility Account exists for one purpose. Section 135(6) opens with the words any amount remaining unspent under sub-section (5), pursuant to any ongoing project, and the third proviso to section 135(5) covers the rest by requiring transfer to a Fund specified in Schedule VII within six months of the expiry of the financial year. The ₹1 crore is not attached to any project, so it leaves the company altogether rather than waiting three years in a bank account.

options.text: Recognise nothing at 31 March 2026 and simply state the reasons for not spending the ₹4 crore in the Board's report under section 134(3)(o)
options.misconception: applies the position before 22 January 2021, when an explanation in the Board's report was the whole of the consequence
options.why: Explaining the shortfall in the Board's report survives as a requirement, but it is no longer the end of the matter. Section 135(5) and section 135(6) as substituted with effect from 22 January 2021 make the transfer compulsory and back it with a penalty of twice the amount required to be transferred or one crore rupees, whichever is less. A compulsory transfer of a determinable amount arising from a past event is a present obligation, so the ₹4 crore is a liability at the reporting date.

citation.ref: section 135(5), third proviso, and section 135(6), both as substituted with effect from 22 January 2021

items.scenario: A company's corporate social responsibility obligation for the year ended 31 March 2026, being two per cent of the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, is ₹10 crore. It spent ₹6 crore during the year. Of the ₹4 crore not spent, ₹3 crore is earmarked for a school building the Board approved as an ongoing project and ₹1 crore was simply not spent on anything.

items.stem: What does the International <IR> Framework actually require?

options.text: The eight content elements are a checklist of required disclosures to be presented in the order the Framework gives them
options.misconception: turns questions into a fixed schedule of disclosures in a fixed sequence, which paras 4.2 and 4.3 rule out
options.why: Para 4.1 says an integrated report includes eight content elements posed in the form of questions to be answered. Para 4.2 says the order as listed is not the only way they could be sequenced and that they are not intended to serve as a standard structure with information appearing in a set sequence or as isolated standalone sections. Para 4.3 says they are stated as questions rather than as checklists of specific disclosures, judgement being needed to decide what is reported.

options.text: The report must be built as six sections, one for each capital, so that a reader can see the movement in every capital in its own place
options.misconception: reads the capitals as a mandatory report structure, which para 2.17 expressly denies
options.why: Para 2.17 says the Framework does not require an integrated report to adopt the categories identified above or to be structured along the lines of the capitals, and gives the two reasons the capitals are in the Framework at all — as part of the theoretical underpinning for value creation, and as a guideline for ensuring organisations consider all the forms of capital they use or affect. Para 4.2 adds that the content elements are not intended to serve as a standard structure either.
keywords: structured along the lines of the capitals

options.text: Five capitals, social and relationship capital being a part of intellectual capital rather than a category of its own
options.misconception: miscounts the categories in para 2.15, which lists social and relationship capital separately
options.why: Para 2.15 lists six capitals and describes social and relationship capital in its own right, as the institutions and relationships within and between communities and groups of stakeholders, including shared norms, key stakeholder relationships, brand and reputation intangibles and the organisation's social licence to operate. Para 2.18 does allow an organisation to categorise differently, but para 2.19 keeps the six as the guideline against which nothing is overlooked.

options.text: Six capitals are described and seven guiding principles and eight content elements set out, but the report need not adopt those categories or be structured along the lines of the capitals, and the content elements are questions to be answered rather than a checklist of specific disclosures
options.why: Para 2.15 categorises and describes six capitals — financial, manufactured, intellectual, human, social and relationship, and natural. Para 3.1 sets out seven guiding principles and para 4.1 eight content elements. Para 2.17 says the Framework does not require an integrated report to adopt the categories identified or to be structured along the lines of the capitals, and para 4.3 says the content elements are stated in the form of questions rather than as checklists of specific disclosures, because the content of a report depends on the individual circumstances of the organisation.
keywords: structured along the lines of the capitals

items.scenario: A listed manufacturer decides to publish its first integrated report alongside its financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2026. Its reporting team argues about how to build it. One member wants six chapters, one for each capital. Another says the company should drop social and relationship capital because its brand work belongs with intellectual capital. A third wants the eight content elements written out as a compliance checklist with a tick against each.

items.stem: At what amount is the group of contracts measured on initial recognition, and what goes to profit or loss on that day?

options.text: A contractual service margin of ₹250 lakh, the ₹60 lakh being carried separately as a provision for uncertainty outside the group
options.misconception: carries the risk adjustment for non-financial risk outside the fulfilment cash flows, as though it were a separate provision
options.why: The risk adjustment for non-financial risk is not a provision standing outside the group. It is one of the three components of the fulfilment cash flows, alongside the estimate of future cash flows and the adjustment for the time value of money and financial risk. Leaving it out overstates the contractual service margin by ₹60 lakh, and that ₹60 lakh would then be released as profit over the coverage period instead of being held back against the uncertainty it was measured for.

options.text: An asset of ₹190 lakh, no contractual service margin arising because a group is measured at its fulfilment cash flows
options.misconception: measures the group at the fulfilment cash flows alone and drops the second component of the model
options.why: The fulfilment cash flows are only the first of two components. Carrying the group at a net inflow of ₹190 lakh on its own would put the whole expected profit on the balance sheet as an asset on day one, which is precisely what the contractual service margin prevents. Adding a contractual service margin of ₹190 lakh brings the carrying amount to nil on initial recognition, and the profit then emerges only as services are provided.

options.text: Fulfilment cash flows are a net inflow of ₹190 lakh and the contractual service margin is set at ₹190 lakh, so the group is carried at nil and nothing at all goes to profit or loss on day one
options.why: The general measurement model carries a group of insurance contracts at the total of the fulfilment cash flows and the contractual service margin. The fulfilment cash flows are the present value of the estimated future cash flows, adjusted for the time value of money and financial risk, plus a risk adjustment for non-financial risk. Here ₹950 lakh of inflows less ₹700 lakh of outflows less the ₹60 lakh risk adjustment for non-financial risk is a net inflow of ₹190 lakh. The contractual service margin is then measured at the amount that leaves no income and no expense arising on initial recognition, which is ₹190 lakh, so the two components cancel and the group is carried at nil.

options.text: A profit of ₹250 lakh recognised in profit or loss on the day the contracts are written, being the excess of expected inflows over expected outflows
options.misconception: takes the expected margin as profit earned on the day the contracts are written, which the contractual service margin exists to defer
options.why: There is no day-one profit in this model. The whole of the expected margin becomes the contractual service margin, which is unearned profit and is released to profit or loss only as insurance contract services are actually provided over the coverage period. The ₹250 lakh also leaves out the risk adjustment for non-financial risk, which is part of the fulfilment cash flows and brings the net inflow down to ₹190 lakh.

citation.ref: the general measurement model — measurement on initial recognition as the fulfilment cash flows plus the contractual service margin (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

items.scenario: A general insurer issues a group of contracts on 1 April 2025. At that date the present value of the expected cash inflows within the contract boundary is ₹950 lakh and the present value of the expected cash outflows, being claims and directly attributable expenses, is ₹700 lakh. The actuary determines the compensation the insurer requires for bearing the uncertainty about the amount and timing of those cash flows at ₹60 lakh. There are no insurance acquisition cash flows still to be paid.

items.stem: How much of the contractual service margin is released to profit or loss in year two, and how is the ₹25 lakh treated?

options.text: ₹125 lakh is released, both the ₹40 lakh and the ₹25 lakh being deducted from the margin first
options.misconception: adjusts the margin for a change relating to past service, which the roll-forward keeps out of it
options.why: Deducting both gives ₹300 lakh plus ₹15 lakh less ₹40 lakh less ₹25 lakh, or ₹250 lakh, half of which is ₹125 lakh. The error is the ₹25 lakh. It arises on claims already incurred, so it relates to past service, and absorbing it into the margin would spread a cost of coverage already given across coverage still to come — the opposite of what the future service test is for.

options.text: ₹157.5 lakh is released, both the ₹40 lakh and the ₹25 lakh going straight to profit or loss
options.misconception: sends every change in fulfilment cash flows to profit or loss, ignoring that a change relating to future service is absorbed by the margin
options.why: Half of ₹315 lakh is ₹157.5 lakh, which is what comes out if the margin is never adjusted. But a change in fulfilment cash flows relating to FUTURE service is absorbed by the contractual service margin, because the service it relates to has not yet been given and the profit on it has not yet been earned. Only a change relating to current or past service goes straight to profit or loss, and here that is the ₹25 lakh alone.

options.text: ₹137.5 lakh is released, and the ₹25 lakh goes straight to profit or loss as an expense of the period
options.why: The roll-forward runs in order. Opening ₹300 lakh plus ₹15 lakh of interest accreted at the discount rate fixed on initial recognition is ₹315 lakh. The ₹40 lakh increase relates to FUTURE service, so it adjusts the margin down to ₹275 lakh. Release comes last and follows the coverage units delivered, one half of ₹275 lakh being ₹137.5 lakh, which also leaves ₹137.5 lakh to carry forward. The ₹25 lakh adverse development is on claims already incurred, so it relates to past service and never touches the margin at all.

options.text: ₹130 lakh is released, the margin being adjusted for the ₹40 lakh but not accreted with interest
options.misconception: leaves the interest accreted on the margin out of the roll-forward
options.why: Three hundred less forty is ₹260 lakh, half of which is ₹130 lakh. What is missing is the ₹15 lakh of interest accreted at the discount rate fixed when the group was first recognised, which is a step of the roll-forward in its own right. The margin is a balance carried forward through time, so it unwinds at a rate, and for a group without direct participation features that rate is the one locked in at initial recognition rather than a current rate.

citation.ref: subsequent measurement of the contractual service margin — the roll-forward and the future service versus past service divide (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

items.scenario: A group of three-year insurance contracts with no direct participation features carries a contractual service margin of ₹300 lakh at the start of year two. During year two, interest accreted on the margin at the discount rate fixed when the group was first recognised is ₹15 lakh. A revised actuarial estimate increases the present value of claims expected on coverage still to be given by ₹40 lakh. Separately, claims already incurred and reported in year one develop adversely by ₹25 lakh. Coverage units delivered in year two are one half of all the coverage units remaining at the start of the year.

items.stem: What does the insurer recognise on initial recognition of this group?

options.text: Nothing on initial recognition, the shortfall emerging as an expense in the periods in which the claims are actually incurred
options.misconception: waits for the claims to arrive before recognising a loss the measurement already shows on day one
options.why: The measurement itself already says the group will cost more than it brings in, so the loss is recognised on initial recognition rather than as claims arrive. Waiting would report profit in the early periods of a group that was known to be loss-making when it was written. That is why the fulfilment cash flows are tested for a net outflow at the outset and why a loss component is established straight away.

options.text: A loss of ₹90 lakh in profit or loss at once, the group carried as a liability of ₹90 lakh with no contractual service margin, and a loss component of ₹90 lakh established within the liability for remaining coverage
options.why: Outflows of ₹560 lakh plus a risk adjustment for non-financial risk of ₹30 lakh against inflows of ₹500 lakh make the fulfilment cash flows a net outflow of ₹90 lakh, which is what makes the group onerous. There is nothing to defer, so the contractual service margin is nil and the whole ₹90 lakh is a loss in profit or loss immediately. The insurer then establishes a loss component of the liability for remaining coverage of the same amount, so that the subsequent release of that liability can be tracked separately from the rest.

options.text: A contractual service margin of negative ₹90 lakh, amortised to profit or loss over the coverage period along with the rest of the margin
options.misconception: allows a negative contractual service margin, which would spread a loss the standard requires immediately
options.why: A contractual service margin represents unearned PROFIT, so it cannot be negative. Where the fulfilment cash flows are a net outflow the margin is nil and the shortfall is a loss recognised at once. Spreading it would delay bad news over the coverage period, which is the asymmetry the loss component exists to prevent.

options.text: A loss of ₹60 lakh, the ₹30 lakh being held outside the group as a separate provision for uncertainty
options.misconception: leaves the risk adjustment for non-financial risk out of the fulfilment cash flows when testing whether the group is onerous
options.why: Five hundred and sixty less five hundred is ₹60 lakh, which is the answer only if the risk adjustment for non-financial risk is treated as something outside the group. It is not: it is a component of the fulfilment cash flows, so it is inside the onerous test and inside the loss. The loss and the loss component are both ₹90 lakh.

citation.ref: onerous contracts — the net outflow test on initial recognition, the immediate loss, and the loss component of the liability for remaining coverage (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

items.scenario: An insurer issues a group of contracts at a price set to win market share. On initial recognition the present value of expected cash inflows is ₹500 lakh, the present value of expected cash outflows is ₹560 lakh, and the compensation the insurer requires for bearing the uncertainty about the amount and timing of those cash flows is ₹30 lakh.

items.stem: What may the insurer do with each group?

options.text: Under the premium allocation approach no onerous test is needed, because the liability for remaining coverage is simply the unearned premium less acquisition costs
options.misconception: drops the onerous requirement on the ground that the simplified liability is formula-driven
options.why: The simplification affects how the liability for remaining coverage is built up and released; it does not remove the requirement to recognise a loss where facts and circumstances indicate a group is onerous. Where they do, the entity measures the fulfilment cash flows relating to remaining coverage and recognises a loss and a loss component just as it would under the general measurement model.

options.text: It MAY choose the premium allocation approach for Group A because the coverage period of every contract in that group is a year or less, it may not use it for Group B because the expected significant variability prevents the insurer from concluding the result would not differ materially from the general measurement model, and either way it must still recognise a loss and a loss component on any group that is onerous
options.why: The premium allocation approach is a permitted simplification of the liability for remaining coverage, and eligibility is tested at the inception of each group. Group A meets the short-coverage gate — six months is a year or less — so the insurer may choose the simplification, but is not obliged to. Group B fails the other gate, because expected significant variability in the fulfilment cash flows is exactly the circumstance in which the insurer cannot reasonably expect a materially similar measurement. The simplification changes how remaining coverage is measured and nothing else, so an onerous group still produces an immediate loss and a loss component.

options.text: It MUST use the premium allocation approach for Group A, because a group whose contracts run a year or less is outside the general measurement model
options.misconception: turns a permitted simplification into a requirement, and treats short-duration contracts as excluded from the general model
options.why: Short coverage opens a gate, it does not close one. The general measurement model remains available for Group A, and an insurer that prefers to apply it may. The premium allocation approach is drafted as something an entity may use to simplify the measurement of the liability for remaining coverage, not as a separate regime that short-duration contracts fall into automatically.

options.text: It may use the premium allocation approach for both groups, since the approach is a presentation simplification open to any insurer that prefers it
options.misconception: skips the eligibility test altogether and reads the approach as a free presentation choice
options.why: It is a measurement simplification, not a presentation choice, and it is gated. An entity may use it for a group only where it reasonably expects the resulting measurement of the liability for remaining coverage would not differ materially from the general measurement model, or where the coverage period of every contract in the group is a year or less. Group B satisfies neither, because ten-year contracts with significant variability in the fulfilment cash flows are the case the gate was drawn to exclude.

citation.ref: the premium allocation approach — its optional character, the two eligibility gates tested at inception, and the onerous requirement surviving (paragraph numbers not verified at source, see the note at the head of this file)

items.scenario: An insurer has two groups of contracts. Group A is motor insurance, and the coverage period of every contract in it is six months. Group B is a group of ten-year contracts on which the insurer expects significant variability in the fulfilment cash flows before any claim is settled, because the claims depend on long-tail liability outcomes. The insurer would like to simplify its reporting as far as the Standard allows.

items.stem: How do these transactions appear in P Ltd's consolidated statement of cash flows for the year ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: A single separately presented investing outflow of ₹440 lakh for the acquisition, the ₹300 lakh share issue disclosed as a non-cash transaction outside the statement, and the ₹150 lakh from the T Ltd sale shown as a financing inflow
options.why: The aggregate cash flows from obtaining control of a subsidiary are presented as a single separate line, classified as investing, and reported net of the cash and cash equivalents acquired — ₹500 lakh of cash consideration less ₹60 lakh of cash acquired is ₹440 lakh. The ₹300 lakh settled in P Ltd's own shares is a non-cash transaction, which para 43 keeps out of the statement and disclosed elsewhere. The sale of 20 per cent of T Ltd did not cost P Ltd control, so it is a transaction with owners in their capacity as owners and its cash flows are financing rather than investing.

options.text: An investing outflow of ₹500 lakh for the acquisition, with the ₹60 lakh of cash acquired shown separately as an operating inflow
options.misconception: fails to net the cash acquired against the cash paid and dresses it up as an operating receipt
options.why: The consideration line is reported net of the cash and cash equivalents acquired with the subsidiary, giving one figure of ₹440 lakh, because the group did not really part with ₹500 lakh of cash — ₹60 lakh of it came straight back inside S Ltd. Nor did the group earn that ₹60 lakh from its operations, so an operating inflow misdescribes it and inflates operating cash flow, which is the number readers watch most closely.

options.text: An investing outflow of ₹800 lakh for the acquisition and an investing inflow of ₹150 lakh from the T Ltd sale
options.misconception: puts the whole consideration through the cash flow statement including the part settled in shares, and classifies an ownership change that kept control as investing
options.why: Two errors compound here. No cash moved on the ₹300 lakh of shares, so it is a non-cash transaction and does not belong in a statement of cash flows at all; and the ₹800 lakh is not reduced by the cash and cash equivalents acquired either. The ₹150 lakh is also misplaced, because a change in ownership interest that leaves control intact is a transaction with owners and is classified as financing.

options.text: An investing outflow of ₹740 lakh, the cash acquired being deducted from the total consideration of ₹800 lakh
options.misconception: nets the cash acquired against the whole consideration instead of against the cash actually paid
options.why: The netting is against the cash consideration, not against the total. Deducting ₹60 lakh from ₹800 lakh mixes a real cash figure with a non-cash transaction of ₹300 lakh and produces ₹740 lakh, an amount that never left any bank account. The cash and cash equivalents acquired come off the ₹500 lakh actually paid, giving ₹440 lakh.

citation.ref: para 39 to 42B, with the exclusion of non-cash transactions in para 43

items.scenario: On 1 December 2025 P Ltd acquired the whole of S Ltd for a total consideration of ₹800 lakh, of which ₹500 lakh was paid in cash and ₹300 lakh was settled by issuing P Ltd's own equity shares to S Ltd's former owners. S Ltd held cash and cash equivalents of ₹60 lakh on that date. Separately, during the same year P Ltd sold a 20 per cent holding in T Ltd, an existing subsidiary, for ₹150 lakh in cash, and retained control of T Ltd afterwards.

items.stem: How are the shares held by the trust reflected in the consolidated financial statements?

options.text: The ₹3.6 crore paid is deducted from equity as treasury shares, the ₹1 crore received on exercise is recognised directly in equity, no gain or loss whatever reaches profit or loss, and the balance still held is disclosed separately
options.why: Para 33 treats an entity's own equity instruments reacquired by the entity or by any other member of the consolidated group as treasury shares, deducted from equity. Two lakh shares at ₹180 is ₹3.6 crore taken out of equity. On transfer, the ₹1 crore of exercise money — 50,000 shares at ₹200 — is consideration received for the entity's own equity instruments, so para 33 puts it directly in equity, and no gain or loss is recognised in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of those instruments. Para 34 requires the amount of treasury shares held to be disclosed separately.

options.text: Nothing appears in the consolidated financial statements, because the trust is a separate legal person and the shares belong to it rather than to the company
options.misconception: stops at the trust's separate legal identity and misses that para 33 reaches shares held by any member of the consolidated group
options.why: Separate legal personality is not the test. The trust is consolidated under Ind AS 110, so it is a member of the consolidated group, and para 33 reaches the entity's own equity instruments reacquired by the entity OR by other members of that group. The ₹3.6 crore is therefore deducted from equity as treasury shares in the consolidated balance sheet even though the company itself bought nothing.

options.text: A gain of ₹10 lakh is recognised in profit or loss on the shares transferred, being the ₹1 crore received less their ₹90 lakh carrying amount
options.misconception: books a profit on a transaction in the entity's own equity instruments, which para 33 forbids outright
options.why: Fifty thousand shares cost ₹90 lakh at ₹180 and brought in ₹1 crore at ₹200, so the ₹10 lakh is arithmetically real. What is wrong is where it goes. Para 33 says no gain or loss shall be recognised in profit or loss on the purchase, sale, issue or cancellation of an entity's own equity instruments, and that the consideration received is recognised directly in equity. An entity cannot make a profit out of dealing in itself.

options.text: The shares are an investment measured at fair value through profit or loss, giving a gain of ₹45 lakh on the 1,50,000 shares still held at the year end
options.misconception: treats the group's holding of its own shares as a financial asset, which the consolidated group cannot own
options.why: One lakh fifty thousand shares at the ₹30 rise from ₹180 to ₹210 is the ₹45 lakh this option reaches, but the group cannot hold an asset representing a claim on itself. The trust is consolidated, so from the group's point of view these are its own equity instruments held within the group, which para 33 requires to be deducted from equity as treasury shares. There is no financial asset, so there is nothing to fair value and no gain or loss to recognise.

citation.ref: para 33 and 34

items.scenario: An employee stock option trust set up by a listed company is consolidated as part of the group under Ind AS 110. During the year ended 31 March 2026 the trust bought 2,00,000 shares of the company in the open market at ₹180 a share. It later transferred 50,000 of those shares to employees on exercise of their options, the employees paying the exercise price of ₹200 a share. The market price on 31 March 2026 was ₹210 a share. The share-based payment expense under Ind AS 102 has been accounted for separately and is not in question.

items.stem: Which positions are presented net in the balance sheet?

options.text: Only the second, presented as a net ₹60 lakh; the first is shown gross because the right of set-off is not currently exercisable, and the third is shown gross because the two amounts are owed to and by different counterparties
options.why: Para 42 permits offsetting only where the entity currently has a legally enforceable right to set off the recognised amounts and intends either to settle net or to realise the asset and settle the liability simultaneously. The bank position satisfies both, so ₹90 lakh less ₹30 lakh is presented as ₹60 lakh. The master netting arrangement fails the first condition, because a right that crystallises only on default is not currently enforceable. The third fails as well, since a right of set-off runs between two parties and there is no such right against a party that owes nothing.

options.text: The first and the second are presented net, since a master netting arrangement is a legally enforceable right of set-off
options.misconception: reads a default-contingent right in a master netting arrangement as a currently enforceable one
options.why: A master netting arrangement of this kind gives a right that becomes exercisable only on a future event, the counterparty's default. That is not a right the entity currently has, and para 42 requires the legally enforceable right to exist now and in the ordinary course of business, not merely in default or insolvency. The receivable stays at ₹80 lakh and the payable at ₹50 lakh.

options.text: None is presented net, because Ind AS 1 para 32 forbids offsetting assets against liabilities
options.misconception: reads the general bar on offsetting as absolute and misses that it yields where another Ind AS permits an offset
options.why: Ind AS 1 para 32 forbids offsetting UNLESS required or permitted by an Ind AS, and Ind AS 32 para 42 is exactly such a permission. Where the entity currently has a legally enforceable right of set-off and intends to settle net, offsetting is not merely allowed but required, because the net amount is what the entity's future cash flows will actually be. The bank position therefore has to be shown at ₹60 lakh.

options.text: All three are presented net, because in every case the amounts will end up cancelling each other out
options.misconception: offsets on the expected outcome rather than on a present enforceable right and a present intention
options.why: Expecting amounts to cancel is not the test. Para 42 asks whether the entity currently has a legally enforceable right of set-off and whether it intends to settle net or realise and settle simultaneously, both at the reporting date. Offsetting on expectation would hide gross exposures — an ₹80 lakh receivable carries ₹80 lakh of credit risk however large the payable beside it — and the whole purpose of the two conditions is to keep that visible.

citation.ref: para 42, read with the conditions elaborated in paras 43 to 50, and Ind AS 1 para 32

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company has three positions. First, a receivable of ₹80 lakh and a payable of ₹50 lakh with the same counterparty under a master netting arrangement whose right of set-off becomes exercisable only if that counterparty defaults. Second, a fixed deposit of ₹90 lakh and an overdraft of ₹30 lakh with the same bank, where the bank documentation gives a currently enforceable right of set-off and the company intends to settle net. Third, a receivable from one group company of ₹20 lakh and a payable to a different group company of ₹20 lakh, both outside the reporting group.

items.stem: What reversal of the impairment loss is recognised on 31 March 2026?

options.text: ₹24 lakh, reinstating in full the impairment loss originally recognised
options.misconception: reverses the original charge in full and forgets the depreciation that has run on the written-down amount since
options.why: The original impairment loss was ₹24 lakh, but two years of depreciation have run since on the reduced amount. Reinstating the whole ₹24 lakh would take the carrying amount to ₹66 lakh, above the ₹60 lakh the asset would have stood at had it never been impaired, and para 117 forbids that. The reversal is the gap between the capped figure and the present carrying amount, ₹18 lakh.

options.text: ₹18 lakh, credited to profit or loss, taking the carrying amount to ₹60 lakh
options.why: After two years the carrying amount was ₹80 lakh and the ₹56 lakh recoverable amount produced a ₹24 lakh impairment loss. Depreciating ₹56 lakh over the remaining eight years is ₹7 lakh a year, so two years later the carrying amount is ₹42 lakh. Para 117 caps the reversal at the carrying amount, net of depreciation, that would have stood had no impairment loss been recognised — four years of ₹10 lakh off ₹100 lakh, which is ₹60 lakh. The reversal is therefore ₹60 lakh less ₹42 lakh, being ₹18 lakh, and para 119 sends it to profit or loss because the asset is carried at cost.

options.text: Nil, because an impairment loss once recognised is not reversed in a later period
options.misconception: applies the goodwill rule in para 124 to an asset that is not goodwill
options.why: Para 124 bars the reversal of an impairment loss recognised for GOODWILL, and only for goodwill. For every other asset, para 110 requires the entity to look at each reporting date for indications that a loss has decreased or gone, and para 114 requires reversal where the estimates used to determine recoverable amount have changed. Winning the contract back is such a change, so a reversal is not merely permitted here, it is required.

options.text: ₹28 lakh, taking the carrying amount up to the recoverable amount of ₹70 lakh
options.misconception: writes the asset back up to recoverable amount and ignores the cap in para 117
options.why: Seventy less forty-two is ₹28 lakh, and that is what a reversal would be if recoverable amount were the ceiling. It is not. Para 117 forbids the increased carrying amount from exceeding the carrying amount, net of depreciation, that would have been determined had no impairment loss been recognised in prior years, which here is ₹60 lakh. Going to ₹70 lakh would let a reversal do what a revaluation does, and the cost model does not permit that.

citation.ref: para 110, 114, 117 and 119, with the goodwill bar in para 124

items.scenario: A machine costing ₹100 lakh was brought into use on 1 April 2022 and is depreciated straight line over ten years with no residual value. On 31 March 2024 its recoverable amount had fallen to ₹56 lakh and an impairment loss was recognised; the remaining useful life was unchanged at eight years. By 31 March 2026 the customer contract that had been lost has been won back and the recoverable amount is ₹70 lakh. The machine is carried under the cost model.

items.stem: At what amount is the restructuring provision recognised?

options.text: ₹160 lakh, being the redundancy payments and the lease termination penalty only
options.why: Para 80 confines a restructuring provision to the direct expenditures arising from the restructuring, which are those both necessarily entailed by the restructuring and not associated with the ongoing activities of the entity. Redundancy of ₹120 lakh and the ₹40 lakh penalty to get out of the lease on the closed site are both, giving ₹160 lakh. Para 81 excludes retraining or relocating continuing staff and marketing by name, since those relate to the future conduct of the business, and para 82 excludes identifiable future operating losses unless they arise on an onerous contract, which none here does.

options.text: ₹215 lakh, adding the retraining and relocation of continuing staff to the redundancy and lease penalty
options.misconception: provides for the cost of settling continuing staff into the new structure, which para 81 names as excluded
options.why: Retraining of ₹30 lakh and relocation of ₹25 lakh on top of ₹160 lakh gives ₹215 lakh. Both are spent on continuing staff, meaning employees who remain part of the ongoing activities of the entity, and para 81 lists retraining or relocating continuing staff as an example of what a restructuring provision does NOT include. The company gets an ongoing benefit from that spending, so it is an expense of the future periods that receive it.

options.text: ₹265 lakh, the whole of the plan's estimated cost
options.misconception: provides for everything in the announced plan, treating the announcement as fixing the amount as well as the obligation
options.why: Announcing the plan creates the obligation; it does not decide what the obligation is measured at. Adding all six figures gives ₹265 lakh, which sweeps in the ₹30 lakh of retraining, ₹25 lakh of relocation, ₹15 lakh of marketing and ₹35 lakh of future operating losses. Paras 81 and 82 keep every one of those out, because they relate to the ongoing activities of the entity and to the future conduct of its business rather than to the restructuring itself.

options.text: ₹195 lakh, adding the operating losses expected up to the closure date
options.misconception: provides for future operating losses, which para 82 excludes unless they arise on an onerous contract
options.why: One hundred and sixty plus thirty-five is ₹195 lakh. Para 82 says identifiable future operating losses up to the date of a restructuring are not included in a provision unless they relate to a contract that is onerous, and the scenario says none is. A loss expected from trading in a future period is not a present obligation at the reporting date, and providing for it would move next year's result into this one.

citation.ref: para 80, 81 and 82, read with the obligating event in para 72

items.scenario: A company announced a restructuring to its affected employees before the year end, so a constructive obligation exists and a provision must be recognised. The plan's costs are estimated at redundancy payments ₹120 lakh, retraining employees who will stay with the company ₹30 lakh, relocating continuing staff to the surviving offices ₹25 lakh, marketing the new structure to customers ₹15 lakh, a lease termination penalty on the site being closed ₹40 lakh, and operating losses expected between the year end and the closure date ₹35 lakh. None of the continuing contracts is onerous.

items.stem: How are the tax balances presented in the consolidated balance sheet?

options.text: All deferred tax balances gross, a deferred tax asset of ₹130 lakh against a deferred tax liability of ₹60 lakh, because offsetting is not available in consolidated statements
options.misconception: refuses an offset that para 74 requires once its two conditions are satisfied
options.why: Ninety plus forty is the ₹130 lakh here, and the refusal to offset is as wrong as offsetting everything. Para 74 is not permissive — it says an entity SHALL offset where the two conditions are met, and for P Ltd's own ₹90 lakh and ₹60 lakh they are, since there is a legally enforceable right against the same taxation authority on the same taxable entity. Showing them gross overstates both sides of the balance sheet.

options.text: A net deferred tax asset of ₹30 lakh for P Ltd and a separate deferred tax asset of ₹40 lakh for S Ltd, a net current tax liability of ₹45 lakh, and no deferred tax balance shown as current
options.why: Para 74 lets deferred tax balances be offset only where there is a legally enforceable right to set off current tax balances and the deferred amounts relate to the same taxation authority on either the same taxable entity or different taxable entities intending to settle net. P Ltd's own ₹90 lakh and ₹60 lakh meet that and net to ₹30 lakh. S Ltd is a different taxable entity with no such intention, so its ₹40 lakh stands alone even though it is consolidated. Para 71 nets the current tax balances to ₹45 lakh, and Ind AS 1 para 56 bars any deferred tax balance from being classified as current.

options.text: A net deferred tax asset of ₹30 lakh presented among current assets, because the underlying temporary differences are expected to reverse within twelve months
options.misconception: classifies a deferred tax balance as current on the strength of when it reverses
options.why: The offsetting is right and the classification is not. Ind AS 1 para 56 says that where an entity presents current and non-current assets and liabilities separately, it shall not classify deferred tax assets or liabilities as current, whatever the expected reversal pattern. No deferred tax balance is ever classified as current on the face of the balance sheet, and the timing of reversal belongs in the notes instead.

options.text: A single net deferred tax asset of ₹70 lakh, since all the balances are assessed by the same taxation authority and appear in one consolidated balance sheet
options.misconception: offsets across two taxable entities on the strength of consolidation and a common tax authority
options.why: Ninety plus forty less sixty is ₹70 lakh, and the same taxation authority is only half of what para 74 asks.
