The other half is that the balances relate to the same taxable entity, or to different taxable entities that intend to settle current tax net or to realise and settle simultaneously in each future period concerned. P Ltd and S Ltd are different taxable entities and have no such intention, and consolidation does not create one — the two companies still file and pay separately.

citation.ref: para 71 and 74, with the classification bar in Ind AS 1 para 56

items.scenario: In P Ltd's consolidated balance sheet at 31 March 2026, P Ltd has a deferred tax asset of ₹90 lakh and a deferred tax liability of ₹60 lakh, both arising on P Ltd's own temporary differences and assessed by the same taxation authority. Its subsidiary S Ltd has a deferred tax asset of ₹40 lakh, assessed by the same authority but on S Ltd as a separate taxable entity, and neither company intends to settle current tax on a net basis with the other. P Ltd also has advance tax and tax deducted at source of ₹25 lakh and a current tax liability of ₹70 lakh for the same assessment year, with a legally enforceable right of set-off and an intention to settle net.

items.stem: What does the company recognise at 31 March 2026?

options.text: A net defined benefit asset of ₹75 lakh, with the ₹125 lakh restriction recognised in other comprehensive income as a remeasurement
options.why: Para 64 measures a net defined benefit asset at the lower of the surplus in the plan and the asset ceiling. The surplus is ₹1,200 lakh less ₹1,000 lakh, being ₹200 lakh, and the asset ceiling is the present value of the economic benefits available as refunds or reductions in future contributions, being ₹75 lakh. The lower is ₹75 lakh. Para 127 makes any change in the effect of the asset ceiling outside net interest a remeasurement, so the ₹125 lakh difference goes to other comprehensive income and, under paras 120 and 122, is never reclassified to profit or loss.

options.text: No asset at all, the ₹200 lakh surplus being written off through other comprehensive income, because a surplus in a funded plan is never recognised
options.misconception: treats the asset ceiling as always nil rather than as an amount to be measured
options.why: The asset ceiling is a measured number, not a prohibition. Where refunds or reductions in future contributions are available, their present value is recognised, and here that is ₹75 lakh. Writing off the whole ₹200 lakh would deny the company a benefit it has, in a case where the actuary has established that some of it can be recovered.

options.text: A net defined benefit asset of ₹200 lakh, being the whole surplus in the plan
options.misconception: recognises the full surplus and ignores the asset ceiling entirely
options.why: A surplus is only an asset to the extent the company can actually get at it. Para 64 sets the asset ceiling as the present value of the economic benefits available in the form of refunds from the plan or reductions in future contributions, which the actuary has put at ₹75 lakh because the deed allows a refund only on winding up. The remaining ₹125 lakh belongs to the plan and cannot be shown as the company's own resource.

options.text: A net defined benefit asset of ₹75 lakh, with the ₹125 lakh restriction charged as an expense in profit or loss
options.misconception: routes a change in the effect of the asset ceiling through profit or loss instead of other comprehensive income
options.why: The amount is right and the destination is wrong. Para 127 lists the remeasurements of the net defined benefit liability or asset as the actuarial gains and losses, the return on plan assets outside net interest, and any change in the effect of the asset ceiling outside net interest. All of them go to other comprehensive income, which is what keeps the operating result clear of movements the company does not control.

citation.ref: para 64, with the remeasurement components in para 127 and the OCI treatment in para 120 and 122

items.scenario: At 31 March 2026 a company's funded gratuity plan has plan assets with a fair value of ₹1,200 lakh and a defined benefit obligation with a present value of ₹1,000 lakh. The trust deed allows a refund to the company only on winding up the plan, and the actuary determines the present value of the economic benefits available to the company as refunds and as reductions in future contributions at ₹75 lakh. The plan was in deficit at the previous year end and no ceiling effect arose then.

items.stem: How is the change in functional currency accounted for?

options.text: The subsidiary continues to report in Singapore dollars, because a functional currency once determined cannot be changed
options.misconception: reads the stability of the functional currency as an absolute bar rather than as a condition on when it may change
options.why: The rule is that the functional currency is not changed UNLESS there is a change in the underlying transactions, events and conditions relevant to it. Here every one of those has changed — sales, purchases, salaries and borrowings have all moved to United States dollars. That is precisely the case paras 35 to 37 are written for, and the change is applied prospectively from the date it happens.

options.text: Prospectively from 1 October 2025 — every item is translated into United States dollars at the rate on that date, the translated amounts of non-monetary items becoming their historical cost from then on, and the ₹48 lakh stays in other comprehensive income
options.why: Paras 35 to 37 apply the translation procedures for the new functional currency prospectively from the date of the change. Everything is translated at the exchange rate at that date, and for non-monetary items the resulting translated amounts are treated as their historical cost thereafter, so the change resets the measurement base without touching any earlier reported figure. The ₹48 lakh already accumulated stays where it is, because para 48 reclassifies exchange differences from equity to profit or loss only on the disposal of the foreign operation, and there has been no disposal.

options.text: Prospectively, but the ₹48 lakh accumulated in other comprehensive income is reclassified to profit or loss on 1 October 2025
options.misconception: treats a change in functional currency as though it were a disposal of the foreign operation
options.why: Nothing has been sold. Para 48 reclassifies the cumulative exchange differences relating to a foreign operation from equity to profit or loss on the DISPOSAL of that operation, when the gain or loss on disposal is recognised. A change in the currency the operation measures itself in is not a disposal, the group's investment is unchanged, and the ₹48 lakh continues to sit in other comprehensive income until the operation actually goes.

options.text: Retrospectively, restating the comparatives and the opening balances as though United States dollars had always been the functional currency
options.misconception: treats a change in functional currency as a change in accounting policy, which is applied retrospectively
options.why: A functional currency is a matter of fact about the economy the entity operates in, not a policy the entity chooses, so a change in it reflects a change in circumstances rather than a change of mind. Paras 35 to 37 therefore apply the new procedures prospectively. Restating would report earlier periods in a currency that did not then determine the subsidiary's selling prices and costs, which would describe those years wrongly.

citation.ref: para 35 to 37 on a change in functional currency, read with the reclassification on disposal in para 48

items.scenario: An Indian parent has a Singapore subsidiary whose functional currency has always been the Singapore dollar. Following a group reorganisation on 1 October 2025 the subsidiary's sales, its purchases, its salaries and its borrowings all shift to United States dollars, and the Singapore dollar is no longer the currency of the economy that determines its selling prices and costs. The consolidated exchange differences accumulated in other comprehensive income from translating the subsidiary in earlier years stand at ₹48 lakh. The subsidiary is not disposed of.

items.stem: At what amount is the plant carried on 31 March 2026, and where does the adjustment go?

options.text: ₹410 lakh, with a charge of ₹60 lakh in profit or loss from continuing operations
options.misconception: applies only the first limb of para 27 and never compares with recoverable amount
options.why: Five hundred less eighteen months of depreciation at ₹60 lakh a year is the ₹410 lakh here, and that is one of the two figures para 27 names. The paragraph takes the LOWER of it and the recoverable amount at the date of the decision not to sell, which is ₹380 lakh. Stopping at ₹410 lakh would carry the plant above what it is worth to the business, which is the very thing an impairment test exists to prevent. The ₹90 lakh charge that does result still lands in profit or loss from continuing operations under para 28.

options.text: ₹470 lakh, the held-for-sale measurement simply continuing now that the asset is back in property, plant and equipment
options.misconception: leaves the asset where held-for-sale measurement left it and never catches up the depreciation that was suspended
options.why: Depreciation was suspended while the plant was held for sale, not cancelled. Once the asset ceases to be classified as held for sale, para 27 rebuilds the carrying amount as though the classification had never happened, adjusting for the depreciation that would have been recognised, and then caps it at recoverable amount. Carrying it at ₹470 lakh would leave an asset that has been used for eighteen months standing at more than it would have if it had never been advertised for sale.

options.text: ₹380 lakh, with a charge of ₹90 lakh in profit or loss from continuing operations
options.why: Para 27 measures an asset that ceases to be classified as held for sale at the lower of two figures. The first is its carrying amount before classification adjusted for the depreciation that would have been recognised had it never been classified — ₹500 lakh less eighteen months at ₹60 lakh a year, being ₹410 lakh. The second is its recoverable amount at the date of the decision not to sell, ₹380 lakh. The lower is ₹380 lakh, so ₹90 lakh comes off the ₹470 lakh carrying amount, and para 28 puts that charge in profit or loss from continuing operations in the period the criteria stop being met.

options.text: ₹500 lakh, the original write-down being reversed in full now that the sale is off
options.misconception: reverses the held-for-sale write-down back to the original carrying amount and ignores both the depreciation catch-up and the recoverable amount cap
options.why: Nothing takes the asset back to ₹500 lakh. Para 27 adjusts the pre-classification carrying amount for the depreciation that would have been recognised, which alone brings it to ₹410 lakh, and then compares that with recoverable amount and takes the lower. Reversing to ₹500 lakh would give the plant eighteen free months of life and ignore the fall in what it can now recover.

citation.ref: para 26, 27 and 28

items.scenario: A plant with a carrying amount of ₹500 lakh was classified as held for sale on 1 October 2024, when its fair value less costs to sell was ₹470 lakh, so it was written down to ₹470 lakh and depreciation stopped. Had it not been classified, depreciation would have been ₹60 lakh a year. On 31 March 2026 the buyer withdrew, the board resolved not to sell, and the held-for-sale criteria are no longer met. The plant's recoverable amount on that date is ₹380 lakh.

items.stem: What may management do?

options.text: Fold the broking arm into the retail segment, since it does not cross ten per cent of combined revenue and is therefore not separately reportable
options.misconception: reads the quantitative thresholds as a licence to aggregate a dissimilar segment into a bigger one
options.why: Failing a quantitative threshold means a segment need not be reported on its own; it does not mean it may be buried in whichever segment is convenient. Para 14 lets below-threshold segments be combined only where they have similar economic characteristics and share a majority of the para 12 respects, and broking shares none of them with supermarkets. Para 16 therefore puts it in an all other segments category.

options.text: Aggregate any segments that have similar economic characteristics, that alone being what para 12 requires once aggregation is consistent with the core principle
options.misconception: takes similar economic characteristics as the whole test rather than as one hurdle standing beside five more
options.why: Similar economic characteristics is necessary and not sufficient. Para 12 adds that the segments must ALSO be similar in each of five respects, and the word each rules out picking two or three. Two businesses can earn comparable margins while selling different things to different customers through different channels, and reporting them as one would hide exactly the difference the segment note exists to show.

options.text: Report the two supermarket segments separately, because they operate in different countries and geography is one of the aggregation criteria
options.misconception: reads geography into the para 12 list, where it does not appear
options.why: Geography is not among the five respects. The list is the nature of the products and services, the nature of the production processes, the type or class of customer, the methods of distribution, and where applicable the nature of the regulatory environment. Two countries may of course differ in regulation or in economic characteristics, but that has to be shown rather than assumed, and here the margins have tracked each other for five years. Geographical information is dealt with separately, in the entity-wide disclosures.

options.text: Aggregate the two supermarket segments, because they have similar economic characteristics and are similar in each of the five respects para 12 lists; but not fold in the broking arm, which must go into an all other segments category or be combined only with other below-threshold segments sharing a majority of those respects
options.why: Para 12 permits aggregation where it is consistent with the core principle of the Standard, the segments have similar economic characteristics, AND they are similar in the nature of the products and services, the nature of the production processes, the type or class of customer, the methods used to distribute, and where applicable the nature of the regulatory environment. The supermarkets satisfy all of that. The broking arm fails every one of the five respects, so para 14 does not help it either, and para 16 sends what is left into an all other segments category.

citation.ref: para 12, read with para 14 and 16

items.scenario: A retail group's chief operating decision maker reviews four operating segments — supermarkets in India, supermarkets in Sri Lanka, an insurance broking arm, and a logistics arm serving external customers. The two supermarket segments sell the same range, buy through the same distribution network, serve the same class of retail customer and have run at similar gross margins for five years. The insurance broking arm sells a different product to a different customer through different channels and is separately regulated, and its revenue is below every quantitative threshold. Management proposes a single retail segment combining the supermarkets and folding the broking arm into it.

items.stem: What does Ind AS 112 require of P Ltd?

options.text: The same disclosures repeated in P Ltd's separate financial statements, so that both sets of statements carry the same information
options.misconception: ignores the scope carve-out that keeps Ind AS 112 out of separate financial statements
options.why: Para 6 says the Standard does not apply to separate financial statements to which Ind AS 27 applies. The narrow exception is for an entity whose only financial statements are separate ones and which has interests in unconsolidated structured entities, and P Ltd is not that entity because it also prepares consolidated financial statements. Repeating the group disclosures in the separate statements would describe a group those statements do not present.

options.text: The subsidiary-level information for every subsidiary it consolidates, B Ltd included, because each of them forms part of the group
options.misconception: applies the disclosure to all subsidiaries rather than to those whose non-controlling interests are material
options.why: The trigger in para 12 is that the NON-CONTROLLING INTERESTS are material to the reporting entity, not that the subsidiary is. B Ltd is wholly owned, so it has no non-controlling interests at all and there is nothing for the paragraph to describe. The disclosure exists to tell a reader how much of the group's results and net assets belong to somebody else, which is a question a wholly owned subsidiary does not raise.

options.text: Disclosure of the significant judgements and assumptions behind the conclusion that it controls C Ltd, and subsidiary-level information for A Ltd because its non-controlling interests are material — with none of it required in the separate financial statements
options.why: Para 7 requires disclosure of the significant judgements and assumptions made in determining that the entity has control, and a conclusion of control on 45 per cent of the votes is exactly such a judgement. Para 12 then requires, for each subsidiary whose non-controlling interests are material to the reporting entity, the name, principal place of business, the proportion of ownership interests and voting rights held by non-controlling interests, the profit or loss allocated to them, their accumulated balance and summarised financial information about the subsidiary. Para 6 keeps all of this out of separate financial statements to which Ind AS 27 applies.

options.text: No disclosure of judgement about C Ltd, since Ind AS 110 already sets out the control test and P Ltd has applied it
options.misconception: confuses the standard that decides consolidation with the standard that requires the reasoning to be published
options.why: Ind AS 110 decides whether there is control; Ind AS 112 makes the entity explain how it got there. Para 7 asks for the significant judgements and assumptions made, and a conclusion that a 45 per cent holder controls the company is precisely the judgement a reader cannot reconstruct from the numbers. Leaving it out would present a contestable conclusion as if it were arithmetic.

citation.ref: para 7 and 12, with the separate financial statements carve-out in para 6

items.scenario: P Ltd prepares consolidated financial statements and, alongside them, separate financial statements under Ind AS 27. It consolidates three subsidiaries. In A Ltd it holds 55 per cent and the non-controlling interests are material to the group. In B Ltd it holds 100 per cent. In C Ltd it holds 45 per cent and has concluded that it controls C Ltd because the remaining 55 per cent is spread across thousands of small holders who have never voted together.

items.stem: At what amount is the land measured?

options.text: ₹60 crore, being what a market participant would pay for residential development after allowing for demolition
options.why: Para 27 measures a non-financial asset on the basis of a market participant's ability to generate economic benefits through its highest and best use. Para 28 asks whether that use is physically possible, legally permissible and financially feasible, and residential development is all three since the rezoning is already granted and runs with the land. Para 29 makes the assessment from the perspective of market participants even where the entity intends a different use, so the company's intention to keep manufacturing is beside the point. The ₹5 crore of demolition is a cost a market participant would bear, so ₹65 crore less ₹5 crore is ₹60 crore.

options.text: ₹65 crore, the price a developer would pay for the site
options.misconception: takes the price for cleared land without deducting what clearing it would cost
options.why: The ₹65 crore is what a developer would pay for land ready to build on, and this land is not. A market participant buying it must spend ₹5 crore demolishing the factory before the legally permissible residential use can be realised, and would price the site accordingly. Fair value reflects the asset as it stands, not as it would stand after somebody else's money had been spent on it.

options.text: The lower of ₹40 crore and ₹60 crore, prudence requiring the more conservative figure to be taken
options.misconception: imports a prudence override into a measurement the Standard defines as an exit price
options.why: Fair value is the price that would be received to sell the asset in an orderly transaction between market participants, and there is no prudence override that lets a lower number be chosen. Paras 27 to 30 point at one figure, the value in the highest and best use, and picking a lower one because it feels safer would make the measurement unverifiable and incomparable between companies.

options.text: ₹40 crore, because an entity's current use is presumed to be the highest and best use of its asset
options.misconception: treats the current-use presumption as conclusive when market factors point to a more valuable use
options.why: Para 29 does presume that current use is the highest and best use, but the presumption falls where market or other factors suggest a different use by market participants would maximise value. A granted rezoning and a developer willing to pay ₹65 crore are exactly such factors. Holding to ₹40 crore would measure the company's plans rather than the asset's fair value.

citation.ref: para 27, 28, 29 and 30

items.scenario: A company owns land in a city on which its factory stands, and intends to keep manufacturing there indefinitely. The municipality rezoned the area for residential use two years ago and the permission runs with the land. Valued as a factory site the land would fetch ₹40 crore. A developer buying it for flats would pay ₹65 crore for cleared land, and would have to spend ₹5 crore demolishing the factory buildings first. The land has to be measured at fair value.

items.stem: At what amount is the lease liability measured on 1 April 2025?

options.text: ₹50 lakh, being the five annual payments of ₹10 lakh added together
options.misconception: measures the liability at the undiscounted total of the payments
options.why: Para 26 measures the lease liability at the PRESENT VALUE of the lease payments not paid at the commencement date, so the five payments have to be discounted. Adding them gives ₹50 lakh, which ignores that ₹10 lakh due in five years is worth less than ₹10 lakh due tomorrow. The difference between ₹50 lakh and ₹37.91 lakh is the interest that will be charged to profit or loss over the lease term as the liability unwinds.

options.text: ₹53.07 lakh, including the present value of the expected turnover rent
options.misconception: discounts an expected variable payment that depends on sales rather than on an index or a rate
options.why: Adding ₹4 lakh a year at the same factor gives ₹15.16 lakh on top of ₹37.91 lakh, hence ₹53.07 lakh. Para 27 admits variable lease payments only where they depend on an index or a rate, such as a consumer price index or a benchmark interest rate, because those can be measured at the commencement date from something outside the lessee's control. A payment that moves with the shop's own sales is an estimate of the lessee's future trading, and para 38(b) leaves it to the period it arises in.

options.text: ₹39.93 lakh, discounting the rent at the weighted average cost of capital of 8 per cent
options.misconception: substitutes a cost of capital for the incremental borrowing rate para 26 names
options.why: Ten lakh times 3.9927 is the ₹39.93 lakh here. A weighted average cost of capital blends the return equity holders expect with the cost of debt and describes the business as a whole; the incremental borrowing rate is narrower and specific, being what this lessee would pay to borrow, over a similar term and with similar security, the funds needed to obtain an asset of similar value in a similar economic environment. Para 26 asks for the second, and using the lower rate here overstates the liability.

options.text: ₹37.91 lakh, with the turnover rent kept out of the liability and charged to profit or loss in the periods the sales occur
options.why: Para 26 discounts at the rate implicit in the lease where it can be readily determined and otherwise at the lessee's incremental borrowing rate, which here is 10 per cent, giving ₹10 lakh times 3.7908, or ₹37.91 lakh. Para 27 lists the payments that go into the liability, and among the variable ones it takes only those that depend on an index or a rate. Turnover rent depends on sales, which is neither, so it stays out, and para 38(b) recognises it in profit or loss in the period in which the event that triggers the payment occurs.

citation.ref: para 26 and 27, with the treatment of excluded variable payments in para 38(b)

items.scenario: A retailer takes a five-year lease of shop space from 1 April 2025. Rent is ₹10 lakh payable at the end of each year, plus turnover rent of 2 per cent of the shop's sales, which the retailer expects to be about ₹4 lakh a year. There is no purchase option, no residual value guarantee and no termination penalty. The retailer cannot readily determine the rate implicit in the lease because it does not know the lessor's initial direct costs or the unguaranteed residual value. It can borrow on similar terms and security at 10 per cent, and its weighted average cost of capital is 8 per cent. The five-year annuity factors are 3.7908 at 10 per cent and 3.9927 at 8 per cent.

items.stem: What must the finished statement show?

options.text: The ₹35 lakh error correction shown as a movement of the current year within retained earnings
options.misconception: buries a retrospective restatement inside this year's movements instead of showing it against the opening balance
options.why: Ind AS 8 para 42 corrects a material prior period error retrospectively, by restating the opening balances of assets, liabilities and equity for the earliest period presented. Para 106 then requires the effects of that retrospective restatement to be shown for each component of equity in their own right. Showing the ₹35 lakh as a movement of this year would make this year's performance look ₹35 lakh worse and leave the earlier year still reported wrongly.

options.text: The ₹40 lakh of dividends presented as an expense in arriving at profit for the year
options.misconception: treats a distribution to owners as a cost of earning the profit it is paid out of
options.why: A dividend is a distribution of profit, not an expense incurred to earn it. Para 107 places it in the statement of changes in equity or in the notes, together with the related amount per share, precisely because it belongs among transactions with owners in their capacity as owners. Running it through profit or loss would understate the return the company actually made and mix a decision of the shareholders with the performance of the business.

options.text: The ₹12 lakh of actuarial losses left in the statement of profit and loss and other comprehensive income only, since the statement of changes in equity deals with transactions with owners
options.misconception: limits the statement to owner transactions and drops other comprehensive income out of the equity reconciliation
options.why: The statement reconciles equity, and other comprehensive income changes equity as surely as profit does. Para 106 requires the reconciliation for each component of equity to disclose separately the changes resulting from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income and from transactions with owners, and para 106A adds an analysis of other comprehensive income by item, in this statement or in the notes. Omitting the ₹12 lakh would leave the reconciliation not reconciling.

options.text: For each component of equity, a reconciliation from opening to closing balance separately disclosing the movements from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income and from transactions with owners, with the ₹35 lakh shown as the effect of a retrospective restatement and the ₹40 lakh of dividends shown here or in the notes with the amount per share
options.why: Para 106 requires total comprehensive income for the period, the effects of retrospective application or retrospective restatement recognised under Ind AS 8, and for each component of equity a reconciliation between the carrying amount at the beginning and at the end of the period, separately disclosing changes from profit or loss, from other comprehensive income and from transactions with owners in their capacity as owners. Ind AS 8 para 42 makes the ₹35 lakh a restatement of the opening balance rather than a movement of this year. Para 107 requires the dividends recognised as distributions to owners and the related amount per share, in this statement or in the notes.

citation.ref: para 106, 106A and 107, read with the restatement requirement in Ind AS 8 para 42

items.scenario: A company's draft statement of changes in equity shows only the opening balance, the profit for the year and the closing balance. During the year it also recognised actuarial losses of ₹12 lakh in other comprehensive income, corrected a prior period error that reduced opening retained earnings by ₹35 lakh, paid dividends of ₹40 lakh, and issued fresh shares for ₹200 lakh.

items.stem: What does the company record on the modification date?

options.text: Continue measuring the award at the fair value of the liability and remeasure it at each reporting date until settlement
options.misconception: ignores the modification and carries on with cash-settled accounting for an award that will now be settled in shares
options.why: Remeasuring at each reporting date is what a cash-settled award requires, and this one is no longer cash-settled. Once the terms change so that the award will be settled in equity instruments, para B44B derecognises the liability on the modification date and there is nothing left to remeasure. Equity-settled awards are not remeasured for later movements in the share price at all.

options.text: Transfer the ₹80 lakh from liabilities to equity, nothing touching profit or loss because the award itself has not changed in value to the employees
options.misconception: treats the reclassification as a movement within the balance sheet and never remeasures the award at the modification date
options.why: The whole point of para B44A is that the equity-settled award is measured afresh at the fair value of the equity instruments on the modification date, which is ₹135 lakh for the full award and ₹90 lakh for the services received so far. That is not the same number as the ₹80 lakh liability, and para B44C requires the difference to go to profit or loss rather than to be absorbed silently in equity.

options.text: Recognise the whole ₹135 lakh in equity on the modification date and derecognise the ₹80 lakh liability, charging ₹55 lakh to profit or loss
options.misconception: recognises the fair value of the entire award instead of the part relating to services already received
options.why: One hundred and thirty-five less eighty is the ₹55 lakh here, and the error is in the first figure. The amount recognised in equity on the modification date is the portion of the modification-date fair value relating to the goods or services already RECEIVED, being two of three years or ₹90 lakh. The remaining third is earned over the final year of the vesting period and is recognised then, as service is rendered.

options.text: Derecognise the ₹80 lakh liability, recognise ₹90 lakh in equity for the services already received, and charge the ₹10 lakh difference to profit or loss immediately
options.why: Para B44A measures the equity-settled award by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments at the MODIFICATION DATE and recognises in equity the portion of that fair value relating to the goods or services received up to that date, which is two of the three years of ₹135 lakh, or ₹90 lakh. Para B44B derecognises the liability for the cash-settled award on that same date, removing the ₹80 lakh. Para B44C sends any difference between the liability derecognised and the amount recognised in equity straight to profit or loss, so the ₹10 lakh is an expense of the period at once.

citation.ref: Appendix B, para B44A, B44B and B44C

items.scenario: A company granted share appreciation rights settled in cash, vesting after three years of service. Two of the three years have elapsed and the liability carried for them stands at ₹80 lakh. On that date the company modifies the terms so that the award will be settled in its own equity shares instead of cash. The fair value of the equity instruments granted in replacement, measured at the modification date, is ₹135 lakh for the whole award. All employees are expected to complete the third year.

items.stem: What segment information must each company give in its interim report?

options.text: The listed company gives the short interim list including a measure of segment profit or loss, the changed segment assets, a description of the change in the basis of segmentation and a reconciliation to the entity's profit or loss; the unlisted company gives none
options.why: Para 16A(g) requires interim segment information only where Ind AS 108 requires that entity to disclose segment information in its ANNUAL financial statements, which is why the unlisted company gives none. For the listed company the paragraph asks for external and intersegment revenues where they are in or provided to the chief operating decision maker's measure, a measure of segment profit or loss, segment total assets and liabilities where regularly provided to that decision maker and materially changed since the last annual balance sheet, a description of any change in the basis of segmentation or measurement, and a reconciliation of the reportable segments' profit or loss to the entity's own.

options.text: Both companies must reproduce the full annual segment note in their interim reports
options.misconception: reads an interim report as a repetition of the annual statements rather than an update on them
options.why: Para 15 frames the interim report as an explanation of the events and transactions significant to understanding the changes since the last annual reporting period, and para 16A(g) accordingly asks for a short list rather than the whole annual note. It also does not reach an entity that is outside Ind AS 108 for its annual financial statements, so the unlisted company has nothing to give at all.

options.text: The listed company must disclose segment assets and liabilities in every interim report, whether or not they have changed since the last annual balance sheet
options.misconception: drops the two conditions the paragraph attaches to segment assets and liabilities
options.why: Para 16A(g) attaches two conditions to that particular disclosure — the amounts must be regularly provided to the chief operating decision maker, and there must have been a material change from the amount disclosed in the last annual financial statements. Both happen to be met here, so the figures do go in, but they would not go in a quarter where nothing had moved. The conditions are what keep an interim report an update rather than a reprint.

options.text: Neither need disclose any segment information, since an interim report carries only condensed financial statements
options.misconception: reads condensed as meaning the interim report carries no notes of its own
options.why: Condensed describes the primary statements, not the notes. Para 15 requires an explanation of what is significant to understanding the changes since the last annual reporting period, and para 16A lists what that explanation must contain, segment information among it for an entity that Ind AS 108 requires to disclose segments in its annual financial statements. A change in the basis of segmentation is exactly the kind of thing that explanation exists to carry, so the listed company must describe it.

citation.ref: para 16A(g), read with para 15

items.scenario: A listed company that discloses segment information in its annual financial statements publishes a half-yearly interim financial report. During the half year it changed the basis on which it identifies segments, and the total assets of one segment rose materially against the figure in the last annual balance sheet; those segment assets are regularly provided to the chief operating decision maker. An unlisted fellow subsidiary in the same group, which is not required by Ind AS 108 to disclose segment information annually, also publishes an interim report.

items.stem: How many of the three propositions are right, and why?

options.text: Only the first — a line item in the prescribed format is authority to recognise the item
options.misconception: reads a presentation format as a recognition rule
options.why: This is the exact confusion the study material warns against. Schedule III prescribes only presentation, and recognition is a subject matter of the Standards. A deferred tax asset is recognised when Ind AS 12 says it may be, and not because a line for it exists on a form.

options.text: Only the third — every company incorporated under the Act, insurers included, presents on the Schedule III format
options.misconception: misses the proviso to section 129(1)
options.why: The proviso to section 129(1) is what carves them out. Insurance companies and banking companies follow formats prescribed by their own regulators, and this has been recognised in the Companies Act, 2013 itself rather than being an industry practice.

options.text: Only the second — the horizontal format survives as an option for smaller companies
options.misconception: treats "minimum requirements" as permission to change the format itself
options.why: Minimum requirements means the minimum that must appear on the face; it is permission to add, not permission to restructure. Only the vertical format is prescribed and no horizontal alternative is offered, whatever the size of the company.

options.text: None of them — Schedule III fixes format and content but not accounting treatment, offers no horizontal alternative, and does not reach insurance or banking companies at all
options.why: Schedule III does not prescribe the accounting treatment to be adopted by the entity; it prescribes only the format and content, so the fact that a particular item has been included in the format of the balance sheet does not imply that the item can be recognised — that is a matter for the notified standards, to which Schedule III grants overriding status. In terms of format, Schedule III prescribes only the vertical format of the balance sheet and does not provide the alternative of using the horizontal format, though it does allow line items, sub-line items and sub-totals to be added or substituted where relevant. And the proviso to section 129(1) implies that the format set out in Schedule III will not apply to insurance companies and banking companies, whose formats are prescribed by their own regulators.

citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — Schedule III, read with the proviso to section 129(1)

items.scenario: A company's finance manager argues three things at a review meeting. First, that a deferred tax asset may be recognised because "Deferred tax assets" appears as a line in the Schedule III balance sheet format. Second, that the group's smallest subsidiary may present a horizontal balance sheet because Schedule III sets only minimum requirements. Third, that the group's insurance subsidiary must be recast into the Schedule III format before consolidation.

items.stem: What does the materiality judgement require here?

options.text: Disclose the commitments but omit the revenue stream, since a stream under five per cent of revenue is below any reasonable threshold
options.misconception: treats materiality as a percentage rule rather than a judgement about users
options.why: Materiality is what could influence the decisions users take on the basis of the financial statements, and a stream the company has publicly named as its strategic direction influences them. A percentage is evidence, not the test.

options.text: Omit both, since an item that fails the materiality test individually cannot be material
options.misconception: applies materiality item by item and never in aggregate
options.why: Aggregation is exactly where this test bites. Eleven immaterial commitments that total a material amount are a material commitment, and treating each in isolation is how an obligation of real size disappears from the notes.

options.text: Disclose everything, since more disclosure is always safer than less
options.misconception: mistakes volume for quality of disclosure
options.why: The lack of clarity in applying materiality is perceived as one of the main drivers of overloaded financial statements. Disclosing the immaterial buries the material, which is the opposite of what the filter is for.

options.text: Disclose both — the commitments because items immaterial individually are material in total, and the revenue stream because materiality is not settled by size alone
options.why: Materiality is the filter in deciding what information to disclose and what to omit, and it runs upwards as well as downwards. Individually each purchase of property, plant and equipment is immaterial, but the total amounts to a material commitment for the company and therefore some disclosure should be made regarding this commitment. The cloud-based revenue is under five per cent of the total, yet the company has communicated a strategic intention to focus its new development efforts there and the revenue has grown rapidly, so it decides to provide separate disclosure about that revenue stream in accordance with Ind AS 108 even though other revenue streams of similar size are typically combined into other revenue.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, materiality

items.scenario: A software company is drafting its notes. It has entered into eleven separate commitments to buy items of plant, each one small enough to be immaterial on its own, which together come to a material amount. It also has a cloud-based revenue stream that is under five per cent of total revenue but has grown rapidly, and about which the company has publicly told its stakeholders it intends to focus its new development efforts. Other revenue streams of similar size are combined into "other revenue". The preparer proposes to omit both, on the ground that neither is material on its own.

items.stem: What does best practice in presenting the notes require?

options.text: Keep every policy in the model set, since completeness protects against a charge of omission
options.misconception: equates completeness with copying a template
options.why: Disclosures should be relevant, specific to the company and explain how it applies its policies. Policy text about transactions the company does not enter into is not completeness; it is dilution.

options.text: Integrate each line item's note with its own policy and the key estimates behind it, keep all policies together, and disclose only the material ones
options.why: Notes cover the largest portion of the financial statements and have the greatest impact on how effectively they communicate, so the main note on a line item is integrated with its accounting policy and with any relevant key estimates and judgements — the inventory note carrying the cost formula, the net realisable value policy and the estimation uncertainty together. Accounting policies should be disclosed in one place and not scattered across various notes, which is why the write-off policy for assets costing less than five thousand rupees belongs with the accounting policy for fixed assets. And the financial statements should disclose only the material accounting policies, removing non-material text that adds no value.

options.text: Move the estimation uncertainty out of the notes entirely into the management commentary
options.misconception: relocates a required disclosure into unaudited narrative
options.why: Effective disclosure about the most difficult, subjective and complex estimates belongs with the item it relates to, with how the estimate was derived, the key assumptions, the review process and a sensitivity analysis. Management commentary sits alongside the financial statements; it does not stand in for them.

options.text: Leave the write-off policy where a reader of the fixed asset note will meet it, since context beats consistency
options.misconception: defends a scattered policy on the ground that it is near its subject
options.why: The study material gives this precise case as an observed failure. A policy stated inside the fixed asset note rather than in the accounting policy for fixed assets is a policy the reader looking for policies will not find.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — best practices, integration of notes

items.scenario: A reviewer finds three things in a draft annual report. The policy of writing off in full every asset costing less than five thousand rupees is stated inside the note on fixed assets rather than with the accounting policies. The estimation uncertainty in net realisable value sits in a separate section eleven pages away from the inventory note. And four pages of accounting policy text have been copied from a model set, covering transactions the company does not enter into.

items.stem: What is the correct treatment for the year ended 31 March 20X2?

options.text: Loan at ₹13,54,602 with the ₹1,45,398 charged to profit or loss on day one as a staff cost
options.misconception: expenses the concession at once rather than deferring it over the loan period
options.why: The difference is a benefit the employee earns by remaining in service, so it is deferred as prepaid employee cost and amortised over the loan period on a straight line basis, at ₹29,080 a year. Charging the whole of it in year one distorts the first year and leaves the following four carrying none of the cost.

options.text: Loan at ₹13,54,602, the ₹1,45,398 difference carried as prepaid employee cost and amortised at ₹29,080 a year, and finance income of ₹1,35,460 for the year
options.why: Ind AS 109 measures the loan on initial recognition at fair value, which is the contracted receipts discounted at the 10% market rate for a similar housing loan, giving ₹13,54,602 rather than the ₹15,00,000 disbursed. The ₹1,45,398 shortfall is not an expense of the year. It is the benefit the employee receives, and because the employee must stay in service to keep the concessional rate it is carried as prepaid employee cost and amortised over the five-year loan period on a straight line basis at ₹29,080 a year as an employee benefit under Ind AS 19, irrespective of the employee not being required to give any specific performance. Interest is then recognised as finance income at the effective interest rate of 10% — ₹13,54,602 at 10% is ₹1,35,460 for the first year — and not at the 6% contracted.

options.text: Loan at ₹15,00,000 with finance income recognised at 10%, being ₹1,50,000, and no employee cost
options.misconception: applies the market rate to the wrong carrying amount and never recognises the benefit
options.why: The effective interest rate is applied to the amortised cost, not to the cash advanced, so ₹1,50,000 is not the finance income of any period. Recognising income at the market rate while holding the asset at cost also makes the concession vanish, when the concession is precisely what the employee has been given.

options.text: The accountant is right — the loan is an asset of ₹15,00,000 and the income is the ₹90,000 actually contracted
options.misconception: records a financial asset at the cash disbursed rather than at fair value
options.why: A loan given to an employee below the market rate has a fair value below its proceeds, so the amount disbursed is not its initial measurement. Carrying it at ₹15,00,000 overstates the asset and understates both the employee cost and the finance income.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Analysis of Financial Statements — case study on a concessional staff housing loan, read with Ind AS 109 and Ind AS 19

items.scenario: On 1 April 20X1 Star Limited advanced a housing loan of ₹15,00,000 to an employee at 6% a year, repayable in five equal annual instalments of principal together with interest at each year end. The employee is not required to give any specific performance against the benefit. The market rate for a similar housing loan from a bank is 10% a year, and the present value of the contracted receipts discounted at 10% is given as ₹13,54,602. The accountant has recognised the loan at ₹15,00,000 and interest income of ₹90,000 for the year.

items.stem: Where is the colleague wrong?

options.text: Nowhere — the five he named are the five in the Code
options.misconception: carries independence across from the assurance rules into the general principles
options.why: Independence belongs to assurance engagements and has its own standards. Substituting it for professional competence and due care drops the principle a member in industry is most often held to, since he issues no audit opinion but does prepare the statements.

options.text: Independence is not one of the five; professional competence and due care is, and it is a principle the accountant must comply with like any other
options.why: The Code sets five fundamental principles of ethics for Chartered Accountants — integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, and professional behaviour — and an accountant shall comply with each of them. Independence is not among them. It is dealt with through the Independence Standards that apply to audits, reviews and other assurance engagements, which the study material expressly leaves to Paper 3. Professional competence and due care requires the accountant to attain and maintain professional knowledge and skill at the level needed to give competent service based on current technical and professional standards, and to act diligently in accordance with them.

options.text: He is right that competence is only a continuing education requirement, since the Code sets no knowledge standard
options.misconception: reduces a principle to an administrative obligation
options.why: Maintaining professional competence requires a continuing awareness and understanding of relevant technical, professional and business developments, and diligence means acting carefully, thoroughly and on time. The accountant must also take reasonable steps to see that those working under his authority have appropriate training and supervision. Hours attended are evidence of none of that on their own.

options.text: He is wrong only about the count — there are six principles, independence among them
options.misconception: adds a principle rather than replacing the wrong one
options.why: The Code lists five, not six. Adding independence to the list does not fix the omission of professional competence and due care, which is the actual error.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the fundamental principles

items.scenario: A newly qualified Chartered Accountant joins a listed company's finance team. A senior colleague tells him the Code of Ethics has five fundamental principles — integrity, objectivity, independence, confidentiality and professional behaviour — and that professional competence is not a principle at all but a matter of completing continuing education hours.

items.stem: What does the conceptual framework actually require?

options.text: Identify the threat, evaluate it and address it to an acceptable level, testing the conclusion against a reasonable and informed third party who need not be an accountant
options.why: The conceptual framework is applied in three steps — identify threats to compliance with the fundamental principles, evaluate the threats identified, and address the threats by eliminating them or reducing them to an acceptable level. Feeling uninfluenced is not any of those steps. The benchmark is the reasonable and informed third party test, which asks whether the same conclusions would likely be reached by another party weighing all the relevant facts and circumstances the accountant knows or could reasonably be expected to know at the time. That third party does not need to be an accountant, but would possess the relevant knowledge and experience to evaluate the appropriateness of the conclusions in an impartial manner.

options.text: Nothing further, since the accountant's own honest belief that he is unaffected settles the matter
options.misconception: substitutes the accountant's self-assessment for the framework
options.why: The framework exists because self-assessment is unreliable in exactly this position. One of the matters professional judgement requires the accountant to consider is whether his own preconception or bias might be affecting that judgement.

options.text: The appearance test can only be applied by another chartered accountant, so an outside opinion must be obtained before proceeding
options.misconception: reads "informed" as "professionally qualified"
options.why: The reasonable and informed third party does not need to be an accountant. The requirement is relevant knowledge and experience sufficient to understand and evaluate the conclusion impartially, which is a much wider group and is why the test is usable at all.

options.text: Every identified threat must be eliminated, so the accountant must in all cases withdraw from the work
options.misconception: allows only elimination where the Code allows reduction
options.why: Threats are addressed by eliminating them or by reducing them to an acceptable level. Withdrawing from the decision-making process is one action that might eliminate a threat, and restructuring or segregating responsibilities and obtaining appropriate oversight are safeguards that might reduce one. Which is right depends on the evaluation.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — the conceptual framework

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant in service is asked to value an investment in which his brother holds a stake. He tells his manager there is no problem because he personally does not feel influenced. The manager agrees, and adds that any question of how the arrangement looks from outside could only be settled by the opinion of another chartered accountant.

items.stem: Which of his three positions, if any, are right?

options.text: Only the refusal to reproduce the model and the refusal to the reviewer — an ICAI reviewer is a third party like any other
options.misconception: misses that a review by the Institute is itself a ground for disclosure
options.why: Complying with a peer review or quality review of the Institute, and responding to an inquiry or investigation by a professional or regulatory body, are both listed as circumstances where there is a professional duty or right to disclose. The reviewer is not an outsider to the profession's own arrangements.

options.text: All three — confidentiality is absolute once information has been acquired in an employment relationship
options.misconception: treats confidentiality as admitting no exception
options.why: Disclosure may be required by law, may be permitted by law and authorised by the client or employer, and may be the subject of a professional duty or right where the law does not prohibit it. An absolute rule would make peer review and the Institute's own investigations impossible.

options.text: Only the refusal to reproduce the model — the peer review carries a duty to disclose, and confidentiality never covers a fraud that ought to be reported
options.why: A Chartered Accountant continues to comply with the principle of confidentiality even after the relationship has ended, and on changing employment is entitled to use prior experience but shall not use or disclose confidential information acquired as a result of the earlier relationship, so the costing model may not be reproduced. Complying with the requirements of peer review or quality review of the Institute is one of the circumstances in which there is a professional duty or right to disclose, so refusing the reviewer is wrong. And hiding material facts which require disclosure, such as reporting fraud, illegal activities or non-compliance with laws and regulations, does not constitute confidentiality at all.
keywords: professional duty or right to disclose

options.text: None of them — once the relationship ends the duty ends, so he may use whatever he knows
options.misconception: reads the duty as expiring with the engagement
options.why: The accountant shall continue to comply with confidentiality even after the relationship with the client or employing organisation ends, and shall not use or disclose confidential information acquired or received during it. Only the general skill and experience he gained travels with him.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — confidentiality

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant leaves one employer for a competitor. Three things follow. His new employer asks him to reproduce the former employer's costing model from memory. A peer review of a former client's file is under way and the ICAI reviewer asks him for information, which he refuses on grounds of confidentiality. And he becomes aware of a fraud at the former employer that ought to be reported, and says confidentiality forbids him from reporting it.

items.stem: What does the Code require of him?

options.text: Sign it off, since he has escalated and the audit committee has taken the decision
options.misconception: treats escalation as discharging the responsibility
options.why: Escalation is a step, not a discharge. Where the accountant continues to have reason to believe the information is misleading after the organisation has failed to act, further actions remain open to him and the endpoint is refusing to remain associated with it.

options.text: Do nothing more, because the estimate is within the range the framework permits and choosing within a permitted range is not misconduct
options.misconception: treats a permitted range as licence to choose the outcome
options.why: The accountant shall not exercise discretion with the intention of misleading others or influencing contractual or regulatory outcomes inappropriately. Determining an estimate in order to misrepresent profit or loss is named as a misuse of discretion, and the intention is what makes it one.

options.text: Report to the regulator immediately, since the audit committee has refused
options.misconception: skips the remaining rungs of the ladder
options.why: Communicating to regulatory and oversight authorities is one of the later steps and is reached after consulting the Institute, the auditors or legal counsel and determining whether any requirement to communicate exists. Jumping to it also puts the principle of confidentiality, to which the accountant must remain alert throughout, needlessly at risk.

options.text: Neither of those two — work the escalation through, and if the information is still misleading after every feasible option, refuse to be or to remain associated with it, resigning if appropriate
options.why: Using an unrealistic estimate with the intention of avoiding violation of a contractual requirement such as a debt covenant is the Code's own example of influencing a contractual outcome inappropriately. The response is a ladder rather than a choice between its two ends. The accountant discusses the concern with his superior, management or those charged with governance and asks that the information be corrected and, where it has already been disclosed to the intended users, that they be told the correct position; consults the employing organisation's own ethics or whistle-blowing policy; then consults the Institute, the internal or external auditor, or legal counsel, and determines whether any requirement exists to communicate to third parties or to regulatory and oversight authorities. If after exhausting all feasible options he still has reason to believe the information is misleading, he shall refuse to be or to remain associated with the information, and in such circumstances it might be appropriate to resign.
keywords: refuse to be or to remain associated

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — preparation and presentation of information

items.scenario: A Chartered Accountant employed by a listed company finds that the draft results rest on an unrealistic estimate whose only effect is to keep the company inside a debt covenant. He raises it with the CFO, then with the audit committee, and both decline to change anything. A colleague tells him he now has two choices only — sign the pack off, or take the matter straight to the regulator.

items.stem: Under what provision, if any, can the CFO be held guilty?

options.text: Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule, for failing to exercise due diligence in the conduct of his professional duties
options.misconception: charges a member in service under a Part written for members in practice
options.why: Part I of the Second Schedule is headed professional misconduct in relation to Chartered Accountants in practice, and its ten clauses reach a member who certifies, reports or expresses an opinion. A CFO with no certificate of practice is outside it, which is why the Council Guidelines and Part II clause 1 exist.

options.text: Clause 1 of Part II of the Second Schedule — contravening any guidelines issued by the Council — read with the Council Guideline that an employee member shall exercise due diligence and not be grossly negligent
options.why: Clauses 5 to 8 of Part I of the Second Schedule are indeed written for a Chartered Accountant in practice, but Part II of the Second Schedule applies to members of the Institute generally, whether in practice or not. Its clause 1 makes a member guilty of professional misconduct where he contravenes any of the provisions of the Act or the regulations made thereunder or any guidelines issued by the Council, and the Council Guidelines state that a member of the Institute who is an employee shall exercise due diligence and shall not be grossly negligent in the conduct of his duties. Presenting receipts from the sale of property, plant and equipment and of investments as cash from operations, when Ind AS 7 classifies them within investing activities, is exactly that failure.
keywords: Part II of the Second Schedule

options.text: No provision reaches him, since the Schedules bind only members in practice
options.misconception: assumes the Act governs practice alone
options.why: Part II and Part III of the First Schedule, and Parts II and III of the Second Schedule, all reach members in service or members generally. The Council has power to inquire into misconduct that does not arise out of professional work at all, because a Chartered Accountant is expected to maintain the highest standards of integrity even in his personal affairs.

options.text: Part III of the Second Schedule, being other misconduct by a member whether in practice or not
options.misconception: reaches for the other-misconduct clause instead of the professional one
options.why: Part III of the Second Schedule holds a single clause, and it is triggered only where the member is held guilty by a civil or criminal court of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months. Misclassifying a cash flow is professional misconduct, and no court conviction is in question.

citation.ref: Ch. Professional and Ethical Duty of a Chartered Accountant — Second Schedule, read with the Council Guidelines and Ind AS 7

items.scenario: The directors of a company are entitled to an incentive computed on cash generated from operations. The company has lost cash from operations, so the CFO, who is a Chartered Accountant in employment and holds no certificate of practice, presents the proceeds of selling under-utilised equipment and investments inside cash from operations, which turns the figure positive. A colleague says he cannot be proceeded against, because clauses 5 to 8 of Part I of the Second Schedule are written for a Chartered Accountant in practice.

items.stem: What can the bots do, and what stays with people?

options.text: Only the data entry — the consolidation adjustments and the statements themselves must stay manual
options.misconception: understates what the technology already covers
options.why: The bots retrieve the consolidated data and apply the necessary consolidation adjustments, perform the calculations for non-controlling interests, equity and comprehensive income attributable to the parent, and generate the four statements. Restricting them to data entry leaves most of the three weeks where it was.

options.text: Everything including the accounting judgements, since the bots can be programmed with the standards
options.misconception: reads automation of rules as automation of judgement
options.why: A bot performs the calculations and applies the rules it has been given, which is why it is good at eliminations and currency conversion. Deciding whether an entity is controlled, or whether an estimate is reasonable, is not a rule waiting to be encoded.

options.text: The bots can extract and consolidate the subsidiary data, convert currencies, identify and eliminate intercompany transactions and produce the statements; the judgement calls stay with people
options.why: Robotic process automation uses software robots to automate manual and repetitive tasks by mimicking human interactions with digital systems. On a consolidation the bots extract the financial data from the subsidiary systems and consolidate it into the parent's, perform the necessary currency conversions, identify the intercompany transactions and generate the elimination entries Ind AS 110 requires so that nothing is counted twice, compute the amounts attributable to non-controlling interests, and generate the consolidated balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, statement of changes in equity and cash flow statement. The gain is accuracy, timely reporting, cost saving and data integrity. What a bot does not do is decide anything: it applies the rules it was given.

options.text: Nothing at all, since robotic process automation needs every subsidiary on one system first
options.misconception: confuses automation with system consolidation
options.why: The bots mimic a person's interactions with the existing systems, which is why they work across subsidiaries each maintaining their own financial data. Putting everyone on one system is an ERP question, not a condition of using bots.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — robotic process automation, read with Ind AS 110

items.scenario: A group with eleven subsidiaries, each on its own accounting system, spends three weeks of every quarter pulling trial balances into spreadsheets, converting currencies by hand, chasing intercompany balances and typing elimination entries. The CFO asks what robotic process automation could take over, and whether it would replace the group reporting manager.

items.stem: What are the two arrangements the CFO wants, and what does the IT head's proposal give up?

options.text: The accounting application is software as a service, and the developers need nothing beyond cloud storage
options.misconception: substitutes file storage for a development platform
options.why: Cloud storage lets users save and synchronise files across devices. It gives developers no runtime, no deployment and no managed infrastructure, which is the whole of what platform as a service provides.

options.text: Software as a service for the accounting application and platform as a service for the developers; buying servers is on-premise, and forgoes the pay-as-you-go scaling infrastructure as a service would give
options.why: Software as a service provides cloud-based applications that users access and use over the internet, which is what a subscription accounting and financial management application is. Platform as a service provides a cloud-based platform enabling developers to build, deploy and manage applications without the complexity of infrastructure management. Installing the application on servers in the company's own building is not cloud computing at all. Infrastructure as a service is what offers virtualised computing resources — servers, storage and networking — on a pay-as-you-go basis, allowing a business to scale its IT infrastructure based on demand without the need for physical hardware.

options.text: Both are infrastructure as a service, since in each case the provider owns the hardware
options.misconception: collapses the three service models into the one that rents hardware
options.why: The models differ by how much of the stack the provider runs. A finished application delivered over the internet is software as a service; a place to build and deploy applications is platform as a service; renting virtualised servers, storage and networking is infrastructure as a service.

options.text: The IT head is right — a private rack in the company's own building is cloud computing, since the finance team reaches it over the network
options.misconception: mistakes network access for the cloud service models
options.why: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet, letting accountants reach their data and software from any device with an internet connection. A traditional client-server architecture in a physical location the entity controls is the arrangement cloud computing is contrasted with.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — common applications of cloud computing

items.scenario: A mid-sized company is moving its finance function. The CFO wants a subscription accounting and financial management application that the team simply logs into, and a place for the in-house developers to build and run a customer portal without anyone managing servers. The IT head proposes instead to buy a rack of servers, install the accounting application on them in the company's own building, and call the result cloud.

items.stem: What does integrating internal control over financial reporting into the ERP actually require here?

options.text: Restrict every finance user to read-only access, since no one then posts anything wrong
options.misconception: replaces segregation of duties with a blanket lockout
options.why: The ERP enables segregation of duties, not the removal of duties. Roles and responsibilities in the closing and reporting process must be clearly defined, documented and communicated, and the people in those roles must have the qualifications, training and accounting knowledge to perform them.

options.text: Move the close out of the ERP into a controlled spreadsheet model, since the ERP has already failed
options.misconception: reads a configuration gap as a reason to abandon the system
options.why: The weaknesses are all things the ERP is designed to control and was not configured to — change management, the access matrix, the period configuration. Moving the close into spreadsheets gives up the audit trail, the segregation of duties and the single source of authentication that made the ERP worth having.

options.text: The monthly spreadsheet review is adequate, since a human reviewer catches anything a system rule would
options.misconception: substitutes a detective review for preventive system controls
options.why: A review after the close cannot stop a posting going into a closed period or record who approved a process change that left no log. Automating and standardising the procedures is what reduces manual effort and minimises the risk of errors; the review is what runs on top of it.

options.text: Use the ERP's own change management with the system logs and audit trail, a responsibility assignment matrix alongside the user access matrix, and the accounting period configuration controls that block backdating
options.why: Integrating internal control over financial reporting into an ERP puts the control inside the system. Changes to the financial closing and reporting process are tracked and validated through the ERP's change management functionality, and it is the system logs and audit trail that confirm the change was authorised by a designated individual with the appropriate authority. Roles are defined by reviewing the user access matrix configurations together with a responsibility assignment matrix, which records who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task. Postings in the wrong period are caught by the accounting period configuration controls and by comparing the posting date with the transaction date, which is also what prevents backdating and unauthorised adjustments. A spreadsheet review outside the system finds these afterwards, if at all.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — illustrative steps for integrating internal control over financial reporting within an ERP

items.scenario: An internal control review at a listed company finds three weaknesses. Changes were made to the financial closing and reporting process with no record of who authorised them. Several journal entries were posted into a period that had already been closed. And nobody can say which finance role is accountable for which step of the close. All the company's transactions run through an ERP. The finance head proposes a monthly spreadsheet review by a manager as the remedy for all three.

items.stem: How should the two incidents be characterised, and is the IT head right on either point?

options.text: A supply chain attack in both cases, because the first email impersonated a client
options.misconception: confuses impersonating a counterparty with compromising one
options.why: A supply chain attack compromises third-party software or hardware in order to gain access to a system or network. An email that merely looks as though it came from a client is phishing; no third-party product was subverted.

options.text: An insider threat followed by a denial of service attack, since a manager's own credentials were used and the firm was locked out
options.misconception: names the threats by their symptoms rather than their mechanism
options.why: An insider threat is a malicious action by an employee or other insider who has access; the manager here was deceived, not malicious. A denial of service attack overwhelms a system or network with traffic; encrypting files and demanding payment is ransomware.

options.text: A phishing attack followed by a ransomware attack; a firewall is one measure among several, and disclosure obligations do not turn on whether cash was lost
options.why: Tricking a user into clicking a malicious link or providing sensitive information is a phishing attack. Encrypting files or locking users out of systems and demanding a ransom payment in exchange for restoring access is a ransomware attack. Network security with firewalls is one proactive measure, but it sits alongside password management, encryption, access control limited to authorised personnel and reviewed as the management or employee structure changes, employee training, regular data backups stored securely, and an incident response plan setting out how an attack is detected, contained and mitigated — and it is training and access control, not a firewall, that address a manager typing his password into a fake page. Organisations have legal and ethical obligations to disclose cybersecurity incidents with financial implications, and the reporting guidelines of regulators such as SEBI and RBI address disclosure of such incidents, so the absence of a cash loss does not close the matter.

options.text: Two malware attacks; the IT head is right that a firewall would have stopped both
options.misconception: folds every incident into malware and treats perimeter security as complete
options.why: Malware is infecting computers or networks with malicious software that steals data or disrupts operations, and it is a different named threat from phishing and from ransomware. No firewall stops a person voluntarily entering credentials on a page he was directed to.

citation.source: ICAI Study Material, Paper 1 Financial Reporting
citation.ref: Ch. Accounting and Technology — common cybersecurity threats and proactive measures

items.scenario: An accounting firm is attacked twice in a fortnight. First a manager receives an email that looks like a client's and enters his credentials on the page it links to. A week later the firm's files are encrypted and a payment is demanded to unlock them. The IT head says a stronger firewall would have prevented both, and that since no money was actually paid and no client complained, nothing further need be considered.

items.stem: What would blockchain change that the group does not already have?

options.text: Past entries could be corrected in place across all systems at once, keeping the group's history consistent
options.misconception: treats an immutable ledger as an editable shared one
options.why: Transactions are recorded and stored in a transparent and tamper-proof manner, and the cryptography exists to prevent unauthorised modification. Consistency comes from there being one record, not from being able to rewrite the old ones everywhere at once.

options.text: The records would be centralised on the parent's server, so the subsidiaries stop keeping their own
options.misconception: describes a central database rather than a distributed ledger
options.why: A blockchain is a distributed network where information is shared and verified by multiple participants, which is what removes the need for intermediaries. Moving everything on to one company's server is the traditional centralised system it is contrasted with.

options.text: The director is right — the gain is speed of data entry and nothing more
options.misconception: reads blockchain as another input automation tool
options.why: Blockchain changes where the record lives and who can alter it, not how fast a document is read. The reconciliation effort the group is describing is precisely what a single shared ledger removes.

options.text: One shared, tamper-proof record instead of five to be reconciled, with an immutable audit trail the auditor can verify directly
options.why: A blockchain is a decentralised ledger in which each transaction is verified and encrypted so that unauthorised modification is prevented.
