citation.ref: the definition of those charged with governance and the determination of the appropriate person or persons within the entity's governance structure with whom to communicate, read with para 15 and para 16

items.stem: Which is the more reliable audit evidence under SA 500?

options.text: The photocopy, provided the client's finance head certifies it a true copy
options.misconception: cures a copy routed through the entity with a certificate from that same entity
options.why: The certificate comes from the party whose balance is being tested, so it adds nothing to the document it certifies. An original document is still more reliable than a photocopy, and evidence obtained directly by the auditor is still more reliable than evidence obtained indirectly.

options.text: The photocopy, because the document started outside the entity and external evidence outranks everything
options.misconception: keeps one reliability generalisation and drops the two the facts actually turn on
options.why: Evidence from independent sources outside the entity is more reliable, but that generalisation does not cancel the others. This document reached you as a copy and through the entity, so where it started is not the only thing to weigh.

options.text: The statement sent to you directly by the customer
options.why: SA 500's generalisations about reliability answer this in one line each. Audit evidence obtained directly by the auditor is more reliable than audit evidence obtained indirectly or by inference, and an original document is more reliable than a photocopy. The copy offered by the client loses on both counts at once, because it is a copy and because it travelled through the client's hands.

options.text: Neither — reliability is fixed by how much evidence is obtained, not by how it arrives
options.misconception: collapses appropriateness into sufficiency
options.why: Sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence and appropriateness the measure of its quality; reliability is one half of quality. How the evidence arrives is precisely what the reliability generalisations are about.

citation.ref: para 7

items.scenario: You need evidence over a customer balance. The client offers you a photocopy of the customer's signed statement of account. You could instead ask the customer to send the statement to you directly.

items.stem: May you describe the inventory misstatement as a key audit matter instead of qualifying the opinion?

options.text: No — communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances require one
options.why: SA 701 states its own limits, and this is the first of them: communicating key audit matters is not a substitute for the auditor expressing a modified opinion when the circumstances of the engagement require it under SA 705 (Revised). The matter is by its nature a key audit matter, but it is reported in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section, and the Key Audit Matters section carries a reference to that section rather than a description of the matter.

options.text: No — and because the opinion is qualified, the report carries no Key Audit Matters section at all
options.misconception: reads the bar on substitution as removing the section altogether
options.why: A qualified opinion does not remove the Key Audit Matters section; it changes what goes into it. The section is dropped only where the auditor disclaims an opinion, and even then only unless law or regulation requires key audit matters to be communicated. Here the section stays and refers to the Basis for Qualified Opinion section.

options.text: Yes, if those charged with governance agree to that treatment
options.misconception: makes a requirement of the standard negotiable with the entity
options.why: Those charged with governance are told about the matter; they do not choose the form of the report. SA 701 leaves no discretion here, and agreement cannot convert a required modification into a key audit matter.

options.text: Yes, provided the description is full enough for a reader to understand the misstatement
options.misconception: treats a well-written description as doing the work of a modification
options.why: However well written, a description in the Key Audit Matters section is not an opinion. SA 701 says communicating a key audit matter is not a substitute for a modified opinion, and the opinion is what a user reads first.

citation.ref: para 4 and para 14

items.scenario: You have concluded that a qualified opinion is required because of an uncorrected material misstatement in inventory. The entity is listed, so your report carries a Key Audit Matters section.

items.stem: What does SA 200 mean by professional skepticism?

options.text: An attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions which may indicate possible misstatement, and a critical assessment of audit evidence
options.why: That is the definition. Professional skepticism is a questioning mind, alertness to conditions which may indicate possible misstatement due to error or fraud, and a critical assessment of audit evidence. It is a way of handling evidence rather than an opinion about people, and SA 200 requires the audit to be planned and performed with it.
keywords: conditions which may indicate possible misstatement

options.text: An attitude required only once fraud risk factors have been identified
options.misconception: switches skepticism on at a trigger, when the standard requires it throughout the audit
options.why: SA 200 requires the audit to be planned and performed with professional skepticism throughout, not from the moment something goes wrong. Waiting for a fraud risk factor to appear is how the conditions that would have shown one get missed.

options.text: A duty to verify every transaction rather than to test a sample
options.misconception: turns an attitude towards evidence into a rule about how much testing is done
options.why: Professional skepticism does not by itself change the extent of testing; it changes how the evidence obtained is weighed. An audit remains selective, and what it delivers is reasonable assurance, not absolute assurance.

options.text: A working assumption that management is dishonest until the evidence shows otherwise
options.misconception: pushes the questioning mind into a presumption of dishonesty the standard does not make
options.why: SA 200 sets neither presumption. The auditor may accept records and documents as genuine unless he has reason to believe the contrary, so professional skepticism does not begin by assuming dishonesty; it begins by refusing to assume honesty either.
keywords: accept records and documents as genuine

citation.ref: para 15

items.stem: Which paragraph does SA 706 (Revised) provide for this, and what must it say about your opinion?

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which qualifies the opinion to the extent of the matter
options.misconception: believes the paragraph modifies the opinion it sits beside
options.why: Neither paragraph modifies the opinion. Modification is governed by SA 705 (Revised), and the Emphasis of Matter paragraph exists precisely for a matter that does not require one — which is why it must state that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.
keywords: opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

options.text: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph, which must state that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter
options.why: An Emphasis of Matter paragraph refers to a matter presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is, in the auditor's judgement, of such importance that it is fundamental to users' understanding of the financial statements. Because the paragraph is not a modification, it must carry a clear reference to the matter and to where the relevant disclosures can be found, and must state that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter.
keywords: presented or disclosed in the financial statements
opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

options.text: No paragraph — a matter already disclosed in a note needs nothing further in the report
options.misconception: reads a disclosure as leaving the auditor nothing to draw attention to
options.why: The Emphasis of Matter paragraph is for a matter that is disclosed and is nevertheless fundamental to users' understanding. Its whole purpose is to point at a disclosure, so the presence of the note is the condition for the paragraph rather than an answer to it.

options.text: An Other Matter paragraph, which must state that the opinion is not modified
options.misconception: reaches for the paragraph reserved for matters the financial statements do not carry
options.why: An Other Matter paragraph is for a matter not presented or disclosed in the financial statements that is relevant to users' understanding of the audit, the auditor's responsibilities or the auditor's report. This matter sits in a note, so the Emphasis of Matter paragraph is the one that fits.
keywords: not presented or disclosed in the financial statements

citation.ref: para 8 on the condition for an Emphasis of Matter paragraph and para 10 on an Other Matter paragraph, with the content requirements including the statement that the auditor's opinion is not modified in respect of the matter

items.scenario: A note to the financial statements sets out an uncertainty over a major litigation. You judge the note fundamental to users' understanding, and the matter does not require you to modify your opinion.

items.stem: Does SA 200 allow that reasoning?

options.text: Yes — reasonable assurance is not absolute assurance, and this shortfall is what that phrase describes
options.misconception: uses the limits on assurance to excuse a procedure that was simply not performed
options.why: Reasonable assurance describes what a properly performed audit delivers, not what an incomplete one may claim. The inherent limitations arise from the nature of financial reporting, the nature of audit procedures and the need to finish in a reasonable time at a reasonable cost — and the standard says in terms that they are not a basis for being satisfied with evidence that is less than persuasive.

options.text: Yes, provided the file records that the procedure was omitted for cost reasons
options.misconception: treats documenting a gap as closing it
options.why: Writing down why a procedure was skipped does not supply the evidence it would have produced. The matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for omitting an audit procedure for which there is no alternative, whether or not the reason is on the file.

options.text: No — but the answer is to disclaim an opinion at once, the budget being a limitation on scope
options.misconception: jumps to a disclaimer without first performing the procedure that is available
options.why: The limitation here is the firm's own budget, not one imposed by the entity or by circumstances, and the first answer is to perform the procedure. A modification follows an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence after the auditor has done what he can, and is not a shortcut past it.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: No — the inherent limitations of an audit are not a basis for being satisfied with evidence that is less than persuasive, and cost is not in itself a reason to omit a procedure with no alternative
options.why: SA 200 does say that reasonable assurance is high but not absolute because an audit has inherent limitations. It then refuses the inference the senior is drawing. Those limitations are not a basis for the auditor to be satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, and the matter of difficulty, time or cost involved is not in itself a valid basis for omitting an audit procedure for which there is no alternative.

citation.ref: para 5 read with the inherent limitations of an audit, the rule that they are not a basis for being satisfied with audit evidence that is less than persuasive, and the rule that difficulty, time or cost is not in itself a valid basis for omitting an audit procedure for which there is no alternative

items.scenario: A procedure over a material balance would take three more weeks and cost more than the fee left in the budget, and there is no alternative procedure that reaches the same assertion. The senior proposes to omit it and to note in the file that an audit gives reasonable assurance and not absolute assurance.

items.stem: What opinion does SA 570 (Revised) require?

options.text: An unmodified opinion with a Material Uncertainty Related to Going Concern section, the disclosure being adequate
options.misconception: applies the treatment for an adequately disclosed uncertainty to a basis that is itself wrong
options.why: That treatment belongs to a different case — where the use of the going concern basis is appropriate but a material uncertainty exists and is adequately disclosed. Here the basis itself is inappropriate, and SA 570 (Revised) gives that case its own outcome.

options.text: An adverse opinion
options.why: Where the financial statements have been prepared using the going concern basis of accounting but, in the auditor's judgement, management's use of that basis is inappropriate, SA 570 (Revised) requires an adverse opinion. A full and accurate note does not rescue it, because the basis of preparation runs through every figure rather than through one disclosure.

options.text: A disclaimer of opinion, the entity's future being unknowable
options.misconception: treats a judgement the auditor has already reached as an inability to obtain evidence
options.why: A disclaimer of opinion answers an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Here the auditor has reached a judgement — that the basis is inappropriate — so the evidence problem the disclaimer exists for does not arise.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: A qualified opinion, the note confining the effect to one disclosure
options.misconception: grades the effect as if it were confined to a single line item
options.why: The going concern basis is not one line item. It touches classification, measurement and every figure that depends on the entity continuing, so its effects are pervasive and the adverse opinion is the one SA 570 (Revised) names for this case.

citation.ref: para 21

items.scenario: Management has prepared the financial statements on the going concern basis of accounting. In your judgement its use of that basis is inappropriate. The position is disclosed fully and accurately in a note.

items.stem: What does Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule require of you?

options.text: Communicate with him in writing before accepting the appointment
options.why: Clause 8 makes it professional misconduct to accept a position as auditor previously held by another chartered accountant without first communicating with him in writing. Two things follow. The communication must be in writing, so a telephone call does not discharge it whatever was said on it. And his permission is not what the clause asks for — a no objection is neither required nor sufficient, because the purpose is to learn whether the change hides something you should weigh.

options.text: Communicate in writing after accepting, so that the company's appointment is not delayed
options.misconception: moves a step the clause puts before acceptance to after it
options.why: The clause says without first communicating with him in writing, so the communication comes before acceptance. Writing afterwards tells the outgoing auditor about a decision instead of informing it.
keywords: first communicating with him in writing

options.text: Nothing further — he has given his no objection, which is what the clause is for
options.misconception: reads the clause as requiring the predecessor's consent rather than a communication from you
options.why: The clause asks you to communicate, not to obtain consent. A no objection given on the telephone leaves nothing in writing at all, and consent was never the test the clause sets.

options.text: Communicate in writing only if he was removed rather than having retired
options.misconception: limits a clause that applies to any position previously held by another chartered accountant
options.why: Clause 8 applies wherever the position was previously held by another chartered accountant, whatever the reason he left. Nothing in it turns on whether that was removal, resignation or retirement.
keywords: previously held by another chartered accountant

citation.ref: First Schedule Part I, Clause 8

items.scenario: You are offered the statutory audit of a company whose retiring auditor is a chartered accountant. You telephone him. He says he has no objection, and asks you not to put anything in writing.

items.stem: What does section 140(1) require before he can be removed?

options.text: A resolution of the Board alone, the Board having a power to remove what it appointed
options.misconception: gives the Board a power of removal that the section gives the members with government approval
options.why: The Board's resolution starts the process — it is the resolution from which the thirty days for the application to the Central Government run — but it removes nobody. Removal needs the approval and then the special resolution.

options.text: A special resolution of the company, passed after the previous approval of the Central Government, with the auditor given a reasonable opportunity of being heard
options.why: Section 140(1) allows removal before the expiry of the term only by a special resolution of the company and only after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government, and its proviso requires that the auditor concerned be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard. The word previous fixes the order — approval first, resolution second.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

options.text: A special resolution first, with the Central Government's approval sought afterwards
options.misconception: reverses an order the section fixes with the word previous
options.why: The section says previous approval of the Central Government, so the approval comes before the general meeting. Rule 7 sets the same sequence — the Board resolves, the application goes to the government, and the special resolution follows the approval.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

options.text: An ordinary resolution of the members in general meeting
options.misconception: downgrades the special resolution the section names and drops the government approval entirely
options.why: Section 140(1) names a special resolution, and that is not the only requirement — the previous approval of the Central Government has to come first. An ordinary resolution would let a simple majority end a tenure the Act deliberately protects.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with Rule 7(1), Rule 7(2) and Rule 7(3) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A company's board is unhappy with its statutory auditor, who was appointed two years ago for a five-year term, and wants him out before that term ends.

items.stem: Which wording does SA 705 (Revised) require in the Opinion section?

options.text: Except for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) uses two phrasings and the difference is the reason for the modification. A qualified opinion arising from a material misstatement says except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section. A qualified opinion arising from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence says except for the possible effects, because the auditor does not know what the missing evidence would have shown.
keywords: inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

options.text: Because of the significance of the matter described, the financial statements do not give a true and fair view
options.misconception: takes the adverse opinion's wording for a qualification
options.why: That sentence is the adverse opinion. It is used where misstatements are both material and pervasive, and it says the statements as a whole are wrong rather than that one area is unresolved.

options.text: We do not express an opinion on the financial statements
options.misconception: takes the disclaimer's wording for a qualification
options.why: That is the disclaimer of opinion, used where the possible effects of an inability to obtain evidence could be both material and pervasive. Here the effects are material but not pervasive, so the report still carries an opinion.

options.text: Except for the effects of the matter described in the Basis for Qualified Opinion section
options.misconception: uses the misstatement wording where the reason for the qualification is missing evidence
options.why: Except for the effects belongs to a known misstatement, whose amount the auditor has measured. Here nothing has been measured, so the wording is except for the possible effects — the qualification is about what might be there.

citation.ref: para 16 on the heading of the Opinion section, read with the wording of a qualified opinion — except for the effects where the modification arises from a material misstatement, and except for the possible effects where it arises from an inability to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence

items.scenario: You are qualifying your opinion because you could not obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over a branch's inventory. The effects are material but not pervasive.

items.stem: Is that interest part of his total income in India?

options.text: Yes, because India taxes its citizens on their worldwide income
options.misconception: makes citizenship the test where the Act uses residential status
options.why: Citizenship decides nothing under section 5. Residential status does, and a non-resident is charged only on income received or deemed to be received in India and on income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India.

options.text: Yes, once he remits the money to India, because it is then received in India
options.misconception: reads a later remittance as a receipt, when received means first received
options.why: Received in section 5 means first received. Money that accrued abroad and was later remitted to India is not received in India, and Explanation 1 to section 5 adds that income once included on the basis of accrual is not included again when it is received.

options.text: No, because neither limb of section 5(2) reaches it
options.why: Section 5(2) limits a non-resident's total income to two limbs — income received or deemed to be received in India, and income accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India. Interest that accrues in Singapore and is credited to a Singapore account satisfies neither. The third limb, income accruing or arising outside India, belongs to a resident and ordinarily resident alone.
keywords: received or deemed to be received in India
accruing or arising or deemed to accrue or arise in India

options.text: No, but a resident but not ordinarily resident would be taxed on it
options.misconception: attaches the not-ordinarily-resident window to a kind of income the proviso does not cover
options.why: The proviso to section 5(1) adds exactly one thing to the charge on a resident but not ordinarily resident — income which accrues or arises outside India from a business controlled in or a profession set up in India. Foreign bank interest is not that, so it would stay out of his total income too.
keywords: business controlled in or a profession set up in India

citation.ref: Section 5(2) read with the proviso to Section 5(1) and Explanation 1 to Section 5

items.scenario: Mr Rao is a non-resident for previous year 2025-26. He earns interest on a deposit with a bank in Singapore, credited to his Singapore account. He controls no business from India.

items.stem: Is he resident for the year?

options.text: Yes, on the first basic condition alone
options.why: Section 6(1) gives two basic conditions and either one is enough. The first is presence in India for 182 days or more in the previous year, which 200 days satisfies. The second — 60 days in the year plus 365 days across the four preceding years — therefore never has to be looked at.

options.text: No, because both conditions must be met and his stay in the four preceding years is not given
options.misconception: reads two alternative conditions as cumulative
options.why: The conditions in section 6(1) are alternatives, joined by or. Satisfying either makes an individual resident, which is why the four preceding years never arise once the 182-day test is met.

options.text: No, because an Indian citizen is tested against 120 days and he becomes resident but not ordinarily resident
options.misconception: applies the visiting-citizen relaxation to a citizen who never left India
options.why: The 120-day figure belongs to a citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India whose Indian income exceeds the prescribed limit, and the stretch to 182 days belongs to a citizen leaving India for employment or as crew. Mr Sethi is neither, so the ordinary conditions apply and the 182-day one is already met.
keywords: person of Indian origin visiting India

options.text: No, because presence alone does not make a person resident unless he also has income in India
options.misconception: adds an income test that the residence section does not contain
options.why: Residence under section 6 is decided by physical presence. What income he has, and where it arises, is what section 5 does with the answer afterwards — it is not part of the test.

citation.ref: Section 6(1)

items.scenario: Mr Sethi, an Indian citizen, was in India for 200 days during previous year 2025-26. He did not leave India for employment or as a member of a crew, and he is not a citizen or person of Indian origin visiting India.

items.stem: Under section 263, in what circumstances may the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner revise an assessment order?

options.text: On an application by the assessee, where the order is prejudicial to him
options.misconception: swaps section 263 for the assessee's own revision route
options.why: Section 263 runs in the revenue's favour and the Commissioner exercises it himself. The assessee's route is section 264, under which the Commissioner may revise an order in a way that is not prejudicial to the assessee.

options.text: Only where the order is both erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue
options.why: Section 263 sets two conditions and they are cumulative. The order must be erroneous, and it must be prejudicial to the interests of the revenue. An order that is wrong but costs the revenue nothing fails the second condition, and an order the Commissioner merely disagrees with fails the first, because a view that is a possible view taken after real enquiry is not erroneous.
keywords: prejudicial to the interests of the revenue

options.text: Wherever the order is erroneous, whether or not any revenue was lost
options.misconception: drops the second of two cumulative conditions
options.why: Erroneous alone is not enough. Section 263 requires the order to be prejudicial to the interests of the revenue as well, so an error that changes no tax is outside the section.
keywords: prejudicial to the interests of the revenue

options.text: Wherever the Commissioner prefers a different view of the same material
options.misconception: treats a difference of opinion as an error in the order
options.why: A view the officer took after real enquiry, being a possible view, is not erroneous merely because the Commissioner would have taken another. What the section reaches is no enquiry where enquiry was called for.
keywords: no enquiry where enquiry was called for

citation.ref: Section 263(1)

items.stem: What does section 154 allow him to do?

options.text: Nothing, since section 154 is exercised only by the authority of its own motion
options.misconception: removes the assessee's express right to apply for a rectification
options.why: Section 154(2)(b) says the opposite. An amendment may be made on an application made by the assessee, and where he applies, the authority must pass an order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is received.

options.text: Apply for rectification, an intimation under section 143(1) being one of the things the section reaches
options.why: Section 154 lets an income-tax authority amend any order it has passed and any intimation under section 143(1), to rectify a mistake apparent from the record. The power is not confined to the authority's own motion — an amendment may be made on an application made by the assessee — and an arithmetical error is the plainest kind of mistake there is.

options.text: Nothing, since an intimation under section 143(1) is not an order and so falls outside section 154
options.misconception: excludes a document that section 154 names in terms
options.why: Section 154 names an intimation under section 143(1) among the things that may be amended, alongside any order passed by the authority. Nothing turns on whether an intimation is called an order.

options.text: Appeal instead, rectification being available only where two views of the point are possible
options.misconception: inverts the test, which excludes debatable points rather than requiring them
options.why: A point on which two views are reasonably possible is outside section 154, not inside it — that is what T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers decided. Rectification is for a mistake apparent from the record, and an arithmetical error is exactly that.

citation.ref: Sections 154(1) and 154(2)(b), read with T.S. Balaram v. Volkart Brothers (1971) 82 ITR 50 (SC)

items.scenario: An assessee spots an arithmetical error in an intimation issued to him under section 143(1) and wants it put right.

items.stem: May the long-term capital loss be set off against the short-term capital gain?

options.text: Yes — a loss under the head capital gains may be set off against any income under that head
options.misconception: applies the rule written for a short-term capital loss to a long-term one
options.why: That freedom belongs to a short-term capital loss under section 70(2). Section 70(3) confines a long-term capital loss to a long-term capital gain, and reading the two the same way deletes a restriction the Act writes out.

options.text: No — a long-term capital loss may be set off only against a long-term capital gain
options.why: The asymmetry is the point of the two sub-sections. Section 70(2) lets a short-term capital loss be set off against income under the head capital gains in respect of any capital asset, long-term or short-term. Section 70(3) runs the other way and confines a long-term capital loss to a long-term capital gain. So the ₹4,00,000 loss waits and the short-term gain is taxed.

options.text: Yes, and any balance may then be set off against his salary income
options.misconception: opens a head that the Act closes to capital losses altogether
options.why: Section 71(3) says a loss under capital gains cannot be set against income under any other head, so a capital loss can never reduce salary, house property or business income. The first half of the answer is wrong too, a long-term loss meeting only a long-term gain.

options.text: No, and the loss lapses, a capital loss not being capable of being carried forward
options.misconception: denies a carry forward that section 74 expressly grants
options.why: Section 74 carries the unabsorbed loss forward for eight assessment years immediately succeeding, and the same restriction follows it. Section 80 adds one condition, that the loss be determined in a return furnished within the time allowed under section 139(1).

citation.ref: Sections 70(2), 70(3) and 71(3), read with Section 74

items.scenario: In previous year 2025-26 Mr Iyer has a long-term capital loss of ₹4,00,000 and a short-term capital gain of ₹4,00,000. He has no other capital transaction.

items.stem: Which of the two survives the late return?

options.text: The business loss, the return having been filed and section 80 asking only that one be filed
options.misconception: reads section 80 as requiring a return rather than a timely one
options.why: Section 80 requires the loss to be determined in a return furnished within the time allowed under section 139(1). A late return is not a timely one, so the business loss does not carry forward.
keywords: within the time allowed under section 139(1)

options.text: Neither — a late return forfeits everything carried from that year
options.misconception: extends a bar written for losses to an allowance that section 32(2) keeps outside it
options.why: Unabsorbed depreciation is not a loss for this purpose. Section 32(2) gives it three privileges a business loss does not have — set off against income under any head except salaries, a carry forward with no eight-year limit, and survival of a return filed late.

options.text: The unabsorbed depreciation
options.why: Section 32(2) deems unabsorbed depreciation to be part of the depreciation allowance of the following year, which puts it outside the machinery that governs a loss. Section 80 makes a timely return the price of carrying a business loss forward and does not reach unabsorbed depreciation. So the business loss is gone and the depreciation survives.

options.text: Both — a late return delays the assessment but takes away no allowance
options.misconception: treats the timing of the return as an administrative matter with no consequence
options.why: The timing is the condition, not a formality. Section 80 withholds the carry forward of a business loss where the return was not furnished in time, which is why two items arising in the same year part company here.

citation.ref: Section 32(2) read with Section 80 and Section 139(1)

items.scenario: A company filed the return for its loss year after the due date under section 139(1). From that year it carries both a business loss and unabsorbed depreciation.

items.stem: Which test does the Article 4(2) tie-breaker apply first?

options.text: The competent authorities settle it by mutual agreement
options.misconception: reaches for the last resort before the tests that precede it
options.why: The mutual agreement procedure is where Article 4(2) ends, not where it begins. It is used only if he is a national of both States or of neither, after the permanent home, the centre of vital interests and the habitual abode have all failed.

options.text: The State in which he has a permanent home available to him
options.why: Article 4(2) is a ladder climbed in order and abandoned the moment one rung decides. The first rung is the State in which he has a permanent home available to him. Only if a permanent home is available to him in both States, or in neither, does the tie-breaker move on to the centre of vital interests, then to the habitual abode, then to nationality, and last of all to mutual agreement between the competent authorities.

options.text: The State of which he is a national
options.misconception: starts at the fourth rung of a ladder that has to be climbed in order
options.why: Nationality is a tie-breaker test, but it is reached only after the permanent home, the centre of vital interests and the habitual abode have each failed to settle the question. Starting there skips three tests the Article puts first.

options.text: The State in which he spent more days during the fiscal year
options.misconception: imports a day-count test from domestic law into a tie-breaker that has none
options.why: Days decide residence under section 6 of the Income-tax Act; Article 4(2) does not count them. The nearest thing in the Article is the habitual abode, and that is the third test rather than the first.

citation.source: OECD Model Tax Convention on Income and on Capital
citation.ref: Article 4(2), as adopted in India's double taxation avoidance agreements, read with Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: An individual is a resident of both India and the other contracting State under each country's own domestic law. The treaty follows the OECD Model.

items.stem: In which previous year is the ₹8,00,000 deductible?

options.text: Previous year 2025-26
options.why: Section 43B allows certain sums, taxes and duties among them, only when actually paid, whatever the books accrue. Its proviso is what rescues this company — where the sum is actually paid on or before the due date for furnishing the return of income under section 139(1) for that previous year, the deduction is allowed in that previous year. So the ₹8,00,000 goes against 2025-26.
keywords: due date for furnishing the return

options.text: In no year — a sum outstanding at the end of the previous year is permanently disallowed
options.misconception: reads section 43B as a disallowance when it is a timing rule
options.why: Section 43B postpones a deduction; it does not destroy one. A sum paid after the due date for furnishing the return is deductible in the year of actual payment, and a sum paid on or before that date is deductible in the year of accrual.
keywords: due date for furnishing the return

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, because the payment had to be made before the end of previous year 2025-26 to count
options.misconception: measures the deadline from the end of the previous year rather than from the due date for the return
options.why: Section 43B's proviso measures the deadline from the due date for furnishing the return of income under section 139(1), not from the last day of the previous year. A payment made in the gap between those two dates still earns the deduction in the earlier year.
keywords: due date for furnishing the return

options.text: Previous year 2026-27, being the year in which the money was paid
options.misconception: applies the main rule and misses the proviso that reads the payment back into the earlier year
options.why: The main rule is stated correctly and the proviso has been missed. A payment made on or before the due date for furnishing the return is read back into the previous year to which the liability relates, so it does not wait for the year of payment.
keywords: due date for furnishing the return

citation.ref: Section 43B with its first proviso, read with Section 139(1)

items.scenario: A company's books for previous year 2025-26 carry unpaid sales tax of ₹8,00,000. It pays the whole amount after the end of that previous year but before the due date for furnishing its return of income under section 139(1) for that year.

items.stem: How much of the ₹1,20,000 is disallowed?

options.text: Nothing, the expense being genuine and the supplier identified
options.misconception: reads a rule about the mode of payment as a rule about bogus expenditure
options.why: Genuineness is not the test. Section 40A(3) looks only at the amount, the person, the day and the mode of payment, which is why a wholly genuine purchase paid in cash above the limit is disallowed in full.

options.text: Nothing this year, the amount becoming deemed profit of the following year instead
options.misconception: applies the sub-section written for a payment made in a year later than the deduction
options.why: Section 40A(3A) is for a different sequence — an expense allowed on accrual in an earlier year and then actually paid in cash beyond the limit, which is deemed profit of the payment year. Here the expense and the cash payment fall in the same year, so the disallowance bites now.

options.text: Only the excess over the prescribed limit
options.misconception: treats the section as a cap on the deduction rather than a disallowance of the payment
options.why: The section is not a cap. Once a payment crosses the limit and fails the mode test, the whole of that payment is disallowed rather than the part above the limit.

options.text: The whole ₹1,20,000
options.why: Section 40A(3) disallows the expenditure in full where the payment, or the aggregate of payments to one person in a day, exceeds the prescribed limit and is made otherwise than by an account payee cheque, an account payee bank draft or a prescribed electronic mode. There is no proportionate disallowance, and the genuineness of the expense and the identity of the payee do not save it.

citation.ref: Section 40A(3) read with Section 40A(3A)

items.scenario: A firm pays one supplier ₹1,20,000 in cash on a single day for goods purchased in the same previous year. The expense is genuine and the supplier is identified. The payment is above the limit prescribed by section 40A(3) and was not made by an account payee cheque, an account payee bank draft or a prescribed electronic mode.

items.stem: How does the Act choose between the prescribed methods of determining the arm's length price of an international transaction?

options.text: By the method that produces the lower income for the assessee, doubt being resolved in his favour
options.misconception: turns a selection test into a taxpayer-favourable presumption
options.why: The outcome does not select the method. Section 92C selects it by appropriateness to the transaction, the functions performed and the data available, so a method chosen because it produces a smaller figure is chosen on the wrong ground.

options.text: By whichever method the Transfer Pricing Officer names, the choice being his
options.misconception: hands a test applied to the facts to an officer's preference
options.why: The most appropriate method is a test applied to the facts, and the assessee applies it in the first place. The Transfer Pricing Officer may disagree, but he too has to show why some other method is the more appropriate one.

options.text: By the comparable uncontrolled price method wherever it can be applied, the rules ranking it first
options.misconception: reads a preference practitioners often have as a statutory order of priority
options.why: No hierarchy ranks the methods. That method is often the strongest where genuine comparables exist, but that is a fact about the data rather than a rule of priority, and the statute asks only for the most appropriate method.

options.text: By the most appropriate method for that transaction, no method ranking above another
options.why: Section 92C requires the arm's length price to be determined by the most appropriate method, having regard to the nature of the transaction, the functions performed and the data available. Rule 10B lists the methods — comparable uncontrolled price, resale price, cost plus, profit split, transactional net margin and the other prescribed method — and no hierarchy ranks them.

citation.ref: Section 92C(1) read with Rule 10B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.stem: Does the warehouse give it a permanent establishment in India?

options.text: Yes, because the list in Article 5(2) names a branch and an office and a warehouse is the same kind of thing
options.misconception: reads an illustrative list as overriding an express exclusion
options.why: Article 5(2) is illustrative and lists a place of management, a branch, an office, a factory, a workshop, a mine or a quarry. A warehouse is not on it, and even a listed place is subject to Article 5(4) where it is maintained solely for an excluded activity.

options.text: No, because Article 5(4) excludes it
options.why: Article 5(1) defines a permanent establishment as a fixed place of business through which the business of the enterprise is wholly or partly carried on, and a warehouse would answer that description. Article 5(4) then takes it back out — a place maintained solely for the storage, display or delivery of goods belonging to the enterprise is excluded, as are places maintained solely for purchasing goods, collecting information, or any other activity of a preparatory or auxiliary character.

options.text: Yes, once the warehouse has been kept for longer than the period the treaty names for a project
options.misconception: applies the construction clause's time test to an ordinary fixed place of business
options.why: Article 5(3) is the construction clause and its time test belongs to a building site or an assembly or installation project. A warehouse is neither, so no length of time converts an excluded storage place into a permanent establishment.

options.text: Yes, a warehouse being a fixed place of business and Article 5(1) being satisfied
options.misconception: stops at the general definition without reading the exclusion that follows it
options.why: Article 5(1) is satisfied on its face, which is exactly why Article 5(4) exists. The exclusion removes a place maintained solely for the storage, display or delivery of goods, so the general definition does not settle the question by itself.

citation.ref: Article 5(1), 5(2), 5(3) and 5(4) of India's double taxation avoidance agreements on the OECD and UN Model pattern, read with Article 7 and Section 90(2) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: A German company keeps a warehouse in Chennai used solely for the storage and delivery of goods belonging to it. It has no other presence in India. The treaty follows the OECD Model.

items.stem: Is it an impermissible avoidance arrangement?

options.text: Yes, unless the company proves that obtaining the tax benefit was not the main purpose
options.misconception: turns the second limb into a burden of proof about the first
options.why: The second limb is not a defence about purpose; it is a separate requirement about the character of the arrangement. Even where a tax benefit is the main purpose, GAAR reaches the arrangement only if one of the four tainted elements is present.

options.text: Yes, obtaining a tax benefit being itself what makes an arrangement impermissible
options.misconception: collapses two cumulative limbs into the first one
options.why: A tax benefit is the trigger, not the offence. Without one of the four tainted elements the arrangement is legitimate planning, and reading the first limb alone would pull every deduction claimed under the Act into GAAR.

options.text: It cannot be decided — GAAR reaches any arrangement whose tax benefit exceeds the threshold in the rules
options.misconception: reads a monetary floor that keeps small arrangements out as a rule that pulls large ones in
options.why: The threshold in the rules is a floor below which GAAR is not invoked, and crossing it does not make an arrangement impermissible. The two limbs still have to be satisfied, and this arrangement fails the second.

options.text: No, because it carries none of the tainted elements
options.why: GAAR has two limbs and both must be satisfied. The main purpose of the arrangement must be to obtain a tax benefit, and the arrangement must also carry a tainted element — non-arm's-length dealings, misuse or abuse of the provisions of the Act, lack of commercial substance, or means not ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes. This arrangement carries none of the four, so what is left is legitimate planning.

citation.ref: Sections 95 and 96 read with Rule 10U of the Income-tax Rules, 1962

items.scenario: An arrangement gives a company a tax benefit. It is entered into at arm's length, has real commercial substance, does not misuse or abuse the provisions of the Act, and is carried out by means ordinarily employed for bona fide purposes.

items.stem: Can section 54 apply to the house she bought before the sale?

options.text: No, a purchase before the transfer counts only if the sale proceeds themselves were used
options.misconception: adds a tracing condition that section 54 does not impose
options.why: Section 54 asks that a residential house be bought or built inside the stated period. It does not ask that the very rupees from the sale be the rupees spent, and a purchase funded from a loan or from savings inside the window is as good.

options.text: No, only construction may straddle the date of transfer, not purchase
options.misconception: swaps the purchase window for the construction window
options.why: Construction has its own period of three years after the transfer and it runs only forwards. It is purchase that carries the one-year backward window, so the position is the reverse of this option.

options.text: No, the new house must be bought after the transfer and never before it
options.misconception: reads section 54 as forward-looking only and drops the backward window
options.why: The section names three periods and only two of them run forwards. A purchase within one year before the transfer is expressly allowed, so a rule that the new house must always come later is not in the text.

options.text: Yes, because section 54 allows a purchase made within one year before the date of transfer
options.why: Section 54(1) gives the assessee three windows for the new house, and one of them looks backwards: a residential house purchased within one year before the date of transfer qualifies exactly as one purchased within two years after it does. A house bought seven months before the sale falls inside that backward window, so the exemption is not lost merely because the purchase came first.
keywords: within one year before the date of transfer

citation.ref: Section 54(1)

items.scenario: Mrs Iyer sold a residential house on 10 December 2025 and the sale gave her a long-term capital gain. She had already bought another residential house in India on 5 May 2025, seven months before that sale. She buys nothing else.

items.stem: Has a transfer taken place for the purposes of capital gains?

options.text: No, a transfer needs consideration in money
options.misconception: requires money where the Act requires only consideration capable of valuation
options.why: Capital gains are computed on the full value of the consideration received, and consideration in kind is valued rather than ignored. If money were needed, an exchange could never be taxed and section 2(47) would not trouble to list it.

options.text: No, nothing was sold, so no transfer took place
options.misconception: reads transfer as sale alone when the definition is wider than that
options.why: Sale is one item on the list in section 2(47), not the whole of it. Exchange, relinquishment, extinguishment of rights and compulsory acquisition each stand on their own, so a transaction with no sale in it can still be a transfer.

options.text: Yes, but only because the two plots are of similar size
options.misconception: makes equality of value the test when the test is the nature of the transaction
options.why: Nothing in section 2(47) turns on whether the two assets are worth the same. The exchange is a transfer whatever the relative values, which affect the computation of the gain rather than whether a transfer happened at all.

options.text: Yes, because section 2(47)(i) counts an exchange as a transfer
options.why: Section 2(47)(i) defines transfer, in relation to a capital asset, to include the sale, exchange or relinquishment of the asset. An exchange is named in the same breath as a sale, so a swap of one plot for another is a transfer even though no money changes hands, and the value of the plot received becomes the full value of the consideration.

citation.ref: Section 2(47)(i) read with Section 45(1)

items.scenario: Mr Bhatt owns a plot in Nashik. He swaps it with his neighbour for a plot of similar size in the same colony. No money passes either way, and both plots are capital assets.

items.stem: Is the resulting capital gain long-term or short-term?

options.text: Short-term, but only because the block ceased to exist
options.misconception: attaches the deeming to one limb of section 50 when it governs both
options.why: Section 50 has two limbs — the excess of the sale money over the written down value where the block survives, and the position where the block ceases to exist. The gain is short-term under either, so the reason given here is too narrow.

options.text: Long-term, because the block itself had existed for more than thirty-six months
options.misconception: moves the holding-period test from the asset to the block and still applies it
options.why: Section 50 offers no holding-period test at any level. It converts the gain to short-term outright, so testing the age of the block answers a question the section never asks.

options.text: Short-term, because section 50 deems it so however long the block was held
options.why: Section 50 provides that where its conditions are met the capital gain shall be deemed to be the capital gain arising from the transfer of a short-term capital asset. The deeming is unconditional as to time, so nine years of holding makes no difference at all and the gain is short-term.
keywords: deemed to be the capital gain arising from the transfer of a short-term capital asset

options.text: Long-term, because the machines were held for more than thirty-six months
options.misconception: applies the ordinary holding-period test to a block on which depreciation was claimed
options.why: The period of holding decides the character of an ordinary capital asset, but section 50 overrides it for a depreciable asset forming part of a block. Once depreciation has been claimed, both the arithmetic and the character come from section 50.

citation.ref: Section 50 read with Section 2(42B)

items.scenario: Sundar Ltd sold the last machine in its plant and machinery block on 2 February 2026. The machines in that block had been bought nine years earlier. The sale money exceeded the written down value of the block, and the block ceased to exist.

items.stem: Is the exemption available to her?

options.text: No, because a gain on unlisted shares is outside the capital gains charge altogether
options.misconception: confuses ineligibility for one exemption with being outside the charge
options.why: Unlisted shares are capital assets and their transfer is fully chargeable under section 45. What fails here is the exemption in section 54EC, not the charge itself.

options.text: Yes, because the bonds are of a body notified for the purposes of section 54EC
options.misconception: checks the bond and forgets the asset that produced the gain
options.why: The identity of the bond issuer is one requirement and the identity of the asset sold is another. Both have to hold, and here the asset sold was shares.

options.text: Yes, any long-term capital gain qualifies if the bonds are bought in time
options.misconception: treats the six-month window as the only condition and drops the asset test
options.why: Time is the second condition and not the first. Section 54EC applies only where the gain arose on land or building or both, and an investment made well inside the period does not repair a gain that never qualified.

options.text: No, because section 54EC covers a gain on land or building or both and not a gain on shares
options.why: Section 54EC(1) opens with a capital gain arising from the transfer of a long-term capital asset, being land or building or both. The nature of the asset sold is a gate rather than a detail, so a gain on shares cannot enter the section however promptly the bonds are bought.

citation.ref: Section 54EC(1)

items.scenario: Ms Kulkarni made a long-term capital gain on the sale of unlisted shares in January 2026. Within a month she invested the whole of that gain in bonds notified for section 54EC and claims the exemption.

items.stem: Can section 50C be applied to this sale?

options.text: Yes, provided the Assessing Officer first refers the matter to a Valuation Officer
options.misconception: treats the valuation reference as a way in when it is a step inside the section
options.why: A reference to a Valuation Officer is machinery that runs once section 50C already applies. It cannot extend the section to an asset the section does not cover.

options.text: No, because section 50C reaches only a capital asset being land or building or both
options.why: Section 50C(1) applies where the consideration received on the transfer of a capital asset, being land or building or both, is less than the value adopted or assessed by a stamp valuation authority. Shares are neither land nor building, and no stamp valuation authority values them, so the section has nothing to bite on.

options.text: No, because the buyer and the seller are unconnected persons
options.misconception: makes the relationship between the parties the test
options.why: Section 50C says nothing about who the buyer is. It fails here because the asset is shares, and it would fail on shares sold to a connected party just the same.

options.text: Yes, section 50C applies to every capital asset sold below its fair market value
options.misconception: reads section 50C as a general rule against undervaluation
options.why: The section is confined by its own words to land or building or both. A general power to substitute fair market value for the stated consideration is not what section 50C gives.

citation.ref: Section 50C(1)

items.scenario: Verma Trading Ltd sold unquoted equity shares of a private company for ₹40,00,000. The Assessing Officer believes the shares were worth far more and proposes to substitute a higher figure under section 50C.

items.stem: In which previous year is the capital gain on the conversion charged?

options.text: Previous year 2025-26, the year in which the stock-in-trade was sold
options.why: Section 45(2) charges the capital gain on a conversion into stock-in-trade as income of the previous year in which such stock-in-trade is sold or otherwise transferred. The gain is measured on the date of conversion but the charge waits for the sale, so previous year 2025-26 is the year of charge.
keywords: the previous year in which such stock-in-trade is sold

options.text: Split between the two years in proportion to the two values
options.misconception: invents an apportionment the section does not contain
options.why: Section 45(2) names one year for the whole of the capital gain. The business profit on the later sale is separate income under the head profits and gains of business or profession, but the capital gain itself is not divided.

options.text: Previous year 2024-25, the year of conversion
options.misconception: charges the gain when it is measured instead of when the section says
options.why: The date of conversion fixes the amount, because the fair market value on that date is taken as the full value of the consideration. Section 45(2) then defers the charge to the year of sale, so measurement and charge fall in different years.

options.text: Previous year 2025-26, but only because the plot was sold within three years of conversion
options.misconception: adds a time limit that section 45(2) does not impose
options.why: There is no outer period in section 45(2). The charge waits however long the stock is held, so the answer would be the same had the sale come ten years after the conversion.

citation.ref: Section 45(2)

items.scenario: Mr Salvi converted a plot he had held for twelve years into stock-in-trade of his property business on 1 July 2024. He sold that plot to a customer on 20 August 2025.

items.stem: Is the exemption under section 54F available to him?

options.text: No, because he owned more than one residential house other than the new asset on the date of transfer
options.why: The proviso to section 54F(1) shuts the section where the assessee owns more than one residential house, other than the new asset, on the date of transfer of the original asset. Two houses is more than one, so the exemption is denied however much of the net consideration he puts into the new flat.

options.text: Yes, the whole net consideration was invested, so the exemption is full
options.misconception: applies the proportion rule and skips the eligibility condition
options.why: Investing the whole net consideration decides how much exemption is given, not whether any is due at all. The ownership condition is tested first, and it fails here.

options.text: Yes, because the two houses are let out and so do not count
options.misconception: reads a self-occupation requirement into the ownership condition
options.why: The proviso counts houses owned, and says nothing about whether they are occupied by the assessee or let to somebody else. A let-out house is owned all the same.

options.text: No, because section 54F applies only to a gain on shares
options.misconception: narrows the original asset when the section deliberately leaves it open
options.why: Section 54F works on a long-term capital gain from any capital asset other than a residential house, so debentures qualify perfectly well as the original asset. It is the two existing houses that defeat the claim.

citation.ref: The proviso to Section 54F(1)

items.scenario: Mr Qureshi sold listed debentures in November 2025 for a long-term capital gain and invested the entire net consideration in a new residential flat. On the date of that sale he already owned two residential houses, both let out.

items.stem: What happens to the unabsorbed ₹2,00,000?

options.text: It is carried forward for eight assessment years and set off only against income from house property
options.why: Section 71B carries the unabsorbed house property loss forward for eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed, and once carried forward it may be set off against income from house property alone.

options.text: It is carried forward indefinitely, in the same way as unabsorbed depreciation
options.misconception: borrows the depreciation rule for a loss that has its own period
options.why: Unabsorbed depreciation under section 32(2) has no outer limit, and that is exactly what makes it unusual. A house property loss carries its own eight-year period under section 71B.

options.text: It lapses, because a house property loss cannot be carried forward at all
options.misconception: treats the current-year restriction as extinguishing the loss
options.why: The restriction bites on how much may be set off against other income this year. Whatever is left over survives under section 71B rather than disappearing.

options.text: It is carried forward for eight assessment years and set off against any head of income
options.misconception: gets the period right and drops the restriction on the head
options.why: Section 71B fixes both the period and the target. Once the loss is carried forward it may be used against house property income only, and not against salary or business income.

citation.ref: Section 71B

items.scenario: Mr Nanda has a house property loss of ₹4,00,000 for previous year 2025-26. After the set-off permitted against his other income this year, ₹2,00,000 of that loss is still unabsorbed. He files his return on time.

items.stem: Which one of the four survives under the default regime?

options.text: The set-off of the house property loss against salary
options.misconception: keeps a set-off that the default regime removes altogether
options.why: Under the default regime a house property loss cannot be set off against income under any other head. The position here is not a lower ceiling; the set-off against salary is gone.

options.text: The house rent allowance exemption under section 10(13A)
options.misconception: treats an exemption as untouched because it sits outside Chapter VI-A
options.why: Section 115BAC(2) reaches exemptions as well as deductions, and the allowance in section 10(13A) is one of the things it withdraws from a person taxed under the default regime.

options.text: The life insurance premium under section 80C
options.misconception: assumes Chapter VI-A survives the default regime intact
options.why: Section 80C is among the deductions that section 115BAC(2) takes away. Chapter VI-A is not kept whole; only named clauses such as section 80CCD(2) and section 80JJAA are saved.

options.text: The employer's contribution to the National Pension System under section 80CCD(2)
options.why: Section 115BAC(2) withdraws most of Chapter VI-A but expressly keeps the deduction for the employer's contribution to the National Pension System under section 80CCD(2). The other three — section 80C, the house rent allowance exemption and the set-off of a house property loss against salary — are all withdrawn by the same sub-section.
keywords: employer's contribution to the National Pension System under section 80CCD(2)

citation.ref: Section 115BAC(2) read with Section 115BAC(1A)

items.scenario: Ms Pillai is salaried and is taxed under the default regime in section 115BAC for assessment year 2026-27. She wants to claim four things: life insurance premium under section 80C, house rent allowance exemption under section 10(13A), a set-off of her house property loss against salary, and her employer's contribution to the National Pension System under section 80CCD(2).

items.stem: Under which head is that ₹12,00,000 chargeable?

options.text: Income from other sources, because an association carries on no business
options.misconception: sends the receipt to the residuary head when a clause of section 28 names it
options.why: The residuary head takes what no other head covers. Section 28(iii) covers this receipt expressly, so it never reaches income from other sources.

options.text: Nothing is chargeable, because it is a receipt from its own members
options.misconception: applies mutuality to a receipt the Act has taken out of it
options.why: Mutuality can keep a members' common fund outside the charge, but section 28(iii) was written precisely to reach fees charged for specific services performed for members. The clause displaces the argument.

options.text: Capital gains, because the fee is consideration for settling a right
options.misconception: treats a service fee as consideration for the transfer of a right
options.why: Capital gains need a capital asset and a transfer of it. An arbitration fee is payment for work done, with no asset changing hands, so no capital gain arises.

options.text: Profits and gains of business or profession
options.why: Section 28(iii) charges under profits and gains of business or profession the income derived by a trade, professional or similar association from specific services performed for its members. Arbitration provided on request is such a specific service, so the fee falls under that head whether or not the association is otherwise carrying on a business.
keywords: specific services performed for its members

citation.ref: Section 28(iii)

items.scenario: The Nagpur Textile Merchants Association, a trade association, charges its member firms a separate fee for arbitrating disputes between them. It collected ₹12,00,000 of such fees in previous year 2025-26.

items.stem: Is the claim good?

options.text: No, because section 37(1) shuts out expenditure in the nature of capital expenditure
options.why: Section 37(1) allows an expenditure only where four things hold at once: it is not described in sections 30 to 36, it is not in the nature of capital expenditure, it is not personal expenditure, and it is laid out wholly and exclusively for the business. A boundary wall is an enduring asset, so the capital gate closes even though the other three conditions are satisfied.
keywords: not in the nature of capital expenditure

options.text: Yes, it is wholly and exclusively for the business, which is what section 37(1) asks
options.misconception: treats the business-purpose gate as the whole of section 37(1)
options.why: Business purpose is one of the four conditions and usually the easiest to satisfy. The section refuses capital expenditure separately, so meeting the purpose test does not carry the claim on its own.

options.text: No, because the wall is personal expenditure
options.misconception: reaches the right answer through a gate that does not apply
options.why: A factory boundary wall is not personal expenditure; that word covers the proprietor's own spending rather than the firm's. The claim fails because the outlay is capital.

options.text: Yes, nothing in sections 30 to 36 covers a boundary wall, so section 37(1) must
options.misconception: reads section 37 as a catch-all for whatever the earlier sections miss
options.why: Section 37 is residuary in the sense that it comes after sections 30 to 36, not in the sense that it takes everything they leave behind. Its own four conditions still have to be met.

citation.ref: Section 37(1)

items.scenario: Havel Industries spent ₹18,00,000 on a new boundary wall around its factory. The wall is entirely for the business, no clause in sections 30 to 36 covers it, and there is nothing personal about it. The firm claims the whole sum under section 37(1).

items.stem: Is the ₹5,00,000 chargeable under section 41(1) in previous year 2025-26?

options.text: No, a business that has closed can have no business income
options.misconception: treats the head of income as needing a live business behind it
options.why: Section 41 is a deeming provision written precisely for the closed business. Its own words carry the charge into a year in which nothing is being carried on.

options.text: Yes, because section 41(1) applies whether or not the business is in existence in that year
options.why: Section 41(1) charges the value of a benefit obtained by remission or cessation of a trading liability in the year the benefit is obtained, and it says in terms that this holds whether the business or profession in respect of which the allowance or deduction was made is in existence in that year or not. Closing the shop in 2023 therefore does not save the receipt.
keywords: in existence in that year or not

options.text: Yes, but only in the hands of a successor who took over the business
options.misconception: applies the successor limb where there was no succession
options.why: Section 41(1)(b) reaches a successor in business where the business has passed to one. Mr Tandel closed his business rather than passing it on, so it is his own position under clause (a) that governs.

options.text: No, the deduction was allowed years ago and that year has become final
options.misconception: looks for a reopening of the old year when the section taxes the new one
options.why: Nothing is reopened. The old year keeps its deduction, and the benefit obtained on the waiver is charged as income of the year in which the waiver came.

citation.ref: Section 41(1)(a)

items.scenario: Mr Tandel discontinued his hardware business in March 2023. A supplier, whose ₹5,00,000 bill had been allowed to him as a deduction in an earlier year, wrote to him in October 2025 waiving the whole amount.

items.stem: Does section 43B(h) push the deduction out of previous year 2025-26?

options.text: Yes, clause (h) covers every enterprise registered under that Act
options.misconception: reads the clause as covering all three categories the MSMED Act defines
options.why: That Act defines micro, small and medium enterprises separately, and clause (h) picks only the first two. Registration on its own does not bring a supplier inside the clause.

options.text: No, because clause (h) covers a micro or small enterprise and not a medium one
options.why: Section 43B(h) speaks of a sum payable by the assessee to a micro or small enterprise beyond the time limit specified in section 15 of that Act. A medium enterprise is a third category which the clause does not name, so the delay carries no consequence under clause (h) and the deduction stands on the mercantile system.

options.text: No, but the deduction moves to the year of payment under the first proviso to section 43B
options.misconception: applies the general proviso to a case the clause never reached
options.why: The first proviso to section 43B rescues a payment made before the due date of the return, and clause (h) is in any event kept outside that proviso. Neither point matters here, because the sum never entered clause (h) at all.

options.text: Yes, because the ninety-day delay is what clause (h) tests
options.misconception: makes the length of the delay the test instead of the identity of the payee
options.why: The delay matters only once the payee is a micro or small enterprise. For a medium enterprise the clause is silent whatever the number of days.

citation.ref: Section 43B(h) read with Section 15 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006

items.scenario: Orbit Engineering owes ₹9,00,000 to a supplier registered as a medium enterprise under the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. The payment is ninety days late, well beyond the time limit in section 15 of that Act, and is still unpaid on 31 March 2026.

items.stem: What is the actual cost of the instrument for depreciation once it enters the business?

options.text: The market value of the instrument on the day it enters the business
options.misconception: substitutes fair value for a rule that works from historical cost
options.why: Market value enters section 43(1) only through particular Explanations aimed at acquisitions designed to inflate the cost. The route here is historical cost less what section 35 has already given.

options.text: ₹10,00,000, because that is what the firm paid for it
options.misconception: uses the purchase price and ignores the deduction already taken
options.why: Actual cost in section 43(1) is the cost to the assessee reduced by any portion met by another person and by the Explanations that follow the definition. Explanation 1 is one of those cuts and it applies squarely here.

options.text: Nil
options.why: Explanation 1 to section 43(1) provides that where an asset is used in the business after it ceases to be used for scientific research related to that business, the actual cost is the actual cost to the assessee as reduced by the deduction already allowed under section 35. The whole ₹10,00,000 was allowed, so the figure reduces to nil and no depreciation follows.
keywords: as reduced by the deduction already allowed under section 35

options.text: The written down value the instrument would have had if depreciation had been claimed all along
options.misconception: reconstructs a depreciation history the asset never had
options.why: No depreciation was ever claimed on this instrument, because its whole cost went out under section 35. Explanation 1 does not ask for a notional written down value; it subtracts the section 35 deduction from the cost.

citation.ref: Explanation 1 to Section 43(1) read with Section 35

items.scenario: Ashok Chemicals bought a laboratory instrument for ₹10,00,000 and was allowed the whole of that cost as a deduction under section 35 for scientific research related to its business. Two years later it stops using the instrument for research and brings it into ordinary factory use.

items.stem: Up to which assessment year may that loss be carried forward?

options.text: Indefinitely, because the return of the loss year was filed on time
options.misconception: treats timely filing as removing the outer limit rather than as the entry condition
options.why: Filing within the due date is what lets the loss be carried forward at all, under section 80. It does not touch the eight-year ceiling, which section 72(3) applies to every business loss.

options.text: Assessment year 2027-28, the eighth assessment year after 2019-20
options.why: Section 72(3) allows no loss to be carried forward for more than eight assessment years immediately succeeding the assessment year for which the loss was first computed. Counting eight from assessment year 2019-20 reaches assessment year 2027-28, after which whatever is left of the loss lapses.

options.text: Assessment year 2028-29, counting eight years from the year the return was filed
options.misconception: starts the eight-year clock at the filing year instead of the loss year
options.why: Section 72(3) counts from the assessment year for which the loss was first computed, which is 2019-20. The date on which the return went in does not start the clock.

options.text: Assessment year 2023-24, four assessment years after 2019-20
options.misconception: borrows the speculation-loss period for an ordinary business loss
options.why: The eight-year period in section 72(3) governs an ordinary business loss. Four years is the period section 73(4) gives a speculation loss, and this loss is not one.

citation.ref: Section 72(3) read with Section 80

items.scenario: Kesar Traders computed a business loss for assessment year 2019-20 and filed the return of that year within the due date. The loss has not been absorbed in any later year.

items.stem: Does section 79 stop the set-off of that carried-forward loss?

options.text: No, because section 79 applies only to a company in which the public are not substantially interested
options.why: Section 79(1) opens by confining itself to a company, not being a company in which the public are substantially interested. Sagar Ports is such a company, so the shareholding-continuity test never runs and the carried-forward loss is untouched by the turnover in its shares.
keywords: not being a company in which the public are substantially interested

options.text: No, because a listed company can never carry forward a business loss
options.misconception: reaches the right conclusion on a reason that is false
options.why: A listed company carries forward its business losses under section 72 like anybody else. What saves the set-off here is that section 79 does not apply to it.

options.text: Yes, unless the shares were sold on a recognised stock exchange
options.misconception: invents an exchange-based exception inside a section that never applies here
options.why: Section 79 carries no exception for trades done on an exchange. The company is outside the section altogether, because the public are substantially interested in it.

options.text: Yes, because more than half the shares changed hands, which is what section 79 tests
options.misconception: applies the continuity test to a company the section does not reach
options.why: The test in section 79 does bite on a change beyond the permitted level, but only for a closely held company. The gate is the kind of company first and the extent of the change second.

citation.ref: Section 79(1) read with Section 2(18)

items.scenario: Sagar Ports Ltd is listed on a recognised stock exchange and is a company in which the public are substantially interested. Over previous year 2025-26 more than eighty per cent of its shares changed hands on the exchange. It carries forward a business loss from an earlier year.

items.stem: Is that rent clubbed with Mr Ghosh's income?

options.text: No, but only because the shop is let out rather than used by her
options.misconception: makes the use of the asset the test
options.why: Section 64(1)(iv) does not ask what the spouse does with the asset. Rent, business profit or interest would all be clubbed had the transfer been without adequate consideration.

options.text: Yes, because they were married at the time of the transfer
options.misconception: takes the subsisting marriage as sufficient by itself
options.why: The marriage must subsist, which it does, but that only opens the clause. It is the consideration that decides the case, and it was adequate.

options.text: No, because the transfer was for adequate consideration
