options.text: As distinct persons only where the registrations are in different States; two registrations inside one State remain one person
options.misconception: drops the words "whether in one State or Union territory or more than one" out of section 25(4)
options.why: Section 25(4) says whether in one State or Union territory or more than one. Two registrations within a single State are distinct persons on exactly the same footing as two across States.

options.text: As distinct persons, one for each registration
options.why: Section 25(4) says a person who has obtained or is required to obtain more than one registration, whether in one State or Union territory or more than one State or Union territory, shall in respect of each such registration be treated as distinct persons for the purposes of the Act. A single permanent account number and a single legal entity make no difference.

options.text: As one person, a company being a single legal entity that cannot supply anything to itself
options.misconception: applies company law's single-entity idea where section 25(4) has written a different rule for GST
options.why: Company law is not the test here. Section 25(4) deliberately splits one legal entity into as many persons as it has registrations, so that a State-wise tax can follow goods and services moving between them.

citation.ref: Sections 25(4) and 25(5), read with paragraph 2 of Schedule I

items.scenario: One company, one permanent account number, two GST registrations — one in Tamil Nadu and one in Kerala. Its finance team asks whether the two registrations are the same person for GST.

items.stem: By when must the tax invoice be issued?

options.text: On 15 August, section 31(1)(b) allowing the invoice at the time of delivery
options.misconception: applies the delivery limb of section 31(1)(b), which is for supplies that do not involve movement
options.why: Section 31(1)(b) covers any other case, meaning a supply that does not involve movement of goods, and there the invoice goes before or at the time of delivery or of making the goods available. This machine moved, so clause (a) governs and removal is the moment.

options.text: By the due date of the return for August, when the supply is first reported
options.misconception: confuses the deadline for reporting a supply with the deadline for documenting it
options.why: The return date is when a supply is declared to the department. Section 31 sets a separate and much earlier deadline for the document itself, and goods may not be removed under a supply without the invoice having been issued by then.

options.text: Before or at the time the machine was removed on 12 August
options.why: Section 31(1)(a) requires a registered person supplying taxable goods to issue a tax invoice before or at the time of removal of goods for supply to the recipient, where the supply involves movement of goods. The machine was removed on 12 August, so that is the outer date and waiting for delivery on 15 August is late.
keywords: before or at the time of removal

options.text: Within thirty days of 12 August, the period rule 47 allows
options.misconception: applies the thirty-day period rule 47 gives for services to a supply of goods
options.why: Rule 47 gives thirty days from the date of supply of the service, and it governs services. A supply of goods runs on section 31(1), which uses removal or delivery and gives no thirty-day grace at all.

citation.ref: Sections 31(1)(a) and 31(1)(b), read with rule 47 of the CGST Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered dealer sells a machine to a buyer in another city. The machine leaves his factory on a truck on 12 August 2026 and reaches the buyer on 15 August 2026. The dealer plans to raise the tax invoice on 15 August, once delivery is confirmed.

items.stem: Where is the place of supply of the hotel accommodation?

options.text: Delhi, the recipient being registered there
options.misconception: applies the general rule in section 12(2) where section 12(3) has a specific rule that overrides it
options.why: Section 12(2) opens with the words "the place of supply of services, except the services specified in sub-sections (3) to (14)". Lodging accommodation is specified in section 12(3)(b), so the general rule is displaced and the recipient's registration decides nothing.

options.text: Delhi, because the guest paid from Delhi and the bill carries a Delhi address
options.misconception: uses the billing address, which section 12(3) never mentions
options.why: Section 12(3)(b) turns on where the immovable property is and on nothing else. Neither the address on the bill nor the source of the payment enters the test.

options.text: Rajasthan, but only because a guest is an ordinary consumer; a registered guest would take the supply to his own State
options.misconception: imports the registered-versus-unregistered split of section 12(2) into section 12(3), which has no such split
options.why: Section 12(3) gives everyone the same answer. The registered-or-not distinction belongs to section 12(2)(a) and (b), and it never reaches a service tied to immovable property.

options.text: Rajasthan, where the hotel stands
options.why: Section 12(3)(b) of the IGST Act covers services by way of lodging accommodation by a hotel, inn, guest house, home stay, club or campsite, and fixes the place of supply as the location at which the immovable property is located. The hotel is in Rajasthan, so that is the answer whatever State the guest is registered in.
keywords: location at which the immovable property is located

citation.ref: Section 12(3)(b), read with section 12(2)

items.scenario: A person registered in Delhi stays two nights at a hotel in Jaipur, Rajasthan. The hotel is registered in Rajasthan.

items.stem: What is the place of supply of the goods?

options.text: Gujarat, where the movement ends for delivery to the buyer
options.why: Section 10(1)(a) of the IGST Act says that where the supply involves movement of goods, whether by the supplier or the recipient or by any other person, the place of supply shall be the location of the goods at the time at which the movement of goods terminates for delivery to the recipient. The movement ends at the warehouse in Gujarat, which makes the supply an inter-State one.
keywords: movement of goods terminates for delivery

options.text: Maharashtra, the supplier's own location
options.misconception: uses the supplier's location, which section 10 never makes the test for a supply of goods
options.why: For goods, section 10 asks where the goods go, not where the supplier sits. The supplier's location is used afterwards, under section 7 of the IGST Act, only to decide whether the supply is inter-State once the place of supply is known.

options.text: Gujarat, but only because the supplier arranged the transport; had the buyer collected the goods himself it would be Maharashtra
options.misconception: makes the answer turn on who moved the goods, which section 10(1)(a) expressly says is irrelevant
options.why: Section 10(1)(a) says whether by the supplier or the recipient or by any other person. Who arranges the transport changes nothing, because the movement still terminates at the buyer's warehouse in Gujarat.

options.text: Maharashtra, where the goods were handed to the transporter and the movement began
options.misconception: reads the section as fixing the place where the movement starts, when its words are where it terminates
options.why: The words of section 10(1)(a) are the location of the goods at the time at which the movement terminates for delivery to the recipient. Where the journey began is not the test, however the transport was arranged.

citation.ref: Section 10(1)(a), read with section 7(1)

items.scenario: A supplier registered in Maharashtra sells goods to a buyer registered in Gujarat. The supplier arranges the transport, and the goods are delivered to the buyer's warehouse in Gujarat.

items.stem: Which date determines the rate of duty?

options.text: The date the goods entered the territorial waters of India
options.misconception: confuses the taxable event, when goods enter India, with the date section 15 uses to pick the rate
options.why: The charge under section 12 attaches to goods imported into India, but section 15 is a separate provision saying which day's rate applies, and it uses the bill of entry, not the crossing of territorial waters.

options.text: 9 June 2026, the date of entry inwards
options.why: Section 15(1)(a) fixes the rate of duty for goods entered for home consumption by the date on which a bill of entry is presented under section 46, and its proviso says that where the bill of entry has been presented before the date of entry inwards of the vessel, it shall be deemed to have been presented on the date of such entry inwards. The relevant date is therefore 9 June.

options.text: 5 June 2026, the date the bill of entry was actually presented
options.misconception: applies the main limb of section 15(1)(a) and ignores its proviso for a filing made ahead of the vessel
options.why: The main limb does use the date of presentation, but the proviso overrides it where the filing runs ahead of the vessel. An early filing is deemed made on the day entry inwards is granted, so the actual date of filing drops out.

options.text: The date the goods were shipped from the foreign port
options.misconception: uses the date of shipment, which section 15 does not mention at all
options.why: Section 15 lists three situations and the date each turns on, and none of them is the date of shipment. What happened abroad does not fix the rate of duty in India.

citation.ref: Section 15(1)(a) with its proviso, read with sections 12 and 46

items.scenario: An importer files a bill of entry for home consumption on 5 June 2026, before the carrying vessel has arrived. The proper officer grants entry inwards to the vessel on 9 June 2026. The rate of basic customs duty on these goods changes between the two dates.

items.stem: Who assesses the duty on these goods in the ordinary course?

options.text: The proper officer, every bill of entry being assessed by the department before clearance
options.misconception: describes the position before self-assessment was introduced, when the officer assessed as a matter of course
options.why: That was the older scheme. Section 17(1) now puts the assessment on the importer and section 17(2) leaves the officer with verification, which he may carry out selectively rather than on every consignment.

options.text: The custodian of the customs area, who holds the goods until the duty is paid
options.misconception: confuses custody of the goods with assessment of the duty on them
options.why: The custodian's duties concern safe keeping of goods in a customs area. Assessment is what section 17 governs, and that section names the importer and the proper officer, nobody else.

options.text: Nobody until clearance — the duty is fixed by the order permitting clearance under section 47
options.misconception: reads the clearance order as the assessment, when section 47 presupposes an assessment already made
options.why: Section 47 lets the proper officer make an order permitting clearance for home consumption where he is satisfied that the goods are not prohibited and that the importer has paid the import duty assessed. The assessment comes first, under section 17; section 47 acts on it.

options.text: The importer himself, the officer's role being verification
options.why: Section 17(1) says that an importer entering any imported goods under section 46, or an exporter entering export goods under section 50, shall self-assess the duty leviable on such goods. Section 17(2) then lets the proper officer verify the entries and the self-assessment, and only where he finds it not done correctly does section 17(4) let him re-assess.
keywords: entering any imported goods under section 46

citation.ref: Sections 17(1), 17(2) and 17(4), read with sections 46 and 47

items.scenario: An importer files a bill of entry for home consumption. There is no dispute about the classification or the value, and the proper officer is satisfied with the declaration.

items.stem: Has the company complied with section 173?

options.text: No — every company must hold at least four board meetings a year, with no more than one hundred and twenty days between consecutive meetings
options.misconception: applies section 173(1) to a company that section 173(5) expressly takes out of it
options.why: Section 173(1) is the general rule and it does require four meetings and a gap of no more than one hundred and twenty days. Section 173(5) is an express relaxation, and a small company is entitled to it.

options.text: Yes — one meeting in each half of the calendar year is enough for a company of this kind
options.why: Section 173(5) says a One Person Company, a small company and a dormant company shall be deemed to have complied with the section if at least one meeting of the Board has been conducted in each half of a calendar year and the gap between the two meetings is not less than ninety days. March falls in the first half and October in the second, and the gap runs well beyond ninety days.
keywords: one meeting of the Board has been conducted in each half of a calendar year

options.text: Yes, and since ninety days is the maximum gap allowed, meetings in March and June would equally have complied
options.misconception: turns the minimum gap in section 173(5) into a maximum
options.why: Section 173(5) says the gap shall be not less than ninety days, which is a floor and not a ceiling. It exists to stop the two meetings being bunched together, and a March and June pairing would also fail the requirement of one meeting in each half of the year.

options.text: No — the relaxation in section 173(5) is available only to a One Person Company
options.misconception: reads one of the three categories named in section 173(5) and drops the other two
options.why: Section 173(5) names three categories together — a One Person Company, a small company and a dormant company. A small company sits squarely inside it.

citation.ref: Sections 173(1) and 173(5)

items.scenario: A small company holds two board meetings in a calendar year, one on 20 March and one on 10 October. Its directors ask whether section 173 is satisfied, since the company held nowhere near four meetings.

items.stem: What is the quorum for a meeting of this Board?

options.text: Six directors, being two-thirds of the total strength
options.misconception: inverts the fraction in section 174(1), which is one-third and not two-thirds
options.why: The fraction in section 174(1) is one-third. Two-thirds appears elsewhere in the Act, in section 152(6) on the proportion of directors liable to retire by rotation, and has nothing to do with quorum.

options.text: Three directors
options.why: Section 174(1) says the quorum for a meeting of the Board shall be one-third of its total strength or two directors, whichever is higher. One-third of nine is three, and three is higher than two, so three directors personally present constitute the quorum.

options.text: Five directors, being a simple majority of the nine
options.misconception: applies the majority needed to carry a resolution as though it were the quorum
options.why: A majority decides whether a resolution is carried once the meeting is properly constituted. The quorum is a different question and section 174(1) answers it with one-third of total strength or two, whichever is higher.

options.text: Two directors, section 174 setting a fixed floor of two whatever the size of the board
options.misconception: takes the floor of two as the whole rule and drops the one-third limb
options.why: Two is only one of the two figures section 174(1) compares. The section takes the higher of one-third of total strength and two, so on a board of nine the one-third figure of three wins.

citation.ref: Section 174(1)

items.scenario: A company's Board consists of nine directors in total. All are validly appointed, none is interested in the business to be transacted, and all are entitled to attend.

items.stem: By when must the annual general meeting for the year ended 31 March 2026 be held?

options.text: By 30 September 2026
options.why: Section 96(1) requires an annual general meeting to be held within six months from the date of closing of the financial year, and separately requires that not more than fifteen months elapse between one such meeting and the next. Six months from 31 March 2026 is 30 September 2026; fifteen months from 20 August 2025 is 20 November 2026. Both tests bind, so the earlier date governs.
keywords: within six months from the date of closing of the financial year

options.text: By 31 December 2026, nine months from the close of the financial year
options.misconception: applies the nine-month period for a first annual general meeting to a subsequent one
options.why: Nine months from the close of the first financial year is the period section 96(1) allows for a company's first annual general meeting. Every meeting after that runs on six months from the close of the financial year.

options.text: By 20 November 2026, fifteen months from the previous meeting being the operative limit
options.misconception: treats the two limits in section 96(1) as alternatives when both have to be satisfied
options.why: The fifteen-month limit is real, but it sits alongside the six-month limit and neither displaces the other. Where the two give different dates the company must meet by the earlier of them, which here is 30 September 2026.

options.text: There is no outer date, so long as one meeting is held in each calendar year
options.misconception: replaces the statutory periods with a loose one-a-year rule
options.why: Section 96(1) fixes both an outer date measured from the close of the financial year and a maximum gap from the previous meeting. Holding one somewhere in the calendar year is not the test, and only the Registrar may extend the time, and never for a first meeting.

citation.ref: Section 96(1) with its provisos

items.scenario: A company well past its first year closes its financial year on 31 March 2026. Its previous annual general meeting was held on 20 August 2025, and no extension has been sought.

items.stem: What does section 139(2) allow?

options.text: He may be reappointed for a second term of five years, in the same way an audit firm may
options.misconception: gives an individual auditor the two terms section 139(2) reserves for an audit firm
options.why: Section 139(2) draws the line between the two. An individual gets one term of five consecutive years; only an audit firm gets two such terms, and that distinction is the point of the sub-section.

options.text: He may be reappointed at once if the members pass a special resolution approving it
options.misconception: treats a shareholder resolution as able to override a statutory ceiling
options.why: The cap in section 139(2) is not a default the members may vary. No resolution, ordinary or special, extends a term the section closes, and the cooling-off period runs whatever the members would prefer.

options.text: He cannot be reappointed, and a cooling-off period follows before he could return
options.why: Section 139(2) says a listed company and the prescribed classes of company shall not appoint or reappoint an individual as auditor for more than one term of five consecutive years, and an audit firm for more than two such terms. Its first proviso then bars an individual auditor who has completed his term from being reappointed in that company for five years from the completion of the term.
keywords: one term of five consecutive years

options.text: He may continue indefinitely, rotation applying only where the auditor is a firm
options.misconception: reads rotation as a firms-only rule when section 139(2) names the individual first
options.why: Section 139(2) begins by naming an individual and then an audit firm, and it caps both. Rotation was written to reach the individual auditor quite as much as the firm.

citation.ref: Section 139(2) with its first proviso

items.scenario: An individual chartered accountant has been the statutory auditor of a listed company for one term of five consecutive years, which is now ending.

items.stem: May the electricity supply be cut off during the moratorium?

options.text: No, and for the same reason the resolution professional need not pay for supply consumed after admission
options.misconception: reads a protection against disconnection as a licence not to pay current dues
options.why: The protection keeps the supply running; it does not make it free. Dues for supply during the process are costs of the process, and section 14(2A) makes the continuation of critical supplies conditional on the corporate debtor paying its dues during the moratorium.

options.text: Yes, but only after thirty days' notice to the resolution professional
options.misconception: converts a prohibition into a notice requirement
options.why: Section 14(2) contains no notice mechanism, because it is not a permission at all. It forbids the interruption for the whole moratorium period, and no length of notice makes the disconnection lawful.

options.text: No — an essential supply may not be interrupted while the moratorium runs
options.why: Section 14(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 protects the supply of essential goods or services to the corporate debtor, which shall not be terminated or suspended or interrupted during moratorium period, and Regulation 32 of the corporate insolvency resolution process regulations specifies electricity among them. Arrears from before admission are a claim to be dealt with in the process, not a lever to switch the factory off.

options.text: Yes — a supplier's contractual right to disconnect for non-payment survives the moratorium
options.misconception: reads the moratorium as binding only courts and creditors pursuing legal action
options.why: Section 14(1) does stop suits and recovery actions, but section 14(2) is a separate protection aimed squarely at suppliers, and it overrides the contractual right to cut off an essential service while the process runs.

citation.ref: Sections 14(1), 14(2) and 14(2A), read with Regulation 32 of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process is admitted against a manufacturing company. The electricity distribution company, owed arrears for the months before admission, threatens to disconnect the factory unless those arrears are cleared. The resolution professional is paying every bill that falls due after admission.

items.stem: What period does the Code allow for completing the process?

options.text: Two hundred and seventy days, being one hundred and eighty days plus the ninety-day extension
options.misconception: assumes the extension is automatic when section 12(2) requires it to be resolved on and granted
options.why: The ninety days exist only once the committee of creditors resolves to seek them and the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that the process cannot be completed in time. With no application made, the one-hundred-and-eighty-day period stands alone.

options.text: No fixed period — the Code sets a target and the Adjudicating Authority allows whatever time the process needs
options.misconception: treats the timeline as merely directory when the Code writes it as a period with a stated ceiling
options.why: Section 12(1) fixes a period and section 12(3) caps both the extension and the total. Timeliness is one of the stated objects of the Code, and there is no open-ended power to add time.

options.text: One hundred and eighty days from 1 April 2026
options.why: Section 12(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 says the corporate insolvency resolution process shall be completed within a period of one hundred and eighty days from the date of admission of the application. Sections 12(2) and 12(3) allow a single extension of up to ninety days beyond that, but nothing is extended unless it is resolved on and granted.

options.text: Three hundred and thirty days, the period the Code gives every process
options.misconception: takes the outer ceiling that includes extensions and litigation time as the ordinary period
options.why: Three hundred and thirty days is the ceiling in the proviso to section 12(3), and it counts any extension granted together with the time taken in legal proceedings. It is a maximum that has to be earned, not the period a process starts with.

citation.ref: Sections 12(1), 12(2) and 12(3) with the proviso to section 12(3)

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process commences on 1 April 2026. No extension has been applied for and no litigation has intervened.

items.stem: How many of them must retire at that meeting?

options.text: Eight, two-thirds of the rotational directors retiring each year
options.misconception: confuses the two-thirds of the board that must be rotational with the one-third that actually retires
options.why: Two-thirds is the proportion of the total board that must be liable to retire by rotation under section 152(6)(a). What retires at each meeting is one-third of that rotational group, which here is four.

options.text: Four
options.why: Section 152(6)(c) says that at every annual general meeting, one-third of such of the directors for the time being as are liable to retire by rotation, or if their number is neither three nor a multiple of three then the number nearest to one-third, shall retire from office. One-third of twelve is four.
keywords: one-third of such of the directors

options.text: None — retirement by rotation applies only where the articles provide for it
options.misconception: treats a statutory requirement as something the articles may switch off
options.why: For a public company section 152(6) applies by force of the statute. The articles may deal with the manner of appointment, but they cannot exempt the company from having two-thirds of its directors liable to retire by rotation.

options.text: Twelve — every rotational director retires and offers himself for reappointment
options.misconception: retires the whole rotational group at once, which defeats the staggering the section creates
options.why: Rotation is staggered on purpose, so that a board is never emptied in one meeting. Section 152(6)(c) retires one-third at each annual general meeting, and each retiring director may then be reappointed.

citation.ref: Sections 152(6)(a) and 152(6)(c)

items.scenario: A public company has twelve directors who are liable to retire by rotation. Its annual general meeting is due.

items.stem: Which whole-time key managerial personnel must such a company have?

options.text: A managing director and an internal auditor, the internal auditor being key managerial personnel
options.misconception: treats the internal auditor as key managerial personnel, which the definition in section 2(51) does not
options.why: Section 138 requires certain companies to appoint an internal auditor, but that office appears neither in the definition of key managerial personnel in section 2(51) nor in the list in section 203(1).

options.text: Only a managing director or chief executive officer, the other offices being recommended rather than required
options.misconception: reduces the three offices section 203(1) requires to the one the company happens to have filled
options.why: Section 203(1) lists three offices and requires all three. A company secretary and a chief financial officer are not optional for a company inside the prescribed class.

options.text: A managing director or chief executive officer or manager and, in their absence, a whole-time director; a company secretary; and a chief financial officer
options.why: Section 203(1) requires every company belonging to the prescribed class to have three whole-time key managerial personnel — a managing director, or chief executive officer or manager and in their absence a whole-time director; a company secretary; and a chief financial officer. The managing director already in place answers the first, so a company secretary and a chief financial officer are still needed.

options.text: A managing director, a company secretary, a chief financial officer and at least one independent director
options.misconception: adds an independent director, whose appointment is governed by section 149 and who is not key managerial personnel
options.why: An independent director is appointed under section 149 and is nowhere in the list of whole-time key managerial personnel. Section 203 is about the executive officers who run the company day to day.

citation.ref: Section 203(1), read with section 2(51)

items.scenario: A company falls within the class that must appoint whole-time key managerial personnel. It has appointed a managing director. The board asks what else section 203 requires.

items.stem: What does section 123(4) require the company to do with the declared dividend?

options.text: Move it into a separate bank account within five days of the declaration
options.why: Section 123(4) says the amount of the dividend, including interim dividend, shall be deposited in a scheduled bank in a separate account within five days from the date of declaration of such dividend. Leaving it in the company's main current account breaks that requirement even if every shareholder is eventually paid.
keywords: within five days from the date of declaration

options.text: Move it into a separate account within thirty days, the same period allowed for paying it
options.misconception: reads the deposit period as matching the payment period when the two are deliberately different
options.why: The two periods differ on purpose. Section 123(4) gives five days to set the money aside, so that the thirty days section 127 allows for payment run against money already secured.

options.text: Nothing in particular, provided every shareholder is paid within thirty days of the declaration
options.misconception: treats the payment deadline in section 127 as discharging the separate-account duty in section 123(4)
options.why: Thirty days is the period in section 127 for actually paying the dividend or posting the warrant. Section 123(4) imposes a different and earlier duty, of ring-fencing the money, and meeting one does not excuse the other.

options.text: Transfer it to the Investor Education and Protection Fund immediately on declaration
options.misconception: applies the destination for long-unclaimed dividends to a dividend just declared
options.why: Money reaches the Investor Education and Protection Fund only after a dividend has remained unpaid or unclaimed for seven years, under section 124(5). A dividend declared this week goes into a separate bank account.

citation.ref: Section 123(4), read with sections 124(5) and 127

items.scenario: A company declares a final dividend at its annual general meeting on 12 August 2026. The finance team plans to keep the money in the company's main current account and pay shareholders as the transfers are processed.

items.stem: What period does section 77(1) allow as of right?

options.text: No fixed period — a charge may be registered any time before the company is wound up
options.misconception: reads the consequence in section 77(3) as though it were the deadline
options.why: Section 77(3) says an unregistered charge shall not be taken into account by the liquidator or any other creditor, which is the penalty for missing the period rather than the period itself. The period is thirty days from creation.

options.text: Sixty days from creation, with no additional fee
options.misconception: takes one of the extended periods the provisos allow and treats it as the ordinary period
options.why: The extensions in the provisos to section 77(1) come at a price and depend on the Registrar allowing them. The period available as of right is thirty days from creation.

options.text: Thirty days from the date the first instalment of the loan is drawn
options.misconception: measures the period from the drawdown rather than from the creation of the charge
options.why: Section 77(1) measures from the creation of the charge, which here is the date the mortgage was made, and not from when money moved under the facility the charge secures.

options.text: Thirty days from the date the charge was created
options.why: Section 77(1) requires a company creating a charge to register the particulars of the charge, signed by the company and the charge-holder, with the Registrar within thirty days of its creation. The provisos then let the Registrar allow registration after that on payment of additional fees, but the period the section itself gives is thirty days.
keywords: within thirty days of its creation
register the particulars of the charge

citation.ref: Section 77(1) with its provisos, read with section 77(3)

items.scenario: A company creates a mortgage over its factory in favour of a bank on 1 July 2026. The company secretary asks by when the particulars of the charge must be filed with the Registrar.

items.stem: Are independent directors liable to retire by rotation?

options.text: Yes — every director of a public company retires by rotation unless the articles say otherwise
options.misconception: applies the general rotation rule to a class the statute expressly removes from it
options.why: Section 152(6) does make two-thirds of the directors liable to retire by rotation, but section 149(13) lifts independent directors out of that count. It is the statute doing so, not the articles.

options.text: Yes, but only in the second half of the five-year term
options.misconception: invents a partial application of a provision that is disapplied entirely
options.why: Section 149(13) disapplies the rotation provisions outright. There is no stage of an independent director's term at which he becomes liable to retire by rotation.

options.text: No — the rotation provisions are switched off for them
options.why: Section 149(13) provides that the provisions of sub-sections (6) and (7) of section 152 in respect of retirement of directors by rotation shall not apply to an independent director. He serves the fixed term section 149(10) gives him instead, so he is neither counted in the rotational group nor put up for retirement at the meeting.
keywords: retirement of directors by rotation shall not apply

options.text: No, because an independent director is not a director at all for the purposes of section 152
options.misconception: over-reads the exemption, treating an exclusion from rotation as an exclusion from directorship
options.why: An independent director is a director in every other respect — he counts towards quorum, he owes the duties in section 166, and he is appointed and removed as a director. What section 149(13) takes away is only the liability to retire by rotation.

citation.ref: Section 149(13), read with sections 149(10) and 152(6)

items.scenario: A listed company is preparing the agenda for its annual general meeting. The company secretary asks whether the independent directors are to be counted among the directors retiring by rotation this year.

items.stem: When does section 184(1) require that disclosure?

options.text: Only when a contract in which he is interested comes before the board
options.misconception: collapses the standing disclosure in section 184(1) into the contract-specific disclosure in section 184(2)
options.why: Section 184(2) is the contract-specific duty, requiring him to disclose his interest in a particular contract or arrangement and to stay out of the discussion and the vote. Section 184(1) is a separate standing duty owed whether or not any contract is on the table.

options.text: Once, at the time of his appointment, with no need to repeat it
options.misconception: treats a recurring duty as a one-off formality
options.why: Section 184(1) says at the first meeting in which he participates and thereafter at the first meeting in every financial year. The duty repeats every year, and again on any change in what has already been disclosed.

options.text: At the annual general meeting, so that the members hear it directly
options.misconception: sends a disclosure the section makes to the Board to the general meeting instead
options.why: The disclosure under section 184(1) is made to the Board and recorded in its minutes. Members learn of the company's related dealings through the board's report and the financial statements, not through a disclosure at the annual general meeting.

options.text: At the first board meeting in which he participates as a director, and then at the first board meeting of every financial year
options.why: Section 184(1) requires every director to disclose his concern or interest in any company, body corporate, firm or other association of individuals at the first meeting of the Board in which he participates as a director and thereafter at the first meeting of the Board in every financial year, and again whenever there is any change in what he has disclosed. The disclosure is made in Form MBP-1.
keywords: first meeting of the Board in which he participates

citation.ref: Section 184(1), read with section 184(2) and rule 9 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A newly appointed director of a public company holds shares and directorships in several other companies. He asks when he must give the board a general disclosure of those interests, quite apart from any particular contract.

items.stem: Which single feature of the plan breaks section 96(2)?

options.text: The community hall, an annual general meeting being lawful only at the registered office itself
options.misconception: drops the words "or at some other place within the city"
options.why: Section 96(2) offers the registered office or some other place within the same city, town or village, in the alternative. A hall in that city satisfies the second limb.

options.text: The 7 p.m. start
options.why: Section 96(2) says every annual general meeting shall be called during business hours, that is, between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., on any day that is not a National Holiday, and shall be held either at the registered office of the company or at some other place within the city, town or village in which the registered office is situate. Seven in the evening is outside the window the sub-section itself defines as business hours. A Sunday is not a National Holiday, and the community hall is inside the same city as the registered office, so those two features are unobjectionable.

options.text: The Sunday, a general meeting being barred on a weekly holiday
options.misconception: reads "National Holiday" as any day the office is shut
options.why: The sub-section bars a National Holiday, a term the Explanation ties to a day declared as such by the Central Government. An ordinary Sunday is not one, and companies hold annual general meetings on Sundays routinely.

options.text: Nothing — section 96(2) fixes only the outer date for the meeting and leaves the hour and the venue to the Board
options.misconception: treats section 96 as a rule about the date alone
options.why: Section 96(1) fixes the outer date. Section 96(2) is a separate sub-section that fixes the hour, the day and the place, and it is the one being tested here.

citation.ref: Section 96(2)

items.scenario: Meridian Ltd, an unlisted public company, calls its annual general meeting for a Sunday evening at 7 p.m., in a community hall standing in the same city as its registered office. The company secretary is asked whether anything about that plan offends section 96.

items.stem: What is the quorum for this meeting?

options.text: Fifteen members personally present, the quorum rising with the number of members on the register
options.misconception: applies the public company slabs to a private company
options.why: The rising slabs of five, fifteen and thirty sit in section 103(1)(a), which opens with the words "in case of a public company". A private company is dealt with separately in clause (b) and takes a flat figure.

options.text: One-tenth of the members, being thirty-four, unless the articles fix a smaller number
options.misconception: invents a proportional quorum the section does not contain
options.why: Section 103 fixes quorum by a number of members and never by a proportion of the register. Articles may provide for a larger number, but the Act's own figure for a private company is two.

options.text: Four, because the proxy is counted along with the three members attending in person
options.misconception: counts a proxy towards quorum
options.why: Section 103 asks for members personally present, and a proxy is not the member in person. The meeting has three for quorum purposes, not four — which is still enough.

options.text: Two members personally present, so the meeting has a quorum
options.why: Section 103(1)(b) gives a private company a single figure: two members personally present shall be the quorum for a meeting of the company. The slabs that rise with the number of members belong to section 103(1)(a) and apply to a public company only, so the 340 members do not move the figure. Three attended in person, which clears the floor of two whether or not the proxy counts.

citation.ref: Section 103(1)(b)

items.scenario: Larkspur Private Ltd has 340 members. Its articles say nothing about quorum. Three members attend the general meeting in person; a fourth sends a proxy. The chairman believes a company with this many members needs fifteen members present before it can begin.

items.stem: How much notice does section 173(3) require for this meeting?

options.text: No notice period is fixed; the Board may meet whenever the chairman convenes it
options.misconception: treats the Board's own procedure as unregulated
options.why: Section 173(3) fixes the period in terms. The Act leaves the Board a great deal of procedural freedom but not the length of its own notice.

options.text: Twenty-one clear days, the same notice a general meeting requires
options.misconception: carries the general meeting notice period across to the Board
options.why: Twenty-one clear days is section 101, and it governs a general meeting of the members. A Board meeting has its own and much shorter period in section 173(3).

options.text: At least seven days in writing to every director at his address registered with the company
options.why: Section 173(3) says a meeting of the Board shall be called by giving not less than seven days notice in writing to every director at his address registered with the company, and such notice shall be sent by hand delivery or by post or by electronic means. Tuesday to Friday is three days, so the meeting cannot be called on that notice for ordinary business.

options.text: Forty-eight hours, the period the Act allows for depositing a proxy
options.misconception: borrows a period from an unrelated provision
options.why: Forty-eight hours is the proxy deposit period in section 105(4). It has nothing to do with calling a Board meeting.

citation.ref: Section 173(3)

items.scenario: The managing director of Harrow Steels Ltd tells the company secretary to call a Board meeting for the coming Friday. It is Tuesday. There is no urgency; the item is the approval of a routine capital budget.

items.stem: What does section 174(4) do with a meeting that fails for want of quorum?

options.text: The directors who did attend may transact the business, quorum being directory for a Board
options.misconception: reads the Board quorum as advisory
options.why: Section 174(1) fixes the quorum and section 174(4) supplies what happens when it is absent. Neither lets the directors present carry the business anyway.

options.text: It stands adjourned automatically to the same day at the same time and place in the next week, or to the next succeeding day that is not a national holiday if that day is one
options.why: Section 174(4) provides that where a meeting of the Board could not be held for want of quorum, then, unless the articles otherwise provide, the meeting shall automatically stand adjourned to the same day at the same time and place in the next week, or if that day is a national holiday, till the next succeeding day which is not a national holiday at the same time and place. The adjournment is automatic, so a fresh notice for a fresh meeting is not what the sub-section calls for.

options.text: It stands adjourned to the same day in the next month, the Board's own cycle being monthly
options.misconception: substitutes a month for the week the sub-section names
options.why: The sub-section says the same day in the next week. There is no monthly cycle in section 174.

options.text: It lapses, and a fresh meeting must be called on seven days' notice
options.misconception: treats the failed meeting as gone rather than adjourned
options.why: Section 174(4) keeps the meeting alive by adjourning it. Seven days' notice under section 173(3) is for calling a meeting, not for one the statute has already carried forward to the next week.

citation.ref: Section 174(4)

items.scenario: A Board meeting of Castleton Ltd is called for Thursday 4 June 2026 at the registered office. Too few directors turn up and no business can be transacted. The chairman asks whether a fresh notice must now go out for a new meeting.

items.stem: Has the ordinary resolution been passed?

options.text: Yes — the votes cast in favour exceed the votes cast against, and the chairman's casting vote is counted with them
options.why: Section 114(1) says a resolution shall be an ordinary resolution where the votes cast in favour of the resolution exceed the votes cast against it, and it says in terms that this includes the casting vote, if any, of the chairman. So the test is a simple majority of the votes actually cast, and the casting vote sits on the favourable side of it. Four thousand against three thousand nine hundred clears that test before the casting vote is even reached.

options.text: Yes, but only if more than half of the total membership voted, an ordinary resolution requiring a majority of all members
options.misconception: measures the majority against the whole register rather than the votes cast
options.why: The sub-section counts votes cast, not members on the register. Members who did not vote are simply absent from both sides of the comparison.

options.text: No — a chairman's casting vote may break a tie but may never be counted in working out the majority
options.misconception: excludes a vote the sub-section expressly includes
options.why: Section 114(1) names the casting vote of the chairman inside the counting rule itself. It is part of the arithmetic, not an extra step outside it.

options.text: No — an ordinary resolution needs three times as many votes in favour as against
options.misconception: applies the special resolution arithmetic to an ordinary one
options.why: The three-to-one requirement is section 114(2) and it defines a special resolution. Section 114(1) asks only that the votes in favour exceed the votes against.

citation.ref: Section 114(1)

items.scenario: At a general meeting of Redwood Ltd an item is put to the vote. 4,000 votes are cast in favour and 3,900 against. The chairman, who holds a casting vote under the articles, uses it in favour. The item is one the Act allows to be carried by an ordinary resolution.

items.stem: What does section 105(2) require the notice to have said?

options.text: It had to say that a proxy may speak at the meeting and vote on a show of hands
options.misconception: states in the notice the opposite of what section 105(1) provides
options.why: Section 105(1) says a proxy shall not have the right to speak at the meeting and shall not be entitled to vote except on a poll. A notice saying otherwise would be wrong.

options.text: It had to name the persons whom a member may appoint, a proxy having to be chosen from the company's own members
options.misconception: adds a membership qualification the sub-section expressly removes
options.why: Section 105(2) says the notice must state that a proxy need not be a member of the company. The Act therefore rules out the very restriction this option assumes.

options.text: It had to state, with reasonable prominence, that a member entitled to attend and vote may appoint a proxy, and that the proxy need not be a member of the company
options.why: Section 105(2) requires that in every notice calling a meeting of a company which has a share capital, there shall appear with reasonable prominence a statement that a member entitled to attend and vote is entitled to appoint a proxy, or, where that is allowed, one or more proxies, to attend and vote instead of himself, and that a proxy need not be a member of the company. A notice that is silent on the point does not answer the sub-section.

options.text: Nothing — the right to appoint a proxy comes from the Act, so the notice need not repeat it
options.misconception: treats a statutory right as excusing the statutory notice about it
options.why: The right does come from section 105(1), and section 105(2) separately obliges the company to tell the members about it in the notice. Both duties run.

citation.ref: Section 105(2)

items.scenario: Kelvin Ltd, a company having a share capital, sends out the notice of its annual general meeting. The notice sets out the business and the venue and says nothing else. A member later complains that he did not know he could send someone in his place.

items.stem: Is a Board resolution enough?

options.text: No — giving time for the repayment of a debt due from a director is one of the four acts section 180 reserves to a special resolution of the members
options.why: Section 180(1)(d) says the Board shall exercise the power to remit, or give time for the repayment of, any debt due from a director only with the consent of the company by a special resolution. It sits in the same list as the sale of an undertaking and the borrowing limit, and each clause of the list bites on its own facts. Whether the company is near its borrowing ceiling is beside the point.

options.text: Yes — section 180 is about selling the undertaking and about borrowing, and neither is happening here
options.misconception: reads section 180(1) as a list of two
options.why: Section 180(1) has four clauses. Clause (d) covers remitting a debt due from a director or giving time for its repayment, and it applies whatever the position under clauses (a) and (c).

options.text: No — an ordinary resolution of the members is required
options.misconception: downgrades the resolution section 180 names
options.why: Section 180(1) opens by requiring the consent of the company by a special resolution for every one of the four powers it lists.

options.text: Yes, provided the interested director does not vote on the resolution at the Board meeting
options.misconception: treats an abstention as a substitute for members' approval
options.why: Abstaining answers section 184. Section 180 asks for the consent of the company by a special resolution, and no arrangement inside the boardroom supplies that.

citation.ref: Section 180(1)(d)

items.scenario: A director of Ashgrove Ltd owes the company ₹40 lakh, repayable on 30 June 2026. The Board resolves to give him a further two years to repay. The company is nowhere near its borrowing limits and no undertaking is being sold.

items.stem: Which part of his proposal does section 128(1) permit?

options.text: The cash basis and single entry, but not the electronic form, books of account having to exist on paper
options.misconception: inverts the sub-section, permitting what it forbids and forbidding what it permits
options.why: The second proviso to section 128(1) expressly allows books to be kept in electronic mode, while accrual and double entry are mandatory.

options.text: Keeping the books in electronic mode, but not the cash basis and not single entry
options.why: Section 128(1) requires every company to keep books of account and other relevant books and papers that give a true and fair view of the state of affairs, and it says those books shall be kept on accrual basis and according to the double entry system. The second proviso to the same sub-section allows the books to be kept in electronic mode in such manner as may be prescribed, so the server is fine and the other two choices are not.

options.text: All three — the section prescribes a place and a period and leaves the method of accounting to the company
options.misconception: reduces section 128(1) to a rule about where the books sit
options.why: The place and the period are in the first proviso and in section 128(5). The basis and the system are written into section 128(1) itself.

options.text: None of the three, because section 128 requires the books to be maintained only in the form the auditor approves
options.misconception: hands the statutory requirement to the auditor
options.why: Section 128 addresses the company and its directors. The auditor reports on the books; he does not choose the basis on which they are kept.

citation.ref: Section 128(1) with its second proviso

items.scenario: A newly appointed accountant at Thornhill Ltd proposes to keep the company's books on a cash basis, using single entry, and to hold them only as scanned images on the company's server. He says the Act is silent on method and only cares that the numbers are right.

items.stem: How does section 152(6) decide who retires?

options.text: Those longest in office since their last appointment go first; and as between the two appointed on the same day, in default of agreement, by lot
options.why: Section 152(6)(c) says the directors to retire by rotation at every annual general meeting shall be those who have been longest in office since their last appointment. Clause (d) then deals with the tie: as between persons who became directors on the same day, those to retire shall, in default of and subject to any agreement among themselves, be determined by lot. So seniority decides first, and the draw decides only the tie the agreement failed to settle.

options.text: The Board chooses, its discretion being unfettered where the articles are silent
options.misconception: gives the Board a choice the section has already made
options.why: Section 152(6)(c) fixes the order by length of service. Nothing is left to the Board's selection.

options.text: The two with the smallest shareholding retire, shareholding being the tie-breaker the Act supplies
options.misconception: invents a test the section does not contain
options.why: Neither clause (c) nor clause (d) mentions shareholding. Length of office decides, and a lot breaks a tie in default of agreement.

options.text: The two most recently appointed retire, so that the longest-serving directors stay on the board
options.misconception: reverses the rule
options.why: The section sends out those longest in office since their last appointment, not the newest arrivals.

citation.ref: Sections 152(6)(c) and 152(6)(d)

items.scenario: Six of Pinewood Ltd's directors are liable to retire by rotation. Two of them must retire at the coming annual general meeting. Four were appointed on different dates over the past six years; the remaining two were both appointed on the same day, and they cannot agree between themselves who should go.

items.stem: Which of the four does section 149(9) rule out?

options.text: The profit related commission, an independent director's pay having to be independent of results
options.misconception: forbids the commission the sub-section permits
options.why: Section 149(9) names profit related commission as approved by the members among the permitted forms of payment. It is allowed, not barred.

options.text: None of the four, section 149(9) leaving the package to the nomination and remuneration committee
options.misconception: treats the committee's recommendation as the whole of the law
options.why: The committee recommends within the law. Section 149(9) shuts out stock options altogether, whatever the committee proposes.

options.text: The stock options, and only those
options.why: Section 149(9) says an independent director shall not be entitled to any stock option and may receive remuneration by way of fee provided under section 197(5), reimbursement of expenses for participation in the Board and other meetings, and profit related commission as may be approved by the members. Three of the four proposals are the very things the sub-section allows; the option grant is the one thing it forbids by name.

options.text: The sitting fees, an independent director serving without fee
options.misconception: assumes independence means unpaid
options.why: The sub-section allows remuneration by way of fee under section 197(5). Sitting fees are the ordinary way an independent director is paid.

citation.ref: Section 149(9)

items.scenario: Bellhaven Ltd wants to reward an independent director who has been of real use on the board. The nomination committee proposes a grant of stock options, sitting fees for the meetings he attends, reimbursement of his travel, and a commission linked to profits approved by the members.

items.stem: May he be appointed?

options.text: No — a conviction involving moral turpitude bars a person from ever being appointed a director
options.misconception: turns a five-year bar into a permanent one
options.why: Only a sentence of imprisonment for seven years or more carries a permanent bar under the proviso. A nine-month sentence engages the five-year clock and nothing longer.

options.text: Yes — section 164 disqualifies only for a failure to file financial statements or annual returns
options.misconception: confines section 164 to sub-section (2)
options.why: The filing default is section 164(2). Sub-section (1) carries its own list of personal disqualifications, including this conviction limb.

options.text: Yes — the disqualification ends the day the sentence is served
options.misconception: stops the clock at release rather than five years later
options.why: The clause runs its five years from the date of expiry of the sentence. Release starts the period; it does not end it.

options.text: No — five years have not passed since the expiry of the sentence
options.why: Section 164(1)(d) disqualifies a person who has been convicted by a court of any offence, whether or not involving moral turpitude, and sentenced in respect thereof to imprisonment for not less than six months, and a period of five years has not elapsed from the date of expiry of the sentence. Nine months is more than the six-month line, and from 1 March 2024 only about two and a half years have gone, so the bar is still running.
keywords: imprisonment for not less than six months

citation.ref: Section 164(1)(d)

items.scenario: Mr Q was convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude and sentenced to imprisonment for nine months. He completed the sentence on 1 March 2024. On 1 September 2026 a company wishes to appoint him as a director. No other disqualification touches him.

items.stem: What does section 184(3) say about the contract?

options.text: It is voidable at the option of the other contracting party
options.misconception: puts the option in the wrong hands
options.why: The sub-section gives the option to the company, whose interest the disclosure duty protects, and not to the counterparty.

options.text: It is void from the beginning, so nothing passed under it
options.misconception: reads voidable as void
options.why: The sub-section says voidable, not void. A void contract never existed; a voidable one stands until the party with the option avoids it.

options.text: It stands, the only consequence being a penalty on the director
options.misconception: leaves the company without the remedy the sub-section gives it
options.why: A penalty on the director under section 184(4) is a separate consequence. Section 184(3) additionally hands the company the power to unwind the transaction.

options.text: It is voidable at the option of the company
options.why: Section 184(3) provides that a contract or arrangement entered into by the company without disclosure under sub-section (2), or with the participation by a director who is concerned or interested in any way, directly or indirectly, in the contract or arrangement, shall be voidable at the option of the company. The company therefore chooses whether to keep the contract or avoid it; the breach does not decide that for it.
keywords: at the option of the company

citation.ref: Section 184(3)

items.scenario: A director of Winterly Ltd is interested in a supply contract the Board approves. He neither discloses his interest nor leaves the room, and the contract is signed. Three months later the company discovers the interest. The supplier has begun performing.

items.stem: What does section 203(2) require instead?

options.text: Nothing more — the managing director may appoint officers below the Board and report the appointment
options.misconception: treats a key managerial appointment as ordinary delegated hiring
options.why: Section 203(2) is written precisely to lift this appointment out of ordinary hiring and onto the Board's own record.

options.text: Appointment by an ordinary resolution of the members in general meeting
options.misconception: moves the appointment to the shareholders
options.why: Section 203(2) puts the appointment of a whole-time key managerial person with the Board. The members appoint directors under section 152, which is a different question.

options.text: Approval of the Central Government before the appointment takes effect
options.misconception: adds a government approval the section does not require
options.why: No Central Government approval features in section 203. The requirement is a Board resolution.

options.text: Appointment by a resolution of the Board containing the terms and conditions of the appointment, including the remuneration
options.why: Section 203(2) says every whole-time key managerial personnel of a company shall be appointed by means of a resolution of the Board containing the terms and conditions of the appointment including the remuneration. The Board makes the appointment itself, in a resolution that carries the terms, rather than noting afterwards a letter someone else issued.

citation.ref: Section 203(2)

items.scenario: Fernhill Ltd is required to have a whole-time company secretary. The managing director issues an appointment letter to a candidate on the company's letterhead, setting out her salary, and tells the Board it can note the matter at its next meeting.

items.stem: What does section 139(1) require on the filing?

options.text: The auditor, not the company, must file the notice with the Registrar
options.misconception: puts the duty on the wrong party
options.why: The sub-section addresses the company: the company shall inform the auditor and the company shall file the notice.

options.text: There is no separate filing; the appointment is reported through the annual return
options.misconception: folds a standalone filing into the annual return
options.why: Section 139(1) imposes its own filing with its own clock. The annual return under section 92 is a different document with a different due date.

options.text: The notice of appointment must be filed with the Registrar within fifteen days of the meeting
options.why: Section 139(1) requires the company to inform the auditor concerned of his appointment and to file a notice of such appointment with the Registrar within fifteen days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed. The period runs from the meeting itself, so waiting for the annual return misses it.

options.text: The notice must be filed within thirty days of the meeting
options.misconception: substitutes a period from a different provision
options.why: Thirty days is the period for registering a charge under section 77 and for an auditor's resignation statement under section 140(2). Section 139(1) says fifteen days.

citation.ref: Section 139(1)

items.scenario: Sandbourne Ltd appoints an audit firm at its annual general meeting held on 20 August 2026. The company secretary writes to the firm the same week. He plans to file the notice of appointment with the Registrar when the annual return goes in, some months later.

items.stem: What does section 140(2) require of the resigning auditor?

options.text: He must file the statement with the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India in every case
options.misconception: applies a government company rule to an ordinary company
options.why: Section 140(2) requires the additional filing with the Comptroller and Auditor-General only where the company is a government company or one covered by section 139(5). This company is neither.

options.text: Nothing — the company files the intimation of the casual vacancy and that is the end of it
options.misconception: lets the company's filing discharge the auditor's separate duty
options.why: The company has its own steps to take on the vacancy under section 139(8). Section 140(2) lays a distinct duty on the outgoing auditor, and section 140(3) penalises him if he ignores it.

options.text: He must file the statement only if the resignation follows a disagreement with the management
options.misconception: adds a condition the sub-section does not carry
options.why: The sub-section applies to every resignation. The reasons go into the statement; they do not decide whether the statement is due.

options.text: He must himself file a statement in the prescribed form with the company and with the Registrar within thirty days of the resignation
options.why: Section 140(2) says the auditor who has resigned from the company shall file within a period of thirty days from the date of resignation, a statement in the prescribed form with the company and the Registrar, indicating the reasons and other facts as may be relevant with regard to his resignation. The duty is the auditor's own, and section 140(3) attaches a penalty on him if he fails to comply.

citation.ref: Sections 140(2) and 140(3)

items.scenario: The statutory auditor of Marlowe Ltd, a company that is not a government company, resigns on 5 May 2026 and writes to the Board explaining why. He assumes the company will deal with any filing that follows, since it is the company that must fill the vacancy.

items.stem: How does section 123(5) treat the two proposals?

options.text: The vouchers are permitted if their face value equals the dividend, since the shareholder receives full value
options.misconception: measures the rule by value rather than by form
options.why: The sub-section is about the form of the payment, not its worth. Anything that is not cash fails it however exactly it matches the amount.

options.text: Neither is permitted, a bonus issue being a distribution in kind and so barred by the same words
options.misconception: ignores the proviso that saves capitalisation
options.why: The proviso to section 123(5) exists exactly to take a bonus issue out of the bar. It names capitalisation of profits or reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares.

options.text: Both are permitted, a dividend in kind being lawful where the members approve it
options.misconception: lets members' consent override the statutory form of payment
options.why: Section 123(5) states the rule without reference to members' approval. A dividend is not payable except in cash, whatever the meeting resolves.

options.text: The vouchers are not permitted, because a dividend must be paid in cash; the bonus issue is permitted, because the sub-section expressly saves capitalisation of profits
options.why: Section 123(5) says no dividend shall be paid by a company in respect of any share except to the registered shareholder of such share or to his order or to his banker, and shall not be payable except in cash. Its proviso then says nothing in the sub-section shall be deemed to prohibit the capitalisation of profits or reserves of a company for the purpose of issuing fully paid-up bonus shares or paying up any amount unpaid on the shares held by the members. So the vouchers fail and the bonus shares stand.

citation.ref: Section 123(5) with its proviso

items.scenario: Oakbourne Ltd has declared a dividend and is short of cash. The Board proposes to satisfy it by sending each shareholder vouchers redeemable at the company's own stores, and separately to capitalise reserves and issue fully paid bonus shares to all members.

items.stem: What does the proviso to section 135(5) say about where the money goes?

options.text: The company shall give preference to the local area and areas around it where it operates
options.why: The proviso to section 135(5) says the company shall give preference to the local area and areas around it where it operates, for spending the amount earmarked for corporate social responsibility activities. It is a preference written into the sub-section, so a Board that spends elsewhere without regard to it has not applied the provision.

options.text: The whole of the amount must be spent within the district in which the registered office is situate
options.misconception: hardens a preference into a geographical cap
options.why: The proviso states a preference, not an exclusive area, and it speaks of where the company operates rather than where its registered office sits.

options.text: Preference must be given to activities in the state that contributed the most tax revenue from the company
options.misconception: invents a link to tax the section does not make
options.why: Section 135 says nothing about tax revenue. The preference attaches to the local area and areas around it where the company operates.

options.text: Nothing — the choice of area is entirely for the Board, section 135 governing only the amount
options.misconception: reads section 135(5) as an arithmetic rule alone
options.why: Section 135(5) fixes the amount in its main limb and then adds the local area preference in its proviso. Both are part of the same sub-section.

citation.ref: Proviso to section 135(5)

items.scenario: Alderman Ltd is covered by section 135 and has a CSR policy. Its factory and its workforce are in one district; the Board proposes to spend the whole of the year's CSR amount on a programme in a distant state chosen because it photographs well.

items.stem: What does section 82 require the company to do?

options.text: Apply to the Tribunal for an order removing the entry from the register of charges
options.misconception: sends a routine filing to the Tribunal
options.why: The Tribunal comes in under section 87 where a filing has been delayed or is defective and rectification is sought. An ordinary satisfaction is filed with the Registrar.

options.text: Nothing — the charge falls away automatically once the debt is repaid, and the register follows
options.misconception: assumes the register updates itself on repayment
options.why: Repayment discharges the security between the parties. The public register changes only when the company files the intimation section 82 requires.

options.text: Give intimation of the payment or satisfaction of the charge to the Registrar in the prescribed form within thirty days of it
options.why: Section 82(1) requires a company to give intimation to the Registrar of the payment or satisfaction in full of any charge registered under Chapter VI, in the prescribed form and manner, within a period of thirty days from the date of such payment or satisfaction. It is a separate filing with its own clock and does not ride on the annual return.

options.text: Report the satisfaction in the annual return, which is the vehicle the Act provides for it
options.misconception: folds a standalone filing into the annual return
options.why: Section 82 fixes its own period of thirty days from the date of payment or satisfaction. The annual return under section 92 is a different filing on a different clock.

citation.ref: Section 82(1)

items.scenario: Bramley Ltd repays a term loan in full on 10 April 2026 and the bank releases its security the same day. The registered charge still shows on the company's index of charges. The finance head says the register will correct itself when the next annual return is filed.

items.stem: Is the dispatch in order under section 62(2)?

options.text: Yes — a twenty-day offer period cures a short dispatch, since every shareholder still has time to apply
options.misconception: sets one requirement off against another
options.why: The offer window in section 62(1)(a) and the dispatch lead time in section 62(2) are two separate conditions. Meeting one does not answer the other.

options.text: No — the notice had to go by registered post, speed post not being an approved mode
options.misconception: shortens a list the sub-section writes out in full
options.why: Section 62(2) names registered post, speed post, electronic mode, courier or any other mode having proof of delivery. Speed post is squarely inside it.

options.text: No — the notice must be dispatched at least three days before the opening of the issue
options.why: Section 62(2) says the notice referred to in sub-clause (i) of clause (a) of sub-section (1) shall be dispatched through registered post or speed post or through electronic mode or courier or any other mode having proof of delivery to all the existing shareholders at least three days before the opening of the issue. Speed post is an approved mode, but two days is short of the three the sub-section fixes.
keywords: before the opening of the issue

options.text: Yes — the sub-section fixes the mode of dispatch and leaves the timing to the company
options.misconception: reads section 62(2) as a rule about the mode alone
options.why: The same sentence carries both. It names the modes and then requires dispatch at least three days before the opening of the issue.

citation.ref: Section 62(2)

items.scenario: Gallowfield Ltd's rights issue opens on Monday 8 June 2026. The company posts the letters of offer by speed post on Saturday 6 June, so that they leave the office two days before the issue opens. The offer period itself is twenty days and renunciation is allowed.

items.stem: What does section 42(8) still require?

options.text: A return of allotment within thirty days, the general period for filings with the Registrar
options.misconception: substitutes a period from a different provision
options.why: Section 42(8) fixes its own figure of fifteen days from the allotment. There is no general thirty-day rule that displaces it.

options.text: A prospectus, a private placement becoming a public offer once the securities are allotted
options.misconception: converts a lawful placement into a public offer
options.why: A private placement becomes a deemed public offer where the company advertises or solicits the public, not merely because it allots.

options.text: A return of allotment filed with the Registrar within fifteen days of the allotment, including a complete list of all security holders with their full names and addresses
options.why: Section 42(8) requires a company making an allotment of securities under this section to file with the Registrar a return of allotment within fifteen days of the allotment, including a complete list of all security holders, with their full names, addresses, number of securities allotted and such other relevant information as may be prescribed. Clean money and a timely allotment do not dispense with it.
keywords: complete list of all security holders

options.text: Nothing further — the separate bank account and the timely allotment are the whole of section 42
options.misconception: stops at the conditions that precede allotment
options.why: Those conditions sit in section 42(6) and its provisos. Sub-section (8) adds a filing after the allotment has been made.

citation.ref: Section 42(8)

items.scenario: Kingsmoor Ltd allots shares under a private placement on 1 July 2026 to sixty identified persons. The money was received through banking channels and kept in a separate account, and the allotment was made well inside the period the Act allows. Nothing further has been filed.

items.stem: When does the moratorium cease to have effect?

options.text: On the date the Adjudicating Authority approves the resolution plan, or passes an order for liquidation, whichever happens first
options.why: Section 14(4) says the order of moratorium shall have effect from the date of the order until the completion of the corporate insolvency resolution process, and that where the Adjudicating Authority approves the resolution plan under section 31(1) or passes an order for liquidation of the corporate debtor under section 33, the moratorium shall cease to have effect from the date of such approval or liquidation order, as the case may be. Approval by the committee alone is not that date.

options.text: On the day the committee of creditors votes to approve the plan
options.misconception: takes the committee's vote as the ending event
options.why: Section 14(4) fixes the date by reference to the Adjudicating Authority's approval under section 31(1), not the committee's vote that precedes it.

options.text: On the one hundred and eightieth day from admission, whatever happens to the plan
options.misconception: ties the moratorium to a fixed period rather than to the process
options.why: Section 14(4) runs the moratorium until the completion of the process. The timeline in section 12 governs how long the process may take, not when the moratorium lapses.

options.text: It continues through the liquidation, so no creditor may sue until the company is dissolved
options.misconception: carries the moratorium past the event that ends it
options.why: Section 14(4) names the liquidation order itself as an event that ends the moratorium. The liquidation then has its own bar in section 33(5).

citation.ref: Section 14(4)

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process is running against Everdon Ltd and a moratorium is in force. The committee of creditors approves a resolution plan and the Adjudicating Authority approves it as well. A creditor asks how much longer the moratorium will keep his recovery suit out.

items.stem: Who becomes the liquidator?

options.text: The Official Liquidator attached to the High Court
options.misconception: imports the winding-up machinery of the Companies Act
options.why: The Official Liquidator belongs to a winding up under the Companies Act, 2013. A liquidation under the Code is run by an insolvency professional under section 34.

options.text: The resolution professional appointed for the resolution process, unless the Adjudicating Authority replaces him
options.why: Section 34(1) says where the Adjudicating Authority passes an order for liquidation under section 33, the resolution professional appointed for the corporate insolvency resolution process under Chapter II shall, subject to submission of a written consent, act as the liquidator for the purposes of liquidation, unless replaced by the Adjudicating Authority under section 34(4). Continuity is the rule and replacement is the exception.

options.text: A liquidator nominated by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India in every case
options.misconception: makes the Board's role routine rather than exceptional
options.why: The Board is asked for a name under section 34(5) only where the Adjudicating Authority has directed a replacement. It does not nominate in the ordinary case.
