options.text: An allottee is a financial creditor, and a dispute is no answer to a section 7 application, but the application still fails on numbers — the joint filing requirement is not less than one hundred allottees under the same real estate project or ten per cent of the total allottees under it, whichever is less, and ninety is the smaller figure here
options.why: The Explanation to section 5(8)(f) deems an amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project to have the commercial effect of a borrowing, which makes a homebuyer a financial creditor and not an operational creditor, so no demand notice arises. A dispute is a defence to a section 9 application; on a section 7 application the Adjudicating Authority looks only at whether a default has occurred, as Innoventive Industries held. The second proviso to section 7(1) is what defeats them: the application must be filed jointly by not less than one hundred allottees under the same real estate project or not less than ten per cent of the total number of allottees under that project, whichever is less, and ten per cent of nine hundred is ninety, so ninety is the smaller of the two and sixty falls short. Section 238A applies the Limitation Act, but three years from the June 2024 default have not run, so staleness is not the answer either.

options.text: The application succeeds, because the sixty applicants are financial creditors and the default exceeds the notified minimum, and the number of applicants is irrelevant where the debt is admitted
options.misconception: ignores the joint-filing gate in the second proviso to section 7(1)
options.why: Being a financial creditor is necessary and not sufficient. The amendment of 2020 added a numerical gate for allottees precisely so that a single disgruntled buyer could not put a project into insolvency, and the Supreme Court upheld it in Manish Kumar v Union of India.

options.text: The application fails because an allottee is an operational creditor, so a demand notice under section 8 had to be served and the developer's dispute would then have defeated it
options.misconception: classifies a homebuyer as an operational creditor
options.why: The Explanation to clause (f) of section 5(8) settles this the other way: an amount raised from an allottee under a real estate project is deemed to have the commercial effect of a borrowing, which is financial debt. Section 8 and the pre-existing dispute defence belong to the operational creditor's route and never arise here.

options.text: The application fails only on limitation, because three years had run from the default and section 238A applies Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963
options.misconception: reaches for limitation and misses the numerical bar
options.why: Section 238A does apply the Limitation Act and Article 137 gives three years from the date of default. The default here is of June 2024 and the application is comfortably inside that period; what defeats it is the joint filing requirement in the second proviso to section 7(1).

citation.ref: Explanation to section 5(8)(f), second proviso to section 7(1), section 7(5) and section 238A

items.scenario: A real estate project has nine hundred allottees. Sixty of them, together owed ₹40 crore on bookings the developer has not delivered, file an application under section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The default occurred in June 2024 and exceeds the amount notified under section 4. The developer resists on three grounds — that an allottee is at best an operational creditor who must serve a demand notice first, that in any case there is a genuine dispute because a municipal approval was delayed, and that the claim is stale.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The decision is premature, because liquidation may be ordered only where the resolution process period expires without a plan or the Adjudicating Authority rejects one
options.misconception: reads section 33(1) as the only route into liquidation
options.why: Section 33(1) is one route and it is the one the scenario has not reached. Section 33(2) is a separate route driven by the committee's own decision, and sections 33(3) and 33(4) supply a third for a contravention of an approved plan.

options.text: The trade creditor may sue, because the moratorium under section 14 ends with the resolution process and nothing replaces it in liquidation
options.misconception: assumes the section 14 moratorium is the only bar on proceedings
options.why: The section 14 moratorium does end with the resolution process, and section 33(5) puts its own bar in place from the liquidation order, subject to the rights a secured creditor has under section 52. A fresh proceeding needs the liquidator and the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority.

options.text: The going concern basis is right, because the liquidator is carrying on the business and a sale of the undertaking as a going concern preserves it
options.misconception: confuses selling a business as a going concern with the entity continuing as one
options.why: Selling the undertaking as a going concern transfers the business to a buyer; the corporate debtor itself is being wound up, and Ind AS 1 asks about the entity preparing the financial statements. Section 33(7) makes the point in its own way by deeming the liquidation order to be a notice of discharge to the officers, employees and workmen except where the liquidator continues the business.

options.text: The decision is valid, because section 33(2) with its Explanation lets the committee resolve to liquidate at any time after its constitution and before confirmation of a resolution plan, including before the information memorandum, on not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share; the trade creditor may not sue, because section 33(5) bars proceedings by or against the corporate debtor; and the going concern basis must be abandoned under Ind AS 1
options.why: Section 33(2) requires the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation where the resolution professional intimates a decision of the committee of creditors, approved by not less than sixty-six per cent of the voting share, to liquidate, and its Explanation says the committee may take that decision at any time after its constitution and before the confirmation of the resolution plan, including before the information memorandum is prepared — so time left on the clock is no objection. Section 33(5) then bars any suit or other legal proceeding by or against the corporate debtor, subject to section 52, and only the liquidator may institute one, with the prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority. Ind AS 1 takes the financial statements off the going concern basis where management has no realistic alternative but to liquidate the entity; carrying on the business under section 35(1)(e) for a beneficial liquidation is a way of selling the assets to advantage, not a decision that the entity will continue.

citation.ref: Sections 33(2) with its Explanation, 33(5), 33(7) and 35(1)(e), read with Ind AS 1 and SA 570

items.scenario: On 12 August 2026 the committee of creditors of a corporate debtor resolves, by seventy-one per cent of the voting share, to liquidate the company. No information memorandum has yet been prepared and ninety days of the resolution process period still remain. The Adjudicating Authority passes a liquidation order on 1 September 2026 and the resolution professional continues as liquidator. He intends to keep the plant running so that the undertaking can be sold whole. The finance team proposes to keep preparing the financial statements on a going concern basis for that reason, and a trade creditor wants to sue the company for its unpaid dues.

items.stem: How should the three transactions be dealt with?

options.text: Nothing can be done about the machinery, because only the resolution professional or the liquidator may apply in respect of an undervalued transaction
options.misconception: overlooks the creditor's independent right under section 47
options.why: Section 47(1) lets a creditor, member, partner or other interested person apply where an undervalued transaction has not been reported by the liquidator or the resolution professional, and section 47(3) lets the Adjudicating Authority order the Board to start disciplinary proceedings against the professional who missed it.

options.text: The plot is outside the relevant period in section 46(1) on any view but is reachable under section 49, which carries no look-back and whose only limit does not protect a buyer with notice; the machinery is an undervalued transaction inside the one-year window and section 47(1) lets the creditor apply where the resolution professional has not; and the bridge loan is taken out of the extortionate credit provision by section 50(2)
options.why: The relevant period in section 46(1) is two years preceding the insolvency commencement date for a related party and one year for anybody else, and a transfer of March 2023 is outside both. Section 49 answers it — where an undervalued transaction was deliberately entered into for keeping assets beyond the reach of a person entitled to make a claim, the Adjudicating Authority may restore the position, and that section fixes no relevant period at all; its only limit is that the order shall not prejudice an interest acquired in good faith, for value and without notice, which a buyer who knew of the decree cannot claim. The machinery sale is undervalued under section 45(2) and sits six months inside the one-year window, and section 47(1) lets a creditor apply where the professional has not reported it. Section 50(2) excludes from the extortionate credit provision any debt extended by a person providing financial services in compliance with any law for the time being in force.

options.text: The bridge loan is an extortionate credit transaction, because it falls inside the two years section 50 measures and the terms require exorbitant payments
options.misconception: ignores the carve-out for a regulated lender in section 50(2)
options.why: The loan does sit inside the two years preceding the insolvency commencement date and the terms may well be exorbitant. Section 50(2) still takes it out, because it excludes any debt extended by a person providing financial services in compliance with any law for the time being in force.

options.text: The plot cannot be touched, because the longest look-back the Code allows is the two years in section 46(1) and it expired long before the process began
options.misconception: reads the section 46 look-back as governing section 49 as well
options.why: Section 46(1) fixes the relevant period for an undervalued transaction reported under section 45. Section 49 is a separate remedy for a transaction deliberately entered into to defeat a claimant, and Parliament gave it no time limit at all, precisely because concealment is what it is aimed at.

items.scenario: A corporate insolvency resolution process commences on 1 July 2026. Three transactions are put to the resolution professional. On 1 March 2023, three days after a money decree was passed against the corporate debtor, it transferred a plot worth ₹30 crore to a buyer for ₹2 crore, and the buyer knew of the decree. On 1 January 2026 it transferred machinery worth ₹8 crore to an unrelated purchaser for ₹1 crore, outside the ordinary course of its business. In March 2025 it took a bridge loan from a non-banking financial company on terms the resolution professional considers exorbitant, though the lender says the terms complied with the law it is regulated under. The resolution professional reports the plot but not the machinery, and a creditor wants to act on the machinery himself.

items.stem: What is the correct treatment of the valuations and of the objection?

options.text: The plan is valid, because the distribution among classes of creditors is a matter of the committee's commercial wisdom and is not justiciable
options.misconception: reads Essar Steel as removing the section 30(2)(b) minimum too
options.why: Essar Steel held that the committee's assessment of the viability and feasibility of a plan and its distribution between classes is not to be second-guessed. It did not touch section 30(2)(b), which fixes a statutory minimum for a dissenting financial creditor by reference to section 53, and a plan below that minimum is not one the Adjudicating Authority may approve.

options.text: The fair value is ₹823.33 crore, the average of all three estimates, and the plan is invalid because the aggregate offered is below it
options.misconception: averages every estimate and treats fair value as a reserve price
options.why: Regulation 35(1) says the average of the two closest estimates shall be considered, not the average of all of them, so the ₹1,050 crore outlier is discarded rather than blended in. And no provision of the Code requires a resolution plan to match fair value; a plan below it can be perfectly valid.

options.text: The third valuer's estimate of ₹720 crore replaces the first two, and the plan is valid because the ₹420 crore offered exceeds the liquidation value of the assets
options.misconception: treats the third valuation as a substitute and liquidation value as the only test
options.why: Regulation 35(1) does not replace the earlier estimates with the third one; it directs that the average of the two closest estimates be considered. And exceeding the liquidation value in aggregate is not the test — the minimum is measured creditor by creditor against what section 53 would have given each of them.

options.text: The fair value is ₹710 crore, being the average of ₹700 crore and ₹720 crore, but that figure is no floor; the plan is nevertheless bad, because section 30(2)(b) requires a financial creditor who did not vote in favour of it to receive not less than the amount payable to him under section 53 in a liquidation
options.why: Regulation 35(1) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016 lets the resolution professional appoint another registered valuer where the two estimates are significantly different, and directs that the average of the two closest estimates shall be considered — ₹700 crore and ₹720 crore are the closest pair, so ₹710 crore is the figure. Nothing in the Code makes fair value a reserve price for a resolution plan. The only floor is in section 30(2)(b), which requires payment to operational creditors and to a dissenting financial creditor of not less than what section 53 would have given them on a liquidation. Essar Steel put the committee's commercial wisdom on the distribution among classes beyond judicial review, but the section 30(2)(b) minimum is statutory and stands outside that.
keywords: average of the two closest estimates

citation.ref: Regulations 27 and 35(1) of the IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, read with section 30(2)(b) of the Code

items.scenario: Two registered valuers appointed under Regulation 27 report a liquidation value of ₹300 crore and ₹310 crore, and a fair value of ₹700 crore and ₹1,050 crore. The resolution professional considers the fair value estimates significantly different and appoints a third registered valuer, who reports ₹720 crore. The committee of creditors then approves a resolution plan offering ₹420 crore in aggregate, under which the operational creditors receive more than they would have under section 53 but a dissenting financial creditor receives less than section 53 would have given him. The dissenting creditor objects that the plan is below fair value.

items.stem: What fails the Regulations?

options.text: Only the resolutions are wrong for the new director, and an ordinary resolution is enough for the independent director because section 152(2) says a director shall be appointed by the company in general meeting
options.misconception: lets the Companies Act default override Regulation 25(2A)
options.why: Section 152(2) allows a director to be appointed by ordinary resolution in general meeting, and for an unlisted company that is the end of it. Regulation 25(2A) raises the bar for an independent director of a listed entity to a special resolution, and the listed entity meets the higher of the two requirements.

options.text: Nothing fails — section 149(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires only three directors in a public company and section 149(4) requires only one-third of a listed public company's board to be independent directors
options.misconception: applies the Companies Act floors to a listed entity
options.why: Section 149(1) does require three directors and section 149(4) does require one-third independent directors, and both are satisfied here. A listed entity has to meet the LODR as well, and where the two differ the Regulation is the stricter — six directors, and at least half independent where the chairperson is an executive director or a promoter.

options.text: Only the age is a problem, and a special resolution at the annual general meeting on 25 September cures everything
options.misconception: reads Regulation 17(1A) as the only condition in play
options.why: A special resolution answers Regulation 17(1A) and nothing else. Board size under Regulation 17(1)(c) and the independence ratio under Regulation 17(1)(b) are composition requirements no resolution can waive, and Regulation 25(2A) needs its own special resolution for the independent director.

options.text: Four things — Regulation 17(1)(c) requires a board of not less than six directors for an entity of this size; Regulation 17(1)(b) requires at least half the board to be independent where the chairperson is an executive director and a promoter; Regulation 17(1A) requires a special resolution to appoint or continue a non-executive director who has attained the age of seventy-five years; and Regulation 25(2A) requires a special resolution for the re-appointment of an independent director
options.why: Regulation 17(1)(c) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 requires the board of a listed entity of this size to comprise not less than six directors, and this one stays at five. Regulation 17(1)(b) requires at least half the board to comprise independent directors where the chairperson is an executive director or is a promoter, so two out of five is short on either count. Regulation 17(1A) forbids a listed entity to appoint or continue the directorship of a non-executive director who has attained the age of seventy-five years unless a special resolution is passed with the justification in the explanatory statement. Regulation 25(2A) separately requires the appointment, re-appointment or removal of an independent director to be approved by a special resolution, so an ordinary resolution will not carry the re-appointment.

citation.ref: Regulations 17(1)(b), 17(1)(c), 17(1A) and 25(2A), read with sections 149(1), 149(4) and 152(2) of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A listed company among the top five hundred listed entities by market capitalisation has five directors — an executive chairperson who is also a promoter, two other executive directors, and two independent directors of whom one is a woman. On 1 June 2026 an executive director resigns and the board appoints in his place a non-executive director aged seventy-eight. The board size therefore stays at five. The company proposes to place the new director's appointment, and the re-appointment of one of the independent directors, before the annual general meeting on 25 September 2026, in each case by ordinary resolution.

items.stem: Where is the company secretary wrong?

options.text: On all three — Regulation 24(6) requires prior approval of the listed entity's shareholders by special resolution where more than twenty per cent of a material subsidiary's assets are sold, disposed of or leased in a financial year; Regulation 24(5) requires the same special resolution before the listed entity reduces its holding to fifty per cent or less or ceases to exercise control; and Regulation 24(1) puts at least one independent director of the listed entity on the board of an unlisted material subsidiary
options.why: Regulation 24(6) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 requires the prior approval of the listed entity's shareholders by special resolution for the selling, disposing of or leasing of assets amounting to more than twenty per cent of the assets of a material subsidiary on an aggregate basis during a financial year, so thirty per cent is caught. Regulation 24(5) requires that same special resolution before the listed entity disposes of shares in a material subsidiary so as to reduce its holding to fifty per cent or less, or ceases to exercise control over it. Regulation 24(1) requires at least one independent director on the board of the listed entity to be a director on the board of an unlisted material subsidiary, which is the case where nobody outside the group is watching. The only carve-out from the two approvals is where the transaction is under a scheme of arrangement approved by a court or tribunal or a resolution plan approved under section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, and neither is present here.

options.text: The resolutions and the independent director are required, but the subsidiary is outside secretarial audit, since section 204 reaches only the listed parent and prescribed public companies
options.misconception: overlooks Regulation 24A
options.why: Section 204 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a secretarial audit for every listed company and for the prescribed classes of public companies, and on its own it would not reach this subsidiary. Regulation 24A of the LODR does, requiring every listed entity and its material unlisted subsidiaries incorporated in India to undertake a secretarial audit and annex the report of a company secretary in practice to the annual report.

options.text: Nothing needs a special resolution, because a subsidiary is material only where its net worth exceeds the prescribed proportion of consolidated net worth, and the scenario speaks of income
options.misconception: reads the material subsidiary test as a single limb
options.why: Regulation 16(1)(c) makes a subsidiary material where its income or its net worth exceeds the prescribed proportion of the consolidated income or net worth respectively of the listed entity and its subsidiaries in the immediately preceding accounting year. The two limbs are alternatives, and crossing either one is enough.

options.text: He is right — section 180(1)(a) puts the special resolution to the members of the company selling the undertaking, which is the subsidiary, and the parent's board can pass it as its sole member
options.misconception: stops at the Companies Act, which does not follow assets down into a subsidiary
options.why: Section 180(1)(a) does put the resolution to the members of the company that is selling, leasing or otherwise disposing of the whole or substantially the whole of its undertaking, and here that company is the subsidiary whose sole member is the parent. That leaves the listed entity's own public shareholders with no vote on a disposal that changes what they own, and Regulation 24(6) exists to give them one.

citation.ref: Regulations 16(1)(c), 24(1), 24(5), 24(6) and 24A, read with sections 180(1)(a) and 204 of the Companies Act, 2013

items.scenario: A listed parent has one wholly owned unlisted Indian subsidiary whose income for the immediately preceding accounting year exceeded the proportion of consolidated income that makes a subsidiary material. During 2026-27 the subsidiary proposes to sell a division amounting to thirty per cent of its assets, and the parent proposes to sell down its holding in the subsidiary from a hundred per cent to forty-five per cent. Neither transaction is under a scheme of arrangement or a resolution plan. The parent's company secretary advises that section 180(1)(a) puts the question to the subsidiary's own members, that the parent's public shareholders therefore do not vote on either, and that no independent director of the parent need sit on an unlisted subsidiary's board.

items.stem: What is right and what is wrong here?

options.text: The chief financial officer is right on the statement, because a Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications is required only for an adverse opinion or a disclaimer, a qualification being a lesser thing
options.misconception: reads a modified opinion as meaning only the two severe modifications
options.why: SA 705 (Revised) calls all three of a qualified opinion, an adverse opinion and a disclaimer of opinion a modified opinion, and the difference between them is the pervasiveness of the effect, not whether the report is modified. Regulation 33(3)(d) attaches the statement to any modified opinion, so a qualification brings it.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the reports themselves, because a full audit gives more assurance than a limited review and a peer review certificate is a matter between the firm and the Institute
options.misconception: treats the peer review certificate as internal to the profession
options.why: An audit does give more assurance than a limited review under SRE 2410, and Regulation 33 lets the quarterly figures be audited instead of reviewed. The certificate is not internal either way — Regulation 33(1)(c) makes it a condition of the report being submitted to the exchange at all, so an audit by a firm without one still does not satisfy the Regulation.

options.text: Both filings are late, because Regulation 33 allows sixty days from the end of every period, quarterly and annual alike
options.misconception: applies the annual clock to the quarterly results
options.why: Regulation 33 runs two different clocks. Quarterly and year-to-date results go in within forty-five days of the end of the quarter under Regulation 33(3)(a); the annual audited results go in within sixty days of the end of the financial year under Regulation 33(3)(d).

options.text: The quarterly filing is in time under the forty-five days Regulation 33(3)(a) allows, but the annual results were due within sixty days of the end of the financial year and are late; a Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications was required because a qualified opinion is a modified opinion; and Regulation 33(1)(c) requires the auditor signing either report to hold a valid peer review certificate
options.why: Regulation 33(3)(a) of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 gives a listed entity forty-five days from the end of a quarter other than the last, and 10 November is the forty-first day from 30 September. Regulation 33(3)(d) gives sixty days from the end of the financial year for the annual audited results, and 12 June is the seventy-third day from 31 March. The same clause attaches a Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications wherever the audit report carries a modified opinion, and SA 705 (Revised) treats a qualified opinion, an adverse opinion and a disclaimer alike as modified. Regulation 33(1)(c) then requires the limited review or audit report submitted to the stock exchanges to be given only by an auditor who has subjected himself to the peer review process of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India and holds a valid certificate from its Peer Review Board.
keywords: Statement on Impact of Audit Qualifications

citation.ref: Regulations 33(1)(c), 33(3)(a) and 33(3)(d), read with SRE 2410 and SA 705 (Revised)

items.scenario: A listed company with a 31 March year end submits its results for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 on 10 November 2026, and its annual audited results for the year ended 31 March 2026 on 12 June 2026. The auditor's report on the annual financial statements carried a qualified opinion, and the company submitted no separate statement with the results. The firm signing both reports has never obtained a peer review certificate. The chief financial officer says the quarterly figures were fully audited rather than reviewed, so nothing further was needed, and that a separate statement is called for only where the auditor gives an adverse opinion or a disclaimer.

items.stem: What is wrong with the grants and with the accounting?

options.text: The vesting date is a matter for the company to fix, and reversing the expense on an unexercised option is right because no shares were ever issued
options.misconception: treats the minimum vesting period as contractual and expiry as undoing the expense
options.why: Rule 12(6)(a) imposes a minimum period of one year between grant and vesting, and the only relaxation is for options granted in lieu of options held under a scheme of a transferor company on a merger or amalgamation. Ind AS 102 does not reverse the expense for a vested award that lapses unexercised, because the entity has already received the services the award paid for; any adjustment is a transfer within equity.

options.text: The grants to the independent director and to the whole-time director are not permitted at all; the grant to the subsidiary's chief executive and the grant of 1.4 per cent to an identified employee each needed a separate resolution; vesting six months after grant breaches the minimum period; and under Ind AS 102 an equity-settled award is measured once at the grant date and no reversal is made where a vested option expires unexercised
options.why: Rule 12(1) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 excludes an independent director from the meaning of employee altogether, and excludes a director who himself or through a relative or a body corporate holds, directly or indirectly, more than ten per cent of the outstanding equity shares — which the whole-time director does at fourteen per cent with his wife. Rule 12(3) requires a separate resolution of the shareholders for a grant to the employees of a subsidiary or holding company and for a grant to identified employees during any one year equal to or exceeding one per cent of the issued capital at the time of grant. Rule 12(6)(a) fixes a minimum period of one year between the grant of options and their vesting, so 1 October 2026 is too early. Ind AS 102 measures an equity-settled award by reference to the fair value of the equity instruments at the grant date and does not remeasure it afterwards, and once an award has vested no reversal is made merely because the option lapses unexercised.

options.text: The grants are defective but the accounting is right, because Ind AS 102 requires a share-based payment to be remeasured at fair value at each reporting date until it is settled
options.misconception: applies cash-settled measurement to an equity-settled award
options.why: Remeasurement at each reporting date until settlement is how Ind AS 102 handles a cash-settled share-based payment, whose liability is carried at fair value throughout. An equity-settled award is measured once, at the grant date, and the only truing up is for the number of awards expected to vest on service and non-market performance conditions.

options.text: All four grants are valid, because section 62(1)(b) leaves the class of employees entitled to participate to the special resolution the shareholders passed
options.misconception: reads section 62(1)(b) as the only condition on an option scheme
options.why: Section 62(1)(b) supplies the special resolution and nothing else. Rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 then decides who may be an employee for the purpose, and no resolution of the shareholders can bring in an independent director or a director holding more than ten per cent of the outstanding equity shares.

citation.ref: Section 62(1)(b) with Rules 12(1), 12(3) and 12(6)(a) of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, read with Ind AS 102

items.scenario: An unlisted public company that is not a start-up grants options on 1 April 2026 to four people — its chief financial officer, an independent director, a whole-time director who together with his wife holds fourteen per cent of the outstanding equity shares, and the chief executive of its wholly owned subsidiary. The grant to the chief financial officer alone equals 1.4 per cent of the issued capital at the time of grant. A single special resolution under section 62(1)(b) covered the scheme, and the scheme provides for vesting on 1 October 2026. The finance head proposes to measure the expense at the fair value of the options at each reporting date, and to reverse the whole expense for any option that vests but is never exercised.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: He is a person resident outside India, and he must therefore dispose of the Mumbai shop within the period prescribed after his status changed
options.misconception: invents a divestment obligation that section 6(5) rules out
options.why: Section 6(5) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 says a person resident outside India may hold, own, transfer or invest in immovable property situated in India if the property was acquired when he was a resident in India. There is no period within which he must sell, and the section was written to make that clear.

options.text: The adviser is right on residence — the one-hundred-and-eighty-two-day count on the preceding financial year is the whole of section 2(v), so he stays a person resident in India until 31 March 2026 and may buy the agricultural land as well
options.misconception: reads the day count in section 2(v) without the purpose exclusion that follows it
options.why: The day count is the opening words of section 2(v) and the exclusions that follow override it. A person who has gone out of India for taking up employment outside India is outside the definition from the day he goes, and no arithmetic on the preceding year brings him back inside it.

options.text: He became a person resident outside India from the day he left, because section 2(v) excludes a person who has gone out of India for taking up employment outside India whatever the preceding year's day count; as a Non-Resident Indian he may buy the flat but not the agricultural land, which can come to him only by inheritance; section 6(5) lets him keep the Mumbai shop; and his income-tax residence is a separate question under section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961
options.why: Section 2(v) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 opens with the one-hundred-and-eighty-two-day test on the preceding financial year and then excludes a person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India for taking up employment outside India, for carrying on a business or vocation, or for any purpose indicating an intention to stay outside India for an uncertain period. Leaving for a job in Dubai puts him outside the definition from the day he goes, so the 210 days of 2024-25 do not help him. A Non-Resident Indian may acquire any immovable property in India other than agricultural land, a farm house or plantation property, which may come to him only by inheritance from a person resident in India, so the Pune flat is open and the Nashik land is not. Section 6(5) preserves what he already owns, letting a person resident outside India hold, own, transfer or invest in immovable property in India acquired when he was a resident in India. Section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 counts his days in the previous year itself and asks nothing about intention, so the two answers need not agree.

options.text: He is a person resident outside India under FEMA, and it follows that he is a non-resident under the Income-tax Act for 2025-26 as well, since both statutes turn on the same one-hundred-and-eighty-two-day test
options.misconception: assumes the two residence tests are one test
options.why: Both statutes use one hundred and eighty-two days and there the resemblance ends. Section 2(v) of FEMA counts days in the financial year preceding the current one and then overrides the count by the purpose of the person's stay; section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 counts days in the previous year itself, adds a sixty-day limb with its own exceptions, and asks nothing about intention. The two answers coincide often and are never the same question.

citation.ref: Sections 2(v) and 6(5) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 with the FEM (Non-debt Instruments) Rules, 2019, read with section 6 of the Income-tax Act, 1961

items.scenario: An Indian citizen who had lived in India all his life left on 1 August 2025 to take up employment with a company in Dubai and has stayed there since. He was in India for 210 days during 2024-25 and for 122 days during 2025-26. On 1 December 2025 he wants to buy a flat in Pune and two acres of agricultural land near Nashik, and he already owns a shop in Mumbai that he bought in 2019 while living in India. His adviser says that because he was in India for more than one hundred and eighty-two days during 2024-25, the financial year preceding the current one, he remains a person resident in India under FEMA for the whole of 2025-26 and may do all three; and that his residential status under the Income-tax Act must follow.

items.stem: Where is the chief financial officer wrong?

options.text: He is wrong on both, because Rule 96A gives an exporter of services three months and fifteen days, the same as an exporter of goods
options.misconception: applies the goods limb of Rule 96A to an export of services
options.why: Rule 96A has two limbs measuring two different events. For goods, the tax becomes payable if the goods are not exported out of India within fifteen days after the expiry of three months from the date of issue of the invoice. For services, the period is fifteen days after the expiry of one year from that date, and what must happen inside it is the receipt of payment in convertible foreign exchange.

options.text: On FEMA and not, yet, on the tax — Regulation 9(1) required the proceeds to be realised and repatriated within nine months from the date of export, so the exchange obligation was already breached on 1 January 2027, while Rule 96A gives one year from the date of issue of the invoice for the payment to be received in convertible foreign exchange
options.why: Regulation 9(1) of the FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015 requires the full export value to be realised and repatriated to India within nine months from the date of export, for all exporters, and section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 obliges the exporter to take all reasonable steps to bring it in. Nine months from 1 April 2026 ran out on 1 January 2027, so the contravention is already complete and an extension has to be sought rather than assumed. Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017 runs a longer clock on the same money: an exporter of services under a letter of undertaking undertakes to pay the integrated tax with interest only if the payment is not received in convertible foreign exchange within fifteen days after the expiry of one year, or such further period as the Commissioner may allow, from the date of issue of the invoice.

options.text: He is wrong on FEMA, but nothing follows, because an exporter may write off unrealised proceeds himself up to the limit the Reserve Bank permits
options.misconception: reads the self write-off facility as an extension of the realisation period
options.why: The self write-off facility lets an exporter write off unrealised export bills up to a limit and subject to conditions, and it is meant for a bill that has genuinely become irrecoverable after all reasonable steps have been taken under section 8. It is not a way of extending the nine months on a bill the exporter still expects to collect.

options.text: He is right on both, because the FEMA period and the Rule 96A period are the same year measured from the same invoice
options.misconception: assumes the exchange rules and the tax rules run the same clock
options.why: They run different clocks on purpose. The exchange rules measure nine months from the date of export and the tax rules measure a year from the date of the invoice, so for an exporter of services the exchange obligation is the first to bite and it bites three months earlier.

citation.ref: Section 8 of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 with Regulation 9(1) of the FEM (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2015, read with Rule 96A of the Central Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017

items.scenario: A registered exporter of software services raises an invoice on 1 April 2026 for USD 500,000 on a customer in Germany and exports the services under a letter of undertaking without payment of integrated tax. On 1 March 2027 the money has still not arrived and no extension has been sought from anybody. The chief financial officer says there is nothing to do on either front until 1 April 2027, a year from the invoice, because both the exchange rules and the tax rules give a year.

items.stem: How should the three be analysed?

options.text: The price list is presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition without any proof of market share; the distributor's resale price maintenance and exclusive dealing fall under section 3(4) and must be shown to cause or be likely to cause such an effect on the section 19(3) factors; and the consultant is caught by the proviso inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023
options.why: Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002 makes an agreement between enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade that determines prices, limits production, shares markets or rigs bids presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition, so the Commission proves the agreement and the parties must displace the effect; how small the four are does not enter into it. Resale price maintenance and exclusive supply sit in section 3(4), where nothing is presumed and the effect has to be established on the factors in section 19(3), which is where a six per cent share becomes relevant. The proviso inserted by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 answers the consultant: an enterprise or person that participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of such an agreement is presumed to be part of it even though it is not engaged in an identical or similar trade.

options.text: The consultant escapes, because he is not engaged in the production or supply of cement and section 3(3) applies only to enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade
options.misconception: reads section 3(3) as it stood before the 2023 amendment
options.why: That was the gap the hub-and-spoke arrangement exploited, and the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 closed it with a proviso presuming an enterprise, association or person that participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of the agreement to be part of it, whatever trade it is in.

options.text: All three must be shown to cause an appreciable adverse effect on the section 19(3) factors, because section 3(1) is the operative prohibition and section 3(3) only illustrates it
options.misconception: erases the presumption that section 3(3) creates
options.why: Section 3(1) is the general prohibition, and section 3(3) does not merely illustrate it — it says such an agreement shall be presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition. That word moves the burden, which is the whole difference between a horizontal case and a vertical one.

options.text: None of the three is caught, because none of the parties is dominant and section 3 requires a dominant position before an agreement can harm competition
options.misconception: imports the section 4 dominance requirement into section 3
options.why: Dominance is what section 4 is about. Section 3 works on agreements, and a cartel of small competitors is as much a cartel as one of large ones — the presumption in section 3(3) does not ask about market share at all.

citation.ref: Sections 3(3) with its provisos as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, and 3(4), read with section 19(3)

items.scenario: Three matters come to the Competition Commission of India together. Four small cement manufacturers, none of them holding a large share of any market, circulate a common price list through their trade association and each adopts it. A software distributor holding about six per cent of its market requires every dealer to resell at the price it fixes and not to stock a rival's product. An industry consultant who sells no cement at all chaired the meetings at which the price list was agreed and carried the numbers between the four manufacturers; he argues that section 3(3) reaches only enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade.

items.stem: What is the correct analysis?

options.text: The below-cost pricing cannot be predatory, because it happened in one state only and a predatory price must be charged across the whole of India
options.misconception: confuses the relevant geographic market with the whole country
options.why: The relevant geographic market is defined under sections 19(5) and 19(6) as the area in which the conditions of competition are distinctly homogeneous and can be distinguished from neighbouring areas, and it may be a single state or smaller. Explanation (b) to section 4 asks whether the price is below the cost of production with a view to reducing competition or eliminating competitors, not how much of India it covers.

options.text: Dominance is found on the section 19(4) factors and not on any share threshold; tying spares and servicing to the machine is abuse under section 4(2)(d) and refusing parts to independent repairers is denial of market access under section 4(2)(c); selling below cost to eliminate a rival is a predatory price within Explanation (b) to section 4; and the penalty base after the 2023 amendment is global turnover derived from all products and services
options.why: Nothing in the Act makes a market share a test of dominance. Explanation (a) to section 4 defines a dominant position as a position of strength enabling the enterprise to operate independently of competitive forces or to affect its competitors, consumers or the relevant market in its favour, and the Commission reaches that finding on the factors in section 19(4), of which market share is one among many — the service network, the dependence of consumers and the barriers to entry all count here. Making the conclusion of a contract subject to supplementary obligations unconnected with its subject is abuse under section 4(2)(d), and shutting independent repairers out of spare parts is abuse under section 4(2)(c). Selling below the cost of production with a view to reducing competition or eliminating competitors is a predatory price under Explanation (b) to section 4. On penalty, the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 defined turnover to mean global turnover derived from all products and services, so the base is not the Indian machine business alone.

options.text: It is dominant, and being dominant is itself the contravention, so all its conduct falls with the finding
options.misconception: treats the holding of a dominant position as the offence
options.why: Section 4(1) forbids the abuse of a dominant position, not the position itself. An enterprise may reach dominance by being better than its rivals and the Act says nothing against it; what it may not do is the conduct listed in section 4(2).

options.text: It is not dominant, because dominance under the Act requires a share of more than half the relevant market
options.misconception: invents a market share threshold the Act does not contain
options.why: The Act sets no figure. Explanation (a) to section 4 describes a position of strength enabling the enterprise to operate independently of competitive forces, and the Commission works to that description through the factors in section 19(4). A firm with a third of a market and a service network everyone depends on can satisfy it; a firm with half a market and easy entry beside it may not.

citation.ref: Section 4(2) with Explanations (a) and (b), read with sections 19(4) to 19(6) and section 27 as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023

items.scenario: An enterprise holds about thirty-four per cent of the Indian market for a specialised machine and has by far the largest service network in the country, on which its customers depend for uptime. It requires every buyer of the machine to buy all spare parts and servicing from it, and refuses to supply spare parts to independent repairers. In one state where a new rival has just launched, it sells its entry-level model below its cost of production. Its counsel argues that thirty-four per cent cannot be dominance, that pricing is a commercial decision, and that any penalty could only be measured on its Indian turnover in machines.

items.stem: How should the four be answered?

options.text: A's managing director is automatically covered by the company's application, and the customer loses his remedy once a lesser penalty is granted
options.misconception: reads a company's leniency as covering its officers and as ending third-party claims
options.why: Section 48 fastens liability on every person who at the time of the contravention was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business, and the benefit of an application reaches only those it covers. A lesser penalty also leaves the finding of contravention standing, on which a person who has suffered loss may claim compensation under section 53N.

options.text: C may apply, because the lesser penalty provisions are available for any contravention of the Act once the applicant co-operates
options.misconception: extends a cartel-only provision to abuse of dominance
options.why: Section 46 is written for a producer, seller, distributor, trader or service provider included in a cartel, and a cartel is a section 3(3) matter. Abuse of a dominant position under section 4 is a unilateral contravention with no co-conspirator to inform on, and no leniency route exists for it.

options.text: A may be given a lesser penalty and, on the second disclosure, the additional reduction the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced; B is too late because the proviso refuses a lesser penalty once the Director General's report has been received; C has no leniency route because the section covers a cartel only; A's managing director stays exposed under section 48; and the customer's claim under section 53N is unaffected
options.why: Section 46 of the Competition Act, 2002 lets the Commission impose a lesser penalty on a member of a cartel who makes a full, true and vital disclosure, and the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 added the further reduction where the same applicant discloses a second, unrelated cartel. Its proviso shuts the door once the report of the Director General has been received, which is what defeats B. The section speaks of a cartel, a section 3(3) matter, so an enterprise facing an abuse of dominance case has nothing to apply for. Section 48 makes every person who at the time of the contravention was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business liable for it, so an officer not covered by the company's application does not share its benefit. And a lesser penalty reduces the penalty without erasing the contravention, so a claim for compensation under section 53N stands untouched.

options.text: B is still in time, because a lesser penalty may be sought at any point before the Commission passes its final order
options.misconception: puts the cut-off at the final order instead of at the Director General's report
options.why: The cut-off is deliberately early. The proviso to section 46 refuses a lesser penalty where the report of the Director General has been received before the disclosure was made, because the disclosure is meant to help the investigation rather than to follow it.

citation.ref: Section 46 with its provisos and section 48, as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023, read with section 53N

items.scenario: Three suppliers rig a public tender. Supplier A applies for a lesser penalty first and makes a full, true and vital disclosure, and some months later discloses a second, unrelated cartel in another product. Supplier B applies only after the Director General's report on the tender has been received. Supplier C is facing a different matter altogether — a complaint that it abused a dominant position in another market — and wants to apply for a lesser penalty in that case. A's managing director, who personally ran the arrangement, is not covered by A's application. A customer who paid inflated prices under the rigged tender wants his money back.

items.stem: Where is the adviser wrong?

options.text: On all three — section 79(2)(c) lifts the shareholding-change restriction where the change is pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Code, the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner having been heard; the proviso to clause (iih) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2) lets a company whose insolvency application has been admitted deduct the aggregate of ₹400 crore and ₹150 crore from book profit; and section 170A allows a modified return within six months from the end of the month in which the Tribunal's order was issued
options.why: Section 79(2)(c) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 removes the section 79(1) bar where the change in shareholding takes place pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard has been given to the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner, so the ₹400 crore loss survives the change of ownership. For minimum alternate tax, clause (iih) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2) ordinarily allows only the lower of the brought forward loss and the unabsorbed depreciation, but its proviso lets a company against which an insolvency application has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority deduct the aggregate of the two, which is ₹550 crore here and not ₹150 crore. Section 170A then lets the successor to a business reorganisation furnish a modified return for the years covered by the order, within six months from the end of the month in which the order was issued.

options.text: He is right on section 79 and wrong on the rest, because the exceptions in section 79(2) cover only a change arising from the death of a shareholder or a gift to a relative
options.misconception: knows two of the section 79(2) exceptions and not the insolvency one
options.why: Death of a shareholder and a gift to a relative are indeed among the exceptions in section 79(2). Clause (c) of the same sub-section adds the change in shareholding pursuant to a resolution plan approved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, subject only to the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner being heard first.

options.text: He is wrong on all three, and in addition the ₹600 crore write-back is entirely outside tax, because a resolution plan approved under section 31 binds the tax authorities
options.misconception: treats section 31's binding effect as an exemption from tax on the write-back
options.why: Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 makes the plan binding on the Central Government and every authority to whom a statutory due is owed, which settles claims for dues of the past. It does not decide the character of an amount written back — a remission or cessation of a trading liability is tested under section 41(1) and the waiver of a capital loan on ordinary principles, so the write-back is analysed line by line.

options.text: He is right on the minimum alternate tax, because clause (iih) of Explanation 1 always allows only the lower of the brought forward loss and the unabsorbed depreciation
options.misconception: reads clause (iih) without the proviso inserted for an admitted insolvency
options.why: The lower of the two is the general rule and it is the one that would apply to a solvent company. The proviso to that clause changes it for a company against which an application for a corporate insolvency resolution process has been admitted by the Adjudicating Authority, letting it reduce the aggregate of the brought forward loss and the unabsorbed depreciation instead.

citation.ref: Sections 79(2)(c), 41(1) and 170A and the proviso to clause (iih) of Explanation 1 to section 115JB(2), read with sections 7 and 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016

items.scenario: An application under section 7 against a closely held company was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority in 2024, and the Tribunal approved a resolution plan on 10 June 2026 under which a new owner takes eighty per cent of the equity. The company carries a brought forward business loss of ₹400 crore and unabsorbed depreciation of ₹150 crore, and the plan writes back ₹600 crore owed to trade creditors, producing a large book profit. The new management's adviser says that section 79 destroys the brought forward loss, that minimum alternate tax is payable on the book profit after deducting only ₹150 crore as the lower of the two figures, and that nothing can now be done about the returns of the earlier years.

items.stem: What is the position under section 94?

options.text: The only consequence of a refusal is the penalty on the company and its officers, and the member must wait for the Registrar to act on it
options.misconception: sees the penalty in section 94(4) and misses the order in the same sub-section
options.why: Section 94(4) carries a penalty and a remedy together, and the remedy is the member's, not the Registrar's. The Tribunal may by order direct an immediate inspection of the document, or direct that the copy required be sent forthwith to the person requiring it.

options.text: The member is entitled to inspect without paying anything, the copy he has asked for must be furnished within seven days, and on a refusal or a delay the Tribunal may order an immediate inspection or direct that the copy be sent forthwith
options.why: Section 94(2) opens the registers, their indices and the copies of the annual return to inspection during business hours by any member, debenture-holder, other security holder or beneficial owner without payment of any fee; the prescribed fee is charged only to any other person. Section 94(3) lets him require a copy on payment of the prescribed fee and requires that copy to be furnished within seven days. Section 94(4) then supplies both a penalty on the company and every officer in default and a remedy, letting the Tribunal by order direct an immediate inspection or direct that the copy be sent forthwith.

options.text: The member has no right of inspection at all, because the shares are held in dematerialised form and the depository's register is the only register that exists
options.misconception: reads section 88(3) as removing the right rather than relocating the register
options.why: Section 88(3) deems the register and index of beneficial owners maintained by a depository to be the corresponding register and index for the purposes of the Act. That saves the company from keeping a second register; it does not close the one that is deemed to be its register, which section 94(2) still opens to a member.

options.text: The company is right about the fee, because the fee prescribed under the Rules is payable by everyone who asks to inspect a statutory register
options.misconception: reads the prescribed fee in section 94(2) as applying to a member as well
options.why: The sub-section splits the two classes in one sentence. A member, debenture-holder, other security holder or beneficial owner inspects without payment of any fee; it is any other person who pays the fee prescribed by Rule 14 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014.

citation.ref: Sections 94(2), 94(3) and 94(4), read with section 88(3) and Rule 14 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014

items.scenario: A member of an unlisted public company goes to its registered office and asks to inspect the register of members and the copies of the annual return. The company secretary tells him that the inspection fee prescribed under the Rules must be paid before he is shown anything, and that the copy of the annual return he has asked for will be posted to him in about a month.

items.stem: Where is the chief financial officer wrong?

options.text: Only on the annual filing; section 129A does apply, because the company is above the turnover limit prescribed for it in the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014
options.misconception: invents a turnover threshold for a section that runs on a class yet to be prescribed
options.why: Section 129A does not work off a turnover figure at all. It works off a class or classes of unlisted companies that the Central Government must prescribe, together with the periodical basis, the form and the manner of the audit or limited review. No figure in the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 supplies what the section leaves to be prescribed.

options.text: Only on section 129A; Regulation 33 applies anyway, because the company has issued non-convertible debentures and those are securities
options.misconception: extends the LODR to an entity none of whose securities is listed
options.why: The SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 apply to a listed entity — one which has any of the designated securities listed on a recognised stock exchange. Privately placed debentures that are not listed bring the company nowhere near Regulation 33, whatever they are called.

options.text: He is right that the annual filing can wait, because a company on which section 129A will eventually bite is relieved of section 137 in the meantime
options.misconception: treats an unnotified power as suspending the duties that already exist
options.why: A power the Central Government has not yet exercised suspends nothing. Section 137(1) requires a copy of the financial statements adopted at the annual general meeting to be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of that meeting, and section 137(2) covers the case where the meeting was not held at all.

options.text: On all three — Regulation 33 of the LODR reaches only a listed entity, so the forty-five-day quarterly clock does not touch this company; section 129A is an enabling power that bites only on a class of unlisted companies the Central Government prescribes and carries its own thirty-day filing clock rather than a forty-five-day one; and the company's annual duties are unaffected, the financial statements being laid at the annual general meeting under section 129(2) and filed with the Registrar under section 137(1) within thirty days of it
options.why: Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 binds a listed entity and requires quarterly and year-to-date results within forty-five days of each quarter other than the last; a company none of whose securities is listed is outside it. Section 129A lets the Central Government require such class or classes of unlisted companies as may be prescribed to prepare periodical financial results, to have them approved by the Board and audited or reviewed, and to file a copy with the Registrar within thirty days of the completion of the relevant period — every limb of it runs on rules, so until the class is prescribed no unlisted company is caught. None of that touches section 129(2) or section 137(1), under which the financial statements are laid at the annual general meeting and a copy filed with the Registrar within thirty days of that meeting.

citation.ref: Section 129A with sections 129(2), 137(1) and 137(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 33 of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015

items.scenario: An unlisted public company with a turnover of ₹1,800 crore has privately placed non-convertible debentures which are not listed on any stock exchange. Its new chief financial officer, who came from a listed group, tells the audit committee that the company must now publish quarterly financial results within forty-five days of each quarter end, that section 129A already requires this of every large unlisted company, and that the annual filing with the Registrar can wait until the quarterly regime is set up.

items.stem: Has section 136 been complied with?

options.text: No, and the company can cure it by filing the financial statements with the Registrar within thirty days of the meeting under section 137(1)
options.misconception: mixes the pre-meeting duty to the members with the post-meeting duty to the Registrar
options.why: Section 137(1) is a separate obligation that arises after the meeting, when a copy of the financial statements adopted at it is filed with the Registrar within thirty days. Filing it does not repair a failure to give the members the documents twenty-one days before the meeting they were meant to vote at.

options.text: Yes, because a listed company only has to send the statement of salient features and the section fixes no time for sending that statement
options.misconception: reads the proviso's alternative without the clock inside it
options.why: The first proviso carries the same twenty-one days as the main sub-section. The statement of salient features in the prescribed form, or copies of the documents as a member may ask for, is to be sent not less than twenty-one days before the date of the meeting, and the inspection at the registered office runs for the same twenty-one days.

options.text: Yes, because the annual report was on the company's website well over twenty-one days before the meeting and a listed company's members are expected to read it there
options.misconception: treats the website duty as discharging the duty to send
options.why: The website requirement sits in the further provisos to section 136(1) and is expressed as an additional obligation on a listed company and on every other company having a website. Nothing in the section makes a posting a substitute for sending, and the deemed-compliance route in the first proviso does not mention a website at all.

options.text: No — the documents or the salient features statement had to go out not less than twenty-one days before the meeting and thirteen days is short of that, the listed company's alternative in the first proviso needs the registered-office inspection for twenty-one days as well, and placing the report on the website is an additional duty rather than a substitute for sending
options.why: Section 136(1) requires a copy of the financial statements, the auditor's report and every other document annexed to them to be sent to every member not less than twenty-one days before the date of the general meeting. The first proviso lets a listed company do it differently, but both of its limbs have to be met — the copies made available for inspection at the registered office during working hours for twenty-one days before the meeting, and the salient features statement in the prescribed form or copies of the documents sent not less than twenty-one days before it. Posting on 12 September for a meeting on 25 September is thirteen days and fails either route, and the further provisos that require the documents to be put on the website add a duty rather than discharge one.

citation.ref: Section 136(1) with its first and further provisos, read with section 137(1)

items.scenario: A listed company has called its annual general meeting for 25 September 2026. It placed the full annual report on its website on 20 August 2026 and posted to every member, on 12 September 2026, a statement containing the salient features of the financial statements in the prescribed form. The documents were never made available for inspection at the registered office. The company secretary says the website posting more than a month ahead settles the matter.

items.stem: What is the correct position?

options.text: The branch auditor's report is to be sent to the auditor of the company, who deals with it in his own report in such manner as he considers necessary rather than reproducing it; a person duly qualified under the laws of Indonesia may lawfully audit that branch; and the branch auditor reports the fraud himself, the reporting duty extending to him to the extent it relates to his branch
options.why: Section 143(8) requires the branch auditor to prepare his report on the accounts of the branch office examined by him and to send it to the auditor of the company, who shall deal with it in his report in such manner as he considers necessary — so the report travels to the company's auditor, not to the Board, and he forms his own opinion on the financial statements as a whole. The same sub-section allows a branch outside India to be audited by an accountant or by any other person duly qualified to act as an auditor of the accounts of the branch office in accordance with the laws of that country. Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 then extends the duty of reporting a fraud to the branch auditor to the extent it relates to the concerned branch, so he reports under section 143(12) with Rule 13 himself.

options.text: The branch auditor's only duty is to pass the fraud to the company's auditor, who alone can report it to the Central Government under section 143(12)
options.misconception: takes the reporting duty away from the person Rule 12 puts it on
options.why: Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 says in terms that the duty of reporting a fraud extends to the branch auditor to the extent it relates to the concerned branch. He therefore follows section 143(12) and Rule 13 himself, routing the matter through the Board or audit committee for their reply and then to the Central Government where the amount requires it.

options.text: The Indonesian branch could only have been audited by a chartered accountant who is qualified for appointment as an auditor under section 141, so the branch audit is void
options.misconception: applies the Indian qualification to a branch that section 143(8) expressly opens to a local auditor
options.why: Section 143(8) provides separately for a branch office situated in a country outside India. It may be audited by the company's auditor, by an accountant, or by any other person duly qualified to act as an auditor of the accounts of the branch office in accordance with the laws of that country. The section 141 disqualifications govern the auditor of the company, not a foreign branch auditor.

options.text: The company's auditor must reproduce the branch auditor's report in his own and adopt its conclusions, having no authority to go behind it
options.misconception: reads "deal with it as he considers necessary" as a duty to adopt
options.why: The statutory words leave the judgement with the company's auditor. SA 600 requires him to perform procedures to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence that the other auditor's work is adequate for his purposes, and where it is not and he cannot do enough more, to qualify his opinion or disclaim it for a limitation on scope — none of which is possible if he is bound to copy out what he was sent.

citation.ref: Section 143(8) with Rule 12 of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, section 143(12) with Rule 13, and SA 600

items.scenario: An Indian listed company has a branch in Indonesia whose accounts are audited by a local firm appointed under section 139, and an Indian branch audited by the company's own auditor. The Indonesian branch auditor uncovers a fraud of about ₹3 crore committed by the branch manager, notes it in his report on the branch accounts and sends that report to the company's Board. The company's management then tells the statutory auditor that the branch report is final, that he must reproduce it in his own report, and that the fraud is now his alone to report because the branch auditor is not the auditor of the company.

items.stem: Were the two resolutions validly passed?

options.text: Both could in any case have been delegated to the managing director under the proviso to section 179(3), so the manner of passing them does not matter
options.misconception: reads the proviso as covering the whole of the section 179(3) list
options.why: The proviso permits delegation of three powers and no others — to borrow monies, to invest the funds of the company, and to grant loans or give guarantee or provide security in respect of loans. Approving the accounts and appointing a key managerial person are outside it, and a delegation the proviso does not allow is no delegation at all.

options.text: Neither was — approving the financial statement and the Board's report, and appointing a key managerial person, are both powers that section 179(3) with Rule 8 requires to be exercised by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Board, and section 175(1) forbids a resolution by circulation on any matter required to be placed before the Board at a meeting
options.why: Section 179(3) lists the powers the Board may exercise only by means of resolutions passed at meetings of the Board, and the approval of the financial statement and the Board's report is one of them. Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014 prescribes further such powers under the last clause of that sub-section, among them the appointment or removal of key managerial personnel, which is what a chief financial officer is. Section 175(1) then says that no resolution shall be passed by circulation on any matter which is required by the Act or otherwise to be placed before the Board at a meeting, so signing an email round cannot carry either of them.

options.text: The accounts resolution was valid because section 134 requires only the Board's approval and does not mention a meeting, and only the chief financial officer's appointment fails
options.misconception: reads section 134 on its own and misses section 179(3)
options.why: Section 134(1) requires the financial statements to be approved by the Board of Directors and signed on its behalf, and it is section 179(3) that says how that approval is to be given — by a resolution passed at a meeting of the Board. The two sections are read together, and the second is the one that decides the manner.

options.text: Both were, because section 175 allows a resolution to be passed by circulation once it is approved by a majority of the directors entitled to vote on it
options.misconception: reads the machinery in section 175 and skips the bar at the front of it
options.why: Section 175 does permit a resolution by circulation approved by a majority of the directors entitled to vote, but only after its opening words have been satisfied: no resolution shall be passed by circulation on any matter which is required by the Act or otherwise to be placed before the Board at a meeting. Both of these matters are on that list.

citation.ref: Section 179(3) with its proviso and Rule 8 of the Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014, read with section 175(1) and section 134(1)

items.scenario: The directors of a public company are scattered across three cities in the week the accounts are due. The company secretary circulates two draft resolutions by email — one approving the audited financial statements and the Board's report for the year, and one appointing a new chief financial officer — and records both as passed when a majority of the directors sign and return them.

items.stem: What is the position?

options.text: The defect can be repaired by having the members ratify the arrangement at the next annual general meeting
options.misconception: overlooks the word "prior" in section 192(1)
options.why: Section 192(1) requires that prior approval for the arrangement be accorded by a resolution of the company in general meeting. An approval obtained after the arrangement has been entered into is not prior approval, and the consequence in section 192(3) attaches to an arrangement entered into in contravention of the section, not to one that stays uncorrected.

options.text: The arrangement is void from the beginning, so the shares issued to Mr R can be cancelled and no third party can take anything under it
options.misconception: reads "voidable at the instance of the company" as void
options.why: Section 192(3) makes the arrangement voidable at the instance of the company, and even that is taken away in two cases — where restitution of the money or other consideration is no longer possible and the company has been indemnified by another person for the loss, and where rights have been acquired bona fide for value and without notice of the contravention by any other person.

options.text: The arrangement needed prior approval by a resolution of the company in general meeting and, Mr R being a director of the holding company, a resolution in general meeting of the holding company too, with the value of the asset calculated by a registered valuer set out in the notice; the arm's-length and ordinary-course finding is irrelevant because section 192 carries no such carve-out; and as things stand the arrangement is voidable at the instance of the company
options.why: Section 192(1) forbids a company to enter into an arrangement by which it acquires assets for consideration other than cash from its own director unless prior approval is accorded by a resolution of the company in general meeting, and where that director is a director of the holding company, by a resolution in general meeting of the holding company as well. Section 192(2) requires the notice for that resolution to include the particulars of the arrangement along with the value of the assets involved, duly calculated by a registered valuer, so the finance team's own figure will not do. The fourth proviso to section 188 exempts a transaction in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis from that section only; section 192 has no value threshold and no such exemption anywhere in it. Section 192(3) then makes an arrangement entered into in contravention of the section voidable at the instance of the company.

options.text: Nothing more was needed, because a transaction in the ordinary course of business on an arm's length basis is outside the related party approval machinery altogether
options.misconception: treats section 192 as though it were a limb of section 188
options.why: The fourth proviso to section 188 carves out an ordinary-course arm's-length transaction from section 188 and from nothing else. Section 192 is a separate prohibition aimed at the kind of consideration rather than at the price, and a payment in shares instead of cash engages it whatever the price was and whatever business the company is in.

citation.ref: Sections 192(1), 192(2) and 192(3), read with the fourth proviso to section 188 and section 247

items.scenario: A logistics company buys and sells warehouses all the time. It acquires a warehouse from Mr R, its whole-time director, who is also a director of its holding company, and pays for it entirely by issuing equity shares to him. The audit committee satisfies itself that the price is on arm's length terms and that the purchase is in the company's ordinary course of business, and concludes on that footing that the fourth proviso to section 188 takes the transaction outside the related party machinery. The Board approves it at a meeting. The value of the warehouse was worked out by the company's own finance team, no resolution was put to any general meeting, and the holding company was merely informed.

items.stem: What is wrong with the appointment?
