options.why: Section 98 lets the Tribunal call a meeting where it is impracticable to call one in the manner the Act prescribes. Here the Act's own manner works perfectly: section 100(4) hands the meeting to the requisitionists, and they need no order to use it.

options.text: Call and hold the meeting themselves within three months of the requisition, and recover their reasonable expenses from the company
options.why: Section 100(2) obliges the Board to call an extraordinary general meeting on a requisition by members holding not less than one-tenth of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights, and thirteen per cent clears that. Section 100(4) then gives the Board twenty-one days from receipt to proceed to call a meeting to be held within forty-five days; on that failing, the meeting may be called and held by the requisitionists themselves within three months from the date of the requisition. Section 100(6) makes the company reimburse their reasonable expenses and recover the sum from the defaulting directors' remuneration.

citation.ref: Sections 100(2), 100(4) and 100(6), read with section 98

items.scenario: Members holding 13 per cent of the paid-up share capital carrying voting rights deliver a signed requisition at the company's registered office on 1 June 2026, setting out a resolution to remove a director. Thirty-five days pass and the Board has taken no step, saying the matter can wait for the annual general meeting in September.

items.stem: Which of the three may be transacted by postal ballot?

options.text: None, because the postal ballot is open only to a company that provides electronic voting
options.misconception: turns a relaxation for e-voting companies into a precondition for everyone else
options.why: The proviso runs the other way. A company required to provide electronic voting under section 108 may transact at a general meeting an item that would otherwise have to go by postal ballot; the ballot itself is not reserved to such companies.

options.text: All three, because a resolution passed by postal ballot is deemed to have been passed at a general meeting
options.misconception: reads the deeming provision as removing the limits on subject matter
options.why: Section 110(2) deems a resolution assented to by the requisite majority by postal ballot to have been duly passed at a general meeting. That fixes the standing of a resolution which could go to a ballot; it says nothing about which resolutions may.

options.text: The removal of the director as well, since removal is special business and not ordinary business
options.misconception: notices that removal is special business and misses the right to be heard
options.why: Being special business is necessary and not sufficient. Section 169(4) entitles the director to be heard on the resolution at the meeting, and section 110 keeps every such item inside a meeting precisely so the hearing can happen.

options.text: Only the change of registered office — the other two are barred, one as ordinary business and one as business on which a person has a right to be heard
options.why: Section 110(1) lets a company transact by postal ballot any item other than ordinary business and any business in respect of which directors or auditors have a right to be heard at any meeting. Adoption of the audited financial statements is ordinary business under section 102(2). A director sought to be removed is entitled by section 169(4) to be heard on the resolution at the meeting. The change of registered office is special business carrying no such right, and it is one of the items the rules list for a postal ballot.

citation.ref: Section 110(1) with its proviso, read with sections 102(2) and 169(4)

items.scenario: A company that is not required to give its members electronic voting proposes to put three matters to a postal ballot instead of a general meeting: adoption of the audited financial statements, removal of a director under section 169, and a change of the registered office outside the local limits of the city.

items.stem: What is defective in the removal?

options.text: The hearing was unnecessary; a special resolution on its own removes an auditor before his term ends
options.misconception: drops the opportunity of being heard that the proviso requires
options.why: The proviso to section 140(1) requires that the auditor concerned be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard before any action is taken. It is not a courtesy the company may waive, and an approval obtained without it is open to challenge.

options.text: Nothing — an ordinary resolution after a hearing is all section 140 asks for
options.misconception: treats removal of an auditor as an ordinary act of the members
options.why: Removal mid-term is the one thing the Act makes hardest, because an auditor who can be dismissed for asking awkward questions is not independent. The special resolution and the Government's previous approval are what stand between the auditor and the board he is auditing.

options.text: The removal stands, but the replacement had to be appointed by the Central Government on the Tribunal's order
options.misconception: borrows section 140(5), which answers a different question altogether
options.why: Section 140(5) lets the Tribunal direct a change of auditor where he has acted fraudulently or colluded in a fraud, and lets the Central Government appoint another where the application to the Tribunal was its own. A routine falling-out never reaches that sub-section.

options.text: It needed a special resolution and the previous approval of the Central Government; the hearing on its own does not carry it
options.why: Section 140(1) allows an auditor to be removed before the expiry of his term only by a special resolution of the company and after obtaining the previous approval of the Central Government in the prescribed manner, and its proviso adds the reasonable opportunity of being heard on top of both. The company supplied the hearing and an ordinary resolution, which is two of the three requirements missing the one that brings an outsider into the decision.
keywords: previous approval of the Central Government

citation.ref: Section 140(1) with its proviso, read with section 140(5)

items.scenario: A company falls out with its statutory auditor in the second year of a five-year term. The Board convenes an extraordinary general meeting, gives the auditor a full hearing at it, and passes an ordinary resolution removing him. A replacement is appointed the same day.

items.stem: What does the ₹2.5 crore contribution need?

options.text: Prior permission of the company in general meeting, because it exceeds five per cent of the average net profits of the three preceding years
options.why: Section 181 lets the Board contribute to bona fide charitable and other funds, but its proviso requires prior permission of the company in general meeting where the aggregate of such contributions in a financial year exceeds five per cent of the average net profits for the three immediately preceding financial years. Five per cent of ₹40 crore is ₹2 crore, and ₹2.5 crore is past it. Meeting the section 135 obligation elsewhere buys no headroom here.

options.text: A special resolution of the members, since the five per cent line has been crossed
options.misconception: upgrades the members' permission into a resolution the section never names
options.why: The proviso asks for prior permission of the company in general meeting, which is an ordinary resolution unless the articles demand more. Reading a special resolution into it makes the requirement harder than Parliament wrote it.

options.text: Nothing, because the amount is inside the two per cent of the same average that section 135 already contemplates
options.misconception: pays a section 181 donation out of the corporate social responsibility allowance
options.why: Section 135 sets a floor on what a covered company must spend on Schedule VII activities; section 181 sets a ceiling on what the Board alone may give away to charitable funds. One is a minimum on a defined kind of spending and the other a limit on a power, and neither is credit against the other.

options.text: Nothing beyond the Board resolution already passed; charitable giving is squarely a Board power
options.misconception: reads the main limb of section 181 and stops before the proviso
options.why: The main limb does give the power to the Board, and the proviso takes it back above the line. Below five per cent of the three-year average the Board acts alone; above it, the members must be asked first.

citation.ref: Section 181 with its proviso, read against section 135

items.scenario: A company's average net profits for the three immediately preceding financial years work out to ₹40 crore — take that figure as given. The Board resolves to contribute ₹2.5 crore during the year to a bona fide relief fund, and separately records that the company's obligation under section 135 is being met in full out of a different budget.

items.stem: How does the application fare?

options.text: It cannot be confirmed — the proviso to section 66(1) bars a reduction while deposit arrears stand, and the auditor's certificate on the accounting treatment is a separate condition
options.why: Section 66(1) lets a company reduce its share capital by special resolution subject to confirmation by the Tribunal, and cancelling paid-up capital lost or unrepresented by available assets is one of the ways it lists. Its proviso then shuts the door where the company is in arrears in the repayment of any deposits accepted by it or of the interest payable thereon. Section 66(3) separately requires the Tribunal to be satisfied that the accounting treatment proposed is in conformity with the accounting standards and that a certificate to that effect from the company's auditor has been filed. Both are missing.

options.text: It succeeds — a write-off of capital already lost takes nothing from any creditor, so the deposit arrears are beside the point
options.misconception: reads an absolute bar as a test of whether creditors are prejudiced
options.why: The proviso does not ask whether this particular reduction hurts the depositors. It bars any reduction while the arrears stand, which is blunt and deliberate: the capital is the depositors' cushion and the company is already failing to pay them.

options.text: It succeeds if the deposit holders are given the three months creditors have to object
options.misconception: converts an absolute bar into an objection period
options.why: Section 66(2) does give the Central Government, the Registrar, the Securities and Exchange Board in a listed company's case and the creditors three months to make representations. That process runs alongside the proviso; it cannot cure a bar that operates before the Tribunal reaches the merits.

options.text: It succeeds, because cancelling lost capital is in substance a buy-back and section 66 does not apply to buy-backs
options.misconception: reaches for section 66(6) to escape section 66 altogether
options.why: Section 66(6) says nothing in the section applies to a buy-back of a company's own securities under section 68. Cancelling capital that is lost or unrepresented by assets buys nothing from anybody — no shares change hands and no money goes out — so the exclusion never engages.

citation.ref: Section 66(1) with its proviso, and sections 66(2), 66(3) and 66(6)

items.scenario: A company carrying ₹90 crore of accumulated losses unrepresented by available assets passes a special resolution to cancel that much of its paid-up capital, and applies to the Tribunal for confirmation. It is in arrears on the interest due to its deposit holders, and its auditor has not certified the accounting treatment the scheme proposes.

items.stem: What does section 236 do here?

options.text: Nothing until the acquirer chooses to act; the section is a power of the majority and gives the minority no right of its own
options.misconception: reads section 236 as running in one direction only
options.why: Section 236(3) is expressly the other direction: the minority shareholders may offer to the majority to purchase their holding at the price determined. The exit does not depend on the acquirer's appetite, which is the point of putting both limbs in one section.

options.text: The acquirer may compulsorily acquire the 8 per cent at the price it names, the valuer's opinion being advisory
options.misconception: leaves the price in the hands of the person paying it
options.why: Section 236(2) fixes the price on the basis of valuation by a registered valuer in accordance with the prescribed rules. Taking the price out of the acquirer's hands is the protection the minority gets in exchange for losing its holding.

options.text: The acquirer must notify the company of its intention to buy the remaining shares at a registered valuer's price, and the minority shareholder may equally offer his shares at that price
options.why: Section 236(1) engages once an acquirer, or a person acting in concert, becomes the registered holder of ninety per cent or more of the issued equity share capital, including where that happens by virtue of an amalgamation, and it requires them to notify the company of their intention to buy the remaining equity shares. Section 236(2) requires the offer to be at a price determined on the basis of valuation by a registered valuer. Section 236(3) turns the right around and lets the minority shareholders offer to the majority to purchase the minority equity shareholding at that same price.

options.text: Nothing, because the ninety per cent has to be reached by purchase and this holding came out of an amalgamation
options.misconception: excludes the very route the section names
options.why: The section reaches a person or group becoming a ninety per cent holder "by virtue of an amalgamation, share exchange, conversion of securities or for any other reason". How the threshold was crossed is exactly what it declines to care about.

items.scenario: After an amalgamation, an acquirer and the persons acting in concert with it hold 92 per cent of the issued equity share capital of a company. The acquirer is content to leave the remaining 8 per cent where it is. One of the minority shareholders wants out at a fair price and is told there is nothing he can do.

items.stem: Where is counsel wrong?

options.text: On neither — an Indian company cannot merge into a foreign company at all, so the whole plan fails for a different reason
options.misconception: carries the position under the 1956 Act into the 2013 Act
options.why: Under the Companies Act, 1956 only the inbound direction was possible, the transferee having to be an Indian company. Section 234(2) of the 2013 Act allows a foreign company to merge into an Indian company "or vice versa", and the rules and the cross-border merger regulations were written for both directions.

options.text: Only on the fast track; the Reserve Bank's approval can follow the Tribunal's sanction, as other regulatory clearances do
options.misconception: treats a prior approval as a clearance that may be collected afterwards
options.why: Rule 25A puts the Reserve Bank's approval ahead of the section 230 application and requires a declaration to that effect when the application is filed. A sanction obtained without it is a sanction of a scheme that was not competent to be presented.

options.text: Only on the sequence; the fast track is available because the parent owns the whole of the Indian company
options.misconception: reads the wholly-owned-subsidiary limb of section 233 without noticing which companies it covers
options.why: Section 233 speaks of companies registered under this Act. A parent incorporated abroad is not one, so the holding-and-wholly-owned-subsidiary limb never reaches it however complete the ownership.

options.text: On both — the Reserve Bank's approval is a prior approval that must be in hand before the Tribunal application, and section 233 is not open to a merger with a company incorporated outside India
options.why: Section 234(2) permits a foreign company to merge into an Indian company or an Indian company into a foreign one only with the prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India, and Rule 25A requires that approval to be obtained before the application under section 230 is made. Section 234(1) also limits the route to jurisdictions the Central Government has notified. Section 233, the fast track, runs between small companies, a holding company and its wholly owned subsidiary and other prescribed classes registered under this Act, which a foreign parent is not.
keywords: prior approval of the Reserve Bank of India

citation.ref: Sections 234(1) and 234(2), read with Rule 25A of the Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules, 2016 and section 233

items.scenario: An Indian company plans to merge into its parent, which is incorporated in a foreign jurisdiction. Counsel proposes to file the scheme with the Tribunal under section 230 first, obtain the sanction, and take the Reserve Bank of India's approval afterwards. He adds that since the parent holds every share of the Indian company, the fast track route under section 233 is available and the Tribunal can be skipped altogether.

items.stem: What can be compounded?

options.text: Neither — the company's offence falls inside the three-year bar on a repeat, and the officer's is punishable with imprisonment and also with fine
options.why: Section 441(2) says nothing in the compounding power applies to an offence committed by a company or its officer within a period of three years from the date on which a similar offence committed by it or him was compounded, and twenty-two months is well inside that. An offence punishable with imprisonment and also with fine is placed outside compounding altogether by section 441, whatever the amount involved and whoever is asked. The fine ceiling only picks the forum, and neither offence gets that far.

options.text: Only the officer's, because an individual may compound where a company cannot
options.misconception: invents a personal exemption the section does not contain
options.why: Section 441 speaks of an offence whether committed by a company or by any officer of it in the same breath, and the repeat bar names both. What shuts this one out is the class of punishment attached to the offence, which is the same for whoever committed it.

options.text: Only the company's, because the three years run from the date of the earlier offence and that is long past
options.misconception: starts the three-year clock at the wrong event
options.why: Section 441(2) measures the three years from the date on which the similar offence was compounded, not from the date it was committed. Starting the clock earlier would reward a company that dragged out its last compounding.

options.text: Both — the first because ₹5 lakh is inside the Regional Director's limit, the second with the permission of the court
options.misconception: treats the fine ceiling as the test of eligibility rather than of forum
options.why: The ceiling on the fine decides who compounds, not whether the offence may be compounded at all. The first offence is barred by the repeat rule whichever forum is approached, and an offence carrying imprisonment together with fine is outside the section by its own words.

citation.ref: Sections 441(1) and 441(2)

items.scenario: A company faces two proceedings. The first is against the company for an offence punishable with fine only, for which the maximum fine is ₹5 lakh; a similar offence by the same company was compounded twenty-two months ago. The second is against an officer for an offence punishable with imprisonment and also with fine. Take as given that the Regional Director may compound where the maximum fine does not exceed ₹25 lakh.

items.stem: What is wrong with the proposed appeal?

options.text: Nothing — an order under the Companies Act is appealable to the Tribunal, and the period is a matter of the Tribunal's rules
options.misconception: assumes the Tribunal is the general appellate forum for everything under the Act
options.why: The Act names the forum provision by provision, and section 454(5) names the Regional Director. An appeal filed in a forum the section did not choose buys nothing except the passage of the sixty days.

options.text: Only the forum is wrong; ninety days is the period the section allows for an appeal
options.misconception: takes the compliance period for the appeal period
options.why: The ninety days is the time within which the company must comply with the order before the consequences in section 454(8) follow. The appeal window is sixty days from receipt of the copy, and the two clocks run for entirely different purposes.

options.text: The appeal lies to the Regional Director and must be filed within sixty days of receiving a copy of the order
options.why: Section 454(5) gives a person aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer an appeal to the Regional Director having jurisdiction in the matter, within sixty days from the date on which a copy of the order is received. The Tribunal has no part in this route: the adjudicating officer is an officer of the Central Government not below the rank of Registrar, and the appeal stays inside that hierarchy.

options.text: Only the period is wrong; the Tribunal is right because an officer of the company has been penalised alongside it
options.misconception: changes the forum according to who was penalised
options.why: Section 454(3) lets the adjudicating officer impose the penalty on the company, on the officer in default or on any other person in the same order, and section 454(5) gives every one of them the same appeal to the Regional Director.

items.scenario: An adjudicating officer appointed under section 454 imposes a penalty on a company and on its company secretary for a filing default. The company wants to challenge the order, and its counsel proposes an appeal to the National Company Law Tribunal, to be filed within the ninety days the company has to comply with the order — take that ninety-day compliance period as given.

items.stem: Which of the three payments does section 202 allow as proposed?

options.text: None as proposed — nothing is payable to a non-executive director, the managing director's ceiling is his unexpired eighteen months, and the resignation into the amalgamated company is an express exclusion
options.why: Section 202(1) permits compensation for loss of office to a managing or whole-time director or manager, "but not to any other director", which disposes of the non-executive director. Section 202(3) caps the payment at the remuneration he would have earned for the remainder of his term or for three years, whichever is shorter, so eighteen months is the managing director's ceiling. Section 202(2) bars payment where a director resigns as a result of the amalgamation and is appointed to office in the company resulting from it.

options.text: Only the managing director's, and in full, because three years is the figure the section names
options.misconception: reads the three years as an entitlement instead of one arm of a "whichever is shorter" test
options.why: The three years is a ceiling and so is the unexpired term, and section 202(3) takes whichever of the two is shorter. With eighteen months left, three years' pay is twice what the section permits.

options.text: All three, provided the members approve each of them by ordinary resolution
options.misconception: treats members' approval as curing a statutory prohibition
options.why: Section 202 is drafted as a restriction on the company, not as a default the members may vary. A payment the section forbids is not made lawful by a resolution, and the excess is recoverable from the recipient.

options.text: Only the whole-time director's, because he is leaving involuntarily as part of the scheme
options.misconception: reads a resignation into the new company as a loss of office
options.why: He is not out of a job; he walks into the same office in the company resulting from the amalgamation. Section 202(2) names that exact case, because compensation is for a loss and he has suffered none.

items.scenario: As it restructures, a company's board proposes three payments: ₹40 lakh to a non-executive director whose seat is being abolished; three years' pay to the managing director, who has eighteen months of his term left; and a severance to a whole-time director who is resigning to take the same office in the company resulting from the amalgamation.

items.stem: Which of the four belongs in the liquidation estate?

options.text: Only the shares in the foreign subsidiary
options.why: Section 36(4) keeps three of the liquidator's four out of the estate: sums due to any workman or employee from the provident fund, the pension fund and the gratuity fund; assets owned by a third party and in the corporate debtor's possession, with bailment expressly named; and the personal assets of a shareholder or partner, unless held on account of a transaction that may be avoided. The exclusion for a subsidiary covers the assets of that subsidiary, not the corporate debtor's own shareholding in it, and shares the debtor owns are its property like any other investment.

options.text: The shares and the promoter's flat, since a promoter cannot shelter behind the corporate form once the company is in liquidation
options.misconception: pierces the veil where the Code declines to
options.why: Section 36(4)(c) excludes the personal assets of a shareholder or partner, and its single exception is an asset held on account of a transaction avoidable under the Chapter. The scenario rules that out, so the flat stays the promoter's.

options.text: The shares, and the provident fund and gratuity money as well, because those dues are ranked in the waterfall under section 53
options.misconception: pays out of the estate a fund that never entered the estate
options.why: Section 53 ranks claims against what the estate actually holds. The Code takes provident fund, pension and gratuity dues out of the estate first, so they are paid in full outside the waterfall rather than queued inside it behind the secured creditors.

options.text: All four, because everything in the corporate debtor's possession vests in the liquidator on liquidation
options.misconception: confuses possession with ownership
options.why: Section 36(4)(a) turns on who owns the thing, not on where it is sitting. Assets owned by a third party and held in trust or on bailment stay the third party's however long the corporate debtor has had them on its floor.

citation.ref: Section 36(4)(a), 36(4)(c) and 36(4)(d), read with section 53

items.scenario: A liquidator taking charge of a corporate debtor lists four things he intends to bring into the liquidation estate: the provident fund and gratuity dues owed to the workmen and lying in the company's fund accounts; machinery held on bailment for a customer under a job-work contract; the shares the corporate debtor holds in its foreign subsidiary; and a promoter-shareholder's personal flat, which is not the subject of any avoidance application.

items.stem: As auditor, what do you require before the report is signed?

options.text: A written representation from the CFO that the banks have been informed separately
options.misconception: routes a reporting defect into a representation
options.why: Whom the bankers heard from privately has no bearing on what the statements must say to every reader. And a representation is never sufficient evidence on its own, least of all about a disclosure that is visibly missing.

options.text: Disclosure of the material uncertainty in the notes to the financial statements themselves
options.why: Ind AS 1 puts the disclosure duty on the financial statements when management is aware of material uncertainties over going concern. The directors' report is not audited to the same standard and is not where SA 570's dedicated section can point. Without the note the statements are misstated, and the opinion — not just a paragraph — is what changes.

options.text: Nothing further, since the auditor's own going concern section will inform readers
options.misconception: uses the auditor's report to carry management's disclosure duty
options.why: The auditor's section draws attention to the note; it does not replace it. Where the note is absent, the statements are wrong and the response is a modified opinion, not a louder auditor's paragraph.

options.text: A more detailed description in the directors' report, cross-referenced from the audit report
options.misconception: accepts other-information disclosure as a substitute for the note
options.why: The directors' report is other information. A cross-reference from the audit report cannot cure an omission inside the statements — it would advertise the very gap it papers over.

citation.ref: para 25

items.scenario: A company has defaulted on its term loans and its net current liabilities are ₹80 crore. The CFO agrees a material uncertainty exists but proposes to describe it in the directors' report only, keeping the financial statements clean "so the bankers do not panic". The audit is in final review.

items.stem: What does section 188 require for this contract?

options.text: No approval, because buying fabric is the company's ordinary course of business
options.misconception: applies half the exemption and drops the arm's length half
options.why: The exemption needs both limbs: ordinary course and arm's length. An 8 per cent premium concedes the second limb, and one failed limb brings the section fully into play.

options.text: Only disclosure in the board's report, since the amount is below ₹50 crore
options.misconception: substitutes a disclosure threshold for the approval requirement
options.why: Thresholds decide when shareholders must approve on top of the board — they never reduce the requirement to disclosure alone. The board resolution is the floor, not the ceiling.

options.text: Approval of the Registrar of Companies before execution
options.misconception: sends a governance decision to the regulator
options.why: Section 188 keeps the decision inside the company — board, and shareholders where thresholds require. The Registrar receives filings; he does not approve contracts.

options.text: Board approval by resolution, with the interested director not participating
options.why: The counterparty is a related party and the pricing is not arm's length, so the ordinary- course-and-arm's-length exemption is unavailable. Section 188 then requires a board resolution — with shareholder approval as well if the prescribed thresholds are crossed — and the interested director stays out of the discussion and the vote.

citation.ref: Section 188

items.scenario: A public company proposes to buy fabric worth ₹12 crore annually from a partnership in which a director's son is a partner, at prices about 8 per cent above the market, citing assured quality. The purchase committee asks what approvals the contract needs.

items.stem: Can the auditor accept this fee arrangement?

options.text: Yes, because fee structure is a private contract between auditor and client
options.misconception: places the engagement contract above the professional schedules
options.why: The Chartered Accountants Act sits over every engagement letter a member signs. A contract cannot authorise what the First Schedule defines as misconduct.

options.text: Yes, if the arrangement is disclosed to shareholders in the general meeting
options.misconception: treats disclosure as curing a prohibited arrangement
options.why: Disclosure cures conflicts that are permissible to hold. This one is prohibited outright; telling the shareholders about it only documents the misconduct.

options.text: No — fees contingent on results or based on a percentage of profits are prohibited
options.why: An auditor paid a share of the profit he certifies holds a stake in the number under audit. The First Schedule makes such fees professional misconduct, outside the narrow exceptions the Council has prescribed for specific engagements — statutory audit is not among them.

options.text: No, unless the percentage is capped at a maximum absolute amount
options.misconception: believes a ceiling converts a contingent fee into a fixed one
options.why: A capped percentage still rises and falls with the profits below the cap — the stake in the certified number remains. The defect is the linkage, not the size.

citation.ref: Clause 10, Part I, First Schedule

items.scenario: A client offers its statutory auditor a fee of 2 per cent of audited net profits, arguing it aligns the auditor's diligence with the company's success and is common for consultants.

items.stem: What does section 143(12) require of you?

options.text: Qualify the audit opinion and treat that as the report
options.misconception: treats the audit report to members as the fraud report to the Government
options.why: The opinion speaks to the financial statements; the 143(12) report is a separate filing to a different addressee with its own form and timeline. One cannot stand in for the other.

options.text: Report to the Central Government, routing it through the board or audit committee for their reply within the prescribed time
options.why: The fraud is by an employee against the company and crosses the one crore threshold, so the report goes to the Central Government in the prescribed manner — the board or audit committee gets the prescribed window to respond, and their comments travel with the report. Handling it quietly is not among the options the section leaves open.

options.text: Resign from the engagement to avoid association with the fraud
options.misconception: substitutes exit for the statutory duty
options.why: Resignation does not discharge section 143(12), and a resigning auditor still carries reporting duties. The Act wants the fraud reported, not the auditor gone.

options.text: Report it to the audit committee only, since internal fraud is a governance matter
options.misconception: applies the below-threshold route to an above-threshold fraud
options.why: Audit-committee-only reporting is the route for frauds under one crore. At ₹1.8 crore the section escalates the duty to the Central Government, and the committee cannot absorb it.

citation.ref: Section 143(12) read with Rule 13, CAAR 2014

items.scenario: During the audit of a listed company you find that a purchase manager, colluding with a vendor, has siphoned ₹1.8 crore through inflated invoices over two years. Management asks you to note it internally and let the audit committee handle it quietly.

items.stem: Does section 135 apply?

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are alternatives, and the profit test is crossed
options.why: Any one of the three gates opens the section, and ₹6.2 crore of net profit is past the ₹5 crore gate. The committee, the policy and the 2 per cent of three-year average net profits all follow, however modest the balance sheet looks beside the other thresholds.

options.text: No, because CSR obligations attach only to listed companies
options.misconception: confuses CSR applicability with listing status
options.why: Section 135 never mentions listing. A private limited company past any threshold is as bound as a listed one.

options.text: Yes, but spending is optional so long as the board explains the shortfall
options.misconception: carries the old comply-or-explain regime past its amendment
options.why: Explain-only died with the 2021 amendments. Unspent money now transfers to an ongoing project account or a specified fund on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: No, because two of the three thresholds are not met
options.misconception: reads the alternative thresholds as cumulative
options.why: Requiring all three would confine CSR to giants. The section says net worth OR turnover OR profit, and one is enough.

citation.ref: Section 135

items.scenario: A company has net worth ₹120 crore and turnover ₹800 crore, but its net profit for the immediately preceding year was ₹6.2 crore. The CFO argues CSR does not apply because the company is nowhere near the net worth or turnover thresholds.

items.stem: How do the two opinions in your report come out?

options.text: Unmodified on the financial statements; adverse on internal financial controls
options.why: Section 143(3)(i) makes controls a separate opinion answering a separate question. A material weakness draws an adverse controls opinion even where extended substantive work let the statements themselves be proved true and fair.

options.text: Unmodified on both, because the statements were ultimately proved right
options.misconception: lets the financial statement outcome absolve the controls
options.why: The controls opinion reports the state of the controls, not the state of the numbers. A material weakness that existed at the year end is reported whether or not it did damage.

options.text: The control failures go only in a management letter, not the audit report
options.misconception: demotes a statutory reporting duty to a private communication
options.why: The management letter supplements; it cannot substitute. Section 143(3)(i) puts the controls opinion in the report to members by force of statute.

options.text: Both must be qualified, since a control failure infects the statements
options.misconception: chains the two opinions together
options.why: The opinions can and do diverge. Broken controls raise the risk of misstatement; they do not prove one occurred, and here the substantive work proved otherwise.

citation.ref: Section 143(3)(i)

items.scenario: Finalising a listed company's audit, you conclude the financial statements are true and fair, but testing showed the purchase-to-pay controls failed repeatedly and a material weakness exists at the year end.

items.stem: Which of the four falls foul of Clause 6?

options.text: The tender response, because concurrent audit was never offered to this firm personally
options.misconception: treats responding to an open invitation as uninvited approach
options.why: A tender is an invitation to everyone qualified. Answering an invitation is the opposite of soliciting; the mischief is approaching those who never asked.

options.text: The letter to the other firm, since work must come from clients directly
options.misconception: bars the one channel the clause expressly keeps open
options.why: Securing work from another chartered accountant in practice is a stated exception — professional sub-engagement is how overflow and specialisation have always moved.

options.text: All four, since each is an attempt to obtain professional work
options.misconception: reads the bar as covering every pursuit of work
options.why: The clause was never a vow of passivity. Its carve-outs exist precisely so that open, invited competition — tenders, empanelment, professional-to-professional requests — stays lawful.

options.text: Only the brochure mailing to the two hundred companies
options.why: Unsolicited circulars to prospective clients are the textbook form of solicitation the clause bars. The other three are its stated exceptions — responding to tenders, applying against announced empanelments, and seeking work from another chartered accountant in practice.

citation.ref: Clause 6, Part I, First Schedule

items.scenario: A firm of chartered accountants does four things in one quarter — mails brochures about its audit expertise to two hundred companies chosen from the registrar's records, responds to a public tender floated by a state bank for concurrent audit, applies against a public empanelment notice of a government corporation, and writes to another CA firm offering to take its overflow tax work.

items.stem: Does the proposed committee comply?

options.text: Yes, provided the committee's recommendations are ratified by the full board
options.misconception: cures defective composition with board ratification
options.why: Ratification cannot rebuild the committee. The statute regulates who deliberates, not just what emerges; a wrongly composed committee stays wrongly composed however its output is later blessed.

options.text: No, because the CFO's relative can never sit on any board committee
options.misconception: invents a blanket relative disqualification
options.why: Relationship to an officer affects independence classification, not committee membership as such. The defect is arithmetic — the independents lack a majority — not the presence of one related non-executive.

options.text: Yes — four exceeds the minimum of three, and independents are represented
options.misconception: checks the headcount and skips the majority condition
options.why: Representation is not the test; majority is. The minimum of three and the independent majority are separate conditions, and the second one fails here.

options.text: No — independent directors must form the majority, and two of four is not one
options.why: Section 177 requires a minimum of three directors with independents in the majority. Two of four fails the majority test, and a committee chaired by the managing director invites exactly the management dominance the composition rules exist to prevent.

citation.ref: Section 177

items.scenario: A listed company proposes an audit committee of four directors — two independent, the managing director, and the CFO's brother as a non-executive director, chaired by the managing director. The company secretary certifies the composition complies with section 177.

items.stem: Does CARO 2020 apply to this company's audit?

options.text: No, since two of the three financial limits are within bounds
options.misconception: reads the cumulative exemption conditions as majority-satisfied
options.why: The exemption is conjunctive. Meeting two limits while breaking the third is simply breaking the conditions — the order does not average them.

options.text: Yes, but only the fraud and statutory dues clauses apply to private companies
options.misconception: invents a partial CARO for private companies
options.why: CARO has no reduced edition. Once applicable, the whole order applies; applicability is the only company-level question.

options.text: Yes — the revenue of ₹14 crore crosses the ten crore limit, and one breach is enough
options.why: The private-company exemption needs every limit honoured together — capital and reserves, borrowings, and revenue. Revenue at ₹14 crore breaks the ten crore ceiling, so the order applies with all its reporting clauses, whatever the other two figures say.

options.text: No, because CARO never applies to private companies
options.misconception: turns a conditional exemption into a blanket one
options.why: Private companies are exempt only inside the size limits. Beyond them, a private company answers every CARO clause a public one does.

citation.ref: Paragraph 1(2)

items.scenario: A private limited company, not a holding or subsidiary of a public company, has paid-up capital and reserves of ₹80 lakh, bank borrowings that peaked at ₹95 lakh during the year, and revenue of ₹14 crore. Its auditor treats CARO 2020 as inapplicable since capital and borrowings are within a crore each.

items.stem: What is the most the company can distribute from current profits?

options.text: ₹28 crore, by adding the securities premium to distributable profit
options.misconception: treats securities premium as a free reserve
options.why: Premium is shareholders' capital contribution, usable only for the purposes section 52 lists. Distribution as dividend is not among them.

options.text: ₹3 crore — after depreciation and after setting off the carried-forward loss
options.why: Section 123 charges depreciation first (₹10 minus ₹3) and then requires previous losses and unabsorbed depreciation to be set off (₹7 minus ₹4), leaving ₹3 crore of distributable profit. The premium and revaluation balances watch from the sidelines.

options.text: ₹7 crore — depreciation must be provided, but old losses concern the balance sheet, not dividends
options.misconception: provides depreciation and skips the loss set-off
options.why: The set-off is a statutory pre-condition, not a presentation nicety. Paying dividends across an unabsorbed loss distributes capital dressed as income.

options.text: ₹18 crore, by drawing on the revaluation surplus
options.misconception: distributes an unrealised book write-up
options.why: A revaluation surplus is an accounting remeasurement, not realised profit. Dividending it hands out money the company never earned and may never see.

citation.ref: Section 123

items.scenario: A company has current-year profit of ₹10 crore before providing ₹3 crore of depreciation, a brought-forward business loss of ₹4 crore, a securities premium of ₹25 crore, and a revaluation surplus of ₹15 crore. The board wants the largest lawful dividend.

items.stem: Can either proposal stand?

options.text: Neither — the cooling-off blocks any reappointment for five years, and the partner-linked firm is equally barred
options.why: Ten years is the ceiling, and the five-year cooling-off admits no short extensions — two years inside a barred window is barred. The fallback fails on the same section's own words: a firm with common partners as at the appointment date stands in the retiring firm's shoes.

options.text: The linked firm works, because it is a distinct legal entity
options.misconception: hides continuity behind a fresh registration
options.why: The statute anticipated the manoeuvre and named it: common partners carry the disqualification across the entity line.

options.text: The two-year extension works, since it is shorter than a term
options.misconception: reads the bar as prohibiting only full terms
options.why: The section bars appointment as auditor during the cooling-off, for any length. Slicing the term thin does not slip it through.

options.text: Both work if the audit committee certifies the firm's independence
options.misconception: lets a committee certify around a statutory bar
options.why: Independence certification supplements eligibility; it cannot manufacture it. A candidate the statute disqualifies stays disqualified with the finest certificate attached.

citation.ref: Section 139(2)

items.scenario: An audit firm completes its second five-year term at a listed company. The shareholders, pleased with its work, propose reappointing it for two more years only, arguing a short extension is not a fresh five-year term. As fallback they suggest a different firm in which three partners of the retiring firm hold a majority.

items.stem: Which of the CFO's three grounds survives section 138?

options.text: The first — private companies are outside internal audit requirements
options.misconception: reads section 138 as a public-company provision
options.why: The rule names private companies with their own thresholds. Two hundred crore of turnover is one of them, and this company is past it.

options.text: The third — the internal auditor must be a practising chartered accountant
options.misconception: narrows the section's deliberately wide eligibility
options.why: The provision expressly allows a cost accountant or such other professional as the board decides, and the rule adds that the appointee may be an employee. Parliament left the choice to the board.

options.text: None — the turnover line is crossed, in-house review is not internal audit, and the board may appoint a qualified employee
options.why: A private company past two hundred crore of turnover is squarely covered. A management team reviewing its own controls is self-review, not the independent function the section contemplates — but the section is generous on who: a chartered accountant, cost accountant or other professional, employee included, as the board decides.

options.text: The second — a documented monthly management review satisfies the requirement
options.misconception: accepts self-review as the audit of self
options.why: The reviewers report to the very management whose controls they review. Internal audit exists to stand outside that loop, reporting toward the audit committee.

citation.ref: Section 138 read with Rule 13

items.scenario: A private company had turnover of ₹230 crore in the preceding year and no borrowings. The CFO resists appointing an internal auditor on three grounds — the company is private, its own accounts team reviews controls monthly, and in any case only chartered accountants can be internal auditors, which would mean hiring outside.

items.stem: Is the company covered, and can unspent CSR sit in the balance sheet?

options.text: Covered — the profit test alone triggers section 135 — and unspent amounts must move to the statutory accounts, not sit in the balance sheet
options.why: The three thresholds are alternatives; net profit of ₹9 crore against the five-crore line is enough on its own. Since the 2019 amendments, unspent money has mandated destinations — an unspent-CSR account within thirty days for ongoing projects, a Schedule VII fund within six months otherwise. A general reserve is neither.

options.text: Covered, but spending remains comply-or-explain, so unspent amounts need only a board explanation
options.misconception: states the pre-2019 regime as current law
options.why: Explanation alone was the original design. The amendments kept the explanation and added teeth — mandatory transfer of unspent amounts on a statutory clock, with penalties behind it.

options.text: Not covered — CSR needs at least two of the three thresholds crossed
options.misconception: reads "or" as "and"
options.why: The section strings its thresholds with "or". One gate open is enough, and the profit gate is open by four crore.

options.text: Covered, and the obligation is two per cent of the preceding year's ₹9 crore profit
options.misconception: computes on one year instead of the three-year average
options.why: Eligibility reads one year; the spend reads three. Two per cent applies to the average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years, which smooths a lumpy profit like this one.

citation.ref: Section 135

items.scenario: A company with turnover of ₹800 crore and net worth of ₹300 crore earned net profit of ₹9 crore in the immediately preceding year. Its CFO argues CSR does not apply since neither the net worth nor the turnover threshold is crossed. The board separately proposes that if CSR does apply, any unspent amount can be carried in the general balance sheet for later use.

items.stem: Which alternatives does section 149 permit?

options.text: The third — a gap of any length resets the two-term count
options.misconception: reads the cooling-off as a courtesy interval rather than a three-year statutory bar
options.why: The reset needs the full three years. A shorter gap leaves him inside the exclusion period, and any association during it is itself prohibited.

options.text: The first, with shareholders' special resolution blessing the third term
options.misconception: lets a resolution extend a statutory maximum
options.why: The special resolution is how a second term is granted. No resolution reaches past two consecutive terms; the statute's ceiling binds the shareholders too.

options.text: None of the three — ten years is the ceiling, and the three-year cooling-off bars any association, consultancy included
options.why: Two consecutive terms exhaust the independent-director route, and section 149(11)'s cooling-off is not merely a pause before reappointment — during those three years he may not be appointed in or associated with the company in any other capacity. The consultancy and the one-year gap both walk into that bar.

options.text: The second — the consultancy is a different capacity outside section 149
options.misconception: routes around the bar through a side door the section explicitly closed
options.why: The subsection's words reach appointment in the company "in any other capacity". A paid consultancy is also precisely the pecuniary relationship that destroyed independence while he served.

citation.ref: Section 149(10) and (11)

items.scenario: A listed company's independent director completes two consecutive five-year terms. The board, valuing his experience, proposes three alternatives: reappoint him for a third term as independent director; appoint him immediately as a paid consultant to the company; or bring him back as an independent director after one year's gap.

items.stem: How many section 186 requirements does the proposal break?

options.text: Three — the limit needs a special resolution, board approval must be unanimous, and the rate is below the statutory floor
options.why: ₹140 crore exceeds both limbs of the limit — sixty per cent of ₹200 crore is ₹120 crore — so shareholders must pass a special resolution first. The board sanction must carry the consent of all directors present, which two dissents defeat. And no loan may be priced below the government-security yield for the matching tenor; a group discount is exactly what the floor exists to stop.

options.text: One — only the shareholder resolution is missing; boards act by majority and price freely
options.misconception: applies ordinary board-majority rules to a section that demands unanimity
options.why: Section 186(5) requires the consent of all directors present at the meeting for these decisions — a deliberate departure from majority rule — and subsection (7) fixes the interest floor.

options.text: Two — resolution and unanimity fail, but interest is a commercial matter for the board
options.misconception: concedes the process points while missing the pricing floor
options.why: Subsection (7) writes the minimum into the statute: not lower than the prevailing yield on government securities closest to the loan's tenor. Commercial freedom starts above that line, not below it.

options.text: None — lending to a group company is exempt from section 186
options.misconception: stretches the wholly-owned-subsidiary carve-outs over the whole group
options.why: The exemptions cover specific cases such as loans to wholly owned subsidiaries. A group company generally is just another body corporate, and every limb of the section applies.

citation.ref: Section 186

items.scenario: A company with paid-up capital plus free reserves of ₹200 crore (free reserves portion ₹90 crore) has existing inter-corporate loans of ₹100 crore. The board wants to lend a further ₹40 crore to a group company at an interest rate below the prevailing government-security yield, approving it by majority vote at a board meeting with two directors dissenting.

items.stem: Which advances can lawfully be made?

options.text: All three, if shareholders approve each by special resolution
options.misconception: reads the whole section as resolution-curable
options.why: The special resolution route exists only for the entities in which directors are interested. For the director personally, the prohibition has no key — that is the section's core.

options.text: The first and third — loans to individuals are personnel matters outside company law
options.misconception: exempts exactly the person the section names first
options.why: "Any loan to any of its directors" is the opening prohibition. The individual director is not the exception; he is the addressee.

options.text: The second with a special resolution, and the third under the employee-scheme exception — never the first
options.why: The direct loan to a director sits in section 185's absolute bar; no resolution reaches it. The interested private company is in the conditional ring — special resolution plus use in the borrower's principal business activities. The managing director's housing loan rides the exception for schemes extended to all employees.

options.text: None — section 185 bans anything that benefits a director directly or indirectly
options.misconception: inflates the bar over the section's own exceptions
options.why: The 2017 rewrite deliberately split the section into a bar, a conditional window and exceptions. Reading it as a wall outlaws employee welfare schemes Parliament expressly saved.

citation.ref: Section 185

items.scenario: A public company's board considers three advances: ₹50 lakh to a director to buy a house; ₹2 crore to a private company in which the same director holds 40 per cent, for that company's working capital; and ₹30 lakh to the managing director under a housing-loan scheme the company extends to all employees.

items.stem: What happens to the section 9 application?

options.text: It fails — the rejection letter is a pre-existing dispute, and section 9 cannot decide whose case is right
options.why: The dispute predates the demand notice by six months in writing, which is exactly what the dispute defence requires. The adjudicating authority only asks whether a plausible dispute existed before the notice — not who would win it — because the Code rescues failing companies rather than collecting contested bills. The supplier's forum is a civil suit or arbitration.

options.text: It succeeds — the undisputed two-thirds alone exceeds the threshold
options.misconception: severs the debt to salvage the application
options.why: A genuine dispute touching the claimed operational debt bars the application; the tribunal does not carve the invoice into clean and contested slices to keep the petition alive.

options.text: It succeeds if the supplier proves the goods were not defective
options.misconception: turns the admission stage into the trial
options.why: Proof of quality is a trial, with evidence and cross-examination — everything the summary admission under the Code is built not to be. Plausibility of the dispute ends the enquiry.

options.text: It fails only if the buyer had also filed a suit before the notice
options.misconception: demands litigation where the Code asks only for a dispute
options.why: The definition covers a dispute including a suit or arbitration — the correspondence raising a real quality claim is enough. Requiring a filed suit would reward the fastest court fee, not the true state of accounts.

citation.ref: Sections 8 and 9

items.scenario: A supplier is owed ₹3 crore for goods delivered. Six months before any insolvency step, the buyer had written rejecting a third of the goods as defective and withholding payment. The supplier now serves a section 8 demand notice and, on non-payment, files under section 9, arguing the defect claim is an afterthought to dodge insolvency.

items.stem: Which section 203 breaches are running?

options.text: None — the search is genuine and the CEO's roles are both disclosed
options.misconception: substitutes good faith and disclosure for statutory limits
options.why: The six-month line and the one-company rule are bright lines. Diligent interviewing past the deadline is still a default, disclosed dual office still a dual office.

options.text: Only the CFO vacancy — CEOs are not key managerial personnel
options.misconception: drops the CEO from the definition
options.why: Section 2(51) lists the chief executive officer among KMP expressly. The whole-time restrictions ride on that definition.

options.text: Two — the CFO vacancy passed its six-month limit in July, and a whole-time KMP cannot hold office in an unrelated company
options.why: The board's window to fill a KMP vacancy is six months from the date it arose; September is past it, and an informal stand-in is not an appointment. The one-company rule for whole-time KMP allows only a subsidiary as the second seat — an unrelated company fails it, and part-time labels do not undo the office.

options.text: Only the CEO's dual role — vacancies may stay open until the right candidate appears
options.misconception: reads the six-month limit as aspirational
options.why: The section commands the board to fill the vacancy within six months, with penalties behind it. Candidate quality is why the window is six months, not why it is open-ended.

citation.ref: Section 203

items.scenario: A listed company's CFO resigns in January. In September, the board is still interviewing, with the finance controller handling the work informally. Meanwhile the company's CEO also serves as CEO of an unrelated private company, describing both as part-time engagements.

items.stem: Is the group barred?

options.text: No — any single shareholder may always petition against oppression
options.misconception: erases the standing requirement altogether
options.why: Open standing would hand every disgruntled member a Tribunal lever against the company. The thresholds filter; the waiver handles the exceptions.

options.text: Yes — thresholds are jurisdictional and the Tribunal cannot relax them
options.misconception: reads the section without its waiver proviso
options.why: The proviso to section 244(1) exists precisely so a meritorious minority is not silenced by arithmetic. Waiver is discretionary, but the power is in the text.

options.text: Not necessarily — the tests are alternatives with a waiver besides; 80 falls short of each, but the Tribunal can waive on merits
options.why: Section 244 offers the least demanding of its routes: one hundred members, one-tenth of members (600 here), or one-tenth of capital. The group misses all three — but the proviso lets the Tribunal waive the requirement for a case worth hearing, and adding 20 consenting members would cure standing outright. The objection opens a door; it does not close the case.

options.text: Yes, unless the group first acquires two more per cent of capital
options.misconception: fixes on the capital route as if it were the only one
options.why: Ten per cent of capital is one of three alternative routes, and the cheapest fix here is twenty more consenting members — or persuading the Tribunal to waive numbers entirely.

citation.ref: Sections 241 and 244

items.scenario: A company has 6,000 members. A group of 80 members holding 8 per cent of the issued capital wants to petition against the promoters for oppression. The promoters' counsel objects: fewer than one hundred members, less than ten per cent of capital — no standing, end of matter.

items.stem: What stops the proposal?

options.text: Nothing — the amount is within the board's ten per cent power
options.misconception: clears the quantum test and stops reading
options.why: Section 68 stacks its conditions; each stands independently. The cooling period exists so buy-backs are considered capital events, not a running price-support tool.

options.text: The absence of a special resolution, required for every buy-back
options.misconception: erases the board-only route
options.why: Up to ten per cent of paid-up equity plus free reserves, the board's resolution suffices — that carve-out is the provision's whole convenience. The defect here is timing, not authority.

options.text: The size — buy-backs are capped at ten per cent of paid-up capital alone
options.misconception: shrinks the base to bare capital
options.why: Both the ten and twenty-five per cent ceilings measure against capital plus free reserves. On ₹400 crore, the board route alone reaches ₹40 crore.

options.text: The one-year cooling period since the last buy-back — the arithmetic is within the board's limit, but the calendar is not
options.why: Ten per cent of ₹400 crore is ₹40 crore, so ₹38 crore sits inside the board-resolution route. What the proposal cannot survive is the bar on a fresh buy-back within one year of the preceding one's completion — a limit that applies whichever organ approves. Wait four months, and the same resolution works.

citation.ref: Section 68

items.scenario: A company with paid-up equity of ₹100 crore and free reserves of ₹300 crore completed a buy-back eight months ago. The board now proposes, by board resolution alone, a fresh buy-back of ₹38 crore, noting it is under ten per cent of capital plus reserves and therefore within the board's own power.

items.stem: How many section 42 violations are running, and which is the gravest?

options.text: Three besides the lapsed timeline — and the forum post is gravest, converting the issue into a deemed public offer
options.why: The 180 identified offerees are fine; everything after is not. Cash application money breaks the banking-channel mandate; spending before allotment and filing breaks the separate-account discipline; week ten has passed the sixty-day allotment-or-refund line. The forum post outranks them all — public solicitation makes the placement a deemed public offer, importing prospectus and penalty consequences wholesale.

options.text: The spending alone, since money once received belongs to the company
options.misconception: mistakes custody for entitlement
options.why: Application money is the applicants' until allotment and the return's filing. That is why it must sit in its own account — spending it early is using other people's money.

options.text: Only the cash collection, curable by depositing it into the separate account now
options.misconception: picks the most fixable breach and forgets the fatal one
options.why: Banking the cash cures nothing already broken, and the deemed-public-offer consequence of the forum post cannot be deposited away.

options.text: None — private companies raising from under two hundred persons are outside section 42's formalities
options.misconception: reads the headcount as the section's only rule
options.why: Two hundred is one gate of several. The banking channel, the escrow discipline, the sixty days and the no-advertisement bar each bind independently of the count.

citation.ref: Section 42

items.scenario: A private company raising ₹15 crore emails its offer letter to 180 hand-picked investors, posts the "opportunity" on a public investor forum "for wider reach", collects some application money in cash for convenience, and starts spending receipts while allotment paperwork is still pending in week ten.

items.stem: Where does the bank stand?

options.text: The loan itself is void and the bank recovers nothing at all
options.misconception: extends the charge's fate to the debt
options.why: Only the security fails. The money remains owed — indeed it becomes immediately payable — and the bank proves for it as an unsecured creditor.

options.text: Unsecured in the liquidation — the unregistered charge is void against the liquidator, and the bank could have filed the charge itself
options.why: Section 77 makes an unregistered charge void against the liquidator and creditors, which is precisely when security earns its keep. The deed binds the company while it lives; in liquidation the bank stands in the unsecured queue for its surviving debt. The sting is self-inflicted — section 78 let the charge-holder register on the company's default, and the bank held the papers for two years.

options.text: Secured — a valid mortgage deed cannot be defeated by a missing form
options.misconception: treats registration as clerical rather than constitutive against third parties
options.why: The register exists so later lenders and the liquidator can see what is already pledged. A secret mortgage defeats that purpose, so the statute defeats the secret mortgage.

options.text: Secured, because the liquidator had actual notice of the mortgage from the company's own records
options.misconception: substitutes notice for registration
options.why: The section voids the unregistered charge against the liquidator without a notice exception. Actual knowledge does not repair a statutory invalidity.

citation.ref: Sections 77 and 78

items.scenario: A bank lends ₹50 crore against a factory mortgage. The company never files the charge with the Registrar, and the bank, holding its own copy of the mortgage deed, does not press. Two years later the company enters liquidation, and the liquidator treats the bank as an unsecured creditor. The bank protests that the mortgage deed is valid between the parties and the loan documentation impeccable.

items.stem: What is wrong with the two proposals?

options.text: Nothing — annexed reports need no response, and any qualified professional may sign
options.misconception: reads the annexure as the end of the board's duty
options.why: The response requirement exists so shareholders see the board answer the criticism. The signature requirement exists because compliance auditing was assigned to the secretarial profession deliberately.

options.text: Only the response point — auditors can hold both offices with member approval
options.misconception: makes eligibility a matter of resolution
options.why: No resolution converts a chartered accountant into a company secretary in practice. The statute names the profession, and approval processes choose within it, not around it.

options.text: The board must explain every qualification in its report, and secretarial audit belongs to a practising company secretary, not the statutory auditor
options.why: Section 204(3) obliges the board to explain in full any qualification or observation in the secretarial audit report — silence is itself a default. And the section reserves the engagement to a company secretary in practice: the statutory auditor holds a different office under a different section, and consolidation would put one professional's certificate where the law demands another's.

options.text: Only the auditor point — boards respond to financial qualifications alone
options.misconception: limits the response duty to the financial audit
options.why: Section 204 carries its own explanation obligation, parallel to the one for the financial auditor's qualifications. Both reports get answered.

citation.ref: Section 204

items.scenario: A large listed company receives a secretarial audit report qualified on delayed stock exchange intimations and a related party approval taken ex post facto. The board proposes to file the report without comment, reasoning that qualifications in an annexure speak for themselves; the CFO separately suggests next year's secretarial audit be given to the statutory auditors to consolidate work.

items.stem: What is the company's true position?

options.text: The plan is fine, and the Registrar can add three months if needed
options.misconception: extends the inextensible first AGM
options.why: The extension proviso carves out the first AGM in terms. Planning that leans on an unavailable extension is planning to default.

options.text: The company defaulted by holding no AGM in 2025 — a meeting is required in every calendar year
options.misconception: applies the old calendar-year rule to the first AGM's own window
options.why: The first AGM clock runs from the first financial year's close, not the calendar. A January 2025 company with a March 2026 year-end lawfully holds its first AGM late in 2026.

options.text: 15 November is lawful — the first AGM window runs nine months from 31 March 2026, but no Registrar extension exists for a first AGM
options.why: A company may take its first financial year to the 31 March following incorporation, and the first AGM is due within nine months of that year-end — by 31 December 2026, with no meeting needed in the incorporation year at all. The comfort the second director seeks is not available: the Registrar's three-month extension power expressly excludes the first AGM. December is a wall.

options.text: The AGM was due by 30 September 2026 — six months from the year-end
options.misconception: applies the subsequent-AGM deadline to the first
options.why: Six months governs later years; the first AGM gets nine. The two windows differ precisely because a new company's first close carries first-time burdens.

citation.ref: Section 96

items.scenario: A company incorporated on 1 January 2025 closes its first financial year on 31 March 2026. The directors plan the first AGM for 15 November 2026, and one director worries they have already defaulted since no AGM happened in calendar 2025. Another proposes seeking the Registrar's extension "as a safety margin" in case preparations slip past December.

items.stem: Can the creditor get the company restored, and did the debt die?

options.text: Yes — a creditor's restoration application runs for twenty years, and liabilities survive striking off as if the company continued
options.why: The three-year clock the ex-directors quote belongs to the aggrieved person's appeal; section 252 separately lets the company, any member, creditor or workman apply within twenty years of the notice. And section 248's own scheme preserves every liability of the company, its directors and members despite the dissolution — the warehouse can answer the decree once the register revives the debtor.

options.text: No — dissolution extinguishes the company and everything it owed
options.misconception: gives an administrative housecleaning the effect of insolvency discharge
options.why: Strike off clears dead names from the register; it is no scheme of creditor settlement. The statute says liabilities continue precisely so debtors cannot die their way out of decrees.

options.text: No — all restoration routes closed three years after the strike off
options.misconception: reads the short window and misses the long one
options.why: Two routes, two clocks. The twenty-year application exists for exactly this discovery-years-later creditor.

options.text: Yes, but only the Registrar can seek restoration once struck off
options.misconception: hands the remedy to the striker alone
options.why: Section 252 names the company, members, creditors and workmen as applicants. The creditor petitions the Tribunal in his own right.

citation.ref: Sections 248 and 252

items.scenario: A company is struck off by the Registrar for two years' inactivity. Four years later a creditor with an unpaid ₹1 crore decree discovers the striking off and wants the company back on the register to execute against its still-existing warehouse; the ex-directors respond that the company's death extinguished its debts and, in any case, all remedies lapsed three years after the strike off.

items.stem: How many defects does the arrangement carry?

options.text: Only the reappointment — an adjourned AGM genuinely extends every director's tenure
options.misconception: gives the adjournment the effect the section pre-empted
options.why: The "date by which the AGM should have been held" language exists precisely for this manoeuvre. Statutory AGM deadlines, not the board's calendar, end the seat.

options.text: Two — a candidate rejected in general meeting is barred from the additional route, and the office ends when the AGM should have been held, adjournment or not
options.why: Section 161(1) closes both doors in its own words. The proviso bars appointing as additional director a person who fails to get appointed at a general meeting — the board cannot overrule the shareholders it answers to. And tenure runs to the AGM or the last date by which it should have been held, whichever is earlier: postponing the meeting postpones nothing for this seat.

options.text: Only the adjournment trick — a fresh board appointment cures a general meeting rejection
options.misconception: lets the appointing organs outrank each other in the wrong order
options.why: The proviso's whole purpose is that a shareholder verdict cannot be reversed in the boardroom. The appointment was void at inception, before the adjournment added the second defect.

options.text: None — the board's power to appoint additional directors is unfettered where the articles allow
options.misconception: reads the power without its proviso and its clock
options.why: The articles enable the power; the statute conditions it. Both conditions here are in the section's text, not in implication.

citation.ref: Section 161(1)

items.scenario: Shareholders reject a promoter's nominee at the AGM. A month later the board appoints the same person as an additional director, and when the next AGM approaches with the shareholders still hostile, the board adjourns the meeting indefinitely so the seat continues. The articles authorise additional directors.

items.stem: Can it claim the small company privileges?

options.text: Yes for accounts, no for meetings — privileges are severable by choice
options.misconception: lets a non-qualifying company pick privileges à la carte
options.why: Status is the gate and it is closed. A company is small or it is not; the privileges flow together from the definition, never individually by preference.

options.text: Yes — the thresholds are the definition, and both are met
options.misconception: reads the limits without the exclusions
options.why: The proviso is half the definition. Size measures the company alone; the exclusions measure what stands behind it, and a listed parent stands behind this one.

options.text: No — a subsidiary is excluded from the definition whatever its size, so every skipped compliance is a default
options.why: The numbers fit — capital under four crore, turnover under forty — but section 2(85)'s proviso excludes holding and subsidiary companies from small company status outright. Group membership means group-scale resources and group-scale stakes, so the concessions for genuinely small standalone businesses are withdrawn: the cash flow statement, the four board meetings and the rotation discipline all apply in full.

options.text: No, but only because turnover must be measured on the consolidated group
options.misconception: fixes the outcome with an invented consolidation test
options.why: The definition tests the company's own figures; the group enters through the subsidiary exclusion, not through aggregation. The right answer needs the right reason — the proviso, not arithmetic.

citation.ref: Section 2(85)

items.scenario: A private company with paid-up capital of ₹3 crore and turnover of ₹35 crore claims small company status: it skips the cash flow statement, holds two board meetings, and keeps its auditor indefinitely. It happens to be the wholly owned subsidiary of a large listed manufacturer.

items.stem: Which two corrections does the plan need?

options.text: The plan works as drafted — 75 per cent of a well-attended meeting suffices
options.misconception: imports the NCLT route's majority into the no-NCLT route
options.why: Three-fourths of those present and voting is section 230's standard, purchased with judicial oversight. The fast track's price is near-unanimity measured on the whole capital.

options.text: Correct thresholds, but once on the fast track no authority can derail the scheme
options.misconception: mistakes no-court-by-default for no-court-ever
options.why: The Regional Director's power to refer objectionable schemes to the Tribunal is the route's safety valve. Fast track means presumption of speed, not immunity from scrutiny.

options.text: The fast track is unavailable — listed companies must always go to the Tribunal
options.misconception: adds a listing bar the section does not contain
options.why: The classes are defined by relationship and size, and holding-WOS is one of them regardless of listing. Securities law adds disclosures, not a different route.

options.text: Holding-WOS mergers qualify, but approval needs ninety per cent of TOTAL shares — not 75 per cent of those voting — and objections can still push the scheme to the Tribunal
options.why: The route fits: holding company with wholly owned subsidiary is a named fast-track class whatever the listing status.
